lessons.label: DNA, Chromosomes, and What a Gene Actually Is

sections.heading: A ladder with a rule for the rungs
sections.body: DNA is two antiparallel strands wound into a right-handed double helix, a structure Watson and Crick proposed in 1953 using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction data (Photo 51) and Erwin Chargaff's earlier observation that A always equals T and G always equals C in any organism's DNA. Antiparallel means the two strands run in opposite chemical directions, one 5'-to-3' and its partner 3'-to-5', which matters mechanically: every enzyme that reads or copies DNA (RNA polymerase, DNA polymerase) synthesizes the new strand only 5' to 3', which means it reads the template strand 3' to 5'. Chargaff's pairing rule has a physical reason — adenine pairs with thymine through 2 hydrogen bonds, guanine pairs with cytosine through 3 — so GC-rich stretches of DNA are measurably more thermally stable and harder to melt apart than AT-rich stretches. The helix completes one full turn roughly every 10.5 base pairs in its normal (B-form) conformation, which sets the spacing that proteins like transcription factors exploit when they dock into the major groove.

sections.heading: Packing two meters of DNA into a nucleus
sections.body: A single human cell holds about 2 meters of DNA that must fit inside a nucleus a few micrometers across, and the first level of compaction is the nucleosome: 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped almost twice around a histone octamer (two copies each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4). Strings of nucleosomes — 'beads on a string' — coil further into chromatin, which condenses into the 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total, one set from each parent) visible under a microscope only during cell division. This packaging isn't just storage; how tightly a region is wound (open euchromatin versus dense heterochromatin) controls whether its genes are accessible for transcription at all.

sections.heading: The anatomy of a gene, and the scale of the genome
sections.body: A gene is not just coding sequence: it includes a promoter (where RNA polymerase and transcription factors assemble), exons (segments retained in mature mRNA), introns (segments spliced out), and untranslated regions at both ends (the 5' UTR and 3' UTR) that flank the coding sequence without being translated into protein. The human genome, sequenced by the publicly funded Human Genome Project and Celera Genomics and declared essentially complete (finished) in 2003, following the working draft announced in 2000, totals about 3.1 billion base pairs but contains only roughly 19,000–20,000 protein-coding genes — a number that surprised researchers who had predicted far more. Coding exons make up only about 1.5% of the genome; the rest is introns, regulatory sequence, and repetitive DNA whose functions are still being mapped.

lessons.workedExample: A student claims their gel shows 'a gene' because they see a band of DNA. A judge asks what fraction of that band is actually coding sequence. Using the scale facts above: if the fragment is a typical human gene averaging tens of thousands of base pairs (introns included), and only ~1.5% of the genome is coding, the student should expect the vast majority of that band to be intron, promoter, and UTR — not exon. A rigorous answer distinguishes 'a segment containing a gene' from 'a segment of coding DNA,' and can point to where a promoter or UTR would sit relative to the start codon, showing the anatomy is understood rather than assumed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe gene anatomy and genome scale because students routinely conflate 'DNA' with 'gene' with 'coding sequence,' and that conflation produces sloppy claims elsewhere in a project — like assuming a mutation anywhere in a gene must change the protein. A student who can state that introns are spliced out, that only ~1.5% of the genome codes for protein, and that ~19,000–20,000 genes are packed into 3.1 billion base pairs has the vocabulary to reason precisely about where a variant of interest actually falls and why that location matters.

questions.prompt: Why does a G-C base pair require more energy to melt apart than an A-T base pair?

options.text: G-C pairs form 3 hydrogen bonds while A-T pairs form 2
G-C pairs are held together by covalent bonds, A-T pairs are not
G and C are physically larger molecules than A and T
G-C pairs occur only in the major groove, which is more stable

explanations.a: Correct — G-C forms 3 hydrogen bonds versus 2 for A-T, so GC-rich DNA is measurably more thermally stable.
explanations.b: Base pairing is hydrogen bonding, not covalent bonding, in both cases; the sugar-phosphate backbone (not the base pairs) is held by covalent bonds.
explanations.c: Purines (A, G) and pyrimidines (C, T) differ in ring structure but size is not what determines pairing energy — bond count is.
explanations.d: The major and minor grooves are helix features present along the whole molecule, not specific to one base pair type.

questions.prompt: A nucleosome is best described as:

options.text: 147 bp of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer
The full condensed chromosome visible during mitosis
A single histone protein bound to one base pair
The promoter region where RNA polymerase binds

explanations.a: Correct — the nucleosome is the first level of DNA packaging: ~147 bp wrapped nearly twice around two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.
explanations.b: A full chromosome is a much higher order of compaction built from thousands of nucleosomes plus further chromatin coiling.
explanations.c: A nucleosome involves eight histone proteins (an octamer), not one, wrapped by far more than a single base pair.
explanations.d: The promoter is a DNA sequence element for transcription initiation, unrelated to the histone-wrapping structure of a nucleosome.

questions.prompt: Match each gene region to its role.

right.text: Retained in mature mRNA and translated into protein
Spliced out of the pre-mRNA before translation
Where RNA polymerase and transcription factors assemble to start transcription
Flanks the coding sequence in mature mRNA but is not translated

questions.explanation: The promoter recruits the transcription machinery; exons are the retained, protein-coding segments of mature mRNA; introns are spliced out; the 5' and 3' UTRs are transcribed and remain in the mRNA but are never translated.

questions.prompt: Approximately what fraction of the human genome's 3.1 billion base pairs is protein-coding exon sequence?

options.text: About 1.5%
About 15%
About 50%
About 90%

explanations.a: Correct — only roughly 1.5% of the ~3.1 billion bp genome is coding exon, spread across ~19,000–20,000 genes.
explanations.b: 15% overstates coding content by an order of magnitude; most of the genome is intron, regulatory, and repetitive sequence.
explanations.c: 50% is far too high — this was a pre-genome-project overestimate that the actual sequence disproved.
explanations.d: 90% would mean almost the entire genome codes for protein, the opposite of what sequencing found.

lessons.label: The Central Dogma: Transcription and Translation

sections.heading: Transcription: making a working copy
sections.body: Francis Crick stated the central dogma of molecular biology in 1958: once sequence information passes from nucleic acid into protein, it cannot flow back out — protein cannot dictate DNA or RNA sequence. It is often mis-simplified as 'DNA makes RNA makes protein only,' but Crick's actual claim was narrower and still holds: RNA-to-DNA transfer (reverse transcription) and RNA-to-RNA replication are allowed, just not protein-to-nucleic-acid. In human cells, RNA polymerase II transcribes protein-coding genes into pre-mRNA. Before that transcript can leave the nucleus it is processed: a 7-methylguanosine cap is added to its 5' end (protecting it from degradation and marking it for translation), a poly-A tail of roughly 50–250 adenines is added at the 3' end after cleavage, and the spliceosome removes introns while stitching exons together. Alternative splicing — including or excluding different exons in different cell types — lets a single gene produce multiple distinct mRNAs and proteins, which is a major reason the ~19,000–20,000 human genes yield a proteome several times larger; most multi-exon human genes are alternatively spliced in at least one tissue.

sections.heading: The genetic code and translation
sections.body: Mature mRNA is read by ribosomes in nonoverlapping triplets called codons. With 4 possible bases per position, there are 4³ = 64 possible codons: 61 code for amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons that halt translation. AUG is both the start codon and codes for methionine, so every protein begins translation at a methionine (often cleaved later). Because 61 codons specify only 20 amino acids, the code is degenerate — most amino acids are specified by multiple codons, usually differing in the third ('wobble') position, a redundancy Crick himself described in the wobble hypothesis. The ribosome, itself built from ribosomal RNA and protein, moves along the mRNA reading each codon while transfer RNAs (tRNAs), each carrying a specific amino acid and a matching anticodon, deliver the correct amino acid to be joined onto the growing peptide chain.

sections.heading: The real exception: reverse transcription
sections.body: Howard Temin and David Baltimore independently discovered reverse transcriptase in 1970, showing that retroviruses like HIV carry an enzyme that copies their RNA genome back into DNA, which then integrates into the host chromosome — RNA to DNA, exactly the direction Crick's dogma permits but that the popular one-way slogan obscures. This is not a violation of Crick's actual 1958 statement, only of its oversimplified retelling.

lessons.workedExample: A student writes in their report: 'The central dogma says genetic information only flows DNA to RNA to protein, so HIV breaks the rule.' A judge would press on this. The corrected version: Crick's 1958 dogma forbids information flowing from protein back into nucleic acid, not RNA-to-DNA transfer — reverse transcriptase (Temin and Baltimore, 1970) converts HIV's RNA genome into DNA, which is an allowed direction, not an exception. The fix isn't just semantic; it shows the student understands what the dogma actually constrains (protein cannot rewrite sequence) versus what it says nothing about (nucleic-acid-to-nucleic-acid transfers, which are common).
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about the central dogma specifically to catch the popular-science misstatement of it, because that misstatement, if uncorrected, makes a student describe reverse transcriptase, retroviruses, or even PCR-adjacent techniques as 'breaking the rules of biology' rather than as well-understood, textbook mechanisms. A student who can state Crick's actual 1958 claim — no protein-to-nucleic-acid information transfer — and correctly place reverse transcription as a permitted RNA-to-DNA step demonstrates they read a primary claim rather than a diagram caption.

questions.prompt: Order the events of mRNA processing and translation from first to last.

items.text: RNA polymerase II transcribes pre-mRNA from the DNA template
A 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail are added; the spliceosome removes introns
Mature mRNA leaves the nucleus and is read by the ribosome in codons
tRNAs deliver amino acids matching each codon to build the protein

questions.explanation: Transcription produces pre-mRNA first; capping, polyadenylation, and splicing process it into mature mRNA; the mature transcript then exits the nucleus for translation; and translation itself proceeds codon by codon as tRNAs deliver matching amino acids.

questions.prompt: Why are there 64 possible codons but only 20 amino acids plus stop signals?

options.text: The genetic code is degenerate — most amino acids are specified by more than one codon
44 of the 64 codons are never used in any organism
Codons are read in overlapping frames, halving the effective number
Only codons starting with A are functional

explanations.a: Correct — with 61 sense codons mapping to only 20 amino acids, most amino acids have multiple synonymous codons, largely varying at the third (wobble) position.
explanations.b: All 64 codons are used: 61 specify amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons; none are simply unused.
explanations.c: Codons are read in a single, nonoverlapping reading frame during normal translation, not overlapping frames.
explanations.d: Codons starting with all four bases are functional; AUG specifically (not just any A-start codon) is the start codon.

questions.prompt: What did Crick's 1958 central dogma actually forbid?

options.text: Information flowing from protein sequence back into nucleic acid sequence
RNA ever being reverse-transcribed into DNA
Any gene being transcribed more than once
Splicing of pre-mRNA in any organism

explanations.a: Correct — Crick's claim was that sequence information cannot flow from protein back into nucleic acid; RNA-to-DNA and RNA-to-RNA transfers were never excluded.
explanations.b: Reverse transcription (RNA to DNA) is consistent with Crick's actual statement — Temin and Baltimore's 1970 discovery in retroviruses does not violate it.
explanations.c: The dogma describes the direction information can flow between molecule types, not how many times a gene can be transcribed.
explanations.d: Splicing was not addressed by the 1958 statement at all; it concerns processing of an RNA transcript, not directional information flow between molecule classes.

questions.prompt: Match each mRNA-processing modification to its function.

right.text: Protects the transcript and marks it for translation
Added after cleavage at the 3' end, roughly 50-250 adenines long
Removes introns and joins exons, enabling alternative splicing

questions.explanation: The 5' cap protects the transcript and signals it is ready for translation; the poly-A tail is added at the 3' end after cleavage; and splicing removes introns while joining exons, with alternative exon choice explaining why gene count understates proteome size.

lessons.label: Alleles, Genotype, and Phenotype

sections.heading: Locus, allele, genotype: the vocabulary
sections.body: A locus is a gene's fixed physical address on a chromosome; an allele is one specific version of the DNA sequence found at that locus. Genotype is the combination of alleles an individual carries at a locus, and phenotype is the observable trait that genotype (interacting with environment) produces. An individual is homozygous if both alleles at a locus are identical, heterozygous if they differ, and hemizygous if only one copy of the locus is present at all — the normal state for most genes on the X chromosome in males, who have only one X. 'Wild-type' is a convention, not a biological fact: it labels whichever allele is most common or was designated the reference in the population or strain a lab happens to be studying, and a wild-type allele in one population can be a minority variant in another.

sections.heading: One molecular change, traced to a phenotype
sections.body: The HBB gene encodes beta-globin, a subunit of hemoglobin. In sickle cell disease, a single DNA base change (GAG to GTG) alters codon 6 from glutamic acid to valine — a Glu6Val substitution first pinned down by Vernon Ingram's 1956 protein sequencing work, building on Linus Pauling's 1949 discovery that sickle hemoglobin migrates differently on electrophoresis, the first disease shown to be caused by a specific molecular defect. That single amino acid swap changes hemoglobin's surface chemistry so that deoxygenated HbS molecules polymerize into rigid fibers, distorting red blood cells into the sickle shape. This is dominance made concrete at three levels: genotype (one base pair), protein (one amino acid), and phenotype (cell shape and downstream disease).

sections.heading: Dominance belongs to the phenotype, not the allele
sections.body: Sickle cell also shows why 'dominant' and 'recessive' describe a relationship between alleles at a specific phenotype level, not a fixed property of an allele. At the level of disease, HbS is recessive: only homozygotes (HbS/HbS) get sickle cell disease. But at the level of the protein itself, HbS and HbA are codominant — a heterozygote (sickle cell trait) produces both hemoglobin types simultaneously, visible on electrophoresis. Loss-of-function alleles can act dominantly through two distinct mechanisms: haploinsufficiency, where one working copy isn't enough to produce a normal amount of protein, and dominant-negative, where the mutant protein actively interferes with the normal protein made from the other allele (common in structural proteins like collagen, where one bad strand can poison an entire triple helix). Gain-of-function mutations, which create a new or amplified activity, are a third route to dominance. Because these mechanisms differ, the same gene can cause both a dominant and a recessive disease depending on exactly what the mutation does to the protein.

lessons.workedExample: A student examines HBB variants and finds one relative has sickle cell trait (one HbS allele, one HbA allele, no disease symptoms but detectable HbS on electrophoresis) and another relative has sickle cell disease (two HbS alleles). Asked whether HbS is 'dominant or recessive,' the precise answer depends on the phenotype level specified: for the clinical disease, HbS is recessive (heterozygotes are unaffected by sickling disease); for the biochemical presence of abnormal hemoglobin, HbS is codominant with HbA (both proteins are made and detectable). Stating 'HbS is recessive' without specifying the phenotype level is technically incomplete — a stronger answer names both levels explicitly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on dominance terminology because 'dominant/recessive' is the single most misapplied vocabulary in student genetics work — treated as a fixed label on an allele rather than a statement about a specific phenotype. A student who can say a loss-of-function allele might act dominantly through haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative interference, or point out that HbS is recessive for disease but codominant for the hemoglobin protein itself, shows they understand dominance as an emergent relationship between molecule, mechanism, and the trait being measured — not a property memorized from a Punnett square legend.

questions.prompt: A male has only one copy of a gene located on the X chromosome, since he has only one X. His genotype at that locus is best described as:

options.text: Homozygous
Heterozygous
Hemizygous
Wild-type

explanations.a: Homozygous requires two identical copies of a locus; a male X-linked gene has only one copy present, not two identical ones.
explanations.b: Heterozygous requires two different alleles at a locus; again, only one copy exists here.
explanations.c: Correct — hemizygous describes having only a single copy of a locus, the normal state for X-linked genes in males (who have one X).
explanations.d: Wild-type describes which specific allele is present (typically the reference/common one), not the number of copies — it is a separate axis of description.

questions.prompt: The single molecular change underlying sickle cell disease is best described as:

options.text: A GAG-to-GTG base change causing a Glu-to-Val substitution at codon 6 of HBB
A large deletion removing the entire HBB gene
A change to the HBB promoter that stops transcription entirely
An extra copy of the whole HBB gene

explanations.a: Correct — this single-base substitution, identified by Ingram's 1956 protein sequencing, changes codon 6 from glutamic acid to valine, altering hemoglobin's surface chemistry.
explanations.b: Sickle cell disease is caused by a point mutation, not a gene deletion; the gene is still transcribed and translated, just with one altered amino acid.
explanations.c: The mutation is in the coding sequence at codon 6, not the promoter, and HBB is still actively transcribed and translated in sickle cell disease.
explanations.d: There is no extra gene copy involved; the mechanism is a single altered codon in the existing gene.

questions.prompt: Why can HbS correctly be called both 'recessive' and 'codominant,' depending on the question asked?

options.text: Dominance is a property of the phenotype level being examined, not a fixed label on the allele itself
HbS actually has two different DNA sequences depending on which parent it came from
The terms are simply used inconsistently by different textbooks with no underlying reason
HbS is recessive in men and codominant in women

explanations.a: Correct — HbS is recessive for the clinical disease phenotype (only homozygotes get disease) but codominant at the protein level (heterozygotes make both HbA and HbS, both detectable).
explanations.b: HbS has one consistent DNA sequence regardless of parental origin; HBB is not an imprinted gene and this isn't the source of the dual description.
explanations.c: There is a precise, non-arbitrary reason: the phenotype level examined (disease vs. protein product) changes which term applies.
explanations.d: HBB is autosomal, not sex-linked, so the dominance relationship does not differ between men and women.

questions.prompt: Match each mechanism of dominance to its description.

right.text: One working copy of the gene isn't enough to make a normal amount of protein
The mutant protein actively interferes with the normal protein from the other allele
The mutation creates a new or amplified protein activity

questions.explanation: Haploinsufficiency is a dosage problem (one copy isn't enough); dominant-negative is active interference by the mutant protein, common in structural proteins like collagen; gain-of-function creates a new or amplified activity rather than losing one — all three are distinct routes by which a loss- or change-of-function mutation can still act dominantly.

lessons.label: Meiosis, Segregation, and Why Gametes Differ

sections.heading: Two divisions, two different jobs
sections.body: Meiosis converts one diploid cell (46 chromosomes in humans, 23 pairs) into four haploid gametes (23 chromosomes each) through two sequential divisions with only one round of DNA replication. Meiosis I is reductional: homologous chromosome pairs (one maternal, one paternal copy of each chromosome) line up and separate from each other, halving the chromosome number. Meiosis II is equational and mechanically resembles mitosis: the sister chromatids of each remaining chromosome separate. Before homologs separate in meiosis I, they physically pair up (synapsis) and exchange segments at points called chiasmata, the visible sites of crossing over, in which non-sister chromatids swap DNA segments. Crossing over is not just a diversity generator — recombination between homologs is typically required for accurate segregation, and human oocyte studies link failed or misplaced crossovers to segregation errors.

sections.heading: Independent assortment and the scale of gamete diversity
sections.body: In meiosis I, each of the 23 homologous pairs orients on the spindle independently of the other 22, so which parental copy (maternal or paternal) of each chromosome ends up in a given gamete is effectively a coin flip repeated 23 times. That alone produces 2^23, about 8.4 million, distinct possible chromosome combinations in a person's gametes before crossing over is even considered; crossing over then shuffles alleles within each chromosome, multiplying the diversity far beyond that figure. This is why full siblings, despite sharing both parents, are genetically distinct at the chromosome level long before any new mutation occurs.

sections.heading: When segregation fails, and inheritance outside the nucleus
sections.body: Nondisjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis I or II, producing gametes with an extra or missing chromosome. When a gamete with an extra copy of chromosome 21 is fertilized, the result is trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), karyotype notation 47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21 (versus a typical 46,XY or 46,XX). The risk rises steeply with maternal age — from roughly 1 in 1,500 live births around age 20 to roughly 1 in 100 by age 40 — because human oocytes are arrested in meiosis for decades and their chromosome-holding machinery (cohesin) degrades over that time. Mitochondrial DNA follows a completely separate inheritance rule: it is passed almost exclusively through the egg, so mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited, and because each cell holds many mitochondria, a person can carry a mix of mutant and normal mitochondrial genomes at once, a state called heteroplasmy.

lessons.workedExample: A genetic counseling scenario: a 42-year-old prospective parent asks why their risk of a trisomy 21 pregnancy is higher than it was at 25. The mechanistic answer chains together this lesson's facts: human oocytes complete meiosis I only at ovulation, sometimes decades after being arrested in prophase I as a fetus; the cohesin proteins holding homologous chromosomes together degrade over that arrest, making nondisjunction at meiosis I more likely with age; a resulting egg with an extra chromosome 21, if fertilized, yields a 47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21 karyotype. The maternal-age curve (about 1/1,500 at 20 to about 1/100 at 40) isn't a vague 'older eggs are riskier' — it's a specific consequence of how long meiosis I stays paused.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe meiosis mechanics because 'genetic diversity' and 'Down syndrome' are both phrases students use fluently without being able to explain the cellular event behind either. Naming independent assortment's 2^23 figure, distinguishing it from the further shuffling crossing over adds, and tracing nondisjunction specifically to meiosis I versus II shows a student has moved past the vocabulary into the actual chromosome mechanics — and it is also the fastest way to catch a student who thinks 'mutation' and 'nondisjunction' are the same kind of error.

questions.prompt: Order these events of meiosis from first to last.

items.text: Homologous chromosomes pair up and crossing over occurs at chiasmata
Homologous pairs separate, halving the chromosome number (meiosis I)
Sister chromatids separate (meiosis II)
Four haploid gametes are produced

questions.explanation: Crossing over occurs during prophase I, before homologs separate in the reductional division (meiosis I); sister chromatids then separate in the equational division (meiosis II); the end result is four haploid gametes.

questions.prompt: Independent assortment of 23 human chromosome pairs, before any crossing over is considered, produces how many possible chromosome combinations in gametes?

options.text: About 8.4 million (2^23)
Exactly 2, since each parent contributes one full set

explanations.a: 23 is just the number of chromosome pairs, not the number of possible combinations they can produce.
explanations.b: 46 is the diploid chromosome number, unrelated to the combinatorics of independent assortment.
explanations.c: Correct — each of the 23 pairs independently contributes either its maternal or paternal copy, giving 2^23 ≈ 8.4 million combinations before crossing over adds further diversity.
explanations.d: Each gamete gets one full haploid set, but which specific maternal/paternal chromosomes make up that set varies combinatorially, not just two ways.

questions.prompt: Why does the risk of a trisomy 21 pregnancy rise steeply with maternal age?

options.text: Human oocytes are arrested in meiosis for decades, and the cohesin holding homologs together degrades over that time, raising the chance of nondisjunction
Older mothers' eggs undergo more rounds of mitosis, accumulating mutations
Sperm chromosome number becomes unstable with paternal age
Trisomy 21 is caused by a new point mutation that accumulates with age

explanations.a: Correct — oocytes are paused in meiosis I for years to decades, during which cohesin proteins degrade, making chromosome mis-segregation (nondisjunction) more likely as maternal age increases.
explanations.b: Oocytes do not undergo repeated mitotic divisions after formation; the age effect is about prolonged meiotic arrest, not mitotic mutation accumulation.
explanations.c: The maternal-age association is specific to oocyte meiotic arrest; sperm chromosome instability is not the mechanism behind the well-documented maternal-age curve for trisomy 21.
explanations.d: Trisomy 21 is a whole-chromosome nondisjunction event, not a point mutation, and its age dependence is mechanical (cohesin degradation), not mutational.

questions.prompt: Why is mitochondrial DNA typically inherited only from the mother, and what does heteroplasmy describe?

options.text: Mitochondria are passed almost exclusively through the egg; heteroplasmy is a mix of mutant and normal mitochondrial DNA within one person's cells
Mitochondrial DNA recombines every generation like nuclear DNA; heteroplasmy means having two nuclear alleles
Sperm contribute no mitochondria at all because they lack the organelle entirely; heteroplasmy is a chromosome abnormality
Mitochondrial DNA is inherited equally from both parents; heteroplasmy describes biparental mitochondrial mixing

explanations.a: Correct — mitochondria (and their DNA) are passed almost entirely through the egg, making inheritance maternal; heteroplasmy is the coexistence of mutant and normal mitochondrial genomes within the same cell or person.
explanations.b: Mitochondrial DNA does not undergo the same nuclear-style recombination between parental copies each generation, and heteroplasmy is specifically about mitochondrial genome variation, not nuclear alleles.
explanations.c: Sperm do contain some mitochondria, but paternal mitochondria are actively degraded after fertilization, which is why inheritance is maternal — not because sperm have none.
explanations.d: Inheritance is maternal, not biparental, which is precisely why mitochondrial DNA is a useful marker for tracing maternal lineages.

lessons.label: Mendel's Laws and the Ratios They Predict

sections.heading: An eight-year experiment before genes had a name
sections.body: Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar working in Brno, bred pea plants (Pisum sativum) across roughly eight years and about 28,000 plants, tracking seven clearly binary traits — seed shape, seed color, pod shape, pod color, flower color, flower position, and stem height — and published his results in 1866, decades before chromosomes or DNA were known. His law of segregation states that an organism carries two 'factors' (alleles) for each trait, which separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one. Crossing two true-breeding plants differing in one trait, then self-pollinating the hybrid offspring, produced a 3:1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes in the second generation — Mendel's own count for seed color was 6,022 yellow to 2,001 green (about 3.01:1), and for his seed-shape cross, 5,474 round to 1,850 wrinkled seeds (about 2.96:1), both close to the 3:1 his model predicted.

sections.heading: Independent assortment, Punnett squares, and the testcross
sections.body: Mendel's second finding, the law of independent assortment, came from dihybrid crosses tracking two traits at once: the alleles for one trait segregate independently of the alleles for another, producing a 9:3:3:1 ratio of phenotype combinations in the second generation (we now know this holds cleanly only when the two genes sit on different chromosomes, or far apart on the same one — a qualification Mendel could not have known: modern linkage mapping shows his seven traits occupy only four of pea's seven chromosomes, so at least two of the trait pairs he tracked are actually on the same chromosome — far enough apart (or simply not among the crosses he published) that independent assortment still appeared to hold). The Punnett square, a grid tool developed by Reginald Punnett in the early 1900s, lets you predict these ratios by crossing every possible gamete type from one parent against every type from the other. Because a dominant phenotype can hide either a homozygous (AA) or heterozygous (Aa) genotype, Mendel also used the testcross: breeding the unknown individual with a homozygous recessive (aa), so that the offspring ratio directly reveals the unknown parent's genotype — a 1:1 split of dominant:recessive offspring means the unknown parent was heterozygous, while all-dominant offspring means it was homozygous.

sections.heading: Fisher's 1936 challenge: too good to be true?
sections.body: In 1936, statistician R.A. Fisher published a chi-square analysis of Mendel's pooled data and found the fit to expected ratios was suspiciously close — closer than chance alone would typically produce, with a probability Fisher estimated at roughly 1 in 20,000 of arising from real sampling variation. Fisher speculated an assistant may have subconsciously (or deliberately) discarded or reclassified ambiguous plants to match expectation. The dispute is still debated: some modern statisticians argue Fisher's own chi-square math or assumptions were flawed, others propose that pea traits Mendel scored as clean binaries have some natural classification ambiguity that a hopeful observer could round toward expectation without any conscious fraud. No one disputes that segregation and independent assortment are correct — only whether Mendel's specific published numbers were exactly as observed.

lessons.workedExample: A student crosses two pea-plant-style traits in a classroom simulation and gets 190 tall:70 short offspring from a monohybrid cross, close to but not exactly 3:1 (195:65 would be exact for the same 260-plant total). Asked whether this supports segregation, the right move is a chi-square check, not visual eyeballing: expected counts of 195 and 65 against observed 190 and 70 would need the formal test from a later lesson to judge whether the deviation is sampling noise. The Fisher episode is the cautionary flip side — a fit that is far too close to 3:1 across many replicated crosses is itself a statistical red flag worth investigating, not just a fit that's too far off.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about Mendel's actual numbers and the Fisher controversy because most students can recite '3:1' and '9:3:3:1' without knowing either came from real, imperfect count data or that the data's near-perfection was itself formally challenged. Citing Mendel's 5,474:1,850 or 6,022:2,001 counts shows the ratios are empirical results, not axioms, and being able to describe what Fisher's 1936 chi-square argument actually claimed — and that it remains disputed rather than settled — shows a student can hold a scientific claim as provisional rather than treating a textbook figure as beyond question.

questions.prompt: Mendel's law of segregation states that:

options.text: The two alleles for a trait separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one
Alleles for different traits are always inherited together
Dominant alleles physically destroy recessive alleles over generations
Every trait is controlled by exactly three alleles

explanations.a: Correct — segregation means the two alleles an organism carries for a trait separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets only one copy.
explanations.b: That describes a version of linkage, not segregation; segregation is about one gene's two alleles separating, and independent assortment (a separate law) concerns how different genes behave relative to each other.
explanations.c: Alleles are not destroyed; a recessive allele persists unexpressed in a heterozygote and can reappear in later generations.
explanations.d: Mendel's model uses two alleles per trait in a diploid individual, not three.

questions.prompt: Mendel's monohybrid seed-shape cross produced 5,474 round to 1,850 wrinkled seeds. This ratio is closest to:

explanations.a: Correct — 5,474:1,850 is about 2.96:1, close to the 3:1 ratio the law of segregation predicts for a monohybrid F2 cross.
explanations.b: 9:3:3:1 is the dihybrid (two-trait) ratio from independent assortment, not the single-trait monohybrid ratio shown here.
explanations.c: A 1:1 ratio is what a testcross of a heterozygote against a homozygous recessive produces, not a self-pollinated F1 monohybrid cross.
explanations.d: 1:2:1 is a genotype ratio (AA:Aa:aa), not the phenotype ratio Mendel counted directly from seed shape.

questions.prompt: What did R.A. Fisher's 1936 chi-square analysis of Mendel's data actually find?

options.text: Mendel's pooled results fit the expected ratios unusually closely — closer than typical sampling variation would predict
Mendel's results consistently deviated far from the 3:1 and 9:3:3:1 ratios he claimed
Mendel had fabricated the existence of his pea experiments entirely
Segregation and independent assortment were mathematically disproven by the analysis

explanations.a: Correct — Fisher found the fit between Mendel's data and expected ratios was implausibly close, with only a small probability of arising from ordinary chance sampling, and proposed possible unconscious or deliberate selection of favorable data.
explanations.b: The opposite is true — Fisher's concern was that the data fit too well, not too poorly.
explanations.c: Fisher's analysis questioned the precision of specific published counts, not the existence of the experiments themselves.
explanations.d: The underlying laws of segregation and independent assortment are well supported by later genetics; Fisher's dispute was about the statistical properties of Mendel's specific published numbers, not the validity of the laws.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or concept to what it is used for.

right.text: Predicting offspring ratios by crossing every possible gamete type from each parent
Determining an unknown genotype by crossing with a homozygous recessive individual
Demonstrating that two genes assort independently of each other

questions.explanation: The Punnett square is a prediction grid for offspring ratios; the testcross reveals an unknown genotype by pairing it with a homozygous recessive, since the offspring ratio directly reflects the unknown parent's gametes; and the dihybrid cross, tracking two traits at once, produces the 9:3:3:1 ratio that demonstrates independent assortment.

lessons.label: Beyond Mendel: Linkage, Epistasis, and Complex Traits

sections.heading: Linkage: when genes don't assort independently
sections.body: Independent assortment assumes genes sit on different chromosomes or far enough apart on the same one that crossing over effectively randomizes them; genes physically close together on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited as a block, breaking the clean 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio. The frequency with which crossing over separates two linked genes — recombination frequency — is a direct proxy for physical distance: 1 map unit, or centimorgan (cM), is defined as roughly 1% recombination frequency. Alfred Sturtevant, then an undergraduate in Thomas Hunt Morgan's fly lab, built the first genetic map in 1913 by measuring recombination frequencies among X-linked Drosophila genes, establishing that recombination frequency could be used to order genes linearly along a chromosome — a technique still conceptually underlying modern genetic mapping.

sections.heading: When one gene doesn't fully mask another: incomplete dominance, codominance, epistasis
sections.body: Incomplete dominance produces a blended intermediate phenotype, classically pink flowers from a cross of red and white snapdragons, because one functional allele copy makes only enough pigment for a partial effect. Codominance instead expresses both alleles fully and separately, as in the ABO blood group system: the IA and IB alleles are codominant with each other (producing type AB blood when both are present) while both are dominant to the i allele, and because there are three alleles circulating in the population, ABO is also a clean example of multiple alleles at one locus. Epistasis occurs when one gene's product masks or modifies another gene's phenotype entirely, distorting the expected dihybrid ratio into patterns like 9:3:4 (as in Labrador retriever coat color, where the E/e gene controls whether pigment is deposited in the coat at all, epistatic to the B/b gene that determines black versus brown) or 9:7 (when two genes' products must both function in the same pathway, so any single loss-of-function combination gives the same 'blocked' phenotype).

sections.heading: Pleiotropy, penetrance, polygenic traits, and parent-of-origin effects
sections.body: Pleiotropy is one gene affecting multiple, seemingly unrelated traits — the HBB sickle mutation, for instance, causes anemia, joint pain, organ damage, and (in heterozygotes) partial malaria resistance, all from one allele. Penetrance is the fraction of carriers of a genotype who show the phenotype at all, while expressivity is how severely it's shown among those who do — a distinction used for variably penetrant disease alleles like some BRCA1 mutations. Traits controlled by many genes of small additive effect, like human height, produce continuous, roughly normal distributions rather than discrete Mendelian classes. Finally, two exceptions break the assumption that both gene copies behave identically: genomic imprinting silences one parent's copy of certain genes regardless of its sequence (deletion of the same chromosome 15 region causes Prader-Willi syndrome if paternally inherited but Angelman syndrome if maternally inherited), and X-inactivation, described by Mary Lyon in 1961, randomly silences one X chromosome per cell in female mammals, producing mosaic tissue (visible as calico cat coat patterns).

lessons.workedExample: A student breeding project on Labrador coat color gets a dihybrid F2 litter with roughly 9 black : 3 brown : 4 yellow puppies instead of 9:3:3:1. Rather than assuming a counting error, the correct read is epistasis: the E/e gene (extension) controls whether pigment is deposited into the coat hair shaft at all, and ee dogs are yellow regardless of their B/b genotype — collapsing what would have been two separate phenotype classes (yellow-from-bb-ee and yellow-from-BB-ee or Bb-ee) into one visible category, converting 9:3:3:1 into 9:3:4. Recognizing the ratio shape itself as diagnostic of epistasis, rather than treating it as noisy data, is the analytical move a judge is looking for.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe non-Mendelian ratios because a student who only knows 3:1 and 9:3:3:1 will misread any real breeding or trait dataset as 'broken' rather than recognizing a specific, nameable mechanism. Naming the mechanism behind a modified ratio (linkage, epistasis, incomplete dominance) — and knowing that recombination frequency measures physical map distance, or that imprinting and X-inactivation break the assumption that both alleles behave equivalently — signals a student who can diagnose deviations from expectation rather than dismissing them as error.

questions.prompt: If two genes show a recombination frequency of 12%, what is their approximate genetic map distance?

options.text: 12 centimorgans
1.2 centimorgans
120 centimorgans
Recombination frequency cannot be converted to map distance

explanations.a: Correct — 1 centimorgan is defined as roughly 1% recombination frequency, so 12% recombination corresponds to about 12 cM, the mapping approach Sturtevant introduced in 1913.
explanations.b: This divides by 10 unnecessarily; the conversion is direct (1% ≈ 1 cM), not scaled by a factor of ten.
explanations.c: This multiplies by 10 unnecessarily; 120 cM would correspond to 120% recombination, which is not a meaningful frequency.
explanations.d: Recombination frequency is precisely the quantity Sturtevant used to build the first genetic map, converting directly (approximately) into map units.

questions.prompt: Match each inheritance pattern to its defining example or mechanism.

right.text: Pink snapdragon flowers — a blended intermediate phenotype from one functional allele copy
ABO blood type AB — both alleles fully expressed and detectable at once
Labrador coat color — one gene masks or modifies another gene's phenotype, distorting the ratio to 9:3:4
Prader-Willi vs. Angelman syndrome from the same chromosome 15 deletion, depending on parent of origin

questions.explanation: Incomplete dominance blends into an intermediate phenotype; codominance expresses both alleles fully and separately; epistasis is one gene's product masking another gene's effect, distorting expected ratios; and imprinting silences a gene copy based on which parent it came from, independent of its sequence.

questions.prompt: What is the key distinction between penetrance and expressivity?

options.text: Penetrance is the fraction of carriers who show any phenotype at all; expressivity is how severe the phenotype is among those who do
Penetrance measures severity; expressivity measures whether the phenotype appears at all
They are two names for the same concept
Penetrance applies only to dominant traits, expressivity only to recessive traits

explanations.a: Correct — penetrance asks 'does the phenotype show up at all in carriers,' while expressivity asks 'how severe is it in those who show it,' two independent axes of variation.
explanations.b: This reverses the definitions; penetrance is about presence/absence, expressivity is about severity.
explanations.c: They describe different properties of a genotype-phenotype relationship and are not interchangeable.
explanations.d: Both concepts apply regardless of dominance pattern; they describe variability in expression, not which allele type is involved.

questions.prompt: Human height is controlled by many genes of small additive effect. What distribution shape does this produce in a population, and why?

options.text: A continuous, roughly normal distribution, because many small independent contributions sum together
A discrete 3:1 ratio, identical to a single-gene Mendelian trait
A bimodal distribution with two distinct peaks
No predictable pattern at all

explanations.a: Correct — polygenic traits, where many genes each contribute a small additive effect, sum to produce continuous, roughly normal (bell-curve) variation rather than discrete classes.
explanations.b: A 3:1 ratio is the signature of a single-gene Mendelian trait with clear dominant/recessive classes, not a polygenic trait.
explanations.c: Bimodal distributions suggest two underlying categories or a major single-gene effect, not the additive small-effect model of typical polygenic traits like height.
explanations.d: Polygenic traits follow a well-characterized, predictable pattern (approximately normal), not an unpredictable one.

lessons.label: Testing an Inheritance Hypothesis: Pedigrees and Chi-Square

sections.heading: Reading a pedigree for inheritance pattern
sections.body: A pedigree tracks a trait through a family tree using standard symbols (squares for males, circles for females, filled shapes for affected individuals), and the pattern of who is affected across generations discriminates between inheritance modes. Autosomal dominant traits appear in every generation, since an affected parent (usually heterozygous) has roughly a 50% chance of passing the allele to each child, and unaffected individuals essentially never have affected children. Autosomal recessive traits often skip generations, appearing when two unaffected carrier parents (each heterozygous) both pass a copy to a child, so an affected child can come from two apparently unaffected parents. X-linked recessive traits show a distinctive asymmetry: affected males are far more common than affected females (since males are hemizygous and need only one copy), and critically, there is no male-to-male transmission — an affected father passes his X (and the trait) only to his daughters, making all of them at least carriers, never to his sons, who get his Y. Mitochondrial inheritance is the most distinctive: only offspring of an affected mother are affected, in every one of her children, while an affected father transmits the trait to none of his children, since mitochondria pass through the egg cytoplasm alone.

sections.heading: Turning a ratio guess into a statistical test
sections.body: A pedigree or a breeding cross gives you an observed count, but genetics claims usually rest on comparing that count to an expected ratio (3:1, 9:3:3:1, 1:1) predicted by a hypothesis. The chi-square goodness-of-fit test formalizes that comparison: χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E, summed across every phenotype category, where O is the observed count and E is the count expected under the hypothesized ratio applied to the same total sample size. Degrees of freedom equal the number of categories minus 1 — a two-category comparison (like testing a 3:1 ratio) has df = 1, and the critical value at the conventional α = 0.05 significance level for df = 1 is 3.84. If the calculated χ² exceeds that critical value, the deviation from the expected ratio is judged too large to attribute to sampling chance, and the hypothesized ratio (and the inheritance model behind it) is rejected; if χ² falls below 3.84, the data are considered consistent with the hypothesis.

sections.heading: Real departure versus sampling noise
sections.body: The chi-square test's whole purpose is separating a genuine biological deviation (linkage, epistasis, incomplete penetrance, or a wrong hypothesis about the inheritance mode) from ordinary sampling noise, which is larger for smaller samples. A small classroom cross of 20 offspring can show a ratio that looks visually far off 3:1 purely by chance and still yield a χ² below 3.84, while a large cross of 2,000 offspring with the same percentage deviation will produce a far larger χ², because the test scales with sample size. This is why chi-square, not eyeballing a ratio, is the standard tool for a school genetics project — and why a small pilot sample that 'looks wrong' should usually prompt collecting more data before rejecting the underlying genetic model.

lessons.workedExample: A student crosses two pea plants and expects a 3:1 ratio (tall:short) from a monohybrid cross. Out of 100 offspring, they observe 82 tall and 18 short. Expected counts under 3:1 are 75 tall and 25 short. χ² = (82−75)²/75 + (18−25)²/25 = 49/75 + 49/25 = 0.653 + 1.96 = 2.61. With df = 1 (two categories), the critical value is 3.84; since 2.61 < 3.84, the deviation is not statistically significant, and the data are consistent with the hypothesized 3:1 segregation ratio — the visually 'off' 82:18 split is within the range expected from ordinary sampling variation at this sample size.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask students to run chi-square on their own cross or pedigree data because it is the single most common (and most commonly botched) analysis in a school genetics project — students routinely eyeball a ratio as 'close enough' or 'clearly wrong' without a formal test, or misapply degrees of freedom. A student who can compute expected counts from a stated hypothesis, correctly set df = categories − 1, and explain why 2.61 does not clear the 3.84 threshold at df = 1 has demonstrated they can distinguish a real biological effect from noise — the difference between a claim and a hypothesis test.

questions.prompt: In a pedigree, a trait appears in every generation, and every affected individual has at least one affected parent, with roughly half of each affected parent's children affected. This pattern is most consistent with:

options.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance
Autosomal recessive inheritance
X-linked recessive inheritance
Mitochondrial inheritance

explanations.a: Correct — appearing in every generation with roughly 50% of an affected (typically heterozygous) parent's children affected is the hallmark of autosomal dominant inheritance.
explanations.b: Autosomal recessive traits typically skip generations, arising from two unaffected carrier parents, not appearing in every generation from an affected parent.
explanations.c: X-linked recessive inheritance shows a male-biased pattern with no male-to-male transmission, not this even, every-generation pattern.
explanations.d: Mitochondrial inheritance would show all children of an affected mother affected and zero transmission from affected fathers, a much more distinctive asymmetric pattern than described here.

questions.prompt: What pedigree observation specifically rules out X-linked recessive inheritance?

options.text: An affected father has an affected son
An affected father has an unaffected daughter
Two unaffected parents have an affected child
More females than males are affected overall

explanations.a: Correct — X-linked recessive traits show no male-to-male transmission, since a father passes his Y (not his X) to sons; an affected father with an affected son points away from X-linked recessive and toward autosomal or Y-linked inheritance.
explanations.b: An affected father's daughters get his X, so they are at least carriers, but wouldn't necessarily show the recessive phenotype themselves unless also inheriting a second affected allele — this alone doesn't rule out X-linked recessive.
explanations.c: Unaffected carrier parents having an affected child is consistent with recessive inheritance generally (both autosomal and X-linked recessive), so it doesn't specifically rule out X-linked.
explanations.d: X-linked recessive traits typically show more affected males than females (since males are hemizygous), but this option describes the opposite pattern being observed as ruling it out indirectly, not the direct diagnostic test that male-to-male transmission provides.

questions.prompt: A student tests observed offspring against an expected 3:1 ratio and calculates χ² = 5.2 with df = 1. What should they conclude at α = 0.05?

options.text: Reject the 3:1 hypothesis — 5.2 exceeds the critical value of 3.84
Accept the 3:1 hypothesis — 5.2 is close to 3.84
The test is inconclusive because df should be 2, not 1
Reject the 3:1 hypothesis only if the sample size is under 50

explanations.a: Correct — with df = 1, the critical value at α = 0.05 is 3.84; since the calculated χ² of 5.2 exceeds 3.84, the deviation is judged too large to be sampling noise, so the 3:1 hypothesis is rejected.
explanations.b: 5.2 is above, not close-and-acceptable relative to, the 3.84 threshold — exceeding the critical value means rejecting, not accepting, the hypothesis.
explanations.c: A 3:1 ratio has two phenotype categories, so df = categories − 1 = 1 is correct; df = 2 would apply to a three-category comparison.
explanations.d: The chi-square decision rule at a fixed α and df does not depend on an arbitrary sample-size cutoff; it depends on comparing the calculated χ² to the critical value for that df.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a chi-square goodness-of-fit test on cross data, from first to last.

items.text: State the hypothesized ratio (e.g., 3:1) and calculate expected counts for the total sample size
Calculate χ² = Σ (O − E)² / E across all categories
Determine degrees of freedom (categories − 1) and find the critical value
Compare calculated χ² to the critical value to accept or reject the hypothesis

questions.explanation: You must first state the hypothesis and compute expected counts, then calculate the χ² statistic from observed versus expected counts, then determine degrees of freedom and look up the corresponding critical value, and finally compare the calculated statistic to that critical value to decide whether to reject the hypothesized ratio.

lessons.label: The Reference Genome and Its Coordinates

sections.heading: A mosaic consensus, not a person
sections.body: GRCh38 (also called hg38) is not a genome anyone has — it is a mosaic consensus stitched from the DNA of a small number of anonymous donors by the Genome Reference Consortium, which released it in 2013 as the successor to hg19 (2009). Roughly 70% of the sequence traces to a single donor, an anonymous Buffalo, New York man given the code name RP11, whose BAC clone library dominated the original Human Genome Project assembly; the rest is patched in from about a dozen other donors. Because it is a composite, GRCh38 is haploid at almost every position — one base per site — even though every real human is diploid, carrying two often-different alleles. Treating the reference as 'normal' and any difference from it as 'variant' is a convenience, not a biological claim: the reference itself carries rare alleles and annotated assembly errors that later patches correct.

sections.heading: The chr:pos:REF:ALT grammar and hg19-to-hg38 pitfalls
sections.body: Every variant is named by its coordinate — chromosome, position, reference base(s), alternate base(s), as in chr7:117559590:A:T — the grammar underlying VCF files, ClinVar entries, and dbSNP records. Coordinates are only meaningful relative to a stated genome build, and hg19 and hg38 disagree on where nearly every locus sits because GRCh38 corrected thousands of assembly gaps, inversions, and misplaced segments. Converting a position between builds without a proper liftOver (UCSC's tool, or CrossMap) does not just apply a fixed offset — the mapping is locus-specific and can fail outright in restructured regions. Mixing an hg19-called variant list with an hg38-annotated database silently produces wrong answers: a variant can appear to land in the wrong gene, or point at an intron instead of an exon, with no error thrown.

sections.heading: Reference bias and the pangenome answer
sections.body: Reference bias arises during alignment: short-read aligners score a read by how well it matches the reference, so a read carrying the non-reference (ALT) allele accumulates mismatches, aligns slightly worse, or gets dropped — systematically undercounting ALT alleles, especially near indels. GRCh38 softened this with alt and patch contigs, extra sequences representing structurally divergent haplotypes (HLA, KIR) a read can align to instead of being forced onto one path, though most pipelines ignore alt contigs by default to avoid double-counting. The field's more structural answer arrived in 2023, when the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium published a draft pangenome built from 94 haplotype assemblies from 47 ancestrally diverse individuals (Liao et al., Nature): using it as an alignment target instead of one linear reference cut small-variant errors by about a third and roughly doubled structural-variant detection per haplotype.

lessons.workedExample: A team downloads candidate variants from an older study reported in hg19 coordinates, then looks each one up directly in gnomAD, which reports frequencies on hg38. Position chr17:41244936 (an hg19 BRCA1-region coordinate) does not name the same base in hg38 — the true hg38 coordinate sits dozens of bases away — so the naive lookup returns 'not found,' or worse, silently returns frequency data for an unrelated position that happens to share the number. Running the list through UCSC's liftOver tool to convert hg19 to hg38 resolves the variants to their correct gnomAD entries. The lesson: any time coordinates cross a database boundary, the genome build must be checked and converted first — matching build names is not optional metadata, it changes which base pair is being discussed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what genome did you compare your data to' is testing whether a student understands that 'the human genome' is an engineering artifact with a version number, not a fixed truth. The tell of real understanding is naming the build (GRCh38/hg38 vs. hg19) and explaining what breaks if two datasets don't share one — coordinates silently pointing at the wrong base, not an error message. A student who cannot say which build their variant calls or reference database used, or who assumes coordinates are portable across builds, has not understood what a reference genome is; one who mentions reference bias or the pangenome shows they know the reference is an approximation with known failure modes, not ground truth.

questions.prompt: What does GRCh38 (hg38) actually represent?

options.text: The exact, complete genome of one identified living person
A haploid mosaic consensus assembled by the Genome Reference Consortium, roughly 70% from a single donor (RP11)
A statistical average of thousands of sequenced human genomes
A fully synthetic sequence with no donor DNA, used only as a coordinate scaffold

explanations.a: No single person's genome is used; GRCh38 is a composite of several anonymous donors.
explanations.b: Correct — GRCh38 is a mosaic, haploid consensus stitched together by the GRC, dominated (~70%) by one donor, RP11, with patches from about a dozen others.
explanations.c: It is not a statistical average; it is a stitched assembly from a small number of real but incomplete donor sequences.
explanations.d: The sequence is real donor DNA, not synthetic — that is precisely why it carries rare alleles and assembly errors of its own.

questions.prompt: Why does reference bias cause reads carrying a non-reference (ALT) allele to be undercounted during alignment?

options.text: Aligners score reads by similarity to the reference, so ALT-carrying reads accumulate mismatches and align worse or get dropped
ALT alleles are always physically shorter fragments that fail to load onto the sequencer
Sequencing chemistry cannot detect any base that differs from the reference
ALT alleles only occur in mitochondrial DNA, which most pipelines exclude

explanations.a: Correct — alignment scoring favors matches to the reference sequence, so reads with real ALT alleles look like worse matches and are systematically undercounted, especially near indels.
explanations.b: Fragment length is a library-prep property unrelated to whether a base matches the reference.
explanations.c: Sequencers read whatever base is physically present; the bias is introduced at alignment/scoring, not detection.
explanations.d: ALT alleles occur genome-wide, including the nuclear genome; this option misattributes the mechanism entirely.

questions.prompt: Order these reference-genome milestones chronologically.

items.text: hg19 released
GRCh38 released, correcting thousands of hg19 assembly gaps and misplaced segments
Draft human pangenome published, using 94 haplotypes from 47 diverse donors instead of one linear reference

questions.explanation: hg19 was released in 2009, GRCh38 superseded it in 2013 with major assembly corrections, and the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium published its draft pangenome in 2023.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in reference-genome coordinate systems.

right.text: Anonymous donor whose DNA makes up roughly 70% of GRCh38
UCSC tool that converts coordinates between genome builds
Extra GRCh38 sequences representing structurally divergent haplotypes like HLA
94 haplotype assemblies from 47 diverse individuals, an alternative to one linear reference

questions.explanation: RP11 is the dominant donor behind GRCh38; liftOver converts coordinates between builds like hg19 and hg38; alt/patch contigs give reads an alternative alignment target for structurally divergent loci; the 2023 draft pangenome replaces a single linear reference with 94 haplotypes from 47 diverse donors.

lessons.label: SNPs, Indels, and How Variation Is Described

sections.heading: SNP, SNV, mutation, polymorphism: same event, different labels
sections.body: A SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism) and a SNV (single nucleotide variant) describe the same event — one base differing from a reference at a given position — but the labels carry different history. Older usage reserved 'polymorphism' for a variant common enough to persist in a population rather than freshly arisen, and textbook convention set that bar at a minor-allele frequency (MAF) of at least 1%; 'mutation' was reserved for rarer, often disease-associated changes. That 1% line is a bookkeeping convention, not a biological threshold — a variant at 0.9% MAF is not mechanistically different from one at 1.1%, and the same allele can be common in one population and rare (crossing the line) in another. Modern sequencing genomics has largely abandoned the distinction, defaulting to the frequency-agnostic term SNV and reserving 'pathogenic mutation' for variants with demonstrated clinical consequence rather than any frequency cutoff.

sections.heading: Indels and the frameshift arithmetic
sections.body: Insertions and deletions (indels) add or remove bases, and their damage depends on arithmetic, not just size. Coding sequence is read in triplets (codons); an indel whose length is not a multiple of three shifts every codon downstream of it into a new reading frame, so a 1 or 2 base-pair indel typically garbles the entire remaining protein and usually creates a premature stop codon within a few dozen downstream codons — a frameshift. An indel of exactly 3 (or 6, 9...) base pairs stays in-frame: it adds or removes whole codons, so the protein gains or loses a few amino acids but the rest of the sequence still reads correctly, which is often — not always — tolerated. This is why a 1-2 bp indel is treated as far more likely to be damaging than a 3 bp indel in the same gene: the difference is whether the frame survives, not raw base count.

sections.heading: Scale and the shared naming system
sections.body: The 1000 Genomes Project found that a typical human genome carries roughly 4 to 5 million variant sites relative to the reference, the overwhelming majority SNVs, with a smaller fraction indels and structural variants. Comparing two unrelated humans directly, the difference rate works out to roughly one variable site per 1,000 base pairs, about 0.1% of the genome — the figure behind the common claim that humans are '99.9% identical.' Cataloging that many variants across millions of sequenced individuals requires a shared naming system: dbSNP, launched in 1998 (Sherry et al., 2001), assigns each distinct variant a reference SNP ID — an 'rs number,' such as rs334, the HBB variant behind sickle-cell disease — that stays stable across genome builds and papers even as chromosome coordinates shift.

lessons.workedExample: CFTR's most common cystic-fibrosis allele, F508del, illustrates in-frame damage: a 3-base-pair deletion that removes exactly one codon, so the resulting CFTR protein is otherwise full-length but missing a single phenylalanine at position 508 — enough to misfold the protein and block its trafficking to the cell membrane. A 1-base-pair deletion at the same codon would be destructive in a different way: it would shift every downstream codon out of frame, scrambling the rest of the amino acid sequence and typically introducing a premature stop within the next few dozen codons, likely triggering nonsense-mediated decay instead of producing a subtly misfolded protein. Same gene, same neighborhood — but the frame-preserving 3 bp deletion and the frame-breaking 1 bp deletion cause qualitatively different kinds of damage.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'is this indel worse than that SNP' is testing whether a student reasons from mechanism instead of intuition. The naive assumption that bigger changes are always worse breaks down immediately: a 1 bp indel is usually far more destructive than a 3 bp one because it breaks the reading frame, while a well-placed 3 bp in-frame deletion — like CFTR's F508del — can be pathogenic through protein misfolding without touching the frame at all. A student who can explain frameshift arithmetic, why length modulo three is what matters rather than raw size, is reasoning about mechanism; one who says 'bigger mutation, bigger effect' is not.

questions.prompt: In older genetics usage, what historically distinguished a 'polymorphism' from a 'mutation'?

options.text: Polymorphisms affect protein-coding regions only; mutations affect noncoding DNA only
A conventional minor-allele-frequency cutoff of about 1%: at or above it, 'polymorphism'; rarer and often disease-linked, 'mutation'
Polymorphisms are inherited from parents; mutations occur only in somatic tissue
Polymorphisms are defined as biologically neutral, mutations as biologically harmful, by direct measurement

explanations.a: The distinction was about frequency, not genomic location; both terms could apply to coding or noncoding variants.
explanations.b: Correct — the traditional convention drew the line at roughly 1% minor allele frequency, an arbitrary bookkeeping cutoff rather than a biological one.
explanations.c: Both terms can refer to inherited (germline) variants; the split was not about inheritance versus somatic origin.
explanations.d: Neither label was assigned by measuring functional effect directly; the cutoff was purely about population frequency.

questions.prompt: Why does a 1 base-pair deletion in a coding exon typically cause more damage than a 3 base-pair deletion at a similar location?

options.text: The 1 bp deletion shifts the reading frame and corrupts every downstream codon, while the 3 bp deletion removes a whole codon and stays in-frame
A 1 bp deletion always physically removes more total DNA than a 3 bp deletion
3 bp deletions can only occur in introns, so they never reach the protein
1 bp deletions are always classified as nonsense mutations regardless of where they occur

explanations.a: Correct — because codons are triplets, a 1 bp deletion is not a multiple of three and shifts the reading frame for everything downstream, while a 3 bp deletion removes exactly one codon and leaves the frame intact.
explanations.b: A 3 bp deletion removes three times as many bases as a 1 bp deletion; the damage difference is about frame, not raw quantity.
explanations.c: 3 bp deletions occur in exons too, as CFTR's F508del demonstrates.
explanations.d: A 1 bp deletion causes a frameshift, which often but not always produces a premature stop; it is not automatically classified as nonsense.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many variant sites does a typical human genome carry relative to the reference, and how often do two unrelated humans differ when compared base-by-base?

options.text: About 4-5 million variants relative to the reference; roughly 1 difference per 1,000 base pairs between two people
About 50,000 variants relative to the reference; roughly 1 difference per 100,000 base pairs
About 4-5 million variants relative to the reference; roughly 1 difference per 10 base pairs
About 500 million variants relative to the reference; roughly 1 difference per 1,000 base pairs

explanations.a: Correct — these are the 1000 Genomes Project figures: roughly 4-5 million variant sites per genome versus the reference, and about one variable site per 1,000 bp between two unrelated humans (~99.9% identity).
explanations.b: This undercounts variant sites by roughly two orders of magnitude.
explanations.c: 1 difference per 10 bp would put humans at only ~90% identity, far more divergent than observed.
explanations.d: 500 million variants would exceed the size of the genome's variable fraction by roughly two orders of magnitude.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: A single base difference from the reference, described without any frequency threshold
An indel whose length is not a multiple of 3, shifting every downstream codon
An indel whose length is a multiple of 3, adding/removing whole codons without shifting frame
A dbSNP reference identifier for a specific variant, stable across genome builds, e.g. rs334

questions.explanation: SNV is the frequency-agnostic term for a single base difference; a frameshift indel breaks the reading frame because its length isn't a multiple of three; an in-frame indel preserves the frame because its length is a multiple of three; an rs number is dbSNP's stable identifier for a cataloged variant.

lessons.label: Structural Variation and Copy Number

sections.heading: Four flavors of structural variation, and copy number
sections.body: Structural variants (SVs) are changes larger than a single base or short indel: deletions and duplications (loss or gain of a segment), inversions (a segment flipped end-to-end), translocations (a segment moved to a different chromosome or location), and copy-number variants (CNVs, the general term for deletions/duplications that change how many copies of a region a genome carries). SVs are dramatically rarer than SNPs — the 1000 Genomes Project's 2015 analysis catalogued about 84.7 million SNPs and 3.6 million short indels across its cohort, but only around 60,000 structural variants. Despite that, SVs collectively alter more total base pairs per genome than SNVs do, because a single SV can span kilobases to megabases while a SNV changes exactly one base — a thousand-fold size difference per event that outweighs the thousand-fold difference in event count.

sections.heading: How SVs form: NAHR, NHEJ, and mobile elements
sections.body: Three mechanisms generate most SVs. Non-allelic homologous recombination (NAHR) happens when nearly identical repeated sequences (segmental duplications or low-copy repeats) flanking a region misalign during meiosis, so crossing over occurs between the wrong copies and produces a deletion in one product and a duplication in the other; this requires flanking repeat homology and tends to recur at the same hotspot loci across unrelated people. Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repairs double-strand breaks by directly ligating broken ends together with little or no sequence homology required; when it joins breaks from two different chromosomes it creates a translocation, and because it needs no matching sequence it can occur almost anywhere, though it is error-prone and can lose bases at the junction. Transposable-element insertion adds a new SV by copying a mobile element (Alu, LINE-1) into a new genomic location, sometimes disrupting a gene it lands in.

sections.heading: Three cases, and why short reads miss them
sections.body: AMY1, the salivary amylase gene, varies from about 2 to 15 copies per person; Perry et al. (2007, Nature Genetics) showed populations with high-starch diets carry significantly more AMY1 copies on average than low-starch hunter-gatherer populations, a plausible case of dietary selection on copy number. 22q11.2 deletion syndrome results from a roughly 3 megabase NAHR deletion between low-copy repeats on chromosome 22, occurring in about 1 in 4,000 births and producing heart defects, thymic hypoplasia, and learning differences. The Philadelphia chromosome, first noted as an abnormally small chromosome 22 by Nowell and Hungerford in 1960 and shown by Rowley in 1973 to be a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, fuses BCR and ABL1 into a constitutively active kinase driving chronic myeloid leukemia. Standard short-read sequencing (~150 bp reads) routinely misses these events: a 150 bp read cannot span a multi-kilobase breakpoint or uniquely align across the very repeats that cause NAHR in the first place.

lessons.workedExample: A clinical team runs standard short-read whole-genome sequencing (150 bp reads, ~30x coverage) on an infant with congenital heart defects and low calcium, suspecting 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. The routine SNV-calling pipeline reports a clean list of point variants and calls the region 'normal,' because a 3 Mb deletion does not look like a mismatch to a short-read aligner — it looks like a stretch where read depth quietly drops to half, a signal the SNV caller was never built to notice. Only when the team reruns a depth-based CNV caller (or orders a targeted FISH or microarray test) does the deletion appear as a clear halving of coverage across the 22q11.2 region. A negative short-read SNV report does not rule out a large deletion — it was never the right tool to find one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'could your sequencing method have missed something' after a student reports a clean SNV-only result is testing whether they know SVs occupy a blind spot standard short-read pipelines are not built to see. The strong answer names the mechanism: a 150 bp read cannot span a multi-kilobase deletion breakpoint or resolve the repeat-rich regions where NAHR-driven CNVs like 22q11.2 occur, so detecting them requires depth-based calling, long reads, or a targeted assay like FISH. A student who assumes 'no SNVs found' means 'no relevant variation' has missed the entire structural-variant category — rarer events that, base for base, matter just as much.

questions.prompt: According to the 1000 Genomes Project's 2015 catalogue, what is the numeric relationship between SNPs and structural variants (SVs) in a genome?

options.text: SVs vastly outnumber SNPs but affect fewer total base pairs
SNPs vastly outnumber SVs (millions vs. roughly 60,000), yet SVs alter more total base pairs because each event spans kilobases to megabases
SNPs and SVs occur in roughly equal numbers
Both SNPs and SVs typically change about one base pair per event

explanations.a: This reverses the relationship — SVs are the rare ones (about 60,000) while SNPs number in the tens of millions.
explanations.b: Correct — about 84.7 million SNPs versus roughly 60,000 SVs, but because SVs can span kilobases to megabases each, they collectively alter more base pairs than the far more numerous single-base SNPs.
explanations.c: SNPs outnumber SVs by roughly three orders of magnitude, not a similar count.
explanations.d: Only SNVs change one base pair per event; SVs by definition span much larger regions.

questions.prompt: Match each mechanism to how it generates structural variation.

right.text: Misaligned crossover between similar flanking repeats, producing a deletion in one product and a duplication in the other
Direct ligation of double-strand break ends with little or no sequence homology; joining breaks on two chromosomes creates a translocation
A mobile element (e.g. Alu, LINE-1) copies itself into a new genomic location, sometimes disrupting the gene it lands in

questions.explanation: NAHR arises from crossover between mismatched copies of similar flanking repeats; NHEJ ligates broken DNA ends with little or no homology and can fuse breaks from different chromosomes into a translocation; transposable-element insertion adds new sequence by copying a mobile element into a new site.

questions.prompt: The Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL fusion) that drives chronic myeloid leukemia arises from which type of structural variant?

options.text: A pericentric inversion on chromosome 22
A reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, shown by Rowley in 1973
A tandem duplication confined to chromosome 9
A large single-chromosome deletion with no second chromosome involved

explanations.a: The event is a translocation between two different chromosomes, not an inversion within one.
explanations.b: Correct — Nowell and Hungerford first noted the abnormal chromosome 22 in 1960, and Rowley showed in 1973 it was a reciprocal translocation t(9;22) fusing BCR and ABL1 into a constitutively active kinase.
explanations.c: The abnormality involves an exchange between two chromosomes (9 and 22), not a duplication confined to one.
explanations.d: A translocation moves material between two chromosomes; it is not a simple one-chromosome deletion.

questions.prompt: Why does standard ~150 bp short-read sequencing routinely miss large structural variants like the 22q11.2 deletion?

options.text: Short reads cannot chemically detect any missing DNA at all
