(2008), which ran PCA on genome-wide SNP data from roughly 1,400 Europeans and found that plotting PC1 against PC2 reproduced a recognizable map of Europe — samples from Spain, Italy, Scandinavia, and the Balkans fell into a scatter whose geometry closely tracked their geographic origin, demonstrating that subtle correlated allele-frequency differences across populations encode real ancestry and migration history. That result is why PCA is now the standard first step in any genome-wide association study: it identifies population substructure that, left uncorrected, causes exactly the stratification-driven inflation described for GWAS Manhattan plots. The second canonical use is in expression data as a quality-control diagnostic rather than a biology result: if samples separate on PC1 or PC2 primarily by which day they were processed, which technician ran them, or which sequencing batch they belong to — rather than by the experimental treatment — that is the classic red flag for a batch effect, and it means the biological question the experiment was designed to answer is confounded until that technical variable is corrected for or included as a covariate.

sections.heading: t-SNE and UMAP: a different promise, a different warning
sections.body: t-SNE and UMAP are nonlinear dimensionality-reduction methods, common in single-cell genomics, that optimize for a different goal than PCA: rather than preserving global variance along ranked axes, they try to preserve local neighborhoods, keeping points that were close in high-dimensional space close on the 2D plot. This makes them excellent at revealing discrete cluster structure (cell types, for instance) that PCA can blur together. But that same design choice makes two visual habits actively misleading: the size of a cluster on a t-SNE or UMAP plot does not reflect how many 'real' distinct subtypes it contains or how variable it is, and the distance between two separate clusters is not a meaningful measure of how biologically different they are — both algorithms can stretch, compress, and reposition clusters arbitrarily as a side effect of preserving local neighbor relationships, so only within-cluster proximity, not between-cluster geometry, should be trusted.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher runs PCA on RNA-seq data from 24 samples (12 treated, 12 control) and finds that PC1 (38% variance) separates samples cleanly into two groups of 12 — but the groups are 'samples processed on Monday' versus 'samples processed on Thursday,' not treated versus control, which split evenly across both days. This is a textbook batch effect: the dominant axis of variation in the entire dataset is a technical artifact of processing day, not biology, and any differential-expression result run without correcting for that batch variable will be confounded. The fix is to add processing day as a covariate in the statistical model (or re-run with batch correction) before trusting any 'treatment effect' downstream.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about PCA specifically to catch the batch-effect trap, because it is the single most common silent confounder in student genomics projects — samples run on different days, different machines, or by different people often separate cleanly on PC1 for reasons that have nothing to do with the hypothesis. A judge asking 'what does PC1 in your plot actually correspond to, and did you check whether it lines up with a technical variable instead of your treatment?' is testing whether the student ran that check at all, since a beautiful PCA separation is meaningless — or actively misleading — if it's tracking batch rather than biology.

questions.prompt: Why must a PCA plot report the percent variance explained by each principal component on its axis labels?

options.text: It's a formatting convention with no analytical meaning
It tells the reader how much of the dataset's real structure that axis captures — a PC explaining 2% is close to noise, one explaining 40% is a dominant axis
It converts the PCA plot into a Manhattan plot
It shows the exact number of samples in the dataset

explanations.a: The percentage carries real analytical weight; it's not decoration.
explanations.b: Correct — variance explained tells you whether an axis reflects substantial real structure or is barely distinguishable from noise, which changes how much weight to put on visual separation along that axis.
explanations.c: These remain entirely distinct plot types regardless of what's on the axis labels.
explanations.d: Variance explained is unrelated to sample count.

questions.prompt: In Novembre et al. (2008), what did plotting PC1 against PC2 from European genotype data reveal?

options.text: That all Europeans are genetically identical
A scatter whose geometry closely tracked the geographic map of Europe, reflecting real ancestry structure
That genotype data cannot be used for ancestry inference
A random cloud with no interpretable structure

explanations.a: The result showed meaningful genetic differentiation correlated with geography, not identity.
explanations.b: Correct — the PC1/PC2 scatter from roughly 1,400 Europeans reproduced a recognizable map of Europe, showing that correlated allele-frequency differences encode real ancestry and migration history.
explanations.c: The study is the canonical demonstration that genotype PCA does capture ancestry structure.
explanations.d: The whole significance of the result is that the structure was interpretable and geographically meaningful, not random.

questions.prompt: In an expression PCA plot, samples separate cleanly on PC1 — but the split matches which day they were processed, not the experimental treatment. What does this indicate?

options.text: A batch effect: PC1 is dominated by a technical variable (processing day), confounding the biological comparison
Strong, unambiguous evidence of a treatment effect
That PCA has failed and should not be trusted for any dataset
That the treatment worked but only on odd-numbered samples

explanations.a: Correct — separation tracking a technical variable like processing date rather than the biological condition is the classic diagnostic red flag for a batch effect confounding the comparison.
explanations.b: The separation tracks a technical variable, not treatment, so it cannot be read as a treatment effect without further correction.
explanations.c: PCA worked correctly here; it's precisely how the batch effect was detected in the first place.
explanations.d: There's no basis in the scenario for an odd/even sample-index explanation.

questions.prompt: In a t-SNE or UMAP plot of single-cell data, which of the following is NOT safe to interpret directly from the plot?

options.text: Whether two points are close neighbors within the same cluster
The distance between two separate clusters as a measure of how biologically different they are
Whether the data shows discrete cluster structure at all
Whether points within one cluster are tightly or loosely grouped locally

explanations.a: Local neighbor relationships are exactly what these algorithms are designed to preserve and are safe to interpret.
explanations.b: Correct — both algorithms can arbitrarily stretch or reposition clusters as a side effect of preserving local structure, so between-cluster distance and relative cluster size are not meaningful.
explanations.c: Revealing discrete cluster structure is the core strength these methods are used for.
explanations.d: Local grouping tightness is part of the preserved neighbor information these methods optimize for.

lessons.label: Trees and Circos: Relationships and Whole-Genome Views

sections.heading: Tips, nodes, branch length, and rooting
sections.body: A phylogenetic tree's tips (the endpoints, usually on the right or at the leaves) represent the sequences or organisms actually sampled; internal nodes represent inferred common ancestors, not sampled organisms — a node is a hypothesis, not a specimen. Branch length usually encodes evolutionary divergence, either as elapsed time (if the tree is calibrated against fossil or mutation-rate data) or as the number of substitutions per site (if uncalibrated), so a long branch means more accumulated change, not necessarily more time unless the tree explicitly says so. Rooting establishes direction: an unrooted tree only shows relative relatedness, while adding a root — conventionally by including an outgroup, a lineage known from outside evidence to have diverged before the rest of the group — lets you read the tree left-to-right (or bottom-to-top) as an actual timeline of divergence events, oldest split nearest the root.

sections.heading: Bootstrap support and the one mistake nearly everyone makes
sections.body: Confidence in a tree's branching pattern is usually reported as bootstrap support values at each internal node, from the method Felsenstein (1985) introduced: resampling the original sequence alignment's columns with replacement many times (typically hundreds to a thousand), rebuilding the tree each time, and reporting what percentage of those replicate trees recovered that same split. Values above roughly 70% are conventionally treated as reasonably well-supported, and above roughly 95% as strongly supported; a node with 30% support is essentially unresolved and shouldn't be treated as a confident claim about relationships. The single most common misreading of a tree, though, has nothing to do with support values: topology (which lineages share which common ancestor, and in what order the branches split) carries all of the biological meaning, while the top-to-bottom order that sibling branches happen to be drawn in is arbitrary — any internal node can be rotated, swapping its children's vertical position, without changing the tree's meaning at all. A reader who infers relatedness from vertical proximity on the page (rather than from shared node ancestry) is reading a tree wrong.

sections.heading: Circos plots and the genome-browser workhorse
sections.body: Circos plots (Krzywinski et al., 2009) arrange chromosomes as a circle and draw arcs (links) connecting regions — commonly used to show structural rearrangements like translocations, or synteny between two species' genomes. They are visually striking, which is exactly the risk: a dense tangle of colorful arcs reads as impressive complexity but often encodes only a handful of underlying breakpoints, with no quantitative axis a reader can extract a number from, so a Circos plot should usually be read as a qualitative map of 'where the interesting connections are,' prompting a follow-up to the actual coordinates, rather than as data to measure by eye. The genuine daily workhorse for looking at real genomic data — not for a poster, but for actually checking a result — is a genome browser track view, such as the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV; Robinson et al., 2011) or the UCSC Genome Browser (Kent et al., 2002): a linear, zoomable view of one genomic region showing annotation tracks, coverage, and individual sequencing reads stacked in place, which is what the next lesson covers in detail.

lessons.workedExample: A phylogenetic tree of four bacterial strains shows strain D branching off first (near the root, using an outgroup to establish direction), then strains A and B splitting from a shared ancestor with 98% bootstrap support at that node, while the split separating C from the A/B pair shows only 42% support. A student should report: strains A and B are confidently sister taxa (98%, well above the ~95% strong-support convention), but the placement of C relative to A/B is essentially unresolved (42%, below even the ~70% convention) and shouldn't be stated as fact. If a colleague redraws the same tree with A and B's branches swapped top-to-bottom, nothing has changed biologically — the topology (D branching first, then A+B as sisters, with C's position uncertain) is identical.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges test tree-reading directly because rotating a node is the cheapest way to check whether a student actually understands topology or is pattern-matching on vertical position — asking 'if I swap these two branches, does the tree still mean the same thing?' has one correct answer (yes) that a student who has memorized the picture rather than the logic will get wrong. A judge will also ask what a specific bootstrap number means, because citing '87% support' without being able to say it comes from resampling the alignment and rebuilding the tree hundreds of times is reciting a number, not demonstrating understanding of confidence in a phylogenetic claim.

questions.prompt: If an internal node in a phylogenetic tree is rotated, swapping the vertical (top-to-bottom) position of its two child branches, what happens to the tree's meaning?

options.text: Nothing changes — topology, not vertical drawing order, carries the meaning
The evolutionary relationships completely reverse
The branch lengths become invalid
The tree becomes unrooted

explanations.a: Correct — topology (which lineages share which common ancestors) is the meaningful content; the vertical order siblings happen to be drawn in is arbitrary and can be freely rotated.
explanations.b: Rotating a node doesn't alter which lineages descend from which ancestor, so relationships are unchanged.
explanations.c: Branch lengths are independent of vertical drawing order and remain valid after rotation.
explanations.d: Rooting is a separate property (whether an outgroup establishes direction) and is unaffected by rotating a node.

questions.prompt: A node has 42% bootstrap support. What should a student conclude?

options.text: That split is essentially unresolved and shouldn't be presented as a confident claim about relationships
That split is strongly supported and can be stated as fact
The tree must be re-rooted before the number means anything
42% means the analysis used 42 resampling replicates

explanations.a: Correct — well below the conventional ~70% threshold for reasonable support, 42% support means that split was recovered in less than half of resampled replicate trees, so it should be treated as unresolved.
explanations.b: 42% is well below both the ~70% and ~95% conventional support thresholds, the opposite of strong support.
explanations.c: Bootstrap support values are interpretable independent of rooting; rooting affects directionality, not support percentages.
explanations.d: The percentage reflects the fraction of replicates (often hundreds) that recovered the split, not the replicate count itself.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of including an outgroup when building a phylogenetic tree?

options.text: To increase the bootstrap support values across all nodes
To root the tree, establishing which end represents older divergences and enabling a directional reading
To reduce the number of tips that need to be sequenced
To eliminate the need for branch lengths

explanations.a: Outgroup choice doesn't mechanically raise support values; support comes from resampling the alignment.
explanations.b: Correct — a lineage known from outside evidence to have diverged before the rest of the group establishes a root, letting the tree be read as a directional timeline rather than just relative relatedness.
explanations.c: Including an outgroup adds a tip to sequence/include, it doesn't reduce sampling needs elsewhere.
explanations.d: Branch lengths remain meaningful (and necessary) regardless of whether the tree is rooted.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson caution against treating a Circos plot's dense web of arcs as quantitative data to be read by eye?

options.text: Circos plots cannot display more than three chromosomes at once
A visually dense, impressive-looking tangle of arcs often encodes only a handful of underlying breakpoints, with no extractable numeric axis
Circos plots are only valid for viewing single genes, not whole chromosomes
Circos plots always use a logarithmic color scale that hides most of the data

explanations.a: Circos plots are specifically designed to show whole-genome, multi-chromosome relationships, not limited to three.
explanations.b: Correct — the visual complexity of a Circos plot can outstrip the actual quantitative information it encodes, so it should prompt a follow-up to real coordinates rather than being measured by eye.
explanations.c: Circos plots are built for chromosome-scale, whole-genome views, the opposite of single-gene focus.
explanations.d: Circos color scale choices vary by plot and are not the stated reason for caution here.

lessons.label: Reading an Alignment: IGV and Variant Calls

sections.heading: What a pileup at one locus actually shows
sections.body: Open a locus in the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV; Robinson et al., 2011) and you see a pileup: a reference sequence track at top, then a stack of individual sequencing reads below it, each a short horizontal bar aligned to the position it maps to, colored where its base disagrees with the reference. Read depth — how many reads stack up at a position — sets your confidence floor; a variant called from 4 overlapping reads is far shakier than one called from 60. For a genuine heterozygous variant in a diploid organism, allele balance (the fraction of reads carrying the alternate allele) should cluster near 50%, since each of the two chromosome copies is sequenced at roughly equal random depth; a variant supported by only 8% of reads at a well-covered site is much more consistent with sequencing error or a subclonal/mosaic event than a true germline heterozygous call, and that distinction — a clean ~50% split versus a thin, ragged smear of a few percent — is often visible by eye before any statistic confirms it.

sections.heading: Three red flags in the pileup
sections.body: Strand bias is a check for whether a variant allele is seen roughly equally on reads sequenced from the forward and reverse strand; a variant that appears almost exclusively on one strand (rather than split reasonably evenly) is a classic sequencing-artifact signature rather than real biology. Mapping quality (MAPQ), often color-coded or grayed out in IGV, reflects how confidently the aligner placed a given read at this exact position versus elsewhere in the genome; MAPQ of zero clustering across a whole region is the signature of a repetitive sequence (a segmental duplication, a transposable element, a paralog) where reads could have come from several near-identical places, and variant calls in a MAPQ-zero region deserve far less trust than the same call in uniquely mapping sequence. Soft-clipping — visible in IGV as reads whose ends are drawn in a lighter shade because that portion didn't align to the reference — means part of the read matched the expected position and part didn't; a cluster of reads all soft-clipped at the same position is frequently the visible signature of a structural event (an insertion, a deletion breakpoint, a translocation junction) that a simple SNP/indel caller wasn't built to fully resolve.

sections.heading: The VCF line underneath, and why eyeballing still matters
sections.body: Variant call format (VCF) encodes each candidate variant as one line with standardized fields: CHROM and POS give the location; REF and ALT give the reference and alternate alleles; QUAL is the caller's confidence (as a Phred-scaled score, so higher means more confident); FILTER records whether the variant passed the caller's internal quality filters ('PASS') or failed one ('LowQual' or similar); INFO carries aggregate annotations like total depth; and the per-sample GT (genotype) field — commonly 0/0 for homozygous reference, 0/1 for heterozygous, 1/1 for homozygous alternate — is the actual call being made about that sample at that site. Every one of these numbers is produced by a probabilistic model applied to messy sequencing data, and pipelines do produce artifacts: a caller can output PASS and a high QUAL for a variant that is, on visual inspection of the pileup, obviously a mapping error in a repeat region. That's why eyeballing the raw alignment in IGV remains standard practice as the last line of defense before trusting a call — the algorithms that generate VCF lines belong to a separate discussion of variant-calling pipelines.

lessons.workedExample: A VCF line reports a heterozygous SNP (GT = 0/1) at a locus with QUAL = 45 and FILTER = PASS. Opening the position in IGV shows 30 reads total, 14 carrying the alternate allele split roughly evenly between forward and reverse strand (consistent with true ~50% allele balance and no strand bias), all with MAPQ near 60 (uniquely mapping), and no soft-clipping — this call looks trustworthy. A second VCF line at a different locus also reports GT = 0/1 with QUAL = 38 and FILTER = PASS, but IGV shows the alternate allele almost entirely on forward-strand reads, at only 9% of total depth, in a region where most reads show MAPQ = 0 — three red flags at once, strongly suggesting this 'heterozygous call' is actually a mapping artifact in a repetitive region and should not be trusted despite passing the caller's filter.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges who ask a student to open IGV at their key variant's coordinates are testing whether the student trusts their pipeline's output or actually verified it, because a PASS-filtered, high-QUAL VCF line can still be a mapping artifact, and 'my software called it' is not evidence. A student who can point at the pileup and say 'allele balance is near 50%, reads are on both strands, mapping quality is high, no soft-clipping' has demonstrated they know what a trustworthy call looks like at the read level; a student who can't explain what they're looking at has only demonstrated they can run a variant caller.

questions.prompt: For a genuine heterozygous variant in a diploid organism, what allele balance (fraction of reads carrying the alternate allele) is expected at a well-covered site?

options.text: Roughly 50%
Roughly 100%
Exactly 0%
Roughly 25%, always

explanations.a: Correct — each of the two chromosome copies is sequenced at roughly equal random depth, so a true heterozygous call should show close to a 50/50 split between reference and alternate alleles.
explanations.b: 100% alternate-allele fraction would indicate a homozygous alternate call, not heterozygous.
explanations.c: 0% would mean no alternate allele is seen at all, i.e., homozygous reference.
explanations.d: There's no biological reason for a fixed 25% expectation at a heterozygous diploid site.

questions.prompt: A variant's alternate allele appears almost exclusively on reads from one sequencing strand (not split reasonably evenly between forward and reverse). What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: A true germline variant, since real variants always favor one strand
A classic sequencing-artifact signature (strand bias), since a real genomic variant shouldn't depend on which strand a read came from
That the sample is definitely from a repetitive region of the genome
That the read depth is too low to call any variant

explanations.a: Real variants have no mechanistic reason to favor one sequencing strand; this pattern is a red flag, not confirmation.
explanations.b: Correct — a true variant is present in the underlying DNA and should be seen roughly evenly regardless of which strand happened to be sequenced, so strong strand skew signals an artifact.
explanations.c: Strand bias and repetitive-region mapping issues (flagged by low MAPQ) are related but distinct red flags; this scenario describes strand bias specifically, not mapping quality.
explanations.d: Strand bias is about allele distribution across strands, not about overall depth.

questions.prompt: A cluster of reads over a locus all show mapping quality (MAPQ) of zero. What does this most directly suggest?

options.text: The reads are of exceptionally high sequencing quality
The region is likely repetitive (e.g., a segmental duplication or transposable element), so reads could plausibly have come from several near-identical genomic locations
The sample must be contaminated with another species' DNA
The variant caller has not yet processed this region

explanations.a: MAPQ reflects placement confidence, not base-calling/sequencing quality; MAPQ 0 signals ambiguous placement, not high quality.
explanations.b: Correct — MAPQ 0 means the aligner could not confidently place the read at one unique position, the classic signature of repetitive sequence where a read matches multiple near-identical locations equally well.
explanations.c: Cross-species contamination is a distinct issue and not what MAPQ specifically measures.
explanations.d: MAPQ is assigned during alignment, before variant calling, so it's unrelated to whether a caller has processed the region.

questions.prompt: In a VCF line, what does the FILTER field of 'PASS' indicate about a variant call?

options.text: That the variant passed the caller's internal quality filters, meaning it should be trusted with no further review
That the variant passed the caller's internal quality filters, but this alone does not guarantee the call is biologically correct — it can still be a mapping or pipeline artifact
That the sample is homozygous reference at this position
That the read depth at this position is exactly zero

explanations.a: The lesson explicitly warns that a PASS-filtered, high-QUAL call can still be a mapping error, so PASS alone doesn't guarantee correctness.
explanations.b: Correct — PASS means the variant cleared the caller's internal thresholds, but pipelines still produce artifacts, which is exactly why eyeballing the alignment in IGV remains standard practice as a last check.
explanations.c: Genotype (homozygous reference vs. heterozygous vs. homozygous alternate) is recorded in the GT field, not FILTER.
explanations.d: FILTER records quality-filter status, not read depth, which is typically found in the INFO field.

lessons.label: The p-value, the Null, and What It Does Not Mean

sections.heading: What p actually measures
sections.body: A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as what you observed, if the null hypothesis were true — nothing more. If you compare gene expression between drug-treated and control cells and get p=0.03, that means: assuming the drug truly does nothing, there is a 3% chance random noise alone would produce a difference this large or larger. It is not the probability the null hypothesis is true, and it is not the probability your result is a fluke — that would require Bayesian reasoning about prior odds, which p-values do not supply. This is the single most common misreading in student projects and in published papers alike.

sections.heading: Choosing the test and the tails
sections.body: For a two-group comparison of a continuous measurement (say, tumor volume in treated versus untreated mice), a Student's t-test assumes the data are roughly normal and the two groups have comparable variance; it asks whether the difference in means is larger than sampling noise predicts. When sample sizes are small or the data are skewed — common in genomics, where a handful of replicates and log-scale expression values are the norm — the Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney U) test is the more honest choice, since it only compares ranks and assumes nothing about the distribution's shape. A two-tailed test asks whether the groups differ in either direction and is the default; a one-tailed test only checks one direction and should be pre-specified before seeing data, never chosen afterward because the result leaned one way.

sections.heading: Why 0.05, and its three classic misreadings
sections.body: The α=0.05 threshold traces to Ronald Fisher's 1925 book Statistical Methods for Research Workers, where he suggested it as a convenient, not sacred, cutoff — a convention the field inherited rather than a law of nature. Three misreadings recur constantly. First, 'p=0.06 means no effect' — 0.06 is just above an arbitrary line; the underlying evidence barely differs from p=0.04. Second, 'p<0.001 means a big effect' — p measures how surprising the data are under the null given the sample size, not how large the effect is; a trivial difference in a huge dataset can produce a tiny p-value. Third, 'non-significant means proven equivalent' — failing to reject the null is not evidence the null is true; it may just mean the study was underpowered to detect a real difference.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares GFP-reporter expression in 6 treated versus 6 control zebrafish embryos and runs a two-tailed Student's t-test, getting p=0.07. They conclude 'the treatment has no effect.' A judge asks for the effect size and the student reports treated embryos averaged 40% higher expression, but with wide variance across only 6 fish. The honest conclusion is not 'no effect' but 'this study, at this sample size, could not distinguish a real 40% difference from noise' — and a Wilcoxon rank-sum test on the same data, appropriate given n=6 and visibly skewed values, is worth reporting alongside the t-test to show the result is not an artifact of the normality assumption.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe p-value interpretation because it is the fastest way to separate a student who ran statistics from one who understands them. The tell is whether a student can correctly state, in one sentence, what their own p-value does and does not claim about their null hypothesis — and whether they distinguish 'not significant' from 'no effect.' A student who defends a p=0.06 result as 'trending' without overclaiming significance, and who can name why they chose a t-test versus a Wilcoxon test for their specific data, has demonstrated real statistical literacy rather than software literacy.

questions.prompt: A student gets p=0.03 comparing two groups. What does this value actually represent?

options.text: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
The probability of observing data this extreme or more, assuming the null hypothesis is true
The treatment effect explains 3% of the variance
There is a 97% chance the treatment works

explanations.a: This inverts the logic — p is calculated assuming the null is true, so it cannot also be the probability that the null is true.
explanations.b: Correct — the p-value is the probability of data this extreme or more extreme, conditional on the null hypothesis being true. It says nothing directly about the probability of any hypothesis.
explanations.c: That description matches an effect-size or variance-explained statistic, not a p-value, which is about surprise relative to the null, not magnitude.
explanations.d: p-values do not translate into a probability that a hypothesis is correct; that requires Bayesian priors p-values do not include.

questions.prompt: Why might a Wilcoxon rank-sum test be preferred over a Student's t-test for comparing gene expression between two small groups?

options.text: It always produces a smaller p-value
It does not assume the data are normally distributed, which matters with small or skewed samples
It is required whenever more than one gene is tested
It measures effect size directly instead of significance

explanations.a: The Wilcoxon test has no systematic bias toward smaller p-values; which test gives a smaller value depends on the actual data.
explanations.b: Correct — the Wilcoxon rank-sum test only uses ranks, so it makes no normality assumption, which suits small-n or skewed expression data common in genomics.
explanations.c: The choice between t-test and Wilcoxon is about distributional assumptions, not the number of genes tested — that is a multiple-testing issue, a separate concept.
explanations.d: Both tests produce a significance measure (a p-value), not an effect size; neither reports magnitude of difference on its own.

questions.prompt: A student reports p<0.001 for a difference in cell count and calls it 'a huge effect.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: p<0.001 is impossible with real biological data
A very small p-value reflects strong evidence against the null given the sample size, not necessarily a large effect magnitude
p-values below 0.05 are always due to batch effects
The student should have used a one-tailed test instead

explanations.a: p<0.001 is common with large samples or careful measurement and is not inherently suspicious.
explanations.b: Correct — with a large enough sample, even a trivially small true difference can produce a very small p-value; p reflects confidence the effect is nonzero, not its size.
explanations.c: A small p-value has many possible causes; batch effects are one confound among several, not the default explanation.
explanations.d: One-tailed versus two-tailed is a separate design choice unrelated to the p-value-versus-effect-size confusion here.

questions.prompt: A study finds p=0.20 for a treatment effect and the student concludes 'this proves the treatment has no effect.' What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing — non-significant results always prove no effect exists
Failing to reject the null is not evidence the null is true; the study may simply be underpowered
The threshold should have been 0.20 instead of 0.05
p=0.20 actually indicates a highly significant effect

explanations.a: This restates the exact misconception the lesson warns against; absence of significance is not proof of absence of effect.
explanations.b: Correct — a non-significant result can mean there truly is no effect, or that the sample size and variance made a real effect undetectable; the two cannot be distinguished without more information like power.
explanations.c: Changing the threshold after seeing the result does not fix the logical error of equating 'not significant' with 'proven equivalent.'
explanations.d: p=0.20 is well above the conventional 0.05 cutoff and would not typically be called significant by any common convention.

questions.prompt: Match each statistical claim to what it actually means.

left.text: p<0.001 with a tiny mean difference in a huge sample

right.text: Just above an arbitrary convention; not meaningfully different from p=0.04
Strong evidence against the null, but not evidence of a large or important effect
Could reflect a truly null effect or simply insufficient power to detect a real one

questions.explanation: p=0.06 sits arbitrarily above the conventional 0.05 line and carries nearly identical evidential weight to p=0.04. A very small p-value with a tiny effect size shows statistical significance without practical significance. A high p-value with low power cannot distinguish 'no effect' from 'underpowered to detect a real effect.'

lessons.label: Effect Size, Fold Change, and Confidence Intervals

sections.heading: Fold change and why genomics uses log2
sections.body: Fold change is the ratio of expression between two conditions — treated divided by control. Reporting raw ratios is awkward because upregulation and downregulation are not symmetric on a linear scale: doubling is 2.0, but halving is only 0.5, so equal-magnitude opposite effects look different in size. Genomics fixes this by working in log2 space: log2 fold change (log2FC) of +1 means the gene doubled (2× up), and log2FC of −1 means it halved (2× down) — symmetric around zero, with magnitude directly readable. A log2FC of +2 is 4× up, +3 is 8× up. RNA-seq tools like DESeq2 and edgeR report log2FC alongside a p-value precisely because a gene can be statistically significant yet trivially small (log2FC=0.1, barely a 7% change) — significance and magnitude are separate questions.

sections.heading: Effect size across data types
sections.body: Different data types use different effect-size metrics. In genetic association studies (does carrying a variant associate with a disease?), the odds ratio (OR) compares the odds of disease in carriers versus non-carriers — OR=1 means no association, OR=2 means carriers have roughly double the odds. Linear regression on continuous traits (height, blood pressure) reports a beta coefficient: the expected change in the trait per copy of the risk allele. For comparing two group means on a continuous measure — the same territory as a t-test — Cohen's d standardizes the mean difference by the pooled standard deviation, with Jacob Cohen's own 1988 rules of thumb treating d=0.2 as small, 0.5 as medium, and 0.8 as large. All three answer 'how big,' which a p-value alone never does.

sections.heading: Confidence intervals and the GWAS calibration
sections.body: A confidence interval (CI) reports a plausible range for the true effect, so a 95% CI on an odds ratio of 1.15 with range 1.10–1.20 tells you both the estimate and its precision in one statement — a p-value alone collapses that into a single pass/fail threshold. This is why reviewers increasingly expect CIs alongside, or instead of, bare p-values. The field's key calibration problem: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) routinely find genuine, replicated associations with odds ratios of only 1.05 to 1.2 per variant. These are real signals, not statistical artifacts, confirmed across independent cohorts of hundreds of thousands of people — but an OR of 1.1 is nearly useless for predicting any individual's risk, since it barely shifts the odds compared to population baseline. This distinction — real and replicated, yet weak at the individual level — is what resolves most 'scientists find the gene for X' headlines: the gene is one small tile in a mosaic of hundreds of variants plus environment.

lessons.workedExample: A DESeq2 analysis reports a gene with log2FC=+2.3 and p=2×10⁻⁸: that gene is roughly 2^2.3 ≈ 4.9× upregulated, and the tiny p-value reflects low noise plus large sample size, not necessarily a bigger fold change than a neighboring gene with log2FC=+0.4 and p=0.001. Meanwhile a GWAS hit for the same phenotype reports OR=1.12 (95% CI 1.09–1.15) — a real, genome-wide-significant, replicated association, but one variant explaining only a sliver of disease risk. A student who reports both the log2FC/CI and the p-value for their strongest hit, and explicitly states what magnitude of change that represents, is doing what the field actually expects; reporting p-value alone leaves the reader unable to judge whether the result matters.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on effect size because 'is it significant' and 'does it matter' are different questions, and conflating them is the most common overclaim in a project's abstract. A student who can convert their own log2FC into a fold-change number, name whether their p-value and their effect size point the same direction, and explain — without prompting — why a genome-wide significant OR of 1.1 would not let you predict an individual's disease status, has shown they understand what their numbers are actually claiming, not just that software produced them.

questions.prompt: A gene has log2 fold change = -2 between treated and control. What does this mean?

options.text: The gene's expression decreased by 2%
The gene's expression is 4× lower in treated versus control
The gene's expression is 2× lower in treated versus control
The result is not statistically significant

explanations.a: log2FC is not a percentage; a value of -2 corresponds to a specific fold-change ratio, not a 2% change.
explanations.b: Correct — log2FC of -2 means 2^2 = 4-fold lower expression in the treated condition; log2FC of -1 would be 2× lower, and -2 doubles that exponent to 4×.
explanations.c: 2× lower corresponds to log2FC=-1, not -2; the relationship is exponential, not linear.
explanations.d: log2FC describes magnitude and direction of change, not statistical significance, which comes from a separate p-value.

questions.prompt: A variant has an odds ratio (OR) of 2.0 for a disease. What does this indicate?

options.text: Carriers of the variant are twice as likely to eventually get the disease with certainty
Carriers have roughly double the odds of the disease compared to non-carriers
The variant causes the disease in 100% of carriers
The p-value for this variant is 2.0

explanations.a: OR describes a ratio of odds, not a certainty or guaranteed outcome for any individual.
explanations.b: Correct — an odds ratio of 2.0 means the odds of disease among carriers are about twice the odds among non-carriers; it says nothing about absolute certainty.
explanations.c: An OR of 2.0 is far from implying full penetrance; most disease-associated variants have much smaller effects and incomplete penetrance.
explanations.d: OR is an effect-size measure, entirely separate from a p-value, which measures statistical evidence against the null.

questions.prompt: Why does reporting a 95% confidence interval alongside an effect size give more information than a p-value alone?

options.text: A CI always excludes the null value, so it is easier to interpret than a p-value
A CI shows both a plausible range for the true effect and its precision, not just a pass/fail cutoff
A CI replaces the need for a sample size
A CI and a p-value always convey identical information, just in different units

explanations.a: CIs can and often do include the null value (e.g., an OR CI spanning 0.95-1.3, including 1); that is not guaranteed.
explanations.b: Correct — a CI communicates the estimated effect's magnitude and how precisely it was measured, whereas a p-value alone only signals whether a threshold was crossed.
explanations.c: Sample size still matters for computing the CI itself; a CI does not eliminate the need to know or report n.
explanations.d: A CI and p-value are related but not equivalent: a CI conveys magnitude and precision, which a bare p-value discards.

questions.prompt: GWAS studies routinely find replicated odds ratios around 1.05-1.2 for common variants. Why does this NOT support a headline like 'scientists find the gene for height/disease X'?

options.text: Because such small odds ratios are usually statistical flukes that fail to replicate
Because even though the association is real and replicated, an OR this small barely shifts an individual's risk and typically reflects one of hundreds of contributing variants
Because odds ratios below 2.0 are not statistically significant by convention
Because GWAS studies never use large enough sample sizes to trust any result

explanations.a: The lesson specifically notes these associations are genuine and replicated across large independent cohorts, not flukes.
explanations.b: Correct — a real, replicated OR of 1.1 has strong statistical evidence behind it but very little individual predictive value, since it represents one small contributor among many variants plus environment.
explanations.c: Statistical significance is governed by the p-value and sample size, not by an arbitrary odds-ratio magnitude threshold.
explanations.d: GWAS consortia typically use very large sample sizes (hundreds of thousands), which is precisely what allows them to detect these small, real effects reliably.

questions.prompt: Match each effect-size metric to the type of comparison it is used for.

right.text: RNA-seq gene expression, treated vs. control
Genetic variant carrier status vs. binary disease outcome
Genetic variant vs. a continuous trait like height in linear regression
Standardized mean difference between two groups on a continuous measure

questions.explanation: log2 fold change quantifies relative expression change in RNA-seq. Odds ratios quantify association between a variant and a binary outcome like disease status. Beta coefficients from linear regression quantify the expected change in a continuous trait per allele copy. Cohen's d standardizes a mean difference between two groups by pooled standard deviation, usable with any continuous outcome.

lessons.label: Multiple Testing: Bonferroni, FDR, and Why Genomics Needs Them

sections.heading: The arithmetic that forces correction
sections.body: A single hypothesis test at α=0.05 accepts a 5% chance of a false positive when the null is true. Genomics rarely runs one test — an RNA-seq differential expression analysis tests every gene in the genome, roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, against the null of no change. If none of those genes actually changed, testing all 20,000 at α=0.05 would still be expected to flag about 1,000 of them as 'significant' by chance alone (20,000 × 0.05 = 1,000). That is the arithmetic that makes uncorrected p-values worthless at genome scale: a list of a few hundred 'significant' genes could be almost entirely noise unless the significance threshold accounts for how many tests were run.

sections.heading: Bonferroni versus Benjamini-Hochberg FDR
sections.body: The Bonferroni correction is the blunt fix: divide α by the number of tests m, so with m=20,000 the per-test threshold becomes 0.05/20,000 = 2.5×10⁻⁶. This controls the family-wise error rate (the chance of even one false positive across all tests) but is highly conservative, especially when tests are correlated — as gene expression tests usually are, since genes in the same pathway rise and fall together, meaning the tests are not independent and Bonferroni over-punishes them. Yoav Benjamini and Yosef Hochberg's 1995 paper introduced the false discovery rate (FDR) instead: rank all p-values, then find the largest one satisfying p(i) ≤ (i/m)×α, and call everything at or below that rank significant. Critically, a Benjamini-Hochberg q-value of 0.05 promises something different from a p-value: among all genes called significant at q<0.05, about 5% are expected to be false positives — not 5% of all 20,000 tests, only 5% of the genes on your final hit list.

sections.heading: Permutation thresholds and the GWAS instance
sections.body: When the correlation structure between tests is complex, an empirical alternative is permutation testing: shuffle the sample labels thousands of times, rerun the whole analysis on each shuffled dataset, and use the distribution of best 'hits' under permutation to set a threshold that accounts for the real correlation structure directly, rather than assuming independence. Genome-wide association studies apply the same correction logic at a different scale: with roughly one million independent tests across the genome (accounting for linkage disequilibrium between nearby SNPs), the field converged on a genome-wide significance threshold of 5×10⁻⁸ — essentially a Bonferroni correction for ~1 million effective independent tests (0.05/1,000,000 = 5×10⁻⁸). Risch and Merikangas first proposed this order of magnitude in 1996, and Dudbridge and Gusnanto's 2008 analysis independently confirmed it, cementing 5×10⁻⁸ as the field-wide reporting standard.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs differential expression on 18,000 genes and finds 400 with raw p<0.05. Without correction, they'd expect roughly 18,000×0.05=900 false positives from chance alone if nothing truly changed — so 400 hits below that noise floor is actually suspicious, not exciting. Applying Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction, only 22 genes survive at q<0.05. The student reports those 22 as the finding, explicitly noting: 'we expect about 1 of these 22 (5%) to be a false discovery, not 5% of the original 18,000 tests' — the correct reading of q<0.05, and evidence to a judge that the raw p<0.05 list was never a defensible result on its own.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about multiple-testing correction because an uncorrected genome-scale hit list is close to meaningless, and whether a student corrected for it — and can explain which correction and why — is a fast, reliable signal of statistical maturity. The trap question is always some version of 'what does q<0.05 promise you,' and the wrong answer ('5% of all genes tested are false') versus the right one ('5% of the genes I'm calling significant are expected to be false') is the exact line between a student who ran a script and one who understands what the script's output means.

questions.prompt: Testing 20,000 genes at uncorrected α=0.05, assuming none actually changed, how many would be expected to appear 'significant' by chance alone?

options.text: About 5
About 1,000
About 20,000
Zero, because chance cannot produce significance

explanations.a: 5 would be far too low; the expected count scales with both the number of tests and α, giving 20,000 × 0.05.
explanations.b: Correct — 20,000 tests × 0.05 false-positive rate = about 1,000 expected false positives from noise alone, which is why uncorrected genome-scale p-values are unusable.
explanations.c: All 20,000 appearing significant would require every test to be a false positive, which is not what a 5% error rate implies.
explanations.d: By definition, a 5% significance threshold guarantees some fraction of true nulls will cross it by chance; that is exactly the problem multiple-testing correction addresses.

questions.prompt: Why is the Bonferroni correction considered overly conservative for correlated tests, like genes in the same biological pathway?

options.text: Bonferroni requires a larger sample size than other methods
Bonferroni assumes tests are independent, so with correlated tests it treats effectively redundant information as if it were m separate independent tests, over-shrinking the threshold
Bonferroni only works for exactly two groups being compared
Bonferroni ignores p-values entirely and uses only effect sizes

explanations.a: Bonferroni's conservatism is about how it divides α by the test count, not about sample size requirements.
explanations.b: Correct — dividing α by the raw number of tests (m) assumes each test contributes independent information; when tests are correlated (as with co-regulated genes), the effective number of independent tests is lower, making Bonferroni's threshold stricter than necessary.
explanations.c: Bonferroni correction applies to any number of tests, not specifically two-group comparisons.
explanations.d: Bonferroni is applied directly to p-values (dividing the significance threshold by m); it does not use effect sizes.

questions.prompt: A gene list is filtered to q<0.05 using Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. What does this q-value threshold actually promise?

options.text: 5% of all genes originally tested are false positives
5% of the genes on this final significant list are expected to be false positives
Every gene on the list has a 95% chance of being biologically important
The family-wise error rate across all tests is exactly 5%

explanations.a: This confuses the denominator — FDR control is about the proportion of false positives within the significant list, not within the entire original test set.
explanations.b: Correct — Benjamini-Hochberg's FDR at q<0.05 promises that, among genes called significant, about 5% are expected to be false discoveries; it says nothing about the untested majority.
explanations.c: A q-value bounds an expected false-discovery proportion; it says nothing about biological importance or individual gene certainty.
explanations.d: Family-wise error rate is what Bonferroni controls; FDR control is a different, generally less conservative, guarantee about the composition of the hit list.

questions.prompt: The GWAS genome-wide significance threshold of 5×10⁻⁸ is best understood as:

options.text: An arbitrary round number chosen for convenience with no relation to test count
Roughly a Bonferroni correction of α=0.05 across about one million effectively independent tests
The false discovery rate threshold used exclusively in GWAS, unrelated to Bonferroni logic
A threshold derived from Cohen's d effect-size conventions

explanations.a: The threshold has a specific derivation from correcting for the number of effectively independent tests across the genome, not an arbitrary choice.
explanations.b: Correct — 0.05 divided by roughly one million effective independent tests (accounting for linkage disequilibrium among SNPs) gives 5×10⁻⁸, the same Bonferroni logic applied at genome-wide scale.
explanations.c: It is derived using Bonferroni-style correction, not the Benjamini-Hochberg FDR procedure.
explanations.d: Cohen's d is an effect-size metric for continuous outcomes and has no role in deriving this significance threshold.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the Benjamini-Hochberg FDR procedure as applied to a list of gene p-values.

items.text: Run the statistical test on every gene, producing one raw p-value per gene
Rank all p-values from smallest to largest, index i = 1 to m
Find the largest rank i where p(i) ≤ (i/m) × α
Call every gene at or below that rank significant at the chosen FDR level

questions.explanation: Benjamini-Hochberg first requires a p-value for every test, then ranks them, then locates the largest rank still satisfying the p(i) ≤ (i/m)×α inequality, and finally declares everything at or below that rank significant — this ordering is what makes the correction adapt to how many true signals appear to be present, rather than applying one flat cutoff to all tests.

lessons.label: Sample Size, Power, and Replication

sections.heading: Power and the four-way trade-off
sections.body: Statistical power is the probability a study detects a true effect, given that one actually exists — conventionally, researchers target 80% power, meaning an 80% chance of catching a real effect and a 20% chance of missing it (a false negative, or Type II error). Power depends on four quantities pulling against each other: the true effect size (bigger effects are easier to detect), the sample size n (more data shrinks noise), the variance in the measurement (noisier assays need more samples to see through the noise), and the significance threshold α (a stricter α, as multiple testing forces in genomics, makes detection harder unless n grows to compensate). A student who says 'my n=3 experiment could only reliably detect large effects, not subtle ones' is stating a real, checkable power fact, not hedging.

sections.heading: Why n=3 is the RNA-seq default, and its real ceiling
sections.body: RNA-seq experiments conventionally use n=3 biological replicates per condition — a convention driven by cost (sequencing runs are expensive) rather than statistical ideal. Tools like DESeq2 and edgeR were specifically engineered with variance-shrinkage methods to extract usable statistics from such small n, borrowing information across genes to stabilize variance estimates that would otherwise be unreliable with only 3 samples. But n=3 has a hard ceiling: it can reliably detect only fairly large, consistent fold changes, and it cannot characterize the population variability well — Soneson and Delorenzi's 2013 benchmark of RNA-seq differential expression methods found that below n=3-5 replicates, power to detect moderate fold changes drops sharply, and subtler true effects are essentially invisible.

sections.heading: Consortium scale and true replication
sections.body: Genome-wide association studies took the opposite path: because individual variant effects are small (odds ratios of 1.05-1.2, as covered in the effect-size lesson), detecting them at genome-wide significance (5×10⁻⁸) requires enormous sample sizes. Early GWAS in the mid-2000s used thousands of subjects; consortium efforts like the UK Biobank now include over 500,000 participants, because only that scale gives enough power to detect small, real effects reliably. The strongest evidence any genomics project can offer is independent replication — rerunning the analysis on a separate cohort collected independently, ideally by a different group, and confirming the same result. This differs fundamentally from a 'validation set' carved out of the same original dataset (a train/test split): a validation set only checks that a model or finding is not overfit to quirks of one dataset's noise, but it cannot catch a batch effect, a shared technical artifact, or a systematic confound present in the whole original collection — only a genuinely independent cohort, collected separately, can do that.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs an RNA-seq experiment with n=3 per condition and finds no significant genes at FDR-corrected q<0.05. Rather than concluding 'nothing changed,' a power-literate write-up says: 'with n=3 and the observed variance in our replicates, a power calculation shows we had roughly 80% power to detect only log2FC ≥ 1.5 (a 2.8-fold change) — smaller true effects were likely undetectable at this sample size.' If the student then splits their existing 3 replicates into a 2-vs-1 'training' and 'validation' comparison and calls that replication, a judge should flag it: that is still one batch, one extraction run, one set of reagents — real replication requires an independently collected cohort, not a re-slice of the same samples.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe sample size and power because 'we found nothing significant' and 'we had no power to find anything' are completely different scientific claims, and only one of them a small student project can usually make honestly. The strongest answer names the specific trade-off — effect size, n, variance, α — and states concretely what magnitude of effect the study's own n could plausibly have detected. The second red flag judges watch for is the same-data validation set being presented as replication; naming why an independent cohort is required, and what confound a within-dataset split cannot catch, is the mark of a student who understands evidence rather than just workflow.

questions.prompt: Statistical power is best defined as:

options.text: The probability that a significant result is a true positive
The probability of detecting a true effect, given that one actually exists
The probability the null hypothesis is false
The sample size required to reach p<0.05

explanations.a: That description matches positive predictive value, a related but distinct concept that also depends on the prior probability of a true effect.
explanations.b: Correct — power is specifically the probability of correctly detecting a real effect when one exists; conventionally researchers target 80% power.
explanations.c: Power is a property of a study design given a true effect size, not a statement about whether the null hypothesis itself is false.
explanations.d: Power is a probability, not a specific sample-size number; the required sample size to achieve a target power is a related but separate calculation.

questions.prompt: Which of these increases statistical power, all else held equal?

options.text: Increasing the sample size n
Increasing the measurement variance
Making the significance threshold α stricter (smaller)
Decreasing the true effect size

explanations.a: Correct — more samples reduce sampling noise, making a true effect, if present, easier to distinguish from noise, which directly raises power.
explanations.b: More measurement variance makes it harder to distinguish signal from noise, which lowers power, not raises it.
explanations.c: A stricter α raises the bar for declaring significance, which — holding n and effect size fixed — reduces power rather than increasing it.
explanations.d: A smaller true effect is inherently harder to detect, which lowers power; effect size and power move together, not oppositely.

questions.prompt: Why do many RNA-seq experiments default to n=3 biological replicates per condition, and what is the resulting limitation?

options.text: n=3 is a regulatory requirement; it detects effects of any size equally well
n=3 is a cost-driven convention, with tools like DESeq2 using variance-shrinkage to make it usable, but it can reliably detect only fairly large, consistent fold changes
n=3 guarantees 80% power for any effect size
n=3 is only used for genome-wide association studies, not RNA-seq

explanations.a: There is no regulatory mandate for n=3, and it does not detect all effect sizes equally — it is specifically limited for subtle effects.
explanations.b: Correct — n=3 is chosen mainly because sequencing is expensive; specialized variance-shrinkage statistics make it workable, but power studies show it reliably catches only large, consistent fold changes, not subtle ones.
explanations.c: 80% power at n=3 depends heavily on effect size and variance; it is not guaranteed for all or even most genes.
explanations.d: n=3 is a convention specific to RNA-seq biological replicates; GWAS instead relies on very large consortium-scale sample sizes, the opposite strategy.

questions.prompt: A student splits their single RNA-seq dataset into a 'training' half and a 'validation' half and calls the matching results 'replication.' What is the flaw?

options.text: There is no flaw; a validation split is equivalent to independent replication
A within-dataset split cannot detect batch effects or systematic confounds shared across the whole original collection, unlike a truly independent cohort
Validation splits are only valid for GWAS, not RNA-seq
The split should use 90% training and 10% validation instead

explanations.a: A same-data split checks for overfitting to that dataset's specific noise, but cannot catch flaws shared by the entire dataset, so it is not equivalent to independent replication.
explanations.b: Correct — because both halves came from the same collection (same extraction batch, same reagents, same processing date), any systematic artifact present in the whole dataset would appear identically in both halves and look like agreement, when it is really a shared confound.
explanations.c: This limitation is general to any single dataset split by any field, not specific to GWAS versus RNA-seq.
explanations.d: Changing the split ratio does not address the underlying problem — both halves remain drawn from the same original, potentially confounded, collection.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the correct interpretation regarding power or replication.

left.text: n=3 RNA-seq study, no genes significant at FDR<0.05
Finding confirmed in a separately collected cohort by a different lab
Finding confirmed only in a held-out split of the same original dataset

right.text: Likely underpowered for subtle effects, not proof of no true difference
Scale needed to reliably detect small, real per-variant effects
True independent replication, the strongest evidence a project can offer
Checks for overfitting but cannot rule out a shared batch or technical confound

questions.explanation: A small-n null result is a power limitation, not proof of absence of effect. Consortium-scale GWAS sample sizes exist because per-variant effects are small and need large n for power. Replication in an independently collected cohort is the strongest form of confirmation. A same-dataset validation split only guards against overfitting, not shared systematic confounds across the whole collection.

lessons.label: Batch Effects, Confounding, and Controls

sections.heading: Genomics' signature failure mode
sections.body: A batch effect is systematic, non-biological variation introduced by when and how samples were processed — processing date, flow cell, sequencing lane, reagent lot, extraction kit, or even which technician ran the protocol. Genomic assays are exquisitely sensitive to these technical details because they measure tens of thousands of features at once from vanishingly small starting material, so tiny shifts in reagent chemistry or machine calibration ripple across the whole dataset. The danger is not that batch effects exist — they always do — but that they become confounded with the biological variable of interest: if all 'treated' samples were processed on Monday and all 'control' samples on Friday, any Monday-versus-Friday technical drift is now statistically indistinguishable from the treatment effect. In real datasets, batch is often the single largest source of variance, larger than the biology the experiment was designed to detect.

sections.heading: The only real fix: randomize and block at prep time
sections.body: Once batch is confounded with biology, no amount of downstream statistics can fully separate the two — the information is simply gone. The only genuine fix happens before the assay runs: randomize samples across batches (mix treated and control samples across processing days, flow cells, and technicians so batch is no longer correlated with condition) and use blocking, deliberately spreading each biological group evenly across every batch so any batch effect hits all groups equally and cancels out in the comparison. Leek and colleagues made this case forcefully in a widely cited 2010 Nature Reviews Genetics paper, arguing that batch effects are a pervasive, under-acknowledged threat to high-throughput biology and that experimental design, not post-hoc correction, is the primary defense.

sections.heading: After-the-fact correction and the control set
sections.body: When randomization at prep time was not done — often because the data already exists — statistical correction is damage control, not a cure. ComBat, from Johnson and colleagues' 2007 paper, uses an empirical Bayes model to adjust for a known batch label directly. Surrogate variable analysis (SVA), developed by Leek and colleagues, instead estimates hidden sources of unwanted variation directly from the data when the batch label itself is unknown or incomplete. Both assume the correction target is separable from biology, an assumption that breaks down if batch and biology are fully confounded rather than merely correlated. A well-designed experiment also carries a control set: a positive control (known to produce a signal, confirming the assay works), a negative control (known to produce no signal, catching contamination), a no-template control (nothing added, catching reagent contamination specifically), a spike-in (a known synthetic sequence added at a fixed amount, calibrating quantification), and both technical replicates (same sample, reprocessed, measuring assay noise) and biological replicates (different samples, same condition, measuring true biological variability) — each catching a different failure mode.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs RNA extraction on all 10 control-group mice on a Tuesday using kit lot A, then all 10 treated-group mice the following Monday using kit lot B, because that is when each cage finished its protocol. When the treated group shows 200 differentially expressed genes, a judge asks how they know this is not kit lot or extraction-day effect. The honest answer, if randomization was skipped, is 'we can't fully separate them' — condition is perfectly confounded with batch. The fixable version: process a mix of treated and control mice each day, alternating kit lots evenly across both groups (blocking), and include a spike-in control in every extraction so any run-to-run quantification drift is directly visible and correctable, rather than invisible and confounded.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe batch effects because they are genomics' most common silent killer of an otherwise well-designed study, and most student projects, run on a tight schedule with samples processed in convenient clumps, are vulnerable to exactly this confound. The strongest answer names the specific batch variable at risk in their own protocol (extraction day, reagent lot, sequencing lane), states whether they randomized or blocked against it, and — if they didn't — is honest that post-hoc tools like ComBat or SVA are damage control, not a substitute for a design that never confounded batch with biology in the first place.

questions.prompt: A student processes all control samples on Monday and all treated samples on Friday. What is the core statistical problem this creates?

options.text: Nothing — as long as the same protocol is used, the day of processing does not matter
Batch (processing day) becomes fully confounded with the biological variable (treatment), so technical drift and biological effect cannot be statistically separated
The sample size is too small to run a t-test
The p-value threshold needs to be corrected for multiple testing

explanations.a: Genomic assays are highly sensitive to processing-date effects (reagent degradation, calibration drift), so day of processing is rarely irrelevant.
explanations.b: Correct — when every control sample shares one batch and every treated sample shares a different batch, any difference between them could be biology, technical drift, or an inseparable mixture of both.
explanations.c: This scenario describes a confounding problem, not specifically a sample-size problem; the confound would remain even with a large n.
explanations.d: Multiple-testing correction addresses a different issue (many simultaneous tests), unrelated to confounding batch with condition.

questions.prompt: What is the only genuine fix for a batch effect that is fully confounded with the biological variable?

options.text: Applying ComBat after the fact to remove the batch signal
Randomizing and blocking sample processing across batches before the assay is run
Increasing the significance threshold to compensate
Running the analysis twice and averaging the results

explanations.a: ComBat can adjust for a known batch label, but if batch and biology are perfectly confounded, there is no statistical way to recover which part of the signal is which; it cannot fix a fully confounded design.
explanations.b: Correct — randomizing which samples go in which batch, and deliberately spreading (blocking) each biological group evenly across batches, is the only way to prevent batch from becoming inseparable from the variable of interest.
explanations.c: Changing the significance threshold does not address confounding; it only changes the bar for calling a (potentially confounded) result significant.
explanations.d: Running the same confounded analysis twice does not introduce new information that would separate batch from biology.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between ComBat and surrogate variable analysis (SVA) as batch-correction tools?

options.text: ComBat adjusts for a known, labeled batch variable; SVA estimates hidden sources of unwanted variation when the batch label is unknown or incomplete
ComBat only works on RNA-seq data, while SVA only works on GWAS data
SVA is a design-time randomization method, while ComBat is a post-hoc statistical method
They are two names for the exact same algorithm

explanations.a: Correct — ComBat (Johnson et al., 2007) uses an empirical Bayes model given a known batch label, while SVA (Leek and colleagues) estimates surrogate variables directly from the data's structure when batch is unknown or only partially recorded.
explanations.b: Both tools are general-purpose and have been applied across microarray, RNA-seq, and other high-throughput data types, not restricted to one assay.
explanations.c: Both ComBat and SVA are post-hoc, after-the-fact statistical corrections; neither is a design-time randomization method.
explanations.d: They use different statistical approaches (a known-label empirical Bayes model versus data-driven latent-variable estimation) and are not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: A no-template control (NTC) in a PCR-based assay is included specifically to catch:

options.text: Whether the biological sample itself produced a signal
Reagent or environmental contamination, since nothing but reagents was added to this reaction
Batch-to-batch variation in sequencing lane
Whether the treatment had a biological effect

explanations.a: A no-template control contains no sample at all, so it cannot address whether a real sample produced a signal — that is what positive/negative controls with actual samples address.
explanations.b: Correct — because nothing but reagents is added, any signal in an NTC reveals contamination in the reagents or environment, a failure mode distinct from what other controls catch.
explanations.c: Lane-level batch variation is better addressed by spike-ins or technical replicates distributed across lanes, not by a no-template control.
explanations.d: Biological effect is assessed by comparing real treated and control samples, not by a control containing no template material at all.

questions.prompt: Match each control type to the specific failure mode it is designed to catch.

right.text: Confirms the assay is capable of detecting a signal at all
Confirms the assay does not falsely detect signal when none should be present
A known synthetic sequence at fixed amount, calibrating quantification accuracy
Same sample reprocessed, measuring assay-level (not biological) noise

questions.explanation: A positive control verifies the assay can detect a real signal; a negative control verifies it does not manufacture false signal; a spike-in gives a known quantity to calibrate measurement accuracy; a technical replicate isolates assay noise from true biological variability, which is instead captured by biological replicates.

lessons.label: Reproducibility: Preregistration, Pipelines, and Reporting Standards

sections.heading: The garden of forking paths in genomic analysis
sections.body: John Ioannidis's widely cited 2005 PLoS Medicine paper 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' argued that, across biomedical research, flexible analysis choices combined with publication pressure make a large share of significant results unreliable — not through fraud, but through the accumulated effect of small, defensible-seeming decisions. Genomics has its own specific version of this problem, sometimes called the garden of forking paths: at multiple points, an analyst chooses between reasonable options — which normalization method (TPM, FPKM, or a more model-based approach), which filtering threshold for low-expressed genes, which covariates to include in the model (age, sex, batch, cell-type proportion) — and each choice can shift which genes end up significant. If those choices are made after peeking at preliminary results, and the analyst unconsciously favors the combination that produces the cleanest story, this is p-hacking even without any single dishonest step.

sections.heading: HARKing and why the fix is procedural, not moral
sections.body: HARKing — Hypothesizing After the Results are Known — is the related practice of discovering a pattern in the data, then writing the introduction and hypothesis as if that pattern had been predicted all along. Both p-hacking and HARKing are usually not conscious cheating; they are the natural consequence of a flexible pipeline plus the very human tendency to rationalize whatever result appears. The field's answer is procedural: preregistration, committing in writing to the hypothesis, primary outcome, normalization method, filtering threshold, and covariate set before looking at the results, converts hidden researcher-degrees-of-freedom into a fixed, checkable plan. A student project that documents its analysis choices before running the differential-expression pipeline is doing, at small scale, exactly what preregistration on platforms like the Open Science Framework does at journal scale.

sections.heading: Concrete practices a judge can check
sections.body: Beyond preregistration, three practices directly answer 'could someone else reproduce this?' First, reporting standards: the MIQE guidelines (Minimum Information for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments), published by Bustin and colleagues in Clinical Chemistry in 2009, specify exactly what must be reported about a qPCR experiment — primer sequences, efficiency, reference gene choice — so another lab can rerun it. Second, data deposition: raw and processed data placed in public repositories — GEO or SRA for sequencing data, dbGaP for controlled-access human genetic data — so the underlying evidence, not just the paper's summary, is available for reanalysis. Third, recording exact software versions, parameter settings, and random seeds used by any stochastic step (many clustering and machine-learning tools are seed-dependent), since 'we used DESeq2' without a version number or parameters is not enough information to rerun the same analysis and get the same numbers.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs three different low-expression filtering thresholds on their RNA-seq count matrix, gets 40, 65, and 22 significant genes respectively, and reports only the 65-gene result because it 'looked the most interesting' and matched their initial hypothesis about a target pathway. A judge asks why that threshold was chosen. The honest, reproducible version: the student pre-specifies one filtering threshold (say, keeping genes with at least 10 reads in at least 3 samples) before running any differential expression test, reports that single result regardless of outcome, deposits the raw counts in GEO, and records the exact DESeq2 version and the random seed used for any permutation step — so a second person running the identical pipeline on the identical deposited data gets the identical 40 (or 65, or 22) genes back.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'could someone else reproduce this?' because it is the fastest test of whether a result is a discovery or an artifact of a flexible pipeline explored until something looked good. The strongest defense a student can give is procedural, not rhetorical: naming the specific choice points in their own analysis (normalization, filtering threshold, covariates) and stating which were fixed before looking at results, plus concretely naming where their data and exact software versions are recorded. A student who cannot say which analysis choices were made before versus after seeing preliminary results has likely HARKed or p-hacked without realizing it — and a judge's job is to surface that gently but directly.

questions.prompt: Ioannidis's 2005 argument in 'Why Most Published Research Findings Are False' is best summarized as:

options.text: Most published findings are the result of deliberate scientific fraud
Flexible analysis choices combined with publication pressure can make a large share of significant results unreliable, even without fraud
Only genomics research suffers from reproducibility problems
p-values below 0.05 are always fabricated

explanations.a: Ioannidis's argument was explicitly not primarily about fraud, but about how flexible, defensible-seeming analysis choices accumulate into unreliable results.
explanations.b: Correct — the paper argued that researcher degrees of freedom plus incentives to publish significant results systematically inflate the rate of false positives across biomedical research, independent of any dishonesty.
explanations.c: The argument was made about biomedical research broadly, not specifically about genomics, though genomics has its own version of the same problem.
explanations.d: The argument concerns systematic bias in which results get published and how they were obtained, not a claim that p-values themselves are fabricated.

questions.prompt: A researcher discovers an unexpected pattern in their genomic data, then writes their paper's introduction as if that pattern had been the original hypothesis all along. This practice is called:

options.text: Preregistration
HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known)
Multiple testing correction
Surrogate variable analysis

explanations.a: Preregistration is the opposite practice — committing to a hypothesis and analysis plan before seeing the results.
explanations.b: Correct — HARKing is presenting a post-hoc discovery as if it had been predicted in advance, which hides how many other patterns could have been 'found' and reported instead.
explanations.c: Multiple testing correction is a statistical adjustment for running many tests, unrelated to how a hypothesis is presented in a write-up.
explanations.d: Surrogate variable analysis is a batch-effect correction technique, unrelated to how a hypothesis is framed in a paper's introduction.
