questions.prompt: Why does preregistration specifically address the 'garden of forking paths' problem in genomic analysis?

options.text: It requires using only one specific software package for all analyses

It commits the analyst in writing, before seeing results, to specific choices like normalization method, filtering threshold, and covariate set — closing off the flexibility that lets a cleaner-looking result get selected after the fact
It guarantees the hypothesis will be statistically significant
It replaces the need for a control set in the experiment

explanations.a: Preregistration is about locking in analysis decisions in advance, not about mandating any particular software tool.
explanations.b: Correct — because the garden of forking paths arises from choosing among multiple defensible analysis options after seeing preliminary results, fixing those choices beforehand removes the opportunity to (even unconsciously) select the most favorable path.
explanations.c: Preregistration says nothing about whether a result will be significant; it only fixes how the analysis will be conducted regardless of outcome.
explanations.d: Preregistration and a control set (positive, negative, spike-in, etc.) address different problems — analysis-choice flexibility versus assay validity — and neither substitutes for the other.

questions.prompt: The MIQE guidelines (Bustin et al., 2009) specifically standardize reporting for which type of experiment?

options.text: Quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) experiments
Genome-wide association studies
Any experiment using a p-value
Field-collected ecological samples only

explanations.a: Correct — MIQE (Minimum Information for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments) specifies exactly what must be reported for qPCR, including primer sequences, amplification efficiency, and reference gene choice, so other labs can rerun the assay.
explanations.b: GWAS reporting has its own conventions (like the genome-wide significance threshold), but MIQE specifically targets qPCR experiments, not GWAS.
explanations.c: MIQE is specific to qPCR methodology and reporting, not a general standard for every experiment that happens to report a p-value.
explanations.d: MIQE is a molecular biology reporting standard for qPCR, unrelated to ecological field sampling.

questions.prompt: Match each reproducibility practice to what it specifically provides.

left.text: Depositing raw sequencing data in GEO or SRA
Recording exact software version and random seed
Following MIQE guidelines for a qPCR experiment
Preregistering the analysis plan before running it

right.text: Makes the underlying evidence, not just the paper's summary, available for independent reanalysis
Ensures a stochastic pipeline produces the identical result when rerun by someone else
Ensures another lab has enough methodological detail to rerun the specific assay
Closes off the garden of forking paths by fixing analysis choices before seeing results

questions.explanation: Data deposition preserves the raw evidence for independent reanalysis. Recording software versions and random seeds makes a stochastic pipeline's output exactly reproducible. MIQE compliance gives another lab the methodological detail to rerun a qPCR assay. Preregistration fixes analysis choices in advance, preventing the garden of forking paths from steering the result toward the cleanest-looking story.

lessons.label: From Mendel to the Double Helix

sections.heading: A monk's paper nobody read for 34 years
sections.body: Gregor Mendel published his pea-plant results in 1866 in the Proceedings of the Natural History Society of Brno, showing that traits segregate as discrete units rather than blending. Across his monohybrid pea crosses — seed shape, flower color, pod color, and others — Mendel consistently observed the dominant and recessive phenotypes reappear in the second generation at roughly a 3:1 ratio, the concrete number underlying his claim that inherited factors segregate as discrete, countable units rather than blending together. It was cited almost nowhere for decades. In 1900, three botanists working independently — Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak — arrived at the same segregation ratios in their own breeding work, went to the literature to check priority, and found Mendel had already done it. This 'rediscovery' is why genetics is often dated to 1900, not 1866: the ideas were correct on arrival but institutionally invisible until three later researchers needed them and made them field-defining.

sections.heading: Morgan's fly room puts genes on chromosomes
sections.body: Mendel's units of inheritance had no known physical location. Thomas Hunt Morgan's lab at Columbia, working with Drosophila melanogaster from 1910, found a white-eyed male fly among red-eyed wild types and bred it to trace how the trait sex-linked. Morgan's group — including Alfred Sturtevant, who as an undergraduate built the first genetic linkage map in 1913 — showed genes sit at fixed positions on chromosomes and that recombination frequency measures physical distance between them, establishing the chromosomal theory of inheritance.

sections.heading: Finding the molecule, then its shape
sections.body: Which molecule carried heredity was unresolved into the 1940s. Frederick Griffith's 1928 pneumococcus experiments showed a 'transforming principle' could convert harmless bacteria into virulent ones. Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty isolated that principle in 1944 and identified it as DNA, not protein — a result many geneticists initially doubted. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase settled it in 1952 with radioactively labeled phage: blending infected bacteria in a kitchen blender showed only DNA, not the protein coat, entered the cell to direct new virus production. Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling then produced Photo 51, the sharp X-ray diffraction image of DNA's helical structure, in 1952. James Watson and Francis Crick published DNA's double-helix model in Nature in April 1953, closing with the now-famous line noting the structure immediately suggested a copying mechanism for genetic material. How Franklin's unpublished diffraction data and a related MRC report reached Watson and Crick — via Maurice Wilkins and a Medical Research Council review — without her direct knowledge remains a documented, still-debated point about credit in the discovery.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to explain why 1953 gets the headline instead of 1866. The chain to walk a judge through: Mendel (1866) found the pattern but had no mechanism and no audience; de Vries, Correns, and Tschermak (1900) independently rediscovered the same ratios, giving Mendel posthumous priority; Morgan's flies (from 1910) located genes on physical chromosomes; Griffith (1928), then Avery-MacLeod-McCarty (1944), then Hershey-Chase (1952) identified DNA, not protein, as the carrier; Franklin's Photo 51 and Watson-Crick (1953) revealed its structure. Each step answered a question the previous step couldn't: what pattern, where, made of what, shaped how.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why did it take from 1866 to 1953?' is testing whether a student sees discovery as a chain of dependent questions rather than one eureka moment. A strong answer names that Mendel's pattern was necessary but not sufficient — you also needed a physical location (Morgan), a candidate molecule (Avery-MacLeod-McCarty), proof of that molecule's role (Hershey-Chase), and its structure (Franklin, Watson-Crick) before the mechanism of heredity was actually understood. It also signals maturity to acknowledge the Franklin credit dispute honestly rather than either erasing her contribution or overstating what is documented.

questions.prompt: Why is 1900, not 1866, often cited as the start of modern genetics?

options.text: Mendel's 1866 paper was scientifically wrong and had to be corrected
Mendel's 1866 results went largely unnoticed until de Vries, Correns, and Tschermak independently found the same patterns in 1900
DNA was not discovered as the hereditary molecule until 1900
Morgan's chromosome work in 1900 replaced Mendel's model entirely

explanations.a: Mendel's segregation ratios were correct; the problem was obscurity, not error.
explanations.b: Correct — three botanists independently reached Mendel's results in 1900 and found his paper already established the priority, triggering the field's 'rediscovery.'
explanations.c: DNA's role as the hereditary molecule was not established until Avery-MacLeod-McCarty (1944) and Hershey-Chase (1952), decades after 1900.
explanations.d: Morgan's fly-room work began around 1910 and built on Mendel's model rather than replacing it.

questions.prompt: What did the Hershey-Chase blender experiment (1952) demonstrate that Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty's 1944 work had not yet settled for many skeptics?

options.text: That chromosomes carry genes
That DNA, not protein, is the genetic material that enters a cell to direct new virus production
That DNA has a double-helix structure
That bacteria can transform from harmless to virulent

explanations.a: That was Morgan's fly-room contribution, decades earlier.
explanations.b: Correct — using radioactive labels to track phage protein versus DNA, Hershey and Chase showed only DNA entered the bacterial cell, convincing remaining skeptics that DNA carried heredity.
explanations.c: The double-helix structure came from Franklin's Photo 51 and the 1953 Watson-Crick model, a separate finding.
explanations.d: Bacterial transformation was Griffith's 1928 finding, which Avery-MacLeod-McCarty later traced to DNA.

questions.prompt: Put these milestones in chronological order.

items.text: Griffith's transforming-principle experiment
De Vries, Correns, and Tschermak rediscover Mendel's ratios
Hershey-Chase blender experiment
Watson and Crick's Nature paper on the double helix

questions.explanation: Mendel's ratios were rediscovered in 1900, Griffith's transformation experiment followed in 1928, Hershey and Chase confirmed DNA as the genetic material in 1952, and Watson and Crick published the double-helix structure in 1953.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher(s) to their contribution.

right.text: Located genes on chromosomes using Drosophila
Identified DNA as Griffith's transforming principle (1944)
Produced Photo 51, the key X-ray diffraction image of DNA

questions.explanation: Morgan's fly-room work established the chromosomal theory of inheritance; Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty identified DNA as the hereditary molecule in 1944; Franklin and Gosling's Photo 51 provided the diffraction data central to solving DNA's structure.

lessons.label: Cracking the Code and Building the Toolkit

sections.heading: Poly-U and the first codon
sections.body: Knowing DNA's structure did not reveal how its sequence specified proteins. In 1961, Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei at the NIH built a cell-free system from ruptured E. coli, fed it a synthetic RNA made of nothing but uracil (poly-U), and got a protein chain made entirely of phenylalanine. That meant the codon UUU coded for phenylalanine — the first word of the genetic code broken, announced at an international conference in Moscow that August. It took another five years, and contributions from Har Gobind Khorana's lab (which synthesized RNA polymers with known repeating sequences to pin down additional codons) and Robert Holley's structural work on transfer RNA, before the full 64-codon table was complete by 1966, including the three stop codons.

sections.heading: The lac operon: genes that switch themselves on and off
sections.body: That same year, François Jacob, working with Sydney Brenner and Matthew Meselson, proposed the messenger RNA concept — a short-lived RNA copy of a gene that carries its code from DNA to the ribosome for translation — giving the codon table a physical courier and linking the code itself to the machinery that reads it. In the same period, Jacob and Jacques Monod at the Pasteur Institute were asking a different question: why do E. coli only make lactose-digesting enzymes when lactose is present? Their 1961 paper described the lac operon — a cluster of structural genes controlled by a single operator site, itself controlled by a repressor protein that unbinds when lactose (specifically its metabolite allolactose) is present. This was the first clear model of gene regulation: genes are not simply 'on,' they are switched by regulatory proteins responding to the cell's environment. Jacob and Monod shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (with André Lwoff) for this work, which became the founding template for every later account of transcriptional control.

sections.heading: Recombinant DNA and the pause the field gave itself
sections.body: By 1972, Paul Berg's lab had combined DNA from SV40 virus with DNA from a bacteriophage, creating the first recombinant DNA molecule and demonstrating that genes from different organisms could be spliced together. The power of the technique — and uncertainty about the biohazard risk of engineered organisms — led leading molecular biologists to call a voluntary moratorium on certain experiments, formalized at the Asilomar Conference on Recombinant DNA in February 1975 in Pacific Grove, California. Attendees, including Berg, drafted tiered containment guidelines (physical and biological containment scaled to a proposed experiment's risk) before resuming the work themselves. Asilomar remains the reference point cited whenever genomics faces a new 'should we do this before we know if we should' moment, from gene drives to germline editing.

lessons.workedExample: A student building a timeline poster for 'how we learned to read and write DNA' should sequence it as: Nirenberg and Matthaei's 1961 poly-U experiment cracks the first codon (UUU = phenylalanine); Khorana's synthetic polymers and Holley's tRNA work complete the full codon table by 1966; Jacob and Monod's 1961 lac operon paper (published the same year as poly-U, a different question — regulation, not the code itself) shows genes can be switched on and off; Berg's 1972 recombinant DNA experiment shows genes can be moved between organisms; the 1975 Asilomar Conference shows scientists pausing to write their own safety rules before scaling that power up. The throughline: reading the code, understanding its regulation, and gaining the power to rewrite it all happened within about a 15-year span.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes Asilomar specifically because it is the field's own answer to 'who decides when a technique is too powerful to use without rules?' — a question every project involving CRISPR, gene drives, or synthetic biology reruns in miniature. A student who can explain that Asilomar was a voluntary, field-initiated pause resulting in tiered containment guidelines (not a government shutdown, and not permanent) shows they understand self-regulation as a real, historically precedented option — not just an abstract ethics platitude tacked onto a discussion section.

questions.prompt: What did Nirenberg and Matthaei's 1961 poly-U experiment establish?

options.text: That the codon UUU codes for the amino acid phenylalanine
That DNA is double-stranded
That the lac operon is regulated by a repressor protein
That recombinant DNA could combine genes from two organisms

explanations.a: Correct — feeding synthetic poly-U RNA into a cell-free system produced a protein made entirely of phenylalanine, cracking the first codon.
explanations.b: DNA's double-stranded helical structure was established by Watson and Crick in 1953, a decade earlier.
explanations.c: The lac operon repressor model came from Jacob and Monod's 1961 paper, a separate line of work on gene regulation rather than the genetic code itself.
explanations.d: Recombinant DNA came from Paul Berg's lab in 1972, over a decade after the poly-U experiment.

questions.prompt: In Jacob and Monod's lac operon model, what causes the structural genes to be transcribed?

options.text: A repressor protein permanently bound to the operator
The absence of any regulatory protein
Lactose's metabolite causing the repressor to unbind from the operator
A separate operon activating the lac genes directly

explanations.a: A repressor permanently bound would keep the genes off, the opposite of what triggers transcription.
explanations.b: The lac operon has an active regulatory system, not an absence of regulation, controlling when genes transcribe.
explanations.c: Correct — when lactose (via its metabolite allolactose) is present, it binds the repressor, causing it to release the operator so the structural genes can be transcribed.
explanations.d: The lac operon regulates itself through its own repressor-operator system, not through a separate operon.

questions.prompt: What was the outcome of the 1975 Asilomar Conference on Recombinant DNA?

options.text: A permanent government ban on all recombinant DNA research
Voluntary, tiered containment guidelines drafted by scientists themselves, after which the moratorium was lifted
Confirmation that recombinant DNA was safe and no guidelines were needed
The first successful use of recombinant DNA in a human patient

explanations.a: The conference produced guidelines, not a permanent ban, and was organized by scientists, not by government mandate.
explanations.b: Correct — attendees including Paul Berg drafted containment guidelines scaled to experimental risk, after which research resumed under those self-imposed rules.
explanations.c: The conference happened precisely because risk was uncertain; it did not conclude the technique was simply safe.
explanations.d: Asilomar addressed research guidelines, not a clinical application; it followed Berg's 1972 lab demonstration of recombinant DNA, not a patient treatment.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: Nirenberg and Matthaei's poly-U experiment
Full genetic code table completed
Berg's recombinant DNA experiment
Asilomar Conference

questions.explanation: The poly-U experiment (1961) cracked the first codon; the full code was completed by 1966 via Khorana and Holley's work; Berg created recombinant DNA in 1972; the Asilomar Conference followed in 1975 to set guidelines for that new power.

lessons.label: The Human Genome Project and the Race with Celera

sections.heading: Two strategies for the same genome
sections.body: The publicly funded Human Genome Project (HGP), launched in 1990 and led by NIH and DOE centers internationally, used hierarchical clone-by-clone sequencing: break the genome into large, mapped BAC clones with known chromosomal positions first, then sequence each clone and assemble with the map as scaffold — slow but reliable for repetitive regions. In 1998, Craig Venter founded the private company Celera Genomics and announced it would sequence the genome faster using whole-genome shotgun sequencing: shred the entire genome into small fragments, sequence all of them, and let computer algorithms reassemble the sequence from overlaps, without a pre-built map. The announcement effectively forced a race, since the public project's funding case rested partly on getting there first with open data.

sections.heading: The Bermuda Principles and the finish
sections.body: In February 1996, HGP leaders meeting in Bermuda adopted the Bermuda Principles, requiring that any sequence assembly over 1 kb be released to public databases within 24 hours of generation — a norm that made data siphoning into a private product much harder and became the template for rapid pre-publication data release across genomics. The rivalry ended not with a winner but with a negotiated tie: a joint White House announcement in June 2000 with President Clinton, Francis Collins (HGP), and Venter (Celera) declaring a working draft complete. The competing papers followed in February 2001 — the public consortium in Nature, Celera in Science — each estimating roughly 30,000-40,000 human genes, a dramatic drop from pre-project estimates that had run as high as 100,000, since the completed sequence showed far less protein-coding content than expected. The gene count kept falling through the 2000s toward the now-accepted figure near 20,000.

sections.heading: 'Complete' in 2003 still left 8% unfinished
sections.body: The HGP declared completion in April 2003, two years ahead of its original schedule and coinciding with the 50th anniversary of Watson and Crick's paper. But that 2003 reference genome still had gaps — roughly 8% of the sequence, concentrated in repetitive, hard-to-assemble regions like centromeres and the short arms of acrocentric chromosomes, remained unresolved. Closing that gap took until 2022, when the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) Consortium published the first truly gapless human genome sequence, CHM13, using long-read sequencing technology unavailable in 2003. Whether the public-versus-private race accelerated genomic science (by pulling the timeline forward years and pressuring open data norms) or distorted it (by rewarding a rushed 'draft' announcement and years of a contested, incomplete reference) is still argued by historians of science.

lessons.workedExample: A student comparing the two sequencing strategies for a poster should frame it as a tradeoff: clone-by-clone (HGP) sequences known-location fragments first, so assembly errors are easier to catch but the process is slower and needs an existing physical map; whole-genome shotgun (Celera) sequences everything at once and relies on computational overlap-matching, which is faster but struggles more with repetitive sequence, since short overlapping reads from different repeat copies can be assembled in the wrong place. Both released a working-draft genome by 2000, both undercounted human genes relative to pre-project guesses of up to 100,000, and both left the same ~8% of repetitive genome unresolved until T2T-CHM13 closed it in 2022 using long-read technology neither strategy had access to in 2000.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about the HGP-Celera race is testing whether a student understands that a scientific 'finish line' is often a negotiated, partial claim rather than a clean endpoint — the 2000 announcement was a working draft, the 2003 'completion' still had an 8% gap, and true completion waited until 2022. It's also a clean test of whether a student can hold two competing methodologies (clone-by-clone versus whole-genome shotgun) in mind and explain their real tradeoff, rather than just naming 'public versus private' as if that alone explained the different results.

questions.prompt: Match each sequencing effort to its strategy.

right.text: Hierarchical clone-by-clone sequencing using a pre-built physical map
Whole-genome shotgun sequencing reassembled computationally from overlaps

questions.explanation: The public consortium sequenced mapped BAC clones in known chromosomal order; Celera, led by Craig Venter, shredded the whole genome into fragments and reassembled it computationally without a prior map.

questions.prompt: What did the Bermuda Principles (1996) require?

options.text: All human genome sequence data over 1 kb be released to public databases within 24 hours of generation
Celera and the public consortium merge into a single organization
A moratorium on all further genome sequencing until ethics review
Gene-count estimates be independently verified before publication

explanations.a: Correct — adopted at a 1996 Bermuda meeting, the principles mandated rapid public release of sequence data, shaping open-data norms across genomics.
explanations.b: The Bermuda Principles were a data-release policy, not a merger; the two efforts remained separate and competing.
explanations.c: The principles concerned data-sharing speed, not a research moratorium (that describes Asilomar in a different context).
explanations.d: The principles governed release speed and openness of raw sequence data, not verification of downstream gene-count estimates.

questions.prompt: How did the 2001 published gene-count estimates compare to pre-project predictions?

options.text: They confirmed the predicted ~100,000 genes
They came in far lower, around 30,000-40,000, later revised down further toward ~20,000
They were higher than any prior estimate
No gene count was reported in either 2001 paper

explanations.a: Pre-project estimates had run as high as 100,000; the actual count was far lower, one of the project's most surprising findings.
explanations.b: Correct — the 2001 Nature and Science papers estimated roughly 30,000-40,000 genes, and later refinement brought the figure down closer to 20,000.
explanations.c: The trend went the opposite direction — the completed sequence showed less protein-coding content than expected, not more.
explanations.d: Both the public consortium's Nature paper and Celera's Science paper reported gene-count estimates as a headline finding.

questions.prompt: What was still missing from the human genome reference after the 2003 'completion' announcement?

options.text: Roughly 8% of the sequence, mainly repetitive regions like centromeres, unresolved until T2T-CHM13 in 2022
The entire Y chromosome, unresolved to this day
All protein-coding genes, identified only after 2010
Nothing — the 2003 sequence was fully gapless

explanations.a: Correct — about 8% of the genome, concentrated in repetitive regions such as centromeres and acrocentric short arms, remained unresolved until the T2T Consortium's gapless CHM13 sequence in 2022.
explanations.b: The Y chromosome was among the harder regions but T2T-CHM13's 2022 assembly resolved essentially all chromosomes, not the Y alone as a permanent exception at that point.
explanations.c: Most protein-coding genes were identified well before 2010; the missing 8% was mostly structural/repetitive sequence, not undiscovered genes.
explanations.d: The 2003 announcement explicitly left gaps; true gapless completion did not arrive until 2022.

lessons.label: ENCODE and the '80% Functional' Fight

sections.heading: A headline number from a huge project
sections.body: The Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) Consortium published its integrated results in Nature in September 2012 after nearly a decade of work mapping biochemical activity across the human genome — transcription factor binding, histone modifications, RNA transcripts, chromatin accessibility. Its widely reported headline claim: at least 80% of the genome is 'biochemically functional.' Given that only a small fraction of the genome codes for protein, this was framed as a dramatic overturning of the old idea that most DNA is 'junk,' and was covered that way by major outlets.

sections.heading: The rebuttal: a definitional sleight of hand
sections.body: Critics moved fast. Dan Graur and coauthors' 2013 paper, titled 'On the immortality of television sets: function in the human genome according to the evolution-free gospel of ENCODE' (Genome Biology and Evolution), argued ENCODE's definition of 'function' — any detectable biochemical activity, such as a region simply being transcribed or bound by a protein — was so loose it would call almost anything functional, the way a television set 'functions' as a paperweight if you define function loosely enough. Ford Doolittle made a related point in a 2013 PNAS commentary: ENCODE's definition ignored evolutionary conservation, the standard genetics test for function, under which a sequence is functional if natural selection acts to preserve it. By that conservation-based standard, only about 8-10% of the human genome shows evidence of purifying selection — an order of magnitude below ENCODE's 80%. Sean Eddy and others raised the same concern: biochemical activity without selective constraint could easily be noise, not function.

sections.heading: The C-value paradox, the onion test, and a walk-back
sections.body: Critics also invoked older evidence ENCODE's claim seemed to ignore. The C-value paradox is the long-known mismatch between genome size and organismal complexity — some amoebas and lungfish have genomes many times larger than the human genome, which is hard to square with 80% of any large genome being tightly functional. Evolutionary biologist T. Ryan Gregory had already formalized this into the 'onion test' back in 2007, later developed further with Alexander Palazzo: onions have a genome roughly five times the size of the human genome, so if genome size scaled with functional content, onions would need to be five times more biologically complex than humans, which they plainly are not. Graur invoked the same test in his 2013 critique of ENCODE. Facing sustained criticism, ENCODE leadership (including Ewan Birney) partially walked back the 80% framing in follow-up writing, clarifying that 'biochemically active' was not the same claim as 'functionally essential,' though the original number kept circulating in press coverage for years. The lasting lesson for any research project: how you define your key term can determine your headline result before a single measurement is taken.

lessons.workedExample: A student designing a project on 'gene expression under stress' should learn from ENCODE's mistake by fixing their own definition before collecting data. If 'active' is defined as 'any detectable transcript above background,' nearly every gene will count as active under stress, just as ENCODE's loose definition made 80% of the genome 'functional.' A tighter, defensible definition — say, at least a 2-fold expression change relative to a control, replicated across samples — produces a smaller, more meaningful result the way conservation-based estimates (~8-10% of the genome under selection) gave a smaller, more defensible functional estimate than ENCODE's biochemical-activity definition.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on the ENCODE 80% figure because it is the cleanest real-world case of a defensible dataset paired with an indefensible headline claim — the biochemical measurements were not wrong, the definition of 'function' built on top of them was. A student who can explain that critics like Graur and Doolittle objected to the definition, not the data, and who can cite the conservation-based ~8-10% figure as the competing number, demonstrates they understand that a single word's definition is itself a methodological choice that needs justifying, not just a measurement to report.

questions.prompt: What was ENCODE's headline 2012 claim?

options.text: At least 80% of the human genome is biochemically functional
Only 8% of the human genome codes for protein
The human genome contains exactly 20,000 genes
80% of the human genome is evolutionarily conserved

explanations.a: Correct — ENCODE's 2012 Nature paper reported that at least 80% of the genome shows some biochemical activity, which it termed 'functional.'
explanations.b: Protein-coding percentage is a separate, much older figure and was not ENCODE's headline claim.
explanations.c: Gene-count estimates came from the Human Genome Project's papers, not ENCODE's function claim.
explanations.d: This is precisely the confusion critics objected to — ENCODE's 80% was based on biochemical activity, not evolutionary conservation, which independent estimates put at only ~8-10%.

questions.prompt: What was the core objection in Graur et al.'s 2013 'immortality of television sets' critique?

options.text: ENCODE's raw biochemical measurements were fabricated
ENCODE defined 'function' so loosely (any detectable biochemical activity) that it would call nearly anything functional, without regard to evolutionary constraint
ENCODE used too small a sample of the genome to draw any conclusion
ENCODE ignored protein-coding genes entirely

explanations.a: The critique targeted the definition of function applied to the data, not the integrity of the underlying measurements.
explanations.b: Correct — Graur and coauthors argued the definition was so permissive it resembled calling a television set 'functional' as a paperweight, and that it ignored the evolutionary-conservation standard for function.
explanations.c: ENCODE's data coverage was extensive across the genome; the objection was about definition, not scope of measurement.
explanations.d: Protein-coding genes were included in ENCODE's analysis; the dispute was about extending 'function' far beyond them.

questions.prompt: What does the 'onion test' illustrate?

options.text: That onions have a smaller genome than humans
That if genome size scaled with functional content, onions (with a genome roughly 5x the human genome) would need to be far more complex than humans, which they are not
That onions and humans share 80% of their DNA sequence
That ENCODE's methods do not work on plant genomes

explanations.a: The onion genome is actually several times larger than the human genome, not smaller.
explanations.b: Correct — the onion test uses the C-value paradox to argue that a genome-size-scales-with-function assumption breaks down badly, since onions are not five times more biologically complex than humans.
explanations.c: The onion test is about genome size versus complexity, not sequence similarity between species.
explanations.d: ENCODE's project was specifically about the human genome; the onion test is a conceptual analogy, not a claim about applying ENCODE's assay to onions.

questions.prompt: By the conservation-based standard critics preferred, roughly what fraction of the human genome shows evidence of functional constraint?

options.text: About 80%
About 50%
About 8-10%
Essentially 0%

explanations.a: 80% was ENCODE's biochemical-activity figure, which critics specifically rejected as the wrong measure.
explanations.b: No credible estimate under either framework lands near 50%.
explanations.c: Correct — evolutionary-conservation estimates, based on purifying selection, put functional sequence at roughly 8-10% of the genome, an order of magnitude below ENCODE's figure.
explanations.d: Protein-coding and known regulatory sequence alone account for more than 0%, so this understates even the conservative estimate.

lessons.label: When Genomics Got It Wrong: Candidate Genes and the Duke Scandal

sections.heading: The candidate-gene era's collapse
sections.body: Through the 1990s and 2000s, a common study design picked one plausible 'candidate gene' and tested whether a variant in it interacted with an environmental factor to predict a disease outcome. The best-known example is 5-HTTLPR, a variant in the serotonin transporter gene, which a highly cited 2003 paper linked to depression risk under stress. Hundreds of follow-up studies chased that interaction. Border and colleagues' 2019 paper in the American Journal of Psychiatry ran a large, well-powered, preregistered test across multiple big cohorts and found no effect of 5-HTTLPR on depression and no gene-by-stress interaction at all — a comprehensive failure to replicate the entire candidate-gene literature on this variant. The pattern behind the collapse: candidate-gene studies were typically underpowered for the small true effect sizes complex traits actually have, and flexible analysis choices (which stress measure, which depression outcome, which subgroup) gave many chances to find a 'significant' result by chance, then publish it while null results stayed in file drawers.

sections.heading: Duke's genomic chemotherapy predictors
sections.body: A parallel collapse happened in cancer genomics. Starting around 2006, Duke researcher Anil Potti published papers claiming gene-expression signatures from a patient's tumor could predict which chemotherapy drugs would work best for that individual patient — a genuinely exciting personalized-medicine result that Duke moved directly into clinical trials, assigning real cancer patients to treatments based on the signatures. Biostatisticians Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes at MD Anderson tried to reproduce the results for an unrelated project and could not. Their forensic bioinformatics investigation, published in the Annals of Applied Statistics, found the underlying spreadsheets contained basic errors: off-by-one row shifts that misaligned sample labels with expression data, and in at least one case drug-sensitive and drug-resistant sample labels appeared to be reversed relative to what the paper reported.

sections.heading: Trials halted, retractions, and the 2012 report
sections.body: Baggerly and Coombes raised these concerns for years before Duke acted. In 2010, after further scrutiny (including discovery that Potti had misrepresented a Rhodes Scholarship on his CV), Duke terminated three clinical trials that had been assigning patients to chemotherapy based on the flawed signatures, and Potti resigned; several papers were later retracted. The case prompted an Institute of Medicine (IOM) committee report in 2012 on the validation of omics-based tests before clinical use, recommending stricter reproducibility and independent-validation standards before any genomic predictor reaches patients. The blunt lesson repeated in bioinformatics courses since: a result that produces a beautiful, cleanly clustered heatmap is not evidence the underlying pipeline is correct — it can just as easily be evidence of a systematic labeling error that a spreadsheet audit would catch.

lessons.workedExample: A student running a genomics-flavored project should treat both cases as a checklist. From 5-HTTLPR: report every stress measure and outcome variable tested, not just the one that came out significant, and estimate whether the sample size can plausibly detect an effect of realistic size before running the test (a small candidate-gene study chasing a subtle interaction is set up to produce false positives). From Potti: before trusting any clustering result or heatmap, manually spot-check that a handful of sample IDs in the raw data match the sample IDs in the final labeled output — Baggerly and Coombes caught the Duke errors essentially by tracing individual sample labels through the pipeline by hand.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who raises 5-HTTLPR or the Duke case is testing whether a student understands that genomics has real, documented failure modes beyond 'the sample size was small' — flexible analysis choices that manufacture false positives, and basic data-handling errors that survive peer review because the output looks convincing. A student who can name Border et al. (2019)'s comprehensive non-replication or Baggerly and Coombes' off-by-one spreadsheet finding, and explain the mechanism (underpowered flexible analysis; unaudited sample-label alignment) rather than just saying 'it was debunked,' shows they understand these as structural risks their own project needs to guard against, not just cautionary trivia.

questions.prompt: What did Border et al. (2019) find when they comprehensively re-tested the 5-HTTLPR gene-by-stress interaction on depression?

options.text: A stronger effect than the original candidate-gene studies had reported
No effect of the 5-HTTLPR genotype on depression and no gene-by-stress interaction
The effect only held in male participants
That 5-HTTLPR causes depression independent of any environmental stress

explanations.a: The large, well-powered re-test found no support for the effect at all, the opposite of a stronger result.
explanations.b: Correct — Border and colleagues' 2019 study found no main effect of 5-HTTLPR genotype and no gene-by-environment interaction, failing to replicate the widely cited candidate-gene literature.
explanations.c: The finding was a general non-replication, not a result restricted to one sex.
explanations.d: The study found no effect of the genotype at all, with or without an environmental interaction.

questions.prompt: What specific type of error did Baggerly and Coombes find in the Duke genomic-predictor spreadsheets?

options.text: The tumor samples had been contaminated in the lab
Off-by-one row shifts that misaligned sample labels with expression data, including apparently reversed drug-sensitive/resistant labels
The gene-expression microarray chips were defective
Duplicate patient IDs across two different hospitals

explanations.a: The problem Baggerly and Coombes identified was in data processing and labeling, not physical sample contamination.
explanations.b: Correct — their forensic bioinformatics review found row-shift misalignments and at least one case of apparently reversed sensitive/resistant labels in the underlying spreadsheets.
explanations.c: The issue was traced to data handling and analysis, not a hardware fault in the microarray platform.
explanations.d: The documented problem was label misalignment within the analysis pipeline, not duplicate IDs across institutions.

questions.prompt: What was the consequence at Duke once the errors could not be resolved?

options.text: The trials continued unchanged while a review was published
Duke terminated three clinical trials that assigned chemotherapy based on the signatures, and Potti resigned amid retractions
The FDA banned all future genomic biomarker research
Duke published the corrected data and the trials proceeded

explanations.a: The trials were not left unchanged — Duke terminated them once the problems became undeniable.
explanations.b: Correct — in 2010, Duke halted three trials using the flawed predictors, Potti resigned, and several related papers were later retracted.
explanations.c: No blanket FDA ban followed; instead the case led to an Institute of Medicine report on validation standards.
explanations.d: The underlying data problems were not simply correctable, which is why the trials were terminated rather than continued with fixed data.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the Duke genomic-predictor case.

items.text: Potti publishes gene-expression chemotherapy-response predictors
Duke begins clinical trials assigning patients using the predictors
Baggerly and Coombes publish their forensic bioinformatics findings
Duke terminates the trials and Potti resigns
IOM publishes its report on validating omics-based tests

questions.explanation: The predictors were published and moved into Duke clinical trials; Baggerly and Coombes' forensic review exposed the underlying errors; Duke then halted the trials and Potti resigned (2010); the IOM report on validation standards followed in 2012.

lessons.label: Live Debates: Missing Heritability, Germline Editing, and Who Owns a Genome

sections.heading: Missing heritability: the GWAS gap
sections.body: Twin studies estimate that height is roughly 80% heritable. But when genome-wide association studies (GWAS) tally up every common variant statistically linked to height, they explain only a modest fraction of that 80% — a gap dubbed 'missing heritability' once GWAS scaled up in the late 2000s. Where the rest is hiding is still contested. One camp points to rare variants, each too infrequent for GWAS (which is built to detect common variants) to catch, but collectively meaningful. Another points to epistasis — gene-gene interactions that don't show up as clean additive effects in standard GWAS models. A third argument, from Evan Boyle, Yang Li, and Jonathan Pritchard's 2017 'omnigenic model' (Cell), reframes the puzzle rather than resolving it: they argue that in tightly interconnected gene-regulatory networks, thousands of 'peripheral' genes with no direct role in a trait can each nudge a handful of 'core' genes, so complex-trait heritability is spread thin across a huge share of the expressed genome rather than concentrated in a few strong hits — which would make it inherently hard for GWAS to fully capture with reasonable sample sizes. A fourth, more skeptical position argues the twin-study heritability estimates themselves were inflated by assumptions baked into the classic twin-study design, meaning there may be less heritability to find than assumed.

sections.heading: He Jiankui and the germline-editing line
sections.body: In November 2018, He Jiankui announced he had used CRISPR to edit the CCR5 gene in human embryos, aiming to confer HIV resistance, resulting in the birth of twin girls (publicly called Lulu and Nana) — the first gene-edited babies, edited at the germline level so the changes are heritable by any offspring they have. The announcement was met with near-universal condemnation from the scientific community for bypassing established ethical review and safety consensus around heritable human editing. A Shenzhen court convicted He of illegal medical practice in December 2019, sentencing him to three years in prison and a fine of 3 million yuan; two collaborators received shorter sentences. The case did not resolve the underlying debate — a broad international moratorium on clinical germline editing is widely supported, but no binding global framework exists, and disagreement continues over whether germline editing should ever be permitted for disease prevention even under strict oversight.

sections.heading: Who owns a genome once it's sequenced
sections.body: Consent and ownership disputes are not hypothetical. Between 1990 and 1994, Arizona State University researchers collected blood from Havasupai tribe members for a diabetes study but also used the samples for unrelated research — including on schizophrenia and population migration — without separate consent; the tribe sued, and a 2010 settlement returned the samples, paid $700,000, and funded some community support. Henrietta Lacks' cells, taken without her consent in 1951 and turned into the widely used HeLa cell line, is the older, still-cited version of the same problem; decades later, researchers published the HeLa genome without her family's involvement, prompting a negotiated data-access agreement with her descendants. A structural version of the same issue persists in GWAS itself: a large majority of GWAS participants have been of European ancestry, so polygenic scores and other genomic tools built on that data are measurably less accurate when applied to people of other ancestries — an equity gap the field acknowledges but has been slow to close.

lessons.workedExample: A student proposing a genomics project involving human samples or public GWAS data should be able to answer three questions a judge is likely to ask, each mapped to a real case above: 'What happens to consent if you reuse this data for a different question later?' (Havasupai and Lacks say get explicit, use-specific consent, or use only fully de-identified public data). 'Would your genomic finding hold up across ancestries?' (GWAS's European-ancestry skew means a polygenic finding tuned on one population may simply not transfer). 'If your project touched heritable human editing, would it clear the current ethical consensus?' (the He Jiankui case is the concrete answer to why the current answer is almost always no for clinical application).
lessons.judgeFraming: This unit's three threads share one underlying question a judge is really asking: who decides what genomic knowledge is used for, and who bears the risk when the field moves faster than its own consensus? Missing heritability tests whether a student understands a genuinely unresolved scientific gap (not a solved problem to summarize); He Jiankui tests whether a student can name a hard, working line the field has actually drawn and enforced; Havasupai and the GWAS ancestry gap test whether a student sees consent and representativeness as science questions, not just ethics footnotes — a genomic tool trained overwhelmingly on European-ancestry data has a real, measurable performance gap, not merely a fairness concern.

questions.prompt: What is the 'missing heritability' problem?

options.text: GWAS-identified common variants explain only a modest fraction of the heritability twin studies estimate for many complex traits
Twin studies cannot be performed on humans for ethical reasons
GWAS studies have found no genetic contribution to any complex trait
Heritability estimates change every generation due to new mutations

explanations.a: Correct — twin-study heritability estimates (e.g., ~80% for height) far exceed what GWAS's tally of common variants can account for, leaving a gap researchers call missing heritability.
explanations.b: Twin studies of humans are a long-established, widely used method; the problem is a data gap, not an ethical block on the method.
explanations.c: GWAS has identified many real genetic contributions; the issue is the total explained variance falling short of twin-based estimates, not zero findings.
explanations.d: The gap is about existing standing genetic variation not being fully captured by GWAS, not about new mutations arising each generation.

questions.prompt: What does the Boyle-Li-Pritchard 'omnigenic model' (2017) propose about missing heritability?

options.text: That heritability is a scientifically meaningless concept and should be discarded
That in interconnected gene-regulatory networks, thousands of peripheral genes each nudge a handful of core genes, spreading trait heritability across far more of the genome than GWAS easily detects
That all missing heritability is explained by rare variants alone
That twin-study heritability estimates are simply wrong and should be ignored

explanations.a: The model works within the concept of heritability, offering a structural explanation for why it's hard to fully capture, not a rejection of the concept.
explanations.b: Correct — the omnigenic model argues gene-regulatory interconnectedness spreads a trait's genetic influence across many peripheral genes acting on core genes, making the effect diffuse and hard for standard GWAS to fully capture.
explanations.c: The omnigenic model is a distinct hypothesis from the rare-variant explanation; it does not claim rare variants alone solve the gap.
explanations.d: The model does not dismiss twin-study estimates; it proposes a mechanism for why GWAS falls short of them, leaving the twin estimates as the reference point being explained.

questions.prompt: What did He Jiankui do in 2018, and what was the legal outcome?

options.text: He performed somatic gene therapy on adult HIV patients; he was fined but not imprisoned
He edited the CCR5 gene in human embryos, resulting in the birth of gene-edited twins; he was sentenced to three years in prison
He published a computational model of germline editing risk; no legal action followed
He led an approved international germline-editing trial that met all regulatory requirements

explanations.a: His editing was germline (embryonic), not somatic, and resulted in a prison sentence, not merely a fine.
explanations.b: Correct — He edited CCR5 in embryos that became twin girls born in 2018; a Shenzhen court sentenced him to three years in prison and a large fine in December 2019 for illegal medical practice.
explanations.c: He performed actual embryo editing resulting in live births, not a computational model.
explanations.d: His work bypassed established ethical review and was widely condemned and prosecuted, not approved.

questions.prompt: Match each consent/ownership case to its outcome.

left.text: Havasupai Tribe v. Arizona Board of Regents

right.text: 2010 settlement: samples returned, $700,000 paid, community support funded
Cells taken without consent in 1951; decades later a negotiated data-access agreement followed publication of the HeLa genome

questions.explanation: The Havasupai case ended in a 2010 settlement after samples were used for unconsented research beyond the original diabetes study. Henrietta Lacks' cells were taken without consent in 1951, and the later publication of the HeLa genome without family involvement led to a negotiated data-access agreement with her descendants.

units.label: Genomics in Practice: Applications and Case Studies

lessons.label: Forensic DNA: From STR Profiles to Genetic Genealogy

sections.heading: Why STRs, not SNPs, became the forensic standard
sections.body: A forensic DNA profile does not sequence a genome; it counts repeats at a handful of chosen sites. Short tandem repeats (STRs) are stretches where a short motif (2-6 base pairs) repeats a variable number of times, and different people carry different repeat counts at the same locus. STRs beat single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) for forensic work because one STR locus can carry a dozen or more alleles, versus typically two for a SNP, so a panel of about 20 STR loci reaches far greater discrimination power than the same number of SNPs would, and standardized multiplex PCR kits can amplify all of them from a few nanograms of degraded crime-scene DNA in one reaction.

sections.heading: CODIS: the database, the loci, and the numbers
sections.body: The FBI's Combined DNA Index System (CODIS) is the software and database letting local, state, and national labs compare profiles. The 13 core STR loci were selected in 1997, and the national database went live with them in October 1998; on January 1, 2017, the FBI expanded the core set to 20 loci, adding seven (including D1S1656, D2S441, and D12S391) to align with the European Standard Set and keep random-match probabilities vanishingly small as the database grows past tens of millions of profiles. Multiplying the match probability at each independent locus (the product rule) routinely yields a combined random-match probability beyond 1 in 10^18 for an unrelated full profile.

sections.heading: Where the science strains: mixtures and touch DNA
sections.body: That figure describes a clean, single-source profile, not what labs often receive. Mixture deconvolution, separating alleles of two or more contributors from one sample, grows combinatorially harder as contributor number rises; probabilistic genotyping software like STRmix is now standard where older binary methods struggled. Low-template ('touch') DNA, amplified from only a few skin cells, is vulnerable to stochastic dropout (a true allele fails to amplify) and drop-in (contamination adds a spurious one), either of which can shift a reported match probability by orders of magnitude. The 1989 People v. Castro case (Bronx, NY) forced an early reckoning: after a 12-week Frye hearing, the court accepted DNA typing's underlying science but ruled the specific lab's execution too flawed to support a match, pushing labs toward standardized protocols and proficiency testing.

sections.heading: Genetic genealogy: solving cases through relatives who never consented
sections.body: Genetic genealogy skips the profile-to-profile match entirely. In 2018, investigator Paul Holes uploaded a crime-scene profile from the decades-old Golden State Killer case to GEDmatch, a public genealogy site; genealogist Barbara Rae-Venter used the resulting list of over 1,000 partial cousin matches to build family trees until they converged on a small candidate pool, narrowed further by DMV photos to Joseph James DeAngelo and confirmed with a covertly collected discarded-DNA sample. No suspect and no relative had to be in CODIS — a handful of relatives' own choices to upload their DNA made DeAngelo findable, which is exactly the privacy argument: people who never consented to forensic searching became reachable through their family.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a lab reports match probabilities of 1 in 500, 1 in 800, and 1 in 1,200 at three independent CODIS loci for a suspect's profile. Applying the product rule, the combined random-match probability is roughly 1 in (500 x 800 x 1,200), about 1 in 480 million -- already far more persuasive than any single locus, and a real 20-locus CODIS profile compounds this across all 20 loci to reach the 1-in-10^18-range figures quoted in court. But a defense expert would immediately ask whether the sample was single-source: if two people contributed to the swab, those same per-locus numbers cannot simply be multiplied, because the observed alleles could belong to either contributor in more than one combination -- which is exactly why mixture cases need probabilistic genotyping software rather than the product rule.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes forensic DNA to test whether a student understands that 'DNA proves it' is not itself a claim -- the strength of a match is a probability computed from a specific statistical model applied to a specific sample type. A student who can explain why a mixed or low-template sample cannot use the same product-rule shortcut as a clean single-source profile, and who can name a real check point in the pipeline (Castro forcing lab standardization, or probabilistic genotyping for mixtures) rather than reciting 'DNA doesn't lie,' has shown they understand forensic genetics as an evidentiary chain with real failure points, not a magic identifier.

questions.prompt: Why are short tandem repeats (STRs) preferred over single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) for forensic profiling?

options.text: STRs are cheaper to sequence than SNPs
A single STR locus has many more possible alleles than a typical SNP, so fewer loci give much greater discrimination power
SNPs cannot be amplified by PCR
STRs never degrade in old or damaged samples

explanations.a: Cost is not the driver here; both can be typed with standard PCR-based kits.
explanations.b: Correct -- an STR locus can carry a dozen or more alleles versus typically two for a SNP, so a panel of about 20 STR loci reaches far greater discrimination power than the same number of SNPs.
explanations.c: SNPs are routinely PCR-amplified; that is not why they are avoided for core forensic panels.
explanations.d: Both STRs and SNPs degrade in old samples; STRs are not immune to degradation, though shorter STR amplicons can sometimes survive better than longer ones.

questions.prompt: What changed in CODIS on January 1, 2017?

options.text: The core loci expanded from 13 to 20, partly to align with the European Standard Set
CODIS switched entirely from STRs to whole-genome sequencing
The database was made searchable by the public for the first time
CODIS began storing full genomic profiles instead of locus-based ones

explanations.a: Correct -- the FBI expanded the core set from 13 to 20 STR loci, adding seven loci to improve international compatibility and keep match probabilities small as the database grows.
explanations.b: CODIS remained STR-based; it did not move to whole-genome sequencing.
explanations.c: CODIS is a law-enforcement database, not a public-search tool -- that description fits GEDmatch, not CODIS.
explanations.d: CODIS profiles remain locus-based repeat counts at the core STR loci, not full genomic sequence.

questions.prompt: Match each forensic DNA term to its correct description.

right.text: A true allele in the sample fails to amplify and so is missing from the profile
Contamination introduces a spurious allele not actually present in the source
Multiplying per-locus match probabilities together to get a combined random-match probability
Case where a Frye hearing accepted DNA typing's underlying science but rejected one lab's flawed execution

questions.explanation: Dropout and drop-in are opposite stochastic failure modes seen in low-template DNA; the product rule is the statistical shortcut used to combine per-locus probabilities for clean single-source profiles; and Castro is the 1989 case that forced forensic labs toward standardized protocols after exposing execution flaws separate from the underlying science.

questions.prompt: How was the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, ultimately identified in 2018?

options.text: His profile was already stored in CODIS and produced a direct database match
A crime-scene profile uploaded to a public genealogy site matched distant relatives, and genealogists built family trees to narrow down a candidate
A confession led police directly to him without any DNA analysis
Local police ran a familial search against the entire state's CODIS database

explanations.a: DeAngelo was never in CODIS; that is precisely why investigators had to turn to a different method.
explanations.b: Correct -- investigator Paul Holes uploaded the crime-scene profile to GEDmatch, genealogist Barbara Rae-Venter used over 1,000 cousin matches to build family trees, and DMV photos plus a discarded-DNA sample confirmed DeAngelo.
explanations.c: No confession initiated the case; genetic genealogy identified him before any admission.
explanations.d: The search was not a state CODIS familial search but a public genealogy-database search using distant relatives' voluntarily uploaded profiles.

questions.prompt: Order the steps that led investigators to Joseph James DeAngelo.

items.text: Crime-scene DNA profile uploaded to the public site GEDmatch
Genealogist builds family trees from over 1,000 partial cousin matches
Candidate pool narrowed using DMV photographs
Identity confirmed with a covertly collected discarded-DNA sample

questions.explanation: The investigation started with uploading the crime-scene profile to GEDmatch, then used the resulting distant-cousin matches to reconstruct family trees, narrowed the pool of candidates using DMV photos, and finally confirmed the match with a discreetly obtained DNA sample before arrest.

lessons.label: Genomics in Agriculture and Conservation

sections.heading: Marker-assisted selection to genome-wide genomic selection
sections.body: Marker-assisted selection (MAS) uses a handful of DNA markers linked to one known trait locus to pick breeding stock without waiting to observe the phenotype. Genomic selection (GS), introduced by Meuwissen, Hayes, and Goddard's 2001 paper 'Prediction of Total Genetic Value Using Genome-Wide Dense Marker Maps,' goes further: it estimates the effects of tens of thousands of markers across the whole genome at once and sums them into a genomic estimated breeding value (GEBV) for traits with no single causal gene. Dairy cattle breeding adopted GS aggressively because it lets breeders rank a bull calf's genetic merit for milk yield from a cheek swab at birth rather than waiting years for his daughters to lactate, shortening the generation interval and raising genetic gain per year.

sections.heading: A pre-genomic precedent, and today's contested cases
sections.body: Genomic tools are recent, but trait-driven crop breeding is not. The Green Revolution of the 1960s relied on semi-dwarfing alleles bred in before anyone knew the genes involved: Norman Borlaug crossed the Rht dwarfing genes from Japan's Norin 10 wheat into high-yield varieties, and IR8 rice carried the sd1 semi-dwarf allele, both letting plants hold heavier, fertilizer-fed grain heads without collapsing (lodging). Modern applied genomics is more contested. Bt crops, engineered with a Bacillus thuringiensis toxin gene, cut insecticide use but push target pests toward resistance, requiring refuge-planting strategies. Golden Rice, engineered by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer to produce beta-carotene against vitamin-A deficiency, spent roughly two decades in regulatory and activist opposition before the Philippines approved commercial planting in 2021.

sections.heading: Conservation genomics: measuring and repairing inbreeding
sections.body: Small, isolated populations accumulate inbreeding, measurable as the inbreeding coefficient F: the probability two alleles at a locus are identical by descent. High F correlates with reduced fertility, birth defects, and disease vulnerability. The Florida panther fell below 30 individuals by the early 1990s with visible inbreeding signs -- kinked tails, cowlicks, heart defects, poor sperm quality. In 1995, managers introduced eight female Texas cougars, the nearest subspecies whose mitochondrial DNA most closely matched pre-bottleneck Florida panthers, as a genetic rescue; heterozygosity rose, defect rates fell, and the population has since grown toward roughly 200. The black-footed ferret suffered a harsher bottleneck: every ferret alive today descends from just seven founders from a single population rediscovered in 1981, and in 2020 conservationists cloned Elizabeth Ann from cryopreserved 1988 cell lines to reintroduce genetic variation lost since that bottleneck.

sections.heading: eDNA: finding species without catching them
sections.body: Environmental DNA (eDNA) surveys detect species from shed cells, mucus, or waste in water or soil samples, amplifying species-specific marker sequences by PCR rather than trapping or observing an organism directly. This makes eDNA fast and non-invasive for tracking invasive-species fronts, such as Asian carp approaching the Great Lakes, or confirming the presence of rare, sparse species that traditional surveys would likely miss.

lessons.workedExample: A dairy breeding program traditionally progeny-tested a bull over about five years: breed him, wait for daughters to calve and complete a lactation, then compute his estimated breeding value from their milk records. Genomic selection collapses this: a chip reads roughly 50,000 SNP markers from a calf's cheek swab at birth, and a genomic estimated breeding value (GEBV) built from a reference population of thousands of already-progeny-tested relatives predicts that same milk-yield merit within weeks rather than years. A GEBV computed at birth is less accurate per animal than a full progeny test, but because it arrives so much earlier, breeders can cycle through more generations per decade -- and the shorter generation interval outweighs the accuracy loss, which is why elite dairy programs shifted to genomic selection within a decade of Meuwissen, Hayes, and Goddard's 2001 method.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about agricultural and conservation genomics to see whether a student can tell apart three things casually lumped together as 'genetic engineering': genomic selection (predicting breeding value from markers -- no DNA is altered), transgenic modification (inserting a gene, as in Bt crops or Golden Rice), and genetic rescue (moving individuals to restore diversity -- no engineering at all). A student who can also name the real risk in genetic rescue, outbreeding depression or swamping a locally adapted gene pool, rather than treating it as an automatic fix, shows they understand these as genuine trade-offs rather than a single undifferentiated idea of 'using genetics.'

questions.prompt: What did Meuwissen, Hayes, and Goddard's 2001 paper introduce that distinguishes genomic selection from earlier marker-assisted selection?

options.text: Using one or two markers linked to a single known trait gene
Estimating the combined effect of tens of thousands of genome-wide markers at once, summed into a genomic estimated breeding value
Sequencing the entire genome of every breeding animal
Replacing DNA-based prediction with pedigree records alone

explanations.a: That description is marker-assisted selection (MAS), the older, narrower approach genomic selection extended beyond.
explanations.b: Correct -- their method estimates effects across tens of thousands of markers spanning the whole genome and sums them into a GEBV, working even for traits without one identified causal gene.
explanations.c: Genomic selection uses dense marker panels (SNP chips), not full genome sequencing, for routine breeding decisions.
explanations.d: Genomic selection uses DNA markers precisely because pedigree-only prediction is less accurate and slower to obtain.

questions.prompt: What problem did the Green Revolution's semi-dwarfing alleles (Rht in wheat, sd1 in rice) solve?

options.text: They made plants resistant to insect pests
They let plants hold heavier, fertilizer-fed grain heads without lodging (collapsing)
They increased a plant's drought tolerance
They eliminated the need for fertilizer entirely

explanations.a: Pest resistance is the goal of Bt crops, a different and later genomic intervention, not the semi-dwarf alleles.
explanations.b: Correct -- shorter, sturdier stalks could support the heavier grain heads produced under heavy fertilizer use without collapsing, which is what let fertilizer inputs translate into yield.
explanations.c: Drought tolerance was not the trait these alleles addressed; lodging resistance under fertilization was.
explanations.d: The alleles worked precisely because they let plants exploit heavy fertilizer input, not because they removed the need for it.

questions.prompt: Match each case to its correct description.

right.text: Carry a Bacillus thuringiensis toxin gene that cuts insecticide use but can drive pest resistance
Engineered to produce beta-carotene against vitamin-A deficiency; delayed roughly two decades by regulatory and activist opposition
Received eight introduced Texas cougars as a genetic rescue after falling below 30 individuals
Descends entirely from seven founders from a single population rediscovered in 1981

questions.explanation: Bt crops and Golden Rice are transgenic applications with contested social and regulatory histories; the Florida panther and black-footed ferret are conservation genetics cases involving inbreeding and genetic rescue rather than genetic engineering.

questions.prompt: How does an environmental DNA (eDNA) survey detect a species?

options.text: By trapping or directly observing individual organisms
By amplifying species-specific marker DNA shed into water or soil, without catching the organism
By sequencing the full genome of every organism in a habitat
By comparing satellite images of habitat range

explanations.a: Direct trapping or observation is the traditional survey method eDNA is meant to avoid or supplement.
explanations.b: Correct -- eDNA amplifies species-specific marker sequences by PCR from shed cells, mucus, or waste in environmental samples, detecting presence without catching the organism.
explanations.c: eDNA typically targets a short marker region by PCR, not whole-genome sequencing of every organism present.
explanations.d: Satellite imagery is a habitat-mapping tool, not a DNA-based detection method.

questions.prompt: Order the events of the Florida panther genetic rescue.

items.text: Population falls below 30 individuals with visible inbreeding defects
Eight female Texas cougars are introduced in 1995
Interbreeding with the introduced cougars raises heterozygosity
Population grows toward roughly 200 with fewer inbreeding defects

questions.explanation: The rescue followed a clear sequence: the population crashed and showed inbreeding depression, managers introduced Texas cougars in 1995 as the closest matching subspecies, interbreeding raised genetic diversity, and defect rates fell as the population subsequently grew.

lessons.label: Pathogen Genomics and Outbreak Tracking

sections.heading: Crowdsourcing an outbreak's cause: Germany, 2011
sections.body: In May 2011 an unusual Shiga toxin-producing E. coli strain, serotype O104:H4, caused an outbreak in Germany that ultimately infected more than 4,000 people and killed about 50, with unusually severe hemolytic uremic syndrome in adults. Rather than one lab working in isolation, the sequencing center BGI produced a draft genome within days and released it publicly, and researchers worldwide organized an open, crowdsourced analysis on GitHub. Within about a day of the data going public, the crowdsourced effort had identified the strain as an enteroaggregative E. coli that had acquired a Shiga-toxin-producing phage plus an unusually broad set of antibiotic-resistance genes -- a hybrid identity that traditional single-lab sequencing would have taken far longer to reach.

sections.heading: Sequencing under fire: Ebola in Sierra Leone, 2014
sections.body: During the 2014 West African Ebola epidemic, a team led by Pardis Sabeti sequenced 99 viral genomes from 78 patients in Sierra Leone within weeks of the local outbreak's start, publishing the results as Gire et al. (2014) in Science. The genomes showed the outbreak traced to a single introduction from an animal reservoir followed entirely by human-to-human transmission, and the observed mutation rate let researchers date how the lineage was branching in near-real time. The paper carries a grim footnote: five of its co-authors, members of the hospital's Lassa fever team who helped collect the samples, died of Ebola before the paper was published -- a reminder that outbreak genomics depends on clinicians working inside the outbreak itself, not just remote desk analysis.

sections.heading: SARS-CoV-2: real-time surveillance and the molecular clock
sections.body: By 2020, outbreak genomics had become continuous rather than after-the-fact. Labs worldwide uploaded SARS-CoV-2 genomes to GISAID (a platform originally built for sharing influenza data), and the open-source tool Nextstrain built and updated a real-time phylogenetic tree from those genomes, letting researchers watch new variants emerge and spread. The method leans on a molecular clock: SARS-CoV-2 accumulates mutations at a roughly steady rate, so counting the mutations separating two genomes estimates how long ago their lineages diverged, which is how researchers dated variant origins and reconstructed transmission chains between countries, often months before contact-tracing interviews could confirm the same links.

sections.heading: Resistance genes, and why a tree is an argument
sections.body: The same sequencing pipeline detects antimicrobial resistance directly, flagging genes like blaNDM-1 or mecA in hours rather than waiting one to two days for culture-based susceptibility testing, which speeds clinical antibiotic choices and hospital-outbreak response. A phylogenetic tree built from a set of isolates is not a decoration; its branching order is a claim about who infected whom. Isolates that cluster tightly, sharing recent mutations, support a single transmission chain, such as a hospital outbreak or superspreading event; isolates falling into separate branches argue for independent introductions instead. Reading that structure correctly, not just generating it, is what turns pathogen genomics into epidemiology.

lessons.workedExample: Say two SARS-CoV-2 genomes sampled from patients in different cities differ by 12 mutations, and surveillance data show the virus accumulates roughly 24 mutations per genome per year (about 2 per month). Because each of the two sampled lineages has been accumulating its own mutations independently since they diverged from their shared ancestor, the observed difference reflects twice the per-lineage rate: dividing 12 mutations by (2 x 24 mutations/year) gives an estimated divergence time of about three months, meaning the two cases likely trace back to a shared ancestor infection roughly a quarter-year earlier rather than a direct, recent transmission between the two patients. This is exactly the logic Nextstrain automates across thousands of genomes at once: instead of one pairwise comparison, it builds a full tree where branch lengths represent mutation counts, letting epidemiologists read off approximate timing and relatedness for an entire outbreak rather than two isolates.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about pathogen genomics because it is easy to present a colorful phylogenetic tree without being able to say what the tree claims. A student who can explain that branch length encodes mutation count, that mutation count implies elapsed time via a roughly constant molecular clock, and that tree topology implies transmission direction -- rather than describing the tree as merely 'showing how related the samples are' -- demonstrates they understand the tree as a testable epidemiological hypothesis. Naming the human cost behind the data, such as the co-authors who died collecting the 2014 Ebola samples, also signals the student understands genomic surveillance as fieldwork, not just downloaded data.

questions.prompt: What made the response to the 2011 German E. coli O104:H4 outbreak unusually fast?

options.text: A single government lab kept the genome confidential until final publication
A draft genome was released publicly and analyzed through open, crowdsourced collaboration
The strain was identical to a previously catalogued outbreak strain
No sequencing was needed because the strain was identified by symptoms alone

explanations.a: The opposite happened -- BGI released the draft genome publicly rather than keeping it confidential.
explanations.b: Correct -- BGI released a draft genome within days, and an open, crowdsourced GitHub effort identified the strain's hybrid identity and resistance genes within about a day of the data going public.
explanations.c: The strain was an unusual hybrid, an enteroaggregative E. coli that had acquired a Shiga-toxin-producing phage, not a match to a known catalogued strain.
explanations.d: Sequencing, not symptoms alone, was what identified the strain's specific hybrid genetic identity and resistance genes.

questions.prompt: What did Gire et al. (2014) conclude about the origin of the Sierra Leone Ebola cases they sequenced, and what happened to several of the paper's co-authors?

options.text: The outbreak traced to a single animal-reservoir introduction followed by human-to-human spread; five co-authors died of Ebola before publication
The outbreak involved dozens of separate animal-to-human introductions; all co-authors survived
The sequencing data were inconclusive about transmission; no co-authors were involved in sample collection
The outbreak was traced to contaminated water rather than animal-to-human transmission

explanations.a: Correct -- the genomic data pointed to one introduction from an animal reservoir followed entirely by human-to-human transmission, and five co-authors from the hospital's Lassa fever team died of Ebola before the paper was published.
explanations.b: The genomic evidence supported a single introduction, not dozens of separate ones.
explanations.c: The sequencing data were conclusive enough to trace a single introduction and transmission pattern, and co-authors were directly involved in sample collection, several fatally.
explanations.d: Ebola virus transmission in this outbreak was traced through an animal reservoir and human-to-human spread, not waterborne contamination.

questions.prompt: Match each tool, platform, or gene example to its role in pathogen genomics.

right.text: Global platform (originally for influenza data) where labs upload pathogen genomes for sharing
Open-source tool that builds real-time phylogenetic trees to track variant emergence and spread
Sequencing-based flagging of resistance genes in hours, faster than culture-based susceptibility testing
Public release of an outbreak genome that let a crowdsourced effort identify a hybrid E. coli strain within about a day

questions.explanation: GISAID is the genome-sharing platform, Nextstrain is the analysis and visualization tool built on that shared data, resistance-gene detection is a direct clinical use of sequencing, and the 2011 BGI release is the earlier precedent for open, crowdsourced outbreak genomics.

questions.prompt: In the 'molecular clock' logic used for SARS-CoV-2 surveillance, what does the number of mutations separating two genomes let researchers estimate?

options.text: The exact geographic location where the virus originated
How long ago the two genomes' lineages diverged from a shared ancestor
The severity of illness the virus causes
Whether the sample was contaminated during sequencing

explanations.a: Mutation count estimates elapsed time, not geographic origin, which requires additional epidemiological and travel data.
explanations.b: Correct -- because the virus accumulates mutations at a roughly steady rate, the number of mutations separating two genomes estimates how long ago their lineages diverged from a common ancestor.
