explanations.c: Mutation count reflects evolutionary time elapsed, not clinical severity, which depends on which specific mutations are present and other factors.
explanations.d: Contamination is a technical sequencing-quality issue, not something the molecular clock calculation is designed to detect.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of using pathogen genomics to argue for a shared transmission chain between two outbreak isolates.

items.text: Collect samples and sequence each pathogen's genome
Compare genomes to count the mutations separating them
Build a phylogenetic tree showing how closely isolates cluster
Interpret tight clustering with few mutations as evidence for a shared transmission chain

questions.explanation: The process starts with sequencing the samples, then quantifying genetic differences between them, then organizing those differences into a tree structure, and finally interpreting that structure epidemiologically -- close clustering with few separating mutations argues for a shared transmission chain rather than independent introductions.

lessons.label: Direct-to-Consumer Genetics: What the Report Can and Cannot Say

sections.heading: Genotyping is not sequencing
sections.body: Direct-to-consumer (DTC) companies like 23andMe and AncestryDNA do not sequence a customer's genome; they run a microarray chip that checks genotype at a fixed, predetermined set of roughly 600,000 to 1,000,000 single-nucleotide sites chosen in advance, reading each one by hybridization rather than reconstructing the full sequence base by base. This keeps the test cheap, well under $200, but means the chip can only report on variants it was designed to look for -- it cannot discover a novel mutation, and its probes, optimized for common variants, are less reliable at the rare, often more clinically important positions a diagnostic sequencing lab would target directly.

sections.heading: What that unreliability costs: the Tandy-Connor findings
sections.body: Tandy-Connor et al. (2018), working with Ambry Genetics, tested this directly: they took 49 patient samples where DTC raw data had flagged a variant and sent them for clinical confirmation sequencing. About 40% of the flagged variants turned out to be false positives, present in the DTC raw data but absent on confirmatory testing, and 94% of those false positives were in cancer-risk genes, exactly the category a worried customer is most likely to act on. The lesson is not that DTC raw data is useless, but that it is a screening signal, not a diagnosis, and any concerning result needs clinical-grade confirmation before it changes a medical decision.

sections.heading: Ancestry estimates and a decade of FDA back-and-forth
sections.body: Ancestry percentages work by comparing a customer's genotype to reference panels of people with known geographic origin and assigning proportions statistically, which means the same raw data can shift noticeably when a company updates its reference panel; the reported number is a best estimate with real uncertainty, not a fact carved into the genome. Health claims went through their own reckoning: the FDA sent 23andMe a warning letter in 2013 ordering it to stop marketing health-related results, citing unvalidated breast-cancer and warfarin-sensitivity reports customers might act on unsupervised, restricting the company to ancestry and raw data only. The FDA authorized carrier-status reports in 2015, and on April 6, 2017, granted 23andMe authorization to market Genetic Health Risk reports for conditions including late-onset Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.

sections.heading: Polygenic risk scores travel poorly across ancestries
sections.body: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) sum the small effects of many common variants into a single risk estimate, but nearly all of them were trained on genome-wide association studies (GWAS) built overwhelmingly from European-ancestry cohorts. Martin et al. (2019) showed the resulting scores lose most of their power outside that training population: predictive accuracy (R-squared) was roughly 4.5 times lower in individuals of African ancestry than in Europeans, because linkage-disequilibrium patterns and allele frequencies differ across populations in ways the training data never captured. A DTC report handing every customer the same-looking risk percentage obscures that the number was calibrated on, and is only reliable for, a narrow ancestral slice of humanity.

lessons.workedExample: A customer runs their 23andMe raw data through a third-party interpretation tool and sees a flagged 'pathogenic' variant at a BRCA1-related position, associated with breast cancer risk. Following the pattern Tandy-Connor et al. (2018) documented, there is roughly a 40% chance this specific flag is a false positive, a miscall from the genotyping array rather than a real variant, and the false-positive rate is especially high for cancer-related genes like this one. The array's probe may have mis-hybridized at that position, or the raw-data file itself may contain an error the interpretation tool did not catch. The scientifically correct next step is not to panic or to dismiss it, but to order a clinical-grade diagnostic sequencing test targeted at that exact position, the same standard Tandy-Connor's team used to confirm or refute each of their 49 flagged variants.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes DTC genetics because these reports are the genetic information most students and their families have actually seen, and it is easy to treat a colorful pie chart or a red 'variant detected' flag as a diagnosis. A student who can state the actual technology (a fixed SNP array, not sequencing), cite the roughly 40% false-positive rate Tandy-Connor's team found for flagged variants, and explain why a risk percentage calibrated on European-ancestry GWAS data does not transfer cleanly to other ancestries is demonstrating they can separate consumer-grade screening from clinical-grade diagnosis -- exactly the distinction the FDA spent 2013-2017 forcing companies to make explicit.

questions.prompt: What does a typical DTC genetics chip actually measure?

options.text: The complete base-by-base sequence of the customer's genome
Genotype at a fixed, predetermined set of roughly 600,000-1,000,000 SNP sites
Only the customer's mitochondrial genome
Gene expression levels across all cell types

explanations.a: Full base-by-base sequencing is more expensive and is not what consumer microarray chips perform.
explanations.b: Correct -- a microarray checks genotype at a fixed, predetermined set of roughly 600,000 to 1,000,000 single-nucleotide sites chosen in advance, rather than reconstructing the whole sequence.
explanations.c: Most DTC chips genotype sites across the nuclear genome, not only mitochondrial DNA, though some mitochondrial markers are included.
explanations.d: Gene expression measurement (transcriptomics) is a different technology from genotype microarrays and is not what these consumer tests report.

questions.prompt: What did Tandy-Connor et al. (2018) find when they sent DTC-flagged variants for clinical confirmation testing?

options.text: Nearly all flagged variants were confirmed as accurate
About 40% of the flagged variants were false positives, most in cancer-related genes
Confirmation testing was impossible for DTC raw data
False positives were evenly spread across all types of genes with no pattern

explanations.a: The opposite was found -- a substantial share of flagged variants did not hold up under confirmation.
explanations.b: Correct -- about 40% of the 49 flagged variants tested were false positives on clinical confirmation, and 94% of those false positives were in cancer-risk genes.
explanations.c: Confirmation testing was performed successfully on all 49 samples; that is how the false-positive rate was measured.
explanations.d: False positives were concentrated in cancer-related genes (94% of them), not evenly distributed.

questions.prompt: Match each finding or event to its description.

right.text: Probes optimized for common variants are less reliable at rare, clinically important positions
Reported ancestry percentages can shift when a company updates its reference panel
Warning letter ordering 23andMe to stop marketing health-related results
Predictive accuracy is roughly 4.5 times lower in African-ancestry individuals than in Europeans

questions.explanation: Each item names a distinct limitation of DTC genetics: the array technology itself, the statistical nature of ancestry estimates, the regulatory history with the FDA, and the documented drop in polygenic risk score accuracy outside the mostly-European populations the scores were trained on.

questions.prompt: Why do polygenic risk scores (PRS) lose accuracy when applied to ancestries different from the training population, per Martin et al. (2019)?

options.text: PRS calculations only work for men, not women
GWAS training data are overwhelmingly European-ancestry, and linkage-disequilibrium patterns and allele frequencies differ across populations
Non-European genomes have fewer SNPs overall
PRS accuracy is identical across all ancestries by mathematical necessity

explanations.a: Sex is not the driver of PRS portability problems; ancestry composition of the training data is.
explanations.b: Correct -- most PRS are trained on European-ancestry GWAS cohorts, and differing linkage-disequilibrium patterns and allele frequencies in other populations mean the score's calibration does not transfer, with R-squared roughly 4.5 times lower in African-ancestry individuals than Europeans.
explanations.c: All human populations carry large numbers of SNPs; the issue is training-data composition, not SNP quantity in non-European genomes.
explanations.d: Accuracy is documented to differ substantially across ancestries, not to be identical by necessity.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the FDA's regulatory history with 23andMe.

items.text: FDA sends a warning letter ordering 23andMe to stop marketing health-related results (2013)
23andMe restricted to selling only ancestry and raw data reports
FDA authorizes carrier-status reports (2015)
FDA authorizes Genetic Health Risk reports, including late-onset Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease (2017)

questions.explanation: The FDA's 2013 warning letter came first, leading 23andMe to restrict its offerings to ancestry and raw data; carrier-status reports were authorized in 2015; and full Genetic Health Risk reports were authorized on April 6, 2017.

lessons.label: Designing a Genetics Project That Holds Up

sections.heading: Four project shapes that fit a school lab
sections.body: Four project shapes reliably fit a school lab's budget and safety envelope. PCR/RFLP genotyping amplifies a short DNA region spanning a known common SNP (a well-worn example is the PTC bitter-taste receptor gene, TAS2R38) and uses a restriction enzyme that cuts differently depending on the allele, so gel band patterns reveal genotype. DNA barcoding amplifies a standardized marker, the COI gene in animals or rbcL/ITS in plants, and compares the sequence against a reference database like BOLD to identify species -- the same method behind studies finding roughly a third of tested seafood mislabeled. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) measures how much a gene's expression changes under a treatment, typically reported as fold-change via the delta-delta-Ct method. Reanalyzing public data, from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) or the 1000 Genomes Project, needs no wet lab at all, just a defensible new question asked of someone else's deposited dataset.

sections.heading: What each shape demands: controls, replicates, blinding
sections.body: Each shape has non-negotiable structure. RFLP genotyping needs known homozygous controls for each allele plus a no-template control to catch contamination, and enough samples that one miscalled band does not decide the result. DNA barcoding needs a reference sequence pulled independently, not just judged 'close enough' by eye, and ideally a blind sample-labeling scheme so whoever reads the gel or sequence does not know which sample is which. qPCR needs a stable reference (housekeeping) gene, biological replicates from separate individuals or cultures rather than just repeated pipetting of one sample (a technical replicate), and a pre-registered comparison rather than fishing through genes until one looks significant.

sections.heading: The rules that trip students up: human subjects, biosafety
sections.body: Two rules catch students by surprise. Under ISEF (Society for Science) regulations, collecting DNA from classmates counts as human-subjects research, requiring Institutional Review Board or Scientific Review Committee approval and signed informed consent (or, for minors, parental permission plus student assent) before any sample is collected, not after and not as a formality once data already exist. Microbiology work is bounded by Biosafety Level 1 (BSL-1): only non-pathogenic organisms, such as standard laboratory E. coli K-12 strains, can be handled in an unmodified school lab without additional institutional biosafety review, ruling out anything isolated from a wild or clinical source without prior clearance.

sections.heading: Demonstrating a technique is not testing a hypothesis
sections.body: The last trap is conceptual, not procedural: running a PCR and showing a clean band on a gel demonstrates that a technique works, but it is not a hypothesis test. A real test needs a stated prediction, an independent variable the experimenter actually manipulates or a comparison group that differs in some defined way, and a way to fail -- a result that would have looked different if the prediction were wrong. 'I extracted and amplified DNA successfully' is a methods-validation step; 'genotype at this locus differs between groups X and Y at a rate better than chance' is a testable claim.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to test whether herbal 'echinacea' supplements sold locally actually contain Echinacea DNA. They buy five supplement brands, extract DNA from each capsule's contents, PCR-amplify the ITS2 barcode region, and Sanger-sequence the product, including a known Echinacea purpurea leaf sample as a positive control and a no-template reaction as a negative control. They BLAST each sequence against GenBank, and the results come back: two brands match Echinacea, one matches a related but non-medicinal Asteraceae species, and two return no clean chromatogram at all, most likely from degraded or below-threshold template DNA. That last result is itself a finding worth reporting, not a failure to hide, because it identifies a detection limit rather than fabricating a false negative for genuine adulteration.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about project design specifically to check whether a student picked a doable, controlled experiment or backed into a demo they are dressing up as research. The tell is whether the student can name their controls unprompted (what would a false positive or a contaminated blank have looked like?), their replicate structure (biological versus technical), and, if human DNA was involved, that they went through IRB/SRC approval and informed consent before collecting a single sample -- because skipping that step is not just a paperwork gap, it is disqualifying at ISEF regardless of how good the science underneath it is.

questions.prompt: Which of the four project shapes requires no wet-lab work at all?

options.text: PCR/RFLP genotyping of a common SNP
DNA barcoding of market fish or herbal supplements
Reanalysis of public data from GEO or the 1000 Genomes Project
qPCR measurement of gene expression under a treatment

explanations.a: RFLP genotyping requires DNA extraction, PCR, restriction digestion, and gel electrophoresis, all wet-lab steps.
explanations.b: DNA barcoding requires DNA extraction, PCR amplification, and sequencing, all wet-lab steps.
explanations.c: Correct -- reanalyzing deposited public datasets from GEO or the 1000 Genomes Project needs no wet lab, only a defensible new question and appropriate statistical analysis of existing data.
explanations.d: qPCR requires cell or tissue treatment, RNA extraction, and quantitative PCR, all wet-lab steps.

questions.prompt: Match each project type to a non-negotiable requirement it needs to hold up.

right.text: Known homozygous controls for each allele plus a no-template control
An independently pulled reference sequence and blind sample labeling
A stable housekeeping gene and true biological (not just technical) replicates
A pre-registered question rather than fishing through variables until one looks significant

questions.explanation: Each project type fails for a different reason without its core safeguard: RFLP without controls cannot rule out contamination or a miscall, barcoding without an independent reference and blinding invites biased matching, qPCR without a housekeeping gene and biological replicates cannot separate a real effect from noise, and public-data reanalysis without a pre-registered question risks capitalizing on chance patterns.

questions.prompt: Under ISEF rules, what must happen before a student collects DNA samples from classmates?

options.text: Nothing extra, since classmates are not considered human subjects for a school project
IRB or Scientific Review Committee approval and signed informed consent (or parental permission and assent for minors) must be obtained first
Approval can be obtained after data collection, as long as it is in place before the fair
Only a teacher's verbal permission is needed

explanations.a: Collecting DNA from classmates does count as human-subjects research under ISEF rules, not an exemption.
explanations.b: Correct -- IRB or SRC approval and informed consent (with parental permission and assent for minors) are required before any sample is collected.
explanations.c: Approval obtained after the fact does not satisfy the requirement; it must precede sample collection.
explanations.d: A verbal teacher permission does not meet the formal IRB/SRC and informed-consent requirements ISEF specifies.

questions.prompt: A student runs PCR on classmate DNA, gets a clean band on a gel, and concludes their project is finished. What is missing for this to count as a hypothesis test rather than a technique demonstration?

options.text: Nothing; a clean band is sufficient evidence for any genetics claim
A stated prediction, a real comparison or manipulated variable, and a result that could have come out differently if the prediction were wrong
A louder gel-imaging light source
A larger PCR machine

explanations.a: A clean band shows the technique worked; it does not by itself test any comparative claim.
explanations.b: Correct -- a hypothesis test needs a stated prediction, a genuine comparison or manipulated variable, and the possibility of a result that would have looked different had the prediction been wrong.
explanations.c: Imaging brightness is a technical detail unrelated to whether the study tests a hypothesis.
explanations.d: Equipment scale does not turn a methods demonstration into a hypothesis test.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a DNA barcoding project testing supplement mislabeling.

items.text: Extract DNA from each supplement sample
PCR-amplify the standardized barcode region (e.g., ITS2)
Sequence the amplified product
Compare the sequence against a reference database to identify the species

questions.explanation: Barcoding proceeds from extracting DNA, to amplifying the standardized marker region by PCR, to sequencing that product, and finally to comparing the resulting sequence against a reference database to determine species identity.

lessons.label: Ethics, Privacy, and the Judge's Hardest Questions

sections.heading: Why genomic data is a uniquely hard privacy problem
sections.body: Genomic data breaks the usual privacy playbook in three ways at once: it is unchangeable (you cannot issue yourself a new genome the way you reset a leaked password), it is inherently familial (your genome reveals information about parents, siblings, and children who never agreed to be tested), and it is re-identifiable even when 'anonymized.' Gymrek et al. (2013) demonstrated the last point starkly: by profiling short tandem repeats on the Y chromosome from supposedly de-identified genomes in public research databases and cross-referencing them against free recreational genealogy websites, they recovered the surnames, and from there the identities, of multiple project participants using nothing but public data. A dataset stripped of names is not the same as a dataset that cannot be traced back to a name.

sections.heading: The legal gap: GINA covers less than people assume
sections.body: Law has not caught up evenly. The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 (GINA) bars employers from using genetic information in hiring decisions and bars health insurers from using it to set premiums or deny coverage. But GINA's protection stops there by design: it does not cover life insurance, disability insurance, or long-term-care insurance, all of which can legally consider genetic test results in some states. A student who assumes 'GINA protects my genetic privacy' without naming this gap has memorized a headline, not the actual scope of the law.

sections.heading: Incidental findings and the ACMG list
sections.body: Clinical sequencing surfaces information the patient never asked for. The American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) maintains a list of genes considered medically actionable enough that labs should report a pathogenic finding back to the patient even when it is unrelated to why the sequencing was ordered, for example discovering a BRCA1 mutation while sequencing for an unrelated childhood condition. The list started at 56 genes covering 24 conditions in 2013 and has grown with each update as evidence accumulates, reflecting a deliberate policy choice: some incidental findings are actionable enough (preventable, treatable) that withholding them would itself be an ethical failure, even though the patient did not specifically consent to learning them.

sections.heading: The ancestry-representation gap has a concrete cost
sections.body: Genomic reference databases are still disproportionately built from European-ancestry participants, and that skew has a measurable clinical cost. Manrai et al. (2016) found that several variants once classified as causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy were actually common, benign polymorphisms that happened to be rare in the mostly-European control populations used to validate them; because those variants are significantly more common in Black Americans, patients of African ancestry were disproportionately given false pathogenic diagnoses. The same imbalance drives higher rates of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in non-European patients, simply because there is less reference data to compare against. Facing 'should this technology be used?', a defensible answer names the specific stakeholders and harms, weighs them against a specific benefit, and cites a concrete safeguard rather than a flat yes or no.

lessons.workedExample: A judge asks a student presenting a DTC ancestry-testing project: 'Should companies sell genetic testing kits without genetic counselors involved?' A weak answer is 'yes, people have a right to know their DNA' or 'no, it's dangerous.' A defensible answer names the actual stakeholders (the customer, untested relatives whose data becomes inferable, future customers relying on panel accuracy), the actual harm (a false-positive cancer flag acted on without confirmation, or a relative re-identified from someone else's raw-data upload), and a concrete existing safeguard that partially addresses it (the FDA's 2017 authorization required proven analytical validity for exactly this reason, and clinical confirmation testing is the actual fix for false positives) -- then states a specific position given those trade-offs.
lessons.judgeFraming: Ethics and privacy questions are the ones most students answer worst, because they default to a gut reaction dressed up as an argument. A judge probing this lesson checks for the reasoning move: identify who exactly is affected, including people who never consented, like relatives; name the specific mechanism of harm, such as Gymrek-style surname re-identification, GINA's insurance coverage gap, or a VUS produced by a thin reference panel; and connect that harm to an existing, real safeguard rather than an invented one. A student who says 'genetic privacy matters' has said nothing a judge cannot already predict; one who names GINA's life-insurance gap has said something checkable.

questions.prompt: What makes genomic data a uniquely hard privacy problem compared to something like a password?

options.text: It is unchangeable, inherently familial, and re-identifiable even when stripped of names
It can be easily reset if it leaks
It only reveals information about the tested individual, never their relatives
It becomes useless once a database is 'anonymized'

explanations.a: Correct -- unlike a password, a genome cannot be reset, it reveals information about relatives who never consented, and Gymrek et al. (2013) showed it can be re-identified from 'anonymized' data using public genealogy databases.
explanations.b: The opposite is true; a genome cannot be reset or reissued the way a compromised password can.
explanations.c: Genomic data is inherently familial -- it reveals information about parents, siblings, and children, not just the tested individual.
explanations.d: Gymrek et al. (2013) demonstrated that 'anonymized' genomic data can still be re-identified using public resources.

questions.prompt: What does GINA (2008) actually protect against, and what does it leave uncovered?

options.text: It bars genetic discrimination in employment and health insurance, but not in life, disability, or long-term-care insurance
It bars genetic discrimination in all forms of insurance, with no exceptions
It only applies to health insurance, not employment
It bans all collection of genetic information by any company
It regulates DTC ancestry percentages but not employment or insurance

explanations.a: Correct -- GINA bars genetic discrimination in employment decisions and health insurance, but by design does not cover life, disability, or long-term-care insurance.
explanations.b: GINA's protections stop short of life, disability, and long-term-care insurance; it is not comprehensive across all insurance types.
explanations.c: GINA covers both employment and health insurance, not just one of the two.
explanations.d: GINA restricts how genetic information can be used in specific contexts; it does not ban collection outright.
explanations.e: GINA is an employment and health-insurance discrimination law; it does not regulate DTC ancestry reporting practices.

questions.prompt: Match each policy or study to its core finding or role.

right.text: Recovered identities from de-identified genomes using Y-STR profiles and public genealogy databases
Bars genetic discrimination in employment and health insurance, but not life/disability/long-term-care insurance
Names medically actionable genes labs should report even when unrelated to the original reason for sequencing
Found cardiomyopathy variants misclassified as pathogenic largely because reference panels underrepresented Black Americans

questions.explanation: Each item addresses a distinct facet of genomic ethics: Gymrek shows re-identification risk, GINA shows the legal protection and its limits, the ACMG list shows the incidental-findings policy, and Manrai shows a concrete downstream cost of ancestry bias in reference data.

questions.prompt: According to Manrai et al. (2016), why were some hypertrophic cardiomyopathy variants misclassified as pathogenic for years?

options.text: They were newly evolved mutations with no prior data available
They were common, benign variants that happened to be rare in the mostly-European control populations used to validate the original classification
Laboratory equipment used at the time could not detect them accurately
The variants were deliberately mislabeled by researchers

explanations.a: The variants were not new mutations; they were long-present, common, benign polymorphisms misjudged as pathogenic.
explanations.b: Correct -- because these variants were rare in the largely European-ancestry control populations used to validate pathogenicity, but significantly more common in Black Americans, they were misclassified as disease-causing.
explanations.c: The issue was reference-population composition and classification methodology, not equipment sensitivity.
explanations.d: There is no indication of deliberate mislabeling; the error traced to underrepresentation in reference control populations.

questions.prompt: Order the steps Gymrek et al. (2013) used to re-identify individuals from supposedly de-identified genomic data.

items.text: Obtain a de-identified genome from a public research database
Extract the Y-chromosome short tandem repeat (Y-STR) profile
Query recreational genetic-genealogy websites for surname matches to that Y-STR profile
Combine the recovered surname with other public metadata (such as age and state) to identify the individual

questions.explanation: The re-identification chain started from a public de-identified genome, extracted its Y-STR profile, matched that profile to a surname using public genealogy databases, and then combined the surname with other available metadata to pin down a specific individual.

lessons.label: What a Read Actually Is

sections.heading: A read is a fragment, not a genome
sections.body: A modern sequencer never hands you a genome. It hands you a pile of short fragments called reads, each a string of base calls (A/C/G/T, plus N for "couldn't tell") paired with a per-base confidence score. A single Illumina run typically produces on the order of 10^8 to 10^9 reads, each only 50-300 bases long, because the sequencing chemistry can only reliably read a short stretch before the signal degrades — the DNA library is chopped into millions of overlapping fragments first, sequenced independently, and reassembled computationally afterward. Nothing about a read tells you where in the genome it came from; that placement is the alignment step's job, not the sequencer's.

sections.heading: Single-end vs. paired-end, and insert size
sections.body: Single-end sequencing reads a fragment from one end only. Paired-end sequencing reads both ends of the same fragment, producing two reads (R1 and R2) that are anchored to each other with a known approximate separation called the insert size — the length of the original DNA fragment between the two sequenced ends. Paired reads are far more informative: they let you span repetitive regions no single short read could resolve, detect structural variants when the pair's orientation or spacing looks wrong, and improve mapping confidence, at roughly double the sequencing cost.

sections.heading: Coverage depth: why 30x means ~90 Gb for a human genome
sections.body: Because a read is a random small sample of the genome, you don't sequence once — you oversample so that most bases are covered by many independent reads, letting you distinguish a true variant from a sequencing error by consensus. Coverage depth (or "read depth") is the average number of reads overlapping a given base. Whole-genome sequencing at 30x — the standard depth for clinical-grade human WGS — means, on average, 30 independent reads cover every base of the roughly 3.1 billion base pair (3.1 Gb) haploid human genome, i.e., 30 x 3.1 Gb ≈ 93 Gb of raw sequence generated per genome. 30x isn't a round number chosen for its own sake: at a heterozygous site, a sequencer samples the two alleles roughly 50/50 by chance, so at low depth a short run of reads drawn from just one allele can look like a homozygous call. Confidently calling heterozygous SNPs against that binomial sampling noise needs roughly 15-20x as a practical floor. 30x sits comfortably above that floor, leaving a margin for the fact that coverage is never perfectly even — GC-rich or repetitive regions sequence less efficiently, and PCR duplicates or off-target reads get filtered out — so the depth that's actually usable stays adequate everywhere, not just on average. Lower depth (e.g., exome sequencing at 50-100x, or low-pass WGS at under 5x) trades base-level confidence for either targeted coverage or cost, and this is a data-volume question, independent of which chemistry produced the reads.

lessons.workedExample: A lab sequences a human sample at a nominal 30x whole-genome depth using 150 bp paired-end reads. To hit ~93 Gb of total sequence (30 x 3.1 Gb genome), they need roughly 93 Gb / 300 bp per read pair ≈ 310 million read pairs (620 million individual reads). If the insert size is 350 bp, each pair samples a 350 bp fragment but only sequences the outer ~150 bp from each end, leaving a ~50 bp gap in the middle unread directly by either mate — that gap is inferred only once the pair is aligned to a reference. A student who reports "we sequenced the genome" without stating read length, pairing, and depth has not specified an experiment; those three numbers are what let anyone else judge whether the data could even detect the variant being claimed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes "what is a read?" because it is the fastest way to tell whether a student who says "we sequenced the genome" understands that a sequencer outputs millions of short, unassembled fragments with per-base confidence, not a finished genome. A strong answer states the read length and depth used, explains why paired-end and insert size matter for the specific question being asked, and can do the back-of-envelope coverage arithmetic (depth x genome size = total bases needed) — showing the number was a design choice, not a black box the pipeline handed them.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much total sequence data (in gigabases) is needed for 30x whole-genome coverage of the ~3.1 Gb human genome?

options.text: About 3 Gb
About 30 Gb
About 93 Gb
About 300 Gb

explanations.a: 3 Gb is roughly one genome's worth of sequence, equivalent to only ~1x coverage, not 30x.
explanations.b: 30 Gb undercounts by a factor of 3 — depth multiplies genome size, so 30x is 30, not 10, times the genome.
explanations.c: Correct — 30x coverage means 30 reads overlapping each base on average: 30 x 3.1 Gb ≈ 93 Gb of total sequence.
explanations.d: 300 Gb would be roughly 100x coverage, far deeper than the standard 30x clinical WGS target.

questions.prompt: What does the insert size describe in paired-end sequencing?

options.text: The length of each individual read
The approximate length of the original DNA fragment spanned by the two paired reads
The number of reads produced per run
The confidence score assigned to each base call

explanations.a: Read length is how many bases are sequenced from each end; insert size is the full fragment length, usually longer than either read.
explanations.b: Correct — insert size is the known approximate distance between the two ends of the original fragment, which the pair of reads brackets even though the middle may go unsequenced.
explanations.c: That describes throughput, a property of the whole run, not of one fragment.
explanations.d: That describes a Phred-style quality score, a separate per-base property covered elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it describes about sequencing output.

right.text: A single short base-call string with per-base confidence, not yet placed in the genome
Sequencing both ends of the same DNA fragment
The average number of reads overlapping a given genomic base
The length of the original fragment spanned by a read pair

questions.explanation: A read is one unplaced base-call string; paired-end sequencing reads both fragment ends; coverage depth is how many reads overlap each base; insert size is the fragment length the pair spans.

questions.prompt: Why does a single Illumina run produce hundreds of millions of short reads rather than one long continuous readout of the genome?

options.text: Because the DNA library is fragmented into many short pieces before sequencing, and each piece is read independently
Because human genomes are only a few hundred bases long
Because the sequencer intentionally skips most of the genome to save cost
Because paired-end sequencing halves the number of reads produced

explanations.a: Correct — the sequencing chemistry can only reliably call bases for a short stretch, so the genome is chopped into millions of overlapping fragments and each is sequenced separately, to be reassembled computationally afterward.
explanations.b: The human genome is about 3.1 billion bases; the mismatch with short reads is a chemistry limit, not genome size.
explanations.c: Whole-genome sequencing aims to cover the full genome via overlapping fragments, not to skip regions; targeted skipping describes exome sequencing, a different design choice.
explanations.d: Paired-end sequencing produces two reads per fragment (more reads, not fewer) and does not explain why reads are short in the first place.

lessons.label: Phred Scores and the FASTQ Format

sections.heading: Phred: turning a base call into a probability
sections.body: Every base a sequencer calls comes with a confidence score, and the standard for expressing that confidence traces to the phred base-calling software Ewing and Green described in 1998 for Sanger trace data, later adopted wholesale by NGS platforms. A Phred quality score Q is defined as Q = -10 log10(P), where P is the estimated probability that the base call is wrong. The scale is logarithmic and each 10-point jump means a tenfold drop in error probability: Q10 means a 1-in-10 chance of error (10% error), Q20 means 1-in-100 (1% error), Q30 means 1-in-1,000 (0.1% error), and Q40 means 1-in-10,000 (0.01% error). Q30 is the conventional bar for "good" sequencing data — most Illumina QC pipelines report the percent of bases at Q30 or higher as a headline run-quality metric.

sections.heading: FASTQ: four lines, one read
sections.body: FASTQ is the plain-text format that pairs a read's sequence with its per-base quality string. Every record is exactly four lines: a header line starting with '@' (read ID and run metadata), the base-call sequence itself, a '+' separator line (optionally repeating the header), and a quality string the same length as the sequence, one character per base. Each quality character is a single ASCII symbol encoding that base's Phred score, so a 150-base read has a 150-character quality line that lines up positionally with the sequence line above it.

sections.heading: The ASCII offset trap and quality decay
sections.body: Quality scores are packed into printable ASCII by adding an offset to Q. The modern standard (Sanger FASTQ, and Illumina pipeline version 1.8 onward) uses offset 33, so Q0 is '!' (ASCII 33) and Q40 is 'I' (ASCII 73). Older Illumina pipelines (versions 1.3 through 1.7) used offset 64 instead, so the same numeric Q30 is a completely different character under the two schemes. A parser that guesses the wrong offset silently misreads every quality score — often by exactly 31 — without throwing an error, which is why offset-64 legacy files (still occasionally exported by old instruments or re-shared archives) remain a real, recurring bug source: tools like FastQC flag suspicious quality ranges specifically to catch this. Within a read, quality is not flat: it is typically highest in the early cycles and decays toward the 3' end as the sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry accumulates phasing error and signal decay over successive cycles, which is why most trimming tools cut low-quality tails rather than treating a whole read as uniformly reliable.

lessons.workedExample: A student inherits a FASTQ file where the quality line for one read is 'hhhhhggggg^^^^^AAAAA' under offset-33 assumptions. Decoding: 'h' is ASCII 104, so Q = 104 - 33 = 71 — an impossible Phred score (max is usually ~41 for Illumina), a red flag that this file is actually offset-64. Re-decoding at offset 64: Q = 104 - 64 = 40 (Q40, 0.01% error) for the 'h' bases, dropping to Q = 94 - 64 = 30 ('^' is ASCII 94, so Q30) in the middle, then Q = 65 - 64 = 1 ('A' is ASCII 65) at the end — a believable decay from confident bases at the read start to near-worthless bases at the tail, matching the expected 5'-to-3' quality drop.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about Phred scores and FASTQ because misreading the offset is a silent, self-inflicted data corruption that a student can commit without any error message — it produces a plausible-looking but wrong dataset. A strong answer states the Q = -10 log10(P) relationship, can convert a Q value to an error rate on the spot (Q30 = 0.1%), names the offset-33-vs-64 distinction as the reason a raw ASCII character is meaningless without knowing the platform version, and explains why trimming targets the 3' tail specifically rather than the whole read.

questions.prompt: A base call has a Phred quality score of Q30. What is its estimated probability of being an error?

explanations.a: 10% error corresponds to Q10, not Q30 — each 10-point increase is a tenfold drop in error probability.
explanations.b: 1% error corresponds to Q20; Q30 is one more tenfold improvement beyond that.
explanations.c: Correct — Q = -10 log10(P), so Q30 means P = 10^(-30/10) = 10^-3 = 0.1% error probability.
explanations.d: 0.01% error corresponds to Q40, one tenfold step more accurate than Q30.

questions.prompt: Why is the FASTQ ASCII offset (33 vs. 64) important to get right when parsing a file?

options.text: It changes the number of lines per record from four to five
It determines which sequencing platform produced the sample
Using the wrong offset silently converts every quality character to the wrong Phred score, with no parse error
It only affects the header line, not the quality scores

explanations.a: The four-line record structure (header, sequence, '+', quality) is fixed regardless of the offset used to encode quality.
explanations.b: The offset reflects the software pipeline version used to generate the file, not the physical instrument model.
explanations.c: Correct — offset-33 and offset-64 map the same ASCII character to different Q values (a difference of 31), and a parser applying the wrong one produces plausible-looking but silently wrong quality scores for every base.
explanations.d: The offset applies specifically to decoding the quality string, not the header line.

questions.prompt: Order the four lines of a single FASTQ record from first to last.

items.text: '@' header line with read ID
Base-call sequence (A/C/G/T/N)
'+' separator line
Quality string, one character per base

questions.explanation: Every FASTQ record is exactly four lines in this fixed order: the '@' header, the sequence, the '+' separator, and the quality string aligned position-for-position with the sequence.

questions.prompt: Within a single read, where does sequencing quality typically decay the most?

options.text: It decays toward the 3' (later-cycle) end of the read as phasing and signal error accumulate
It decays toward the 5' (earliest-cycle) end of the read
Quality is uniform across the whole read by design
Quality decays only in paired-end reads, never in single-end reads

explanations.a: Correct — quality is typically highest in early cycles and drops toward the read's 3' tail as sequencing-by-synthesis error accumulates cycle over cycle, which is why trimming tools target the tail.
explanations.b: This reverses the actual pattern; early cycles are the most reliable, not the least.
explanations.c: Quality reliably declines across a read; treating it as uniform is exactly the mistake quality-trimming is meant to correct.
explanations.d: The 5'-to-3' decay pattern arises from the sequencing chemistry itself and applies to both single-end and paired-end reads.

lessons.label: Reference Genomes and Coordinate Systems

sections.heading: A position number is meaningless without a build
sections.body: "Chromosome 7, position 117,559,590" only identifies a real location if you also say which reference genome assembly that number is drawn from. GRCh37 (released 2009, also called hg19 in UCSC's naming) was the human reference for roughly a decade and still underlies huge amounts of legacy clinical and research data. GRCh38 (released December 2013) fixed thousands of assembly errors, added alt/decoy contigs, and shifted coordinates across the genome — the same biological base can sit at a different position number, or even a different chromosome arm's worth of offset, between the two builds. More recently, the Telomere-to-Telomere Consortium's CHM13 assembly (Nurk et al., published in Science in 2022) closed nearly all remaining gaps, including centromeres and repetitive regions GRCh38 left unresolved, giving a third coordinate system in active use. Any coordinate reported without its build is not actually reproducible.

sections.heading: Naming conventions and alt/decoy contigs
sections.body: Even within one build, chromosome names are not standardized: UCSC's browser and file formats use 'chr1', 'chr2', ..., 'chrX', while Ensembl and NCBI conventionally drop the prefix ('1', '2', ..., 'X'). Mixing the two silently produces zero overlap between two files that actually describe the same genome, because 'chr1' and '1' are different strings to a naive tool. GRCh38 also introduced alt contigs (alternate sequence representations of highly variable regions, like the MHC locus, where one linear reference can't capture real population diversity) and decoy sequences (contigs added purely to absorb reads that would otherwise misalign to the primary assembly) — a reference file with alts/decoys included is not a strict superset of one without them for alignment purposes, since decoys change where reads land.

sections.heading: 0-based half-open vs. 1-based inclusive: the classic off-by-one
sections.body: Genomic file formats split into two incompatible counting conventions. BED format is 0-based, half-open: the first base of a chromosome is position 0, and an interval [start, end) excludes its end coordinate, so a BED interval '0 10' covers exactly the first 10 bases. VCF, GFF, and SAM are 1-based, inclusive: the first base is position 1, and an interval's end coordinate is itself included. Converting between them requires adding or subtracting exactly 1 at the boundary, and getting it backward is the single most common off-by-one bug in bioinformatics — it silently shifts every reported feature by one base rather than crashing, so it often survives into published results. When coordinates must move between genome builds (not just formats), tools like UCSC's liftOver use build-to-build alignment chain files to remap positions; a meaningful fraction of positions — especially in repetitive, structurally rearranged, or newly resolved regions — fail to lift over at all or map ambiguously to multiple locations, so liftOver output must be checked, never trusted blindly.

lessons.workedExample: A team has a BED file listing a gene's exon as 'chr7 117559592 117559644' (0-based half-open) and needs to report the same exon in VCF-style 1-based inclusive coordinates for a paper. The correct conversion adds 1 to the start only: the BED start 117559592 becomes VCF start 117559593, while the BED end 117559644 stays 117559644 as the VCF end (since BED's exclusive end already equals the last included base index once you're in 1-based counting). Reporting 'start 117559592, end 117559644' as if it were 1-based, or reporting both boundaries shifted by 1, both create an off-by-one error that shrinks or grows the exon by exactly one base — the kind of error that looks fine at a glance and only surfaces when someone tries to reproduce the region.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about coordinate systems because it is the fastest test of whether a student actually handled real genomic files or just plotted numbers someone else already aligned. A strong answer names the specific reference build used (not just "the human genome"), can state whether a given file format is 0-based half-open or 1-based inclusive, and — if the project crossed genome builds — can say what fraction of their positions liftOver failed to remap and how they handled that failure rather than silently dropping it.

questions.prompt: Why is a genomic position like "chr7:117559590" ambiguous on its own?

options.text: Because chromosome 7 does not have that many bases
Because the same numeric position can refer to different underlying bases depending on the reference genome build (e.g., GRCh37 vs. GRCh38)
Because positions are always reported in scientific notation
Because chromosome 7 is not present in the human genome

explanations.a: Chromosome 7 is about 159 million base pairs, so a position around 117.5 million is well within range; that is not the issue.
explanations.b: Correct — GRCh37, GRCh38, and T2T-CHM13 assign different coordinates to the same biological base, so a position number is meaningless without stating which build it came from.
explanations.c: Positions are reported as plain integers, not scientific notation; formatting is not the source of ambiguity here.
explanations.d: Chromosome 7 is a standard human autosome present in every build; it is not the problem.

questions.prompt: Match each reference-genome concept to its description.

right.text: Released 2009; also called hg19; underlies much legacy clinical/research data
Released 2013; fixed assembly errors and shifted coordinates genome-wide relative to the prior build
Published 2022 (Nurk et al., Science); closed remaining gaps including centromeric and repetitive regions
Extra reference sequence added only to absorb reads that would otherwise misalign to the primary assembly

questions.explanation: GRCh37 (2009, hg19) was the reference for roughly a decade; GRCh38 (2013) fixed errors and shifted coordinates; T2T-CHM13 (Nurk et al. 2022) closed the remaining gaps GRCh38 left unresolved; decoy contigs exist purely to catch misaligning reads, not to represent real annotated sequence.

questions.prompt: A student merges a UCSC-style BED file (chromosomes named 'chr1', 'chr2', ...) with an Ensembl-style annotation file ('1', '2', ...) and gets zero overlapping features, even though both describe the same genome build. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The two files use different genome builds entirely
The chromosome-naming mismatch ('chr1' vs '1') makes every feature fail to match as a naive string comparison
BED files cannot contain gene annotations
One of the files must be corrupted

explanations.a: The scenario states both files describe the same build; the failure is about naming convention, not build mismatch.
explanations.b: Correct — 'chr1' and '1' are different strings to a naive tool even though they name the identical chromosome, so every comparison silently fails to match without an explicit renaming step.
explanations.c: BED is a general interval format and is commonly used for gene or feature annotations; that is not the limitation here.
explanations.d: Neither file needs to be corrupted for this failure — the naming convention mismatch alone fully explains zero overlaps.

questions.prompt: What does the UCSC liftOver tool do, and what is the important caveat when using it?

options.text: It converts FASTQ quality encodings between offset-33 and offset-64; it has no failure cases
It remaps coordinates from one genome build to another using alignment chain files; some positions fail to lift over or map ambiguously and must be checked, not assumed to succeed
It converts SAM files to BAM; failures are always reported as fatal errors
It renames 'chr1'-style chromosome names to Ensembl-style names; it always succeeds

explanations.a: That describes a FASTQ encoding fix, an unrelated tool and problem.
explanations.b: Correct — liftOver uses chain files built from build-to-build alignments to remap positions, and a meaningful fraction of positions (especially in repetitive or rearranged regions) fail or map to multiple places, so output needs verification.
explanations.c: That describes format conversion (e.g., samtools), not build-to-build coordinate remapping.
explanations.d: Renaming chromosome prefixes is a simpler, separate operation; liftOver's job and risk is coordinate remapping across builds, not renaming.

lessons.label: Alignment Files: SAM, BAM, and CRAM

sections.heading: SAM's 11 mandatory fields
sections.body: Once a read is aligned to a reference, the result is stored as a SAM (Sequence Alignment/Map) record — one line per read, tab-separated, with 11 mandatory fields: QNAME (read name), FLAG (a bitfield of yes/no properties, below), RNAME (reference chromosome), POS (1-based leftmost mapping position), MAPQ (mapping-quality score), CIGAR (how the read matches the reference, below), RNEXT and PNEXT (the mate read's reference and position, for paired data), TLEN (observed template/insert length), SEQ (the read's base calls), and QUAL (the read's Phred quality string). Optional tagged fields follow for aligner-specific metadata. A raw text SAM file is human-readable but large; BAM is its binary, compressed, indexable equivalent, and is what pipelines actually pass around.

sections.heading: FLAG bits and CIGAR strings
sections.body: FLAG packs several independent booleans into one integer via bitwise flags: bit 0x4 means the read is unmapped, 0x10 means it aligned to the reverse strand, and 0x400 marks the read as a PCR or optical duplicate (an artifact of library prep, not a true independent observation, typically excluded from variant calling). A FLAG of 0 means none of the flagged conditions apply — a simple, forward-strand, mapped, non-duplicate read. CIGAR describes, base by base, how a read's sequence lines up against the reference: M means match or mismatch (aligned, not necessarily identical), I is an insertion relative to the reference, D is a deletion relative to the reference, S is soft-clipping (bases present in the read but excluded from the alignment, still stored in SEQ), H is hard-clipping (bases removed entirely from the record), and N is a skipped reference region, used for RNA-seq reads spanning an intron. A CIGAR string like '76M2D24M' means 76 aligned bases, then a 2-base deletion relative to the reference, then 24 more aligned bases — reading it lets you reconstruct exactly how the 100-base read maps onto the reference coordinates starting at POS.

sections.heading: MAPQ, sorting/indexing, and CRAM's tradeoff
sections.body: MAPQ estimates confidence in the read's placement the same way Phred estimates confidence in a base call: MAPQ = -10 log10(P), where P is the probability the alignment position is wrong — so MAPQ 30 means roughly a 0.1% chance the read is actually mismapped, often because the sequence is repetitive and could equally fit elsewhere. For downstream tools to query a region efficiently, a BAM file must be coordinate-sorted (records ordered by RNAME then POS) and indexed, producing a companion .bai file that lets tools jump directly to a region instead of scanning the whole file. CRAM compresses further by storing only the differences between each read and the reference sequence rather than the full read sequence — often roughly halving file size versus BAM — but this means a CRAM file is not self-contained: decoding it correctly requires access to the exact reference sequence (and build) it was compressed against, and losing or mismatching that reference makes the file unreadable or silently wrong.

lessons.workedExample: A 100 bp read has FLAG 16, POS 1001, MAPQ 60, and CIGAR '10S85M5I'. FLAG 16 (binary for 0x10) means the read aligned to the reverse strand and nothing else unusual applies. The CIGAR says: the first 10 bases are soft-clipped (not part of the alignment, e.g., adapter sequence), the next 85 bases align to the reference starting at position 1001 (covering reference positions 1001-1085), and the final 5 bases are an insertion relative to the reference (present in the read, absent from the reference, so they don't consume reference coordinates). MAPQ 60 signals very high confidence — this read maps essentially uniquely, unlike a repetitive read that might land at MAPQ 0-3 because it fits several genomic locations equally well.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes SAM/BAM/CRAM because being able to read a CIGAR string and a FLAG value by hand is the clearest proof a student actually inspected their own alignment data rather than trusting a pipeline's summary plot. A strong answer can decode a FLAG into its component bits, walk through what a CIGAR string like '76M2D24M' implies about the underlying biology (here, a 2-base deletion), state what MAPQ is estimating and why repetitive regions produce low values, and knows that a CRAM file is unusable without its exact matching reference — a real failure mode when data gets shared without that reference attached.

questions.prompt: A SAM record has CIGAR '76M2D24M'. What does this describe?

options.text: 76 aligned bases, a 2-base insertion, then 24 more aligned bases
76 aligned bases, a 2-base deletion relative to the reference, then 24 more aligned bases
A read entirely unmapped except for 2 matching bases
76 soft-clipped bases followed by 26 aligned bases

explanations.a: 'I' denotes an insertion; this CIGAR uses 'D', which denotes a deletion relative to the reference, not an insertion.
explanations.b: Correct — 'M' is aligned bases (match/mismatch), 'D' is a deletion relative to the reference (reference bases the read skips over), so this is 76 aligned, a 2-base gap in the read relative to reference, then 24 more aligned bases.
explanations.c: The record describes 100 aligned/gapped bases total (76M + 24M), not an unmapped read with only 2 matching bases.
explanations.d: 'S' denotes soft-clipping; this CIGAR contains no 'S' operator at all, so no bases are soft-clipped here.

questions.prompt: What does a FLAG value with bit 0x400 set indicate about a read?

options.text: The read is unmapped
The read aligned to the reverse strand
The read is a PCR or optical duplicate, an artifact of library prep rather than an independent observation
The read is paired with a mate on a different chromosome

explanations.a: Unmapped status is bit 0x4, a separate flag from 0x400.
explanations.b: Reverse-strand alignment is bit 0x10, a separate flag from 0x400.
explanations.c: Correct — bit 0x400 marks a PCR or optical duplicate, typically excluded from variant calling since it does not represent an independent sampling of the original DNA fragment.
explanations.d: Mate-chromosome information lives in the RNEXT field, not in the FLAG bitfield.

questions.prompt: A read has MAPQ 3. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The read has excellent base-call quality throughout
The read's alignment position is highly uncertain, often because its sequence is repetitive and fits multiple genomic locations about equally well
The read is a PCR duplicate
The read failed to align entirely

explanations.a: Base-call quality is Phred/QUAL, a separate per-base measure from MAPQ, which is about mapping-position confidence.
explanations.b: Correct — MAPQ = -10 log10(P wrong location), so a low MAPQ like 3 means a high estimated chance the reported position is wrong, typically because the read's sequence matches several places in the genome nearly equally well.
explanations.c: Duplicate status is recorded via the FLAG bit 0x400, independent of MAPQ.
explanations.d: An unmapped read is marked by FLAG bit 0x4 and would not carry a meaningful mapping position at all, rather than a low but present MAPQ.

questions.prompt: What is the key risk of using CRAM instead of BAM for long-term storage?

options.text: CRAM files are always larger than BAM files
CRAM cannot store paired-end reads
CRAM stores only differences from the reference, so decoding it correctly requires the exact matching reference sequence — losing or mismatching that reference breaks the file
CRAM files cannot be coordinate-sorted or indexed

explanations.a: CRAM is typically smaller than BAM, often roughly half the size, since it avoids storing full read sequences that match the reference.
explanations.b: CRAM supports the same alignment information as BAM, including paired-end data; format is not the limitation.
explanations.c: Correct — CRAM's reference-based compression means the file is not self-contained; without access to the identical reference sequence used to compress it, the file cannot be decoded correctly.
explanations.d: CRAM files support coordinate sorting and indexing much like BAM; that is not where the tradeoff lies.

lessons.label: Variant Files: VCF and the Representation Problem

sections.heading: VCF's core columns and per-sample fields
sections.body: The Variant Call Format (VCF) records one variant per line with eight fixed columns: CHROM and POS locate it (1-based), ID is an optional database identifier (like an rsID), REF and ALT give the reference and alternate allele sequences, QUAL is a Phred-scaled confidence that the variant call is real, FILTER records whether the site passed quality filters (or names which one it failed), and INFO carries site-level annotations as key=value pairs. When samples are genotyped, a FORMAT column defines which per-sample fields follow, most commonly: GT (genotype, e.g., 0/1 for heterozygous, where 0 is the reference allele and 1 is the first ALT allele), DP (read depth at that site for that sample), GQ (Phred-scaled genotype quality — confidence in the called genotype specifically, distinct from QUAL), AD (allelic depth, the read count supporting each allele), and PL (Phred-scaled likelihoods for each possible genotype, the raw evidence GQ is derived from).

sections.heading: Multiallelic sites
sections.body: A single position can have more than one alternate allele across a cohort or even within one sample — a multiallelic site lists them comma-separated in ALT (e.g., 'A,T' for a position with two possible non-reference bases seen), and each sample's GT then indexes into that list (0/2 means heterozygous for the reference and the second listed ALT allele). Many older tools assume biallelic sites and either error or silently mishandle multiallelic ones, so splitting multiallelic records into one biallelic record per alternate allele is a common, necessary normalization step before running such tools.

sections.heading: Left-normalization and why one indel has many valid spellings
sections.body: Indels (insertions/deletions) inside a repetitive stretch — a homopolymer run like 'AAAAA' or a short tandem repeat — genuinely have more than one equally correct VCF representation, because deleting any one of several identical repeated bases produces the identical resulting sequence. For example, deleting the 3rd 'A' versus the 5th 'A' from a run of five A's yields the exact same final DNA sequence, so both are valid descriptions of the same underlying variant, just anchored at different POS/REF/ALT values. Left-normalization (also called left-alignment) is the convention of always shifting an indel's representation as far left/5' as it can go and trimming any redundant shared bases between REF and ALT, giving every tool a single canonical spelling for the same biological event. Without left-normalization, two variant callers — or even the same caller run twice with different parameters — can report the identical true variant with different CHROM/POS/REF/ALT, so a naive line-by-line diff between two VCFs will report a false difference even though the underlying biology matches; this ambiguity is exactly what motivates representation-aware comparison tools rather than plain text diffing.

lessons.workedExample: Two variant callers both correctly detect a single-base deletion in a homopolymer run of five A's (reference 'CAAAAAT', position 100-106). Caller 1 reports POS=101, REF='AAAAA', ALT='AAAA' (deleting the last A). Caller 2 reports POS=103, REF='AAA', ALT='AA' (deleting a middle A). Both descriptions produce the identical final sequence 'CAAAAT' when applied — they are the same variant. A script that does a plain string comparison of POS/REF/ALT between the two VCFs sees two different records and reports a disagreement, when the correct, left-normalized representation (shift the deletion as far left/5' as possible, e.g., POS=101, REF='AAAAA', ALT='AAAA', trimmed to its minimal indel form) would reveal them as identical.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks about VCF representation is testing whether a student who compared "my calls" to "the truth set" and reported a false-positive or false-negative rate actually accounted for the fact that indels in repetitive sequence have multiple valid spellings. A strong answer explains why a homopolymer deletion is ambiguous, names left-normalization as the fix, and — critically — states that they normalized both VCFs before diffing rather than comparing raw text lines, because an unnormalized comparison inflates apparent disagreement with an artifact of representation, not biology.

questions.prompt: In a VCF sample's genotype field, GT = 0/1 means:

options.text: The sample is homozygous for the reference allele
The sample is heterozygous, carrying one reference allele and one copy of the first alternate allele
The read depth at this site is 0.1x
The variant failed quality filtering

explanations.a: Homozygous reference would be written 0/0, both alleles indexing to REF.
explanations.b: Correct — in GT, 0 indexes the REF allele and 1 indexes the first ALT allele, so 0/1 means one copy of each: a heterozygous call.
explanations.c: Read depth is recorded in the separate DP field, not encoded in GT.
explanations.d: Filter status is recorded in the FILTER column, a site-level field, not in the per-sample GT.

questions.prompt: Match each VCF FORMAT field to what it represents.

right.text: The called genotype (which alleles this sample carries)
Total read depth at this site for this sample
Phred-scaled confidence in the called genotype specifically
Read count supporting each allele individually

questions.explanation: GT is the genotype call itself; DP is total depth; GQ is genotype-specific confidence (distinct from site-level QUAL); AD breaks depth down per allele, the evidence underlying the genotype call.

questions.prompt: Why can a single-base deletion inside a run of five identical bases (a homopolymer) be validly represented in more than one way in VCF?

options.text: Because VCF allows arbitrary, non-standardized formatting of any field
Because deleting any one of the identical repeated bases produces the exact same resulting sequence, so multiple POS/REF/ALT combinations describe the identical biological event
Because homopolymer regions cannot be sequenced accurately, so the representation is arbitrary
Because VCF requires deletions to always be reported at the first base of the chromosome

explanations.a: The core VCF columns are standardized; the ambiguity here is a real biological/representational fact, not a lax format spec.
explanations.b: Correct — within a homopolymer, removing any one of the identical repeated bases yields the same final sequence, so several different POS/REF/ALT triples are all technically correct descriptions of the same underlying deletion.
explanations.c: This is a representation-ambiguity issue independent of base-calling accuracy; even a perfectly sequenced homopolymer deletion has multiple valid spellings.
explanations.d: VCF has no such rule; the convention that resolves the ambiguity is left-normalization, not a fixed chromosome-start requirement.

questions.prompt: Why does comparing two VCF files by naive line-by-line text diff risk reporting false differences?

options.text: Because VCF files are always sorted differently by every tool
Because the same true indel can be legitimately represented with different POS/REF/ALT values unless both files are left-normalized first
Because VCF files do not contain a QUAL column
Because VCF is a binary format that cannot be read as text

explanations.a: Sort order is a separate, fixable issue (files are typically coordinate-sorted); it is not the core cause of representation-driven false differences.
explanations.b: Correct — two callers (or the same caller under different settings) can report the identical biological indel with different coordinates/alleles in an unnormalized homopolymer or repeat region, so a raw text diff sees a mismatch that left-normalization would resolve as identical.
explanations.c: VCF does include a QUAL column; its presence or absence is unrelated to representation ambiguity.
explanations.d: VCF is a plain-text, tab-delimited format (sometimes gzip-compressed as VCF.gz, but still fundamentally text), not a binary format.

lessons.label: Annotation, Intervals, and Gene Models

sections.heading: GFF3, GTF, and BED: the interval languages
sections.body: Genomic annotation — where genes, exons, and other features sit along a chromosome — is stored as intervals in a handful of standard formats. GFF3 (General Feature Format version 3) and GTF (Gene Transfer Format, a stricter, gene-centric dialect of GFF2) both describe hierarchical features: a gene contains transcripts, a transcript contains exons and a coding sequence, linked together by ID/Parent attribute fields on each line. BED is the simpler, more general interval format — just coordinates plus optional name/score/strand columns — commonly used for anything from ChIP-seq peaks to custom regions of interest, without GFF/GTF's structured gene hierarchy. Because GFF3/GTF use 1-based inclusive coordinates while BED is 0-based half-open, converting annotation between the two formats runs into the same off-by-one hazard as any other coordinate conversion in the field.

sections.heading: Browsers: IGV, UCSC, and Ensembl
sections.body: To actually look at these intervals against sequence and aligned reads, researchers use genome browsers. IGV (Integrative Genomics Viewer, developed at the Broad Institute and described by Robinson and colleagues in 2011) is a desktop/web application for loading a user's own BAM, VCF, and BED/GFF files and visually inspecting them against a reference — the standard way to eyeball whether a called variant looks real or looks like an alignment artifact. The UCSC Genome Browser and the Ensembl browser instead serve public, pre-loaded annotation tracks (genes, conservation, regulatory marks) for browsing published data online, each with its own coordinate display conventions and its own underlying gene-model source.

sections.heading: RefSeq, Ensembl, and GENCODE disagree with each other
sections.body: There is no single, universally agreed-upon gene model for the human genome. RefSeq (curated by NCBI), Ensembl (curated by EMBL-EBI), and GENCODE (produced by the Ensembl/Havana collaboration and used as the reference annotation for projects like ENCODE) each apply different criteria for what counts as a gene or a transcript, and they disagree — not just in transcript boundaries and exon structure, but in the total number of protein-coding genes and transcripts annotated for the identical genome build. This is not a rare edge case: it is common enough that the Matched Annotation from NCBI and EMBL-EBI (MANE) project was created specifically to reconcile RefSeq and Ensembl/GENCODE onto a shared set of representative transcripts. The practical consequence is that a variant's predicted functional consequence — synonymous vs. missense, in-frame vs. frameshift, which exon it falls in — depends on which annotation set and which version of it you ran your variant effect predictor against; the identical genomic coordinate can be classified as coding in one transcript set's model and non-coding (e.g., intronic to a different transcript) in another's, so re-annotating with a different or updated gene set can change a variant's reported consequence without the underlying DNA changing at all.

lessons.workedExample: A student annotates a variant at a specific coordinate using RefSeq's gene model and reports it as a missense (protein-changing) variant in exon 4 of a gene. A classmate runs the identical coordinate through Ensembl/GENCODE's gene model and gets a different transcript structure for that gene, where the same coordinate falls in exon 5, or even in an intron of an alternative, longer transcript isoform not present in the RefSeq model — producing a different predicted consequence for the same physical base pair. Neither student made an arithmetic error; they annotated against different, legitimately disagreeing gene models. A rigorous report states both the annotation source (RefSeq/Ensembl/GENCODE) and its version, the same discipline coordinates require with a reference-genome build.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about gene models because "I annotated the variant and it's missense" sounds definitive but is not, unless the student also names which transcript set and version produced that call. A strong answer explains that RefSeq, Ensembl, and GENCODE are independently curated and genuinely disagree on transcript structure and even gene counts, that a variant's predicted consequence is therefore annotation-set-dependent rather than an intrinsic fact about the DNA, and can name IGV as the tool they used to visually confirm a call rather than trusting a text report alone.

questions.prompt: Why can the identical genomic coordinate be classified as a missense variant under one gene-model annotation and as intronic under another?

options.text: Because the DNA sequence itself changes depending on which browser is used to view it

Because RefSeq, Ensembl, and GENCODE are independently curated and legitimately disagree on transcript structure, so the same coordinate can fall in coding sequence under one gene model and outside it under another
Because variant callers randomly assign consequences
Because only one of the two annotations can be correct, and the other contains a data error

explanations.a: The underlying DNA sequence and coordinate are fixed; only the interpretive gene model overlaid on top of it differs.
explanations.b: Correct — RefSeq, Ensembl, and GENCODE apply different curation criteria and genuinely disagree on transcript boundaries and structure, so a variant's predicted consequence is dependent on which annotation set was used, not solely a property of the DNA.
explanations.c: Consequence prediction is deterministic given a transcript model; the variability comes from differing transcript models, not randomness.
explanations.d: Both annotation sets can be legitimately curated and correct on their own terms; they simply model transcript structure differently, which is exactly why the MANE project was created to reconcile them.

questions.prompt: What is the main structural difference between BED and GFF3/GTF as annotation formats?

options.text: BED can only store single-base positions, while GFF3 can store ranges
GFF3/GTF encode a hierarchical gene structure (gene contains transcript contains exons, via ID/Parent links), while BED is a simpler flat interval format without that hierarchy
BED is 1-based inclusive while GFF3/GTF are 0-based half-open
GFF3 cannot represent strand information

explanations.a: BED represents ranges (start/end coordinates) just as GFF3 does; the limitation is not to single bases.
explanations.b: Correct — GFF3/GTF link features hierarchically (genes to transcripts to exons/CDS via attribute fields), while BED is a flat, general-purpose interval format without that structure.
explanations.c: This reverses the actual convention: BED is 0-based half-open, while GFF3/GTF are 1-based inclusive.
explanations.d: GFF3 includes a strand column and does represent strand; that is not a distinguishing limitation.

questions.prompt: What was the MANE (Matched Annotation from NCBI and EMBL-EBI) project created to address?

options.text: Converting BAM files to CRAM for storage savings
Reconciling RefSeq and Ensembl/GENCODE onto a shared set of representative transcripts, since the two annotation sources disagree
Lifting coordinates over from GRCh37 to GRCh38
Standardizing FASTQ quality-score encoding across sequencing platforms

explanations.a: That describes CRAM compression, an unrelated file-format concern.
explanations.b: Correct — MANE was created specifically to reconcile the disagreements between RefSeq and Ensembl/GENCODE gene models by defining a shared set of representative transcripts.
explanations.c: That describes liftOver's function, a different tool solving a coordinate-build problem, not an annotation-source disagreement.
explanations.d: That describes the FASTQ offset-33/offset-64 issue, an unrelated data-encoding problem.

questions.prompt: What is IGV primarily used for?

options.text: Running variant callers to generate VCF files from BAM input
Visually inspecting a user's own aligned reads, variants, and annotation tracks against a reference genome
Compressing BAM files into CRAM format
Assigning Phred quality scores to raw sequencer signal

explanations.a: IGV displays existing alignments and calls; generating VCFs is the job of a separate variant-calling tool, not IGV itself.
explanations.b: Correct — IGV is a browser for loading a user's own BAM, VCF, and BED/GFF files and visually inspecting them against the reference, the standard way to eyeball whether a call looks like real biology or an alignment artifact.
explanations.c: Compression to CRAM is handled by tools like samtools, not IGV.
explanations.d: Base-calling and quality scoring happen in the sequencer's onboard software (e.g., phred-derived base callers), a stage upstream of anything IGV touches.

lessons.label: Global Alignment: Needleman-Wunsch

sections.heading: A 1970 recurrence for the whole-sequence problem
sections.body: Needleman and Wunsch published the first practical algorithm for aligning two full sequences end to end in 1970, in the Journal of Molecular Biology. The problem: given sequence X of length m and sequence Y of length n, find the arrangement of matches, mismatches, and gaps across their entire lengths that maximizes total score. Their insight was dynamic programming — build a table F where F(i,j) holds the best score for aligning the first i characters of X against the first j characters of Y, then define every cell from three smaller cells already solved: F(i,j) = max of F(i-1,j-1) + s(xi,yj) [diagonal: align xi to yj, scoring a match or mismatch], F(i-1,j) + gap [align xi to a gap], and F(i,j-1) + gap [align yj to a gap].

sections.heading: Filling the (m+1)x(n+1) matrix
sections.body: The matrix has m+1 rows and n+1 columns because row 0 and column 0 represent aligning against nothing — pure gap. F(0,j) = j x gap and F(i,0) = i x gap, since the only way to align i letters against zero letters is i gaps. Every other cell is filled left-to-right, top-to-bottom from the recurrence, so each cell is computed exactly once from cells already known: this is what makes the algorithm O(mn) in both time and space — every one of the (m+1)(n+1) cells does constant work. The final answer, the optimal global alignment score, sits in the bottom-right corner, F(m,n).

sections.heading: Why the optimum is guaranteed, not guessed
