explanations.b: Correct — at historical Nanopore/PacBio error rates (10-15%), exact matches (MEMs) become short and unreliable, whereas a per-window minimizer often survives an isolated substitution, giving more robust anchors to chain.
explanations.c: Minimap2 still runs bounded alignment after chaining minimizer anchors; sketching only replaces the seeding step.
explanations.d: The limitation is about seeding robustness to errors, not an inherent inability to build a BWT/FM-index over long-read data.

questions.prompt: In a spliced RNA-seq alignment, what does the 'N' operation in a CIGAR string represent?

options.text: A deletion relative to the reference caused by a sequencing error
A large intronic gap where the read is split across an exon-exon junction
A soft-clipped region at the end of the read
A mismatch between the read base and the reference base

explanations.a: A sequencing-error deletion is represented by 'D', a much smaller gap than an intron and not splice-specific.
explanations.b: Correct — 'N' specifically marks a large skipped region in the reference corresponding to an intron, distinguishing spliced alignment from an ordinary indel.
explanations.c: Soft-clipping is represented by 'S' and marks unaligned read ends, not intronic gaps.
explanations.d: Mismatches are encoded within the 'M' alignment operation (or 'X' in extended CIGAR), not 'N'.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to its seeding/alignment strategy.

right.text: Seeds with maximal exact matches, chains and extends via local alignment
Seeds with minimizer sketches, tolerant of high per-base error
Finds maximal mappable prefixes via suffix-array search, stitches across splice gaps
Uses a graph-extended FM-index incorporating known splice sites to jump introns

questions.explanation: BWA-MEM chains MEMs for short/moderate reads; minimap2 uses minimizer sketches suited to high-error long reads; STAR finds maximal mappable prefixes via suffix-array search and stitches splice-consistent gaps; HISAT2 uses a graph-extended FM-index seeded with known splice-site information to jump introns directly.

lessons.label: Multi-Mapping, MAPQ, and the Unmappable Genome

sections.heading: Roughly half the genome is not unique
sections.body: Studies of the human reference estimate that a large share of the genome — commonly cited around half — is composed of repetitive elements: LINEs, SINEs (including the ~1.1 million Alu elements), satellite DNA, segmental duplications, and processed or unprocessed pseudogenes. A short read originating from inside one of these repeats can align equally well to many genomic locations, not because the aligner is failing but because the sequence genuinely is not unique. This is what multi-mapping means: the aligner correctly reports that a read fits several places with identical or near-identical scores, and there is no additional information in the read itself to break the tie.

sections.heading: MAPQ is a confidence score, not a quality score
sections.body: Mapping quality (MAPQ), stored in every SAM/BAM record, encodes the aligner's confidence that a read is placed at the reported position rather than somewhere else — typically computed from the score gap between the best and second-best alignment, on a Phred-like scale capped at 60 in tools like BWA. A MAPQ of 0 specifically means 'this read maps equally well to at least one other location,' not 'this is a bad or low-quality read' — the base calls can be perfect and the read still get MAPQ 0 if it originated from a duplicated region. Mappability tracks (precomputed genome-wide scores such as Umap, from Karimzadeh, Ernst, Kundaje & Hoffman, 2018, or GEM-mappability, from the CRG's GEM team — independent academic tools whose tracks are hosted and used by resources like ENCODE and UCSC, not tools ENCODE itself built) mark exactly which reference positions are expected to have low MAPQ for a given read length, letting analysts flag regions where variant calls should be discounted before they ever look at the data.

sections.heading: Named blind spots where this actually breaks clinical calls
sections.body: The clinical stakes are concrete. SMN1 and SMN2, the genes underlying spinal muscular atrophy, are near-identical paralogs differing by a handful of bases, and standard short-read mapping frequently misassigns reads between them, which is exactly why clinical SMA testing uses targeted assays (MLPA, ddPCR) rather than trusting standard exome/genome MAPQ. The HLA region on chromosome 6 is so polymorphic and repetitive that standard linear-reference aligners routinely misplace or misgenotype it, driving the field toward dedicated HLA callers and graph-based references. More broadly, any gene with a close paralog or processed pseudogene (for example, PMS2 and its pseudogene PMS2CL in Lynch syndrome screening) risks a real pathogenic variant being systematically assigned to the wrong copy or diluted across both, silently producing a false negative unless the pipeline specifically accounts for it.

lessons.workedExample: A clinical lab runs exome sequencing on a patient suspected of spinal muscular atrophy. Reads covering the SMN1/SMN2 region map with MAPQ 0 across both nearly identical gene copies because the sequence difference is only a few bases — not enough for the aligner to confidently favor one copy over the other. A pipeline that simply filters out MAPQ 0 reads (a common default QC step) would discard this region entirely and miss the causal variant. The correct response, and the reason SMA is not diagnosed from standard short-read WGS/WES alone, is to recognize the region as a known low-mappability blind spot in advance and route it to a targeted assay (MLPA or ddPCR) that can distinguish the paralogs directly, rather than trusting alignment-based genotyping there.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who raises MAPQ or multi-mapping is testing whether the student can distinguish 'the sequencing failed' from 'the genome itself is ambiguous here,' which is a much more sophisticated and correct framing. The strongest answers name a specific real blind spot — SMN1/SMN2 in SMA, the HLA locus, or a pseudogene pair like PMS2/PMS2CL — and explain that low MAPQ there reflects genuine sequence similarity between paralogs, not poor data, and that the practical fix is a targeted orthogonal assay rather than trying to force short-read alignment to resolve it. A student who treats MAPQ 0 as simply 'bad data to filter out' has missed that filtering is exactly what causes the false negative.

questions.prompt: A read has MAPQ 0 in a BAM file. What does this most precisely indicate?

options.text: The read's base calls are low quality and likely contain sequencing errors
The read aligns equally well (or nearly so) to more than one genomic location
The read failed to align anywhere in the genome
The read overlaps a known SNP

explanations.a: MAPQ reflects placement confidence, not base-call quality — those are tracked separately as per-base quality scores.
explanations.b: Correct — MAPQ 0 specifically signals that the aligner found (at least) one other position with an equal or near-equal alignment score, so it cannot confidently pick one location.
explanations.c: An unaligned read is typically flagged as unmapped entirely, not given a mapped record with MAPQ 0.
explanations.d: MAPQ has nothing to do with whether a position overlaps a known variant; that is separate annotation.

questions.prompt: Why do SMN1 and SMN2 create a specific problem for short-read alignment in spinal muscular atrophy testing?

options.text: They are on different chromosomes, so no aligner can compare them
They are near-identical paralogs differing by only a few bases, so reads are frequently misassigned between them
SMN1 has no reference sequence available at all
SMN2 is entirely composed of repetitive satellite DNA

explanations.a: Both genes are located on chromosome 5 in close proximity, which if anything worsens rather than resolves the ambiguity.
explanations.b: Correct — SMN1 and SMN2 differ by only a handful of bases, so short reads from one frequently align with equal or near-equal confidence to the other, producing low MAPQ and misassignment.
explanations.c: Both genes have reference sequence in standard genome builds; the issue is similarity between them, not absence of one.
explanations.d: The mapping difficulty comes from paralog similarity, not from satellite-DNA repeat content specifically.

questions.prompt: A pipeline's default QC step discards all reads with MAPQ 0 before variant calling. What is the main risk of this policy in regions like SMN1/SMN2 or PMS2/PMS2CL?

options.text: It has no downside; MAPQ 0 reads never carry useful variant information
It can discard the region entirely, producing a false negative for a real pathogenic variant
It only affects mitochondrial DNA variant calls
It increases sequencing cost for future runs

explanations.a: MAPQ 0 reads can still carry a real, causal variant; discarding them by default removes that evidence from consideration.
explanations.b: Correct — in known paralog-confusion regions, blanket MAPQ-0 filtering can eliminate the only reads covering a real pathogenic variant, which is why such regions need targeted follow-up assays rather than reliance on filtered short-read alignment.
explanations.c: The problem generalizes to nuclear paralog/pseudogene regions like SMN1/SMN2 or PMS2/PMS2CL, not specifically mitochondrial DNA.
explanations.d: This is a data-analysis and diagnostic-accuracy risk, not a cost issue.

questions.prompt: Match each genomic region or feature to the mapping challenge it illustrates.

right.text: Near-identical paralogs where SMA-causing variants can be misassigned between copies
Highly polymorphic, repetitive locus that standard linear aligners routinely misgenotype
Gene/processed-pseudogene pair risking false negatives in Lynch syndrome screening
Precomputed genome-wide score flagging positions expected to have low MAPQ

questions.explanation: SMN1/SMN2 illustrates paralog confusion relevant to SMA diagnosis; the HLA region illustrates polymorphism-driven mapping failure needing dedicated callers/graph references; PMS2/PMS2CL illustrates a pseudogene pair risking missed variants in Lynch syndrome screening; mappability tracks are the precomputed tool used to flag such low-confidence regions genome-wide in advance.

lessons.label: Post-Alignment Processing

sections.heading: Marking duplicates before they masquerade as evidence
sections.body: PCR amplification during library prep and optical crosstalk on the sequencer both produce duplicate reads — copies that trace back to the same original DNA fragment, not independent sampling of it. Tools like Picard MarkDuplicates (or samtools markdup) identify these by comparing the mapped start coordinates of read pairs: identical outer coordinates flag PCR duplicates, while optical duplicates are flagged by proximity on the flow cell itself. Left unmarked, duplicates inflate apparent read depth at a site and let a single PCR artifact masquerade as several independent reads supporting a variant, which can push a false call over a caller's confidence threshold. Marking (not deleting) duplicates lets downstream tools exclude them from depth and genotype-likelihood calculations while preserving the record for audit.

sections.heading: Base quality score recalibration
sections.body: Illumina's reported per-base quality scores are systematically biased by machine cycle, sequencing context, and position in the read, in ways that do not track the true error rate exactly. Base Quality Score Recalibration (BQSR), part of the GATK best-practices pipeline, corrects this empirically: it excludes any base overlapping a known-variant site (from a database such as dbSNP or Mills/1000-Genomes indels) so real variation is not mistaken for error, then models the residual mismatch rate against covariates like cycle number and dinucleotide context, and rewrites each base's quality score to better reflect its true empirical error probability. This matters because variant callers weight evidence by quality score — a mis-calibrated score either buries a real low-frequency variant under artificially low confidence or lets a systematic sequencer error look confidently real.

sections.heading: Soft-clips as signal, and why realignment moved into the caller
sections.body: A soft-clipped base (CIGAR 'S') is part of the read that the aligner chose not to align — trimmed off, not deleted — often because that stretch of the read does not match the reference at all near an otherwise-good alignment. Rather than noise to discard, a cluster of soft-clips at the same genomic position across many reads is a classic clue to a structural variant breakpoint: an insertion, a translocation, or a large deletion edge, since the clipped tail is exactly the part of the read that belongs on the other side of the breakpoint. Older pipelines also ran a dedicated local indel realignment step (GATK's IndelRealigner) to fix alignments that BWA-style single-read mapping scored suboptimally around an indel. GATK4 dropped the standalone realigner because haplotype-based callers like HaplotypeCaller do something strictly better: when they detect a region showing signs of variation, they discard the existing per-read alignments entirely and locally reassemble all overlapping reads into candidate haplotypes via a de Bruijn graph, which resolves indel placement more accurately than realigning individual reads ever could — making a separate realignment pass redundant.

lessons.workedExample: A tumor sample is PCR-amplified before sequencing to boost low-input DNA, then sequenced to nominal 100x depth. At one site, 40 of the 100 reads turn out to be PCR duplicates of just 4 original template molecules, all carrying the same somatic variant by chance amplification bias. Without duplicate marking, a variant caller sees 40 supporting reads out of 100 (40% variant allele frequency) and calls it confidently. After Picard MarkDuplicates collapses those 40 reads down to their 4 true independent templates, the effective supporting evidence is 4 reads out of an effective ~64 non-duplicate reads at that site — a very different, much weaker signal that changes whether the variant clears a somatic-calling confidence threshold at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks about post-alignment processing is checking whether the student understands that a BAM file from an aligner is not yet analysis-ready data — several steps sit between mapping and a trustworthy variant call, each fixing a distinct failure mode. The strongest answers can explain why duplicate marking is about independence of evidence (not just tidiness), why BQSR is an empirical correction rather than a fixed formula, why a soft-clip cluster is a structural-variant clue rather than noise to trim away, and specifically why GATK4 removed the standalone indel realigner — because haplotype-based callers now reassemble the region from scratch, making a prior realignment pass redundant rather than simply outdated.

questions.prompt: Why does failing to mark PCR duplicates risk inflating false confidence in a variant call?

options.text: Duplicates are always low-quality reads that should be removed for base-call accuracy
Duplicates are copies of the same original template, so counting them as independent evidence overstates how many separate molecules actually support the variant
Duplicates change the reference genome coordinates of nearby variants
Duplicates only affect indel calls, never single-nucleotide variant calls

explanations.a: Duplicate status is about PCR/optical origin, not intrinsic base-call quality; a duplicate read can otherwise be perfectly accurate.
explanations.b: Correct — because duplicates trace to the same original fragment, treating them as independent reads inflates the apparent number of molecules supporting a variant, which can push a weak or artifactual signal past a caller's confidence threshold.
explanations.c: Duplicate marking does not alter genomic coordinates; it only flags read redundancy for downstream tools to exclude.
explanations.d: Duplicate inflation affects both SNV and indel evidence, since both rely on counting supporting reads/depth.

questions.prompt: What does Base Quality Score Recalibration (BQSR) specifically correct?

options.text: It re-aligns reads to a different reference genome build
It empirically adjusts reported per-base quality scores using covariates like sequencing cycle and context, excluding known-variant sites
It removes all reads below a fixed minimum quality score
It merges overlapping paired-end reads into a single consensus read

explanations.a: BQSR operates on quality scores of already-aligned reads; it does not change the reference build being used.
explanations.b: Correct — BQSR models the empirical mismatch rate against covariates (cycle, dinucleotide context, etc.), excluding known-variant sites from the model, and rewrites quality scores to better reflect true error probability.
explanations.c: BQSR recalibrates scores rather than filtering reads outright by a fixed threshold.
explanations.d: Merging paired-end overlap is a separate step from a different tool category; BQSR only adjusts quality values.

questions.prompt: Why did GATK4 drop the standalone IndelRealigner step from its recommended pipeline?

options.text: Indel realignment was found to be scientifically invalid
Haplotype-based callers like HaplotypeCaller locally reassemble reads into candidate haplotypes around variant regions, making a separate realignment pass redundant
Modern sequencers no longer produce indel-adjacent alignment errors
IndelRealigner was replaced by BQSR, which performs the same function

explanations.a: Realignment was a valid and useful correction; it became unnecessary, not invalid, once callers began reassembling regions themselves.
explanations.b: Correct — HaplotypeCaller (and similar haplotype-based callers) discard existing alignments in an active region and rebuild candidate haplotypes via de Bruijn graph assembly, which resolves indel placement at least as well as a prior realignment step, making the standalone realigner redundant.
explanations.c: Alignment errors near indels are a property of single-read local alignment scoring, not something new sequencer chemistry eliminated.
explanations.d: BQSR corrects quality scores, an entirely different function from indel realignment; it does not perform reassembly.

questions.prompt: A cluster of soft-clipped reads all clip at the same genomic position. What should this most likely be treated as?

options.text: Sequencing noise that should be discarded before any analysis
A possible structural variant breakpoint, since the clipped portions are the part of the read that belongs on the other side of the breakpoint
Evidence that the reads are PCR duplicates
Proof that the reference genome build is incorrect

explanations.a: Soft-clips at a shared position are a coordinated pattern, not random noise, and discarding them loses structural-variant evidence.
explanations.b: Correct — a shared soft-clip position across many reads is a classic signature of a structural variant breakpoint (insertion, translocation, or deletion edge), since the clipped tail represents sequence that maps elsewhere.
explanations.c: Duplicate status is about identical mapped start coordinates from PCR/optical origin, unrelated to soft-clipping patterns.
explanations.d: A local soft-clip cluster reflects a real structural feature at that locus, not a genome-build error.

lessons.label: Alignment-Free Methods

sections.heading: When base-level alignment is wasted work
sections.body: Every method in this unit so far computes a base-by-base alignment: where exactly does each nucleotide of the read sit relative to the reference, with which mismatches and gaps. That precision is essential for variant calling, but it is overkill for some genuinely common questions — 'which transcript did this RNA-seq read come from' or 'how similar are these two bacterial genomes overall' rarely need per-base coordinates, only a good count or a good distance estimate. Alignment-free methods answer these questions by comparing k-mer content directly, skipping the dynamic-programming alignment step entirely, which trades away per-base positional detail for order-of-magnitude speed.

sections.heading: Pseudoalignment and selective alignment for transcript quantification
sections.body: Kallisto (Bray et al., 2016) introduced pseudoalignment for RNA-seq quantification: instead of aligning a read base-by-base to the genome or transcriptome, it breaks the read into k-mers, looks up which transcripts each k-mer is compatible with in a precomputed index (a colored de Bruijn graph over all reference transcripts), and intersects those compatibility sets across the read's k-mers to determine which transcript(s) the read is consistent with — no alignment, no CIGAR, just set membership. This is dramatically faster than genome alignment plus counting and made routine transcript-level quantification of large RNA-seq cohorts computationally cheap. Salmon (Patro et al., 2017) refined the idea with selective alignment: it still avoids full base-level alignment for speed, but adds a validation step that checks whether a read's mapping is actually consistent enough to trust, filtering out the spurious k-mer-compatibility matches that pure pseudoalignment can accept, at a modest speed cost for materially better accuracy on repetitive or paralogous transcripts.

sections.heading: MinHash sketching for whole-genome distance
sections.body: Mash (Ondov et al., 2016) applies alignment-free comparison at the scale of whole genomes rather than individual reads, using MinHash sketching: it hashes all k-mers of a genome and retains only the smallest few thousand hash values as a compact 'sketch,' then estimates genome-to-genome distance (an approximation of average nucleotide identity) by comparing two sketches' overlap — a task that took hours with full alignment-based comparison and takes seconds with Mash, enabling researchers to search or cluster thousands of bacterial genomes by similarity in a practical amount of time. The honest tradeoff across all these methods is the same: orders-of-magnitude speedups, at the cost of having no per-base alignment to inspect when a result looks wrong — if kallisto assigns a read to the wrong transcript or Mash reports a surprising distance, there is no CIGAR string or mismatch column to open and diagnose; the analyst has to fall back to a true aligner to see what actually happened at the sequence level.

lessons.workedExample: A lab wants to quantify transcript expression across 200 RNA-seq samples for a differential-expression study. Aligning each sample's ~40 million reads to the genome with STAR and then counting reads per transcript would take hours per sample and require gigabytes of intermediate BAM files, adding up to days of compute for the full cohort. Running kallisto instead — building one pseudoalignment index over the transcriptome once, then pseudoaligning each sample's reads by k-mer compatibility — finishes each sample in minutes on a laptop, because no base-level alignment or BAM file is ever produced. The tradeoff shows up when one transcript's quantification looks anomalous: with STAR's BAM output the analyst can open a genome browser and see exactly which bases disagree; with kallisto's pseudoalignment there is no positional alignment to inspect, so diagnosing the anomaly requires re-running that region through a real aligner.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing alignment-free methods wants to see that the student can articulate a genuine tradeoff rather than presenting speed as a free win. The strong answer names the specific mechanism (k-mer compatibility sets for kallisto's pseudoalignment, MinHash sketch overlap for Mash's genome distance) and states plainly what is given up: no base-level positional evidence to inspect, so an unexpected result cannot be diagnosed within the tool itself and requires falling back to true alignment. A student who can also explain why Salmon's selective alignment exists — as a deliberate partial retreat from pure pseudoalignment to buy back some accuracy — shows they understand this as a spectrum of speed-versus-evidence choices, not a single alignment-free category.

questions.prompt: What does kallisto's pseudoalignment fundamentally do differently from a standard base-level aligner like STAR?

options.text: It uses a longer k-mer size but otherwise performs the same dynamic-programming alignment
It determines which transcripts a read's k-mers are compatible with via set intersection, without computing a base-by-base alignment
It aligns reads to the genome first and then infers the transcriptome afterward
It only works on single-end reads, never paired-end

explanations.a: Pseudoalignment skips dynamic-programming alignment entirely; it is not merely a k-mer-size variant of the same process.
explanations.b: Correct — kallisto looks up each k-mer's transcript-compatibility set in a precomputed index and intersects these sets across the read, determining transcript consistency without ever computing per-base alignment.
explanations.c: Kallisto pseudoaligns directly against a transcriptome index; it does not require a genome alignment step first.
explanations.d: Pseudoalignment handles both single-end and paired-end RNA-seq data; the method is not restricted to one read layout.

questions.prompt: What specific improvement does Salmon's selective alignment add over pure pseudoalignment?

options.text: It removes the need for a reference transcriptome index entirely
It adds a validation step that filters out k-mer-compatibility matches that are not actually consistent alignments, improving accuracy on repetitive transcripts
It performs full genome alignment before quantification, unlike kallisto
It eliminates all speed advantage over traditional alignment-based quantification

explanations.a: Salmon still requires a reference transcriptome index; it does not remove that requirement.
explanations.b: Correct — selective alignment adds a check on whether a k-mer-compatible mapping is genuinely a good match, discarding spurious hits that pure pseudoalignment would accept, which improves accuracy for repetitive or paralogous transcripts at some added computational cost.
explanations.c: Salmon still avoids full base-level alignment for speed; it does not fall back to genome-scale alignment for every read.
explanations.d: Salmon retains a substantial speed advantage over traditional alignment-based pipelines, just somewhat less than pure pseudoalignment alone.

questions.prompt: How does Mash estimate the distance between two whole bacterial genomes?

options.text: By running full genome-wide Smith-Waterman alignment between the two sequences
By comparing the overlap of MinHash sketches — small retained subsets of each genome's k-mer hash values
By counting the total number of genes annotated in each genome
By aligning both genomes to a shared reference and comparing coordinates

explanations.a: Full alignment is exactly what Mash avoids; that is the slow, alignment-based approach it replaces.
explanations.b: Correct — Mash hashes each genome's k-mers, retains only the smallest values as a compact sketch, and estimates distance from the overlap between two genomes' sketches, approximating average nucleotide identity in seconds.
explanations.c: Gene annotation counts are unrelated to Mash's sequence-similarity estimate, which operates purely on k-mer content.
explanations.d: Mash compares genomes directly to each other via sketches; it does not require a shared third reference for coordinate-based comparison.

questions.prompt: What is the main honest tradeoff of alignment-free methods like kallisto, Salmon, and Mash compared to base-level alignment?

options.text: They are more accurate but much slower than traditional aligners
They gain large speed advantages but leave no per-base alignment evidence to inspect when a result looks wrong
They can only be used on bacterial genomes, never human data
They require more memory than a full BWT/FM-index aligner

explanations.a: The tradeoff runs the opposite direction — these methods are typically faster, with accuracy that is good but not verifiable at base-pair resolution.
explanations.b: Correct — the consistent tradeoff across pseudoalignment, selective alignment, and MinHash sketching is orders-of-magnitude speed at the cost of having no CIGAR-level, per-base evidence to diagnose an unexpected result.
explanations.c: Kallisto and Salmon are routinely used on human RNA-seq quantification; the alignment-free approach is not species-restricted.
explanations.d: These methods are generally designed to be lighter-weight (smaller sketches or compatibility indexes) than a full genome aligner index, not heavier.

units.label: Variant Calling and Pipeline Quality Control

lessons.label: Quality Control Across the Pipeline

sections.heading: What FastQC's modules are actually telling you
sections.body: FastQC runs a fixed battery of checks on raw reads before anything else touches them. Per-base quality plots Phred scores across read cycle; on Illumina chemistry, quality reliably degrades toward the 3' end as phasing and pre-phasing errors accumulate cycle over cycle, so a downward slope late in the read is expected chemistry, not a red flag by itself. GC content distribution is compared against the expected genome-wide value (about 41% for human); a clean single peak near that value is normal, while a second peak or a broad shoulder signals exogenous DNA mixed into the library. Adapter content tracks how much of each read is actually sequencing-adapter rather than insert; overrepresented sequences flag reads dominated by a handful of identical sequences, usually PCR over-amplification from low-input DNA or leftover adapter dimers; and sequence duplication level estimates what fraction of reads are exact or near-exact copies, which inflated PCR cycles will drive up.

sections.heading: Trimming and aggregating across a run
sections.body: Trimmomatic, fastp, and cutadapt all remove adapter sequence and low-quality bases, but differently: Trimmomatic applies a sliding-quality-window trim plus explicit adapter clip lists (ILLUMINACLIP); cutadapt is adapter-sequence-driven and fast for known adapter sets; fastp combines trimming with its own QC report in one pass, which is why it has largely displaced running FastQC and a trimmer as two separate steps. None of these fix a sample-level problem — they only clean up sequencing noise. MultiQC then aggregates FastQC (and other tools') reports across every sample in a run into one HTML dashboard, which is the only practical way to notice that one lane, not just one sample, is failing.

sections.heading: Contamination and coverage that actually matter
sections.body: FastQ Screen aligns a subsample of reads against multiple reference genomes at once (human, mouse, common bacteria, PhiX) to catch cross-species contamination — a mouse-derived xenograft sample bleeding into a human tumor library, for instance. VerifyBamID instead estimates within-species contamination, comparing observed allele frequencies at known-variable sites against expected patterns to output a contamination percentage even when the contaminating DNA is also human. For coverage, mean depth alone is a weak summary; the metrics that matter are percent of target bases at or above 20x (a floor below which heterozygous calls start being lost to sampling chance) and uniformity — GC-rich or GC-poor regions are systematically under-amplified during library prep, so a caller can be started on a run that pads out an acceptable mean depth while whole exons sit at 5x.

lessons.workedExample: A WGS run's FastQC report shows per-base quality dropping below Phred 20 only in the last 30bp of 150bp reads (normal 3' decay — trim it) but also a sharp rise in adapter content starting around cycle 120, meaning many fragments were shorter than the read length and sequencing ran into adapter. fastp trims both issues in one pass. MultiQC then shows mean depth of 32x across the cohort, which looks fine, but only 84% of target bases reach 20x with a visible dip in GC-rich exons — a uniformity problem library prep caused, not something trimming or a better caller can rescue. That sample gets flagged before variant calling starts, not after a caller returns confident-looking but under-supported homozygous-reference calls in the low-coverage exons.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on QC because it separates a student who trusted the variant caller's output from one who first checked whether the input deserved trust. The tell is distinguishing sequencing noise you fix with trimming (3' quality decay, adapter read-through) from a sample-level problem no downstream step can rescue (contamination, uneven coverage from library prep) — a student who can point to a specific plot and say which bucket it falls in, and why, has done real QC rather than clicked through a report.

questions.prompt: A FastQC report shows adapter content rising sharply in the last third of 150bp reads. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: Cross-species contamination in the sample
Many DNA fragments were shorter than the read length, so sequencing read through the insert into adapter
PCR duplication from low-input DNA
A failed sequencing lane with random base calls

explanations.a: Contamination shows up as a bimodal GC distribution or cross-species alignment hits, not adapter content.
explanations.b: Correct — when the insert is shorter than the read length, sequencing runs past the end of the DNA fragment and into adapter sequence, which FastQC reports as rising adapter content late in the read.
explanations.c: PCR duplication shows up as elevated sequence duplication levels and overrepresented sequences, not specifically an adapter-content spike.
explanations.d: A failed lane typically shows collapsed per-base quality across most cycles, not a localized adapter signal.

questions.prompt: Why is percent of target bases at ≥20x tracked instead of relying on mean depth alone?

options.text: Mean depth is not computable from a BAM file
A single mean can hide regions sitting well below the depth needed to confidently call heterozygous sites, especially where library prep under-amplifies GC-extreme regions
20x is the depth required to detect any contamination
Mean depth only applies to RNA-seq, not DNA sequencing

explanations.a: Mean depth is a standard, easily computed BAM metric; that isn't the issue.
explanations.b: Correct — a cohort or sample can hit an acceptable mean depth while GC-rich or GC-poor exons sit far below it due to uneven library amplification, and low-depth heterozygous sites are lost to sampling chance well before mean depth would suggest a problem.
explanations.c: Contamination detection uses allele-frequency-based tools like VerifyBamID, not a depth threshold.
explanations.d: Depth metrics apply broadly to DNA sequencing, including WGS and exome data, not only RNA-seq.

questions.prompt: Match each QC tool or module to what it detects.

right.text: Cross-species contamination, via alignment against multiple reference genomes
Within-species sample contamination, estimated from allele frequency mismatches
Aggregates per-sample QC reports across a whole run or cohort into one view
Read quality degradation across sequencing cycle

questions.explanation: FastQ Screen aligns reads to several reference genomes to catch contamination from another species; VerifyBamID detects same-species contamination from allele-frequency patterns; MultiQC rolls up individual reports (FastQC and others) across many samples; and the per-base quality module shows how Phred scores change across read cycle.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a standard pre-alignment QC workflow.

items.text: Run FastQC on raw reads
Trim adapters and low-quality bases (e.g., with fastp)
Re-run FastQC on trimmed reads
Aggregate all sample reports with MultiQC
Check coverage metrics (mean depth, % ≥20x, uniformity) before variant calling

questions.explanation: QC starts on raw reads to characterize the problem, trimming addresses sequencing-level noise, a second FastQC pass confirms the trim worked, MultiQC gives the cohort-level view needed to catch systematic issues, and coverage metrics — which only make sense after alignment — are checked last before trusting a caller's output.

lessons.label: Calling SNVs and Small Indels

sections.heading: Pileup likelihoods versus local reassembly
sections.body: bcftools mpileup treats each genomic position independently: it stacks every aligned read that overlaps a site, uses each base's Phred quality as an error-rate estimate, and computes a Bayesian genotype likelihood for each possible genotype given the caller's assumed ploidy, then reports the most probable one. It is fast and works directly from the alignment the mapper already produced. GATK's HaplotypeCaller instead identifies active regions — windows with evidence of variation such as mismatches, soft clips, or an unusual insert size — and inside each one performs local de novo assembly of all overlapping reads into a de Bruijn graph, reconstructing candidate haplotypes rather than trusting the mapper's original per-base alignment. It then realigns every read against those candidate haplotypes using a pair-HMM and calls variants from the haplotypes that best explain the reads.

sections.heading: Why reassembly wins near indels
sections.body: A short-read aligner like BWA places each read independently and greedily; near an indel, especially inside a homopolymer or short repeat, different reads covering the same true indel can get aligned with the gap positioned slightly differently from one read to the next, since several placements are equally parsimonious. A pileup caller sees this as scattered mismatches across several adjacent positions rather than one clean indel, and can miss the real variant or emit several spurious low-confidence SNVs instead. Local reassembly sidesteps the problem by not trusting the original per-read placement at all: it rebuilds one consistent haplotype for the whole region from all the reads together, then realigns every read to that shared haplotype, so the indel resolves to a single call with consistent support rather than a smear of noise.

sections.heading: Ploidy, allele balance, and joint calling
sections.body: Callers assume a ploidy per region: diploid (2) for human autosomes, haploid (1) for X/Y in males, and much higher effective ploidy for mitochondrial DNA given its many copies per cell. Allele balance — the fraction of reads at a site supporting the alt allele — should sit near 0.5 for a true heterozygous call and near 1.0 for a true homozygous-alt call under diploid assumptions; a site reporting 0.9 when called heterozygous, or 0.1 when called homozygous, is a signal to re-inspect, not necessarily discard. For cohorts, GATK's GVCF workflow runs HaplotypeCaller once per sample in a mode that records likelihoods at every site (not just variant sites), then combines and jointly genotypes all samples together with GenotypeGVCFs. This avoids the 'N+1 problem': without it, adding one new sample to a cohort would require re-calling every sample from scratch to keep genotypes comparable.

lessons.workedExample: Consider a 4bp deletion sitting inside a homopolymer run. BWA aligns some overlapping reads with the deletion placed at the start of the repeat and others with it placed a few bases later, since both placements explain the read equally well. A pileup caller sees this as mismatches scattered across four or five adjacent positions and either misses the deletion entirely or emits several low-confidence spurious SNVs in its place. HaplotypeCaller, working on the same reads, performs local assembly across the whole active region, builds one deletion haplotype, realigns every read to that single haplotype, and calls one clean 4bp deletion with allele balance near 0.5 — consistent with a true heterozygous call — instead of a cluster of ambiguous single-base calls.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about caller choice because near indels and repeats the 'obvious' per-base approach systematically breaks, and picking mpileup versus HaplotypeCaller for a repeat-rich target reveals whether a student understands what local realignment actually buys rather than just naming a tool. A student who can explain why reassembly resolves ambiguous indel placement — not just that HaplotypeCaller is 'more accurate' — has understood the mechanism.

questions.prompt: Why does HaplotypeCaller typically outperform a pure pileup caller near indels in repetitive sequence?

options.text: It uses a higher base-quality threshold than pileup callers
It rebuilds one consistent haplotype for the region via local assembly and realigns all reads to it, instead of trusting each read's independent per-base alignment
It ignores reads that overlap indels entirely
It only calls variants supported by paired-end reads

explanations.a: Both approaches use base quality in their likelihood models; the difference is not a quality threshold.
explanations.b: Correct — local de novo assembly reconstructs one shared haplotype from all overlapping reads, so an indel that different reads' original alignments placed inconsistently gets resolved to a single consistent call.
explanations.c: HaplotypeCaller uses reads overlapping indels directly; it does not discard them.
explanations.d: The reassembly approach applies to single-end and paired-end data alike; pairing is not the mechanism.

questions.prompt: Under diploid assumptions, what allele balance (fraction of reads supporting the alt allele) is expected at a true heterozygous site?

options.text: Near 0.0
Near 0.25
Near 0.5
Near 1.0

explanations.a: Near-zero alt support would suggest homozygous reference, not heterozygous.
explanations.b: 0.25 is skewed enough from the diploid expectation to warrant re-inspection for artifact, not a typical heterozygous value.
explanations.c: Correct — with one reference and one alt copy, reads should sample each allele roughly equally, giving allele balance near 0.5.
explanations.d: Near-1.0 alt support is the expectation for homozygous alt, not heterozygous.

questions.prompt: What problem does GATK's GVCF-based joint genotyping workflow avoid?

options.text: The need to trim adapters before alignment
The 'N+1 problem' — having to re-call every sample from scratch each time a new sample joins the cohort
The need for a reference genome
Strand bias in Illumina sequencing

explanations.a: Adapter trimming is a QC step unrelated to joint genotyping.
explanations.b: Correct — recording per-sample likelihoods in a GVCF lets a new sample be combined and jointly genotyped with existing ones without re-running every prior sample.
explanations.c: A reference genome is still required for alignment and calling regardless of this workflow.
explanations.d: Strand bias is addressed by filtering annotations, not by the GVCF joint-calling workflow.

questions.prompt: Order the steps HaplotypeCaller takes when calling a variant.

items.text: Identify active regions showing evidence of variation
Perform local de novo assembly of overlapping reads into candidate haplotypes
Realign all reads to the candidate haplotypes using a pair-HMM
Call variants from the haplotypes that best explain the realigned reads

questions.explanation: HaplotypeCaller first flags regions worth reassembling, builds candidate haplotypes from all reads in that region, realigns every read against those haplotypes rather than the original mapper placement, and only then calls variants from the haplotypes with the best read support.

lessons.label: Filtering: Hard Filters, VQSR, and Learned Callers

sections.heading: What the standard annotations actually measure
sections.body: QD (QualByDepth) normalizes a variant's confidence score by the depth at that site, since raw quality otherwise scales with coverage and would make deep regions look artificially more confident. FS (FisherStrand) is a Phred-scaled p-value from Fisher's exact test comparing how often the alt allele appears on forward versus reverse strand reads; SOR (StrandOddsRatio) is a related but more symmetric statistic that avoids over-penalizing strand imbalance at high depth, where FS tends to inflate. MQ is the root-mean-square mapping quality of reads supporting the variant — low MQ means the reads could plausibly map elsewhere, a hallmark of repetitive or paralogous regions. ReadPosRankSum applies a Mann-Whitney rank-sum test comparing where in the read the alt allele falls between alt- and ref-supporting reads; alt support clustered near read ends (rather than spread through the read body) suggests a misalignment artifact rather than a true variant. GATK's Best Practices hard-filter thresholds (e.g., QD < 2.0, FS > 60.0, MQ < 40.0) are empirically chosen cutoffs derived from what separates known-true from known-false sites in validation callsets — not universal physical laws.

sections.heading: VQSR: a learned multivariate threshold, and where it breaks
sections.body: Variant Quality Score Recalibration builds a Gaussian mixture model across several annotations jointly, rather than applying independent univariate cutoffs, training the model on 'true' positive sites from resources like HapMap, Omni, and 1000 Genomes. Each candidate variant gets a VQSLOD score reflecting how closely its annotation profile matches the density of known-true sites in that multivariate space, and the user picks a tranche — for example, a threshold retaining 99.5% sensitivity to the training sites — trading recall against precision as a tunable knob rather than a fixed yes/no. VQSR needs many thousands of true-positive sites to fit a reliable multivariate density; a small gene panel or a shallow exome simply doesn't supply enough variants for the mixture model to converge meaningfully, which is why VQSR is a whole-genome or large-cohort tool, not a small-panel one.

sections.heading: DeepVariant: learning the filter directly from pileups
sections.body: DeepVariant takes a different approach entirely: instead of hand-selected annotations, it converts the pileup of reads around a candidate site into an image-like tensor — read bases, base qualities, strand, and other properties encoded as channels, analogous to color channels in a photo — and feeds it to a convolutional neural network (built on an Inception-v3-style architecture) trained on labeled truth sets such as Genome in a Bottle. The network directly classifies the likely genotype from what the pileup 'looks like,' with no explicit QD- or FS-style thresholds anywhere in the decision. Whichever method is used, every filtering choice trades false positives against false negatives: tightening a threshold raises precision at recall's expense, loosening it does the reverse, so selecting a filter is always choosing a point on a precision-recall curve, not searching for one universally correct answer.

lessons.workedExample: A candidate SNV has QD = 1.2 (below the default QD < 2.0 hard-filter cutoff), but FS = 15, MQ = 58, and ReadPosRankSum = -1.0 all look clean. Under a hard-filter pipeline, this variant is discarded outright because of the single low QD value, even though every other annotation looks like a true call. Under VQSR, the same variant's full annotation profile — not QD alone — is compared against the density of known-true sites in multivariate space; if the combination as a whole still sits close to that true-site cloud, VQSLOD can keep the variant despite the marginal QD. This is the concrete difference between a hard threshold, which can only look at one number at a time, and a joint model, which can rescue (or reject) sites a single cutoff cannot judge correctly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on filter choice because 'why QD < 2.0' is not a trivia question about a magic number — it's a probe for whether the student can say what moving that threshold costs and buys. A student who explains the precision-recall tradeoff behind a specific cutoff, or why VQSR needs many training sites a small panel can't supply, has understood filtering as a calibrated decision; one who can only recite the threshold has memorized a setting.

questions.prompt: Why is a variant's raw confidence score normalized by depth (QD) rather than used directly?

options.text: Because deeper regions are always more repetitive
Because raw quality scores scale with coverage, so unnormalized scores would make deeply covered sites look artificially more confident regardless of actual support
Because depth has no effect on variant confidence
Because QD replaces the need for a reference genome

explanations.a: Depth and repetitiveness are separate properties; MQ, not QD, tracks mapping ambiguity.
explanations.b: Correct — QualByDepth divides confidence by depth specifically to remove the systematic inflation that coverage alone would otherwise cause.
explanations.c: Depth strongly affects raw confidence scores, which is exactly why QD exists to correct for it.
explanations.d: QD is an annotation on called variants; it has nothing to do with reference genome requirements.

questions.prompt: Why does VQSR tend to perform poorly on a small targeted gene panel?

options.text: Small panels have too few reads per site
The Gaussian mixture model needs many thousands of true-positive training sites to fit a reliable multivariate density, and a small panel doesn't contain enough variants
VQSR cannot process VCF files smaller than a certain size
Small panels always have low mapping quality

explanations.a: Read depth on a panel can be very high; the limitation is the number of distinct training-relevant sites, not per-site depth.
explanations.b: Correct — VQSR fits a multivariate model from known-true training sites, and a small panel simply doesn't contain enough variant sites for that density estimate to be reliable.
explanations.c: VQSR has no hard file-size limitation; the failure mode is statistical, not a format restriction.
explanations.d: Mapping quality depends on genomic context, not panel size.

questions.prompt: What does DeepVariant use in place of hand-selected annotation thresholds like QD or FS?

options.text: A fixed set of stricter hard-filter cutoffs
A convolutional neural network trained on pileup images to directly classify genotype
A larger training set for VQSR's Gaussian mixture model
Manual review of every candidate site

explanations.a: DeepVariant does not use hard-filter cutoffs at all; that's the pileup-annotation approach it replaces.
explanations.b: Correct — DeepVariant encodes the pileup around a candidate site as an image-like tensor and classifies it with a CNN trained on labeled truth data, with no explicit annotation thresholds.
explanations.c: DeepVariant is a distinct approach from VQSR, not an extension of its mixture model.
explanations.d: The entire point of DeepVariant is automated classification, not manual review.

questions.prompt: Match each annotation to what it is designed to detect.

right.text: Strand bias in alt-allele support
Low mapping confidence, suggesting a repetitive or multi-mapping region
Alt-allele support clustered near read ends rather than spread through the read body
Variant confidence normalized for site depth

questions.explanation: FS and SOR both quantify strand bias; MQ reflects mapping quality of supporting reads; ReadPosRankSum flags alt support concentrated near read ends, a misalignment signature; and QD removes the confound of depth from the raw confidence score.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the VQSR workflow.

items.text: Build a Gaussian mixture model from known-true training sites (HapMap, Omni, 1000 Genomes)
Score each candidate variant's annotation profile against the model to get a VQSLOD
Choose a sensitivity tranche (e.g., 99.5% of training sites retained)
Apply the resulting threshold to filter the candidate call set

questions.explanation: VQSR first fits its model on trusted training sites, then scores every candidate variant against that model, then the user selects a sensitivity tranche that sets the actual VQSLOD cutoff, and only then is that cutoff applied to filter the full call set.

lessons.label: Structural Variants and Copy Number

sections.heading: Four short-read signatures of a structural variant
sections.body: Short reads can't span most structural variants outright, so callers infer them from four indirect signatures. Discordant read pairs are pairs whose mapped distance, orientation, or chromosome disagrees with what the library preparation expects — a pair mapping too far apart implies a deletion between them, one mapping in the wrong orientation implies an inversion. Split reads are single reads that must be broken into two or more segments mapping to distant or differently oriented locations, which pinpoints a breakpoint down to the base pair rather than a fuzzy interval. Read depth is the classic copy-number signal: a region with roughly double the expected coverage implies a duplication, half implies a deletion, used by depth-based callers like CNVnator. Local assembly reconstructs the actual breakpoint sequence by de novo assembling reads around a candidate region, which is especially needed for insertions, where the inserted sequence itself has to be recovered rather than just located. Manta combines discordant pairs, split reads, and local assembly for base-pair breakpoint precision; DELLY integrates paired-end and split-read evidence similarly; LUMPY unifies multiple evidence types into a single per-breakpoint probabilistic score rather than treating them as separate filters.

sections.heading: Long reads call SVs directly instead of inferring them
sections.body: Sniffles and pbsv call structural variants from PacBio or Oxford Nanopore long reads, which individually span an entire breakpoint including any inserted or rearranged sequence. An SV then shows up as one aligned read with a large gap in its CIGAR string, or a soft-clip that resolves cleanly once locally realigned, rather than being statistically reconstructed from indirect evidence scattered across many short reads. This matters most for insertions: short reads systematically underdetect insertions longer than the library's insert size, since there is no way to split-map or fully span sequence that was never captured within a single fragment, while a long read that simply reads through the inserted sequence resolves it directly.

sections.heading: Few variants, disproportionate footprint
sections.body: The 1000 Genomes Project's Phase 3 structural variant map (Sudmant et al., 2015), built from 2,504 genomes, found that a typical genome carries roughly 4 to 5 million SNV and small-indel sites but only about 2,100 to 2,500 structural variants — three orders of magnitude fewer sites. Yet those few thousand SVs collectively affect roughly 20 megabases of sequence per genome, more total bases than all SNVs combined, because a single deletion or duplication can span thousands to millions of bases while each SNV changes exactly one. This asymmetry is why SV calling matters disproportionately for phenotype despite the small variant count: one large deletion can remove an entire gene, something no single SNV can do.

lessons.workedExample: A student calling variants in a family trio gets roughly 4.3 million SNVs and indels per genome from a standard pipeline, in line with 1000 Genomes expectations, but their SV caller (Manta) reports only about 2,300 structural variants per genome. At first this looks like the SV caller is underperforming — until they sum the total bases those SVs affect and get roughly 21 megabases per genome, larger than expected and comfortably ahead of the total bases changed by all the SNVs combined. The lesson is that SV count and SV impact are different axes entirely: structural variants are rare events with an outsized genomic footprint, not simply a smaller category of the same thing SNV calling finds.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this 'few but big' asymmetry because it's the single most testable insight in the lesson — a student who only says 'SVs matter more per site' has understood half of it; one who can explain why (breakpoints require different evidence than single-base mismatches, and variant count and affected-base footprint are separate currencies) has understood the underlying biology and methodology, not just repeated a statistic.

questions.prompt: A read pair maps much farther apart than the library's expected insert size, but in the correct orientation. What does this discordant pair most likely indicate?

options.text: A deletion between the two mates
A single nucleotide variant at one mate's position
Normal sequencing noise with no biological cause
An inversion at that locus

explanations.a: Correct — if the reference sequence between the mates is missing in the sample, the same two reads will map farther apart than the library's true insert size implies, signaling a deletion.
explanations.b: An SNV doesn't change mapped distance between mates at all; that's not what discordant-pair signatures detect.
explanations.c: A systematic distance discordance across supporting reads at one locus is a structural signal, not random noise.
explanations.d: An inversion is signaled by discordant orientation, not simply increased distance with normal orientation preserved.

questions.prompt: Why can long-read technologies (PacBio, Nanopore) call many structural variants directly rather than inferring them statistically?

options.text: Long reads have higher per-base accuracy than short reads
A single long read can span an entire breakpoint, including any inserted or rearranged sequence, rather than relying on indirect evidence spread across many short reads
Long-read sequencers use a different reference genome
Long reads eliminate the need for alignment entirely

explanations.a: Historically long reads have had lower raw per-base accuracy than short reads; that isn't why they directly resolve SVs.
explanations.b: Correct — spanning the whole breakpoint and any inserted sequence within one read lets the SV appear directly in that read's alignment (a large CIGAR gap or resolvable soft-clip) instead of being reconstructed from scattered indirect signals.
explanations.c: Long and short reads are both aligned to the same standard reference genomes.
explanations.d: Long reads still require alignment; local realignment around candidate SVs is part of tools like Sniffles and pbsv.

questions.prompt: Per the 1000 Genomes Project Phase 3 structural variant map (Sudmant et al., 2015), roughly how many structural variants does a typical genome carry, compared to its 4-5 million SNV/indel sites?

options.text: Roughly 200,000
Roughly 50
Roughly the same, 4-5 million

explanations.a: Correct — the Phase 3 map found approximately 2,100 to 2,500 structural variants per genome, several orders of magnitude fewer than the SNV/indel count.
explanations.b: 200,000 is far too high; that figure isn't supported by the Phase 3 SV map.
explanations.c: 50 undercounts even the low end of the study's per-genome SV estimate.
explanations.d: SVs are far rarer than SNVs/indels per genome; the two counts are not comparable in scale.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to the primary evidence it relies on for structural variant calling.

right.text: Discordant read pairs, split reads, and local assembly combined
Read-depth signal (coverage above or below expected)
Direct spanning of the breakpoint by individual long reads

questions.explanation: Manta integrates discordant pairs, split reads, and local assembly for breakpoint precision; CNVnator relies primarily on read-depth deviations to call copy-number variants; and long-read callers like Sniffles and pbsv call SVs directly because individual reads span the whole breakpoint.

lessons.label: Annotating and Prioritizing Variants

sections.heading: Consequence prediction depends on which transcript you pick
sections.body: VEP (Ensembl's Variant Effect Predictor), SnpEff, and ANNOVAR all take a VCF and annotate each variant against gene models to predict functional consequence — missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, and so on. The complication is that a single genomic position often overlaps multiple transcripts of the same gene, or transcripts of different genes entirely, and exon boundaries differ between transcripts, so the same variant can be missense in one isoform and intronic in another. 'The' consequence therefore depends on which transcript is chosen as canonical, and picking the longest transcript or an arbitrary default can silently give a wrong-feeling answer. MANE Select (Matched Annotation from NCBI and EMBL-EBI), finalized around 2019-2020, fixes this by defining one representative transcript per protein-coding gene that RefSeq and Ensembl agree on identically, giving pipelines a stable default instead of an arbitrary pick.

sections.heading: Population frequency is the highest-yield filter
sections.body: gnomAD (the Genome Aggregation Database, maintained by the Broad Institute and spanning hundreds of thousands of individuals across its v2 through v4 releases) reports allele frequency across large, mostly healthy reference populations. A variant present at appreciable frequency in gnomAD — commonly used cutoffs sit around 1% or lower depending on the disease model — is unlikely to cause a rare, severe Mendelian condition, since such variants would be far rarer in the population if they were highly deleterious. Frequency filtering against gnomAD is typically the single step that removes the largest fraction of candidate variants in an exome, before any structural or functional reasoning is applied.

sections.heading: In-silico predictors, and their shared blind spot
sections.body: SIFT and PolyPhen-2 predict whether a missense change is damaging using sequence conservation and structural context; CADD integrates many genomic annotations into a single score trained to separate simulated deleterious variants from common ones; REVEL is an ensemble meta-predictor specifically for missense variants, combining outputs from several individual tools; SpliceAI is a deep-learning model that predicts splicing disruption directly from sequence context. The shared limitation is that many of these tools are trained on overlapping data — the same catalogs of known pathogenic and benign variants — and ensemble tools like REVEL and CADD literally take other predictors' scores (including SIFT and PolyPhen-2) as input features. That means their errors are correlated, not independent, so stacking several of them as corroborating evidence inflates confidence far less than treating them as separate votes would suggest.

lessons.workedExample: A candidate missense variant sits in exon 4 of one transcript of a gene but falls in an intron of a shorter alternative transcript of the same gene. Without a fixed transcript convention, two students annotate the same variant differently: one, using the longer transcript, calls it a damaging missense change (SIFT deleterious, PolyPhen-2 probably damaging); the other, using the shorter transcript, calls it a likely-benign intronic variant — a disagreement created entirely by transcript choice, before biology or frequency even enters the picture. Standardizing on the MANE Select transcript resolves the ambiguity. Checking gnomAD then shows the variant absent across roughly 800,000 observed alleles, which keeps it as a plausible rare candidate worth further review with REVEL and SpliceAI, rather than something either predictor result alone should settle.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on transcript choice and correlated predictors specifically because this is the step where good-looking numbers can be one opinion wearing five labels: five tools all saying 'damaging' is weak evidence if several of them share training data or literally take each other's scores as inputs. A student who can say how many of their predictors are actually independent evidence, rather than just counting votes, has understood ensemble bias rather than just run a pipeline.

questions.prompt: Why can VEP, SnpEff, and ANNOVAR report different predicted consequences for the exact same variant?

options.text: They use different reference genome builds by default in every configuration
The variant overlaps multiple transcripts with different exon/intron boundaries, so the predicted consequence depends on which transcript is used
Two of the three tools do not support indels
Only ANNOVAR checks population frequency

explanations.a: All three tools can be configured to the same reference build; that mismatch isn't the typical cause of disagreement.
explanations.b: Correct — when a position lies within overlapping transcripts whose exon boundaries differ, the same variant can be missense in one and intronic in another, so the reported consequence depends on transcript choice.
explanations.c: All three tools handle indels; that isn't the source of disagreement described here.
explanations.d: Population frequency is a separate annotation step from consequence prediction and isn't unique to ANNOVAR.

questions.prompt: What problem does MANE Select specifically solve?

options.text: It removes the need for population frequency filtering
It defines one representative transcript per gene, identically agreed upon by RefSeq and Ensembl, replacing an arbitrary transcript choice
It predicts splicing disruption directly
It replaces CADD as the deleteriousness score of choice

explanations.a: MANE Select addresses transcript choice, not allele frequency filtering.
explanations.b: Correct — MANE Select gives a single canonical transcript per protein-coding gene, matched between RefSeq and Ensembl, so consequence annotation has a stable default instead of an arbitrary pick.
explanations.c: Splicing prediction is what SpliceAI does; MANE Select is about transcript selection, not splicing.
explanations.d: MANE Select is unrelated to CADD's scoring function; the two solve different problems.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to treat agreement among SIFT, PolyPhen-2, CADD, and REVEL as five independent pieces of evidence for a missense variant?

options.text: Because they are trained on overlapping data, and ensemble tools like REVEL and CADD directly use other predictors' scores as input features, so their errors are correlated
Because only one of the four tools actually works on missense variants
Because these tools disagree with each other more often than they agree
Because CADD and REVEL require a different reference genome than SIFT and PolyPhen-2

explanations.a: Correct — shared training data and direct incorporation of other tools' scores as features means these predictors' errors are correlated rather than independent, so stacking them overstates the actual corroborating evidence.
explanations.b: All four are commonly applied to missense variants; applicability isn't the issue here.
explanations.c: The concern in this lesson is correlated agreement inflating confidence, not typical disagreement rates.
explanations.d: Reference genome build compatibility is a separate technical concern from the correlated-training-data problem described.

questions.prompt: Match each resource or tool to what it primarily predicts or provides.

right.text: Whether a missense change is damaging, from conservation and structural context
An integrated deleteriousness score built from many genomic annotations
Whether a variant disrupts splicing, predicted from sequence context via deep learning
Allele frequency across large reference populations

questions.explanation: SIFT and PolyPhen-2 score missense damage from conservation/structure, CADD combines many annotations into one integrated score, SpliceAI predicts splicing disruption from sequence with a deep-learning model, and gnomAD supplies population allele frequencies rather than a functional prediction.

lessons.label: Benchmarking a Caller Honestly

sections.heading: Precision, recall, and what the denominator has to be
sections.body: The Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) consortium provides reference samples such as NA12878/HG001 with a high-confidence truth VCF and, critically, a high-confidence BED file marking exactly which regions that truth VCF is trusted for — built by combining many sequencing technologies and callers so that sites where methods disagree are excluded from truth rather than adjudicated by guesswork. Precision is TP / (TP + FP) among the calls a pipeline actually made; recall is TP / (TP + FN) among the truth variants that exist in the confident region; F1 is their harmonic mean. Computing these over the whole genome rather than the confident region is a common and serious mistake: regions with no established truth get silently miscounted as either errors or successes, which makes the resulting number uninterpretable regardless of how precise the arithmetic looks.

sections.heading: One F1 number hides where callers actually differ
sections.body: GIAB and the related GA4GH benchmarking framework stratify performance separately by region class: easy high-confidence regions, low-complexity or repetitive sequence, homopolymer runs (where PCR and sequencing slippage cause systematic indel errors), and segmental duplications (near-identical paralogous sequence where reads from two different genomic locations map ambiguously together, producing false heterozygous calls from cross-paralog contamination of the pileup). Two callers can post nearly identical genome-wide F1 scores while one is dramatically better specifically inside homopolymers and the other inside segmental duplications — a difference a single aggregate number erases completely, even though it is exactly the difference that matters for a given application.

sections.heading: Comparing representations, not just positions
sections.body: The same underlying indel can be written as more than one valid VCF representation — different combinations of position, REF, and ALT that describe an equivalent sequence change, which happens routinely in repetitive or homopolymer contexts where an indel can be shifted left or right within the repeat with no change in meaning. Naive comparison that matches calls to truth purely by position and allele string can therefore score one genuinely correct call as both a missed truth variant (false negative) and a spurious extra call (false positive) — double-penalizing a caller for a formatting difference rather than an actual error. Tools built for this, such as RTG vcfeval and Illumina's hap.py, normalize and realign variant representations before comparing sets, so equivalent indels correctly match as true positives. This step is essential for indel-heavy comparisons, where naive scoring can inflate apparent error rates substantially.

lessons.workedExample: A caller correctly identifies a 2bp deletion sitting in a homopolymer run but represents it left-aligned at position 1000, while the GIAB truth VCF represents the exact same deletion right-aligned at position 1003 — both are valid, equivalent descriptions of one real event. A homemade comparison script matching purely on position and allele string counts this as a missed truth variant plus an extra spurious call, visibly dropping the computed F1 for a caller that made zero actual errors at that site. Running the same two VCFs through hap.py, which normalizes representation before matching, correctly scores it as a single true positive, and the caller's real F1 turns out noticeably higher than the naive script suggested.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this because 'my caller got 99% F1' should never be accepted at face value — the follow-up question, F1 on what confident region, stratified by which region class, compared with what matching tool, tests whether a student understands that one aggregate number can hide both where a caller actually fails and artifacts introduced by the comparison method itself, not the caller.

questions.prompt: Which formula correctly defines precision for variant calling?

options.text: TP / (TP + FN)
TP / (TP + FP)
FP / (TP + FP)
(TP + TN) / (TP + FP + FN + TN)

explanations.a: TP / (TP + FN) is recall — the fraction of true variants actually called — not precision.
explanations.b: Correct — precision is the fraction of calls a pipeline actually made that are true positives.
explanations.c: This is the false discovery rate, the complement of precision, not precision itself.
explanations.d: This is an accuracy-style formula that isn't standard for variant-calling benchmarks and requires a meaningful true-negative count, which isn't well-defined genome-wide.

questions.prompt: Why can two callers with nearly identical genome-wide F1 scores actually differ substantially in real-world usefulness?

options.text: F1 scores are always identical regardless of caller, so this cannot happen
A single aggregate F1 hides performance differences that only show up when stratified by region class, such as homopolymers or segmental duplications
F1 only measures speed, not accuracy
Genome-wide F1 cannot be computed for more than one caller at a time

explanations.a: F1 scores vary substantially between callers; that isn't the reason for this discrepancy.
explanations.b: Correct — one caller can excel in homopolymers while another excels in segmental duplications, and these opposite strengths can average out to similar overall F1 scores that erase the real difference.
explanations.c: F1 is an accuracy measure combining precision and recall; it has nothing to do with runtime speed.
explanations.d: F1 can be computed independently for any number of callers on the same truth set; that isn't a limitation.

questions.prompt: Why can naive position-and-allele-string comparison of indels generate a false negative and a false positive for one genuinely correct call?

options.text: Because indels are never represented correctly by any caller

Because the same indel can have more than one valid VCF representation (different position/REF/ALT describing the same event), especially in repetitive sequence, and naive matching treats these as different variants
Because truth sets never include any indels
Because FP and FN cannot both occur in the same comparison

explanations.a: Correctly called indels happen routinely; the issue here is representation, not caller failure.
explanations.b: Correct — an indel shifted within a homopolymer or repeat can be validly written at different positions, and comparing by raw position/allele string treats one real event as two mismatched variants.
explanations.c: GIAB truth sets include indels specifically, which is why representation-aware comparison matters for them.
explanations.d: Both an FN and an FP can occur from the same underlying event when representations differ, which is exactly the double-penalty problem described.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct definition.

right.text: Fraction of a pipeline's actual calls that are true positives
Fraction of true variants in the truth set that were successfully called
The region where a truth VCF is established as reliable, defined by a BED file
Normalizing/realigning variant encodings before matching, so equivalent indels aren't scored as separate events

questions.explanation: Precision measures correctness among calls made, recall measures completeness against known truth, the confident region defines where that truth is trustworthy, and representation-aware comparison prevents equivalent variant encodings from being double-penalized.

lessons.label: Reading Output Like a Skeptic

sections.heading: A checklist for looking at a call in IGV
sections.body: Loading a candidate variant in IGV and looking at the pileup directly catches artifacts that pass a caller's automated filters. First, check strand distribution of alt-supporting reads: a real variant is usually supported by roughly even numbers of forward- and reverse-strand reads, while support concentrated almost entirely on one strand is the same strand-bias signal FS and SOR quantify numerically, now visible by eye. Second, check where in each read the alt allele falls: support clustered only in soft-clipped ends — the portion of a read the aligner gave up on mapping and left unaligned — rather than solid matches through the read body, points to a misalignment artifact, not a true call. Third, check the reference context around the site: a variant sitting inside a homopolymer run or a short tandem repeat is in a region where PCR and sequencing slippage routinely manufacture spurious indels that can look like a confident heterozygous or even homozygous call.

sections.heading: Two damage signatures with a fixed chemical identity
sections.body: OxoG damage arises when guanine is oxidized to 8-oxoguanine during sample shearing or library preparation — a real chemical event, not a sequencing error — which then mispairs with adenine during PCR, producing characteristic false G>T substitutions (or C>A read from the opposite strand). Costello and colleagues (2013) characterized this systematically in deep targeted-capture sequencing data, showing the artifact rate scales with library prep method and, critically, that OxoG artifacts are strongly biased toward one strand or read orientation, while a true G>T mutation shows no such asymmetry — giving a concrete computational check, not just a name to recognize. FFPE deamination is a separate, unrelated signature: formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue, common in archival and clinical tumor samples, accumulates cytosine deamination to uracil over time and during fixation, which reads out as artifactual C>T (or G>A) substitutions, typically at low variant allele fraction, and is likewise distinguishable through orientation-bias filtering similar to the OxoG check.

sections.heading: Building a defensible call, not a guess
sections.body: No single check settles the question alone, but a variant with balanced strand support, alt-allele reads matched well into the read body rather than only in soft-clipped tails, a reference context free of homopolymer or repeat structure, and a substitution pattern that doesn't match a known damage signature for the library prep used, is one a student can defend as real. A call missing several of these should be argued as likely artifactual — and naming which specific signature it resembles (OxoG, FFPE deamination, homopolymer slippage, or generic strand bias) is what separates a defensible answer from an unsupported guess.

lessons.workedExample: A pileup screenshot shows a G>T call at 15% variant allele fraction in a tumor-only sample known to be FFPE-derived, with every single alt-supporting read on the same strand and no repeat structure in the reference context. The strand restriction and low VAF match the OxoG artifact pattern Costello and colleagues (2013) described — oxidative damage introduced during shearing — not the FFPE deamination pattern, which would present as C>T or G>A rather than G>T. The defensible read of this pileup is 'likely OxoG artifact, needs orientation-bias filtering before trusting this call,' not 'likely real somatic mutation,' even though the caller may have passed it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge uses a pileup screenshot specifically because it's the fastest way to tell whether a student can move past a caller's PASS label into actual judgment.
