Naming the specific artifact — not just 'this might be wrong' — and the specific tell that identifies it (strand restriction, soft-clip-only support, homopolymer context, characteristic substitution) is exactly the skill an automated filter can't replace, and it's what a judge wants performed live in front of them.

questions.prompt: A candidate variant's alt-allele support comes only from the soft-clipped ends of reads, never from solid matches within the read body. What does this suggest?

options.text: A confident, well-supported true variant
A likely misalignment artifact rather than a real call
FFPE deamination specifically
Normal sequencing depth

explanations.a: A true variant is typically supported by matches within the read body, not only unaligned soft-clipped tails.
explanations.b: Correct — support restricted to soft-clipped ends, portions the aligner already gave up on placing confidently, is a hallmark of a misalignment artifact.
explanations.c: FFPE deamination has a specific substitution signature (C>T/G>A), not a soft-clip-location signature.
explanations.d: This pattern is about where support falls within reads, not overall depth.

questions.prompt: OxoG oxidative damage, as characterized by Costello and colleagues (2013), characteristically produces which false substitution?

options.text: C>T
G>T
A>G
T>A

explanations.a: C>T is the characteristic signature of FFPE deamination, a different damage mechanism.
explanations.b: Correct — oxidation of guanine to 8-oxoguanine causes mispairing with adenine during PCR, producing a characteristic false G>T substitution.
explanations.c: A>G is not the signature associated with either OxoG or FFPE damage in this lesson.
explanations.d: T>A is not the OxoG signature; the damaged base is guanine, producing G>T.

questions.prompt: What false substitution pattern does FFPE (formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded) tissue deamination characteristically produce?

options.text: G>T
C>T
A>C
Indels only, never substitutions

explanations.a: G>T is the OxoG oxidative-damage signature, not FFPE deamination.
explanations.b: Correct — cytosine deamination to uracil during formalin fixation reads out as artifactual C>T (or G>A) substitutions, typically at low variant allele fraction.
explanations.c: A>C is not the deamination signature described; deamination affects cytosine specifically.
explanations.d: FFPE deamination produces substitution artifacts, not indel artifacts; homopolymer slippage is the indel-producing mechanism.

questions.prompt: Match each artifact to the pileup signature that identifies it.

right.text: Alt-allele support restricted almost entirely to one strand
Spurious indel appearing inside a homopolymer or short tandem repeat
Strand-restricted false G>T substitutions from oxidized guanine during shearing
Low-VAF false C>T substitutions from cytosine deamination during fixation

questions.explanation: Generic strand bias shows as one-sided strand support without a specific substitution identity; homopolymer slippage produces spurious indels in repeat runs; OxoG damage produces strand-restricted G>T substitutions from oxidized guanine; FFPE deamination produces low-VAF C>T substitutions from formalin-driven cytosine deamination.

questions.prompt: Order the checklist steps for inspecting a candidate variant in IGV before deciding whether it is real or artifactual.

items.text: Check strand balance of alt-allele support
Check whether support falls in the read body or only in soft-clipped ends
Check the reference context for homopolymer or repeat structure
Check the substitution pattern against known damage signatures (OxoG, FFPE)
Conclude whether the call is defensible as real or likely artifactual

questions.explanation: A systematic inspection checks strand balance, then where within reads support falls, then the local sequence context for repeat structure, then whether the substitution matches a known chemical-damage pattern, and only after gathering all four checks reaches a conclusion about the call.

lessons.label: Clone-by-Clone vs Whole-Genome Shotgun

sections.heading: A proposal and a public rebuttal, in the same journal issue
sections.body: In 1997, Jim Weber and Gene Myers published "Human Whole-Genome Shotgun Sequencing" in Genome Research, arguing the human genome could be sequenced by shattering the whole genome into small fragments, sequencing them, and letting a computer reassemble the pieces from overlaps — cheaper and faster than the plan already underway. Phil Green published a direct rebuttal in the same issue, "Against a Whole-Genome Shotgun," arguing that repetitive DNA (which makes up roughly half the human genome) would create ambiguous overlaps a shotgun assembler could not resolve, and that the coverage needed to close gaps was underestimated. The public Human Genome Project (HGP) sided with Green's caution and used a hierarchical clone-by-clone strategy: break the genome into large, mapped BAC clones with known chromosomal positions, then shotgun-sequence each clone separately, where local repeats are far less confusing than genome-wide ones.

sections.heading: Two strategies, two 2001 papers
sections.body: Craig Venter's company Celera Genomics bet on whole-genome shotgun anyway, racing the public consortium. Both efforts published draft genomes within a day of each other in February 2001: the International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium's Nature paper ("Initial sequencing and analysis of the human genome") appeared February 15, and Celera's Science paper ("The Sequence of the Human Genome") appeared February 16. Both were declared successes, and the rivalry pushed both efforts to finish years ahead of pre-project estimates — the public consortium had originally targeted 2005.

sections.heading: The 2002 PNAS argument over whose assembly it really was
sections.body: The dispute did not end there. In 2002, Robert Waterston, Eric Lander, and John Sulston published "On the Sequencing of the Human Genome" in PNAS, arguing that Celera's assembly was not an independent demonstration of whole-genome shotgun: Celera had shredded the public consortium's already-assembled sequence into a uniform tiling path and mixed it into their own shotgun reads before reassembling, so the result leaned heavily on public mapping data rather than resolving the genome from Celera's shotgun reads alone. Their computational argument had a specific number behind it: a perfect tiling path built from the public map, at just 2-fold sequence coverage, is sufficient on its own to recover virtually an entire genome assembly — meaning Celera's reported accuracy could be explained by that borrowed tiling path doing the real work, not by whole-genome shotgun resolving the genome unaided. Myers and Celera colleagues replied in the same journal, arguing this mixing was a legitimate way to gain coverage, not a dependency that invalidated the whole-genome shotgun method.

lessons.workedExample: A judge asks why the public project didn't just do what Celera did. The strong answer: in 1997 Green's specific worry was that genome-wide repeats (transposons, segmental duplications) would make a shotgun assembler stitch together the wrong pieces without an independent map to check against. Clone-by-clone sidesteps this because each BAC clone is only ~150kb and already positioned on the chromosome, so an assembler only has to disambiguate repeats within that small window, not across 3 billion bases. The 2002 PNAS exchange (Waterston, Lander, Sulston vs. Myers et al.) is exactly this argument continuing: did Celera's result prove pure whole-genome shotgun works, or did it prove whole-genome shotgun works when quietly given a map for free?
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this history will ask which strategy a student's own project depends on, and whether they can name the actual failure mode (ambiguous repeat overlaps) rather than a vague "it's more accurate." Naming Green's specific technical objection, not just "there was a rivalry," and being able to state what the 2002 PNAS dispute was actually about — whether Celera's assembly used public data as scaffolding — separates a student who read past the popular Human Genome Project narrative from one who only knows the two-companies-raced framing.

questions.prompt: What was Phil Green's core technical objection to Weber and Myers' 1997 whole-genome shotgun proposal?

options.text: It would be too slow compared to clone-by-clone sequencing
Repetitive DNA across the genome would create ambiguous overlaps an assembler could not resolve without independent positional information
Shotgun sequencing could not be automated
It required a computer that did not yet exist

explanations.a: Speed was actually shotgun's selling point; Green's objection was about assembly correctness, not speed.
explanations.b: Correct — Green argued that genome-wide repeats would produce ambiguous overlaps a shotgun assembler could not correctly resolve, unlike within a small, mapped clone.
explanations.c: Automation was not the disputed issue; sequencing machines already existed and were used by both strategies.
explanations.d: The proposal was a strategy/algorithm dispute, not a hardware-availability one.

questions.prompt: Why does clone-by-clone sequencing reduce the repeat-ambiguity problem Green raised?

options.text: Because each BAC clone is small and already mapped to a chromosomal position, so an assembler only resolves repeats within that small window
Because BAC clones contain no repetitive DNA at all
Because clone-by-clone does not require any computational assembly
Because it sequences only coding regions

explanations.a: Correct — a ~150kb mapped clone confines the repeat-disambiguation problem to a small, positioned window instead of the whole genome.
explanations.b: Repeats still occur within clones; the strategy reduces the scale of the ambiguity, not its existence.
explanations.c: Clone-by-clone still requires assembling reads within each clone — it just does so at much smaller scale.
explanations.d: Both strategies sequence the whole genome, not just coding regions.

questions.prompt: Match each publication to its role in this history.

right.text: Proposed whole-genome shotgun sequencing of the human genome
Rebutted the proposal, citing repeat-driven assembly ambiguity
Argued Celera's genome assembly leaned on public consortium data
Defended Celera's approach as a legitimate use of available coverage

questions.explanation: Weber & Myers proposed whole-genome shotgun in 1997; Green rebutted it in the same issue over repeat ambiguity; Waterston, Lander & Sulston argued in 2002 that Celera's published assembly depended on the public consortium's tiling path; Myers and colleagues replied defending the approach.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.

items.text: Weber & Myers propose whole-genome shotgun; Green publishes a rebuttal in the same Genome Research issue
The public consortium and Celera each publish a draft human genome (Nature and Science)
Waterston, Lander & Sulston publish a PNAS critique of Celera's assembly method
Myers and Celera colleagues publish a PNAS reply defending their method

questions.explanation: The 1997 proposal-and-rebuttal came first, followed by the 2001 dueling draft-genome papers, then the 2002 PNAS critique from Waterston, Lander, and Sulston, and finally Myers and colleagues' reply in the same journal.

lessons.label: How Sequence Search Became Biology's Most-Used Tool

sections.heading: A database first, then a reason to search it
sections.body: GenBank was founded in 1982 (originally run out of Los Alamos National Laboratory, later moved to NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information) as a public archive where any researcher who sequenced a gene could deposit it and anyone else could retrieve it. That single decision — free, public deposition — is what made sequence search worth building: without a shared, growing pool of known sequences, there was nothing to compare a new sequence against. GenBank's early growth was slow, but the norm it set, that sequence data gets shared rather than hoarded, became the foundation the rest of bioinformatics was built on.

sections.heading: FASTA: fast enough to actually use
sections.body: David Lipman and William Pearson published the FASTA algorithm in Science in 1985 ("Rapid and sensitive protein similarity searches"), refined in a 1988 PNAS paper. FASTA's trick was to first find short, exact-matching "words" (k-mers) shared between the query and database sequences, then only run a full, slower alignment on the regions around those hits. This heuristic — filter cheaply first, align expensively second — made searching a growing database computationally feasible instead of requiring a full dynamic-programming alignment (Smith-Waterman). Smith-Waterman guarantees the single best local alignment, but it does so at O(n·m) time and space for a query of length n against a database sequence of length m — costs that make running it against every sequence in a large archive, one comparison at a time, impractical at database scale.

sections.heading: BLAST and the cost of being fast
sections.body: Stephen Altschul, Warren Gish, Webb Miller, Gene Myers, and David Lipman published BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) in the Journal of Molecular Biology in 1990. BLAST pushed the same word-then-extend strategy further with better statistics — an E-value estimating how many hits that good would be expected by chance, computed using a substitution scoring matrix such as BLOSUM62 for protein searches that scores each possible amino-acid pairing by how often it's observed to substitute in related proteins — and became one of the most-cited papers in the history of science, with well over 100,000 citations. BLAST is a heuristic: because it only extends alignments from short exact-match seeds, it can miss a true optimal alignment that a full Smith-Waterman search would find, especially for short or highly divergent sequences. That tradeoff — sometimes wrong, but fast enough to search millions of sequences in seconds instead of Smith-Waterman's far costlier full alignment — is precisely why it won: a slightly-less-than-perfect answer researchers could actually get, beat a perfect answer they couldn't afford to compute, on free software anyone could run against a free public database.

lessons.workedExample: A student sequences an unknown gene from a soil bacterium and wants to know what it does. Running full Smith-Waterman alignment against every sequence in GenBank (hundreds of millions of entries) would take an impractically long time on a laptop. Running BLAST instead: it finds short exact-match seeds between the query and database sequences in seconds, extends only the promising ones, and returns ranked hits with E-values — say, a top hit to a known nitrogen-fixation gene with E-value 1e-120 (essentially certain to be real homology, not chance). The student now has a testable hypothesis about function, obtained in under a minute, because BLAST traded a guarantee of finding the single best alignment for speed across a huge search space.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about BLAST because so many student projects report a BLAST hit as if it were a definitive identification, without understanding that it's a heuristic. A student who can explain that BLAST seeds on exact short matches and extends them — and can therefore miss true but weakly-similar homologs, or misrank hits for short/repetitive queries — shows they understand the tool's limits, not just its output. It also tests whether a student knows the free-and-public culture (GenBank, and BLAST itself as freely available software) is what let a heuristic algorithm become a universal default rather than a niche shortcut.

questions.prompt: Why did GenBank's 1982 founding matter for the eventual usefulness of tools like BLAST?

options.text: It provided the computing hardware BLAST needed to run
It created a large, shared, growing pool of public sequence data, without which there would be nothing to search against
It invented the BLAST algorithm itself
It restricted sequence deposition to approved labs, ensuring data quality

explanations.a: GenBank is a data archive, not a hardware provider.
explanations.b: Correct — a search tool is only useful if there is a large, shared database to search; GenBank's free public deposition model created exactly that.
explanations.c: GenBank and BLAST were separate developments; GenBank predates BLAST by eight years and was not an algorithm.
explanations.d: GenBank's model was open deposition, not restricted access — that openness is the point.

questions.prompt: What is the core heuristic shared by FASTA and BLAST that makes them fast?

options.text: They only search the first 100 bases of any sequence
They find short exact-matching words first, then run full alignment only around those seed hits
They compress the database before searching
They ignore protein sequences and search DNA only

explanations.a: Neither tool truncates sequences; they search the whole sequence, just via a filtering strategy.
explanations.b: Correct — both use a seed-and-extend approach: cheap exact-match filtering first, expensive full alignment only where a seed hit suggests it's worthwhile.
explanations.c: Database compression is not the mechanism; the speedup comes from avoiding full alignment against every entry.
explanations.d: Both tools handle both nucleotide and protein sequences (BLASTN, BLASTP, and related variants).

questions.prompt: Because BLAST is a heuristic rather than a guaranteed-optimal aligner, what is a realistic limitation a student should acknowledge?

options.text: BLAST can never return a true positive hit
BLAST may miss a true but weak or short homologous match because it requires an initial exact-match seed to extend from
BLAST cannot report an E-value
BLAST only works on sequences deposited after 1990

explanations.a: BLAST returns true positives constantly; that is why it is the field's default tool.
explanations.b: Correct — because it seeds on short exact matches before extending, a real but weakly similar or very short homology can lack a seed and go undetected, unlike a full Smith-Waterman search.
explanations.c: E-values are a core part of BLAST's output, used to judge statistical significance.
explanations.d: BLAST searches any sequence data present in the database, regardless of deposition date.

questions.prompt: Order these developments chronologically.

items.text: GenBank founded as a public sequence archive
Lipman & Pearson publish FASTA in Science
Pearson & Lipman publish the improved FASTA in PNAS
Altschul, Gish, Miller, Myers & Lipman publish BLAST

questions.explanation: GenBank (1982) came first, giving sequence search something to search against; FASTA followed in 1985 and was refined in 1988; BLAST, building on the same seed-and-extend idea with better statistics, was published in 1990.

lessons.label: The Assembly Wars: OLC vs de Bruijn

sections.heading: Overlap-layout-consensus: assembly as a graph of reads
sections.body: Gene Myers built the overlap-layout-consensus (OLC) approach behind the Celera Assembler, used for Celera's 2000 Drosophila genome and the 2001 human genome: find all pairwise overlaps between reads, lay the reads out into a consistent order along the genome, then vote on a consensus base at each position. OLC is intuitive — it directly mirrors how a person would piece together overlapping fragments — but computing all pairwise overlaps among millions of reads is expensive, and the resulting overlap graph gets tangled fast wherever repeats make two different genomic locations look identical.

sections.heading: de Bruijn graphs: assembly as an Eulerian path
sections.body: In 2001, Pavel Pevzner, Haixu Tang, and Michael Waterman published "An Eulerian Path Approach to DNA Fragment Assembly" in PNAS, reframing assembly entirely: instead of comparing whole reads pairwise, break every read into short fixed-length k-mers and build a de Bruijn graph where each k-mer is an edge; assembling the genome becomes finding an Eulerian path that uses every edge (k-mer) exactly once. This sidesteps all-against-all read comparison — a huge win once short-read sequencing (Illumina) started producing hundreds of millions of short reads a machine could never afford to compare pairwise. Velvet (Daniel Zerbino & Ewan Birney, Genome Research 2008) and later SPAdes (Bankevich et al. 2012) built practical short-read assemblers on this de Bruijn foundation, and it became the dominant approach for the short-read era.

sections.heading: GAGE and Assemblathon: the reckoning over what 'good' means
sections.body: By the early 2010s, dozens of assemblers existed, and two coordinated bake-offs asked the uncomfortable question: given the identical raw data, do different assemblers even produce comparable genomes? GAGE (Salzberg et al., Genome Research 2012) and Assemblathon 1 (Earl et al., Genome Research 2011) and Assemblathon 2 (Bradnam et al., GigaScience 2013) ran many assemblers on the same real or simulated datasets and found wildly different results — assembly length, contiguity, and error rates varied enormously between tools on identical input. The most consequential finding: N50 (a standard contiguity statistic, the contig length at which half the assembly is contained in equal-or-longer contigs) did not reliably track actual correctness. An assembler could post an impressively high N50 while stitching together misassembled, chimeric contigs that merged the wrong genomic regions — meaning the single number the field had been using to rank assemblies could reward confidently wrong answers over honestly fragmented but correct ones.

lessons.workedExample: A team assembles the same bacterial genome from identical reads using two tools and gets N50 = 250,000 bp from one and N50 = 90,000 bp from the other. Naively, the higher-N50 assembly looks better — longer contigs, less fragmented. But GAGE-style validation against a known reference showed this reasoning fails in practice: the high-N50 assembler had, in some benchmark genomes, bridged over a repeat incorrectly and joined two non-adjacent regions into one falsely long contig, while the lower-N50 assembler had honestly broken the assembly at the repeat rather than guess. Checking with an independent measure — aligning contigs back to a trusted reference or a genetic map, not just reporting N50 — is what GAGE and Assemblathon showed is required before trusting a contiguity statistic.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is a favorite judge probe because it tests whether a student trusts a single summary statistic or understands what it measures. Anyone can report an N50 from assembler output; a judge wants to hear that N50 measures contiguity, not correctness, and that GAGE and Assemblathon caught assemblers achieving a high N50 through misassembly. A student who says "I checked contig accuracy against a reference, not just N50, because Assemblathon showed N50 rankings can disagree with correctness rankings" has understood the actual lesson of that history.

questions.prompt: What computational problem does the de Bruijn graph approach (Pevzner, Tang & Waterman, 2001) avoid that overlap-layout-consensus (OLC) requires?

options.text: It avoids needing any sequencing reads at all
It avoids computing all pairwise overlaps between reads, instead breaking reads into k-mers and finding an Eulerian path
It avoids the need for a consensus sequence
It avoids repeats entirely by ignoring them

explanations.a: Both approaches still require sequencing reads as input; the difference is how those reads are related to each other.
explanations.b: Correct — de Bruijn assembly reframes the problem as an Eulerian path over k-mer edges, avoiding the expensive all-against-all pairwise overlap computation OLC needs.
explanations.c: Both approaches still ultimately produce a consensus sequence; that step isn't eliminated, just reached differently.
explanations.d: Repeats still cause tangles in a de Bruijn graph (branch points); the approach doesn't ignore them, it represents them differently.

questions.prompt: What did GAGE and Assemblathon (2011-2013) find about N50 as a quality metric?

options.text: N50 perfectly predicted assembly correctness across all tested assemblers
A high N50 could come from a misassembled genome, so N50 rankings did not reliably track correctness rankings
N50 could not be computed for short-read data
N50 only applies to protein sequences, not genome assemblies

explanations.a: The opposite was found — N50 could be high on an assembly containing real misassembly errors.
explanations.b: Correct — assemblers could achieve impressive N50 by incorrectly bridging repeats into falsely long contigs, decoupling the statistic from actual correctness.
explanations.c: N50 is computed routinely for short-read assemblies; that wasn't the issue these studies raised.
explanations.d: N50 is a genome/contig-assembly statistic about contig lengths, unrelated to protein sequences.

questions.prompt: Match each name/tool to its role in the assembly wars.

right.text: Built the overlap-layout-consensus approach used for Drosophila and human genomes
Introduced the Eulerian-path de Bruijn graph formulation of assembly
A practical short-read assembler built on the de Bruijn graph approach
Benchmarked assemblers on identical data and found N50 didn't track correctness

questions.explanation: Myers built OLC-based Celera Assembler; Pevzner, Tang & Waterman introduced the de Bruijn/Eulerian-path formulation; Velvet applied de Bruijn graphs to short-read data; GAGE and Assemblathon benchmarked assemblers and exposed the N50-vs-correctness gap.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: Celera Assembler (OLC approach) used for the Drosophila and human genomes
Pevzner, Tang & Waterman publish the Eulerian-path de Bruijn graph approach
Velvet is published as a de Bruijn short-read assembler
GAGE and the Assemblathon competitions benchmark many assemblers on identical data

questions.explanation: OLC-based Celera Assembler (2000-2001) came first, followed by the 2001 de Bruijn/Eulerian-path proposal, then Velvet's 2008 practical short-read implementation, then the GAGE/Assemblathon benchmarking effort of 2011-2013.

lessons.label: Genome in a Bottle and the Truth-Set Problem

sections.heading: You can't grade a variant caller without an answer key
sections.body: A variant caller reports which positions in a genome differ from a reference. To know if it's right, you need ground truth — a genome whose real variants are already known. But no sequencing technology is itself perfectly accurate, so the "truth" can't just come from running one more sequencer; it has to be built by cross-checking many independent technologies against each other. NIST's Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) consortium, led by Justin Zook and Marc Salit, tackled this starting around 2014: rather than trust any single platform, GIAB combines Illumina short-read, PacBio HiFi and Oxford Nanopore long-read, and mapping- and linked-read-based technologies on the same DNA samples, keeps only the calls multiple independent methods agree on, and — critically — publishes explicit "confident regions" (a BED file) marking exactly where the consensus is considered trustworthy, so a caller is only scored inside regions where the truth itself is solid. Zook and colleagues published the original high-confidence call sets in a 2016 Scientific Data paper, "Extensive sequencing of seven human genomes to characterize benchmark reference materials."

sections.heading: The reference samples: HG001 and two family trios
sections.body: GIAB's original pilot sample is HG001, the well-studied NA12878 cell line from the CEPH/Utah pedigree already used throughout genomics. GIAB then added family trios, because a trio lets you check Mendelian inheritance (a child's genotype should be explainable from the two parents) as an independent consistency check on the calls: the Ashkenazi trio (HG002 son, HG003 father, HG004 mother, from the Personal Genome Project) and a Chinese trio (HG005-HG007). HG002 in particular became the most heavily characterized human genome sample in the field, used to develop and test benchmarks for the hardest regions of the genome, including ones previously too repetitive to resolve confidently.

sections.heading: PrecisionFDA Truth Challenges — and the circularity critique
sections.body: The FDA ran public benchmarking competitions against GIAB truth sets: the 2016 precisionFDA Truth Challenge and the 2020 Truth Challenge V2, which focused specifically on difficult regions. These became the field's open bake-off — any team could submit a caller and get scored transparently against the same reference. But the design has a known circularity: because the confident regions and consensus calls were originally built substantially from short-read and mapping-based technologies, the truth set is weakest exactly where short reads are weakest — highly repetitive regions, segmental duplications, and structurally complex loci. A caller can look artificially strong by doing well precisely where the truth set is easiest to build, while the hardest real biology remains under-benchmarked.

lessons.workedExample: A team benchmarks their new variant caller against HG002 and reports 99.9% precision and recall inside GIAB's confident regions — genuinely impressive. But a judge asks what happens outside those regions, in the segmental duplications and centromeric-adjacent sequence GIAB originally excluded because no technology could confidently call them either. The honest answer: performance there is unmeasured, not necessarily good, because the truth set the team is comparing against was itself built with technologies (largely short reads) that struggle in the same places. This is exactly the circularity GIAB's own confident-region BED files are designed to be transparent about — they mark the boundary of what the benchmark can actually vouch for.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is a favorite judge probe because it tests whether a student understands that a benchmark result is only as good as its ground truth, and that ground truth in genomics is itself an engineered consensus, not an independent oracle. A student who reports "99.9% accuracy" without mentioning GIAB's confident regions, or without acknowledging that hard-to-sequence regions are systematically under-represented in the truth set, hasn't grappled with circularity. Naming HG002, the confident-region concept, or the precisionFDA Truth Challenges shows they know where the benchmark's edges are.

questions.prompt: Why does GIAB combine multiple independent sequencing technologies rather than trust a single platform to define "truth"?

options.text: Because a single platform is too expensive to run at scale
Because no sequencing technology is itself perfectly accurate, so consensus across independent methods is used to build reliable ground truth
Because journals require at least three technologies per paper
Because a single platform cannot sequence a human genome at all

explanations.a: Cost isn't the stated rationale here; the issue is that any single technology has its own systematic errors.
explanations.b: Correct — since every sequencing platform has its own error modes, only agreement across independent methods gives confidence a call is real, which is why GIAB used consensus plus explicit confident regions.
explanations.c: This is not a journal policy; it is GIAB's specific methodological choice for building a trustworthy benchmark.
explanations.d: Any modern sequencing platform can sequence a human genome; the concern is accuracy of specific calls, not feasibility.

questions.prompt: Why did GIAB add family trios (like HG002-HG004) rather than only unrelated individual samples?

options.text: Trios are cheaper to sequence than individuals
Mendelian inheritance between parents and child provides an independent consistency check on variant calls
Trios eliminate the need for confident-region annotation
Only trio DNA can be sequenced with short-read technology

explanations.a: Cost is not the reason given; trio structure serves a specific validation purpose.
explanations.b: Correct — a child's genotype should be explainable by inheritance from the two parents, so disagreement flags a likely calling error, adding an independent check beyond cross-platform consensus.
explanations.c: Confident regions are still needed for trio samples; trio structure adds a check, it doesn't replace region annotation.
explanations.d: Short-read sequencing works on any DNA sample, related or not; this isn't a trio-specific requirement.

questions.prompt: What is the circularity critique of GIAB-based benchmarking, as tested by the precisionFDA Truth Challenges?

options.text: The truth sets were built substantially from short-read and mapping-based methods, so they under-represent exactly the repetitive/complex regions those methods struggle with
The Truth Challenges were not open to public submission
GIAB samples cannot be used more than once
The FDA does not allow benchmarking of research-use callers

explanations.a: Correct — because the confident regions were built largely from technologies that struggle with highly repetitive or structurally complex DNA, those same difficult regions are under-benchmarked, making high scores look stronger than they are for whole-genome performance.
explanations.b: The Truth Challenges were public bake-offs open to submissions; that is precisely why they mattered as a field-wide benchmark.
explanations.c: GIAB samples like HG002 are reused constantly across many benchmarking efforts; there's no one-use restriction.
explanations.d: The FDA specifically ran these as open, research-oriented benchmarking competitions.

questions.prompt: Match each GIAB reference sample or set to its description.

right.text: The NA12878 pilot sample from the CEPH/Utah pedigree
The Ashkenazi trio (son, father, mother) from the Personal Genome Project
The Chinese trio

questions.explanation: HG001 is the original NA12878 pilot sample; HG002-HG004 form the Ashkenazi trio (son HG002, father HG003, mother HG004); HG005-HG007 form the Chinese trio.

lessons.label: Deep Learning Enters the Pipeline

sections.heading: DeepVariant: variant calling as a picture-recognition problem
sections.body: For years, variant callers like GATK's HaplotypeCaller worked by explicit statistical models built by hand: probability models of sequencing error, base quality scores, and rules tuned by experts to decide whether a mismatch was a real variant or noise. In 2018, Ryan Poplin and colleagues at Google published DeepVariant in Nature Biotechnology, taking a completely different approach: convert the pileup of aligned reads around a candidate site into a multi-channel image (read bases, base quality, strand, mapping quality encoded as image channels) and hand that image to a convolutional neural network — the same kind of architecture used for photo classification — to classify the site as homozygous-reference, heterozygous, or homozygous-alternate. DeepVariant won the SNP category of the 2016 precisionFDA Truth Challenge and again performed strongly in the 2020 Truth Challenge V2, in both cases outperforming hand-tuned statistical filters on the GIAB benchmarks.

sections.heading: AlphaFold2: the same lesson at a much larger scale
sections.body: Two years later, DeepMind's AlphaFold2 delivered a far more dramatic version of the same pattern at CASP14 (the 2020 Critical Assessment of protein Structure Prediction). Protein structure prediction — inferring a protein's 3D shape from its amino acid sequence — had been worked on for decades using physics-based and heuristic modeling, with slow, incremental progress. AlphaFold2 achieved a median GDT_TS (a 0-100 score measuring how closely a predicted structure matches the true experimentally-solved structure) of about 92.4 across CASP14's targets, a jump assessors described as without precedent in the competition's history, functionally comparable in accuracy to experimental methods for many targets. Between them, DeepVariant and AlphaFold2 made the case that learned models trained end-to-end on data could displace decades of hand-built expert heuristics — not just match them.

sections.heading: The live argument: black boxes in a clinical pipeline
sections.body: The unresolved debate is what to do with these tools in settings where a wrong answer has consequences. A hand-built statistical caller can, in principle, be inspected: you can point to the specific probability model and threshold that produced a genotype call. A trained neural network's decision is distributed across millions of learned weights, making it much harder to say exactly why it called a given site the way it did. This matters because training data has known bias: GIAB's benchmark samples, and much of the training data such callers rely on, skew toward certain ancestries and toward regions of the genome that were already easy to sequence, so performance on chromosomally similar samples is well characterized while performance on underrepresented ancestries or genomically difficult regions is not. The open question for clinical reporting is what "explainable" should even mean for a genotype call — a confidence score, a saliency map over the pileup image, or something else — and how much explainability should be required before a black-box call is allowed to inform a patient's diagnosis.

lessons.workedExample: A team builds a variant caller using a small CNN modeled loosely on DeepVariant's pileup-image approach and reports it matches GATK's accuracy on HG002. A judge asks: does it perform equally well on a genome from an ancestry group underrepresented in GIAB's trio samples? If the team hasn't tested that, they've replicated DeepVariant's architecture without replicating the caution its real-world deployment requires — because a model's benchmark accuracy on well-represented samples says nothing about its accuracy on samples that look statistically different from its training distribution, exactly the training-bias concern raised about clinical use of these tools.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson gets probed because deep learning is an easy buzzword to drop and a hard one to justify. A judge wants to know whether a student understands what the neural network actually replaced (a hand-tuned statistical model, evaluated as a pileup image classification problem) and what tradeoff came with it (opacity, and training-data bias toward well-represented ancestries and easy regions). Citing DeepVariant's specific mechanism, or AlphaFold2's actual CASP14 result rather than a vague "it solved protein folding," shows real engagement rather than name-dropping a headline.

questions.prompt: How did DeepVariant (Poplin et al., 2018) reframe the variant-calling problem?

options.text: As an image-classification task over pileup images of aligned reads
As a database lookup against known variants
As a physics simulation of DNA polymerase behavior
As a text-translation task between species

explanations.a: Correct — DeepVariant encodes the read pileup around a candidate site as a multi-channel image and classifies it with a CNN, borrowing image-classification architecture.
explanations.b: A lookup against known variants couldn't call novel variants; DeepVariant is a learned classifier, not a database matcher.
explanations.c: No physics simulation is involved; the approach is purely a learned image classifier.
explanations.d: This is not a translation task between sequences or species; it is a per-site classification problem.

questions.prompt: What was AlphaFold2's approximate median GDT_TS score at CASP14 (2020), and why did assessors consider it remarkable?

options.text: About 92, a leap described as without precedent in the competition's history
About 50, a modest improvement over prior methods
About 30, roughly matching random structure guessing
About 99.9, indicating perfect prediction on every target

explanations.a: Correct — AlphaFold2 achieved a median GDT_TS around 92.4 across CASP14 targets, a jump assessors called without historical parallel in the competition.
explanations.b: 50 would represent only a middling result, well below what CASP14 assessors actually reported.
explanations.c: A score near random guessing would not have been treated as a landmark result at all.
explanations.d: AlphaFold2's result was very strong but not literally perfect on every target; 99.9 overstates it.

questions.prompt: What is the specific training-data concern raised about black-box variant callers in clinical use?

options.text: Neural networks cannot process DNA sequence data at all
Benchmark and training data skew toward certain ancestries and easier-to-sequence regions, so performance elsewhere is less well characterized
Black-box models are always less accurate than hand-tuned models on every benchmark
Clinical labs are legally barred from using any machine-learning tool

explanations.a: Neural networks clearly do process sequence/pileup data; that's the basis of DeepVariant's success.
explanations.b: Correct — because GIAB benchmark samples and training data skew toward certain ancestries and toward easier genomic regions, a model's strong benchmark score doesn't guarantee equally strong performance on underrepresented samples or harder regions.
explanations.c: DeepVariant outperformed hand-tuned filters on GIAB benchmarks; the concern is about generalization and bias, not raw accuracy on the benchmark itself.
explanations.d: No such blanket legal bar exists; the debate is about how much explainability and validation should be required, not outright prohibition.

questions.prompt: Order these events chronologically.

items.text: DeepVariant wins the SNP category of the precisionFDA Truth Challenge
Poplin et al. publish DeepVariant in Nature Biotechnology
AlphaFold2 achieves its landmark result at CASP14
DeepVariant performs strongly in the precisionFDA Truth Challenge V2

questions.explanation: DeepVariant won the 2016 Truth Challenge before its 2018 journal publication; AlphaFold2's CASP14 result came in 2020, the same year DeepVariant performed strongly again in Truth Challenge V2.

lessons.label: The Reproducibility Reckoning

sections.heading: Ioannidis and the failed replication of 18 papers
sections.body: In 2009, John Ioannidis and colleagues published "Repeatability of Published Microarray Gene Expression Analyses" in Nature Genetics, attempting to reproduce one key result from each of 18 papers published in that same journal. The outcome was stark: only 2 of the 18 could be reproduced in principle; 6 were partially reproducible with discrepancies; 10 could not be reproduced at all, mostly because the data or the exact processing steps were unavailable or underspecified. This wasn't an accusation of fraud — it exposed that standard reporting practice in genomics simply didn't require enough detail (exact software versions, parameters, filtering steps) for an independent team to redo the analysis.

sections.heading: Forensic bioinformatics and the Duke chemosensitivity scandal
sections.body: Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes went further than pointing out missing detail — they reverse-engineered a flawed analysis from its published output. Their 2009 paper, describing this work as "forensic bioinformatics," painstakingly reconstructed how Duke researcher Anil Potti's gene-expression signatures for predicting chemotherapy response had been built, and found the underlying code contained basic errors, including sample mislabeling that had inflated apparent predictive accuracy. The signatures had already been used to enroll patients into clinical trials that assigned chemotherapy based on the flawed predictions. The investigation eventually forced those trials to be halted and led to multiple paper retractions — a case study in how a bioinformatics error, unnoticed for years, propagated all the way into decisions about real patients' treatment.

sections.heading: Unrecorded parameters, and gene names Excel quietly rewrote
sections.body: Anton Nekrutenko and James Taylor's 2012 Nature Reviews Genetics paper argued the reproducibility gap in sequencing analysis specifically came from unrecorded software versions and parameters — a pipeline run today with tool version 2.3 and default settings can give a different answer than the same nominal pipeline run last year with version 2.1, if no one wrote down which was used. A more mechanical failure surfaced in 2016: Mark Ziemann, Yotam Eren, and Assam El-Osta scanned supplementary files from thousands of genomics papers and found that about one in five papers with a supplementary gene list had gene names silently corrupted by Microsoft Excel's autocorrect — for example the gene SEPT1 getting auto-converted to a date. The fix wasn't in the papers; it was upstream, in the names themselves. In 2020 the HGNC (the body that officially names human genes) renamed SEPT1 to SEPTIN1 and similarly renamed other affected genes, because getting spreadsheet software to stop autocorrecting proved less tractable than renaming the genes.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to replicate a published RNA-seq analysis for their project and finds the paper reports "differential expression analysis was performed using standard methods" with no software name, version, or parameter values listed. Applying the Nekrutenko & Taylor lesson, they realize this sentence alone makes exact replication impossible — different tools (or even different versions of the same tool) can call different sets of genes significant from identical raw data. The fix in their own project is to record and report the exact tool, version, and every non-default parameter used, the specific gap Ioannidis's team ran into when trying to reproduce 16 of 18 microarray papers.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes reproducibility because it is the most direct test of whether a student's result would survive someone else trying to redo it. Naming Ioannidis's 2/18 finding, or the Duke chemosensitivity retraction Baggerly and Coombes uncovered, shows a student understands reproducibility failures aren't hypothetical — they have derailed real clinical trials. Mentioning the Excel gene-name problem specifically tests whether a student has thought about mechanical, boring failure modes (a spreadsheet autocorrecting a gene name) as seriously as they think about their headline statistical result — because judges know those boring failures are far more common than dramatic fraud.

questions.prompt: In Ioannidis et al.'s 2009 Nature Genetics study, how many of the 18 microarray papers examined could be fully reproduced?

options.text: 18 of 18 — full reproducibility
2 of 18
0 of 18

explanations.a: The study found the opposite — most results could not be cleanly reproduced.
explanations.b: Correct — only 2 of the 18 papers' results could be reproduced in principle; 6 partially, and 10 not at all.
explanations.c: 10 was the number that could not be reproduced at all, not the number successfully reproduced.
explanations.d: A small number (2) were reproducible in principle, so the true count is not zero.

questions.prompt: What did Baggerly and Coombes' 2009 "forensic bioinformatics" investigation into Duke's chemosensitivity signatures find, and what was its consequence?

options.text: The signatures were sound; the investigation confirmed the trials were safe to continue

Basic errors, including sample mislabeling, had inflated apparent predictive accuracy; the flawed signatures had already been used to guide chemotherapy assignment in clinical trials, which were eventually halted with papers retracted
The signatures were accurate but used an outdated statistical test
The issue was limited to a typo in the paper's abstract with no effect on the underlying analysis

explanations.a: The investigation found serious errors, not confirmation of soundness.
explanations.b: Correct — Baggerly and Coombes reverse-engineered the analysis and found errors like sample mislabeling that inflated accuracy; the signatures had already influenced treatment assignment in trials that were later halted, with retractions following.
explanations.c: The problem was in the underlying code and data handling (mislabeling), not just a choice of statistical test.
explanations.d: This was a substantive analytical error with real clinical consequences, not a cosmetic typo.

questions.prompt: According to Ziemann, Eren & El-Osta (2016), roughly what fraction of scanned genomics papers with a supplementary gene list showed Excel-autocorrect gene name errors?

options.text: About one in twenty
About one in five
About three in four
Essentially none — the problem was theoretical, not observed

explanations.a: One in twenty understates the scale the scan actually found.
explanations.b: Correct — roughly one-fifth (about 20%) of scanned papers with a supplementary Excel gene list had autocorrect-corrupted gene names.
explanations.c: Three in four substantially overstates the scanned rate.
explanations.d: The problem was empirically documented across thousands of scanned supplementary files, not merely theoretical.

questions.prompt: Match each name/body to their contribution to the reproducibility reckoning.

right.text: Found most of 18 microarray papers could not be reproduced
Reverse-engineered the flawed Duke chemosensitivity signature analysis
Argued unrecorded software versions/parameters undermine sequencing-analysis reproducibility
Renamed genes like SEPT1 to SEPTIN1 to stop Excel autocorrect corruption

questions.explanation: Ioannidis's team found most of 18 microarray papers were not reproducible; Baggerly and Coombes forensically unraveled the Duke chemosensitivity analysis; Nekrutenko and Taylor pointed to unrecorded parameters/versions as a sequencing-specific reproducibility gap; HGNC renamed vulnerable genes in 2020 to end the Excel autocorrect problem.

lessons.label: Open Questions Right Now

sections.heading: Is a single linear reference genome obsolete?
sections.body: Every reference genome since the Human Genome Project has been a single linear sequence — one representative version of "the" human genome, against which every new sample is aligned. In 2022, Sergey Nurk and colleagues published "The Complete Sequence of a Human Genome" in Science, the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) consortium's CHM13 assembly, finally filling in the roughly 8% of the genome (centromeres, segmental duplications, acrocentric chromosome arms) that decades of prior references had left as unresolved gaps. T2T-CHM13 added nearly 200 million base pairs of previously missing sequence and around 2,000 new gene predictions. But CHM13 is still one linear genome from one individual (a hydatidiform mole cell line), and no single person's genome represents human genetic diversity well — a reference built from one ancestry systematically aligns worse to samples from underrepresented ancestries, a bias called reference bias.

sections.heading: The pangenome answer, and what it costs
sections.body: The Human Pangenome Reference Consortium's 2023 Nature paper (Liao et al., "A Draft Human Pangenome Reference") took a different approach: instead of one linear sequence, build a graph genome from 94 haplotype assemblies across 47 ancestrally diverse individuals, so a sample can be aligned against a structure that already contains much of the variation a linear reference would treat as "different from normal." The pangenome added over 100 million base pairs of previously-missing sequence relative to the standard GRCh38 reference and measurably reduced reference bias in downstream analysis. The cost is real: a graph doesn't have the same simple, universal coordinate system a linear genome does — "position 12,345 on chromosome 7" means one thing on a linear reference and requires translation or a different addressing scheme on a graph, complicating decades of tools, databases, and papers built around linear coordinates.

sections.heading: Can genomic data ever really be anonymized?
sections.body: A parallel open debate concerns data sharing. In 2013, Melissa Gymrek, Amy McGuire, David Golan, Eran Halperin, and Yaniv Erlich published "Identifying Personal Genomes by Surname Inference" in Science, showing that Y-chromosome short tandem repeats (Y-STRs) — a small set of markers — could be cross-referenced against public genealogy databases to recover the surnames of men whose "anonymized" genomes were in research datasets, then combined with age and state to narrow down actual identities; the technique successfully identified dozens of individuals. Separately, researchers demonstrated re-identification attacks against GA4GH "Beacon" systems — services designed to answer only a minimal yes/no question ("does this dataset contain a genome with variant X?") — showing that repeated beacon queries could still infer whether a specific individual's genome was present in a supposedly private dataset. Together these results argue that genomic data carries enough uniquely identifying signal that conventional anonymization (stripping names) is not the same as making re-identification impossible, an unresolved tension for consortiums like GIAB and HPRC that depend on broad, open data sharing.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to reduce ancestry-related bias in their variant-calling pipeline and has to choose between aligning to T2T-CHM13 (still one linear genome, but far more complete than the old GRCh38) or to the HPRC pangenome graph (built from 47 diverse individuals, but requiring graph-aware tools their existing pipeline doesn't support). Naming this exact tradeoff — completeness and simplicity of a single improved linear reference versus reduced reference bias at the cost of tooling complexity in a graph — is what shows a judge the student understands why this is still an open engineering question in 2026, not a solved one.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about open questions specifically to see whether a student can talk about unresolved tradeoffs rather than presenting bioinformatics as a solved field. Naming T2T-CHM13's actual contribution (filling ~200 Mb of gap sequence) versus the pangenome's actual contribution (reduced reference bias from 47-individual diversity, at the cost of linear coordinates) shows real grasp of the reference-genome debate. On privacy, citing Gymrek's 2013 surname-inference result specifically — not a vague "genomic data isn't private" — shows the student understands the actual mechanism (Y-STR cross-referencing against genealogy databases) rather than just repeating a slogan.

questions.prompt: What did the T2T-CHM13 assembly (Nurk et al., Science 2022) specifically add to the human reference genome?

options.text: Nearly 200 million base pairs of previously missing sequence, filling gaps like centromeres and acrocentric arms
A complete second copy of the genome from a different ancestry
Only mitochondrial DNA sequence
A graph-based coordinate system replacing linear coordinates

explanations.a: Correct — T2T-CHM13 filled the roughly 8% of the genome prior references left as gaps, adding nearly 200 Mb of new sequence and about 2,000 new gene predictions.
explanations.b: CHM13 is still a single linear genome from one cell line, not a second ancestry's genome added alongside the first.
explanations.c: T2T-CHM13's contribution was nuclear genome completion (centromeres, segmental duplications, acrocentric arms), not mitochondrial sequence specifically.
explanations.d: T2T-CHM13 remains a linear reference; the graph-based coordinate approach is what the pangenome project introduced instead.

questions.prompt: What is the main tradeoff of the HPRC pangenome graph (Liao et al., 2023) compared to a linear reference genome?

options.text: It reduces reference bias by representing diversity from many individuals, but loses the simple universal linear coordinate system tools were built around
It is smaller in total sequence than GRCh38
It removes the need for any sequence alignment
It only works for non-human genomes

explanations.a: Correct — building a graph from 94 haplotypes across 47 diverse individuals reduced reference bias, but sacrificed the simple linear coordinate addressing that decades of tools depend on.
explanations.b: The pangenome added sequence relative to GRCh38, rather than being smaller.
explanations.c: Alignment is still required against a pangenome graph; the representation changes, not the need for alignment itself.
explanations.d: The HPRC pangenome is specifically a human pangenome reference.

questions.prompt: How did Gymrek et al. (2013) recover identities from supposedly anonymized genomic data?

options.text: By cross-referencing Y-chromosome short tandem repeats (Y-STRs) against public genetic genealogy databases to infer surnames, then narrowing with age/state metadata
By hacking into the sequencing lab's servers
By using only the participant's stated age
By requesting the data be de-anonymized by the original researchers

explanations.a: Correct — Y-STR markers correlate with surname inheritance, so cross-referencing them against public genealogy databases let the team infer surnames and, with added metadata, identify dozens of individuals.
explanations.b: The method used only public genetic and genealogical data, no unauthorized server access.
explanations.c: Age alone was used only as a narrowing factor after surname inference, not as the primary re-identification method.
explanations.d: The point of the demonstration was that re-identification was possible without any cooperation from the original researchers.

questions.prompt: Order these developments chronologically.

items.text: Gymrek et al. publish the Y-STR surname-inference re-identification study
Nurk et al. publish the complete T2T-CHM13 human genome
Liao et al. publish the draft human pangenome reference

questions.explanation: The Gymrek re-identification study was published in 2013, T2T-CHM13 in 2022, and the HPRC draft pangenome reference in 2023.

lessons.label: Overlap-Layout-Consensus

sections.heading: The original shotgun assembly recipe
sections.body: Shotgun sequencing breaks a genome into millions of fragments and reads each one; assembly has to put the puzzle back together with no picture on the box. Overlap-Layout-Consensus (OLC) does this in three stages. Overlap: compare every read against every other read to find pairs that share a suffix-prefix match long enough to be real (not chance). Layout: chain those pairwise overlaps into a graph and infer an ordering of reads along the genome. Consensus: for each position, vote across all the reads that cover it to call the final base, correcting individual sequencing errors. This is the approach behind the Sanger-era genome projects — the Celera Assembler used OLC to assemble the human genome draft in 2001, working from ~500-800 bp Sanger reads.

sections.heading: Myers' string graph: trimming edges you can already infer
sections.body: A raw overlap graph is bloated: if read A overlaps read B and read B overlaps read C, and A's overlap with B implies A also overlaps C transitively, drawing all three edges is redundant. Eugene Myers' 2005 string graph formulation ("The fragment assembly string graph," Bioinformatics) removes these transitively inferable edges, keeping only the irreducible ones needed to represent the true layout. The result is a much sparser graph whose paths correspond directly to candidate contigs, making layout tractable and making repeats visible as places where the graph branches instead of running straight.

sections.heading: Why O(n^2) killed OLC for short reads and long reads brought it back
sections.body: All-versus-all overlap detection compares every read against every other read, an O(n^2) cost in the number of reads. Sanger sequencing produced relatively few, relatively long reads, so this was affordable. Illumina sequencing flipped that: hundreds of millions to billions of reads per genome, each only ~100-150 bp. Running O(n^2) overlap detection at that scale was computationally infeasible, which is exactly why the field moved to de Bruijn graph methods for short reads in the 2000s. OLC came back once long-read platforms (PacBio, Oxford Nanopore) arrived: a human genome needs only a few million long reads instead of billions of short ones, so all-versus-all comparison is affordable again — and it was made fast, not just smaller, by MinHash-sketch overlap indexing (MHAP, Berlin et al., 2015), which represents each read as a small set of hashed minimizers and finds candidate overlaps by comparing those sketches instead of aligning full reads, avoiding brute-force pairwise alignment. Canu builds on this sketch-based indexing, and OLC-style assemblers such as Canu and FALCON became the standard tools for long-read genome assembly.

lessons.workedExample: A student assembling a 5 Mb bacterial genome from long reads has two options: chop every read into k-mers and build a de Bruijn graph, or run pairwise overlap detection. With ~50x coverage from long reads, that is roughly 50,000 reads — an all-versus-all comparison is about 2.5 billion pairwise checks, feasible on a laptop-scale cluster in minutes with an indexed seed-and-extend overlapper. If the same student tried the same approach on Illumina data for the same genome (covering it with 150 bp reads at 50x means ~1.7 million reads), the pairwise comparison count balloons to ~2.8 trillion, which is why no production short-read assembler does raw all-versus-all OLC — they use a de Bruijn graph instead.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "why did you pick this assembler" is really asking whether the student understands that assembly algorithm choice is dictated by read length and count, not preference. A strong answer names the O(n^2) overlap cost as the reason short-read projects abandoned OLC for de Bruijn graphs, and explains that long reads made all-versus-all comparison affordable again because there are far fewer reads to compare. A student who cannot say why their pipeline chose OLC over a k-mer graph (or vice versa) has run a tool without understanding what problem it solves.

questions.prompt: Order the three stages of the Overlap-Layout-Consensus pipeline as they are applied.

items.text: Find all pairwise overlaps between reads
Chain overlaps into an inferred read ordering along the genome
Vote across overlapping reads to call the final base at each position

questions.explanation: OLC first detects which reads share sequence (overlap), then uses those overlaps to infer how reads line up along the genome (layout), and finally calls a consensus base at each position from all reads covering it (consensus).

questions.prompt: What specifically does Myers' 2005 string graph remove from the raw overlap graph?

options.text: Reads with fewer than two overlaps
Edges that are transitively inferable from other overlaps already in the graph
All overlaps shorter than the read length
Reads that map to repetitive regions

explanations.a: The string graph does not filter reads by overlap count; it removes redundant edges, not nodes.
explanations.b: Correct — if A overlaps B and B overlaps C such that A's overlap with C is already implied, the string graph drops that redundant edge, keeping only the irreducible overlaps needed to represent the layout.
explanations.c: Overlap length thresholds are a separate quality filter used before graph construction, not what the string graph formulation itself removes.
explanations.d: Repeats are not removed; they remain visible in the string graph as branch points, which is part of why the representation is useful.

questions.prompt: Why did all-versus-all overlap detection become infeasible for Illumina short-read data?

options.text: Illumina reads are too long to compare pairwise
Short reads cannot be indexed for fast comparison
Covering a genome with short reads requires hundreds of millions to billions of reads, making the O(n^2) pairwise comparison cost intractable
Short reads have too few sequencing errors to build a meaningful overlap graph

explanations.a: Illumina reads are short (~100-150 bp), not long; that is exactly why so many are needed to cover a genome.
explanations.b: Indexing methods exist for short reads; the bottleneck is the sheer number of pairwise comparisons required, not indexability.
explanations.c: Correct — reaching adequate coverage with ~100-150 bp reads takes hundreds of millions to billions of reads per genome, and comparing every read to every other read is an O(n^2) operation that becomes computationally infeasible at that scale.
explanations.d: Error rate is unrelated to why all-versus-all comparison is infeasible; the issue is purely the number of reads.

questions.prompt: Why did OLC-style assembly become practical again with long-read platforms like PacBio and Oxford Nanopore?

options.text: Long reads have zero sequencing errors, so no consensus step is needed
Long reads reduce the number of reads needed to cover a genome, making all-versus-all comparison affordable again
Long-read platforms do not require an overlap step at all
Long reads are shorter than Illumina reads, so fewer bases need comparing

explanations.a: Long reads still carry sequencing errors, which is exactly why the consensus step remains necessary in OLC pipelines like Canu.
explanations.b: Correct — a human genome needs only a few million long reads to reach good coverage instead of billions of short reads, so the O(n^2) all-versus-all comparison becomes computationally affordable again.
explanations.c: Long-read OLC assemblers such as Canu and FALCON still perform an overlap step; it is the first stage of the pipeline.
explanations.d: Long reads (PacBio, Nanopore) are longer than Illumina reads, not shorter; that is the entire premise of the question.

lessons.label: De Bruijn Graphs

sections.heading: Shattering reads into k-mers instead of comparing reads directly
sections.body: Instead of comparing whole reads pairwise, de Bruijn graph assembly breaks every read into overlapping substrings of fixed length k (k-mers) and builds a graph where each unique (k-1)-mer is a node and each observed k-mer is a directed edge connecting its prefix node to its suffix node. Two reads never need to be compared to each other directly — they only need to share k-mers, which the graph structure captures automatically. Pevzner, Tang, and Waterman formalized this as an Eulerian path problem in a 2001 PNAS paper: if you can find a path through the graph that uses every edge exactly once, that path spells out a candidate genome sequence. This sidesteps the O(n^2) pairwise-overlap bottleneck entirely, which is why de Bruijn graphs became the dominant approach once Illumina sequencing produced hundreds of millions of short reads per run.

sections.heading: The k tradeoff, tips, and bubbles
sections.body: Choosing k is a real tradeoff, and the pivot point is how k compares to the length of a repeat. If a repeated sequence is at least as long as k, then at least one k-mer lies entirely inside the repeat, and that k-mer is byte-for-byte identical in every copy — so every copy of the repeat is forced onto the same node, collapsing distinct genomic locations into one tangle and destroying the information about which flank connects to which. A repeat shorter than k causes no such collapse: every k-mer spanning it also carries some unique flanking sequence, so the copies stay distinguishable. That is why raising k resolves more repeats — it pushes more of them below the collapse threshold — but a large k also demands higher sequencing coverage, because two reads must share a full exact k-mer to link up at all; at low coverage or in the presence of sequencing errors, large-k graphs fragment into disconnected pieces. Errors themselves create two characteristic graph defects: tips, short dead-end branches created by an error near a read's end that never gets confirmed by another read, and bubbles, two parallel paths that diverge and rejoin because of a single mismatched base. Bubbles are not always errors — in a diploid organism, a true heterozygous SNP produces the same bubble shape, since each haplotype contributes a different k-mer at that position, so assemblers must decide whether to collapse a bubble (losing haplotype information) or keep both paths.

sections.heading: Memory cost and the tools that made it practical
sections.body: Storing every distinct k-mer in a genome-scale dataset in a hash table is memory-intensive: a human genome at 30x coverage can generate billions of k-mer instances, and naive storage of all of them (plus their graph edges) can require tens to hundreds of gigabytes of RAM. Velvet (Zerbino and Birney, 2008) was among the first practical de Bruijn assemblers for short reads, followed by SOAPdenovo (Li et al., 2010) which scaled the approach to the human genome using more memory-efficient hash structures, and SPAdes (Bankevich et al., 2012), which introduced multi-k assembly — building and merging graphs at several k values — to better handle the uneven coverage typical of single-cell and bacterial sequencing.

lessons.workedExample: A student assembling a bacterial genome with 150 bp Illumina reads tries k=55 first and gets a fragmented assembly with thousands of short contigs. Checking coverage, they find several genomic regions were sequenced at only 8x instead of the genome average of 40x — at k=55, those low-coverage stretches don't have enough overlapping reads sharing a full 55-mer to link consecutive nodes, so the graph simply breaks apart there. Dropping to k=15 reconnects those regions (shorter k-mers need less coverage to overlap) but now a 40 bp transposon repeat that occurs at three locations in the genome collapses into a single tangled node: because 40 bp is longer than k=15, the 15-mers sitting inside the repeat are identical no matter which copy they came from, and all three copies land on the same nodes. That same 40 bp repeat is shorter than k=55, so it never collapsed in the first, large-k attempt — every 55-mer touching it still carries unique flanking sequence. The fix used by SPAdes-style tools is exactly this observation formalized: build graphs at multiple k values and reconcile them, so the low-coverage regions are rescued by the small-k graph while the repeat stays resolved in the large-k graph, rather than committing to one k for the whole genome.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing de Bruijn assembly wants to see that a student understands k is not a tuning knob picked by trial and error but a real tradeoff tied to coverage and repeat length — small k links sparse data but collapses any repeat as long as k or longer, large k resolves those repeats but fragments where coverage is thin. The strongest answers name what a tip versus a bubble means mechanistically (an error-driven dead end versus a diverging-then-rejoining path) and can explain why a bubble in a diploid sample might be biology, not noise. A student who says "I used k=21 because that's the default" has not engaged with the tradeoff; one who says "I chose k based on my coverage and my longest expected repeat, and checked for a spike in short dead-end contigs" has.

questions.prompt: In a de Bruijn graph assembly, what does finding the genome sequence correspond to, per Pevzner, Tang, and Waterman's 2001 formulation?

options.text: Finding a Hamiltonian path that visits every node exactly once
Finding an Eulerian path that uses every edge exactly once
Finding the shortest path between the two most distant nodes
Finding a minimum spanning tree over the k-mer nodes

explanations.a: Hamiltonian path (visiting every node once) is the NP-hard formulation used by OLC-style graphs; the whole point of the de Bruijn reformulation is to avoid that.
explanations.b: Correct — Pevzner, Tang, and Waterman (2001, PNAS) framed assembly as finding an Eulerian path, using every edge (each observed k-mer) exactly once, which is solvable in linear time, unlike the Hamiltonian formulation.
explanations.c: Shortest-path search does not use every k-mer edge and would discard real sequence data.
explanations.d: A spanning tree does not preserve the edge-multiplicity structure needed to reconstruct a linear sequence.

questions.prompt: Match each de Bruijn graph structure to its cause.

left.text: A bubble (two paths diverge then rejoin)
Every copy of a repeat collapsing onto one node

right.text: A sequencing error near a read end, unconfirmed by other reads
A mismatch from either a sequencing error or a true heterozygous SNP
k chosen no longer than the repeat, so a k-mer sits entirely inside it

questions.explanation: Tips arise from uncorroborated errors near read ends; bubbles arise from a single mismatched base, which can be either a sequencing error or a genuine heterozygous variant; and collapse happens when the repeat is at least as long as k, because then some k-mer lies wholly inside the repeat and is identical in every copy. Raising k above the repeat length forces every k-mer to include unique flanking sequence, which pulls the copies back apart — so the size relationship runs the opposite way from the common misconception: a repeat SHORTER than k is absorbed into its unique flanks and causes no tangle at all.

questions.prompt: Why does choosing a larger k value require higher sequencing coverage to avoid graph fragmentation?

options.text: Larger k-mers take longer to compute, so fewer reads can be processed
Two reads must share a full exact k-mer to be linked in the graph, and a longer shared substring is less likely to be present when coverage is sparse or reads carry errors
Larger k always increases the total number of sequencing errors
Larger k-mers cannot be stored in a hash table

explanations.a: This is a computational cost concern, not the reason fragmentation occurs at low coverage.
explanations.b: Correct — connectivity depends on reads sharing a full exact k-mer; with sparse coverage the odds that two overlapping reads share a long enough error-free exact match drop, so the graph breaks into disconnected fragments across low-coverage regions.
explanations.c: k does not change the error rate of the underlying reads, only how those errors manifest in the graph.
explanations.d: Larger k-mers are simply longer strings and are routinely stored in hash tables; the issue is graph connectivity, not storage feasibility.

questions.prompt: What innovation did SPAdes (Bankevich et al., 2012) introduce to handle uneven coverage, such as in single-cell sequencing?

options.text: Building and merging de Bruijn graphs at multiple k values instead of committing to one
Switching entirely to an Overlap-Layout-Consensus approach
Discarding all reads from low-coverage regions
Using only the largest possible k-mer size for every dataset

explanations.a: Correct — SPAdes builds graphs across several k values and reconciles them, so regions poorly served by one k (fragmented at large k, or collapsed at small k) can be rescued by information from another k.
explanations.b: SPAdes remained a de Bruijn graph assembler; it did not switch paradigms to OLC.
explanations.c: Discarding low-coverage reads would worsen fragmentation rather than fix it; SPAdes was designed specifically to handle uneven coverage without discarding data.
explanations.d: Using only the largest k would worsen fragmentation in low-coverage regions, which is the opposite of what multi-k assembly is meant to solve.

lessons.label: Why Assembly Is Hard, and How to Grade One

sections.heading: The unresolvable case: repeats longer than the read
sections.body: If a repeated sequence in the genome is longer than any single read spanning it, no algorithm — OLC or de Bruijn — can determine which copy of the repeat connects to which flanking sequence, because no read ever captures both a repeat's edge and its unique context at once. This is a fundamental limit, not an engineering gap: the ambiguity is genuinely present in the data. Human genomes are full of such repeats — segmental duplications, satellite arrays, transposon families — many exceeding even PacBio HiFi read lengths, which is part of why even modern assemblies leave gaps or collapse repeat copies together. Beyond repeats, real assemblies also suffer coverage gaps (regions sequencing happened to undersample, by chance or GC bias), haplotype collapse (a diploid genome's two divergent haplotypes get merged into one artificial mosaic sequence at heterozygous sites), and contamination (bacterial, viral, or even human cross-contamination reads getting assembled into contigs that don't belong to the target organism).

sections.heading: N50 and its trap
sections.body: N50 is the standard contiguity metric: sort contigs from longest to shortest, walk down the list summing lengths, and N50 is the length of the contig at which that running sum first reaches 50% of the total assembly length. L50 is the number of contigs it took to get there. The trap is that N50 rewards length, not correctness — an assembler that aggressively joins contigs together, even across weak or wrong evidence, produces fewer, longer contigs and a higher N50, even though some of those joins misplace sequence. NG50 fixes part of this by dividing against an independently estimated genome size instead of the assembly's own total length, making N50-style numbers comparable across assemblies of different total sizes (an assembly that is missing large chunks of the genome can't inflate its NG50 just by being shorter).

sections.heading: Checking correctness, not just length
sections.body: Because N50 can be gamed by misassembly, real evaluation pairs it with tools that check accuracy. BUSCO (Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs, Simão et al., 2015) searches an assembly for a curated set of genes expected to occur as a single copy in nearly every species in a lineage, reporting the fraction found complete, duplicated (a sign of haplotype collapse gone wrong or contamination), fragmented, or missing. QUAST (Gurevich et al., 2013) aligns an assembly against a trusted reference genome and counts explicit misassembly events — places where a contig's alignment breaks or jumps discontinuously. Merqury (Rhie et al., 2020) needs no reference at all: it builds a k-mer database from the raw sequencing reads and checks how well the assembly's own k-mers agree with it, producing a consensus quality value (QV) that flags errors even for a species with no existing reference genome.

lessons.workedExample: Two teams assemble the same bacterial genome. Team A's assembler is tuned conservatively and produces 40 contigs with an N50 of 180 kb; Team B's assembler joins more aggressively and produces 12 contigs with an N50 of 410 kb. On N50 alone, Team B looks better. Running QUAST against a reference relative shows Team B has 6 misassemblies — places where the aggressive joiner stitched together sequence from two different genomic regions because they shared a repeat — while Team A has zero. Running BUSCO shows Team A recovers 98% of single-copy orthologs complete versus Team B's 91%, with several genes fragmented exactly at Team B's misassembly junctions. The higher N50 was a symptom of overconfident joining, not a better assembly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how good is your assembly?" is testing whether a student reports a single number or a mix of metrics that catch different failure modes.
