Citing N50 alone is a red flag, because N50 can be inflated by exactly the kind of misassembly a careful judge expects a student to know about. The strongest answer names at least one contiguity metric and at least one correctness metric — for instance N50 alongside BUSCO completeness or a Merqury QV — and can explain in one sentence why contiguity and correctness are not the same thing.

questions.prompt: Why is a repeat longer than any sequencing read fundamentally unresolvable, not just hard?

options.text: Because no algorithm has been invented yet that is fast enough
Because no single read ever spans both the repeat and enough unique flanking sequence to show which copy connects to what
Because repeats always contain sequencing errors
Because repeats are always shorter than a read, so this scenario cannot occur

explanations.a: This is not a speed limitation — more compute cannot recover information that was never captured in any read.
explanations.b: Correct — if the repeat exceeds read length, no read ever captures both an edge of the repeat and the unique sequence beside it, so the true connections are genuinely ambiguous in the data, regardless of algorithm.
explanations.c: Error rate is unrelated to this specific ambiguity, which would occur even with a perfectly accurate but too-short read.
explanations.d: The premise of the scenario is exactly a repeat longer than the read, which does occur in real genomes (segmental duplications, satellite arrays).

questions.prompt: How does NG50 differ from N50?

options.text: NG50 divides against an independently estimated genome size instead of the assembly's own total length
NG50 only counts contigs longer than 1 Mb
NG50 is calculated from BUSCO completeness scores
NG50 and N50 are the same metric with different names

explanations.a: Correct — N50 uses the assembly's own total length as the denominator, which lets an incomplete assembly inflate its N50 simply by being shorter overall; NG50 uses an independent genome-size estimate, making the metric comparable across assemblies of different completeness.
explanations.b: NG50 uses no fixed contig-length cutoff; it is defined by the running-sum-to-50%-of-genome-size rule, same as N50's rule but against a different denominator.
explanations.c: NG50 is a contiguity metric computed from contig lengths, unrelated to BUSCO's gene-completeness search.
explanations.d: They differ specifically in the denominator used, which is the entire point of NG50 existing as a separate metric.

questions.prompt: Match each assembly evaluation tool to what it checks.

right.text: Contig length distribution (how few, how long the contigs are)
Presence/completeness of expected single-copy genes
Misassembly events found by aligning to a trusted reference
Reference-free base-level accuracy from raw-read k-mers

questions.explanation: N50/L50 summarize contig length distribution; BUSCO checks for expected single-copy orthologs; QUAST aligns to a reference genome to count explicit misassemblies; Merqury compares the assembly's k-mers against the raw reads' k-mer spectrum with no reference required.

questions.prompt: In the worked example, why was Team B's higher N50 misleading?

options.text: N50 cannot be computed for assemblies with fewer than 40 contigs
Team B's aggressive joining produced longer contigs partly by stitching together sequence from different genomic regions, which QUAST and BUSCO exposed as misassemblies
Team A's assembler used a reference genome and Team B's did not
N50 is only valid for eukaryotic genomes

explanations.a: N50 is computable for any number of contigs; contig count is not a validity constraint.
explanations.b: Correct — the higher N50 reflected fewer, longer contigs, but some of that length came from wrongly joining sequence across a shared repeat, which QUAST flagged as misassemblies and BUSCO flagged as fragmented orthologs at the same junctions.
explanations.c: Neither team's assembler is described as using a reference during assembly; the reference was only used afterward for QUAST evaluation.
explanations.d: N50 applies to any genome assembly, prokaryotic or eukaryotic; the worked example is explicitly a bacterial genome.

lessons.label: Long Reads Change the Problem

sections.heading: PacBio HiFi: accuracy through repetition, not longer chemistry
sections.body: PacBio's HiFi (High-Fidelity) reads solve accuracy by reading the same short DNA molecule multiple times rather than by improving raw per-base accuracy. The molecule is circularized and the polymerase sequences around it repeatedly, producing several passes that are then collapsed into a circular consensus sequence (CCS). The result is reads of roughly 15-25 kb with accuracy above Q30 (99.9%+) — a striking jump from the raw single-pass accuracy of the same chemistry, which is far noisier. This trades some read length (HiFi reads are shorter than Nanopore's longest reads) for base-level trustworthiness, which matters directly for variant calling and for keeping small-scale graph errors out of an assembly.

sections.heading: Oxford Nanopore: length without a hard ceiling
sections.body: Oxford Nanopore sequencing reads a molecule by threading it through a protein pore and measuring changes in electrical current as bases pass through, with no theoretical upper limit on read length — reads over 100 kb are routine for ultra-long protocols, and multi-megabase reads have been reported. Jain et al. (2018) demonstrated assembly of a human genome using ultra-long Nanopore reads with an N50 above 100 kb, showing that raw read length alone could span repeats that had defeated earlier assemblies. Nanopore's historical weakness was per-base error rate, often in the 5-15% range for older chemistries, but the R10.4 pore chemistry sharply improved raw accuracy, and duplex reads (sequencing both strands of the same molecule and combining the signal) now approach HiFi-level accuracy while keeping Nanopore's characteristic length advantage.

sections.heading: What length and phase buy: T2T continuity and separated haplotypes
sections.body: Long reads matter for assembly because they can span repeats that defeated short-read and even early long-read methods: a read longer than a repeat carries unique flanking sequence on both sides, resolving what was structurally ambiguous. Combining PacBio HiFi with Nanopore ultra-long reads let the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) Consortium produce the first complete, gapless human genome assembly, T2T-CHM13 (Nurk et al., 2022, Science), closing centromeric and other repeat-rich regions every prior reference had left as gaps. A separate long-read payoff is haplotype phasing during assembly itself: hifiasm (Cheng et al., 2021) can use trio binning — sorting reads by parent-specific k-mers derived from short-read sequencing of both parents — or Hi-C chromosome-conformation data to assign long reads to the correct parental haplotype before assembly, producing two separate, phased haplotype assemblies instead of a single collapsed mosaic that mixes both parents' sequence at every heterozygous site.

lessons.workedExample: A lab wants a diploid human genome assembly that keeps maternal and paternal sequence separate rather than collapsed. They sequence the proband with PacBio HiFi for base accuracy, sequence both parents with cheap short reads just to build parent-specific k-mer sets, and run hifiasm with trio binning: any long read whose k-mers match the paternal-specific set gets assigned to the paternal bin, and likewise for maternal, before assembly graphs are even built. The output is two haplotype-resolved assemblies rather than one merged sequence — critical if the research question is which parental copy of a gene carries a disease variant, since a collapsed assembly would average over that distinction and could hide it entirely.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "why did you choose this sequencing platform" wants a tradeoff, not a brand preference. A strong answer distinguishes HiFi's accuracy-through-repeated-reading (CCS) from Nanopore's length-through-a-different-physical-mechanism (pore current), and can say what each buys for the specific biological question — repeat-spanning continuity, phasing, or raw base accuracy for variant calling. A student who cannot explain why phasing (trio binning or Hi-C) matters, versus just running a plain assembler, hasn't grasped that a genome has two haplotypes and a collapsed assembly quietly discards that information.

questions.prompt: How does PacBio HiFi sequencing achieve its Q30+ accuracy?

options.text: By using a longer, more error-prone raw chemistry and correcting errors computationally afterward
By circularizing the molecule and sequencing it multiple times, then collapsing the repeated passes into a circular consensus sequence
By threading the molecule through a nanopore and measuring current changes
By using trio binning to remove erroneous reads before assembly

explanations.a: HiFi's accuracy gain comes from repeated reading of the same molecule, not post-hoc correction of a single noisy pass.
explanations.b: Correct — HiFi circularizes the template and passes it through the polymerase multiple times, and the circular consensus sequence (CCS) built from those repeated passes reaches Q30+ (99.9%+) accuracy even though any single pass is much noisier.
explanations.c: Pore-based current sensing describes Oxford Nanopore sequencing, not PacBio's HiFi chemistry.
explanations.d: Trio binning is a haplotype-assignment technique used during assembly, unrelated to how HiFi achieves per-base accuracy during sequencing.

questions.prompt: What specifically improved with Oxford Nanopore's R10.4 chemistry?

options.text: Maximum theoretical read length
Raw per-base accuracy, sharply reduced from the historically higher error rates of older chemistries
The need for circular consensus sequencing
The cost of the sequencing instrument

explanations.a: Nanopore read length was never chemistry-limited in principle; R10.4's advance was accuracy, not a length ceiling that didn't exist.
explanations.b: Correct — Nanopore's historical weakness was raw per-base error, often 5-15% in older chemistries; R10.4 sharply improved raw accuracy, and duplex reads push it further toward HiFi-level accuracy.
explanations.c: Circular consensus sequencing (CCS) is a PacBio HiFi concept, not part of the Nanopore pore-based sequencing mechanism.
explanations.d: Instrument cost is unrelated to what R10.4 chemistry specifically changed about sequencing accuracy.

questions.prompt: Match each haplotype-phasing input hifiasm can use to how it identifies which reads belong to which parent.

right.text: Short-read sequencing of both parents to build parent-specific k-mer sets, then matching long reads to those sets
Chromosome-conformation contact frequencies that indicate which sequences are physically co-located on the same chromosome copy

questions.explanation: Trio binning uses parent-specific k-mers (from separately sequencing both parents) to sort a child's long reads by parental origin before assembly; Hi-C uses chromosome-conformation contact data, which reflects physical proximity within a haplotype, to phase without needing parental sequencing at all.

questions.prompt: What did combining PacBio HiFi and Nanopore ultra-long reads achieve in the T2T-CHM13 assembly (Nurk et al., 2022)?

options.text: The first complete, gapless human genome assembly, closing repeat-rich regions like centromeres that prior references left as gaps
The first human genome assembly of any kind
A reduction in the cost of Illumina short-read sequencing
The first assembly to use a de Bruijn graph

explanations.a: Correct — T2T-CHM13 was the first telomere-to-telomere, gapless human genome assembly, closing centromeric and other repeat-rich regions that had defeated every prior reference by combining HiFi accuracy with Nanopore ultra-long read length.
explanations.b: Human genome assemblies existed long before T2T-CHM13, including the original draft and subsequent GRCh references; what was new was completeness, not existence.
explanations.c: T2T-CHM13's contribution was assembly completeness using long-read platforms, unrelated to Illumina short-read pricing.
explanations.d: T2T-CHM13 relied on long-read OLC-style methods suited to PacBio and Nanopore data, not a short-read de Bruijn graph approach.

lessons.label: Phasing and Imputation

sections.heading: Read-backed phasing: let physical reads settle it
sections.body: A standard genotype call tells you a person is heterozygous at two nearby SNPs but not which alleles sit together on the same physical chromosome copy — the A at position 1 could be paired with the G at position 2, or with the C, and unphased genotyping alone cannot tell them apart. Read-backed phasing resolves this directly when a single sequencing read (or read pair) is long enough to span both heterozygous sites at once: whatever two alleles appear together on that one physical molecule must be on the same haplotype. WhatsHap (Patterson et al., 2015) implements this by collecting reads spanning multiple heterozygous positions and finding the haplotype assignment that is most consistent with all of them, weighted by base quality. Its main limit is coverage geometry: it can only phase pairs of variants close enough that some read or read pair actually bridges them, which is why long reads extend phasing much further than short reads can.

sections.heading: Statistical phasing: borrowing from population structure
sections.body: When no read spans two variants, phasing can still be inferred statistically from population haplotype patterns. Tools like SHAPEIT and Eagle (Loh et al., 2016) build on the Li and Stephens (2003) copying model: they treat each individual's unknown haplotype as an imperfect mosaic, stretches copied from other haplotypes already observed in a reference panel, with occasional "switches" between which panel haplotype is being copied from (modeling recombination) and occasional mutations away from the copied allele (modeling genotyping error or true novel variation). This is formalized as a hidden Markov model, and it works because real haplotypes are not random combinations of alleles — nearby variants travel together across generations due to linkage disequilibrium, so a large panel of known haplotypes strongly constrains which combinations are plausible.

sections.heading: Imputation: filling in genotypes you never measured
sections.body: Imputation extends the same copying-model logic to genotypes that were never directly assayed at all — common on SNP arrays, which only genotype a fixed set of a few hundred thousand positions out of tens of millions of possible variant sites. Using a reference panel of fully sequenced haplotypes such as the Haplotype Reference Consortium (HRC, McCarthy et al., 2016, roughly 65,000 haplotypes) or TOPMed (Taliun et al., 2021, 53,831 diverse genomes), an imputation algorithm finds which reference haplotypes best match an individual's measured genotypes and fills in the unmeasured positions from that match. Accuracy is strong for common variants well represented in the panel, but drops sharply for rare variants (too few copies in any panel to establish a reliable copying pattern) and for individuals from ancestries underrepresented in the panel, since reference panels have historically skewed heavily European, leaving imputation systematically less accurate for African, Indigenous, and admixed American populations — a well-documented equity gap in clinical and research genomics.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher genotypes a cohort on a SNP array covering 700,000 positions but wants genotypes at 10 million common variant sites for a genome-wide association study. They run imputation against the TOPMed reference panel: for each stretch of the genome, the algorithm finds which TOPMed haplotypes best match the person's directly measured genotypes nearby, then fills in the untyped positions using those matched haplotypes' known alleles there. For a common variant with high minor allele frequency, imputation accuracy (measured as squared correlation with true genotype, r^2) is typically well above 0.9. For a rare variant carried by only a handful of haplotypes in the panel, or for a participant of an ancestry underrepresented in TOPMed relative to their study population, that same imputation accuracy drops substantially, meaning any downstream association test involving that variant is noisier and more likely to miss a real signal, or in rare cases, produce a spurious one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing phasing or imputation wants to know the student understands these are inference, not measurement, and that inference has different failure modes than measurement error. The strongest answers distinguish read-backed phasing (a direct physical fact from a spanning read) from statistical phasing and imputation (a probabilistic borrowing from population structure), and can name the specific failure mode — rare variants and underrepresented ancestries getting worse imputation accuracy because reference panels don't have enough matching haplotypes to copy from. A student who treats an imputed genotype as equivalent to a directly sequenced one hasn't understood what the method is actually doing.

questions.prompt: What makes read-backed phasing (as in WhatsHap) different from statistical phasing?

options.text: Read-backed phasing uses a reference panel of population haplotypes; statistical phasing does not
Read-backed phasing infers phase directly from reads that physically span two heterozygous sites on the same molecule; statistical phasing infers phase from population haplotype patterns
Read-backed phasing only works on RNA sequencing data
Statistical phasing requires no sequencing data at all

explanations.a: This is backwards — statistical phasing is the approach that relies on a reference panel of population haplotypes; read-backed phasing relies on physical reads.
explanations.b: Correct — WhatsHap-style read-backed phasing uses reads (or read pairs) spanning multiple heterozygous positions to read off phase directly from the physical molecule, while statistical phasing infers phase from patterns of linkage disequilibrium across a population.
explanations.c: Read-backed phasing works on any sequencing data type where reads can span multiple heterozygous sites, not specifically RNA sequencing.
explanations.d: Statistical phasing still requires genotype data for the individual being phased; it just doesn't need reads spanning the specific variant pair.

questions.prompt: What core idea from the Li and Stephens (2003) model underlies tools like SHAPEIT and Eagle?

options.text: Every individual's haplotype is a random, independent combination of alleles
An individual's haplotype can be modeled as an imperfect mosaic copied from haplotypes already observed in a reference panel
Phasing requires directly sequencing both parents
Linkage disequilibrium has no effect on haplotype structure

explanations.a: The opposite is true — the model works precisely because haplotypes are not random combinations; linkage disequilibrium makes nearby alleles travel together.
explanations.b: Correct — Li and Stephens (2003) modeled a haplotype as an imperfect copy of a mosaic of known reference haplotypes, formalized as a hidden Markov model with switches (recombination) and mutations (errors or novel variation).
explanations.c: Statistical phasing is explicitly the approach that does not require parental sequencing; that describes a different technique (trio-based phasing).
explanations.d: Linkage disequilibrium is the reason the copying model works at all — without it, nearby alleles would carry no information about each other.

questions.prompt: Why does imputation accuracy drop for individuals from ancestries underrepresented in a reference panel like HRC or TOPMed?

options.text: Because SNP arrays cannot genotype individuals from underrepresented ancestries at all
Because the reference panel has fewer haplotypes carrying that population's characteristic variation, so the copying model has less accurate material to match against
Because imputation algorithms apply a fixed accuracy penalty based on self-reported ancestry
Because underrepresented ancestries have systematically higher sequencing error rates

explanations.a: SNP arrays genotype directly measured positions regardless of ancestry; the accuracy gap is specifically in imputing the unmeasured positions.
explanations.b: Correct — since reference panels like HRC and TOPMed have historically skewed heavily European, individuals from underrepresented ancestries have fewer well-matching haplotypes in the panel to copy from, so the statistical copying model performs worse for them.
explanations.c: Imputation accuracy emerges from panel composition and matching quality, not an explicit ancestry-based penalty applied by the algorithm.
explanations.d: Sequencing error rate is a property of the assay, not of ancestry, and is not the mechanism behind the imputation accuracy gap.

questions.prompt: Order these steps in a typical imputation workflow, from raw data to final result.

items.text: Genotype the individual on a SNP array covering a limited set of positions
Match the individual's measured genotypes against haplotypes in a reference panel
Fill in genotypes at untyped positions using the best-matching reference haplotypes

questions.explanation: Imputation starts from a limited set of directly measured genotypes (from a SNP array), then finds which reference-panel haplotypes best explain that measured pattern, and only then fills in the genotypes at positions the array never measured, using the matched reference haplotypes.

lessons.label: Pangenomes and Graph References

sections.heading: From one linear string to a graph of many genomes
sections.body: GRCh38, like every reference genome before it, is a single linear sequence — one path through one mosaic of donor DNA, even though no two humans share identical sequence at every position. A variation graph represents many genomes at once: nodes are sequence segments and edges connect segments that occur adjacent to each other in at least one included genome, so a site where individuals differ by a SNP, insertion, or deletion becomes a branch point where the graph offers multiple paths instead of forcing one arbitrary choice. The vg toolkit (Garrison et al., 2018, Nature Biotechnology) built practical tools for constructing these graphs and aligning reads directly to them, showing that graph-based mapping reduced reference bias — the tendency for a linear reference to poorly represent reads carrying sequence that differs from it, especially around structural variants and insertions the linear reference simply never included at all.

sections.heading: Storing many haplotypes efficiently: GBWT and minigraph-cactus
sections.body: A pangenome graph is only useful if you can also record which specific path each individual genome actually takes through it — otherwise the graph has no notion of a real haplotype, only abstract possible ones. The GBWT (Graph Burrows-Wheeler Transform, Sirén et al., 2020) indexes thousands of haplotype paths through a graph in compressed form, letting tools query which known haplotypes pass through a given node without storing every path explicitly. Building the graph itself at genome scale is its own problem: minigraph-cactus, the pipeline used by the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium, aligns many complete haplotype-resolved assemblies (built with the long-read and phasing methods from earlier lessons) against each other and merges shared sequence into a single graph structure. The HPRC's 2023 draft human pangenome (Liao et al., Nature) was built from 47 individuals' phased diploid assemblies (94 haplotypes), deliberately sampled for ancestral diversity that GRCh38 and its predecessors lacked.

sections.heading: GFA, and what breaks when the reference isn't a line
sections.body: Graphical Fragment Assembly (GFA) is the standard text file format for representing these sequence graphs — segments, links between them, and paths that trace a specific haplotype through the graph — playing the role FASTA plays for linear sequence. Moving to a graph reference breaks a huge amount of tooling built on one assumption: that every genomic position can be named as a single chromosome plus a single integer offset. BED intervals, VCF coordinates, and essentially every alignment, visualization, and annotation tool (BWA, GATK, IGV) were built assuming that linear chrom:pos coordinate system. Using pangenome results with this tooling requires projecting graph coordinates back onto a chosen linear reference path through the graph, which recovers compatibility but also reintroduces some of the very bias the graph was built to avoid for the sequence that path leaves out. The measured payoff is real: the HPRC pangenome captured structural variation and sequence entirely absent from GRCh38, and graph-based mapping against it reduced small-variant call errors and improved sensitivity to structural variants relative to standard linear-reference mapping, with the largest gains in individuals of non-European ancestry, the population GRCh38's mosaic construction represented most poorly.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher studying a population with African ancestry maps their sequencing reads to GRCh38 and finds a structural variant region shows suspiciously low, patchy coverage — reads carrying an insertion present in their population but absent from GRCh38 either fail to align or align with so many mismatches they get filtered out, a classic reference bias signature. Remapping the same reads to the HPRC pangenome graph, built from 47 diverse phased assemblies including individuals of African ancestry, the same reads now align cleanly because the insertion sequence is already represented as an alternate path in the graph. The variant caller run on the graph-based alignment recovers the structural variant that the linear-reference pipeline had essentially made invisible — but the researcher then has to project the graph coordinates back onto a linear chrom:pos system before their existing BED-based annotation pipeline can process the result at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "why not just use GRCh38" wants to see the student understand reference bias as a concrete, non-hypothetical failure mode, not an abstract fairness talking point. The strongest answer names a specific mechanism — reads carrying sequence absent from a linear reference either fail to align or get filtered as too-mismatched, and this disproportionately affects populations underrepresented in that reference's original donor mosaic — and can also name the concrete cost of switching to a graph, that most existing genomic tooling assumes linear chrom:pos coordinates and graph coordinates must be projected back to interoperate with it.

questions.prompt: What structural change does a variation graph make relative to a linear reference like GRCh38?

options.text: It stores multiple genomes as separate, unconnected FASTA files
It represents sequence differences as branch points, with edges connecting segments that co-occur in at least one included genome, instead of forcing a single fixed path
It removes all repetitive sequence from the reference
It only stores SNPs, not insertions or deletions

explanations.a: A variation graph is a single connected structure, not a collection of separate linear files; the connections between segments are the entire point.
explanations.b: Correct — nodes are sequence segments and edges connect segments adjacent in at least one genome, so a site of variation becomes a branch offering multiple paths instead of one arbitrary linear choice.
explanations.c: Variation graphs still represent repetitive sequence; graphs do not remove it, though repeats can create complex tangles in the graph structure.
explanations.d: Variation graphs represent insertions, deletions, and structural variants as alternate paths, not just SNPs.

questions.prompt: Match each pangenome component to its role.

right.text: Constructs graphs and aligns reads directly to them
Compressed indexing of many haplotype paths through a graph
Pipeline that aligns many phased assemblies to build the graph structure itself
Text file format representing graph segments, links, and haplotype paths

questions.explanation: vg builds graphs and aligns reads to them; GBWT compactly indexes many haplotypes' paths through an existing graph; minigraph-cactus constructs the graph itself from many phased assemblies (as used by the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium); GFA is the file format that represents the resulting graph structure.

questions.prompt: Why does switching to a graph reference break most existing genomic tooling like BED intervals, GATK, and IGV?

options.text: Because those tools cannot process any text file format
Because that tooling assumes every genomic position can be named as a single chromosome plus a single integer offset, which a graph with multiple paths does not have
Because graph references are always larger than linear references
Because BED and VCF formats were designed specifically to be incompatible with graphs

explanations.a: These tools process text-based formats fine; the incompatibility is about coordinate semantics, not file parsing.
explanations.b: Correct — BED, VCF-style coordinates, and tools like GATK and IGV assume a single linear chrom:pos coordinate system, which does not map cleanly onto a graph where a position can lie on one of several alternate paths.
explanations.c: File size is not the reason for the tooling break; the issue is the coordinate model these tools were designed around.
explanations.d: BED and VCF predate widespread pangenome graphs and were designed for linear references, not deliberately designed to exclude graphs.

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, what population saw the largest measured benefit from pangenome-based mapping relative to GRCh38, and why?

options.text: European-ancestry individuals, because GRCh38's mosaic construction represented them best
Non-European-ancestry individuals, because GRCh38's donor mosaic represented them most poorly, so more of their sequence was missing from the linear reference
All populations benefited equally regardless of ancestry
Only individuals sequenced with PacBio HiFi reads benefited

explanations.a: European-ancestry individuals were already relatively well represented by GRCh38's original donor mosaic, so they had less to gain from switching to a pangenome.
explanations.b: Correct — because GRCh38 represented non-European ancestries most poorly, those individuals had more sequence and structural variation missing from the linear reference, so mapping to a diverse pangenome graph produced the largest measured reduction in reference bias for them.
explanations.c: The benefit was not uniform; it was concentrated in populations underrepresented in GRCh38's original construction.
explanations.d: The benefit of pangenome mapping applies to short-read and long-read data alike being mapped to the graph; it is not restricted to individuals sequenced with a particular long-read platform.

units.label: Pipelines in the Wild: Applications and Case Studies

lessons.label: Reproducible Pipelines and What They Cost

sections.heading: "We ran GATK" is not a methods section
sections.body: A bioinformatics pipeline is not one program, it is a chain: trim reads, align, sort, mark duplicates, call variants, filter, annotate. Every step has a tool, a version, and parameters, and every one of those can change the output. GATK's HaplotypeCaller has shifted its default model more than once across major versions; aligning to GRCh37 versus GRCh38 changes coordinates and can flip calls near structural differences between the builds; a minimum base-quality or mapping-quality cutoff set at 20 versus 30 changes which low-confidence sites survive. A methods section that says "we ran GATK" tells a judge nothing reproducible — it omits the tool version, the reference genome build, and the exact parameters, any one of which another team could rerun differently and get a different variant list from the same raw reads.

sections.heading: Workflow managers pin the chain, not just one step
sections.body: Workflow managers exist to make the whole chain, not just one tool, reproducible. Nextflow and Snakemake both let you describe a pipeline as a graph of steps with declared inputs and outputs, so the manager can resume from a failed step, parallelize independent branches, and rerun the identical graph later. WDL, paired with the Cromwell execution engine, is the format the Broad Institute uses for its production genomics pipelines. Curated pipeline collections such as nf-core wrap Nextflow workflows that a community has already tested and versioned end to end (nf-core/sarek for variant calling, nf-core/rnaseq for expression), so a student does not have to hand-assemble each step from scratch. Containers (Docker or Singularity) go one layer deeper: they freeze the exact tool binary and its library dependencies, so "GATK 4.5.0.0 in this container" runs identically on a laptop or a cluster years later, immune to whatever the system's default samtools has drifted to since.

sections.heading: The resource math behind a single genome
sections.body: Reproducibility also has to survive a resource budget. A 30x-coverage human whole-genome sequencing run — each base of the ~3.1 billion-bp genome read about 30 times on average, the standard clinical depth — produces roughly 100 GB as an aligned BAM file; switching to the reference-compressed CRAM format (which stores differences from the reference rather than full sequence) cuts that to roughly 60 GB. Getting from raw reads to a filtered variant call set takes on the order of tens of CPU-hours end to end, which is why pipelines are written to run in parallel across genome regions rather than as one long serial job. A team that cannot state its tool versions, reference build, and rough compute footprint has not fully specified what it did — and cannot promise the same numbers if it ran the pipeline again tomorrow.

lessons.workedExample: A student re-runs a public RNA-seq dataset and gets a different list of differentially expressed genes than the original paper. Before assuming a coding error, they check the pipeline: the paper aligned to GRCh38 with STAR 2.5, the student used GRCh37 with STAR 2.7 and the default parameter set, which shifted read placement near a handful of genes whose annotations differ between builds. Pinning the same reference build and tool version in a container, rather than "whatever is installed," resolves the discrepancy and turns an apparent contradiction into a documented version difference.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "what version, what reference, what parameters" because bioinformatics results are only as reproducible as the exact software stack that produced them — a different GATK version or genome build can change variant calls without any error in the student's logic. A project that names its workflow manager (Nextflow, Snakemake) or container, states the reference build, and can roughly justify its compute cost shows the student understands their pipeline is a specific, versioned artifact, not a black box they ran once and trusted.

questions.prompt: Why is "we ran GATK to call variants" an incomplete methods statement?

options.text: GATK cannot call variants at all, only align reads
It omits the tool version, reference genome build, and parameters, any of which can change the resulting variant calls
GATK requires a paid license, so the statement implies an undisclosed cost
Variant calling never depends on software version, only on the raw reads

explanations.a: GATK's HaplotypeCaller is specifically a variant-calling tool; the problem isn't what it does but what the statement fails to specify.
explanations.b: Correct — different GATK versions have changed default calling models, GRCh37 versus GRCh38 shifts coordinates and can flip calls near build differences, and parameter choices like base-quality cutoffs change which sites pass filtering.
explanations.c: Licensing cost is irrelevant to reproducibility of the scientific result.
explanations.d: The opposite is true — version and parameters are exactly what can change the output from identical raw reads.

questions.prompt: What is the main reproducibility advantage a container (Docker/Singularity) adds beyond a workflow manager like Nextflow alone?

options.text: It freezes the exact tool binary and its library dependencies, not just the order of pipeline steps
It automatically corrects sequencing errors in the raw reads
It removes the need to specify a reference genome build
It makes the pipeline run without needing any compute resources

explanations.a: Correct — a workflow manager pins the graph of steps and can resume/parallelize, but a container additionally pins the exact software version and its dependencies so the same command produces the same behavior years later.
explanations.b: Containers package software; they have no effect on sequencing chemistry or error rates.
explanations.c: The reference build is a pipeline input a container does not decide; it still must be specified separately.
explanations.d: Containers still require CPU and memory to execute; they only standardize the software environment.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much smaller is a 30x human WGS file stored as CRAM compared to BAM?

options.text: About 100 GB down to roughly 60 GB
About 60 GB down to roughly 100 GB
About 100 GB down to roughly 1 GB
CRAM and BAM are always the same size

explanations.a: Correct — a 30x WGS BAM is roughly 100 GB, and CRAM's reference-compression brings that down to roughly 60 GB.
explanations.b: This reverses the direction; BAM is the larger format, CRAM the compressed one.
explanations.c: CRAM compresses relative to the reference but does not shrink a whole genome's worth of reads that far.
explanations.d: CRAM's reference-based compression is specifically why it is smaller than BAM.

questions.prompt: Match each tool/format to its role in a reproducible genomics pipeline.

right.text: Describes a pipeline as a graph of steps that can resume and parallelize
Workflow language and execution engine used for Broad Institute production pipelines
Community-curated, versioned collection of ready-made Nextflow pipelines
Freezes the exact tool binary and library dependencies for identical reruns

questions.explanation: Nextflow and Snakemake define the pipeline as a resumable, parallelizable graph of steps; WDL/Cromwell is the workflow language and engine behind Broad Institute production pipelines; nf-core packages tested, versioned Nextflow pipelines like sarek and rnaseq; containers pin the exact software environment so results reproduce years later.

lessons.label: Pathogen Genomics: SARS-CoV-2 as a Case Study

sections.heading: Amplicon sequencing and its signature failure
sections.body: The ARTIC Network protocol, developed for fast field sequencing of outbreak viruses, tiles the roughly 30-kb SARS-CoV-2 genome with about 98 overlapping PCR amplicons (in its widely used V3/V4 primer sets) split across two pools so that neighboring amplicons don't compete for the same primer-binding site. The design has one structural weakness: if a mutation arises exactly where a primer binds, that primer can no longer anneal, and the amplicon covering that stretch fails to amplify — amplicon dropout. This is not just a nuisance; it turned into an accidental surveillance signal. The Alpha variant (B.1.1.7) carried a deletion in the spike gene that happened to sit in the binding site of a target used by a specific diagnostic PCR assay, causing that one gene target to fail — S-gene target failure (SGTF) — while the other PCR targets in the same test still came back positive. Because routine UK diagnostic PCR used that exact assay at huge scale, SGTF became a free, real-time proxy for Alpha's spread through late 2020, months before enough genomes were sequenced to confirm the same trend directly.

sections.heading: From reads to a placed lineage
sections.body: After amplicon reads are trimmed of primer sequence and aligned to the reference genome, a consensus sequence is built by taking the majority base at each position (masking or dropping any dropout region rather than guessing). Genomes over a coverage threshold are named systematically as Pango lineages, a nomenclature framework Rambaut and colleagues proposed in 2020 specifically so genomic epidemiologists could track transmission chains at finer resolution than broad clade labels — B.1.1.7, B.1.617.2, and their many sublineages all come from this system. Nextclade then places a new genome onto the Nextstrain global phylogenetic tree by comparing it to reference sequences, flagging quality issues (like too many masked or ambiguous sites) and reporting which mutations it carries relative to the ancestral genome, all without the slower step of rebuilding the whole tree from scratch.

sections.heading: The GISAID-versus-open-data fight
sections.body: Nearly all of this analysis needs a shared genome database, and that is where SARS-CoV-2 genomics became genuinely contentious. GISAID, which grew out of influenza data-sharing, became the dominant repository — holding many millions of SARS-CoV-2 genomes — but requires users to register, credit data-generating labs, and agree not to redistribute the raw sequences, terms defended as necessary to get labs in lower-resource settings to share data at all. Critics countered that fully open archives such as INSDC (GenBank/ENA/DDBJ) let anyone reanalyze and redistribute freely, and argued GISAID's restrictions slowed independent verification and made some published findings hard to fully reproduce. Both camps agree sharing matters; they disagree about whether access controls help or hinder the science built on top of it.

lessons.workedExample: A UK lab in late 2020 notices a growing share of routine diagnostic PCR tests coming back positive on two targets but negative on the S-gene target specifically. Rather than treating this as assay failure, epidemiologists cross-reference a small number of genomes and confirm the pattern matches a spike-gene deletion carried by the emerging B.1.1.7 (Alpha) lineage. Because millions of routine PCR tests were already being run for diagnosis, SGTF frequency became a real-time, low-cost tracker of Alpha's growth advantage across the country — a case where an amplicon dropout, normally a data-quality problem, became the surveillance signal itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes SARS-CoV-2 pipeline projects on amplicon dropout specifically because it is the failure mode most likely to silently corrupt a student's own consensus genomes if they don't know to look for it, and because the SGTF story shows dropout can be informative rather than purely a defect. A student who can explain why a primer-site mutation causes a gap in coverage, and who has checked their own genome for masked or low-coverage regions, is demonstrating they understand their pipeline's failure modes rather than trusting whatever consensus sequence came out the other end.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an ARTIC-based SARS-CoV-2 pipeline from raw reads to a placed lineage.

items.text: Trim primer sequences from amplicon reads
Align trimmed reads to the reference genome
Build a consensus sequence, masking dropout regions
Assign a Pango lineage and place the genome on the Nextstrain tree via Nextclade

questions.explanation: Primer sequence must be trimmed before alignment so primer-derived bases don't distort mapping; alignment must happen before a per-position consensus can be built; only once a consensus genome exists can it be assigned a Pango lineage and placed on the phylogenetic tree.

questions.prompt: What caused S-gene target failure (SGTF) in routine UK PCR tests during the rise of Alpha (B.1.1.7)?

options.text: A spike-gene deletion in Alpha sat in the binding site of one PCR target, causing that target to fail while others in the same test stayed positive
Alpha infections produced too little viral RNA for any PCR target to detect
Laboratories ran out of S-gene reagent during the surge
SGTF was a sequencing artifact unrelated to any real viral mutation

explanations.a: Correct — Alpha's spike-gene deletion disrupted one PCR target's binding site specifically, so that target failed while the assay's other targets still detected the virus, making SGTF a real-time proxy for Alpha's spread.
explanations.b: SGTF affected only one specific target within a multi-target PCR test, not overall detection sensitivity.
explanations.c: The failure was caused by a genetic mismatch, not a reagent shortage.
explanations.d: SGTF was a genuine PCR signal tied to a real mutation, not a sequencing artifact, and it was used precisely because it reflected biology.

questions.prompt: Amplicon dropout in an ARTIC-based protocol most directly occurs when:

options.text: A mutation arises at a primer-binding site, preventing that primer from annealing and that amplicon from being produced
The virus genome is too large to fit in any amplicon tiling scheme
Two overlapping amplicons are sequenced with identical reads
The consensus caller ignores all positions with any coverage

explanations.a: Correct — dropout is a structural weakness of primer-based amplification: a mutation exactly where a primer binds stops that primer from annealing, so the amplicon it should have produced is missing.
explanations.b: Amplicon tiling is designed around genome size (around 98 amplicons cover SARS-CoV-2's ~30-kb genome); size itself isn't the failure mode.
explanations.c: Overlapping amplicons are a deliberate design feature for redundancy, not a cause of dropout.
explanations.d: Consensus callers use available coverage; dropout is about missing coverage in the first place, not how the caller treats coverage that exists.

questions.prompt: What is the central disagreement in the GISAID-versus-open-data controversy?

options.text: Whether GISAID's access terms (registration, no redistribution) help secure data sharing or instead hinder independent reanalysis, compared with fully open archives like GenBank/ENA/DDBJ
Whether SARS-CoV-2 genomes should be sequenced at all
Whether Pango lineages or Nextstrain clades are the correct nomenclature
Whether amplicon or shotgun sequencing produces higher coverage

explanations.a: Correct — GISAID's defenders argue its terms (registration, crediting labs, no redistribution) were needed to get broad participation, while critics argue those same restrictions slowed independent verification compared to fully open INSDC archives.
explanations.b: The controversy assumes sequencing happens; it is about the terms under which the resulting genomes are shared, not whether to sequence.
explanations.c: Pango and Nextstrain nomenclature serve different purposes and are not the subject of the GISAID access dispute.
explanations.d: Sequencing method is a separate technical question from database access policy.

lessons.label: Metagenomics and the Contamination Problem

sections.heading: Two ways to survey a microbial community
sections.body: 16S amplicon sequencing PCR-amplifies one marker gene — the bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA gene, whose sequence is conserved enough to amplify broadly but variable enough in specific regions to distinguish taxa — and sequences just that fragment across every organism in a sample. Older pipelines clustered similar reads into OTUs at a fixed similarity threshold; Callahan and colleagues' 2016 DADA2 method replaced that with amplicon sequence variants (ASVs), which model the sequencer's actual per-base error rates to resolve single-nucleotide differences between organisms rather than lumping them into a coarse cluster. Shotgun metagenomics instead sequences all the DNA in a sample indiscriminately, which costs more but captures genes beyond the marker, including functional and antibiotic-resistance genes. Its reads are typically classified by k-mer matching against reference genome databases — Kraken2 breaks each read into fixed-length k-mers and looks up which taxon's genome each k-mer belongs to, assigning the read via the lowest common ancestor of its matches. Shotgun reads can also be assembled and grouped by shared coverage and composition into metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), recovering draft genomes for organisms that were never cultured in a lab.

sections.heading: The kitome: contamination that scales with how little DNA you started with
sections.body: Salter and colleagues' 2014 study demonstrated that the reagents used to extract and amplify DNA — enzymes, water, spin-column kits — carry their own trace bacterial DNA, dubbed the "kitome." In a high-biomass sample like stool, that trace signal is negligible against the real microbial DNA present. In a low-biomass sample — blood, tissue, or a hospital surface swab — the reagent contamination can rival or exceed the genuine signal, so a chunk of what looks like "the sample's microbiome" is actually the kit's. The fix is procedural, not computational: sequence extraction-blank and no-template controls alongside real samples and subtract or flag whatever taxa show up in the blanks.

sections.heading: When the field didn't run that control: the tumor microbiome dispute
sections.body: Poore and colleagues published a high-profile 2020 Nature paper claiming distinct microbial DNA signatures could be found in blood and tumor tissue across many cancer types, useful as a diagnostic signal. A re-analysis by Gihawi, Salzberg, and colleagues argued that much of the reported signal was better explained by exactly the low-biomass contamination problem Salter had described nearly a decade earlier, compounded by normalization choices in the analysis pipeline that could manufacture apparent cancer-type-specific patterns from batch effects. The dispute escalated for years; Nature retracted the original paper in June 2024, with all authors agreeing to the retraction even as some maintained the biological signal was still partly real. The episode is now a standard cautionary example: an exciting low-biomass finding needs contamination controls built in from the start, not argued about after publication.

lessons.workedExample: A high-school team wants to compare the gut microbiome of two mouse diet groups using 16S sequencing. If they only sequence the mouse stool samples, any reagent contamination is a rounding error against the enormous real bacterial signal in stool, so a DADA2 ASV pipeline can proceed with reasonable confidence. If instead they were sampling something low-biomass — say, a hospital swab or dilute environmental water — the same pipeline without an extraction-blank control could report the kit's contaminating bacteria as if they were the sample's own community. The lesson generalizes: the amount of caution a metagenomics pipeline needs scales inversely with how much real DNA the sample actually contains.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the kitome and the tumor-microbiome retraction because low-biomass metagenomics is exactly where enthusiasm most easily outruns rigor — a compelling result can be built entirely from reagent contamination and never get caught without a blank control. A student who can name Salter's 2014 finding, explain why it matters more in low- than high-biomass samples, and describe running (or at least discussing) an extraction-blank control has shown they understand the field's most consequential failure mode, not just its taxonomy pipeline.

questions.prompt: Match each metagenomics method to what it does.

right.text: Models per-base sequencer error to resolve amplicon sequence variants from 16S reads
Classifies reads by matching k-mers against a reference database
A draft genome recovered by assembling and binning shotgun reads by coverage/composition
Sequences all DNA in a sample rather than one marker gene

questions.explanation: DADA2 (Callahan et al. 2016) resolves ASVs from 16S amplicon data using an error model; Kraken2 classifies shotgun reads via k-mer matching against reference genomes; a MAG is a draft genome assembled and binned from shotgun data; shotgun metagenomics sequences all DNA in a sample rather than a single marker gene.

questions.prompt: Why does reagent ("kitome") contamination matter more in a low-biomass sample than a high-biomass one like stool?

options.text: Low-biomass samples have less real microbial DNA, so trace bacterial DNA from extraction kits can rival or exceed the genuine signal
Extraction kits only contaminate low-biomass samples and never touch high-biomass ones
High-biomass samples cannot be sequenced with 16S amplicon methods
Low-biomass samples require a different sequencer that is more error-prone

explanations.a: Correct — Salter et al. (2014) showed reagents carry their own trace bacterial DNA; in stool that trace is negligible against the real signal, but in blood or tissue it can dominate.
explanations.b: The same reagents are used regardless of sample type; it's the ratio of contamination to real signal that changes with biomass.
explanations.c: High-biomass samples are routinely sequenced with 16S methods; biomass affects contamination risk, not sequencing feasibility.
explanations.d: The issue is the sample's own DNA quantity relative to reagent background, not the sequencing instrument.

questions.prompt: What was the central criticism Gihawi, Salzberg, and colleagues raised against the 2020 Poore et al. tumor-microbiome paper?

options.text: That much of the reported microbial signal was better explained by low-biomass contamination and pipeline normalization artifacts than by real tumor biology
That the original samples had been physically switched between patients
That tumors cannot contain any microbial DNA under any circumstances
That the paper used 16S sequencing instead of shotgun metagenomics

explanations.a: Correct — the re-analysis argued the reported signal was largely explainable by the same kitome-style contamination Salter described, compounded by normalization choices in the analysis, leading to Nature's June 2024 retraction with all authors' agreement.
explanations.b: The dispute was about computational and contamination artifacts in the analysis, not sample mix-ups.
explanations.c: The critique was about how much of the specific reported signal was real versus artifact, not a blanket claim that tumors have no microbial DNA.
explanations.d: The critique centered on contamination and normalization, not on which sequencing strategy (16S versus shotgun) was used.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended procedural fix for kitome contamination, rather than a purely computational one?

options.text: Sequence extraction-blank and no-template controls alongside real samples, then subtract or flag taxa that appear in the blanks
Always switch from 16S to shotgun sequencing
Increase the k-mer size used by the taxonomic classifier
Discard any sample with fewer than a million reads

explanations.a: Correct — running blank controls through the same extraction and amplification process reveals which taxa are reagent-derived, so they can be subtracted or flagged in real samples.
explanations.b: Switching sequencing strategy does not address reagent contamination, which affects both amplicon and shotgun workflows.
explanations.c: K-mer size affects classification specificity, not whether contaminating reagent DNA was present in the first place.
explanations.d: Read depth alone does not distinguish real signal from kit contamination; a blank control is needed for that distinction.

lessons.label: Ancient and Forensic DNA

sections.heading: Reading DNA that has been falling apart for millennia
sections.body: DNA degrades after death: enzymes and environmental chemistry fragment it into very short pieces, often well under 100 base pairs by the time a sample is tens of thousands of years old, far shorter than the intact molecules a modern sequencing library expects. Chemical damage adds a second, diagnostic signature — cytosine bases near the fragment's exposed ends spontaneously deaminate into uracil, which sequencing machinery reads as thymine, producing an excess of C-to-T substitutions concentrated at the 5' ends of reads (and the complementary G-to-A pattern at 3' ends). Jónsson and colleagues' 2013 tool mapDamage quantifies this exact pattern from aligned reads, and a real ancient sample should show it decaying smoothly away from the fragment ends; a modern contaminant sequence, by contrast, shows no such damage curve. Because ancient samples are handled by modern humans in modern labs full of modern DNA, every ancient-DNA pipeline also runs an explicit contamination estimate — checking, for example, what fraction of mitochondrial or X-chromosome reads look modern rather than damaged — before trusting any downstream population-genetic conclusion.

sections.heading: What these signatures made possible: the Neanderthal and Denisovan genomes
sections.body: Green and colleagues' 2010 Science paper produced a draft Neanderthal genome by sequencing degraded bone material and using exactly this damage-and-contamination framework to argue the recovered sequence was authentically ancient, not a mix of lab contamination — the analysis found Neanderthal-derived DNA in non-African modern humans, evidence of ancient interbreeding. Reich and colleagues' 2010 Nature paper applied the same logic to a finger bone from Denisova Cave in Siberia, identifying an entirely new archaic human population, the Denisovans, from DNA alone, before any comparable skeletal description existed. This body of work — recovering and authenticating genomes from fossils that were previously unreadable — won Svante Pääbo the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

sections.heading: Forensic pipelines and the genealogy controversy
sections.body: Forensic DNA typing profiles short tandem repeats (STRs) — short repeated sequences that vary in copy number between people — at a standard panel of loci, or increasingly single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), to match a sample against a suspect or database. Investigative genetic genealogy pushed this further: instead of matching a crime-scene profile against known offenders, it uploads a much denser SNP profile to genealogy databases to find distant relatives and reconstruct a family tree back to the suspect. In April 2018, investigators used GEDmatch this way to identify Joseph James DeAngelo as the Golden State Killer suspect, decades after his crimes, by triangulating distant cousins' matches down to one family line before confirming with a discarded-item DNA sample. The technique's power triggered a real consent debate: the relatives whose DNA cracked the case had uploaded their own profiles for genealogy, not law enforcement, and never consented to their DNA implicating a family member in a criminal investigation.

lessons.workedExample: A lab receives a 40,000-year-old bone fragment and a modern comparison sample, both sequenced identically. Running mapDamage on the aligned reads from each, the ancient sample shows the expected C-to-T spike concentrated at the first few bases of reads, decaying by base 15-20, while the modern sample shows a flat, near-zero rate throughout. A read that maps to the ancient sample's data but lacks any damage signature is flagged as likely modern contamination (from excavation, storage, or lab handling) and excluded before any population-genetic inference is drawn from the dataset.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks how you know an ancient sample is authentically ancient because the entire field's credibility rests on distinguishing real archaic DNA from modern contamination introduced during excavation or lab work — a claim about a 40,000-year-old genome is worthless if it is actually a contaminating lab technician's DNA. A student who can point to the C-to-T damage signature mapDamage quantifies, and who ran an explicit contamination estimate rather than assuming the sample is clean, is showing they understand what actually authenticates ancient DNA rather than taking the sequencer's output on faith.

questions.prompt: What pattern does mapDamage look for to distinguish authentic ancient DNA from modern contamination?

options.text: An excess of C-to-T substitutions concentrated near the 5' ends of reads, decaying with distance from the fragment end
Fragments that are longer than 10,000 base pairs
A complete absence of any sequencing errors
An even, uniform substitution rate across the entire length of every read

explanations.a: Correct — post-mortem cytosine deamination produces C-to-T misincorporations concentrated at read ends, a pattern that decays away from the fragment terminus and is absent in modern contaminant DNA.
explanations.b: Ancient DNA is characteristically very short (often under 100 bp), not unusually long.
explanations.c: Damage patterns are a specific, structured type of miscall, not a general absence of errors.
explanations.d: The damage signature is concentrated near read ends and decays inward; a uniform rate would not distinguish ancient from modern DNA.

questions.prompt: Match each study or achievement to what it established.

right.text: Draft Neanderthal genome showing interbreeding evidence in non-African modern humans
Identification of the Denisovans as a new archaic population from a single finger bone's DNA
Recognized for recovering and authenticating genomes from extinct hominins
Used to identify the Golden State Killer suspect via distant-relative genealogy matching

questions.explanation: Green et al. (2010) produced the draft Neanderthal genome and found interbreeding evidence; Reich et al. (2010) identified the Denisovans from Denisova Cave finger-bone DNA alone; Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize for this body of ancient-genome work; GEDmatch's dense SNP database enabled investigators to identify Joseph James DeAngelo as the Golden State Killer suspect in 2018.

questions.prompt: What is the core consent controversy raised by investigative genetic genealogy cases like the Golden State Killer identification?

options.text: Distant relatives who uploaded their DNA for genealogy purposes never consented to it being used to implicate a family member in a criminal investigation
STR profiling is scientifically unreliable and should not be used in court
GEDmatch charged suspects a fee to access their own genetic data
Genetic genealogy cannot legally be used to identify any suspect

explanations.a: Correct — relatives uploaded profiles for family-history genealogy, not law enforcement use, and had no say in their DNA being leveraged to identify a family member as a criminal suspect.
explanations.b: The controversy is about consent and privacy, not about the scientific reliability of STR typing itself.
explanations.c: Access fees are not the source of the ethical controversy described.
explanations.d: The technique was legally used and led to a real identification in 2018; the debate is about the ethics of using relatives' data this way, not its legality at the time.

questions.prompt: Why does every rigorous ancient-DNA pipeline include an explicit contamination estimate?

options.text: Because ancient samples are handled by modern humans in modern labs, so modern DNA can mix with the ancient signal and must be quantified before drawing conclusions
Because ancient DNA never actually contains any real genetic information
Because government regulations require it regardless of sample source
Because contamination estimates replace the need for a reference genome

explanations.a: Correct — excavation, storage, and lab handling all introduce opportunities for modern DNA to mix with an ancient sample, so pipelines check, for example, what fraction of mitochondrial or X-chromosome reads look modern rather than damaged before trusting downstream results.
explanations.b: Ancient samples do contain real, sequenceable DNA; the concern is separating it from contaminant DNA, not an absence of signal.
explanations.c: The practice is a scientific safeguard driven by the biology of degraded samples, not a regulatory mandate.
explanations.d: A reference genome is still needed for alignment; contamination estimation is a separate quality check, not a substitute.

lessons.label: Transcriptome and Single-Cell Pipelines

sections.heading: Two ways to quantify expression from reads
sections.body: RNA-seq reads come from mature mRNA, which has had introns spliced out, so a read can span an exon-exon junction that does not exist contiguously in the genome. STAR handles this with spliced alignment — it finds the actual genomic coordinates of each read, including splitting reads across splice junctions, which is essential if you also want to detect novel splice isoforms or genomic variants. kallisto and Salmon take a faster route called pseudoalignment (or lightweight/selective alignment): rather than pinning down exact genomic coordinates, they determine only which transcripts a read is compatible with, which is enough to quantify expression and runs far faster with far less memory than full alignment, at the cost of not producing a genome-coordinate BAM file for variant calling or novel-junction discovery.

sections.heading: Why raw counts are not the number you report
sections.body: A raw read count for a gene is not directly comparable across genes or samples: a longer transcript accumulates more reads at the same expression level simply because it has more positions reads can start from, and a sample sequenced twice as deep produces roughly twice the counts for everything. TPM (transcripts per million) corrects for both: it normalizes each transcript's count by its length first, then scales so that all transcripts per sample sum to one million, making within-sample and cross-sample comparisons meaningful in a way raw counts are not. Differential-expression tools such as DESeq2 or edgeR instead work from raw counts but apply their own library-size and dispersion-based normalization internally as part of their statistical model — the point is that some form of length and depth correction is mandatory before counts mean anything, whether it happens explicitly (TPM) or inside the statistical model.

sections.heading: What single-cell adds on top
sections.body: Single-cell RNA-seq multiplexes thousands of cells into one sequencing run, so the pipeline must first sort reads back to their cell of origin using a cell barcode sequenced alongside each transcript, then collapse PCR-duplicate reads using a unique molecular identifier (UMI) tagged onto each original mRNA molecule before amplification — UMI deduplication is what turns amplified read counts back into an estimate of original molecule counts. Two cleanup steps are single-cell-specific: empty-droplet filtering distinguishes real cells from droplets that captured only ambient RNA floating free in the cell suspension (tools like EmptyDrops model the ambient background to draw this line statistically rather than by a fixed count cutoff), and doublet detection flags droplets that accidentally captured two cells at once, which would otherwise look like one cell with an impossible hybrid expression profile. None of this substitutes for the expression biology and differential-expression statistics themselves — those live on the transcriptomics branch — this lesson is only the plumbing that gets from raw reads to a clean cell-by-gene count matrix.

lessons.workedExample: A student processing 10x Genomics single-cell data notices one cluster in their analysis has roughly double the total RNA content of every other cluster and expresses two mutually exclusive marker genes at once, which no single real cell type should show. Rather than treating it as a novel cell state, they suspect a doublet — two cells captured in one droplet whose reads share a barcode. Running a doublet-detection step on the raw count matrix flags exactly that cluster as high-doublet-probability, and removing it before downstream analysis restores marker genes to mutually exclusive, biologically sensible clusters.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about barcode demultiplexing, UMI deduplication, and doublet detection specifically because single-cell data looks deceptively like a simple table of numbers, but a student who skipped these steps can easily present PCR duplication or two-cells-in-one-droplet as if it were real biological variation. A student who explains why UMIs (not raw reads) estimate molecule counts, and who can describe how they distinguished a real rare cell type from a doublet artifact, has shown they understand what their count matrix actually represents rather than trusting an output file blindly.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between STAR's spliced alignment and kallisto/Salmon's pseudoalignment?

options.text: STAR finds exact genomic coordinates including splice junctions, while pseudoalignment only determines which transcripts a read is compatible with, trading positional precision for speed
STAR can only align DNA, never RNA-seq reads
Pseudoalignment produces a genome-coordinate BAM file while STAR does not
There is no meaningful difference; both produce identical outputs

explanations.a: Correct — STAR's spliced alignment pins down genomic coordinates and splice junctions, useful for novel isoforms or variant calling, while kallisto/Salmon skip that precision for much faster, lower-memory transcript-compatibility quantification.
explanations.b: STAR is specifically designed for spliced RNA-seq alignment, handling reads that span exon-exon junctions.
explanations.c: This reverses the tools' outputs — STAR produces genome-coordinate alignments; pseudoalignment tools generally do not.
explanations.d: The two approaches trade off precision and speed differently and are not interchangeable for every downstream use (e.g., novel-junction discovery needs STAR-style alignment).

questions.prompt: Why can't raw read counts be compared directly across genes within the same sample?

options.text: A longer transcript accumulates more reads at the same expression level simply because it offers more positions for reads to start from
Raw counts are always identical for every gene regardless of expression
Longer transcripts are sequenced with lower accuracy than short ones
Read counts only reflect sequencing errors, not expression

explanations.a: Correct — transcript length biases raw counts upward for longer transcripts at equal expression, which is exactly why TPM normalizes by length before scaling to a per-million total.
explanations.b: Raw counts vary substantially with expression level; the issue is a length bias on top of that signal, not an absence of variation.
explanations.c: Sequencing accuracy is not systematically tied to transcript length in this way.
explanations.d: Read counts primarily reflect transcript abundance and length, not error rate.

questions.prompt: Match each single-cell pipeline step to what it does.

right.text: Sorts reads back to their cell of origin using a per-cell tag sequence
Collapses PCR-amplified duplicate reads back to original molecule counts
Distinguishes real cells from droplets containing only ambient RNA
Flags droplets that captured two cells, which show an impossible hybrid expression profile

questions.explanation: Cell barcodes sort reads to their originating cell; UMIs let deduplication collapse PCR-amplified reads back to true molecule counts; empty-droplet filtering (e.g., EmptyDrops-style models) separates real cells from ambient-RNA-only droplets; doublet detection flags droplets with two cells' worth of mutually exclusive expression signal.

questions.prompt: A cluster in a single-cell analysis shows roughly double the total RNA content of other clusters and co-expresses two normally mutually exclusive marker genes. What should be suspected first?

options.text: A doublet — two cells captured in one droplet and sharing a barcode
A failure of cell-barcode demultiplexing to run at all
A missing reference genome
Ambient RNA contamination from an empty droplet

explanations.a: Correct — two cells sharing one droplet and barcode produce an artificially high RNA content and a mixed expression profile that looks like co-expression of markers no single real cell type shares.
explanations.b: If demultiplexing failed entirely, reads would not be assignable to cells at all, not produce a coherent but doubled cluster.
explanations.c: A missing reference would prevent alignment entirely, not produce this specific expression pattern.
explanations.d: Empty droplets contain very little RNA and would show low, not doubled, total content.

lessons.label: Running a Bioinformatics Project at a Science Fair

sections.heading: Where the free data actually lives
sections.body: Raw sequencing reads for essentially any published study sit in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) or its European mirror ENA, downloadable by anyone with an accession number. GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) hosts processed expression data alongside the raw reads, making it the easiest entry point for a project that reanalyzes an existing dataset rather than generating new sequence. ENCODE catalogs functional genomic data (chromatin state, transcription-factor binding) across cell types, and the 1000 Genomes Project provides openly downloadable population-scale human variant data. For a project that specifically needs a genome with a known, trustworthy "truth set" of variants to check answers against, the Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) consortium sequences a small number of extensively characterized reference individuals and publishes high-confidence variant calls precisely so other pipelines can be benchmarked against them. Not all data is this open: dbGaP and the UK Biobank hold individual-level human genetic data behind a controlled-access tier, requiring an institutional application and a stated research purpose — appropriate for professional research, not a route a student project should plan around.

sections.heading: Free compute that doesn't need a cluster
sections.body: A full pipeline does not require owning a server. Galaxy is a free, browser-based platform that wraps common bioinformatics tools (aligners, variant callers, quality-control steps) behind a point-and-click interface, so a student can run a real pipeline without installing anything locally. Google Colab provides free cloud compute with a Python environment already configured, workable for smaller-scale analysis, custom scripting, or plotting once intermediate files exist. Many high schools also have access to a local university's or partner institution's compute cluster through an outreach program — worth asking about directly, since cluster time solves the memory and CPU-hour ceiling that a laptop hits fast on a whole-genome-scale task.

sections.heading: A scoped project a judge can actually evaluate
sections.body: A defensible bioinformatics fair project narrows scope deliberately rather than promising to "analyze the whole genome." One concrete template: download a GIAB reference sample's chromosome 20 reads (small enough to process on modest hardware, large enough to be real), call variants with two different callers (for example GATK and a second tool), and benchmark each call set against GIAB's published high-confidence truth set using vcfeval — a comparison tool that correctly handles the fact that the same variant can be represented in more than one equivalent way in a VCF file, and reports precision and recall rather than a naive line-by-line diff. Stratifying results by genomic region (using GIAB's published difficult-region files, such as repetitive or low-mappability regions) turns a single accuracy number into a real finding: most callers agree easily in most of the genome and diverge specifically in the hard regions, which is a more honest and more interesting result than one overall percentage. Any project that touches real human data, even public GIAB data, should still include a short consent and data-use note: GIAB samples come from consented volunteers under stated terms, and a project must not attempt to re-identify individuals or combine datasets in ways the original consent didn't cover.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants a project bigger than "run one tool on one file" but has a laptop, not a cluster. They download NA12878 (a GIAB reference sample) chromosome 20 reads from ENA, run the alignment and variant-calling steps on Galaxy's free web interface with two different callers, then use vcfeval to compare each caller's output against GIAB's published truth set for that region. The result is a precision/recall table for each caller, split by whether the site falls in a GIAB-flagged difficult region — a project with a clear, falsifiable comparison, built entirely from free data and free compute, that a judge can actually check the logic of.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about data provenance and scope specifically because "I downloaded a huge public dataset and got some numbers" is not evaluable, while "I benchmarked two callers against GIAB's truth set on one chromosome, stratified by difficult regions" is a claim with a specific method a judge can probe end to end. A student who can name where their data came from (accession, consent terms), what tool ran each step, and how they measured accuracy against a real ground truth (not just eyeballing) has built something a judge can actually assess for rigor, not just for ambition.

questions.prompt: Why would a student project use a GIAB reference sample specifically, rather than an arbitrary public genome?

options.text: GIAB publishes high-confidence variant truth sets for its reference individuals, so a pipeline's output can be benchmarked against a known correct answer
GIAB samples are the only human genomes that have ever been sequenced
GIAB data requires no reference genome for alignment
GIAB samples are smaller in genome size than other human samples

explanations.a: Correct — GIAB's extensively characterized reference individuals come with published high-confidence variant calls, giving a project a ground truth to benchmark accuracy against rather than just an unverifiable output.
explanations.b: Many thousands of human genomes are publicly available (e.g., via 1000 Genomes); GIAB's distinction is its curated truth set, not being the only data.
explanations.c: GIAB samples still need alignment to a standard reference genome like any other sequencing data.
explanations.d: All human genomes are approximately the same size; GIAB's value is its validated truth set, not sample size.

questions.prompt: What does vcfeval add beyond a naive line-by-line comparison of two VCF files?

options.text: It correctly handles equivalent-but-differently-represented variants and reports precision/recall rather than a naive diff
It re-sequences the sample to generate new reads
It replaces the need for a reference genome entirely
It only works on RNA-seq data, not variant calls

explanations.a: Correct — the same variant can be written multiple valid ways in a VCF, so a naive diff would miscount matches as mismatches; vcfeval resolves this and reports proper precision and recall against a truth set.
explanations.b: vcfeval compares existing call sets; it does not generate new sequencing data.
explanations.c: A reference genome is still required upstream for alignment and calling; vcfeval operates on the resulting VCFs.
