explanations.d: vcfeval is specifically a variant-call benchmarking tool, not an RNA-seq expression tool.

questions.prompt: Match each resource to what it provides.

right.text: Raw sequencing reads for published studies, open by accession number
Processed expression data alongside raw reads
High-confidence variant truth sets from extensively characterized reference individuals
Individual-level human genetic data requiring controlled-access application

questions.explanation: SRA/ENA host open raw sequencing reads by accession; GEO hosts processed expression data alongside raw reads; GIAB publishes high-confidence variant truth sets for benchmarking; dbGaP and UK Biobank gate individual-level human genetic data behind controlled access requiring an institutional application.

questions.prompt: Why does stratifying variant-calling accuracy by GIAB's difficult-region files produce a more honest result than one overall accuracy percentage?

options.text: It reveals that callers typically agree easily across most of the genome and diverge specifically in repetitive or low-mappability regions, which a single number hides
It eliminates the need for a truth set entirely
It always produces a higher accuracy number than the unstratified result
Difficult regions are randomly distributed, so stratification has no effect on the result

explanations.a: Correct — a single overall percentage can mask that most disagreement between callers concentrates in specific hard regions, while performance elsewhere is near-perfect; stratification surfaces that structure.
explanations.b: A truth set is still required to know what counts as correct in each stratum; stratification is applied on top of, not instead of, a truth set.
explanations.c: Stratified results in difficult regions are typically worse, not better, than the genome-wide average, which is exactly the point.
explanations.d: Difficult regions (repetitive, low-mappability) are specific, mapped genomic features, not randomly distributed, which is why stratifying by them is informative.

units.label: Cutting and Repairing DNA: The Foundations of Genome Editing

lessons.label: What Counts as a Genome Edit

sections.heading: A targeted, permanent change to the sequence itself
sections.body: Genome editing means deliberately changing the DNA sequence at a chosen chromosomal address, so the change is copied into every daughter cell and read by the cell's own machinery from then on. That definition does real work by excluding two things people often lump in with it. First, transgenesis: making a transgenic mouse by pronuclear injection or a Bt corn plant by Agrobacterium delivery inserts foreign DNA, but at a random, uncontrolled genomic location — you cannot say in advance which gene you have landed in or disrupted. Editing specifies the address before you touch the cell; transgenesis specifies only the cargo. Second, anything that is transient and reversible does not count as editing even if it looks like a loss-of-function experiment. RNA interference (RNAi), synthetic siRNA, and morpholino oligonucleotides all work downstream of the genome, degrading or blocking messenger RNA so a gene's product drops without its DNA sequence ever changing. Because mRNA and the silencing complex both turn over, the effect wears off — days for siRNA in mammalian cells, until the morpholino is diluted out across cell divisions in an embryo. Epigenetic silencing (DNA methylation, histone modification via tools like dCas9-KRAB) is the same category: the sequence is untouched, and the mark can in principle be erased.

sections.heading: Somatic vs. germline: a fact about which cells inherit it
sections.body: Somatic and germline are not about method or ethics in the first instance — they are a technical fact about which cells carry the edit forward. A somatic edit changes cells that make up the body but are not passed to offspring: correcting hepatocytes in a liver, editing T cells ex vivo for a CAR-T therapy. The change dies with the patient. A germline edit changes the sperm, egg, or a very early embryo, so it propagates into every cell of the resulting organism, including its own future germ cells — heritable, permanent in the population. This is the technical basis for why He Jiankui's 2018 germline editing of twin embryos (targeting CCR5) drew near-universal condemnation while somatic clinical trials proceed under standard regulatory review: the same enzyme, aimed at a different cell type, has irreversible population-level consequences.

sections.heading: The vocabulary: knockout, knock-in, correction, knockdown
sections.body: Four words recur through every later lesson. A knockout disrupts a gene's function, usually by cutting it and letting error-prone repair introduce a frameshift indel. A knock-in inserts new sequence at a specific site — a fluorescent tag, a point mutation, a whole cassette. A correction is a knock-in that restores wild-type sequence at a disease-causing mutation. A knockdown reduces (not eliminates) a gene product's abundance without touching DNA, typically via RNAi — the transient category above. Keeping knockout and knockdown distinct matters because they fail differently: a knockout is permanent and heritable through cell division; a knockdown decays and must be reapplied.

lessons.workedExample: A lab wants to test whether gene X causes a phenotype in zebrafish. Team A injects siRNA against X's mRNA into one-cell embryos and sees the phenotype at 48 hours, but by 5 days post-fertilization the phenotype has faded as the siRNA is diluted across dividing cells — a knockdown, transient by nature. Team B instead injects a CRISPR ribonucleoprotein targeting X's DNA sequence, producing a heritable frameshift indel; every descendant cell, and the fish's own offspring if it is a germline edit in the embryo, carries the disrupted gene permanently. Only Team B has performed a genome edit; Team A has performed a knockdown that looks similar for two days and diverges by day five.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this distinction because 'I edited gene X' is a claim with a specific, checkable meaning, and students often use it loosely for any loss-of-function trick. A judge who asks 'is that change in the DNA sequence, and does it persist through cell division?' is testing whether the student can tell a permanent genotype change from a transient knockdown or an epigenetic mark — and whether the student knows which cells (somatic or germline) actually carry whatever they made. A vague answer ('we turned the gene off') collapses four technically distinct interventions into one; a precise answer names which one was actually done and why that distinction changes what the result can support.

questions.prompt: A researcher uses siRNA to reduce a gene's mRNA level in cultured cells, and the effect fades within about a week. What is this an example of?

options.text: A genome edit, because the gene's function was disrupted
A knockdown, because the DNA sequence is untouched and the effect is transient
A germline edit, because it will be passed to offspring
A knock-in, because new sequence was introduced

explanations.a: Genome editing requires a permanent change to the DNA sequence; siRNA acts on mRNA and leaves DNA unchanged.
explanations.b: Correct — siRNA degrades mRNA downstream of the genome, so the DNA sequence never changes, and the effect decays as the siRNA and its complex turn over.
explanations.c: Germline status depends on which cells carry a change into offspring; siRNA in cultured cells has no bearing on inheritance and produces no DNA change at all.
explanations.d: A knock-in inserts new DNA sequence at a target site; siRNA inserts nothing into DNA.

questions.prompt: What technically distinguishes a targeted genome edit from classic transgenesis (e.g., pronuclear injection to make a transgenic mouse)?

options.text: Transgenesis always uses viral vectors; editing never does
Editing specifies the genomic location in advance; transgenesis inserts DNA at a random, uncontrolled location
Transgenesis only works in animals, editing only in plants
Editing cannot insert new DNA, only delete it

explanations.a: Vector choice does not define the distinction; both approaches can use various delivery methods.
explanations.b: Correct — transgenesis delivers DNA that integrates wherever chance permits, while editing targets a chosen chromosomal address before the cell is touched.
explanations.c: Both transgenesis and editing are used across animals and plants; species is not the distinguishing factor.
explanations.d: Knock-in editing routinely inserts new sequence; the distinction is about targeting location, not insertion capability.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: Disrupts gene function, typically via an indel from error-prone repair
Inserts new sequence (a tag, mutation, or cassette) at a specific site
A knock-in that restores wild-type sequence at a disease-causing mutation
Reduces gene product abundance transiently without changing DNA

questions.explanation: Knockout and knock-in both change DNA permanently (disruption vs. insertion); correction is the disease-fixing special case of knock-in; knockdown is the transient, DNA-untouched RNA-level category.

questions.prompt: What determines whether an edit is 'germline' rather than 'somatic'?

options.text: Whether the edit was made with CRISPR versus an older tool
Whether the edited cells include sperm, egg, or early-embryo cells that pass the change to offspring
Whether the edit is a knockout or a knock-in
Whether the edit occurred in a human versus a model organism

explanations.a: The tool used (CRISPR, TALEN, etc.) is irrelevant to germline status; the same tool can make either kind of edit.
explanations.b: Correct — germline vs. somatic is strictly about which cells carry the change forward to offspring, not about method, edit type, or species.
explanations.c: Knockout vs. knock-in describes what the edit does to sequence, not which cells inherit it.
explanations.d: Germline and somatic edits are made in both humans and model organisms; species does not define the category.

lessons.label: The Double-Strand Break Is the Engine

sections.heading: A break the cell cannot ignore
sections.body: Every nuclease-based editor — meganucleases, zinc-finger nucleases, TALENs, CRISPR-Cas — does the same fundamental thing: it cuts both strands of the DNA double helix at a chosen site, producing a double-strand break (DSB). A single-strand nick is tolerated and quietly patched by base- or nucleotide-excision repair without much drama. A DSB is different in kind: it severs the chromosome, threatens loss of the distal fragment at the next cell division, and can trigger apoptosis or senescence if left unrepaired. Because a DSB is a lethal-if-ignored lesion, the cell responds within minutes — the MRN complex (Mre11-Rad50-Nbs1) detects the break, ATM kinase signals cell-cycle arrest, and one of several repair pathways is recruited to physically rebuild the locus. The editor's job is only ever to make the cut at a chosen address; the repair pathway the cell chooses is what actually rewrites the sequence into a knockout, a knock-in, or a silent repair back to wild type. This is the single idea that unifies the whole unit: cutting is not editing, repair is editing, and a DSB is simply the trigger that forces repair to happen at a site of your choosing rather than wherever chance and replication stress would otherwise produce one.

sections.heading: The Jasin lab result that made targeted nucleases worth building
sections.body: Why bother engineering a protein or an RNA-guided complex just to make one cut? Because Rouet, Smih, and Jasin answered a quantitative question in 1994 that justified the entire subsequent engineering effort. Spontaneous homologous recombination between a chromosomal locus and a co-transfected donor sequence in mammalian cells is extremely rare — on the order of one event per million cells (roughly 1e-6), because cells have no reason to invoke recombination unless something is broken. Rouet, Smih, and Jasin expressed the yeast homing endonuclease I-SceI, engineered to cut a unique 18-base-pair site they had inserted into a mouse cell chromosome, and measured how often a co-transfected homologous donor was used to repair that exact locus. A single site-specific DSB raised the homologous recombination frequency at that locus by roughly three orders of magnitude — a thousandfold jump over the ~1e-6 background. That single number is the entire economic case for programmable nucleases: recombination-based gene targeting was already possible without a break, but it was too rare to be practical at any scale beyond heroic embryonic-stem-cell screens. A targeted DSB turns a one-in-a-million event into something workable in a standard transfection.

sections.heading: One trigger, many possible outcomes
sections.body: A DSB at a given locus does not commit the cell to any particular repair pathway or outcome — it only forces a choice. The next lesson covers the competing pathways (NHEJ, MMEJ, HDR) that can resolve the same break differently depending on cell-cycle phase, the presence of a homologous donor, and which repair factors are most active in that cell type. What stays constant across every editing platform, from I-SceI in 1994 to Cas9 today, is the logic: engineer specificity for where the cut lands, and let the cell's own repair machinery do the actual writing.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to insert a 2 kb reporter cassette at a specific locus in mouse embryonic stem cells. Without any nuclease, co-transfecting a homologous donor plasmid and screening surviving clones for correct integration yields roughly 1 correctly targeted clone per million cells screened — the ~1e-6 spontaneous HR rate — which meant weeks of drug selection and colony picking in the pre-nuclease era. Following the logic Rouet, Smih, and Jasin established with I-SceI, the researcher instead co-transfects a nuclease engineered to cut once at that exact locus alongside the same donor. Homologous recombination at the cut site rises roughly a thousandfold, so the same screen that once required scanning a million colonies for one hit now finds correctly targeted clones at a rate practical to screen across a handful of 96-well plates instead of a million-colony hunt.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does a double-strand break matter, and why not just nick one strand?' to check whether a student understands the mechanism rather than reciting 'CRISPR cuts DNA.' The strong answer distinguishes a DSB (chromosome-severing, cell treats as an emergency, forces a repair-pathway choice) from a nick (quietly patched, no pathway competition), and can explain why targeted nucleases exist at all: without a site-specific break, homologous recombination at a chosen locus is a roughly one-in-a-million event, so the entire practical value of a programmable nuclease is the thousandfold jump in usable repair frequency a DSB buys.

questions.prompt: Why is a double-strand break (DSB) treated so differently by the cell than a single-strand nick?

options.text: A nick is always more mutagenic than a DSB
A DSB severs the chromosome and threatens loss of genetic material, so it is a lethal-if-unrepaired lesion the cell must actively resolve
Nicks only occur in bacteria, so mammalian cells have no response to them
A DSB is repaired identically to a nick, just twice as fast

explanations.a: The opposite is true in terms of consequence — a nick is routinely patched without drama, while an unrepaired DSB threatens chromosome loss.
explanations.b: Correct — a DSB severs both strands, risking loss of the distal chromosome fragment and triggering damage signaling (MRN complex, ATM), which is why the cell must recruit a repair pathway rather than quietly patching it.
explanations.c: Nicks occur in mammalian cells too and are handled by base- or nucleotide-excision repair without triggering the same emergency response.
explanations.d: DSBs and nicks are repaired by different mechanisms entirely; a DSB requires pathway choice (NHEJ, MMEJ, or HDR), not simple patching.

questions.prompt: In the Rouet, Smih, and Jasin (1994) experiment, roughly how much did a site-specific I-SceI-induced DSB raise homologous recombination frequency at that locus, compared to the spontaneous background?

options.text: About twofold
About tenfold
Roughly three orders of magnitude (about a thousandfold)
It had no measurable effect

explanations.a: A twofold change would not have justified the subsequent decades of nuclease engineering; the actual effect was far larger.
explanations.b: Tenfold understates the result — the measured jump was roughly a thousandfold, not tenfold.
explanations.c: Correct — the site-specific DSB raised HR frequency at that locus roughly a thousandfold (about three orders of magnitude) above the ~1e-6 spontaneous background, the result that justified building targeted nucleases.
explanations.d: The DSB had a dramatic, measurable effect — this result is precisely what launched targeted-nuclease engineering.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate spontaneous (background) rate of homologous recombination at a chosen chromosomal locus without a targeted break, as described in this lesson?

options.text: About 1 in 10
About 1 in 1,000
About 1 in 1,000,000 (roughly 1e-6)
About 1 in 2

explanations.a: This rate is far too high; spontaneous HR at a specific locus is a rare event, not a common one.
explanations.b: Still far too frequent — the actual background rate is roughly a thousand times rarer than this.
explanations.c: Correct — spontaneous HR at a chosen locus occurs at roughly one event per million cells (~1e-6), which is why a targeted DSB's thousandfold boost was so significant.
explanations.d: This rate would make gene targeting trivial without any nuclease; the actual background frequency is vastly lower.

questions.prompt: Order the events in a targeted-nuclease editing experiment, from the nuclease binding DNA to the locus being rebuilt.

items.text: The nuclease binds and cuts its target site, producing a double-strand break
The MRN complex detects the break and ATM signals damage response
The cell recruits and commits to a specific repair pathway
Repair machinery physically rebuilds the locus, determining the final edit outcome

questions.explanation: The nuclease cuts first; the cell's damage-sensing machinery (MRN/ATM) detects the break next; a repair pathway is then recruited and chosen; and only that repair step actually determines the final sequence outcome — cutting triggers the process, but repair writes the edit.

lessons.label: NHEJ, MMEJ, and HDR: The Repair Pathways You Are Betting On

sections.heading: Classical NHEJ: fast, always on, imprecise
sections.body: Non-homologous end joining is the cell's default, high-speed fix for a double-strand break. The Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer clamps onto each broken end within seconds, recruits the kinase DNA-PKcs to hold the two ends in proximity, and Ligase IV (LIG4, with its partner XRCC4) seals them back together. NHEJ is active in every phase of the cell cycle, including G1 when no sister chromatid exists for a homology-based repair, which is why it is by far the dominant pathway in most cell types, including non-dividing ones. The tradeoff is fidelity: because the enzymes doing the trimming and ligating do not check for a template, rejoining a Cas9-style blunt-ish cut frequently leaves a small insertion or deletion (indel) of a few base pairs at the junction. This is exactly what a knockout strategy exploits — a frameshift indel in an early exon disrupts the reading frame and, usually, the protein.

sections.heading: MMEJ: a scrappier, more predictable alternative
sections.body: Microhomology-mediated end joining (also called alternative end joining) kicks in especially when NHEJ is compromised or when the break ends happen to expose short complementary sequences. DNA polymerase theta (POLQ) is the central enzyme: it recognizes microhomologies of roughly 2 to 20 base pairs on either side of the break, anneals them, and fills in the rest, which necessarily deletes the sequence between the two microhomologous stretches. Because the deletion size is set by the distance between whichever microhomologies exist near the cut, MMEJ outcomes at a given target site are not random noise — they are reproducible across experiments and even across labs, which is why deep-sequencing tools can predict a site's dominant indel before you ever run the experiment. Some genome-editing strategies deliberately design in flanking microhomologies to steer MMEJ toward one specific, predictable deletion — a precision use of an 'imprecise' pathway.

sections.heading: HDR: the template-copying pathway, and why it is rare
sections.body: Homology-directed repair is the only pathway of the three that can write new sequence exactly as specified, because it uses a homologous template — normally the sister chromatid, or in editing experiments a designed donor — to resynthesize the region around the break. RAD51, loaded onto resected single-stranded DNA with help from BRCA2, drives the strand-invasion step that finds and pairs with the template. That dependence on a sister chromatid is also HDR's fundamental limitation: sister chromatids exist only after S phase, so HDR is essentially restricted to S and G2. In dividing cell lines, HDR-mediated knock-in typically succeeds in only a low single-digit-to-low-double-digit percentage of edited alleles, with NHEJ and MMEJ consuming the rest. In post-mitotic cells — neurons, cardiomyocytes, skeletal muscle fibers — that never re-enter S phase, HDR is functionally close to zero, which is precisely why precise correction in the brain or heart is one of the hardest open problems in the field, and why so much editing there instead relies on base or prime editing strategies built to avoid HDR entirely.

lessons.workedExample: A lab CRISPR-targets the same gene in two cell populations: a rapidly dividing HEK293 line and post-mitotic primary neurons, both with an HDR donor designed to correct a point mutation. In HEK293 cells, deep sequencing of the edited locus shows roughly 5-8% of alleles carrying the precise HDR-mediated correction, with the remainder split between NHEJ indels and MMEJ deletions bounded by nearby microhomologies. In the neurons, sequencing the same locus shows the HDR-corrected allele essentially absent — under 1% — because neurons are permanently post-mitotic and never enter S/G2, so RAD51-BRCA2-driven strand invasion has no sister-chromatid-equivalent template pathway to draw on; nearly all repair reads out as NHEJ or MMEJ indels instead.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this because 'we used CRISPR to correct the mutation' hides a crucial fork: correction only happens if HDR wins the competition against NHEJ and MMEJ, and that competition is rigged by cell-cycle phase and cell type before the experiment even starts. A student who can say 'HDR needs S/G2 because RAD51-BRCA2 requires a sister chromatid, so our correction rate will be low in dividing cells and near zero if we tried this in neurons' has understood that repair-pathway choice, not nuclease activity, is what determines whether an edit is a knockout, an unpredictable deletion, or the precise correction the project actually wanted.

questions.prompt: Match each repair pathway to its defining molecular machinery.

right.text: Ku70/Ku80, DNA-PKcs, and LIG4
POLQ (DNA polymerase theta) using 2-20 bp microhomologies
RAD51 loaded with help from BRCA2, driving strand invasion into a homologous template

questions.explanation: NHEJ relies on Ku70/80, DNA-PKcs, and LIG4 to rejoin ends directly; MMEJ relies on POLQ to anneal short microhomologies flanking the break; HDR relies on RAD51/BRCA2-driven strand invasion into a homologous template.

questions.prompt: Why is HDR restricted mainly to S and G2 phases of the cell cycle?

options.text: DNA-PKcs is only expressed during S/G2
HDR requires a homologous template, normally the sister chromatid, which only exists after DNA replication
Ku70/Ku80 actively blocks HDR outside of S/G2
Microhomologies only form during S/G2

explanations.a: DNA-PKcs is an NHEJ factor, not an HDR factor, and its expression is not the reason for HDR's cell-cycle restriction.
explanations.b: Correct — HDR's strand-invasion step (RAD51/BRCA2) needs a homologous template, and the sister chromatid that normally serves as that template is only present after S phase replication.
explanations.c: Ku70/Ku80 is part of the competing NHEJ pathway, but the fundamental limit on HDR is template availability, not active blocking by Ku.
explanations.d: Microhomologies are a feature of MMEJ, a different pathway, and are not cell-cycle restricted in the way HDR is.

questions.prompt: Why does MMEJ produce reproducible, predictable deletions rather than random ones?

options.text: Because POLQ always deletes exactly 10 base pairs regardless of sequence
Because the deletion size is set by the distance between microhomologous sequences flanking the break, which is fixed for a given target site
Because MMEJ only occurs in cells lacking any other repair pathway
Because MMEJ uses a homologous donor template like HDR

explanations.a: POLQ does not delete a fixed length; deletion size depends on where microhomologies happen to sit relative to the break.
explanations.b: Correct — because the microhomologies flanking a given cut site are fixed by the local sequence, the deletion POLQ produces at that site is reproducible across experiments.
explanations.c: MMEJ competes with NHEJ and HDR in cells that have all three pathways available; it is not restricted to pathway-deficient cells only.
explanations.d: MMEJ uses short microhomologies on the broken ends themselves, not an external homologous donor, which is what distinguishes it from HDR.

questions.prompt: In a post-mitotic neuron, which outcome is most likely for a CRISPR-induced double-strand break at a target locus?

options.text: Near-complete HDR-mediated precise correction
Predominantly NHEJ or MMEJ repair, with HDR-mediated correction close to zero
No repair at all, leaving the break permanently open
Exclusively HDR, since neurons lack Ku70/Ku80

explanations.a: Neurons are post-mitotic and never enter S/G2, so HDR's sister-chromatid-dependent mechanism has no template pathway available.
explanations.b: Correct — without S/G2 access, HDR is functionally near zero in neurons, so the break resolves almost entirely through NHEJ or MMEJ.
explanations.c: A DSB is a lethal-if-unrepaired lesion, so cells actively resolve it through available pathways rather than leaving it open indefinitely.
explanations.d: Neurons still express Ku70/Ku80 and NHEJ remains fully active in non-dividing cells; it is HDR, not NHEJ, that is cell-cycle restricted.

lessons.label: Designing a Repair Template for a Knock-In

sections.heading: Choosing a donor: ssODN versus plasmid or AAV
sections.body: The template you supply determines what HDR can build. For a point mutation correction or a short epitope tag, the workhorse donor is a single-stranded oligodeoxynucleotide (ssODN), typically on the order of 60 to 200 nucleotides total — short enough to synthesize cheaply and to deliver efficiently by electroporation alongside the nuclease. For larger insertions — a full fluorescent-protein cassette, a several-kilobase gene replacement — an ssODN cannot carry enough sequence, so labs switch to double-stranded donors: a plasmid (cheap, easy to clone, but can trigger innate immune sensing and integrates less efficiently) or an adeno-associated virus (AAV) donor, which delivers single-stranded DNA directly into the nucleus and is the standard for in vivo and clinical-grade knock-ins because of its efficient, largely episomal delivery.

sections.heading: Homology arms, proximity, and blocking re-cutting
sections.body: Every donor is built the same way conceptually: the edit sits in the middle, flanked by two homology arms that match the genomic sequence on either side of the cut so RAD51-driven strand invasion has something to pair with. Arm length and symmetry matter — ssODN donors commonly use asymmetric arms (a longer arm on the PAM-distal side relative to the PAM-proximal side has been shown empirically to improve HDR efficiency for Cas9 cuts), while plasmid and AAV donors typically use longer, more symmetric arms of several hundred base pairs to a few kilobases. Distance from the cut site is the other dominant variable: HDR efficiency falls off sharply as the intended edit moves away from the DSB, because the resection and strand-invasion machinery operates locally — an edit placed even 10-20 base pairs from the cut can see a large drop in incorporation relative to one placed directly at the cut. This is why guide selection and edit design are not separable steps: you often have to accept whichever nearby PAM gets you closest to the intended base, not whichever guide has the best predicted on-target score. Finally, every functional knock-in donor should carry a silent mutation in the PAM or the guide's seed region alongside the intended edit — without it, the nuclease will simply re-cut the newly repaired, correct allele and expose it to another round of NHEJ, potentially destroying the very edit you just installed.

sections.heading: Boosting HDR: real tactics, real controversy
sections.body: Because HDR competes with a much faster NHEJ pathway, several tactics attempt to tip the balance. Synchronizing cells into S/G2 (e.g., with a double-thymidine block) restricts editing to the window when HDR machinery is active, and reproducibly raises HDR rates in cultured cells, though it is impractical in vivo. Chemically inhibiting NHEJ — most famously SCR7, a Ligase IV inhibitor reported by Chu and colleagues (2015) to raise HDR several-fold — looked promising but has been contested by subsequent labs reporting inconsistent or non-reproducible gains across cell types and delivery methods, and the toxicity of blocking a genome-wide DNA repair pathway is a legitimate concern for any therapeutic use. A newer approach covalently or non-covalently tethers the donor DNA directly to the Cas9 protein, increasing its local concentration right at the break the instant it forms; reports of this tethering strategy (e.g., Savic and colleagues, 2018) show meaningful HDR gains without the genome-wide off-target risk of inhibiting a repair pathway everywhere.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to correct a single point mutation in a cultured cell line using Cas9 and an ssODN donor. Their first design places the mutation to fix 15 bp from the nearest usable PAM and uses symmetric 40-nt homology arms, but does not alter the PAM sequence in the donor. Sequencing shows correction in under 2% of alleles, and closer inspection reveals many corrected alleles were re-cut and disrupted by residual Cas9 activity, since the intact PAM let the nuclease keep finding and cutting the repaired site. The redesigned ssODN keeps the edit but adds a silent PAM-disrupting substitution and shifts to an asymmetric arm layout favoring the PAM-distal side; the corrected-allele fraction rises several-fold and the corrected alleles now persist because Cas9 can no longer recognize and re-cut them.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes donor design because it is where 'we designed an HDR template' either holds up or falls apart under one follow-up question: 'how far is your edit from the cut, and did you block re-cutting?' A student who cannot answer either question likely copied a donor sequence without understanding why HDR efficiency depends on proximity to the DSB, or why an unmodified PAM lets the nuclease erase its own successful edit. Naming a specific boosting tactic (cell-cycle sync, SCR7, Cas9-donor tethering) and, crucially, acknowledging that these tactics are contested rather than guaranteed, signals a student who read primary literature rather than a single tutorial.

questions.prompt: A researcher needs to insert a several-kilobase fluorescent-protein cassette via HDR. Which donor type is appropriate, and why?

options.text: An ssODN, because it is the cheapest option regardless of insert size
A plasmid or AAV donor, because an ssODN (roughly 60-200 nt) cannot carry a several-kilobase insert
No donor is needed; NHEJ alone can insert kilobase-scale cassettes precisely
An ssODN, because longer donors always reduce HDR efficiency

explanations.a: ssODNs are limited to roughly 60-200 nucleotides, far too short to carry a several-kilobase cassette; cost is not the deciding factor here.
explanations.b: Correct — a several-kilobase insert exceeds ssODN capacity, so a double-stranded donor (plasmid or AAV) is required to carry the full cargo.
explanations.c: NHEJ does not use a homologous template and cannot precisely insert a defined multi-kilobase cassette; that requires HDR with an appropriate donor.
explanations.d: Donor length is chosen based on insert size requirements, not a general rule that shorter is always more efficient regardless of what needs to be delivered.

questions.prompt: Why does HDR efficiency typically fall off sharply as the intended edit is placed farther from the double-strand break?

options.text: Because RAD51 cannot bind DNA more than 1000 bp from any cut
Because the resection and strand-invasion machinery act locally around the break, so edits farther away are less efficiently incorporated
Because farther edits always trigger NHEJ instead of HDR
Distance from the cut has no effect on HDR efficiency

explanations.a: This specific distance threshold is not the mechanism; the lesson describes a general local dependence, not a hard 1000 bp cutoff.
explanations.b: Correct — because resection and strand invasion operate in the region immediately around the break, edits placed farther from the cut are incorporated less efficiently, sometimes dropping sharply within just 10-20 bp.
explanations.c: Pathway choice (NHEJ vs. HDR) is determined by cell-cycle phase and repair-factor availability, not simply by edit distance from the cut.
explanations.d: Distance is one of the most important variables in donor design precisely because it strongly affects HDR incorporation efficiency.

questions.prompt: Why must a functional HDR donor typically include a silent mutation in the PAM or seed region, in addition to the intended edit?

options.text: To make the donor sequence longer for easier synthesis
To prevent the nuclease from re-cutting the successfully repaired allele and disrupting it via NHEJ
Because silent mutations always increase protein expression
To shorten the homology arms needed

explanations.a: The mutation's purpose is functional (blocking re-cutting), not to adjust donor length.
explanations.b: Correct — an unmodified PAM or seed region on the corrected allele remains a valid target, so the nuclease can re-cut it and expose it to NHEJ, potentially destroying the edit just installed.
explanations.c: Silent mutations by definition do not change the encoded protein sequence and have no direct effect on expression level.
explanations.d: Homology arm length is determined by insert size and empirical HDR optimization, not by whether a PAM-blocking mutation is present.

questions.prompt: Match each HDR-boosting tactic to its described mechanism or status.

right.text: Restricts editing to S/G2 when HDR machinery is active; impractical in vivo
A Ligase IV inhibitor reported by Chu and colleagues (2015) to raise HDR, but with contested reproducibility across labs
Increases local donor concentration at the break by linking donor DNA directly to the Cas9 protein

questions.explanation: Cell-cycle synchronization restricts editing to the HDR-permissive window but does not translate well to living organisms; SCR7 blocks NHEJ's Ligase IV and showed early promise but inconsistent replication; Cas9-donor tethering raises local donor concentration exactly where the break forms.

lessons.label: Before CRISPR: Meganucleases, Zinc Fingers, and TALENs

sections.heading: Meganucleases: exquisitely specific, almost impossible to retarget
sections.body: Long before CRISPR, homing endonucleases from yeast and other microbes — I-SceI is the classic example, used in the Rouet-Smih-Jasin experiments covered earlier in this unit — recognize very long DNA sequences, typically around 18 base pairs. An 18-bp recognition site is long enough to be statistically unique even across a genome of billions of base pairs, which is exactly why I-SceI made such a clean tool for proof-of-concept DSB experiments: it cuts nowhere else in a mammalian genome unless that site is deliberately inserted. The catch is that the recognition sequence is baked into the protein's folded structure across its whole binding surface, not assembled from separable, swappable parts. Retargeting a meganuclease to a new, naturally occurring sequence means re-engineering large parts of the protein's structure through laborious structure-guided mutagenesis or directed evolution — projects that could consume a PhD to redirect one enzyme to one new site.

sections.heading: Zinc-finger nucleases: modular fingers, an obligate-dimer cut
sections.body: Zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs) solved the retargeting problem partway by building recognition from modular parts. Each zinc-finger domain is a small folded unit that reads roughly 3 base pairs of DNA, and arrays of three to six fingers are strung together to recognize 9-18 bp of target sequence — in principle, swap a finger, change which triplet it reads, and reuse the rest of the array. The cutting domain, borrowed from the bacterial enzyme FokI, only cleaves as a dimer, so ZFN design requires engineering two separate zinc-finger arrays that bind two half-sites on opposite DNA strands, spaced a fixed number of base pairs apart, so that two FokI domains — one fused to each array — can come together and cut in the middle. That dimerization requirement was a deliberate specificity safeguard: a stray single array binding elsewhere in the genome cannot cut anything alone. In practice, though, finger-to-finger context effects meant a finger that worked well in one array often behaved unpredictably when moved into another, so assembling a working ZFN pair for a new target still required substantial empirical screening rather than pure plug-and-play design.

sections.heading: TALENs: one repeat, one base, and where they still win
sections.body: Transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs), built from TALE proteins found in the plant pathogen Xanthomonas, cracked the modularity problem more cleanly. Each TALE repeat is a near-identical ~34-amino-acid block whose specificity comes down to two variable residues (the repeat-variable diresidue, or RVD) that read a single base: NI reads A, HD reads C, NG reads T, and NN reads G. Because the code is one repeat to one base, stringing repeats together lets a designer read out an arbitrary DNA sequence, unlike the context-sensitive triplets of zinc fingers. TALE binding also requires a thymine immediately 5' of the target sequence. TALENs, like ZFNs, dimerize FokI across two half-sites. Both platforms still required engineering a new protein for every new target — expensive and slow compared to reprogramming an RNA guide — which is why CRISPR-Cas9 displaced them for most routine editing after 2012. But TALENs retain real advantages: their long, modular recognition footprint gives tighter intrinsic specificity than early Cas9 designs, they are not blocked by CpG methylation at a target site the way some Cas9 guides can be, and because they require no separate guide RNA import into a compartment, they remain a leading tool for editing mitochondrial DNA, where CRISPR's RNA-guide delivery into mitochondria is a persistent unsolved problem.

lessons.workedExample: A lab in 2010 needs to disrupt a specific gene in zebrafish and has no access to CRISPR, which had not yet been adapted for genome editing. Using a meganuclease is ruled out immediately, since the target sequence does not match any known homing endonuclease site and re-engineering one would take years. The lab instead designs a TALEN pair: for each 15-18 bp half-site flanking the target, they select TALE repeats using the RVD code (NI for each A, HD for each C, NG for each T, NN for each G) so each repeat reads one base of the target, confirm a 5' T immediately precedes each half-site, and fuse each array to a FokI half-domain. Because the RVD-to-base mapping is a direct code rather than a context-dependent one, the array assembly proceeds far faster and more predictably than an equivalent zinc-finger design would have.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who has read about CRISPR but also asks 'what came before it, and why did people stop using it?' is testing whether a student understands programmable nucleases as a lineage of engineering tradeoffs rather than CRISPR appearing from nowhere. The strong answer names the specific bottleneck at each stage — meganucleases' recognition site is inseparable from protein structure, ZFN fingers show unpredictable context effects when recombined, TALEN repeats give a clean one-repeat-one-base code but still require a new protein per target — and can explain why TALENs specifically remain the tool of choice for a niche case like mitochondrial DNA editing, where CRISPR's RNA-guide delivery mechanism does not work.

questions.prompt: Why were homing meganucleases like I-SceI nearly impossible to retarget to new sequences?

options.text: Their recognition sequence is only 3 bp long, too short to be specific
Their ~18 bp recognition sequence is embedded across the protein's folded structure rather than built from separable, swappable parts
They require a guide RNA that cannot be resynthesized
They only function in yeast cells

explanations.a: Meganuclease recognition sites are long (around 18 bp), not short — length is not the problem.
explanations.b: Correct — because the recognition sequence is read out by the protein's overall folded structure rather than modular, swappable domains, retargeting requires laborious structure-guided re-engineering.
explanations.c: Meganucleases are protein-only enzymes; they do not use a guide RNA, which is a CRISPR-specific feature.
explanations.d: Meganucleases like I-SceI function in mammalian cells too, as demonstrated in the Jasin lab experiments; species restriction is not the retargeting bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Why must zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs) be designed to bind as pairs at two half-sites?

options.text: Because a single zinc-finger array cannot bind DNA at all
Because the FokI cleavage domain only cuts as a dimer, so two arrays are needed to bring two FokI domains together
Because each zinc finger reads 18 bp, so two are needed to cover a full gene
Because ZFNs require a 5' thymine on each strand

explanations.a: A single zinc-finger array can bind DNA on its own; the dimerization requirement is about the cleavage domain, not DNA binding.
explanations.b: Correct — FokI, the borrowed cleavage domain, requires dimerization to cut, so ZFN design pairs two arrays at adjacent half-sites so their fused FokI domains can come together.
explanations.c: Each zinc finger reads roughly 3 bp, not 18; arrays of several fingers together cover 9-18 bp.
explanations.d: The 5' thymine requirement belongs to TALE binding, not zinc-finger binding.

questions.prompt: Match each TALE repeat-variable diresidue (RVD) to the base it reads.

right.text: Adenine (A)
Cytosine (C)
Thymine (T)
Guanine (G)

questions.explanation: The TALE RVD code maps directly: NI reads A, HD reads C, NG reads T, and NN reads G, giving one repeat per base — a cleaner, more direct code than the context-sensitive triplets read by zinc fingers.

questions.prompt: Despite CRISPR-Cas9 displacing TALENs for most routine editing, in what context do TALENs still have a real practical advantage?

options.text: Editing mitochondrial DNA, since CRISPR's RNA-guide delivery into mitochondria remains an unsolved problem
Any editing task, since TALENs are always faster to design than CRISPR guides
Editing RNA rather than DNA
Only in plant genomes, since TALE proteins originate from a plant pathogen

explanations.a: Correct — because TALENs are protein-only and require no separate guide RNA import into a compartment, they remain a leading tool for mitochondrial DNA editing, where CRISPR's guide-RNA delivery is a persistent obstacle.
explanations.b: TALEN design requires engineering a new protein per target, which is generally slower than reprogramming a CRISPR guide RNA — this is exactly why CRISPR displaced TALENs for routine use.
explanations.c: TALENs, like the other nucleases in this lesson, act on double-stranded DNA, not RNA.
explanations.d: TALE proteins originate in a plant pathogen, but TALENs have been used across many organisms including mammalian cells and are not restricted to plant genomes.

lessons.label: Recombinases, Integrases, and Transposons

sections.heading: Cre/loxP and Flp/FRT: cutting and pasting without a DSB
sections.body: Not every DNA-writing tool relies on a double-strand break at all. Cre recombinase, from bacteriophage P1, recognizes a 34-bp site called loxP and recombines DNA between any two loxP sites present in the genome — excising the intervening sequence if the sites point the same direction, or inverting it if they point opposite ways. Flp recombinase, from the yeast 2-micron plasmid, does the analogous job at its own FRT sites. Both are tyrosine recombinases that never create a free DSB during the reaction — they proceed through a controlled series of strand exchanges via a Holliday-junction-like intermediate, so there is no window where an unrepaired chromosome break could cause loss of material or trigger an error-prone repair pathway. This is exactly why Cre/loxP became the standard tool for conditional knockouts (flanking, or 'floxing,' a gene with loxP sites so it can be deleted only in tissues expressing Cre) and for lineage tracing (a Cre-triggered reporter permanently marks a cell and all its descendants), work built on Brian Sauer's and others' adaptation of the phage system into mammalian cells starting in the late 1980s.

sections.heading: Serine integrases: one-way insertion at attB and attP
sections.body: Serine integrases such as phiC31 (from a Streptomyces phage) and Bxb1 (from a mycobacteriophage) work on a related but distinct principle: they recombine a phage-derived attP site with a bacterial-derived attB site, and the reaction is unidirectional — attB x attP recombine into attL and attR, but the reverse reaction does not occur without a separate recombination-directionality factor. That irreversibility is a feature, not a limitation, for stable, permanent insertion: once a payload landing pad (attP) is installed at a genomic site and a donor carrying the matching attB is delivered, the integrase locks the cargo in with no risk of it being excised back out later by the same enzyme. Because these sites are unrelated to loxP or FRT, phiC31 and Bxb1 systems are used orthogonally to Cre/Flp in the same cell without cross-reacting.

sections.heading: Transposons: self-contained delivery, and the pre-installed landing pad problem
sections.body: Sleeping Beauty and piggyBac are DNA transposons — mobile genetic elements that cut themselves out of one location and paste into another via a transposase enzyme. Sleeping Beauty was reconstructed by Ivics and colleagues in 1997 from inactive, fossilized transposon sequences found across fish genomes, engineered back into an active enzyme. PiggyBac, isolated from the cabbage looper moth, integrates precisely at TTAA tetranucleotide sites and, unusually among transposons, can be removed later without leaving a scar, since its transposase excises cleanly back out of TTAA sites. Both are popular for stable cargo delivery in cell and gene therapy manufacturing because a single transposase enzyme can integrate a payload without engineering a target-specific protein at all. Every system here shares one limitation: each recognizes only a fixed site (loxP, FRT, attB/attP, TTAA) that must already exist or be pre-installed, unlike a programmable nuclease redirectable to nearly any sequence. That fixed-site limitation is exactly why later engineering bolted integrases onto CRISPR's programmable targeting: use a nuclease-free or nickase-based CRISPR system to write the attB or attP landing pad at a chosen genomic address, then let a serine integrase do the large, precise, irreversible cargo insertion — the strategy this unit's PASTE-style tools build on.

lessons.workedExample: A lab wants to create a mouse where a gene is deleted only in liver cells, not throughout the body. They breed in loxP sites flanking the gene ('floxed' allele) using standard embryonic-stem-cell targeting, then cross that line with a mouse expressing Cre recombinase under a liver-specific promoter (Albumin-Cre). Only in cells where Albumin-Cre is active does Cre find both loxP sites and excise the intervening gene; every other tissue retains two intact floxed copies. If the lab instead wanted to permanently and irreversibly insert a large reporter cassette at one specific genomic address across the whole animal, they would use a serine integrase like Bxb1 with a pre-installed attP landing pad, since Bxb1's attB x attP reaction is unidirectional and will not later reverse itself the way a hypothetical Cre-based insertion at loxP sites could.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about recombinases and transposons to check whether a student understands that not all DNA engineering runs through a nuclease and a repair pathway, and to test whether they grasp the central limitation of every system in this lesson: fixed recognition sites. A student who says 'we used Cre/loxP because we needed conditional, reversible control, and it doesn't require a DSB at all' shows real understanding; one who cannot explain why phiC31 or Bxb1 can insert cargo at an arbitrary genomic site (they cannot, without a pre-installed attP landing pad) reveals they have not grasped why these tools are fundamentally different from a programmable nuclease.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't Cre/loxP recombination require or create a double-strand break?

options.text: Cre recombinase works only on single-stranded DNA
Cre proceeds through a controlled series of strand exchanges via a Holliday-junction-like intermediate, never leaving a free break
loxP sites are too short for any nuclease to recognize
Cre first repairs any existing DSB before recombining

explanations.a: Cre acts on double-stranded DNA at loxP sites, not single-stranded DNA.
explanations.b: Correct — as a tyrosine recombinase, Cre performs a controlled series of strand exchanges through a Holliday-junction-like intermediate, so the chromosome is never left as a free double-strand break.
explanations.c: loxP is a defined 34-bp site that Cre recognizes specifically; site length is not why no DSB forms.
explanations.d: Cre does not act on pre-existing DSBs; its recombination mechanism at loxP sites simply never produces one in the first place.

questions.prompt: What makes phiC31 and Bxb1 integrase reactions especially useful for stable, permanent cargo insertion?

options.text: The attB x attP recombination reaction is unidirectional, so the integrated cargo is not later excised by the same enzyme
They can target any DNA sequence without a pre-installed site
They require a double-strand break to function
They only work in bacteria, ensuring safety in mammalian cells

explanations.a: Correct — because attB x attP recombination into attL/attR does not spontaneously reverse without a separate directionality factor, cargo inserted this way stays locked in place.
explanations.b: Like the other tools in this lesson, serine integrases require a pre-installed matching site (attP or attB); they cannot target arbitrary sequences.
explanations.c: Serine integrases, like tyrosine recombinases, do not rely on a double-strand break mechanism.
explanations.d: phiC31 and Bxb1 are used successfully in mammalian cells; they are not restricted to bacteria.

questions.prompt: What is the central limitation shared by Cre/loxP, Flp/FRT, phiC31/Bxb1, and Sleeping Beauty/piggyBac, in contrast to a programmable nuclease?

options.text: They all require a guide RNA to function
Each recognizes a fixed site that must already exist or be pre-installed, rather than being redirectable to any arbitrary sequence
None of them can be used in mammalian cells
They all create indels at their target site

explanations.a: None of these systems use a guide RNA; that is a CRISPR-specific feature, not something these tools share.
explanations.b: Correct — loxP, FRT, attB/attP, and TTAA are all fixed recognition sequences; none of these enzymes can simply be redirected to a new arbitrary sequence the way a CRISPR guide can be reprogrammed.
explanations.c: All of these systems are routinely used in mammalian cells; that is not the shared limitation.
explanations.d: These systems generally avoid indel-producing repair altogether, which is the opposite of the shared limitation being tested here.

questions.prompt: Match each system to its origin or recognition feature.

right.text: Originates from bacteriophage P1; recognizes loxP sites
Reconstructed by Ivics and colleagues (1997) from inactive sequences found across fish genomes
Isolated from the cabbage looper moth; integrates at TTAA sites and can excise cleanly

questions.explanation: Cre comes from bacteriophage P1 and acts on loxP; Sleeping Beauty was resurrected by Ivics and colleagues in 1997 from dormant fish-genome transposon sequences; piggyBac, from the cabbage looper moth, integrates at TTAA sites and uniquely can excise itself scarlessly.

lessons.label: What an Edit Can and Cannot Prove

sections.heading: Genotype evidence is not phenotype evidence
sections.body: Sequencing an edited locus and finding a frameshift indel tells you the genotype changed — it does not tell you the protein is gone, or that any downstream phenotype is caused by that loss. A frameshift is a hypothesis about protein loss, not a demonstration of it, for several concrete reasons: nonsense-mediated decay of the mutant transcript is often incomplete, alternative translation start sites downstream of the edit can sometimes restore a truncated but partially functional protein, and exon skipping around the edited region can occasionally preserve a near-normal reading frame entirely. The only way to close that gap is to check the protein directly — a western blot showing the band is gone, or an antibody-based assay confirming loss of the specific protein — rather than inferring loss of function purely from the DNA sequence trace.

sections.heading: The bulk-pool confound: not every cell in your sample is edited
sections.body: No genome-editing delivery method achieves 100% editing efficiency in every cell of a population. A transfected or transduced pool of cells is a mixture of edited and unedited cells in unknown proportion, and any phenotype measured on that bulk pool is diluted and confounded by the unedited fraction still behaving normally. A 30% editing efficiency does not mean you can expect a phenotype at 30% strength and call it confirmed — it means roughly 70% of your measured signal is coming from cells that were never edited at all, which can mask a real effect, exaggerate an artifact, or make a modest true effect look statistically noisy. The fix is either single-cell cloning to isolate a pure edited (and pure unedited) population before phenotyping, or measuring editing efficiency by sequencing the same pool being phenotyped so the analysis can account for the mixture rather than ignore it.

sections.heading: Isogenic controls, two guides, and rescue: the standard of proof
sections.body: Three practices together are what separates a defensible causal claim from a correlation. An isogenic control is a cell line or organism genetically identical to the edited line except at the intended locus — ideally a sibling clone from the very same transfection that happened not to acquire the edit, so genetic background, clonal drift, and culture history are matched rather than confounded. Using two independent guide RNAs against the same gene, rather than one, protects against the specific failure mode where a single guide's phenotype is actually driven by an off-target cut elsewhere in the genome — if two unrelated guides targeting the same gene from different sequences produce the same phenotype, an off-target explanation becomes far less plausible, since two guides would need to share the same off-target site by coincidence. Rescue, or complementation, is the strongest evidence of all: reintroducing a wild-type copy of the edited gene (typically one engineered to resist re-cutting or delivered as cDNA from a different locus) into the edited cells and showing the phenotype reverses. If the phenotype rescues, it was caused by loss of that gene specifically; if it does not rescue, the original phenotype likely had another cause entirely, including an off-target event the two-guide check might have missed.

lessons.workedExample: A team edits gene Y in a cell line, sees reduced cell growth in the bulk transfected pool, and sequences the pool to find 40% of alleles carry frameshift indels. Before concluding gene Y is required for growth, they run the full check: they single-cell clone to isolate a pure knockout line and a pure isogenic sibling-clone control from the same transfection, confirm by western blot that the Y protein band is absent in the knockout, repeat the whole experiment with a second, independent guide RNA targeting a different part of gene Y and see the same growth defect, and finally re-express a re-cutting-resistant wild-type copy of Y in the knockout clone and watch growth return to normal. Only after all four steps does the team have a defensible claim that gene Y itself, not an off-target cut or the unedited fraction of a bulk pool, causes the growth defect.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is close to the single most common failure mode judges see in editing-based projects, so it gets probed hard: a student reports 'we knocked out gene Y and saw phenotype Z' after sequencing a bulk pool and observing a difference, with no isogenic control, no second guide, and no rescue. A judge asking 'how do you know the phenotype is due to loss of Y and not an off-target cut, and how do you know your control is genetically matched otherwise?' is testing whether the student understands that an indel is genotype evidence, a bulk-pool phenotype is confounded by editing efficiency, and only a second independent guide plus a rescue experiment together constitute a real causal claim.

questions.prompt: Why is finding a frameshift indel by sequencing not, by itself, proof that the protein is lost?

options.text: Because sequencing can never detect indels accurately
Because incomplete nonsense-mediated decay, downstream alternative start sites, or exon skipping can sometimes preserve partial or full protein function despite the frameshift
Because frameshifts only occur in non-coding DNA
Because a frameshift always increases protein expression

explanations.a: Sequencing reliably detects indels; the issue is not detection accuracy but what a detected indel does or does not guarantee about the protein.
explanations.b: Correct — a frameshift is a hypothesis about protein loss, not a demonstration of it, precisely because these mechanisms can sometimes rescue partial or complete function despite the DNA-level change.
explanations.c: Frameshifts specifically disrupt the reading frame of a coding sequence; the concept does not apply to non-coding DNA.
explanations.d: A frameshift typically disrupts or truncates a protein rather than increasing its expression.

questions.prompt: A bulk transfected cell pool has 30% editing efficiency, and a phenotype is measured on the whole pool. What is the main problem with interpreting that measurement?

options.text: There is no problem; 30% editing efficiency is sufficient for any phenotype assay
Roughly 70% of the measured cells are unedited and behaving normally, diluting and confounding the signal
Bulk pools cannot be sequenced to determine editing efficiency
The unedited cells will always show a stronger phenotype than the edited ones

explanations.a: A large unedited fraction directly confounds bulk-pool phenotyping; 30% editing efficiency does not make the measurement clean.
explanations.b: Correct — the unedited majority of the pool continues behaving normally, which can mask, exaggerate, or add noise to whatever true effect exists in the edited minority.
explanations.c: Sequencing the pool is precisely how editing efficiency (like the 30% figure) is measured in the first place.
explanations.d: There is no general rule that unedited cells show a stronger phenotype; the problem is dilution and confounding, not a directional bias favoring unedited cells.

questions.prompt: Why does observing the same phenotype with two independent guide RNAs targeting the same gene strengthen a causal claim?

options.text: Because two guides always have identical off-target sites
Because it is far less likely that two unrelated guides would coincidentally share the same off-target site, so a shared phenotype is more likely due to the intended gene
Because using two guides doubles the editing efficiency
Because two guides eliminate the need for an isogenic control

explanations.a: Two independent guides targeting different sequences are expected to have different off-target profiles, not identical ones — that is exactly why the comparison is informative.
explanations.b: Correct — if an off-target effect explained the phenotype, it would need to arise from two guides with different sequences and different off-target sites, which is a much less likely coincidence than the phenotype simply being due to loss of the shared intended gene.
explanations.c: The two-guide strategy is about ruling out off-target explanations, not about increasing on-target editing efficiency.
explanations.d: Two guides address a different confound (off-target effects) than an isogenic control (genetic background matching); one does not replace the other.

questions.prompt: Order these steps as they would be performed to build a defensible causal claim that gene Y's loss causes an observed phenotype.

items.text: Observe a phenotype difference in a bulk transfected pool
Single-cell clone to isolate a pure edited line and a matched isogenic control
Repeat editing with a second, independent guide RNA and confirm the same phenotype
Re-express a re-cutting-resistant wild-type copy of the gene and confirm the phenotype reverses

questions.explanation: The process starts with an initial bulk-pool observation, which must then be purified via single-cell cloning against an isogenic control to remove the unedited-fraction confound, corroborated with a second independent guide to rule out off-target effects, and finally confirmed with a rescue experiment, the strongest evidence that the phenotype is specifically caused by loss of that gene.

units.label: CRISPR-Cas9: Mechanism and Guide RNA Design

lessons.label: CRISPR as a Bacterial Immune System

sections.heading: A genomic diary of past infections
sections.body: CRISPR loci — Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats — were first noticed in 1987 by Ishino and colleagues as an odd stretch of repeated sequence in E. coli, with no known function. It took until the early 2000s for Francisco Mojica to survey these repeat arrays across dozens of bacterial and archaeal genomes and coin the acronym CRISPR (with Ruud Jansen) around 2002. The key clue came in 2005, when Mojica and others noticed that the unique 'spacer' sequences sitting between the repeats matched phage and plasmid DNA — the array looked like a chronological record of past infections. Barrangou and colleagues at Danisco confirmed this experimentally in 2007: adding a new spacer to Streptococcus thermophilus made the bacterium resistant to the matching phage, and removing it restored susceptibility. CRISPR was an adaptive, heritable immune system in a single-celled organism.

sections.heading: Adaptation, expression, and self/non-self discrimination
sections.body: Three stages keep the system running. In adaptation, the Cas1–Cas2 complex captures short fragments of invading DNA and integrates them as new spacers at the leader end of the array, so the array's order preserves a timeline of exposures. In expression, the whole array is transcribed as one long pre-crRNA and processed into individual crRNAs, each carrying one spacer plus repeat fragments. In type II systems this processing requires a second small RNA, the tracrRNA, which base-pairs with the repeat and recruits host RNase III to cut the pre-crRNA. Critically, the bacterium's own array does not carry a PAM (protospacer-adjacent motif) next to its spacer sequences, only the invader's DNA does — so the effector complex ignores the CRISPR locus itself and only cuts matching sequence flanked by a PAM. This PAM requirement is the self/non-self switch that keeps the immune system from destroying its own genome.

sections.heading: Two classes, one that became a tool
sections.body: CRISPR systems split into two classes based on how the spacer sequence gets used to find and destroy the target. Class 1 systems (types I and III) use large multi-subunit effector complexes — Cascade being the best-studied example — built from several different Cas proteins. Class 2 systems (types II, V, VI) use a single, large multidomain protein to do the whole job: Cas9 for type II, Cas12 for type V, Cas13 for type VI. Type II Cas9 became the genome-editing workhorse precisely because it is class 2 — one protein plus two small RNAs (crRNA and tracrRNA) is a far simpler system to reconstitute and reprogram than a multi-protein Cascade complex. Jinek, Doudna, Charpentier and colleagues showed in 2012 that the crRNA and tracrRNA could be literally fused into one synthetic single guide RNA (sgRNA), reducing Cas9 targeting to two components: one protein, one RNA.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher sequences a Streptococcus thermophilus strain that survived a phage outbreak in a yogurt starter culture and finds its CRISPR array has one more spacer than the parent strain, inserted right at the leader end. Sequencing the phage genome shows that new spacer is an exact match to a phage gene, immediately adjacent to a PAM in the phage DNA. This is exactly the Barrangou 2007 result: acquiring the spacer via Cas1–Cas2 integration made the strain immune, and the position at the leader end (rather than scattered through the array) tells you it was the most recent exposure, not an old one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing native CRISPR biology is checking whether a student understands that Cas9 is a repurposed bacterial defense system, not an engineered tool from scratch — and specifically whether they can explain why the bacterium doesn't shred its own genome. The strong answer names the PAM as the self/non-self discriminator (present on invader DNA next to the protospacer, absent next to the array's own spacers) rather than vaguely saying 'it recognizes foreign DNA.' A student who can also explain why type II (Cas9) was the class chosen for engineering — one protein instead of a multi-subunit Cascade complex — shows they understand the practical reason CRISPR-Cas9 exists as a lab tool at all.

questions.prompt: What prevents the CRISPR-Cas system from cutting the bacterium's own CRISPR array, which contains sequences identical to its spacers?

options.text: The array is physically shielded by a protein coat
The array's own spacer sequences are not flanked by a PAM, so the effector complex does not recognize them as targets
Cas9 only becomes active outside the cell
The spacers in the array are chemically different from the phage DNA they matched

explanations.a: There is no such shielding protein; the discrimination is sequence-based, not physical.
explanations.b: Correct — the PAM sits adjacent to the protospacer in invader DNA but not adjacent to the corresponding spacer in the host's own array, so this PAM requirement is the self/non-self switch.
explanations.c: Cas9 acts inside the bacterial cytoplasm on invading DNA; location is not the discriminator.
explanations.d: The spacer sequence is chemically identical DNA copied from the invader; the difference is the flanking PAM, not the base chemistry.

questions.prompt: Barrangou and colleagues' 2007 experiment in Streptococcus thermophilus demonstrated CRISPR immunity by showing that:

options.text: Bacteria without any CRISPR array were more resistant to phage
Adding a phage-matching spacer conferred resistance, and removing it restored susceptibility
CRISPR repeats alone, without spacers, blocked phage infection
Phage resistance was unrelated to spacer content

explanations.a: The opposite is true — CRISPR arrays provide resistance when they carry a matching spacer, not when absent.
explanations.b: Correct — this gain-and-loss-of-function result was the direct experimental proof that CRISPR spacers confer sequence-specific, heritable phage immunity.
explanations.c: Repeats alone carry no targeting information; the spacer sequence is what determines specificity.
explanations.d: The whole point of the experiment was to show resistance tracked precisely with spacer content.

questions.prompt: Match each CRISPR-Cas component or stage to its role.

right.text: Captures invader DNA fragments and integrates them as new spacers
Base-pairs with the repeat and recruits RNase III to process pre-crRNA
Short motif required next to a target for Cas9 to cut it, absent from the array's own spacers
Site where new spacers are added, preserving a chronological infection record

questions.explanation: Cas1-Cas2 performs adaptation by integrating new spacers at the leader end; tracrRNA partners with RNase III to process the pre-crRNA transcript in type II systems; the PAM is the sequence motif that lets Cas9 distinguish invader DNA from the host's own array.

questions.prompt: Why was type II Cas9 the CRISPR system engineered into a genome-editing tool, rather than a class 1 system like Cascade?

options.text: Cas9 is a single multidomain protein needing only two small RNAs, far simpler to reprogram than a multi-subunit complex
Cascade cannot bind DNA at all
Type II systems are found in more bacterial species
Cas9 does not require a guide RNA

explanations.a: Correct — class 2 systems like type II use one large effector protein plus crRNA and tracrRNA (later fused into a single sgRNA), which is dramatically simpler to reconstitute than Cascade's multiple Cas subunits.
explanations.b: Cascade does bind and target DNA in class 1 systems; the issue is complexity of reconstitution, not capability.
explanations.c: Prevalence across species was not the deciding factor; molecular simplicity was.
explanations.d: Cas9 absolutely requires guide RNA (crRNA plus tracrRNA, or the fused sgRNA) to find its target.

lessons.label: Cas9 Architecture and the Chemistry of the Cut

sections.heading: Two lobes, one clamp
sections.body: Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) is a 1,368-residue protein folded into two lobes connected by a bridge helix: the alpha-helical recognition (REC) lobe, which grips the guide RNA and the RNA:DNA heteroduplex, and the nuclease (NUC) lobe, which houses the two cutting domains (HNH and RuvC) plus the PAM-interacting (PI) domain. Structures solved by Nishimasu, Ran, Hsu, Konermann and colleagues (2014, Cell) resolved the Cas9-sgRNA-target DNA ternary complex, while Jinek and colleagues (2014, Science) separately solved the apo (RNA-free) Cas9 structure, showing the apo protein is bilobed and relatively open, closing around its RNA and DNA substrates as it loads — a clamp that only becomes catalytically competent once fully assembled.

sections.heading: PAM first, then a directional R-loop
sections.body: Cas9 does not search DNA by trying to base-pair the guide everywhere; it first scans for its PAM (5'-NGG for SpCas9) using the PI domain, without needing to unwind the duplex. Sternberg and Doudna's 2014 single-molecule study (Nature 507) showed that both binding and cleavage require this PAM contact, and that once a PAM is found, DNA strand separation and RNA:DNA heteroduplex formation initiate right there and proceed directionally away from the PAM into the rest of the protospacer — forming a structure called an R-loop, where the guide strand pairs with the target DNA strand and the non-target strand is displaced as single-stranded loop. A guide with a perfect match near the PAM but mismatches far from it can still bind detectably; the reverse is not true, which is why PAM-proximal mismatches are so much more disruptive than PAM-distal ones.

sections.heading: A conformational checkpoint gates the cut
sections.body: Cas9 carries two nuclease domains that each cut one strand: HNH cuts the target strand (the one base-paired to the guide), and RuvC cuts the non-target (displaced) strand, together producing a blunt double-strand break positioned about 3 base pairs upstream (5') of the PAM. But HNH does not simply sit next to its substrate — Sternberg and colleagues' 2015 Nature work on conformational control showed HNH must physically swing into a docked, catalytically active position once the R-loop is fully formed, and this repositioning event also licenses RuvC to cut, coupling the two cuts to one conformational checkpoint. Mismatches, particularly in the PAM-proximal region, stall R-loop completion and block HNH docking — this conformational proofreading step is a major structural basis of Cas9's target discrimination. After cleavage, Cas9 does not release quickly: it remains bound to the cut DNA ends, behaving as a slow, single-turnover enzyme in biochemical assays rather than a fast catalytic recycler.

lessons.workedExample: A biochemist compares two guide RNAs targeting nearly identical sequences: guide A has one mismatch 2 nucleotides from the PAM, guide B has one mismatch 18 nucleotides from the PAM (near the far end of the 20-nt spacer). In cleavage assays, guide A shows almost no cutting, while guide B cuts nearly as efficiently as a perfect match. This matches the PAM-first, directional R-loop model: the mismatch in guide A falls in the region where heteroduplex formation initiates and HNH docking is most sensitive, so R-loop propagation stalls early; guide B's distal mismatch is tolerated because the R-loop nucleates successfully near the PAM before the mismatch is ever encountered, letting the checkpoint pass.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about Cas9's mechanism wants to know if a student understands cleavage as a multi-step, checkpointed process rather than 'the guide finds the gene and Cas9 cuts it.' The revealing detail is naming which domain cuts which strand (HNH: target strand; RuvC: non-target strand) and explaining why PAM-proximal mismatches matter more than distal ones — that asymmetry is direct evidence a student grasps the directional R-loop model, not just memorized vocabulary. It also sets up why guide design (Unit 4) weights the seed region so heavily: it is downstream of this exact biochemistry.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Cas9 target recognition and cleavage from first to last.

items.text: PAM-interacting domain recognizes the 5'-NGG PAM
DNA unwinds and the guide RNA base-pairs with the target strand, forming an R-loop that propagates away from the PAM
HNH domain docks into its catalytically active conformation
HNH cuts the target strand and RuvC cuts the non-target strand, producing a blunt break near the PAM

questions.explanation: PAM recognition happens first and does not require unwinding; only after the PAM is found does the R-loop form directionally from the PAM; full R-loop formation licenses HNH to dock; docking then permits both HNH and RuvC to cut, producing the blunt double-strand break.

questions.prompt: Which nuclease domain of Cas9 cuts the DNA strand that is base-paired to the guide RNA (the target strand)?

options.text: RuvC
HNH
The PAM-interacting domain
The REC lobe

explanations.a: RuvC cuts the non-target (displaced) strand, not the guide-paired strand.
explanations.b: Correct — HNH cuts the target strand, the one that is base-paired with the guide RNA in the R-loop.
explanations.c: The PI domain reads the PAM sequence; it has no catalytic cutting function.
explanations.d: The REC lobe binds RNA and DNA structurally but does not carry catalytic nuclease activity.

questions.prompt: Why does a mismatch near the PAM-proximal end of the guide typically block cleavage much more effectively than a mismatch at the PAM-distal end?

options.text: Because R-loop formation initiates at the PAM and proceeds directionally, so proximal mismatches disrupt heteroduplex formation before it can propagate
Because the PAM-distal end of the guide is chemically degraded before binding
Because RuvC only reads the PAM-proximal sequence
There is no positional difference; all mismatches are equally disruptive

explanations.a: Correct — since heteroduplex formation nucleates at the PAM and extends away from it, a mismatch near the PAM interrupts that process early, while a distal mismatch is encountered only after the R-loop has largely already formed.
explanations.b: Guide RNA is not selectively degraded at one end during targeting; this is not the mechanism.
explanations.c: RuvC's activity depends on the conformational checkpoint triggered by full R-loop formation, not direct PAM-proximal sequence reading.
explanations.d: Position matters enormously — this asymmetry is a well-established, mechanistically explained feature of Cas9 targeting.

questions.prompt: After cutting its target DNA, how does Cas9 typically behave, based on single-molecule and biochemical studies?

options.text: It releases immediately and moves rapidly to cut additional target sites
It remains bound to the cleaved DNA ends, acting as a slow, single-turnover enzyme
It degrades itself immediately after cleavage
It re-anneals the cut DNA strands back together

explanations.a: This is the opposite of what is observed — Cas9 is notably slow to release product, not a fast recycling enzyme.
explanations.b: Correct — biochemical assays show Cas9 stays bound to the cut ends for an extended period, behaving as a single-turnover rather than multi-turnover enzyme.
explanations.c: Cas9 is not self-degrading upon cleavage; its persistence at the site is a protein-DNA binding phenomenon, not proteolysis.
explanations.d: Cas9 has no ligase activity; it cuts DNA but does not rejoin it.

lessons.label: PAMs, Orthologs, and the Reachable Genome

sections.heading: The PAM sets your targeting density
sections.body: Every Cas ortholog has its own PAM requirement, and that requirement determines how densely you can find usable cut sites across a genome. SpCas9's 5'-NGG PAM is short and permissive — GG dinucleotides occur often enough in the human genome that an NGG site shows up roughly every 8 to 12 base pairs on average, giving near-continuous coverage for guide design.
