Staphylococcus aureus Cas9 (SaCas9) needs the longer, more restrictive 5'-NNGRRT motif (R = A or G), which cuts down targetable sites substantially, but SaCas9's real advantage is size: at roughly 1,053 residues versus SpCas9's 1,368, its coding sequence plus an sgRNA cassette fits inside a single adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector, which has a tight ~4.7 kb packaging limit — a major reason SaCas9 shows up in in vivo and therapeutic delivery contexts where SpCas9 does not fit.

sections.heading: Cas12a: a different PAM position, a different cut
sections.body: Cas12a (originally called Cpf1, discovered by Zetsche and colleagues in 2015) is a class 2, type V effector with several mechanistic differences from Cas9. Its PAM, 5'-TTTV (V = A, C, or G), sits on the 5' side of the protospacer rather than the 3' side, and instead of a blunt cut near the PAM, Cas12a cuts distal to the PAM and leaves a staggered break with 5-nucleotide 5' overhangs — sticky ends that some applications (like directional insertion) can exploit. Cas12a is also self-sufficient at RNA processing: it uses its own RuvC-like domain to process its own crRNA array without needing a separate tracrRNA or host RNase III, which makes it well suited to multiplexed editing from a single compact array of guides.

sections.heading: Engineering around the PAM constraint
sections.body: Because the PAM is the single biggest constraint on where you can cut, several labs engineered SpCas9 variants with relaxed PAM requirements. Hu and colleagues' 2018 xCas9 recognized a broadened set including NG, GAA, and GAT PAMs. Walton, Kleinstiver and colleagues went further in 2020 (Science), engineering SpG to recognize the simpler NGN PAM and then SpRY, a near-PAMless variant active on NRN PAMs (and with lower but still usable activity on NYN PAMs) — dramatically expanding which genomic positions, including specific disease-associated single-nucleotide variants, become reachable. But this targeting range comes at a cost: the broader a variant's PAM tolerance, the less selective its PI domain is being for any one motif, and in practice these expanded-PAM variants generally show lower on-target activity and can show reduced specificity at any given site compared to wild-type SpCas9 working at its native NGG PAM — a real trade-off between reach and precision that a guide-design decision has to weigh.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to correct a single disease-associated point mutation, but the only NGG PAM near that base sits 25 base pairs away — too far for the HDR editing window to reliably reach the mutation. Switching to SpRY reveals an NRN PAM positioned just 4 base pairs from the mutation, well within range. The trade-off is real: the SpRY guide at that near-PAMless site shows lower cleavage efficiency in pilot tests than a typical SpCas9/NGG guide would, so the student has to weigh reachability against raw editing efficiency, potentially by testing several PAM-adjacent options and picking the best empirical performer rather than assuming any near-PAMless option works as well as wild-type.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing PAM choice is testing whether a student picked their Cas ortholog and PAM deliberately or defaulted to 'Cas9' without considering constraints. The strong answer connects a specific design need — delivery vector size, targeting a base with no nearby NGG, needing multiplexed cuts — to a specific ortholog or engineered variant, and can state the associated cost (SaCas9's more restrictive PAM, or PAM-relaxed variants trading away on-target activity and specificity). Reciting that 'Cas12a is another CRISPR enzyme' without connecting it to its distinct PAM position, staggered cut, or self-processing crRNA signals memorization rather than design reasoning.

questions.prompt: Match each Cas ortholog or variant to its defining PAM or design trait.

right.text: 5'-NGG PAM, targetable site roughly every 8-12 bp in the human genome
5'-NNGRRT PAM; smaller protein that fits an AAV vector with sgRNA
5'-TTTV PAM on the 5' side of the protospacer; staggered cut distal to the PAM
Near-PAMless engineered variant active on NRN (and weaker on NYN) PAMs

questions.explanation: SpCas9 uses the common, permissive NGG PAM; SaCas9 uses the more restrictive NNGRRT PAM but is small enough for AAV packaging; Cas12a's PAM sits 5' of the protospacer and it cuts distally with a staggered overhang; SpRY was engineered by Walton, Kleinstiver and colleagues (2020) to work on almost any PAM.

questions.prompt: What is the main practical reason SaCas9 is favored over SpCas9 for AAV-delivered in vivo gene editing?

options.text: SaCas9 has a more permissive PAM than SpCas9
SaCas9's smaller protein size lets it plus an sgRNA cassette fit within AAV's tight packaging limit
SaCas9 does not require a PAM at all
SaCas9 cuts DNA without a guide RNA

explanations.a: SaCas9's NNGRRT PAM is actually more restrictive than SpCas9's NGG, not more permissive.
explanations.b: Correct — at roughly 1,053 residues versus SpCas9's 1,368, SaCas9 plus its guide RNA cassette fits within AAV's ~4.7 kb packaging capacity, which is the main delivery-driven reason to choose it.
explanations.c: SaCas9 still requires its own specific PAM (NNGRRT); it is not PAM-independent.
explanations.d: Like SpCas9, SaCas9 is guide-RNA dependent for target recognition.

questions.prompt: What is the general trade-off of PAM-relaxed engineered Cas9 variants like SpG and SpRY compared to wild-type SpCas9 at its native NGG sites?

options.text: They reach more target sites but generally show lower on-target activity and can show reduced specificity
They reach fewer target sites but are always more specific
There is no trade-off; they are strictly superior in every respect
They eliminate the need for a guide RNA entirely

explanations.a: Correct — broadening PAM tolerance expands the reachable genome but generally comes at the cost of lower on-target efficiency and potentially reduced specificity relative to wild-type SpCas9 at an NGG site.
explanations.b: The relaxed-PAM variants reach more sites, not fewer, which is their whole design purpose.
explanations.c: There is a documented efficiency/specificity trade-off; they are not simply better in all respects.
explanations.d: These variants still require a guide RNA for targeting; only the PAM constraint is relaxed.

lessons.label: Anatomy of a Guide RNA

sections.heading: Spacer plus scaffold, fused into one molecule
sections.body: The single guide RNA (sgRNA) that Jinek, Doudna, Charpentier and colleagues engineered in 2012 is a literal fusion of two natural RNAs: a 20-nucleotide spacer, derived from the crRNA, that base-pairs with the target DNA strand, and a scaffold, derived from the tracrRNA, that folds into a structure Cas9 physically grips. The scaffold is not just filler — it contains the repeat:anti-repeat duplex (where the original crRNA repeat and tracrRNA sequence pair with each other) followed by three stem-loops that dock against the REC and NUC lobes of the protein. Truncating or disrupting these stem-loops measurably reduces Cas9 activity, because the scaffold's job is to hold the RNA in the exact conformation Cas9 needs to load and activate, not merely to link spacer to protein.

sections.heading: The seed region and where mismatches actually matter
sections.body: Within the 20-nt spacer, the roughly 10-12 nucleotides closest to the PAM form the 'seed region' — the segment where Jinek's 2012 work and Hsu and colleagues' 2013 systematic mismatch study both found mismatches were least tolerated, consistent with the PAM-first, directional R-loop mechanism (Unit 2). A guide designed with a seed-region mismatch to its intended target will typically fail to cut; the same mismatch in the PAM-distal 8-10 nucleotides is often tolerated. This asymmetry is the first thing a guide-design tool checks, both for on-target confidence and, in reverse, for predicting where a guide might cut somewhere it shouldn't (Unit 5).

sections.heading: Practical constraints and empirical scoring
sections.body: Real guide design has to satisfy the biochemistry of both Cas9 and however the guide gets made. GC content in the 40-70% range is generally preferred — too low destabilizes the RNA:DNA heteroduplex, too high can hinder unwinding. If the sgRNA is transcribed in cells from a Pol III promoter such as U6, two constraints follow directly from Pol III biology: a run of four or more T's acts as a Pol III terminator, so a spacer containing poly-T will truncate transcription mid-guide, and the U6 promoter requires the transcript to start with a G, so spacers not naturally starting with G often get an extra G appended at the 5' end. Chemically synthesized guides, used for RNP delivery (Unit 7), instead carry end modifications like 2'-O-methylation and phosphorothioate linkages to resist nucleases and reduce innate immune activation. On top of these hard constraints, empirical on-target scoring — most notably Doench and colleagues' Rule Set 2 (also called the Azimuth score), trained on a large multi-gene panel of guides tiling NGG sites and published in Nature Biotechnology in 2016 — uses machine learning on positional and dinucleotide nucleotide frequencies, GC content, and predicted melting temperatures to rank candidate guides by predicted cutting efficiency before anyone touches a pipette.

lessons.workedExample: A student designs a guide against a target exon and picks the top candidate purely because it has the highest Rule Set 2 score. Checking the sequence, they find it contains a run of four T's, TTTT, five bases in, and it will be delivered via a U6-driven plasmid — a real problem, since that poly-T stretch risks premature Pol III termination and truncating the transcript. They also notice the spacer starts with an A rather than a G, so under a U6 promoter they append an extra 5' G (a one-nucleotide mismatch to the genomic target, but at the very PAM-distal end where mismatches are best tolerated) to satisfy the promoter's transcription-start requirement, rather than picking a lower-scoring guide unnecessarily.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why did you choose this specific guide?' is testing whether a student treated guide design as a real engineering decision with named constraints, or just grabbed the first 20-mer next to an NGG. The strong answer distinguishes constraints that are hard requirements of the delivery method (poly-T truncation and the U6 5'-G rule only matter for Pol III-transcribed guides, not chemically synthesized RNPs) from constraints that are about predicted efficiency (GC content, an empirical Rule Set 2 score) — showing the student understands these are different categories of concern, not one undifferentiated checklist.

questions.prompt: Why is a mismatch in the seed region (the ~10-12 nucleotides closest to the PAM) generally more damaging to Cas9 activity than a mismatch at the far end of the spacer?

options.text: The seed region is chemically less stable RNA
R-loop formation nucleates at the PAM and proceeds toward the distal end, so a seed mismatch disrupts heteroduplex formation early
Cas9 only reads the seed region and ignores the rest of the spacer
The seed region is not part of the guide RNA

explanations.a: There is no special chemical instability in the seed region; the effect is mechanistic, not chemical.
explanations.b: Correct — this directly follows from the PAM-first, directional R-loop mechanism: mismatches near the PAM interrupt heteroduplex formation before it can propagate, while distal mismatches are encountered after the R-loop is largely formed.
explanations.c: Cas9 does use the full 20-nt spacer for binding; distal mismatches are simply better tolerated, not ignored entirely.
explanations.d: The seed region is the PAM-proximal ~10-12 nucleotides of the spacer itself, not a separate element.

questions.prompt: A guide RNA transcribed from a U6 (Pol III) promoter contains the sequence ...TTTTG... within its 20-nt spacer. What problem does this create?

options.text: None — poly-T runs are irrelevant to Pol III transcription
The TTTT run acts as a Pol III terminator, likely truncating the guide transcript
It increases GC content above the acceptable range
It prevents the guide from folding its scaffold stem-loops

explanations.a: Poly-T runs are highly relevant — they are a known Pol III termination signal.
explanations.b: Correct — a run of four or more T's is a Pol III terminator, so this guide would likely have its transcription cut short by the U6 promoter system.
explanations.c: A poly-T run lowers, not raises, local GC content.
explanations.d: The scaffold stem-loops are downstream of the spacer and are a separate structural element from this transcription-termination issue.

questions.prompt: Match each guide RNA design constraint to its underlying cause.

left.text: Guide should start with a 5' G

right.text: U6 promoter requires the transcript to begin with G
Poly-T acts as a Pol III transcription terminator
Too low destabilizes the RNA:DNA heteroduplex, too high hinders unwinding
Resist nuclease degradation and reduce innate immune activation for RNP delivery

questions.explanation: Poly-T runs terminate Pol III transcription prematurely; the U6 promoter's transcription-start requirement is a 5' G; GC content in a moderate range balances heteroduplex stability against unwinding; chemical modifications like 2'-O-methylation and phosphorothioate linkages protect synthetic guides used in RNP delivery.

questions.prompt: Doench and colleagues' Rule Set 2 (Azimuth) score, published in 2016, was trained on what kind of data to predict guide efficiency?

options.text: A large multi-gene panel of guides tiling NGG PAM sites, using positional/dinucleotide features and GC content
A single guide's activity extrapolated to the whole genome
Only the guide's predicted melting temperature, with no other features
Off-target cleavage data exclusively, with no on-target measurements

explanations.a: Correct — Rule Set 2 was trained on a large multi-gene panel of sgRNAs tiling NGG sites, using a machine-learning model over nucleotide position/frequency, GC content, and melting-temperature features to predict on-target cutting efficiency.
explanations.b: The model's strength comes from a large multi-gene dataset, not extrapolation from a single guide.
explanations.c: Melting temperature is one of several features used, not the only one.
explanations.d: Rule Set 2 is an on-target activity predictor; off-target scoring uses separate schemes like CFD (Unit 5).

lessons.label: Predicting Off-Targets Before You Cut

sections.heading: Mismatch tolerance is uneven, not absolute
sections.body: Hsu and colleagues' 2013 systematic study tested guides against thousands of near-matching genomic sites and confirmed what Unit 4's seed-region logic predicts: Cas9 tolerates mismatches unevenly depending on position, with PAM-distal mismatches tolerated far more readily than PAM-proximal ones, and tolerance also depending on how many mismatches cluster together and how far apart they are. This means an off-target site is not simply 'close enough' or 'not close enough' by total mismatch count — a site with three mismatches all clustered in the PAM-distal 8 nucleotides can be cut nearly as efficiently as a perfect match, while a single mismatch placed in the seed region can abolish cutting almost entirely. Any off-target search that just counts total mismatches without weighting position will misrank real risk.

sections.heading: Bulges: the off-targets naive alignment misses
sections.body: A second complication is that Cas9 can tolerate small insertions or deletions between guide and target, not just substitutions. A DNA bulge (an extra, unpaired base in the target DNA) or an RNA bulge (an extra, unpaired base in the guide) lets the guide bind and sometimes cut a site that would be invisible to a simple mismatch-counting alignment, because the sequences only align if you allow a one- or two-base gap rather than a straight base-for-base comparison. These bulge-tolerant off-targets were a documented blind spot of early naive seed-matching searches, and modern off-target search tools explicitly search for small insertions/deletions alongside substitution mismatches for exactly this reason.

sections.heading: Scoring schemes and honest limits
sections.body: Two scoring schemes aggregate this positional complexity into a single usable number. The MIT specificity score (Hsu et al., 2013) assigns a weighted penalty to a mismatch based on its position and combines penalties across all predicted off-target sites into one specificity score for a guide. The Cutting Frequency Determination (CFD) score, from Doench and colleagues' 2016 Rule Set 2 paper, instead uses empirically measured cutting frequencies for specific mismatch types at specific positions, generally considered a better-calibrated predictor of real off-target cutting than pure positional weighting. Tools like CRISPOR (Haeussler et al., 2016) run a candidate guide against a reference genome, list predicted off-target sites with both MIT and CFD scores, and flag bulge-tolerant matches, while Cas-OFFinder (Bae et al., 2014) is a fast standalone search engine that finds sites within a specified number of mismatches and bulges genome-wide. The honest limit to state plainly: these tools rank and filter candidate guides by predicted risk, they do not certify that a guide is off-target-free — only empirical genome-wide off-target assays can confirm what a guide actually cut in cells, which is exactly why those assays exist as a separate, necessary step.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs a candidate guide through CRISPOR and gets an MIT specificity score of 62 (out of 100) with one predicted off-target site in an intron, flagged as a 3-mismatch match all falling in the PAM-distal region. A second candidate guide scores 89 with no predicted off-targets under 3 mismatches. Picking the second guide on specificity score alone, the student still notes in their methods that CRISPOR's prediction did not include a bulge search at relaxed stringency, and that they cannot claim the guide is off-target-free from the score alone — only a downstream empirical assay would confirm the actual cut sites in their cell line.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about off-target prediction is checking whether a student can distinguish computational risk-ranking from experimental proof — a common overclaim is saying 'I checked CRISPOR and there were no off-targets, so my guide is specific.' The strong answer states plainly that in silico tools rank candidates by predicted risk using position-weighted and empirically-calibrated scores (naming MIT score or CFD specifically), while acknowledging bulges and imperfect prediction mean a clean computational score is not proof — only an empirical off-target assay closes that gap.

questions.prompt: Why is counting total mismatches alone an unreliable way to predict whether Cas9 will cut a near-matching off-target site?

options.text: Mismatch tolerance depends on position — PAM-distal mismatches are tolerated much more than PAM-proximal ones — not just total count
Cas9 never tolerates any mismatches, so counting is unnecessary
Total mismatch count is actually the only factor that matters
Off-target sites always have zero mismatches

explanations.a: Correct — Hsu and colleagues (2013) showed tolerance is strongly position-dependent, so a guide with several clustered PAM-distal mismatches can still cut efficiently while a single PAM-proximal mismatch can block cutting, making raw mismatch counts an unreliable proxy.
explanations.b: Cas9 does tolerate mismatches, especially PAM-distal ones, which is exactly why off-target cutting is a real concern.
explanations.c: Total count matters less than position and clustering pattern, per the position-weighted evidence.
explanations.d: Off-target sites by definition have at least one mismatch or bulge relative to the intended target; a perfect match is the on-target site.

questions.prompt: What is a DNA or RNA 'bulge' in the context of Cas9 off-target binding, and why does it matter for prediction?

options.text: An extra, unpaired base in the target DNA or guide RNA that lets binding occur at a site invisible to simple substitution-only alignment
A physical swelling of the Cas9 protein during catalysis
A type of PAM variant found only in Cas12a
A mismatch that always prevents any binding

explanations.a: Correct — a bulge is an extra unpaired base on one side of the guide:DNA duplex, and because it requires a small gap in the alignment rather than a straight substitution comparison, naive mismatch-only searches can miss these off-target sites entirely.
explanations.b: This is not a description of any physical conformational phenomenon of the protein; 'bulge' refers to the nucleic acid duplex geometry.
explanations.c: Bulges are a general Cas9 off-target phenomenon, not a PAM-related concept specific to Cas12a.
explanations.d: Bulges are notable precisely because they can still permit binding and cutting, not prevent it.

questions.prompt: Match each off-target prediction tool or score to its description.

right.text: Aggregates position-weighted mismatch penalties across predicted off-target sites into one score (Hsu et al., 2013)
Uses empirically measured cutting frequencies for specific mismatch types/positions (Doench et al., 2016)
Web tool that lists predicted off-targets with both MIT and CFD scores, flagging bulge-tolerant matches (Haeussler et al., 2016)
Fast standalone genome-wide search engine for sites within a set number of mismatches and bulges (Bae et al., 2014)

questions.explanation: The MIT score is Hsu and colleagues' position-weighted aggregate specificity metric; CFD is Doench and colleagues' empirically calibrated mismatch-type/position score; CRISPOR is a web platform reporting both scores plus bulge-aware off-target lists; Cas-OFFinder is a fast dedicated genome-wide search tool for mismatch- and bulge-tolerant matches.

questions.prompt: What is the honest limit of in silico off-target prediction tools like CRISPOR or Cas-OFFinder?

options.text: They rank and filter candidate guides by predicted risk but cannot certify that a guide is off-target-free in cells
They provide a legally binding guarantee of guide specificity
They eliminate the need for any empirical off-target assay
They can only be used for Cas9, never for other Cas orthologs

explanations.a: Correct — these tools rank candidates by predicted risk using positional and empirical scoring, but only empirical genome-wide assays can confirm actual off-target cutting in a given cell type.
explanations.b: No prediction tool offers any such guarantee; they are computational estimates, not certifications.
explanations.c: Prediction narrows candidates but does not replace empirical validation, which remains a necessary downstream step.
explanations.d: These tools are generally usable across Cas orthologs with appropriate PAM settings, not restricted to Cas9 alone.

lessons.label: Choosing the Cut Site for the Experiment You Want

sections.heading: Which exon, and how far from the start codon
sections.body: For a full loss-of-function knockout, the cut site needs to land in an exon that is present in every transcript isoform of the gene — an alternatively spliced exon skipped in some isoforms leaves those transcripts untouched and still functional. Position matters too: cutting immediately at or just after the start codon seems intuitive, but it is often a trap, because ribosomes can reinitiate translation at a downstream in-frame ATG if the first one is disrupted, producing a truncated but sometimes partially functional protein from an internal start site. The safer target is an early constitutive exon that is far enough past the annotated start codon to make downstream reinitiation land somewhere that actually disrupts function, rather than the very first codons of the gene.

sections.heading: Frameshift escape routes
sections.body: A CRISPR cut relies on the cell's error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair to create small insertions or deletions, and not every indel is a knockout. An indel of a length divisible by three preserves the reading frame, potentially producing an internally-shortened but still-folded, partially functional protein rather than a null allele — this in-frame escape is a real and commonly observed outcome, not a rare edge case. Premature stop codons from out-of-frame indels usually trigger nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), which degrades the mutant transcript, but NMD is itself position-dependent: a premature stop codon in the last exon, or very close to it, typically escapes NMD surveillance and can still produce a stable truncated protein. Because of these two escape routes, targeting an exon that encodes a known functional domain (not just any constitutive exon) raises the odds that even an in-frame or NMD-escaping indel still breaks something essential. Cutting at a splice acceptor or donor site is a related but distinct strategy: it can force exon skipping rather than simple indel formation, which is sometimes the goal (modeling a specific isoform loss) and sometimes an unwanted confound (an in-frame skipped exon can also restore a reading frame).

sections.heading: Sequence identity and copy number outside the target gene
sections.body: Two more traps sit outside the gene model itself. Paralogs and pseudogenes with near-identical sequence to the target exon can share a guide's binding site closely enough to be cut as unintended off-targets (Unit 5's mismatch-tolerance logic applies directly here), so a guide needs to be checked against the whole genome, not just aligned to the one gene of interest. And copy number at the locus determines how many alleles actually need editing to get a full knockout: a diploid autosomal gene needs both alleles disrupted, but a locus with a segmental duplication, a copy-number variant, or (in the case of some clinical or cell-line contexts) aneuploidy may carry more than two copies, meaning a bulk-edited population can retain a residual functional allele even when editing efficiency looks high per-allele.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to knock out a signaling gene and initially designs a guide 15 base pairs downstream of the annotated start codon in exon 1. Sequencing edited clones shows several still express a faint but detectable protein band on a western blot. Checking the gene model, they find an in-frame ATG 40 codons downstream of their cut site that can serve as an alternative start, and their target exon is also alternatively spliced out in one minor isoform. They redesign against a constitutive exon encoding the kinase domain, further downstream, where even reinitiation or an in-frame indel is far more likely to land inside a domain required for function rather than upstream of it — and the redesigned clones show a clean loss of the protein band.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why did you cut there and not somewhere else in the gene?' is testing whether a student treated exon and position choice as a real design decision or just picked the first NGG they found. The strong answer names a specific trap they considered and avoided — downstream ATG reinitiation, an alternatively spliced exon, in-frame indel escape, NMD escape near the last exon, a near-identical paralog, or locus copy number — and explains how their chosen site avoided it, rather than offering a generic claim that 'we picked an early exon to make sure the gene was knocked out.'

questions.prompt: Why is cutting immediately at the very start codon of a gene sometimes a poor choice for a knockout, even though it seems like the earliest possible disruption point?

options.text: The start codon region is never accessible to Cas9
A downstream in-frame ATG can serve as an alternative translation start, producing a truncated but sometimes partially functional protein
Cutting at the start codon always produces the largest possible deletion
The start codon has no PAM sites nearby in any gene

explanations.a: Accessibility is not generally the limiting issue at start codons; the concern is downstream translational reinitiation.
explanations.b: Correct — ribosomal reinitiation at a downstream in-frame ATG can rescue a functional or partially functional protein even when the first start codon is disrupted, so cutting immediately at the start is not automatically a clean knockout.
explanations.c: Deletion size is determined by NHEJ repair outcomes, not by proximity to the start codon.
explanations.d: PAM site availability varies by local sequence, but that is not the reason this position is risky.

questions.prompt: A CRISPR-induced indel that is a multiple of 3 base pairs in length is a design concern because:

options.text: It preserves the reading frame, potentially producing an internally-shortened but still partly functional protein rather than a true null
It always triggers nonsense-mediated decay
It cannot occur through NHEJ repair
It only happens when targeting splice sites

explanations.a: Correct — an in-frame indel does not introduce a premature stop codon, so translation can continue and yield a protein that may retain partial function, undermining a clean knockout.
explanations.b: In-frame indels lack a premature stop codon, so they typically do not trigger NMD, which targets transcripts with premature stops.
explanations.c: In-frame indels are a routine possible outcome of NHEJ's error-prone repair, occurring alongside frameshifting indels.
explanations.d: In-frame indels can occur at any NHEJ-repaired cut site, not only at splice sites.

questions.prompt: A premature stop codon introduced very close to the last exon of a gene is more likely than one introduced mid-gene to:

options.text: Escape nonsense-mediated decay and still produce a stable truncated protein
Be immediately degraded by NMD with total certainty
Prevent transcription of the gene entirely
Have no effect on protein product at all

explanations.a: Correct — NMD surveillance is position-dependent, and premature stop codons located in the last exon (or very close to it) typically escape NMD, allowing a stable truncated protein to be produced.
explanations.b: NMD efficiency drops sharply for stop codons near the last exon; this option describes the opposite of the position-dependence.
explanations.c: NMD acts post-transcriptionally on the mRNA transcript, not by blocking transcription itself.
explanations.d: An NMD-escaping premature stop still changes the protein product by truncating it, even if the transcript is stable.

questions.prompt: Why does gene copy number at a target locus matter when evaluating whether an edited cell population is a true knockout?

options.text: A locus with more than two copies (e.g., via segmental duplication or copy-number variation) may retain a functional, unedited allele even with high per-allele editing efficiency
Copy number never varies between cells or cell lines
Editing efficiency is always 100% regardless of allele count
Copy number only matters for genes on the Y chromosome

explanations.a: Correct — if the locus has extra copies beyond the standard diploid two, a bulk-edited population can retain a residual functional allele even when the reported editing efficiency per allele looks high, because not every copy in every cell was necessarily hit.
explanations.b: Copy number does vary — segmental duplications, CNVs, and aneuploidy in certain cell lines are real and relevant considerations.
explanations.c: Editing efficiency is never assumed to be 100%; that is exactly why allele count and residual wild-type alleles matter.
explanations.d: Copy number variation is a general genomic phenomenon relevant to any locus, not restricted to the Y chromosome.

lessons.label: Getting Cas9 to Behave: Plasmid, mRNA, and RNP

sections.heading: The axis that matters: how long active nuclease persists
sections.body: Cas9 and its guide RNA can be delivered into a cell in three basic formats, and the choice between them mostly comes down to one variable: how long active, cutting-competent Cas9 persists inside the cell. Longer persistence gives more chances for the intended cut, but also more chances for off-target cutting and unwanted genomic side effects, since every extra hour of active nuclease is another window for a rare mismatched site to get hit. Plasmid DNA encoding Cas9 and the sgRNA is transcribed and translated continuously as long as the plasmid persists, giving expression that can last for days; it is cheap to produce, easy to scale, and can carry a selection marker (such as a puromycin-resistance gene) to enrich for transfected cells. The cost is that plasmid DNA is itself a piece of foreign genetic material, and there is a documented risk of fragments of the plasmid backbone integrating at the cut site during repair, contaminating the edited locus with vector sequence.

sections.heading: mRNA and RNP: shorter windows, cleaner edits
sections.body: Delivering Cas9 as in vitro-transcribed mRNA shortens that window: the mRNA is translated into protein and then degraded by normal cellular turnover, giving a shorter burst of Cas9 activity than a continuously-expressing plasmid, without introducing any DNA into the cell. Going further, delivering Cas9 as a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) — the Cas9 protein pre-complexed with its sgRNA in a tube before ever entering the cell — compresses the active window the most: RNP-delivered Cas9 becomes active within hours of delivery and is cleared by normal cellular protein degradation within roughly 24-48 hours. Because the nuclease is active for such a short, defined window, RNP delivery generally gives the best specificity per unit of on-target editing achieved, and since no Cas9-encoding DNA or plasmid backbone ever enters the cell, there is no risk of foreign DNA integration into the genome at all.

sections.heading: Multiplexing and why RNP is now the default for primary cells
sections.body: Any of these formats can be multiplexed by delivering an arrayed set of several distinct guide RNAs alongside Cas9, targeting multiple genes or multiple sites in one gene simultaneously — Cas12a is naturally suited to this because it processes its own crRNA array from a single transcript, while Cas9 multiplexing typically means delivering several separate sgRNAs together. RNP electroporation has become the default delivery method for primary cells (T cells, hematopoietic stem cells) and for ex vivo clinical editing specifically because these cell types are sensitive to prolonged nuclease exposure and to foreign DNA, and RNP sidesteps both concerns. The clearest real-world example is exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy), the CRISPR-Cas9 therapy that the FDA approved for sickle cell disease on December 8, 2023, and later for transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia on January 16, 2024: it works by editing a patient's own CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells ex vivo via RNP electroporation before returning them to the patient, precisely the short-exposure, no-foreign-DNA profile that makes RNP the preferred format for this kind of therapeutic cell editing.

lessons.workedExample: A lab needs to edit primary human T cells for a short-term functional assay and is choosing between a Cas9-expressing plasmid and RNP electroporation. Plasmid transfection into primary T cells triggers a strong innate immune (interferon) response and poor cell viability, a common problem with introducing foreign DNA into primary immune cells, and the multi-day expression window also raises off-target risk in an already stressed cell population. Switching to RNP electroporation — Cas9 protein pre-complexed with sgRNA delivered directly, active within hours and cleared within about two days — improves both viability and editing specificity, which is exactly why RNP is the standard choice for primary and therapeutic cell editing rather than a corner case.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why did you deliver Cas9 this way and not another way' wants a student to reason from the actual biology — nuclease exposure time versus off-target risk versus foreign-DNA risk — rather than just naming a delivery method by rote. The strong answer explains the persistence gradient (plasmid: days: RNA: shorter burst; RNP: hours, cleared within ~24-48h) and ties a specific delivery choice to a specific cell type's sensitivities, ideally citing that this is the same logic behind why an approved therapy like Casgevy uses RNP electroporation on primary stem cells rather than a plasmid.

questions.prompt: Order these three Cas9 delivery formats from longest to shortest duration of active nuclease persistence in the cell.

items.text: Plasmid DNA encoding Cas9 and sgRNA
In vitro-transcribed Cas9 mRNA
Ribonucleoprotein (Cas9 protein pre-complexed with sgRNA)

questions.explanation: Plasmid DNA gives continuous expression that can last days as long as the plasmid persists; mRNA gives a shorter translational burst before normal turnover degrades it; RNP is active within hours and cleared within roughly 24-48 hours, the shortest window of the three.

questions.prompt: What is a documented risk specifically associated with delivering Cas9 via plasmid DNA rather than RNP?

options.text: Fragments of the plasmid backbone can integrate at the cut site during repair
Plasmid delivery cannot produce any detectable editing
Plasmid-delivered Cas9 is cleared within minutes, too fast to cut
Plasmids cannot carry a selection marker

explanations.a: Correct — because plasmid DNA is present in the cell during repair of the Cas9-induced break, fragments of the vector backbone can become integrated at the cut site, contaminating the edited locus.
explanations.b: Plasmid delivery is a standard, effective method that does produce editing; the concern is a specific integration risk, not lack of efficacy.
explanations.c: Plasmid-driven expression is the longest-lasting of the three formats, not the fastest to clear.
explanations.d: Plasmids commonly do carry selection markers (e.g., puromycin resistance), which is actually cited as one of their practical advantages.

questions.prompt: Why has RNP electroporation become the default Cas9 delivery method for primary cells like T cells and hematopoietic stem cells, and for clinical ex vivo editing such as Casgevy?

options.text: RNP's short active window and absence of foreign DNA minimize prolonged nuclease exposure and DNA-integration risk in cells that are especially sensitive to both
RNP is the cheapest delivery format available
RNP requires no guide RNA at all
RNP produces permanent, continuous Cas9 expression for maximal editing

explanations.a: Correct — primary and therapeutic cell types are sensitive to prolonged nuclease exposure and to introduced foreign DNA, and RNP's short (hours, cleared by ~24-48h) active window with no DNA payload directly addresses both concerns, which is why Casgevy's ex vivo hematopoietic stem cell editing uses RNP electroporation.
explanations.b: Cost is not the deciding factor here; RNP protein production is often more expensive than plasmid DNA production, but it is chosen for its safety/specificity profile.
explanations.c: RNP still requires a pre-complexed sgRNA together with the Cas9 protein; it is not guide-free.
explanations.d: RNP gives the shortest exposure window of the three formats, the opposite of continuous expression.

questions.prompt: Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), the first FDA-approved CRISPR-based therapy, approved December 8, 2023, treats sickle cell disease by:

options.text: Injecting Cas9 mRNA directly into the patient's bloodstream
Editing a patient's own CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells ex vivo via RNP electroporation, then returning them to the patient
Using a plasmid-based in vivo gene therapy delivered by AAV
Editing cells inside the patient's body without ever removing them

explanations.a: Casgevy does not involve direct bloodstream injection of Cas9 mRNA; editing happens ex vivo on isolated cells.
explanations.b: Correct — Casgevy edits the patient's own CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells outside the body via RNP electroporation before reinfusing them, exactly the short-exposure, no-foreign-DNA delivery profile RNP is chosen for.
explanations.c: Casgevy is an ex vivo cell therapy, not an in vivo AAV-delivered plasmid approach.
explanations.d: The cells are removed from the patient, edited ex vivo, and then reinfused — editing is not performed inside the body.

units.label: Plasmids, Cloning, and Delivery: Building and Shipping the Editor

lessons.label: Reading a Plasmid Map

sections.heading: An editing plasmid is several genes sharing one circle
sections.body: The vector Cong et al. (2013) built to bring CRISPR into mammalian cells, pX330, still shows the anatomy every SpCas9 plasmid inherits. A bacterial origin of replication (often a high-copy pUC-derived ori, hundreds of copies per cell, versus a low-copy pBR322 ori around 15-20) sets how much plasmid a prep yields. An antibiotic-resistance gene — usually bla, conferring ampicillin resistance via beta-lactamase — lets only plasmid-bearing E. coli survive on a selective plate. Neither element does anything in a human cell; they exist purely so the plasmid can be propagated and selected in bacteria before it is ever delivered. The whole backbone is a useful anchor for reading any map like it: pX330 runs about 8.5 kilobases end to end, small enough that a single Sanger read or a quick restriction digest can sanity-check the whole construct.

sections.heading: Two promoters, because Cas9 and the guide are transcribed differently
sections.body: The guide RNA is driven by a U6 promoter, recognized by RNA polymerase III, which is chosen because Pol III initiates transcription at a precise, defined nucleotide and terminates at a simple poly-T stretch without needing a 5' cap or poly-A tail — exactly what a short, unmodified sgRNA needs. Cas9 itself is a protein-coding gene, so it needs Pol II machinery: a promoter such as CBh, CMV, EF1a, or CAG, followed downstream by a polyadenylation signal (commonly bovine growth hormone or SV40 polyA) that cleaves the transcript and adds the poly-A tail required for nuclear export and stability. Cas9's coding sequence is flanked by nuclear localization signal (NLS) tags — typically an SV40 NLS and a nucleoplasmin NLS on opposite termini — because the ~160 kDa protein cannot cross the nuclear envelope unassisted to reach genomic DNA.

sections.heading: The cloning site, and Addgene as shared infrastructure
sections.body: Between the U6 promoter and the guide scaffold sits a filler sequence about 2 kilobases long, flanked by BbsI sites — the multiple cloning site a researcher cuts out and replaces with their own 20-nucleotide targeting sequence. The filler is deliberately sized to be large relative to the tiny guide insert, so a gel or a quick size check immediately shows whether the cloning worked: an uncut or re-ligated vector still carrying the ~2 kb filler runs visibly larger than one that swapped it for a 20-nt guide. Rather than re-clone from scratch, most labs order the exact plasmid used in a published paper from Addgene, a nonprofit repository founded in 2004 where depositing a plasmid on publication is now a near-universal norm. An Addgene entry lists the catalog number, the depositing lab, a full annotated sequence map, and any required co-transfection components — turning a plasmid described in a methods section into a physical tube that arrives in the mail.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to knock out a gene using a plasmid resembling pX330. They search Addgene, find the deposited plasmid, and check its map before ordering: a pUC-type ori (high copy, for a large miniprep yield), an ampicillin-resistance gene (so LB-amp plates select for it), a U6 promoter feeding into a BbsI-flanked filler upstream of the sgRNA scaffold, and a CBh promoter driving SpCas9-2xNLS, terminated by a bGH polyA signal. Recognizing that the U6/BbsI cassette is where their guide sequence must be cloned in — and that nothing else on the map needs to change — tells them exactly which single step separates the stock plasmid from a working, gene-specific editor.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks a student to walk through their plasmid map is testing whether the student understands the tool they used, not just that they used it. A student who can point to the ori and explain why it affects yield, name which promoter drives the guide versus Cas9 and why they differ (Pol III versus Pol II), and explain what the NLS tags are for shows they engineered a construct. A student who says 'it's the CRISPR plasmid' and cannot locate a single labeled element on their own map is a signal the plasmid was used as a black box.

questions.prompt: Why is the sgRNA in a plasmid like pX330 driven by a U6 (Pol III) promoter instead of a Pol II promoter like CBh?

options.text: Pol III initiates and terminates transcription precisely without needing a 5' cap or poly-A tail, which suits a short unmodified RNA
Pol III promoters are stronger in bacteria, where the plasmid is first grown
Cas9 requires Pol II, so the guide must use a different polymerase to avoid competition
U6 is the only promoter small enough to fit on a plasmid

explanations.a: Correct — Pol III gives a precisely defined transcription start and a simple termination signal, matching what an unmodified, uncapped, non-polyadenylated sgRNA needs.
explanations.b: Promoter activity in bacteria is irrelevant; these elements only function once the plasmid is delivered into a mammalian cell.
explanations.c: The two genes do not compete for polymerase in a way that would require this split — the split reflects what each transcript needs structurally, not resource competition.
explanations.d: Promoter size is not the driving reason; U6 is chosen for the properties of Pol III transcription, not compactness.

questions.prompt: The bacterial origin of replication and the ampicillin-resistance gene on an editing plasmid are used for:

options.text: Editing the genome once the plasmid reaches a mammalian cell
Propagating and selecting the plasmid in E. coli before delivery
Localizing Cas9 to the nucleus
Terminating transcription of the sgRNA

explanations.a: The ori and resistance gene have no function inside a mammalian cell; they only matter during bacterial propagation.
explanations.b: Correct — the ori sets copy number for the miniprep yield, and the resistance gene lets only plasmid-bearing bacteria grow on selective plates.
explanations.c: Nuclear localization is the job of the NLS tags fused to Cas9, not the ori or resistance gene.
explanations.d: Transcription termination of the sgRNA is handled by the Pol III terminator sequence, unrelated to these bacterial elements.

questions.prompt: Match each plasmid element to its function.

right.text: Directs the Cas9 protein into the nucleus
Cleaves the Cas9 transcript and adds a poly-A tail
Removed and replaced with the researcher's 20-nt guide sequence
Lets other labs order the exact published plasmid instead of re-cloning it

questions.explanation: NLS tags import Cas9 into the nucleus; the polyA signal terminates and stabilizes the Cas9 transcript; the BbsI filler is the cloning site swapped for a specific guide; and depositing on Addgene lets the field share exact, verified constructs instead of everyone re-cloning from the paper's methods section.

questions.prompt: A plasmid with a high-copy pUC-type origin of replication, compared to one with a low-copy pBR322 ori, will generally:

options.text: Edit the genome more efficiently once delivered to a human cell
Yield more plasmid DNA per miniprep, because more copies exist per bacterial cell
Be resistant to a broader range of antibiotics
Express Cas9 from a stronger promoter

explanations.a: Copy number in bacteria has no direct bearing on editing efficiency in a mammalian cell — that depends on the mammalian promoter, NLS, and delivery method.
explanations.b: Correct — a high-copy ori like pUC can push plasmid copy number into the hundreds per bacterial cell versus roughly 15-20 for a low-copy pBR322 ori, directly increasing miniprep yield.
explanations.c: Antibiotic resistance is conferred by a separate resistance gene, not by the origin of replication.
explanations.d: Promoter strength for Cas9 expression is set by the chosen Pol II promoter (e.g., CBh, CMV, EF1a, CAG), independent of the bacterial origin.

lessons.label: Cloning a Guide into a Vector

sections.heading: The standard oligo-annealing workflow
sections.body: The most common way to install a specific guide into a plasmid like pX330 does not use a full restriction/ligation reaction with two separate DNA fragments. Instead, a researcher orders two short complementary single-stranded oligonucleotides — one for the top strand, one for the bottom — each carrying the 20-nucleotide target sequence plus a few extra bases on the ends that, once annealed to each other, form overhangs matching the sticky ends left after the vector is cut with BbsI. The two oligos are mixed, heated to around 95°C, and slowly cooled so they anneal into a short double-stranded fragment with the correct overhangs, then ligated directly into the BbsI-digested backbone with T4 DNA ligase — no PCR, no gel purification of an insert, because the 'insert' is synthesized as oligos in the first place.

sections.heading: Golden Gate: cutting outside the recognition site
sections.body: BbsI and BsaI belong to the Type IIS restriction enzyme class, which cut DNA a fixed distance outside their own recognition sequence rather than within it — the basis of Golden Gate assembly, formalized by Engler et al. (2008). Because the cut site is separate from the recognition site, the recognition sequence is removed from the final ligated product, so the assembled construct is no longer a substrate for the same enzyme; digestion and ligation can run in one pot without the enzyme re-cutting its own output, and the designed 4-nucleotide overhangs enforce a specific order and orientation for multiple fragments at once. This is why Golden Gate became the standard for arrayed multi-guide libraries and for assembling TALEN repeat-variable-diresidue modules, where many fragments (often a dozen or more repeat units) must snap together in one defined sequence in a single reaction.

sections.heading: Gibson assembly and Gateway as alternatives
sections.body: Gibson assembly (Gibson et al., 2009) takes a different route: fragments are designed with 20-40 base pairs of shared sequence at their ends, and a single isothermal reaction at 50°C combines a 5' exonuclease (chews back ends to expose single-stranded overhangs), a DNA polymerase (fills remaining gaps), and a DNA ligase (seals the nicks) — sequence-independent, so it does not require any particular restriction site and scales well to assembling several large fragments at once. Gateway cloning, built around bacteriophage lambda att recombination sites, instead uses proprietary recombinase enzyme mixes (BP and LR clonase) to shuttle an insert between a Gateway 'entry' vector and any number of compatible 'destination' vectors without restriction enzymes or ligase at all, which is efficient when the same insert needs to move into many different expression backbones.

lessons.workedExample: A lab needs to build a library of 200 distinct sgRNA-expressing plasmids targeting 200 different genes for a pooled screen. Ordering and individually restriction-digesting 200 separate insert fragments would be slow and error-prone. Instead they design 200 oligo pairs, each with the same BbsI-compatible overhangs but a different 20-nt targeting sequence in the middle, anneal each pair, and ligate each into BbsI-cut backbone in parallel, one-pot reactions — the identical overhangs on every pair let the same Golden Gate protocol run uniformly across all 200 constructs without redesigning the cloning strategy for each guide.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing the cloning step wants to know whether a student can explain why their specific method was chosen rather than reciting 'we cloned in the guide.' The strong answer names the enzyme class (Type IIS, cutting outside its recognition site) and explains why that property — not just 'it worked' — allows scarless, directional, one-pot assembly, or contrasts it correctly against Gibson's overlap-based mechanism. A student who cannot say whether their enzyme cuts within or outside its recognition sequence has memorized a protocol step without understanding why it works.

questions.prompt: Why can Golden Gate assembly run digestion and ligation together in a single one-pot reaction without the enzyme destroying the final product?

options.text: The ligase permanently inactivates the restriction enzyme
Type IIS enzymes like BsaI and BbsI cut outside their recognition sequence, so the recognition site is removed from the ligated product and cannot be re-cut
The reaction is run at a temperature too low for the restriction enzyme to function
Golden Gate does not actually use any restriction enzyme

explanations.a: Ligase does not inactivate the restriction enzyme; both remain active throughout the reaction.
explanations.b: Correct — because the recognition site sits outside the cut site, it ends up on the discarded fragment rather than the assembled product, so the final construct is no longer a substrate and the reaction can proceed to completion in one pot.
explanations.c: The enzymes used are chosen to be active at the reaction temperature; temperature is not what prevents re-cutting.
explanations.d: Golden Gate specifically relies on Type IIS restriction enzymes such as BsaI or BbsI.

questions.prompt: In Gibson assembly, what role does the 5' exonuclease play?

options.text: It chews back the 5' ends of each fragment to expose single-stranded overhangs that anneal to complementary overlaps on adjacent fragments
It seals nicks left after the fragments anneal
It fills in gaps left after annealing
It recognizes and cuts a specific 6-8 bp restriction site

explanations.a: Correct — the exonuclease creates single-stranded 5' overhangs that let fragments with shared 20-40 bp end sequences anneal to each other.
explanations.b: Sealing nicks is the ligase's job in the Gibson cocktail, not the exonuclease's.
explanations.c: Gap-filling is done by the DNA polymerase in the same reaction, not the exonuclease.
explanations.d: Gibson assembly is sequence-independent and does not rely on restriction sites at all.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the standard oligo-annealing workflow for cloning a single guide into a BbsI-cut vector.

items.text: Order two complementary oligos carrying the target sequence and matching overhangs
Heat and slowly cool the oligos so they anneal into a short double-stranded fragment
Digest the vector backbone with BbsI to expose compatible sticky ends
Ligate the annealed insert into the digested backbone with T4 DNA ligase

questions.explanation: The oligos are designed and ordered first, the vector is separately digested to expose the correct overhangs, the oligos are annealed to each other, and finally the annealed insert is ligated into the cut backbone.

questions.prompt: Why is Golden Gate assembly the standard choice for building TALEN repeat-variable-diresidue arrays, which require assembling many repeat modules in a defined order?

options.text: TALEN repeats cannot be joined by any other cloning method
Golden Gate's designed overhangs enforce a specific order and orientation for many fragments assembled in a single one-pot reaction
Golden Gate is the cheapest method regardless of the number of fragments
TALEN repeats have no repetitive sequence, so any method works equally well

explanations.a: Other methods exist in principle, but the ordering problem for many nearly identical repeat modules makes some methods impractical, not impossible.
explanations.b: Correct — because each junction's 4-nt overhang is custom-designed, a dozen or more repeat modules can only ligate in the intended order, which is exactly what an array of similar repeats needs.
explanations.c: Cost is not the reason Golden Gate is favored here; the ordering/orientation control is.
explanations.d: TALEN repeat modules are highly repetitive in sequence, which is precisely why a method with sequence-independent, overhang-defined ordering (like Golden Gate) is needed instead of relying on unique sequence for correct assembly.

lessons.label: Transformation and Confirming the Construct

sections.heading: Getting the ligated plasmid into bacteria
sections.body: A ligation reaction is a soup of DNA, not a usable reagent, until it is propagated inside living bacteria. Chemically competent E. coli — cells treated with calcium chloride to make their membranes transiently permeable to DNA — take up plasmid via heat shock, briefly raising the temperature to around 42°C for 30-45 seconds then returning cells to ice, which is thought to create a transient thermal imbalance that drives DNA across the destabilized membrane. Electroporation instead uses a brief high-voltage pulse to open transient pores in the membrane, and electrocompetent cells reach far higher transformation efficiencies — up to roughly 10^9-10^10 colony-forming units (cfu) per microgram of DNA, versus roughly 10^6-10^8 cfu/µg for chemically competent cells — but the ligation mix must first be desalted, since residual salt causes arcing during the electric pulse.

sections.heading: From a plate of colonies to a confirmed clone
sections.body: Transformed cells are plated on agar containing the plasmid's antibiotic (an LB-ampicillin plate for a bla-marked vector), so only colonies carrying the plasmid grow overnight. Individual colonies are screened by colony PCR — touching a pipette tip to a colony and running it directly in a PCR with primers flanking the insert site — a fast way to distinguish colonies likely to carry the insert from those with an empty or unmodified backbone, before committing to a full prep. A colony that PCR-screens positive is grown in liquid culture overnight and miniprepped (alkaline lysis, the method described by Birnboim and Doly in 1979) to purify enough plasmid DNA for further analysis: a diagnostic restriction digest, cutting with an enzyme chosen to give predictable, distinguishable fragment sizes on a gel if the insert and orientation are correct.

sections.heading: Why sequencing, not a digest, is the final gate
sections.body: A restriction digest can only confirm a fragment of the expected size is present — it says nothing about whether the 20-nucleotide guide sequence inside is exactly correct, since a single wrong base would not change fragment size at all. The rule in the field is that no construct is used in an experiment until it has been sequence-verified by Sanger sequencing (the chain-termination method Sanger et al. described in 1977) across the entire insert and its junctions with the vector. Three failure modes recur: empty-vector background, where incomplete restriction digestion leaves some uncut or self-re-ligated backbone that transforms and grows just as well as insert-bearing plasmid, inflating the fraction of 'wrong' colonies; recombination of repetitive elements, where repeat-rich inserts (TALEN repeat arrays, lentiviral LTRs) recombine out during bacterial growth, especially in recA+ strains, which is why repetitive constructs are typically propagated in recombination-deficient strains such as Stbl3; and toxic inserts, where a gene product or regulatory element is mildly toxic to E. coli, causing slow growth, plasmid instability, or selection for spontaneous mutations that inactivate the insert.

lessons.workedExample: A student ligates their annealed guide oligo into a BbsI-cut backbone, transforms chemically competent cells, and gets 40 colonies on their amp plate. Colony PCR on eight colonies shows six give the expected band size and two give a band matching the uncut empty vector — evidence of incomplete BbsI digestion leaving some background. They miniprep two of the six PCR-positive colonies, run a diagnostic digest confirming the expected fragment pattern on both, then Sanger sequence across the guide insertion site. One clone reads perfectly; the other has a single base deleted from the guide sequence, undetectable by the digest alone. Only the sequence-verified clone is carried forward into cell culture.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how do you know your construct was actually correct?' is checking whether a student can distinguish confirmation from wishful thinking. 'I ran a digest and got the right size' is a weaker answer than naming Sanger sequencing across the full insert as the actual gate, because a digest cannot catch a single-base error that would still leave the guide non-functional. A student who can also explain one specific failure mode they screened for — empty-vector background, recombination, or a toxic insert — shows they understand why the verification steps exist, not just that a protocol says to run them.

questions.prompt: Why is a diagnostic restriction digest insufficient on its own to confirm a cloned guide sequence is correct?

options.text: It only confirms fragment sizes are as expected; a single incorrect base inside the guide would not change fragment size
Restriction digests cannot be run on miniprepped plasmid DNA
Restriction enzymes destroy the insert during digestion
A digest can only be performed after Sanger sequencing

explanations.a: Correct — a digest confirms the presence and rough size of an insert, but a point mutation or single-base error within it would not alter fragment size and would go undetected.
explanations.b: Restriction digests are routinely run on miniprepped plasmid DNA; that is their standard use.
explanations.c: A properly designed diagnostic digest cuts at intended sites without destroying the region being analyzed.
explanations.d: The two are independent confirmatory steps; sequencing does not need to precede a digest.

questions.prompt: A researcher wants to transform a large ligation reaction and needs the highest possible transformation efficiency. Which approach is best suited, and what must be done first?

options.text: Heat-shock chemically competent cells directly with the ligation mix, no preparation needed
Electroporate electrocompetent cells, after first desalting the ligation mix
Electroporate chemically competent cells directly with the ligation mix
Heat-shock electrocompetent cells at a higher temperature than usual

explanations.a: Chemically competent heat shock works but yields lower efficiency (roughly 10^6-10^8 cfu/µg) than electroporation.
explanations.b: Correct — electrocompetent cells give the highest efficiency (up to roughly 10^9-10^10 cfu/µg), but salt in the ligation mix causes arcing during the electric pulse, so it must be desalted first.
explanations.c: Electroporation requires electrocompetent cells prepared for that method; chemically competent cells are not interchangeable for this purpose.
explanations.d: Electrocompetent cells are transformed by electric pulse, not heat shock; mixing the two methods is not how either protocol works.

questions.prompt: Match each construct failure mode to its likely cause.

right.text: Incomplete restriction digestion leaves uncut or self-re-ligated backbone that transforms alongside true recombinants
Repeat-rich sequence (e.g., TALEN repeat arrays) is lost during growth in a recA+ strain
The insert's gene product slows bacterial growth or selects for spontaneous inactivating mutations

questions.explanation: Empty-vector background comes from incomplete digestion allowing insert-free backbone to re-transform; recombination loss affects repeat-rich inserts in recombination-proficient (recA+) strains; and toxic inserts impair bacterial growth or get selected against, both of which are reasons every construct must be sequence-verified before use.

questions.prompt: What is the field's rule regarding when a newly cloned construct may be used in an experiment?

options.text: As soon as colony PCR shows the expected band
As soon as a diagnostic restriction digest matches the predicted pattern
Only after it has been sequence-verified by Sanger sequencing across the entire insert and its junctions
As soon as colonies grow on the antibiotic selection plate

explanations.a: Colony PCR is a fast preliminary screen to prioritize which colonies to prep further, not a final confirmation.
explanations.b: A digest confirms size but cannot catch single-base errors within the insert.
explanations.c: Correct — the standard rule is that no construct is used until full Sanger sequencing across the insert and vector junctions confirms the exact expected sequence.
explanations.d: Growth on selective plates only confirms the antibiotic-resistance gene is present and functional, saying nothing about the insert.

lessons.label: Viral Delivery: Lentivirus, AAV, and Adenovirus

sections.heading: Lentivirus: integration for stable lines and screens
sections.body: Lentiviral vectors package roughly 8-9 kilobases of transgene, comfortably fitting a Cas9-plus-guide cassette, and their defining feature is that the viral genome integrates into host chromosomal DNA. That integration is semi-random — studies of integration site preference show a bias toward actively transcribed genes rather than a uniform genome-wide scatter — which creates a real insertional-mutagenesis risk (integration near a proto-oncogene or tumor suppressor can alter its expression) but also gives permanent, heritable expression through every cell division. That permanence is exactly why lentivirus is the standard for building stable cell lines and for pooled CRISPR screens such as the GeCKO libraries (Shalem et al., 2014), where tens of thousands of guides are delivered at low multiplicity of infection so each cell integrates roughly one guide, and that guide's identity persists through selection and expansion.

sections.heading: AAV: small, episomal, and tissue-selective
sections.body: Adeno-associated virus carries a single-stranded DNA genome and packages only about 4.7 kilobases, and unlike lentivirus it remains predominantly episomal — it does not efficiently integrate into the host chromosome, though rare low-frequency integration does occur. Its tropism (which tissues it efficiently transduces) is set by the capsid serotype: AAV8 efficiently transduces liver, AAV9 is notable for reaching the CNS by partially crossing the blood-brain barrier and also transducing muscle, and other serotypes such as AAV2 are used for the eye. Because AAV triggers a comparatively mild immune response and has a long clinical track record — including approved gene therapies such as Luxturna for a retinal disease and Zolgensma for spinal muscular atrophy — it is the workhorse vector for in vivo somatic genome editing in both research and therapeutic settings.

sections.heading: Adenovirus, and the AAV packaging problem
sections.body: Adenoviral vectors accommodate much larger cargo (helper-dependent 'gutless' versions can carry up to roughly 36 kilobases) but provoke a strong innate and adaptive immune response — the risk that caused the death of Jesse Gelsinger in a 1999 gene-therapy trial — making it poorly suited to repeat dosing or long-term expression. AAV's small capacity creates a genuine engineering constraint: SpCas9's coding sequence alone is about 4.2 kilobases, and once a promoter, NLS tags, the guide expression cassette, and a polyA signal are added, the full construct exceeds what a single AAV can carry. Two fixes are used. The first is a dual-vector split-intein strategy (Truong et al., 2015): SpCas9 is divided into two halves, each fused to a self-splicing intein, packaged into two separate AAVs that co-infect the same cell, where the inteins excise themselves and rejoin the two Cas9 halves into a full functional protein. The second is switching to a naturally smaller Cas9 ortholog — Staphylococcus aureus Cas9 (SaCas9), about 3.2 kilobases (Ran et al., 2015) — which is compact enough to fit alongside its guide and promoter in a single AAV, at the cost of a different, longer PAM requirement.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to edit a gene in mouse liver in vivo. Lentivirus is ruled out immediately — integration risk is unacceptable for a therapeutic-style application, and lentivirus does not efficiently transduce non-dividing hepatocytes in vivo the way it transduces dividing cells in culture. Adenovirus could carry full-length SpCas9 easily given its larger capacity, but its strong immunogenicity makes it a poor choice for an approach that might need re-dosing. They choose AAV8, selected specifically for its liver tropism, and because full SpCas9 plus a guide cassette exceeds AAV's ~4.7 kb limit, they switch to SaCas9 (~3.2 kb) so the whole payload fits in one vector rather than needing the split-intein dual-AAV approach.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why did you pick that viral vector?' is testing whether a student chose based on the biology of the vector or just used whatever protocol was handed to them. The strong answer names the specific constraint that ruled out alternatives — integration risk for lentivirus, immunogenicity for adenovirus, packaging capacity for AAV — and, if AAV was used with SpCas9, can explain the packaging problem and which fix (split-intein or a compact ortholog like SaCas9) was chosen and why. A student who cannot say why lentivirus wasn't used instead has not engaged with the actual delivery decision.

questions.prompt: Why does AAV delivery of full-length SpCas9 plus a guide RNA create a packaging problem?

options.text: AAV's genome cannot be single-stranded, and SpCas9 requires double-stranded packaging
SpCas9's coding sequence (~4.2 kb) plus the promoter, NLS tags, guide cassette, and polyA signal exceeds AAV's ~4.7 kb packaging capacity
AAV cannot package any DNA sequence longer than a single gRNA
SpCas9 is toxic to the AAV capsid protein during assembly

explanations.a: AAV packages a single-stranded DNA genome by nature; that is not the source of the SpCas9 packaging problem.
explanations.b: Correct — SpCas9 alone is about 4.2 kb, and adding the required regulatory elements pushes the full cassette past AAV's roughly 4.7 kb limit.
explanations.c: AAV can package cargo well beyond the size of a single guide RNA; the constraint is the combined size of Cas9 plus all needed elements, not guide size.
explanations.d: The limitation is capsid packaging capacity (genome size), not any toxicity between Cas9 and capsid assembly.

questions.prompt: A researcher needs stable, heritable Cas9 expression in a dividing cell line for a pooled CRISPR screen. Which vector is the standard choice, and why?

options.text: AAV, because it has the mildest immune response
Adenovirus, because of its large cargo capacity
Lentivirus, because it integrates into the genome and gives permanent expression through cell division
Any of the three, since they are functionally interchangeable for this purpose

explanations.a: AAV's mild immunogenicity is an advantage for in vivo delivery, but it is largely episomal, so it does not give the permanent, heritable expression a pooled screen in dividing cells needs.
explanations.b: Adenovirus's large capacity is not the relevant property here; it also does not integrate, so expression would not persist reliably through many divisions.
explanations.c: Correct — lentivirus's semi-random genomic integration is exactly what makes expression permanent and heritable, which pooled screens like GeCKO rely on.
explanations.d: The three vectors differ fundamentally in integration behavior, capacity, and immunogenicity, and are not interchangeable for this application.

questions.prompt: Match each AAV serotype-related fact to the tissue tropism it enables.

right.text: Efficient liver transduction
Partial blood-brain-barrier crossing, reaching CNS and muscle
Used for ocular/retinal delivery

questions.explanation: AAV capsid serotype determines tissue tropism: AAV8 is liver-selective, AAV9 is notable for reaching the CNS and muscle, and AAV2 is used for eye-directed delivery such as in approved retinal gene therapies.

questions.prompt: Which two strategies specifically solve the problem of fitting a full CRISPR editor into a single AAV vector?

options.text: Using adenovirus capsids on an AAV genome, and increasing the multiplicity of infection
A dual-vector split-intein Cas9 approach, and switching to a compact ortholog like SaCas9
Removing the guide RNA entirely, and using a stronger promoter
Switching to lentivirus, and removing the NLS tags

explanations.a: This mixes vector components in a way that is not how either vector system works and does not address the size constraint.
explanations.b: Correct — splitting SpCas9 across two intein-fused halves delivered by two AAVs, or substituting a smaller ortholog such as SaCas9 (~3.2 kb), are the two established fixes for AAV's packaging limit.
explanations.c: Removing the guide RNA would eliminate targeting entirely; a promoter change does not address cargo size.
explanations.d: Switching vector families changes the underlying tropism and integration properties entirely rather than solving AAV's specific capacity limit; removing NLS tags would impair nuclear delivery of Cas9.

lessons.label: Non-Viral Delivery: LNPs, Electroporation, and Injection

sections.heading: Lipid nanoparticles: four lipids and a liver bias
sections.body: A lipid nanoparticle (LNP) is built from four components: an ionizable lipid, neutral at blood pH but positively charged at the acidic pH inside an endosome, which is what lets it interact with and destabilize the endosomal membrane; a helper phospholipid providing structural support; cholesterol for particle stability; and a PEG-lipid that controls particle size and reduces aggregation. Once injected, LNPs adsorb apolipoprotein E (ApoE) from the bloodstream onto their surface, and ApoE is recognized by the LDL receptor (LDLR), which is highly expressed on hepatocytes — this single interaction is why LNPs are strongly liver-tropic by default, with no targeting ligand engineered in. The bottleneck for LNP delivery is endosomal escape: after a cell takes up the particle by endocytosis, only a small fraction of the cargo — commonly estimated around 1-2% — actually escapes the endosome into the cytoplasm before the endosome matures and degrades its contents; nearly all engineering effort on ionizable lipid chemistry targets improving that single step.

sections.heading: Redosability, and delivering into cells taken out of the body
sections.body: Because an LNP delivers Cas9 mRNA or a Cas9-guide RNP transiently, with no viral capsid proteins for the immune system to recognize and remember, LNPs can generally be re-administered without the anti-vector immunity that limits repeat dosing of a viral vector — though PEG itself can provoke anti-PEG antibodies with repeated use, a distinct and real caveat. NTLA-2001, published by Gillmore et al. (2021), was the first systemic in vivo CRISPR therapy in humans, using a liver-targeted LNP to deliver Cas9 mRNA and a guide against the TTR gene to reduce transthyretin protein levels in patients with transthyretin amyloidosis. For cells that can be removed from the body, a different non-viral route dominates: electroporation or nucleofection delivers a pre-assembled Cas9 protein-guide RNA complex (RNP) directly into cells ex vivo — standard in manufacturing CAR-T cells and in editing induced pluripotent stem cells — and because RNP is transient and rapidly degraded rather than continuously expressed, it also tends to reduce off-target editing relative to plasmid- or virus-expressed Cas9.

sections.heading: Injection and plant-specific routes
sections.body: Zygote microinjection — direct injection of Cas9 mRNA or protein plus guide RNA into a fertilized egg's pronucleus or cytoplasm — has been the standard way to generate edited mouse models since methods like the one-step approach described by Wang et al. (2013) made it possible to produce gene-modified mice in a single generation rather than through multi-step targeting and breeding. Plants require their own routes because of the cell wall: Agrobacterium tumefaciens naturally transfers a segment of its Ti plasmid, the T-DNA, into plant cell chromosomes, and this natural mechanism is co-opted to deliver editing constructs; biolistics (the 'gene gun,' developed by Sanford and colleagues in the 1980s) physically shoots DNA-coated gold or tungsten particles into cells; and protoplast transfection first enzymatically strips the cell wall, then uses polyethylene glycol (PEG) to deliver DNA or RNP directly — notably enabling DNA-free RNP editing of plant cells, which in some regulatory jurisdictions avoids classification as a genetically modified organism since no foreign DNA is ever integrated.

lessons.workedExample: A company wants to lower a disease-causing liver protein in patients and needs the therapy to be redosable if the edit's effect wanes. They rule out AAV, whose capsid triggers lasting neutralizing antibodies after a single dose, and instead formulate an LNP carrying Cas9 mRNA and a guide against the target gene. They rely on the LNP's natural ApoE-LDLR uptake pathway to reach hepatocytes without engineering a targeting ligand, accept that only a small fraction of each dose will escape the endosome and count on dosing to compensate, and confirm the transient nature of mRNA-delivered Cas9 (rather than a DNA plasmid, which could persist and re-express) limits off-target exposure per dose — the same LNP-mRNA logic that underlies NTLA-2001, the first systemic in vivo CRISPR therapy in humans.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about non-viral delivery is checking whether a student understands that 'no virus' does not mean 'no targeting mechanism' — the strong answer explains that LNPs reach the liver by default through ApoE binding to LDLR, not through any deliberate targeting the student engineered, and can name endosomal escape as the actual efficiency bottleneck rather than something vaguer like 'getting the particle into the cell.' A student who cannot explain why LNPs go to the liver without being told to, or who cannot distinguish an ex vivo RNP electroporation approach from an in vivo LNP approach, has not thought through which delivery problem they were actually solving.

questions.prompt: Why are lipid nanoparticles strongly liver-tropic by default, even without an engineered targeting ligand?

options.text: The ionizable lipid is chemically identical to a hepatocyte membrane receptor
LNPs adsorb apolipoprotein E (ApoE) from serum, which is recognized by the LDL receptor highly expressed on hepatocytes
PEG-lipid binds directly to bile acid transporters in the liver
The liver is the only organ large enough to filter nanoparticles from the blood

explanations.a: The ionizable lipid's role is pH-dependent charge for endosomal escape, not molecular mimicry of a receptor.
explanations.b: Correct — ApoE adsorption onto the LNP surface, followed by LDLR-mediated uptake in hepatocytes, is the mechanism behind the default liver tropism of unmodified LNPs.
explanations.c: PEG-lipid's role is controlling particle size and reducing aggregation, not receptor binding.
explanations.d: Liver tropism is receptor-mediated (ApoE-LDLR), not a simple size-filtration effect.

questions.prompt: What is described as the major efficiency bottleneck in LNP-based delivery?
