options.text: Cellular uptake of the LNP itself
Endosomal escape, where only a small fraction of cargo reaches the cytoplasm before the endosome degrades it
PEGylation preventing any cellular uptake
The ionizable lipid degrading before injection

explanations.a: Cellular uptake via endocytosis generally occurs efficiently; the bottleneck is what happens after uptake.
explanations.b: Correct — after endocytosis, an estimated 1-2% of cargo escapes the endosome into the cytoplasm before the endosome matures and degrades its contents, making this the dominant inefficiency.
explanations.c: PEGylation modulates particle behavior in circulation but does not prevent uptake outright.
explanations.d: Lipid degradation before injection is a formulation/stability concern, not the described mechanistic bottleneck of delivery itself.

questions.prompt: Match each delivery route to the setting it is used for.

right.text: Systemic in vivo delivery, e.g. to hepatocytes
Ex vivo editing of cells such as T cells or iPSCs before reinfusion
Generating gene-edited mouse models in a single step
Delivering editing constructs into plant cell chromosomes

questions.explanation: LNPs are the standard for systemic in vivo delivery (notably to liver); electroporation/nucleofection of RNP is used for ex vivo cell engineering like CAR-T and iPSC editing; zygote microinjection generates edited mouse models directly; and Agrobacterium's natural T-DNA transfer mechanism is co-opted to deliver constructs into plant genomes.

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, which tissues/settings remain the central unsolved delivery problem for genome editing?

options.text: Liver, eye, and cells that can be removed from the body for ex vivo editing — these are considered largely solved
Tissues beyond liver, eye, and cells amenable to ex vivo editing, such as most of the rest of the body's organs and tissues
There is no remaining delivery problem once LNPs and AAV are both available
Only skeletal muscle remains an unsolved delivery target

explanations.a: Liver, eye, and ex vivo-accessible cells are framed as the tissues delivery already reaches reasonably well, not the unsolved problem.
explanations.b: Correct — the lesson frames the central unsolved problem as efficient, targeted delivery to the many tissues beyond liver, eye, and cells removable from the body, since even a working editing reagent is limited by whether it can reach the target tissue.
explanations.c: Having LNP and AAV as tools does not mean delivery is solved broadly; each has a fairly narrow set of tissues it reaches well.
explanations.d: The unsolved problem is described broadly across many tissues, not narrowed to skeletal muscle specifically.

lessons.label: Selection, Enrichment, and Making a Clonal Line

sections.heading: Enriching a mixed pool before cloning
sections.body: After delivery, only a fraction of cells actually took up and expressed the editor, so the first step is enriching for those cells rather than immediately isolating single clones from an unenriched pool. Antibiotic selection — puromycin or blasticidin resistance co-delivered on the same construct — kills untransfected cells within roughly 24-72 hours, but the working concentration must first be established with a kill curve: a dose-response titration on non-transfected cells to find the minimum concentration that reliably kills every cell, since too low a dose leaves resistant escapers and too high a dose can kill even resistant cells through off-target toxicity. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) offers an alternative or complementary route, gating on a fluorophore co-expressed from the same cassette as the editor, or on a surrogate reporter — for instance, a construct that only fluoresces once a nearby site has been cut and repaired by the error-prone indel-forming pathway — letting cells be enriched for successful editing activity itself, not just for construct uptake.

sections.heading: From an enriched pool to single-cell clones
sections.body: An enriched pool is still a mixture of many different edits, or no edit at all, in different cells, so a defined line requires isolating individual cells and letting each grow into a genetically uniform colony. Limiting dilution serially dilutes the cell suspension to a target of roughly 0.5 cells per well across a 96-well plate, using Poisson statistics so that wells with any growth are highly likely to have started from a single cell; single-cell FACS sorting directly into individual wells is a faster alternative when the sorter is available. Each surviving clone is then expanded and genotyped — typically by PCR amplifying across the target site and Sanger sequencing, sometimes deconvolved with tools like TIDE or ICE when the trace is mixed — and critically, genotyping must check both alleles in a diploid cell, since a clone can be heterozygous (one allele edited, one wild-type), compound heterozygous (both alleles edited but with different indels), or homozygous (identical edits on both alleles); only a clone with a frameshifting, loss-of-function edit on every allele can be treated as a functional knockout, and even then protein loss should be separately confirmed, for example by western blot.

sections.heading: Why one clone is never enough
sections.body: Single-cell expansion imposes a genetic bottleneck: whichever cell happens to grow fastest in culture dominates the resulting clone, so a clone's growth behavior or phenotype can reflect an unrelated passenger mutation, a karyotype change acquired during expansion, or simple selection for fitness in culture rather than the intended edit. A closely related hazard is an off-target clonal artifact: an unintended cut elsewhere in the genome, or a pre-existing genetic variant unique to that particular founder cell, can produce a phenotype that gets misattributed to the on-target edit simply because it appears in the edited clone and not the parental line. The standard defense against both hazards is to genotype and phenotype several independent clones rather than trusting one, since a phenotype specific to a single clone but absent from other independently derived clones carrying the same intended edit is far more likely to be a clonal artifact than a true consequence of the edit — and, where feasible, to perform a rescue experiment, re-introducing the wild-type gene into the edited clone to confirm the phenotype reverts, the same logic as a positive control.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher edits a diploid cell line with a guide against a gene of interest, sorts on a co-expressed GFP to enrich transfected cells, then limiting-dilutes into 96-well plates at roughly 0.5 cells/well. Of 40 wells that grow into colonies, sequencing shows 15 are unedited, 12 are heterozygous, 9 are compound heterozygous with different frameshift indels on each allele, and 4 are precisely homozygous. They select three independent compound-heterozygous or homozygous clones — not just one — for phenotyping, and observe the same loss-of-function phenotype in all three, while a fourth clone shows an unrelated growth defect not seen in the other two, correctly interpreted as a clone-specific artifact rather than a consequence of the edit.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how many clones did you test, and why?' is checking whether a student understands that a single edited clone is an anecdote, not a result. The strong answer explains the clonal bottleneck directly — that single-cell expansion can fix an unrelated mutation or karyotype change alongside the intended edit — and states that multiple independent clones showing the same phenotype, ideally alongside a rescue, is what separates a real effect of the edit from a clone-specific artifact. A student who tested one clone and reports its phenotype as 'the effect of the knockout' has skipped the step that makes the claim credible.

questions.prompt: Why is a kill curve necessary before applying antibiotic selection to an edited cell pool?

options.text: To find the minimum antibiotic concentration that reliably kills all non-resistant cells, since too low a dose leaves resistant escapers and too high a dose risks toxicity to resistant cells
To determine how long the cells need to grow before FACS sorting
To confirm the guide RNA sequence is correct
Kill curves are only needed for viral, not plasmid, delivery

explanations.a: Correct — a dose-response titration on non-transfected cells establishes the working concentration, avoiding both under-selection (resistant escapers survive) and over-selection (toxicity even to genuinely resistant cells).
explanations.b: Kill curves determine antibiotic dosing, not FACS timing, which is a separate, unrelated enrichment method.
explanations.c: Guide sequence correctness is confirmed by sequencing the construct before delivery, not by an antibiotic kill curve.
explanations.d: Kill curves are relevant whenever antibiotic selection is used, regardless of delivery method.

questions.prompt: A clone has different frameshift indels on each of its two alleles at the target site. How should this genotype be classified?

options.text: Heterozygous, since only one allele shows an edit
Compound heterozygous, since both alleles are edited but with different indels
Homozygous, since both alleles are non-wild-type
Wild-type, since no single allele matches a reference edit

explanations.a: Heterozygous means one edited allele and one wild-type allele; here both alleles are edited.
explanations.b: Correct — compound heterozygous describes both alleles being edited but with distinct indels from each other, distinct from homozygous where both alleles carry the identical edit.
explanations.c: Homozygous specifically means both alleles carry the same edit; different indels on each allele is the compound heterozygous case.
explanations.d: Both alleles carry edits (frameshift indels), so this is not a wild-type genotype.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of going from a mixed edited pool to a validated clonal line.

items.text: Enrich the pool by antibiotic selection or FACS
Isolate single cells by limiting dilution or single-cell sorting
Expand each isolated cell into a colony and genotype both alleles
Compare phenotypes across several independent clones, ideally with a rescue

questions.explanation: The mixed pool is first enriched for edited cells, then single cells are isolated, each resulting colony is expanded and genotyped at both alleles, and finally multiple independent clones are compared (with a rescue where feasible) before trusting a phenotype.

questions.prompt: Why is a phenotype seen in only one edited clone, but absent from other independently derived clones carrying the same intended edit, treated with suspicion?

options.text: Because single-cell expansion imposes a genetic bottleneck, so a clone-specific passenger mutation, karyotype change, or off-target artifact can produce a phenotype unrelated to the intended edit
Because CRISPR editing is inherently less reliable in the first clone isolated from any pool
Because Sanger sequencing cannot detect indels reliably
Because FACS sorting always introduces the same artifact in every experiment

explanations.a: Correct — the clonal bottleneck means each isolated clone can carry unrelated mutations or changes acquired during single-cell expansion, so a phenotype unique to one clone is more likely a clonal artifact than a true consequence of the edit unless it replicates across independent clones.
explanations.b: There is no inherent unreliability tied to which clone is isolated first; the concern is about clone-specific artifacts generally, from any clone.
explanations.c: Sanger sequencing reliably detects indels at the target site; that is not the source of this concern.
explanations.d: FACS sorting is one enrichment method among several and is not described as inherently introducing a consistent artifact across experiments.

units.label: Validating an Edit: Measuring What You Actually Made

lessons.label: Mismatch-Cleavage Assays and Their Ceiling

sections.heading: The gel-based screen: T7E1 and Surveyor
sections.body: The fastest, cheapest way to ask "did my guide cut?" is a mismatch-cleavage assay. You PCR-amplify a few hundred base pairs spanning the cut site from a bulk-edited cell population, then heat-denature and slowly re-anneal the pool. Because the population is a mix of unedited and variously-indeled alleles, single strands from different alleles randomly pair up, and any strand carrying an indel forms a bulged heteroduplex against a wild-type strand. Two enzymes are used to find that bulge: T7 Endonuclease I, originally a bacteriophage enzyme that resolves Holliday junctions and branched DNA, and the Surveyor nuclease, a plant (celery) CEL-I nuclease that nicks at mismatches and small loops. Either one cleaves the heteroduplex at the mismatch, and running the digest on a gel produces two smaller cleavage bands alongside the uncut full-length band. Band intensities, measured by densitometry (commonly in ImageJ), estimate percent indels.

sections.heading: Why the number it gives you is only approximate
sections.body: The raw band-intensity ratio systematically misreads efficiency at both ends. At low editing, cleaved bands near the detection floor (roughly 2-5% indels) are hard to distinguish from gel background and enzyme star activity — non-specific nuclease cleavage that occurs under low-stringency reaction conditions (for example excess enzyme or a high-glycerol buffer), cutting DNA irrespective of a true mismatch and producing spurious extra bands that mimic a real signal — so small effects can be invisible. At high editing, the assay under-reports: as more alleles carry indels, edited strands increasingly re-anneal with each other into homoduplexes that carry no mismatch and never get cut, so the cleaved fraction plateaus below the true editing rate. The field's rough correction is Guschin et al.'s (2010) formula, fraction modified equals 1 minus the square root of the uncleaved fraction. For example, a digest where 49% of the lane's intensity sits in the uncut band corrects to an estimated modified fraction of 1 minus the square root of 0.49, or 30%, rather than the raw 51% cleaved reading. But even corrected the assay is blind to a further category: homozygous alleles carrying the identical indel reanneal into a perfect duplex, cannot be told apart from wild-type, and are simply never counted. Natural SNPs anywhere in the amplicon also form heteroduplexes and cleave, producing false-positive bands unrelated to editing.

sections.heading: What it is good for
sections.body: Given all that, T7E1/Surveyor is a same-day yes/no screen for whether a guide is cutting at all before committing to slower, quantitative methods — never the number reported in a figure claiming a precise editing percentage.

lessons.workedExample: A student screens four candidate guides against a target exon by PCR, T7E1 digest, and gel imaging. Guide 3 shows the strongest cleavage bands, so it is chosen for the main experiment. Two weeks later, Sanger-based deconvolution of the same samples shows Guide 3 is actually only 55% edited while Guide 2, which looked weaker on the gel, is 78% edited — because Guide 2's higher efficiency pushed more alleles into homoduplex reannealing, suppressing its own band intensity. The gel screen correctly said "both guides cut" but was the wrong tool to rank them.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a T7E1 gel image reported as "our editing efficiency was X%" is checking whether the student understands that this assay measures presence of cutting, not its true magnitude, and that its own detection ceiling can flip a ranking between guides. The strong answer names the reannealing-suppression mechanism and states that a quantitative claim needs a follow-up method like Sanger deconvolution or amplicon sequencing; the weak answer treats the gel band as the final number.

questions.prompt: In a T7E1 or Surveyor assay, what physically gets cleaved to produce the diagnostic gel bands?

options.text: The PCR primers themselves
A heteroduplex formed where an edited strand re-anneals with an unedited strand, creating a mismatched bulge
Any double-stranded DNA regardless of sequence
Only strands containing a premature stop codon

explanations.a: Primers are short oligos consumed during PCR; they are not part of the denature/reanneal pool being probed.
explanations.b: Correct — denaturing and slowly re-annealing a mixed population lets edited and unedited strands cross-pair into a mismatched heteroduplex, which T7E1 or Surveyor nuclease then cleaves at the mismatch site.
explanations.c: The enzymes are mismatch-specific; a perfectly matched homoduplex (wild-type/wild-type or identical-indel/identical-indel) is not cleaved.
explanations.d: The assay detects any sequence mismatch or small indel loop, not specifically stop codons — it has no way to read the reading frame at all.

questions.prompt: Why does a T7E1/Surveyor assay systematically under-report editing efficiency as the true efficiency gets high?

options.text: The enzyme degrades at high DNA concentrations
Edited strands increasingly re-anneal with each other into mismatch-free homoduplexes that are never cleaved
High-efficiency editing always produces indels too small to detect
PCR fails when too many alleles are edited

explanations.a: Enzyme degradation is not the mechanism the assay's known bias comes from.
explanations.b: Correct — as more of the pool carries indels, edited strands are more likely to re-anneal with other edited strands during the denature/reanneal step, forming homoduplexes with no mismatch to cleave, which plateaus the cleaved-band signal below the true rate.
explanations.c: Indel size is unrelated to overall editing efficiency; small and large indels both occur at any efficiency.
explanations.d: PCR amplifies whatever template is present regardless of editing status; it does not selectively fail.

questions.prompt: A gel shows a cleavage band even in a sample from an unedited, unrelated cell line. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: A natural SNP within the amplified region creates a heteroduplex mismatch against the reference sequence used for PCR design
The cell line spontaneously acquired the intended edit
T7 Endonuclease I cannot cut unedited DNA under any circumstance
The PCR primers bound the wrong locus entirely

explanations.a: Correct — any natural sequence variant (SNP or small indel) within the amplicon, unrelated to CRISPR editing, forms a mismatch when strands from different alleles or from the sample versus reference reanneal, and it cleaves just like a genuine edit, producing a false-positive band.
explanations.b: Spontaneous acquisition of a specific engineered edit is not a plausible explanation for a background band.
explanations.c: The enzyme's mechanism is mismatch-driven and does not distinguish the biological source of the mismatch.
explanations.d: Wrong-locus amplification would typically show no clean expected-size product at all, not a defined cleavage pattern consistent with the target.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate use of a T7E1/Surveyor result in a science-fair write-up?

options.text: As the final reported editing percentage for the experiment
As a fast qualitative screen for whether a guide cuts, followed by a quantitative method for the actual reported number
As proof that no off-target edits occurred
As a replacement for sequencing entirely

explanations.a: The assay's own detection floor and high-efficiency under-reporting make its raw number unreliable as a final quantitative claim.
explanations.b: Correct — its speed and low cost make it well suited to screening several guides for activity before investing in slower quantitative methods like Sanger deconvolution or amplicon sequencing.
explanations.c: The assay only probes the on-target amplicon supplied to it; it says nothing about genome-wide off-target activity.
explanations.d: It is complementary to, not a substitute for, sequencing-based quantification.

lessons.label: Sanger Deconvolution: TIDE and ICE

sections.heading: Reading a messy trace as a sum of clean ones
sections.body: A Sanger chromatogram from a bulk-edited cell population is not one sequence but a superposition: unedited alleles and every distinct indel allele are all being sequenced in the same reaction, so past the cut site the trace becomes a jumble of overlapping peaks. TIDE (Tracking of Indels by Decomposition), published by Brinkman and colleagues in 2014, and Synthego's ICE (Inference of CRISPR Edits) both exploit a simple insight: every indel just shifts the downstream trace by some number of bases relative to the wild-type trace. So the edited sample's chromatogram, from the cut site onward, can be modeled as a linear combination of copies of a control (unedited) trace, each shifted by -10, -9, ... 0 ... +9, +10 bases and weighted by how much of the population carries that size indel. Fitting that regression against the observed trace recovers the indel spectrum directly, without ever needing to clone or Sanger-sequence individual alleles.

sections.heading: What the output tells you
sections.body: Both tools return an overall percent-edited efficiency and a per-indel-size frequency breakdown, but they differ in framing: TIDE reports the decomposition alongside an R-squared goodness-of-fit and a statistical significance per indel size against control noise, while ICE additionally computes a knockout score, the fraction of the indel spectrum whose length is not a multiple of three and therefore predicted to cause a frameshift. A high R-squared (typically above 0.9) is the signal that the fit is trustworthy; a poor fit means the underlying assumption, that the sample differs from control by simple indels only, has broken down. Under the hood, the regression is fit under a non-negative-least-squares constraint, meaning no indel size is ever allowed a negative population weight; TIDE's default alignment window for that regression spans roughly bases 115 through 685 relative to the start of the aligned trace, giving the fit enough clean downstream sequence to distinguish each shifted copy from the next.

sections.heading: What breaks the fit
sections.body: The method needs a genuinely clean single-peak wild-type control trace and correct guide/cut-site coordinates to anchor the alignment window. The sequencing primer must sit far enough from the cut site, typically at least 50-100 base pairs upstream, that a clean, unambiguous run of sequence precedes the point where the traces start to diverge. Both tools degrade badly on large deletions (which shift the reading frame of the alignment itself, not just the local trace), on low-efficiency edits where the edited signal is barely above chromatogram noise, and on complex alleles carrying combinations of indels and substitutions that no simple shift-and-weight model captures.

lessons.workedExample: A lab edits a cell pool and gets 74% editing by ICE with a knockout score of 51% and R-squared of 0.97 — a clean, trustworthy fit. A second sample from a guide targeting a repeat-rich region returns 40% editing but R-squared of 0.62. Rather than reporting 40% at face value, the researcher rechecks the sequencing primer position and discovers it sits only 15 base pairs from the cut site, too close for the traces to align cleanly before decomposition; moving the primer back and re-sequencing raises R-squared to 0.94 and reveals the true efficiency was closer to 68%.
lessons.judgeFraming: Sanger deconvolution is popular precisely because it is cheap and fast, so a judge probes whether a student trusts the output number blindly or checks the fit. The tell of real understanding is citing the R-squared (or knockout score) alongside the percent-edited figure and explaining what a low fit quality implies — primer placement, low efficiency, or complex alleles the linear model cannot represent — rather than reporting a single percentage as if it were exact.

questions.prompt: What is the core mathematical idea behind TIDE and ICE?

options.text: They count colonies on a bacterial plate after cloning each allele separately
They model the edited sample's chromatogram as a weighted linear combination of the control trace shifted by different indel sizes
They measure the total fluorescence intensity of the chromatogram
They align the sample trace to a reference genome using BLAST

explanations.a: Both tools work directly on bulk Sanger data from a mixed population; no per-allele cloning is involved.
explanations.b: Correct — each possible indel size simply shifts the downstream trace by that many bases, so the mixed trace can be decomposed as a regression against shifted copies of the wild-type control.
explanations.c: Total fluorescence intensity is not the quantity being fit; the shape and shift pattern of the trace after the cut site is.
explanations.d: BLAST-style alignment is a different technique used for other sequencing formats, not the shift-and-regress decomposition these tools use.

questions.prompt: What does ICE's "knockout score" specifically represent?

options.text: The percent of cells that died during editing
The overall percent of alleles carrying any indel, regardless of size
The fraction of the indel spectrum with a length not divisible by three, predicted to cause a frameshift
The R-squared of the decomposition fit

explanations.a: Cell viability is not measured by chromatogram decomposition at all.
explanations.b: That broader figure is the overall percent-edited efficiency; the knockout score is a narrower subset of it.
explanations.c: Correct — indels whose length is a multiple of three preserve the reading frame and may not disrupt the protein, so the knockout score isolates the frameshift-causing fraction as the best predictor of functional knockout.
explanations.d: R-squared measures fit quality, a separate diagnostic from the biological interpretation of the indel spectrum.

questions.prompt: A TIDE analysis returns 40% editing with an R-squared of 0.62. What should this prompt?

options.text: Reporting 40% editing directly, since the tool gave a number
Concluding the guide simply does not work
Investigating the fit quality itself — for example checking primer placement relative to the cut site, or whether large or complex alleles are present that the linear model cannot represent
Repeating the exact same PCR and resequencing with no changes

explanations.a: A low R-squared signals the underlying model assumption is not holding, so the 40% figure should not be trusted at face value.
explanations.b: A low fit quality is a statement about measurement reliability, not evidence the editing failed.
explanations.c: Correct — poor fit quality is diagnostic of a real problem with the assay (wrong primer distance, low signal, or complex alleles), and a well-designed follow-up should address the fit rather than accept the number.
explanations.d: Repeating an identical, unmodified protocol would reproduce the same underlying issue rather than resolve it.

questions.prompt: Why must the sequencing primer sit well upstream of the cut site rather than immediately adjacent to it?

options.text: Sanger sequencing cannot read through a CRISPR cut site at all
A clean, unambiguous stretch of trace before the divergence point is needed to properly anchor the alignment before decomposition begins
Primers too close to the cut site physically block Cas9 from cutting
It has no effect on the analysis; primer placement is arbitrary

explanations.a: Sanger sequencing reads straight through the cut site; the DNA itself is not damaged at the sequencing step.
explanations.b: Correct — the decomposition needs a well-aligned, noise-free reference region before the traces begin to diverge, which requires enough distance between the primer and the cut site.
explanations.c: Primer binding for sequencing happens on purified, already-cut/repaired DNA, long after any Cas9 activity; it cannot interfere with cutting.
explanations.d: Placement materially affects fit quality, as shown by cases where moving the primer back resolves a poor R-squared.

lessons.label: Amplicon Sequencing as the Reference Standard

sections.heading: Reading every allele instead of fitting an average
sections.body: Where TIDE and ICE infer an indel spectrum by fitting a mixed Sanger trace, targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) of the same PCR amplicon reads each individual DNA molecule separately, tens of thousands of times over. CRISPResso2, published by Clement and colleagues in 2019, is the standard tool for turning those raw reads into an answer: it aligns every read to the reference and the (if supplied) intended edited allele, then builds an allele table listing every distinct sequence observed and its frequency, plus a full indel-size-distribution plot showing exactly how big each insertion or deletion is and how often it occurs. Because it counts individual reads rather than fitting a curve, it directly reports separate NHEJ (indel) and HDR (precise edit matching a supplied donor) percentages side by side, something Sanger deconvolution cannot cleanly do once a donor template is in the mix.

sections.heading: Sensitivity and its price
sections.body: With adequate read depth, on the order of thousands of reads per sample, amplicon sequencing can reliably detect variant alleles down to roughly 0.1% frequency, roughly 20-50x more sensitive than the ~2-5% floor of a mismatch-cleavage gel. That sensitivity is what makes it the reference standard for validating a low-efficiency or off-target site, but it is not free: library prep, sequencing runs, and read-depth requirements make it slower and costlier than a Sanger reaction, so it is typically reserved for the sites that matter most rather than every candidate guide screened.

sections.heading: Where the numbers still lie
sections.body: Several artifacts distort the read counts even here. PCR itself is biased against large deletions, because a shorter deleted template amplifies more efficiently than the full-length wild-type template in the same tube, which can inflate the apparent deletion frequency or, if the deletion removes a primer-binding site entirely, cause that allele to drop out of the amplicon pool and be invisible rather than counted. Index hopping, in which reads carrying one sample's barcode are misassigned to another sample on a shared, multiplexed sequencing run, can leak a small false-positive signal across samples. Finally, every sequencer has its own background substitution error rate, so an unedited control sample processed identically is required to establish the noise floor a true edit must rise above. A standard mitigation for a related artifact, PCR duplication and PCR-introduced errors inflating or distorting the read counts, is tagging each original DNA molecule with a unique molecular identifier (UMI) before amplification, so that reads sharing a UMI can be collapsed back into a single count of the original molecule and PCR-cycle errors are recognized as noise rather than real variants.

lessons.workedExample: A team edits a target locus with a donor template for a 3-base-pair tag insertion and sends the amplicon for CRISPResso2 analysis at roughly 20,000 reads per sample. The allele table shows 31% precise HDR, 22% NHEJ indels, and 47% unedited, with an indel-size plot showing a cluster of -1 and +1 events typical of NHEJ. Their unedited control sample shows a 0.3% background "edit" rate from sequencer error, so they correctly report their HDR rate as 31% against that established noise floor rather than as an unqualified raw number. Because the deletion allele's primer sites remained intact, PCR dropout was not a concern for this locus.
lessons.judgeFraming: Amplicon sequencing is the gold standard, so a judge probing this section is checking whether a student can name what could still make even a reference-standard method wrong. The strong answer names a specific artifact — PCR bias against large deletions, primer-site loss, index hopping, or missing an unedited control — and explains its direction of distortion; a weak answer treats 'we did NGS' as automatically authoritative with no caveats.

questions.prompt: Match each artifact to what it does to the reported numbers.

left.text: Index hopping on a shared sequencing run

right.text: Can inflate the apparent frequency of the shorter, more efficiently amplified allele
Makes that allele invisible/undercounted since it can no longer be amplified
Leaks a small false-positive signal across pooled samples
Leaves no established noise floor to distinguish true low-frequency edits from sequencer error

questions.explanation: Shorter deleted templates outcompete full-length templates during PCR (inflating that allele's apparent share); a deletion spanning a primer site drops that allele from the amplicon pool entirely; index hopping misassigns a fraction of reads to the wrong sample on multiplexed runs; and without a sequenced unedited control there is no baseline to know what background error rate a true low-frequency edit must exceed.

questions.prompt: Roughly what variant-frequency sensitivity can targeted amplicon sequencing (via a tool like CRISPResso2) achieve with adequate read depth?

options.text: About 2-5%, similar to a mismatch-cleavage gel
About 0.1%
About 25%
It cannot detect frequencies below 50%

explanations.a: That range is the detection floor of gel-based mismatch-cleavage assays, well above what deep sequencing achieves.
explanations.b: Correct — with thousands of reads per sample, deep amplicon sequencing can reliably call variants down to roughly 0.1% frequency, which is why it is used to validate low-efficiency or rare off-target sites.
explanations.c: That figure vastly understates the sensitivity that deep sequencing provides over gel-based screens.
explanations.d: The whole value of the method is resolving frequencies far below 50%, including single-digit and sub-1% variants.

questions.prompt: Why does CRISPResso2 require an intended-edit (donor) sequence as an optional input to report HDR percentage specifically?

options.text: It uses the donor sequence to distinguish reads matching the precise intended edit from reads that are merely indel-containing NHEJ outcomes
The donor sequence is required to run any alignment at all
It uses the donor sequence to correct for PCR bias automatically
The donor sequence sets the read-depth threshold

explanations.a: Correct — without a defined intended-edit sequence to align against, the tool can only report generic indel (NHEJ) frequencies; supplying the donor lets it separately classify reads as matching the precise intended edit (HDR) versus other indel outcomes.
explanations.b: Basic alignment to the reference genome sequence does not require a donor; NHEJ-only analyses run without one.
explanations.c: PCR bias correction is not something the donor sequence provides; it remains a known limitation regardless.
explanations.d: Read-depth requirements are set by the sequencing run design, not by the donor sequence.

questions.prompt: A large on-target deletion removes one of the two PCR primer-binding sites used to amplify the locus. What happens to that allele in the CRISPResso2 report?

options.text: It is correctly counted at its true frequency
It is systematically undercounted or entirely missing, because it can no longer be amplified into the sequenced pool
It is automatically flagged and reported separately
It gets counted twice due to PCR duplication

explanations.a: Accurate counting assumes the allele is present in the amplified pool at all, which a lost primer site prevents.
explanations.b: Correct — PCR requires both primer sites; an allele that has lost one through a large deletion simply fails to amplify and disappears from the sequenced pool, undercounting exactly the class of large structural changes that matter most.
explanations.c: No automatic flag exists for this; the loss is silent unless the analyst independently checks for it (for example with orthogonal methods).
explanations.d: PCR duplication concerns read redundancy in sequencing depth, not double-counting of an allele that cannot amplify at all.

lessons.label: Genome-Wide Off-Target Discovery

sections.heading: Tagging real breaks inside living cells
sections.body: Amplicon sequencing tells you what happened at one predicted site, but Cas9 can cut sequences it was never designed for, and predicting those sites computationally from sequence similarity alone misses many real ones. GUIDE-seq, developed by Tsai and colleagues in 2015, solves this empirically and in vivo: a short blunt double-stranded oligonucleotide (dsODN) is co-delivered with Cas9 and the guide, and cellular double-strand-break repair machinery integrates that tag directly into genomic breaks via NHEJ, wherever in the genome they occur. Sequencing that pulls out tag-flanking DNA then maps every site in that living cell population where a break actually formed and got repaired by that pathway. Because it happens inside real chromatin, with real nucleosome occupancy and accessibility, GUIDE-seq reflects what actually happens to that guide in that cell type — but it is limited by tag-integration efficiency, so very rare cutting events can be missed.

sections.heading: The in vitro alternative: maximal sensitivity, no chromatin
sections.body: CIRCLE-seq (Tsai et al., 2017) and CHANGE-seq (Lazzarotto et al., 2020) instead digest purified, naked genomic DNA in a test tube with Cas9 RNP, entirely outside a cell. CIRCLE-seq circularizes genomic DNA first so only cleaved, re-linearized fragments get sequenced, giving extremely low background and very high sensitivity; CHANGE-seq uses a tagmentation-based readout that scales to many guides more cheaply. Digenome-seq (Kim et al., 2015) takes a related in vitro approach, digesting whole genomic DNA and inferring cut sites from the characteristic aligned-read-end pattern in standard whole-genome sequencing. All three, because they use naked DNA, will find any site the sequence chemistry allows Cas9 to cut, including ones chromatin would have kept inaccessible in a real cell — they are highly sensitive but also prone to nominating sites that are never actually cut inside living cells.

sections.heading: DISCOVER-seq and the convention that ties it together
sections.body: DISCOVER-seq (Wienert et al., 2019) takes a third route: it performs ChIP-seq for MRE11, a protein recruited to genuine double-strand breaks during repair, directly capturing real in vivo cutting events across many guides and cell types without needing to pre-deliver a tag. Given the trade-off — in vitro assays over-call, in-cell assays under-call rare events — the field convention is two-step: nominate candidates broadly with a sensitive method (often in vitro), then confirm each candidate individually by deep targeted amplicon sequencing in the actual cell type of interest, where a site only counts as a validated off-target if it shows real edits above background.

lessons.workedExample: A lab runs CIRCLE-seq on their guide and gets 340 candidate off-target sites from naked-DNA digestion. Rather than reporting all 340 as off-targets, they rank by cleavage score, take the top 40, and deep-sequence each locus by targeted amplicon sequencing in the actual therapeutic cell type. Only 6 of the 40 show editing above the unedited-control background rate, and just 2 exceed 1% frequency. The final off-target report lists those 2 validated sites, explicitly noting that CIRCLE-seq's remaining 300+ nominations were either inaccessible in cellular chromatin or represent an in-vitro-only artifact, not a false report by the confirmation assay.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "how do you know you found all the off-targets, and how do you know the ones you found are real?" is testing whether a student understands that no single assay answers both halves. The strong response names the in-cell-versus-in-vitro trade-off explicitly and describes the nominate-then-confirm workflow; a student who reports a raw CIRCLE-seq or Digenome-seq hit list as "our off-targets" without amplicon-sequencing confirmation has skipped the step that separates a candidate from a validated finding.

questions.prompt: Match each off-target discovery method to its core mechanism.

right.text: A dsODN tag is integrated by cellular NHEJ repair at real breaks in living cells
Purified genomic DNA is circularized so only Cas9-cleaved fragments are captured and sequenced
Whole-genome sequencing of in vitro Cas9-digested DNA, with cut sites inferred from aligned-read-end patterns
ChIP-seq for MRE11, a protein recruited to genuine in vivo double-strand-break repair events

questions.explanation: GUIDE-seq (Tsai et al., 2015) tags real cellular breaks via NHEJ-mediated dsODN integration; CIRCLE-seq (Tsai et al., 2017) circularizes purified DNA before in vitro digestion for a low-background, highly sensitive readout; Digenome-seq (Kim et al., 2015) infers cut sites from whole-genome sequencing of in vitro-digested DNA; DISCOVER-seq (Wienert et al., 2019) uses MRE11 ChIP-seq to capture genuine in vivo repair events.

questions.prompt: Why do in vitro assays like CIRCLE-seq and Digenome-seq tend to nominate more candidate sites than actually get cut inside living cells?

options.text: They use a different, more error-prone version of the Cas9 enzyme
They digest naked purified DNA, so there is no chromatin/nucleosome accessibility barrier limiting which sequences Cas9 can reach
They have lower sensitivity than in-cell assays
They only test one guide RNA at a time

explanations.a: The same Cas9 chemistry is used; the difference is the substrate, not the enzyme.
explanations.b: Correct — in a real cell, chromatin packaging and nucleosome occupancy restrict which genomic sites are physically accessible to Cas9, but naked DNA in a test tube has no such barrier, so in vitro assays cleave sites that would never be cut inside a cell.
explanations.c: In vitro assays are generally more sensitive, not less, than in-cell methods — that is exactly why they over-call.
explanations.d: Guide throughput is a practical design choice, not the reason for the accessibility discrepancy.

questions.prompt: Order the standard workflow for validating genome-wide off-target sites.

items.text: Run a sensitive discovery assay (e.g., CIRCLE-seq or GUIDE-seq) to nominate a broad candidate list of possible off-target sites
Rank candidates and select a manageable subset for follow-up
Deep-sequence each candidate locus by targeted amplicon sequencing in the actual cell type of interest
Report only candidates showing editing above an unedited-control background rate as validated off-targets

questions.explanation: The field convention nominates candidates broadly with a sensitive discovery method, narrows to a practical subset by ranking, confirms each by deep targeted amplicon sequencing in the relevant cell type, and only reports sites clearing the background noise floor as validated off-targets — never the raw discovery-assay hit list.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes DISCOVER-seq's approach from GUIDE-seq's?

options.text: DISCOVER-seq detects real breaks via a naturally recruited repair protein (MRE11), without needing to pre-deliver a synthetic tag alongside Cas9
DISCOVER-seq only works on purified DNA outside cells
DISCOVER-seq cannot detect any in vivo cutting events
GUIDE-seq and DISCOVER-seq use an identical mechanism

explanations.a: Correct — DISCOVER-seq captures MRE11 recruitment to genuine repair sites via ChIP-seq, so it can survey many guides and cell types in vivo without engineering a dsODN tag delivery step the way GUIDE-seq requires.
explanations.b: DISCOVER-seq works in living cells, capturing real repair events, not purified DNA in a tube.
explanations.c: In vivo detection of real cutting events is the entire point of the DISCOVER-seq approach.
explanations.d: The two rely on different biological readouts — tag integration via NHEJ versus ChIP for a repair-recruited protein — even though both are in-cell methods.

lessons.label: Genotype Is Not Phenotype: Validating at the Protein Level

sections.heading: An indel percentage is not a knockout percentage
sections.body: Sequencing can report that 80% of alleles carry a frameshifting indel, and it is tempting to treat that as "80% knockout," but the indel percentage describes DNA, not the protein a cell actually makes. Closing the case requires looking downstream: a western blot or intracellular flow cytometry directly measures whether the target protein is still present, which is the claim that actually matters for a phenotype. A separate check, qPCR on the transcript, tests whether a premature stop codon triggered nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) — the cell's surveillance pathway that degrades transcripts carrying a stop codon positioned more than roughly 50-55 nucleotides upstream of the last exon-exon junction, which lowers measurable mRNA levels. RT-PCR across the targeted exon adds a third check: it can reveal exon skipping, where the spliceosome removes the entire edited exon from the mature transcript rather than including the disrupted sequence.

sections.heading: How a 'confirmed' knockout still makes protein
sections.body: Several escape routes let a cell with a frameshifting indel keep producing a working protein. Downstream ATG reinitiation lets ribosomes skip the disrupted start of the reading frame and begin translation at an internal methionine further along the transcript, producing an N-terminally truncated but still-functional protein — a mechanism documented as a major source of false CRISPR knockouts by Smits and colleagues (2019). Exon skipping, when it removes a whole exon whose length is a multiple of three, can restore the reading frame around the deletion entirely, again yielding a near-normal protein despite genomic evidence of editing. And even a plain in-frame 3n indel — a 3, 6, or 9 base-pair insertion or deletion — simply adds or removes a codon or two without shifting the frame at all, which sequencing correctly calls "edited" but which may barely dent protein function.

sections.heading: The standard remedy
sections.body: Because any single guide can be defeated by one of these routes, the standard fix is to target the same gene with a second, independent guide at a different exon and confirm the phenotype reproduces, then run a rescue experiment: re-introducing an edit-resistant cDNA (recoded at the guide's seed sequence or PAM so Cas9 cannot re-cut it) and showing it restores the wild-type phenotype confirms the observed effect is really due to loss of that gene product, not an off-target or clonal artifact.

lessons.workedExample: A team knocks out a gene with 85% frameshift indels by sequencing and sees no phenotype change, so they suspect the assay rather than concluding the gene is irrelevant. A western blot shows the protein is still present at roughly wild-type levels. RT-PCR reveals the answer: the targeted exon, which is a multiple of three bases long, is being skipped by the spliceosome in most transcripts, restoring the reading frame around the disrupted exon and yielding a near-normal protein despite the genomic indels. Switching to a guide in a different, non-skippable exon finally produces both loss of protein on the blot and the expected phenotype.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how do you know the protein is actually gone?" after a student cites an indel percentage is testing exactly this gap. The strong answer names a protein-level assay (western blot or flow) plus an escape mechanism it would catch — reinitiation, exon skipping, or an in-frame indel — and describes the two-guide-plus-rescue design used to confirm specificity; citing only a sequencing-derived indel percentage as proof of knockout is the single most common shortcut judges are trained to catch.

questions.prompt: Match each validation method to what it directly measures.

right.text: Whether the target protein itself is still present
Whether nonsense-mediated decay has reduced transcript levels
Whether the spliceosome is skipping the edited exon entirely

questions.explanation: A western blot or intracellular flow assay reads protein abundance directly; qPCR on the transcript detects the mRNA depletion characteristic of nonsense-mediated decay triggered by a premature stop codon; RT-PCR across the exon reveals exon-skipping isoforms that bypass the targeted disruption in the mature transcript.

questions.prompt: How can downstream ATG reinitiation defeat an apparently successful frameshift knockout?

options.text: It prevents the indel from occurring in the first place
Ribosomes can begin translation at an internal start codon downstream of the disrupted region, producing a truncated but still-functional protein
It repairs the DNA back to wild-type sequence
It increases the rate of nonsense-mediated decay

explanations.a: Reinitiation happens at the translation step, well after the indel has already been introduced into the DNA and transcribed into mRNA.
explanations.b: Correct — as documented by Smits et al. (2019), ribosomes can skip a disrupted N-terminal region and reinitiate at an internal methionine, yielding a shorter protein that can retain partial or full function despite genomic evidence of a frameshift.
explanations.c: The genomic sequence remains edited; reinitiation is a translational workaround, not DNA repair.
explanations.d: Reinitiation is a separate translational phenomenon unrelated to the transcript-degradation pathway of NMD.

questions.prompt: Why would an in-frame 3-base-pair deletion be correctly flagged as "edited" by sequencing yet potentially preserve much of the protein's function?

options.text: Because sequencing tools cannot detect indels smaller than 6 base pairs
Because a multiple-of-three indel removes or adds whole codons without shifting the downstream reading frame
Because 3-base-pair deletions always occur outside the coding sequence
Because such deletions trigger nonsense-mediated decay, which restores wild-type protein

explanations.a: Sequencing-based tools reliably detect indels of any size, including single base pairs; detection is not the issue here.
explanations.b: Correct — a deletion or insertion whose length is a multiple of three removes or adds intact codons, so translation continues in the original frame past the edit, which can leave the protein largely intact even though the site is genuinely edited.
explanations.c: In-frame indels can and do occur within coding sequence; their defining feature is frame preservation, not location.
explanations.d: NMD is triggered by premature stop codons from frameshifts, not by preserved-frame indels, and it degrades transcript rather than restoring wild-type protein.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the standard rescue experiment — re-expressing an edit-resistant cDNA after a knockout?

options.text: To increase the editing efficiency at the original locus
To confirm the observed phenotype is specifically due to loss of that gene product, ruling out off-target or clonal artifacts
To replace the need for a western blot
To generate a second independent guide RNA

explanations.a: The rescue cDNA is introduced after editing is complete and does not affect the original locus's editing efficiency.
explanations.b: Correct — if restoring expression of the gene product (via a cDNA recoded so Cas9 cannot re-cut it) reverses the observed phenotype, that is strong evidence the phenotype was caused by loss of that specific gene, not by an off-target effect or an unrelated clonal difference.
explanations.c: A rescue experiment complements protein-level assays like a western blot rather than substituting for them.
explanations.d: A second guide is a separate strategy (targeting a different exon); rescue is about re-expressing the gene product, not generating new guides.

lessons.label: Structural Damage the Standard Assays Cannot See

sections.heading: What a short amplicon cannot show you
sections.body: Every method covered so far — mismatch cleavage, Sanger deconvolution, even standard targeted amplicon sequencing — reads a few hundred base pairs centered on the cut site. Kosicki, Tomberg, and Bradley (2018) showed why that window is dangerous: repairing a Cas9-induced double-strand break can produce deletions spanning kilobases, far larger than a typical amplicon, along with complex local rearrangements. If the deletion's edge falls outside the primers, the PCR either fails to amplify that allele at all (making it invisible) or amplifies a shorter, rearranged product that a pipeline expecting a small indel may mis-call or discard. Loss of heterozygosity is a related on-target risk documented by Adikusuma and colleagues (2018): a large deletion on one chromosome can eliminate not just the targeted gene but neighboring heterozygous variants along with it, silently converting a heterozygous locus to hemizygous.

sections.heading: Damage that scales beyond the cut site
sections.body: The consequences can extend past the local sequence entirely. Leibowitz and colleagues (2021) showed that a Cas9 double-strand break can, in some fraction of cells, trigger loss of the entire chromosome arm or missegregation of a whole chromosome into a micronucleus, which then undergoes chromothripsis — the chromosome inside the micronucleus shatters and is stitched back together in a scrambled, rearranged order. In multiplexed editing, where several guides cut simultaneously, the risk compounds further: translocations, where a piece of one chromosome fuses to another, become more likely as the number of simultaneous double-strand breaks in the genome increases, because free DNA ends from different breaks can be joined to each other by repair machinery instead of being correctly resolved.

sections.heading: Finding it, and a hidden selection bias
sections.body: Catching structural damage needs tools built for scale: long-read sequencing (nanopore or PacBio) spans the whole locus in single reads and directly shows kilobase deletions and rearrangements that short-read amplicon sequencing would miss; droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) compares the copy number of an on-target amplicon against a reference locus, flagging a copy loss consistent with a large deletion; karyotyping or array CGH detects chromosome-scale gains and losses; and allele-specific PCR can directly test for loss of heterozygosity. A final wrinkle compounds all of this: Haapaniemi and colleagues (2018) and Ihry and colleagues (2018) independently showed that cells with an intact, functional p53 DNA-damage response tend to arrest or die in response to a Cas9 cut, while cells with a weakened p53 pathway survive editing more readily — so the surviving, expandable clones researchers pick from are enriched for p53 dysfunction, a serious concern for any therapeutic application.

lessons.workedExample: A team validates their edit with a 400-base-pair amplicon around the cut site and reports clean, simple indels with no evidence of large damage. Suspicious because their cell line shows slower growth than expected, they run ddPCR comparing on-target copy number to a reference locus and find a 40% signal reduction, consistent with a large deletion removing one primer site in a subset of alleles. Long-read sequencing across a wider window then reveals a 3.8 kilobase deletion in those alleles, invisible to the original short amplicon, and karyotyping confirms no additional chromosome-scale abnormality. The team also checks p53 status in their surviving clones and finds reduced p53 pathway activity relative to unedited controls, consistent with a damage-response-driven survival bias.
lessons.judgeFraming: This is the deepest cut a judge can make: "your amplicon looks clean — how do you know there isn't a kilobase deletion just outside your primers, or a chromosome-scale change your assay was never built to see?" A strong answer names a specific orthogonal tool — ddPCR copy number, long-read sequencing, or karyotyping — and, for anything claiming clonal or therapeutic relevance, raises the p53 selection bias unprompted; treating a clean short-amplicon result as proof of a clean edit is the gap this lesson exists to close.

questions.prompt: Why can a short-amplicon PCR/sequencing assay completely miss a kilobase-scale deletion at the on-target site?

options.text: Because Cas9 physically cannot cause deletions larger than a few base pairs
If the deletion's edge falls outside the primer binding sites, that allele either fails to amplify or amplifies as an unexpected product the pipeline may mis-call or discard
Because large deletions always convert to point mutations during PCR
Because sequencers cannot read DNA longer than 400 base pairs under any circumstance

explanations.a: Kosicki, Tomberg, and Bradley (2018) directly demonstrated that double-strand-break repair can produce deletions spanning kilobases, well beyond a small indel.
explanations.b: Correct — PCR requires both primer-binding sites intact; a deletion large enough to remove one leaves that allele unamplifiable or amplifying an unexpected product, so a short-amplicon assay simply never sees it.
explanations.c: Large deletions remain large deletions through PCR; they do not convert into a different mutation type.
explanations.d: Sequencing platforms read fragments of many different lengths; the limitation here is about which fragment gets amplified at all, not a fixed sequencer read-length ceiling.

questions.prompt: Match each detection tool to the structural damage it is best suited to catch.

right.text: Kilobase-scale deletions and complex rearrangements spanning a single long read across the locus
Copy loss at the on-target locus relative to a reference amplicon
Whole-chromosome or chromosome-arm-scale gains and losses
Loss of heterozygosity at the targeted locus

questions.explanation: Long reads span the whole locus and directly reveal large deletions or rearrangements a short amplicon would hide; ddPCR compares on-target versus reference copy number to flag large deletions; karyotyping/CGH arrays are built to detect chromosome- and arm-scale abnormalities; allele-specific PCR directly tests whether one allele's sequence has been lost, catching loss of heterozygosity.

questions.prompt: According to Leibowitz and colleagues (2021), how can a single Cas9 double-strand break lead to chromothripsis?

options.text: The cut directly rearranges the DNA sequence at the break site into a scrambled order
The break can cause a whole chromosome to missegregate into a micronucleus, where it later shatters and is stitched back together in a scrambled, rearranged order
Chromothripsis only occurs in cells that were never exposed to Cas9
The break immediately triggers apoptosis in every affected cell, so no rearranged genome survives

explanations.a: Chromothripsis is a chromosome-scale shattering event, not a local rearrangement confined to the cut site itself.
explanations.b: Correct — a Cas9 cut can, in some cells, cause a whole chromosome to be lost into a micronucleus during division, where it later undergoes chromothripsis and is reassembled in scrambled form, a mechanism only detectable by chromosome-scale tools, not local amplicon sequencing.
explanations.c: The whole point of the finding is that Cas9 editing can be a direct on-target trigger for chromothripsis in some fraction of edited cells.
explanations.d: If every affected cell died, the resulting rearranged genomes could not be observed in surviving edited populations, which contradicts the documented finding.

questions.prompt: Why does p53 pathway status create a selection bias in the surviving clones researchers pick after editing?

options.text: p53-competent cells tend to arrest or die in response to a Cas9 cut, so surviving, expandable clones are enriched for weakened p53 function
p53 status has no effect on which cells survive editing
p53-competent cells edit more efficiently, so they dominate surviving clones
p53 only affects off-target editing rates, not on-target survival

explanations.a: Correct — Haapaniemi et al. (2018) and Ihry et al. (2018) independently found that an intact p53 DNA-damage response causes cells to arrest or die after a Cas9 cut, so the clones that survive and get expanded for downstream use are disproportionately those with a weakened p53 pathway.
explanations.b: The documented finding is specifically that p53 status strongly shapes which cells survive editing, not that it is irrelevant.
explanations.c: It is the opposite direction — a functional p53 response tends to remove cells from the surviving pool rather than help them dominate it.
explanations.d: The effect described is about on-target damage-response survival, not a claim about off-target cutting frequency.

units.label: Beyond the Double-Strand Break: Base, Prime, and Epigenome Editing

lessons.label: Nickases and Dead Cas9: Repurposing the Scaffold

sections.heading: Two nuclease domains, two switches
sections.body: Cas9 is a bilobed enzyme with two independent nuclease domains, each cutting one strand of the target DNA: RuvC cleaves the strand not bound by the guide RNA (the protospacer strand, the one sharing sequence with the guide and carrying the PAM), while HNH cleaves the strand base-paired with the guide RNA (the target strand). Wild-type Cas9 uses both to leave a blunt double-strand break a few base pairs upstream of the PAM. Mutating either domain's catalytic residue silences only that domain. The D10A substitution knocks out RuvC, so the enzyme becomes a nickase using only its intact HNH domain, cutting just the guide-complementary target strand. H840A does the reverse: it knocks out HNH, leaving RuvC active and nicking only the non-target, PAM-containing strand. A single nick is repaired quietly by high-fidelity base-excision repair rather than the error-prone non-homologous end joining a full double-strand break triggers, so a lone nickase is far less mutagenic than wild-type Cas9 at both on-target and off-target sites.

sections.heading: dCas9: a programmable anchor, not a pair of scissors
sections.body: Combine both mutations, D10A and H840A together, and neither nuclease domain functions at all: the resulting dCas9 ('dead' Cas9) still folds correctly and still uses its guide RNA to find and bind a matching genomic sequence with high specificity, but it cuts nothing. That inertness is the entire point. dCas9 converts Cas9 from programmable scissors into a programmable anchor: a protein sent to almost any 20-nucleotide address in the genome that then simply sits there, or drags along whatever is fused to it. Every editor covered later in this unit, cytosine and adenine base editors, prime editors, transcriptional activators and repressors, methylation writers and erasers, starts from this same dead or nicking scaffold and swaps in a different cargo domain.

sections.heading: Paired nickases square the specificity
sections.body: A single nickase is gentle but not necessarily specific: a lone guide RNA can still nick at unintended, similar-looking sites elsewhere in the genome. Ran et al. (2013) addressed this with paired nickases: two nCas9(D10A) complexes with two separate guide RNAs targeting opposite strands, offset by a defined spacing near the intended site. Neither nick alone does much damage, but the two nicks together, positioned close together and on opposite strands, create a staggered double-strand break with short overhangs that the cell repairs like a normal Cas9 cut. Off-target mutagenesis now requires two independent guide RNAs to each find a nearby off-target match at the correct spacing and orientation, an event whose probability is roughly the product of two independent low probabilities rather than one, squaring the specificity of single-guide targeting.

lessons.workedExample: A lab wants to knock out a gene that has a near-identical pseudogene elsewhere in the genome, so a single guide RNA risks cutting both. Wild-type Cas9 with the best available guide still produces a detectable double-strand break at the pseudogene in sequencing data. Switching to a paired-nickase design, the team picks two guides, one on each strand, offset by about 20 base pairs and both overlapping the small stretch of sequence unique to the real gene. Each guide alone, paired with nCas9(D10A), only nicks; only at the true target locus do both guides land close enough, on opposite strands, to produce the staggered double-strand break NHEJ needs to disrupt the gene. Off-target sequencing on the pseudogene comes back clean.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why not just use regular Cas9?' is testing whether a student understands that specificity, not just cutting ability, is the real engineering problem. The strong answer distinguishes what a single nick versus a double-strand break does to repair fidelity, and explains the paired-nickase logic in probabilistic terms: two independent guides must both find a nearby off-target match for damage to occur, so specificity is squared, not just improved. A student who cannot explain why dCas9 (both mutations) is useless for gene disruption but essential for base editors and CRISPRi has not understood that the same protein scaffold is being repurposed as a delivery vehicle, not a tool that always cuts.

questions.prompt: The D10A mutation inactivates which nuclease domain of Cas9, and what is the resulting effect?

options.text: It inactivates HNH, so the enzyme nicks only the non-target (PAM-containing) strand.
It inactivates RuvC, so the enzyme nicks only the target strand base-paired with the guide RNA.
It inactivates both nuclease domains, producing catalytically dead Cas9.
It inactivates the PAM-recognition domain, blocking DNA binding entirely.

explanations.a: That describes the effect of H840A, not D10A; H840A inactivates HNH and leaves RuvC active.
explanations.b: Correct: D10A knocks out RuvC's catalytic activity, leaving HNH intact, so the nickase cuts only the strand paired with the guide RNA.
explanations.c: Both domains are inactivated only when D10A and H840A are combined, which is dCas9, not the single D10A nickase.
explanations.d: D10A is a catalytic-residue mutation in RuvC, not a change to PAM recognition; the enzyme still binds DNA normally.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes dCas9 from a single Cas9 nickase?

options.text: dCas9 carries only the D10A mutation.
dCas9 carries only the H840A mutation.
dCas9 carries both D10A and H840A, so neither strand is cut and the protein only binds.
dCas9 lacks a guide RNA entirely, so it binds DNA non-specifically.

explanations.a: D10A alone is a nickase (HNH still active), not dCas9.
explanations.b: H840A alone is also a nickase (RuvC still active), not dCas9.
explanations.c: Correct: combining both catalytic mutations silences both nuclease domains, giving a protein that still finds its target via the guide RNA but cuts nothing, turning it into a programmable binding scaffold.
explanations.d: dCas9 still requires a guide RNA for sequence-specific targeting; it is the cutting, not the targeting, that is lost.

questions.prompt: Why does the paired-nickase strategy improve specificity compared to a single guide RNA with wild-type Cas9?

options.text: Because nCas9 nicks DNA faster than wild-type Cas9 cuts it.
Because unintended cutting now requires two independent guide RNAs to each find a correctly spaced, correctly oriented off-target match, multiplying two low probabilities together.
Because paired nickases no longer require a PAM sequence.
Because two guide RNAs bind DNA with twice the affinity of one.

explanations.a: Nicking speed is not the mechanism; the gain comes from requiring two coincident low-probability binding events.
explanations.b: Correct: an off-target double-strand break can only form if both guides happen to find nearby off-target sites in the right orientation and spacing, an event far rarer than a single guide finding one off-target site.
explanations.c: Paired nickases still use SpCas9 and still require a PAM adjacent to each guide's target.
explanations.d: Binding affinity per guide is unchanged; the specificity gain is combinatorial, not a change in binding strength.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a paired-nickase edit, from guide design to double-strand break repair.

items.text: Two guide RNAs are designed to bind opposite DNA strands near the target, offset by a defined spacing
nCas9(D10A) enzyme-guide complexes bind their respective target sites
Each complex nicks only the single strand base-paired with its own guide RNA
The two offset nicks combine into a staggered double-strand break, which the cell repairs by NHEJ or HDR

questions.explanation: Guide design and offset spacing come first, then binding, then each nickase makes its single-strand cut, and only once both nicks exist nearby does the cell see a double-strand break to repair, the same repair pathways used by wild-type Cas9, but reached only when both guides land correctly.

lessons.label: Cytosine Base Editors

sections.heading: A deaminase riding a nickase
sections.body: Komor et al. (2016), in Nature, fused a cytidine deaminase, rat APOBEC1 (rAPOBEC1), to catalytically impaired Cas9 to edit a single base without ever cutting both DNA strands. The guide RNA unwinds the target DNA into an R-loop, exposing a short stretch of single-stranded DNA on the non-edited strand; APOBEC1 can only act on single-stranded DNA, so it deaminates a cytosine within that exposed window, converting it to uracil. Left alone, the cell's base-excision repair machinery would recognize and remove that uracil, so the construct (BE3) also fused a uracil glycosylase inhibitor (UGI), a small protein blocking uracil-DNA glycosylase, letting the U survive until replication, when it is read as a T on the new strand, a net C•G to T•A change with no double-strand break and no donor. BE3 pairs the deaminase with nCas9(D10A), which nicks the strand opposite the edited base, biasing mismatch repair to copy the edited, uracil-containing strand rather than reverting it.

sections.heading: The editing window and bystander edits
sections.body: Deamination only happens where APOBEC1 can physically reach single-stranded DNA, limiting editing to a window roughly at protospacer positions 4 through 8, counting the PAM-distal end of the 20-nucleotide protospacer as position 1. That window is the base editor's central limitation: if more than one cytosine sits inside it, all of them convert, not just the intended one. These unintended conversions, bystander edits, can turn a clean single-amino-acid correction into an edit that also changes a neighboring codon, sometimes producing an unwanted missense change or a new stop codon. Narrowing the window with engineered deaminase variants, or choosing guide RNAs where the target cytosine is the lone C in range, are the two practical mitigations.

sections.heading: From BE3 to BE4max, then the off-target reckoning
sections.body: BE3 was quickly improved: BE4 added a second UGI copy in tandem, more thoroughly blocking base-excision repair, and further linker and codon optimization gave BE4max, which edits more efficiently and with fewer unwanted indels than BE3. A bigger problem emerged in 2019: two independent Science papers, Zuo et al. in mouse embryos and Jin et al. in rice, both reported that cytosine base editors generate thousands of single-nucleotide variants scattered across the genome and transcriptome that do not depend on the guide RNA at all, the deaminase domain, once tethered inside a cell, can act on any exposed single-stranded DNA or RNA it randomly encounters, unguided by Cas9's targeting. That guide-independent DNA and RNA deamination forced a new engineering push toward deaminase variants with reduced intrinsic affinity for single-stranded nucleic acid, trading a little on-target activity for far less stray mutation.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to correct a single pathogenic C that should become a T, but sequencing of the target region shows two more cytosines sitting four and six bases away, inside the same predicted editing window. Using BE4max with the obvious guide RNA, the intended C is corrected, but sequencing of edited cells shows the two bystander C's have also flipped to T, silently changing a second codon. The team redesigns the guide to shift the protospacer register so the bystander cytosines fall outside positions 4-8, at the cost of a slightly weaker PAM match, and re-tests: the intended correction rate holds and the unwanted bystander conversions disappear from the sequencing traces.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a base-editing project will almost always ask 'did you check the other C's near your target?' because bystander editing is the single most common way a student's 'precise' single-base correction turns out to carry an unintended second change. A strong answer names the roughly-position-4-to-8 window explicitly, shows the sequence around the target with any bystander cytosines flagged, and explains the guide-design trade-off made to avoid them. A student who can also mention that even a perfectly designed guide does not eliminate genome-wide, guide-independent off-target deamination, the 2019 Science findings, shows they understand the limitation is not fully solvable by guide design alone.

questions.prompt: What does the uracil glycosylase inhibitor (UGI) do in a cytosine base editor?

options.text: It deaminates cytosine to uracil directly.
It blocks the cell's uracil-DNA glycosylase from excising the newly formed uracil, letting the edit persist until replication.
It nicks the non-edited DNA strand.
It prevents the guide RNA from unwinding the DNA.

explanations.a: That is the job of the cytidine deaminase (rAPOBEC1), not UGI.
explanations.b: Correct: without UGI, base-excision repair would remove the uracil and revert the edit before replication fixes it as a T.
explanations.c: The strand nick is performed by the Cas9 nickase domain, not UGI.
explanations.d: DNA unwinding into an R-loop is driven by Cas9-guide RNA binding, not UGI.

questions.prompt: Bystander editing in cytosine base editors happens because:

options.text: the deaminase converts every cytosine in the genome at once
any cytosine within the roughly position-4-to-8 editing window of exposed single-stranded DNA gets deaminated, not only the intended one
the guide RNA binds multiple unrelated genomic sites simultaneously
UGI selectively fails only at bystander cytosines

explanations.a: Deamination requires the deaminase to physically reach exposed single-stranded DNA in the R-loop; it does not act genome-wide at once.
explanations.b: Correct: the deaminase cannot distinguish the intended cytosine from any other cytosine sitting in the same window of exposed single-stranded DNA.
explanations.c: A single guide RNA binds one matching site (plus rare off-targets); bystander editing is a within-window effect at the same site, not multi-site binding.
explanations.d: UGI's job is blocking base-excision repair everywhere it is present, not selectively protecting or failing at specific cytosines.

questions.prompt: What did the 2019 Science reports by Zuo et al. and Jin et al. demonstrate about cytosine base editors?

options.text: They have no off-target activity beyond what wild-type Cas9 produces.
They produce guide-independent, genome- and transcriptome-wide off-target deamination unrelated to Cas9 targeting.
They only affect the intended target locus, but with lower efficiency than expected.
They cannot function at all in mammalian embryos.

explanations.a: The point of both papers was that base editors have a distinct, additional off-target problem beyond Cas9's own targeting.
explanations.b: Correct: both papers, in mouse embryos and in rice respectively, found stray DNA and RNA edits scattered across the genome and transcriptome that did not depend on where the guide RNA directed Cas9.
explanations.c: The reported off-target variants were genome-wide, not confined to the intended locus.
explanations.d: Zuo et al. specifically demonstrated base editing, including its off-target effects, does occur in mouse embryos.

questions.prompt: Match each component or version to its function.

right.text: Deaminates cytosine to uracil on exposed single-stranded DNA
Blocks base-excision repair from removing the new uracil
Biases repair toward copying the edited strand
Improved BE3 with a second UGI copy, better efficiency, and fewer indels

questions.explanation: rAPOBEC1 performs the chemistry (C to U), UGI protects that uracil from repair, the strand nick directs the cell's repair toward the edited strand, and BE4max is the later-engineered, higher-efficiency, lower-indel version of the original BE3.

lessons.label: Adenine Base Editors

sections.heading: No natural DNA adenine deaminase existed
sections.body: Cytosine deamination was a well-characterized reaction: APOBEC and AID family enzymes had been studied for decades. No enzyme was known to deaminate adenine within DNA at all; the only known adenosine deaminases acted on RNA, converting adenosine to inosine in tRNA anticodon loops or mRNA. Gaudelli et al. (2017), in Nature, built an adenine base editor anyway by taking one such enzyme, the bacterial tRNA adenosine deaminase TadA, and evolving it in E. coli through multiple rounds of directed evolution and selection, screening for rare variants able to act on adenine within a DNA context inside an R-loop rather than only within a folded tRNA. The evolved TadA* was fused, as a heterodimer with wild-type TadA, to a Cas9 nickase, giving ABE, the first editor able to write A•T to G•C changes without cutting both DNA strands.

sections.heading: Inosine reads as guanine
sections.body: Mechanistically ABE mirrors CBE: the guide RNA opens an R-loop, exposing single-stranded DNA that TadA* can reach, and it deaminates adenine to inosine. Inosine is not one of the four standard bases, but DNA polymerase treats it as guanine during replication and repair, so the paired thymine on the other strand is eventually replaced by cytosine, a net A•T converted to G•C. Like CBE, ABE works within a limited editing window on the single-stranded DNA exposed by the R-loop, and edits happen without a donor template or a double-strand break.

sections.heading: Transitions only, but that covers half of disease mutations
sections.body: Both base editor families are restricted to transitions, purine-to-purine or pyrimidine-to-pyrimidine swaps (C to T for CBE, A to G for ABE), never a transversion such as a purine converting to a pyrimidine. That restriction sounds narrow, but transitions account for roughly half of all known human pathogenic point mutations, so a tool limited to transitions still reaches a large share of disease-relevant single-base changes, without ever needing a double-strand break or a donor template the way correcting a transversion by HDR would.

sections.heading: ABE7.10 to ABE8e
sections.body: The original optimized editor, ABE7.10, was efficient but slow. Later directed-evolution rounds produced ABE8e, whose evolved TadA variant deaminates adenine far faster, enabling high efficiency with shorter windows of editor exposure, useful for hard-to-transfect or hard-to-edit cell types. That speed comes with a cost: ABE8e's faster kinetics also widen its effective editing window and increase bystander adenine editing, the same window-versus-precision trade-off seen in cytosine base editor engineering.
