lessons.workedExample: A pathogenic mutation has converted a normal G•C base pair to A•T at a specific codon position, exactly the kind of change ABE can reverse, since ABE converts A•T back to G•C. The design team places the target adenine, on the strand where correcting it restores the wild-type G, inside the editing window using ABE7.10 first; efficiency in patient-derived cells comes back around 15%, too low for the intended timeline. Switching the same guide RNA to ABE8e raises editing efficiency substantially, but sequencing of edited cells also reveals a second, bystander adenine three bases away has now been converted in a fraction of alleles, a trade the team accepts because that bystander sits in a non-coding intron.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why can't a base editor just fix any point mutation?' is testing whether a student understands the transition/transversion distinction, not just that base editors 'change one letter.' The strong answer states plainly that CBE and ABE only make transitions, gives the C-to-T / A-to-G rule, and connects it to the roughly-half figure for human pathogenic point mutations, so the student can explain both the tool's reach and its hard boundary. Asking why anyone would choose the slower ABE7.10 over the faster ABE8e checks whether the student grasps the efficiency-versus-bystander trade-off, not just that a newer version exists.

questions.prompt: Why did Gaudelli et al. need directed evolution to build an adenine base editor, unlike the cytosine base editor?

options.text: No enzyme was known that could deaminate adenine within a DNA context, so TadA had to be evolved from its native RNA-editing role.
Cytosine base editors do not use a deaminase at all.
DNA adenine deaminases are toxic and had to be weakened by evolution.
TadA was already known to edit DNA and only needed a new guide RNA.

explanations.a: Correct: TadA naturally deaminates adenosine in tRNA, not DNA, so directed evolution in E. coli was needed to select variants active on DNA within an R-loop.
explanations.b: Cytosine base editors use rAPOBEC1, a cytidine deaminase; the issue was the total absence of a known DNA adenine deaminase, not the absence of deaminases generally.
explanations.c: The engineering problem was that no DNA-active adenine deaminase existed at all, not that an existing one was too strong.
explanations.d: TadA's native activity was on RNA (tRNA anticodon loops); it had no known DNA activity before evolution.

questions.prompt: During DNA replication, inosine (the product of adenine deamination) is read as which base?

options.text: Adenine
Guanine
Cytosine
Thymine

explanations.a: Inosine is the deamination product of adenine, but it is not read back as adenine, that would produce no net change.
explanations.b: Correct: DNA polymerase treats inosine as guanine, so the paired base on the opposite strand becomes cytosine, giving A to G.
explanations.c: Cytosine is the eventual base on the opposite strand after replication, not what inosine itself is read as.
explanations.d: Thymine is the original pairing partner of adenine before deamination, not what inosine is read as.

questions.prompt: A transition mutation is best described as:

options.text: A purine-to-pyrimidine or pyrimidine-to-purine substitution
A purine-to-purine or pyrimidine-to-pyrimidine substitution
Any insertion or deletion of a single base
A substitution that changes the reading frame

explanations.a: That describes a transversion, the category base editors cannot make.
explanations.b: Correct: transitions swap within the same chemical class, purine for purine (A/G) or pyrimidine for pyrimidine (C/T), which is exactly what CBE and ABE do.
explanations.c: Insertions and deletions are indels, a different category of mutation entirely, not a substitution type.
explanations.d: A single-base substitution does not shift the reading frame; only indels not in multiples of three do that.

questions.prompt: Compared with ABE7.10, what does ABE8e trade for what?

options.text: Lower on-target efficiency for a narrower, cleaner editing window
Faster deamination kinetics for a wider editing window and more bystander adenine editing
DNA specificity for RNA specificity
Transition editing for transversion editing

explanations.a: ABE8e has higher, not lower, on-target efficiency; the trade-off runs the other direction.
explanations.b: Correct: later directed-evolution rounds made ABE8e's TadA variant deaminate much faster, which raises efficiency but also widens the window in which bystander adenines get edited.
explanations.c: Both ABE7.10 and ABE8e act on DNA; the difference is speed and window width, not target molecule.
explanations.d: Both remain transition-only editors; ABE8e does not gain transversion capability.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in adenine base editing.

right.text: Native tRNA adenosine deaminase, evolved in E. coli to act on DNA
Nature paper introducing the first working adenine base editor
First optimized ABE, efficient but slower-acting
Faster-kinetics ABE variant with a wider window and more bystander editing

questions.explanation: TadA was repurposed from RNA editing to DNA editing by directed evolution; Gaudelli et al. (2017) published the resulting ABE; ABE7.10 was the first optimized version; ABE8e later traded window width and bystander editing for faster kinetics.

lessons.label: Prime Editing

sections.heading: A reverse transcriptase bolted onto a nickase
sections.body: Anzalone et al. (2019), in Nature, introduced prime editing: a fusion of Cas9 nickase (H840A, which nicks only the non-target, PAM-containing strand) to an engineered Moloney murine leukemia virus (M-MLV) reverse transcriptase, guided by a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA). A pegRNA is a standard guide RNA extended at its 3' end with two extra elements: a primer-binding site (PBS) that base-pairs with the free 3' end created by the nick, and an RT template encoding the desired new sequence. Once the nick exposes a single-stranded 3' end, it anneals to the PBS and the reverse transcriptase extends it, copying the RT template directly into the genomic DNA as new, edited single-stranded DNA, no donor template, no double-strand break, and unlike base editors, not limited to a single transition.

sections.heading: PE2, PE3, PE3b
sections.body: PE2 is the minimal system: nickase-RT fusion plus pegRNA, editing one strand and relying on cellular repair to resolve the resulting heteroduplex, often inefficiently. PE3 adds a second, ordinary sgRNA nicking the opposite, non-edited strand, which biases mismatch repair toward copying the new edited strand and substantially raises efficiency, but reintroduces indel risk, because two simultaneous nicks on opposite strands can again behave like a double-strand break. PE3b fixes this by designing the second nicking guide to match only the edited sequence, not the original, so it cannot cut until after the edit is already installed, capturing most of PE3's efficiency gain with far fewer indels.

sections.heading: Suppressing mismatch repair: PE4 and PE5
sections.body: Chen et al. (2021) found that DNA mismatch repair itself was reverting a fraction of correctly installed edits, recognizing the heteroduplex intermediate as an error. Co-expressing a dominant-negative MLH1 (MLH1dn) transiently disables mismatch repair long enough for the edit to be sealed in; PE4 pairs MLH1dn with PE2, and PE5 pairs it with PE3, each raising editing efficiency several-fold over its unsuppressed counterpart in mismatch-repair-proficient cells.

sections.heading: twinPE and the honest trade-off
sections.body: twinPE uses two pegRNAs to write two new sequences on opposite strands flanking a site, for example installing a short attB integrase landing site, enabling larger programmed insertions, deletions, or inversions than a single pegRNA can reach, especially when paired with a site-specific integrase for multi-kilobase cargo. The trade-off across the whole prime editing family: it can write essentially any small substitution, insertion, or deletion at single-nucleotide precision, but unlike base editing, efficiency varies widely and unpredictably by genomic locus and by pegRNA design, so a working pegRNA is usually found empirically rather than by pure prediction.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to insert a 3-base-pair sequence to correct a small deletion. With PE2 alone, editing efficiency in their cell line comes back around 5%, too low to be useful. Adding a second nicking guide (PE3) on the opposite strand raises efficiency to about 20%, but indel byproducts also appear in roughly 8% of edited alleles. Redesigning the second guide as PE3b, so it only cuts once the correct sequence is already installed, keeps efficiency near 18% while indels drop to under 2%. Pushing further, the team co-expresses MLH1dn, combining PE3b's nicking design with mismatch-repair suppression (PE5), and efficiency climbs past 40%, at the cost of one more construct to deliver and validate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a prime-editing project will ask why the student did not just use PE3 everywhere, since it is more efficient than PE2. The strong answer names the specific trade-off, a second nick raises efficiency but reintroduces indel risk, and explains whether PE3b or mismatch-repair suppression (PE4/PE5) was used to manage that risk, and why. It also distinguishes prime editing's flexibility, any small edit, no donor, no double-strand break, from its cost: efficiency is locus- and pegRNA-dependent, so a student who tested only one pegRNA and reports a single efficiency number has not demonstrated they understand that pegRNA design is itself an empirical variable.

questions.prompt: What two extra elements does a pegRNA add beyond a standard guide RNA?

options.text: A second spacer sequence and a PAM-interacting domain
A primer-binding site (PBS) and an RT template, both in a 3' extension
A UGI domain and a second nuclease domain
Two MS2 hairpin loops

explanations.a: pegRNAs keep the standard spacer; the addition is a 3' extension, not a second spacer or PAM domain.
explanations.b: Correct: the PBS anneals to the nicked strand's exposed 3' end, and the RT template is the sequence the reverse transcriptase copies into the genome.
explanations.c: UGI belongs to cytosine base editors, not prime editing, which has no analogous glycosylase-inhibitor step.
explanations.d: MS2 hairpins are used in CRISPRa systems like SAM, not in pegRNAs.

questions.prompt: What specific problem does PE3b solve relative to plain PE3?

options.text: PE3 cannot edit at all without PE3b.
PE3's second nick, made immediately on the unedited sequence, raises indel risk; PE3b delays that nick until after the edit is installed.
PE3b removes the need for a reverse transcriptase.
PE3b eliminates the need for a pegRNA.

explanations.a: PE3 edits on its own, just with more indels than PE3b produces.
explanations.b: Correct: because PE3b's second guide only matches the already-edited sequence, it cannot nick until the edit exists, avoiding the near-simultaneous double-nick that causes indels in PE3.
explanations.c: The reverse transcriptase fusion is required in every prime editing variant, including PE3b.
explanations.d: The pegRNA is the core guide of prime editing and is still required in PE3b.

questions.prompt: What does MLH1dn accomplish in PE4/PE5?

options.text: It directly reverse-transcribes the RT template into DNA.
It transiently suppresses mismatch repair, preventing the correctly installed edit from being reverted.
It nicks the opposite DNA strand.
It permanently deletes the MLH1 gene.

explanations.a: Reverse transcription is performed by the fused M-MLV RT domain, not by MLH1dn.
explanations.b: Correct: MLH1dn is a dominant-negative form of a mismatch-repair protein, and its transient expression stops mismatch repair from recognizing and reverting the edited heteroduplex.
explanations.c: Nicking the opposite strand is the role of the second sgRNA in PE3/PE3b, not MLH1dn.
explanations.d: MLH1dn acts as a dominant-negative protein transiently; it does not delete the endogenous MLH1 gene.

questions.prompt: Order the core steps of a prime-editing reaction.

items.text: pegRNA-guided nCas9(H840A) nicks the non-target strand, exposing a free 3' DNA end
The exposed 3' end anneals to the primer-binding site (PBS) in the pegRNA's 3' extension
The fused reverse transcriptase extends the DNA end, copying the RT template into new genomic DNA
Cellular repair resolves the resulting heteroduplex, ideally incorporating the new edited strand

questions.explanation: The nick must come first to create a free 3' end; that end then primes off the PBS; the reverse transcriptase then writes the new sequence; only afterward does the cell's own repair machinery decide whether to keep the edit, which is what PE3, PE3b, and mismatch-repair suppression are all designed to influence.

lessons.label: CRISPRi, CRISPRa, and Epigenome Editing

sections.heading: CRISPRi and CRISPRa: silencing and switching on without cutting
sections.body: Fusing an effector domain to dCas9 turns it into a programmable transcriptional dial instead of a pair of scissors. Gilbert et al. (2013) showed that dCas9 fused to the KRAB repressor domain (dCas9-KRAB), directed to a gene's promoter or transcription start site, recruits corepressor complexes that install repressive chromatin and block transcription, CRISPR interference (CRISPRi). Activation runs the other direction and is harder: a single dCas9-VP64 fusion is usually too weak alone, so activation systems amplify it. SAM (Synergistic Activation Mediator, Konermann et al. 2015) modifies the guide RNA scaffold itself to include MS2 RNA hairpins that recruit MS2 coat protein fused to the p65 and HSF1 activation domains. SunTag (Tanenbaum et al. 2014) instead appends a repeating peptide array to dCas9 that recruits many copies of an antibody fragment fused to VP64, multiplying the number of activation domains at a single site.

sections.heading: Writing and erasing chromatin marks directly
sections.body: Beyond transcription factors, dCas9 can deliver chromatin-modifying enzymes to a specific locus: dCas9-DNMT3A installs DNA methylation to silence a target region, dCas9-TET1 does the reverse, promoting demethylation to reactivate it, and dCas9-p300, using only p300's catalytic acetyltransferase core (Hilton et al. 2015), acetylates histone H3 at lysine 27, a mark associated with active enhancers, letting a distal regulatory element rather than just a promoter be switched on.

sections.heading: Reversible is the feature, until it isn't
sections.body: CRISPRi, CRISPRa, and most dCas9-chromatin fusions require the fusion protein to keep being expressed; remove it and the target gene's activity typically returns toward baseline, exactly why these tools are prized for reversible, dose-controllable perturbation screens. Nuñez et al. (2021) built the deliberate exception: CRISPRoff installs DNA methylation durable enough that, once the editing machinery is withdrawn, the cell's own maintenance methylation machinery keeps copying the mark through every subsequent cell division, silencing the gene long-term from a single transient treatment, reversible only by a separate CRISPR-on (TET1-based) construct that actively removes the methylation.

sections.heading: Screens read dosage
sections.body: Pooled CRISPRi/a screens differ from CRISPR knockout screens in what they measure: instead of a binary gene loss from an indel, they read out graded gene dosage, partial knockdown or degrees of overexpression. Gilbert et al. (2014, Cell, 'Genome-Scale CRISPR-Mediated Control of Gene Repression and Activation') established this at genome scale, building parallel genome-wide CRISPRi and CRISPRa libraries and screening them alongside a CRISPR knockout library in the same cell line. For genes essential to viability, the knockout screen could only report a dropout: cells carrying a knockout guide simply died and vanished from the population, erasing any finer information about how strongly the gene mattered. The CRISPRi screen instead recovered a graded fitness effect, guides producing weaker knockdown left cells only mildly impaired, while guides producing near-complete knockdown were strongly depleted, letting the screen rank essential genes by the severity of their fitness defect rather than merely flagging that a defect existed. That dosage resolution is what makes CRISPRi/a screens uniquely suited to studying essential genes, where a full knockout would kill the cell before any phenotype beyond death could be scored.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to silence a gene essential for cell survival, ruling out a knockout screen. Using dCas9-KRAB directed at the promoter, gene expression drops to about 20% of baseline within 48 hours, enough to see a phenotype without killing the cell outright, and the effect fully reverses within a week of removing doxycycline-induced dCas9-KRAB expression, confirming it is reversible. To test whether the silencing could instead be made permanent for a stem-cell differentiation experiment that needs the gene off for months without continuous drug treatment, the team switches to CRISPRoff: a single transient transfection installs stable, methylation-based silencing that persists through repeated cell division without further intervention, exactly the behavior a transient dCas9-KRAB treatment could not provide.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will often ask why a student used CRISPRi instead of a CRISPR knockout for an essential gene, and the strong answer is that CRISPRi gives graded, reversible dosage control rather than a binary, permanent loss the cell might not survive. A second common probe is what happens when the dCas9 fusion is removed, a student who says 'it reverses' has described the default behavior of KRAB, VP64, DNMT3A, or TET1 fusions, while a student who has read about CRISPRoff can explain the important exception: durable, heritable silencing from a single treatment, a fundamentally different tool for a fundamentally different question.

questions.prompt: What does dCas9-KRAB do when directed to a gene's promoter?

options.text: It cuts the DNA, disrupting the promoter permanently.
It recruits corepressor complexes that install repressive chromatin, silencing transcription.
It methylates the gene irreversibly, matching CRISPRoff.
It activates transcription by recruiting p65 and HSF1.

explanations.a: dCas9 is catalytically dead; KRAB works through chromatin repression, not DNA cutting.
explanations.b: Correct: the KRAB domain recruits corepressor machinery that installs repressive chromatin marks at the target site, silencing transcription while the fusion protein remains bound.
explanations.c: Standard dCas9-KRAB silencing is reversible when the fusion is withdrawn; only the separate CRISPRoff design is built for durable, irreversible-by-default methylation.
explanations.d: Recruiting p65 and HSF1 is the SAM activation mechanism, the opposite effect of KRAB.

questions.prompt: Match each dCas9 fusion to its typical action.

right.text: Represses transcription by installing repressive chromatin
Installs DNA methylation to silence the target region
Removes methylation to promote reactivation
Acetylates H3K27 to activate enhancers

questions.explanation: KRAB recruits repressive chromatin machinery, DNMT3A directly writes methylation, TET1 removes it, and the p300 catalytic core acetylates H3K27 to switch on enhancers rather than promoters specifically.

questions.prompt: What makes CRISPRoff different from standard dCas9-KRAB silencing?

options.text: It only works transiently, exactly like KRAB.
It installs DNA methylation-based silencing that persists through cell division after the editing machinery is withdrawn.
It permanently deletes the target gene's DNA sequence.
It only works on RNA transcripts, not the genome.

explanations.a: The defining feature of CRISPRoff is that, unlike standard KRAB silencing, it does not need continued expression to persist.
explanations.b: Correct: CRISPRoff's methylation mark is copied by the cell's own maintenance methylation machinery through repeated division, so silencing outlasts the initial treatment.
explanations.c: CRISPRoff modifies chromatin, not the underlying DNA sequence; the gene is still present, just silenced.
explanations.d: CRISPRoff acts on genomic DNA methylation, not on RNA transcripts.

questions.prompt: Why are CRISPRi/a pooled screens especially useful for studying essential genes?

options.text: They produce complete gene knockouts, which is required for essential genes.
They allow graded, partial knockdown or overexpression rather than a lethal full loss-of-function.
They physically cannot target essential genes.
They only work in non-dividing cells.

explanations.a: A full knockout of an essential gene would typically kill the cell, preventing any downstream phenotype from being measured; that is the opposite of the advantage.
explanations.b: Correct: because CRISPRi/a modulate dosage rather than eliminating the gene, cells survive with a partial effect, letting a graded phenotype be scored.
explanations.c: CRISPRi/a can target any gene with a suitable guide RNA, essential genes included.
explanations.d: CRISPRi/a screens are routinely run in actively dividing cell populations.

lessons.label: Programmable Insertion and RNA Targeting

sections.heading: CRISPR-associated transposases: insertion without a double-strand break
sections.body: Homology-directed repair is inefficient and largely confined to dividing cells, which limits it as a way to insert large sequences. In 2019, two independent groups found a different route already built by nature: Tn7-like bacterial transposons that had co-opted CRISPR effectors to choose where they insert. Klompe et al. described a Vibrio cholerae system, and Strecker et al. described a cyanobacterial Tn7-like system, both using a CRISPR-associated effector to guide the transposase-transposon complex to a programmed genomic address, where it inserts DNA cargo directly, no double-strand break, no reliance on the cell's own repair pathways, and capacity for cargo well beyond what typical HDR donor templates support.

sections.heading: PASTE: prime editing writes the landing site
sections.body: PASTE-style approaches split large-cargo insertion into two precise steps. First, prime editing installs a short Bxb1 attB sequence at the exact target site, small enough, and precise enough, for prime editing's single-nucleotide accuracy. Second, a separately delivered Bxb1 serine integrase recognizes that attB site and recombines it with a matching attP site carried on a donor construct, splicing in cargo that can run to multiple kilobases, an entire gene, not just a point mutation, at a defined locus, again without depending on a double-strand break or the cell's own homologous recombination machinery.

sections.heading: Cas13: RNA knockdown with a collateral catch
sections.body: Cas13 is guided by an RNA to a complementary RNA target and cleaves it, knocking down a transcript while leaving the genome completely untouched, useful where a change needs to be reversible or where editing DNA at all is undesirable. Once a Cas13 complex binds its intended target, its nuclease becomes promiscuously active and cleaves nearby RNA indiscriminately, collateral trans-cleavage. That behavior is the working principle of SHERLOCK (Gootenberg et al., 2017): a target RNA activates Cas13, which then shreds an added reporter RNA and produces a detectable signal, making Cas13 the engine of a sensitive diagnostic. The same collateral activity is a liability inside living cells, where indiscriminate RNA cleavage is toxic.

sections.heading: REPAIR and RESCUE: editing the message, not the gene
sections.body: REPAIR (Cox et al., 2017) fuses catalytically dead Cas13 to an ADAR2 deaminase domain, converting adenosine to inosine, read as guanosine, directly on RNA transcripts. RESCUE extends the same logic to cytosine-to-uridine RNA editing. Because both act on RNA rather than DNA, the change is transient, decaying as the edited transcript turns over, and the genome itself is never altered, a deliberately reversible, dosable alternative to a permanent DNA edit.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to insert a 4.2-kilobase reporter gene at a defined genomic locus without triggering a double-strand break, since their cell type repairs breaks poorly and mostly through error-prone pathways. HDR with a donor plasmid gives under 1% correct insertion. Switching to a PASTE-style strategy, they first use prime editing to install a 38-base-pair Bxb1 attB site precisely at the target locus, a small, single-nucleotide-precision edit well within prime editing's normal range, then deliver Bxb1 integrase along with a donor plasmid carrying a matching attP site and the 4.2-kb reporter cassette. The integrase recombines the two att sites, inserting the full cassette at the programmed locus in a substantial fraction of cells, without any double-strand break at any step.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks how to insert something bigger than a base pair or two without HDR is testing whether a student knows the field has moved past homology-directed repair as the only route to large insertions. The strong answer names either CRISPR-associated transposases or the two-step PASTE logic, prime editing to write a small, precise landing site, then an integrase to deliver the large cargo, and explains why splitting the problem this way avoids a double-strand break at any point. For the RNA branch, a judge probing Cas13 will listen for whether the student can name collateral trans-cleavage as both SHERLOCK's mechanism and a cellular liability, not just 'it cuts RNA.'

questions.prompt: What do the Klompe et al. and Strecker et al. 2019 CRISPR-associated transposase systems have in common?

options.text: Both use homology-directed repair to insert cargo at a target site.
Both use a CRISPR effector to direct a Tn7-like transposase to insert DNA at a programmed site without a double-strand break.
Both are RNA-only editing systems with no DNA activity.
Both require a donor plasmid with long homology arms.

explanations.a: The point of both systems is that they bypass HDR entirely, using transposition instead.
explanations.b: Correct: both systems repurpose naturally occurring Tn7-like transposons whose insertion site is chosen by a CRISPR-associated effector, inserting cargo without a double-strand break.
explanations.c: Both systems insert DNA cargo into DNA; they are not RNA-targeting tools.
explanations.d: Transposon insertion does not depend on long homology arms the way HDR donor design does.

questions.prompt: In a PASTE-style strategy, what is prime editing's specific role?

options.text: It delivers the multi-kilobase cargo directly.
It installs a short Bxb1 attB landing site precisely at the target locus, which the integrase later uses.
It cleaves the target RNA transcript.
It performs the final integrase recombination step.

explanations.a: Prime editing writes small sequences; the large cargo is delivered separately and joined in by the integrase.
explanations.b: Correct: prime editing's single-nucleotide precision is used only to write the short attB site, which is well within its normal editing range.
explanations.c: Prime editing acts on genomic DNA, not RNA transcripts.
explanations.d: Recombination between attB and attP is carried out by the Bxb1 integrase, not by the prime editor.

questions.prompt: What is Cas13's collateral trans-cleavage activity?

options.text: Sequence-specific cleavage of only the intended target RNA.
Once activated by its target, indiscriminate cleavage of nearby RNA, the basis of SHERLOCK diagnostics and a liability in living cells.
Cleavage of double-stranded DNA near the target.
A repair pathway that fixes Cas13's own off-target cuts.

explanations.a: Collateral cleavage is specifically the non-specific activity that goes beyond the intended target.
explanations.b: Correct: target binding switches Cas13 into a state where it cleaves any nearby RNA indiscriminately, which SHERLOCK exploits for detection but which is toxic inside living cells.
explanations.c: Cas13 acts on RNA, not DNA; it has no DNA-cleaving activity.
explanations.d: There is no repair pathway involved; collateral cleavage is an unwanted side activity, not a correction mechanism.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to what it does.

right.text: Cleaves a targeted RNA transcript, leaving the genome untouched
A-to-I RNA editing via dCas13 fused to ADAR2
C-to-U RNA editing
Installs a Bxb1 landing site by prime editing, then integrates multi-kilobase DNA cargo

questions.explanation: Cas13 alone degrades its target transcript; REPAIR and RESCUE repurpose catalytically dead Cas13 to edit individual bases on RNA (A-to-I and C-to-U respectively) rather than destroying it; PASTE combines prime editing and a serine integrase to insert large DNA cargo into the genome.

lessons.label: From Repeats to an Immune System: 1987-2011

sections.heading: An accidental repeat, then a name
sections.body: In 1987, Yoshizumi Ishino's group in Osaka was sequencing the E. coli iap gene when they noticed odd, evenly spaced repeated sequences downstream of it — repeats they could not explain and mentioned almost in passing. Nobody knew what they were for. It was Francisco Mojica, a graduate student in Alicante, Spain, who took the repeats seriously: starting in 1993 he found near-identical repeat clusters in halophilic archaea, then across dozens of bacterial and archaeal genomes, and became convinced they were too widespread and too structured to be junk. In 2002, Mojica and Ruud Jansen coined the acronym CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) to standardize what had been called by half a dozen different names.

sections.heading: The 2005 spacer-match papers, rejected before they were accepted
sections.body: The breakthrough came when Mojica compared the unique 'spacer' sequences sitting between repeats against public databases and found in 2005 that many spacers matched bacteriophage and plasmid DNA — meaning the array looked like a record of past infections. The implication (an adaptive immune system in bacteria) was radical enough that his manuscript was rejected by several journals — reportedly including Nature, PNAS, and Nucleic Acids Research — before the Journal of Molecular Evolution accepted it in 2005. That same year, Alexander Bolotin's group identified a conserved motif flanking the spacers — the protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) — later shown essential for the system to distinguish self from invader.

sections.heading: Proof, target, and the missing RNA
sections.body: A hypothesis needed an experiment. In 2007, Rodolphe Barrangou and Philippe Horvath, working at the food-industry company Danisco, published in Science the first direct test: they infected Streptococcus thermophilus (used in yogurt fermentation) with phage, showed surviving bacteria had acquired new phage-derived spacers, and demonstrated that adding or deleting spacers changed phage resistance accordingly — CRISPR was a heritable, programmable immune system. In 2008, Luciano Marraffini and Erik Sontheimer showed the system targets DNA directly, not RNA as some had assumed. In 2010, Sylvain Moineau's lab (Josiane Garneau, Marie-Ève Dupuis, and colleagues) identified Cas9 itself as the nuclease that actually cuts the invading phage or plasmid DNA during natural CRISPR immunity, publishing in Nature — pinpointing the enzyme that would later become the tool's cutting blade. Then in 2011, Elitza Deltcheva and Emmanuelle Charpentier's group discovered tracrRNA (trans-activating crRNA), a second small RNA required to process the CRISPR array and guide Cas9 — the final piece before the system could be reprogrammed as a tool.

lessons.workedExample: A judge asks a student presenting on CRISPR's history: 'Who actually proved CRISPR was an immune system, and how?' The strong answer names Barrangou and Horvath's 2007 Science paper: they didn't just observe a correlation, they intervened — deliberately adding a phage-derived spacer to Streptococcus thermophilus and showing it gained resistance to that specific phage, then deleting it and showing resistance was lost. That causal manipulation, not Mojica's 2005 sequence-matching alone, is what turned a strong hypothesis into an experimentally confirmed mechanism, twenty years after Ishino's first accidental sighting of the repeats.
lessons.judgeFraming: This history is a clean case study in how a hypothesis becomes an accepted mechanism, and judges probe it to see if a student can tell the difference between observation, hypothesis, and proof. Mojica's 2005 spacer-match paper was a strong hypothesis built on bioinformatic pattern-matching — and it was rejected by multiple journals precisely because pattern-matching isn't proof. Barrangou and Horvath's 2007 experiment is what actually tested the hypothesis by manipulating the variable (spacer content) and observing the predicted effect (resistance). A student who conflates 'discovered' with 'proved' hasn't understood how the field itself worked through the doubt.

questions.prompt: Which experiment provided the first direct, causal proof that CRISPR functions as an adaptive immune system?

options.text: Ishino's 1987 sequencing of repeats near the E. coli iap gene
Barrangou and Horvath's 2007 Science paper adding/deleting spacers in Streptococcus thermophilus
Mojica's 2005 discovery that spacers match phage sequences
Deltcheva and Charpentier's 2011 discovery of tracrRNA

explanations.a: Ishino's group noted the repeats' existence but had no functional explanation for them at all.
explanations.b: Correct — Barrangou and Horvath manipulated spacer content directly and observed the predicted change in phage resistance, converting a hypothesis into a tested mechanism.
explanations.c: Mojica's 2005 finding was a strong correlational hypothesis (spacers resemble phage DNA) but not an experimental test of function.
explanations.d: tracrRNA's discovery explained a mechanistic component of the system but came four years after CRISPR's immune function was already proven.

questions.prompt: Why was Mojica's 2005 manuscript rejected by several journals before publication?

options.text: It contained a data-fabrication error later corrected
It proposed a radical function (bacterial adaptive immunity) supported only by sequence comparison, not experiment
It was submitted to journals outside his field of archaea genetics
Reviewers had already published the same finding first

explanations.a: There is no record of a fabrication issue; the paper's core observations held up.
explanations.b: Correct — reviewers were skeptical of a striking functional claim resting on bioinformatic spacer-matching alone, without a manipulation experiment behind it.
explanations.c: The rejections were about the strength of the evidence for the claim, not journal scope.
explanations.d: No competing group had already published this specific spacer-phage match hypothesis before Mojica.

questions.prompt: Order these events from earliest to latest.

items.text: Ishino's group notes unexplained repeats near E. coli iap
Mojica and Jansen coin the acronym CRISPR
Barrangou and Horvath show spacer acquisition confers phage resistance
Deltcheva and Charpentier discover tracrRNA

questions.explanation: Ishino's observation (1987) came first, followed by Mojica and Jansen naming the phenomenon (2002), then Barrangou and Horvath's causal proof of immune function (2007), and finally the tracrRNA discovery (2011) that completed the mechanistic picture needed to later reprogram the system.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher(s) to their contribution.

right.text: Identified the protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM), 2005
Showed the CRISPR system targets DNA, not RNA, 2008
Discovered tracrRNA, 2011
Proved spacer acquisition confers phage resistance, 2007

questions.explanation: Bolotin identified the PAM in 2005; Marraffini and Sontheimer established DNA as the target in 2008; Deltcheva and Charpentier found tracrRNA in 2011; Barrangou and Horvath supplied the 2007 causal proof of immune function at Danisco.

lessons.label: 12012-2013: The Papers That Made It a Tool

sections.heading: June 2012: cutting DNA to order, in a test tube
sections.body: In June 2012, Martin Jinek, Krzysztof Chylinski, Ines Fonfara, Michael Hauer, Jennifer Doudna, and Emmanuelle Charpentier published in Science the paper that reframed CRISPR-Cas9 as a tool rather than a bacterial curiosity. Working with purified components in vitro, they showed that Cas9 could be guided to cut any DNA sequence if given a matching crRNA plus tracrRNA — and, critically, that the two RNAs could be fused into one synthetic single guide RNA (sgRNA), simplifying the system to two parts: Cas9 protein and one programmable RNA. A separate group — Virginijus Siksnys's lab in Vilnius, with Giedrius Gasiunas, Rodolphe Barrangou, and Philippe Horvath — had submitted similar dual-RNA-guided cleavage findings to PNAS earlier that spring; PNAS published it in September 2012, after Science's paper had already appeared.

sections.heading: The contested step: from a test tube to a nucleus
sections.body: Cutting purified DNA in a dish is not the same as cutting a chromosome packaged in chromatin, inside a living human cell, without killing it — and this gap was the real, contested engineering problem in 2012. Would a bacterial enzyme even fold and function correctly with human codon usage and nuclear import signals? Would guide RNAs work reliably against a three-billion-base-pair genome without wrecking the cell? Several labs raced to answer this simultaneously. In January 2013, Science published back-to-back papers answering yes: Le Cong and Feng Zhang's group, and George Church and Prashant Mali's group, each independently demonstrated CRISPR-Cas9 editing in human cells, using codon-optimized Cas9 and nuclear localization signals. Jinek's own group followed in early 2013 with a detailed eLife paper on optimizing the system for mammalian genome editing. What actually converts a Cas9 cut into an edit is the cell's own DNA repair response: the double-strand break is resolved either by error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), which typically leaves small insertions or deletions that disrupt the gene (a knockout), or, if a repair template is supplied, by homology-directed repair (HDR), which can copy a precise, researcher-specified sequence into the break — the difference between merely disabling a gene and rewriting it.

sections.heading: From four papers to thousands of labs
sections.body: Editing quickly proved portable across organisms — labs applied the same reagents to zebrafish and to plants within months, confirming CRISPR-Cas9 was not a human-cell fluke but a general tool. What made the explosion possible was that the reagents were cheap and simple: order a short guide RNA (about $10-20) and use an off-the-shelf Cas9, instead of engineering a custom protein per target the way zinc-finger nucleases or TALENs required. Plasmids were deposited in nonprofit repositories like Addgene, and within roughly two years of the January 2013 human-cell papers, thousands of labs worldwide were routinely editing genomes that previously required specialized engineering teams.

lessons.workedExample: A student claims 'CRISPR was invented in 2012.' A judge presses: invented for what? The precise answer separates two achievements. The June 2012 Jinek/Doudna/Charpentier paper demonstrated programmable DNA cleavage in vitro — a biochemistry result, not yet a genome-editing tool, because no one had shown it worked inside a living nucleus. The January 2013 Cong/Zhang and Mali/Church papers closed that gap by showing the same two-component system (Cas9 + sgRNA) could cut targeted sequences inside human cells and trigger the cell's own repair machinery to make edits. Both steps were necessary; conflating them erases the seven-month engineering problem that made human genome editing possible.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'what year was CRISPR invented' specifically to catch this collapse of two distinct achievements into one. A student who can name both the June 2012 in vitro cleavage paper and the January 2013 human-cell papers — and explain why the second required real engineering (codon optimization, nuclear localization, working through chromatin) rather than being a trivial extension — demonstrates they understand that going from 'it can cut DNA' to 'it can edit a genome inside a living cell' was itself a scientific accomplishment, not a formality.

questions.prompt: What was the key technical contribution of the June 2012 Jinek, Chylinski, Fonfara, Hauer, Doudna, and Charpentier Science paper?

options.text: First demonstration of CRISPR-Cas9 editing inside a living human cell
Showing dual-RNA-guided DNA cleavage in vitro and that the guide RNAs could be fused into one synthetic single guide RNA
First use of CRISPR-Cas9 in a zebrafish embryo
Discovery of the tracrRNA molecule itself

explanations.a: That milestone came seven months later, in the January 2013 human-cell papers, not the June 2012 paper.
explanations.b: Correct — the paper demonstrated programmable cleavage of purified DNA in vitro and introduced the fused single guide RNA that simplified the system to two components.
explanations.c: Zebrafish and plant editing followed later in 2013, after the human-cell demonstrations.
explanations.d: tracrRNA was discovered by Deltcheva and Charpentier in 2011, a separate, earlier paper.

questions.prompt: Why was moving CRISPR-Cas9 editing into human cells considered a genuinely contested engineering step, not a formality?

options.text: Because human cells lack any DNA repair machinery
Because a bacterial protein needed codon optimization and nuclear localization signals to fold, enter the nucleus, and function amid chromatin without killing the cell
Because human cells cannot be cultured in a laboratory
Because guide RNAs cannot be synthesized outside of bacteria

explanations.a: Human cells have robust DNA repair pathways; in fact CRISPR editing relies on hijacking that repair machinery.
explanations.b: Correct — a bacterial-derived Cas9 had to be codon-optimized for human expression and fitted with nuclear localization signals to reach and function on chromatin-packaged chromosomal DNA.
explanations.c: Human cell culture was already routine well before 2012 and was not the barrier.
explanations.d: Guide RNAs are short synthetic oligonucleotides that can be made chemically or transcribed in any cell type; this was not the obstacle.

questions.prompt: Order these publications from earliest to latest.

items.text: Jinek, Chylinski, Fonfara, Hauer, Doudna, Charpentier — Science, in vitro dual-RNA cleavage
Gasiunas, Barrangou, Horvath, Siksnys — PNAS, dual-RNA-guided cleavage
Cong/Zhang and Mali/Church — Science, human-cell editing
Jinek et al. — eLife, mammalian genome-editing optimization

questions.explanation: The Science in vitro paper appeared June 2012; the PNAS paper (submitted earlier but published later) appeared September 2012; the back-to-back human-cell Science papers appeared January 2013; Jinek's detailed eLife optimization paper followed shortly after in 2013.

questions.prompt: What made CRISPR-Cas9 spread to thousands of labs within about two years of the human-cell papers, unlike earlier tools such as zinc-finger nucleases or TALENs?

options.text: It required no guide molecule at all
Retargeting it only required ordering a new cheap guide RNA rather than engineering a new custom protein per target
It was the first genome-editing tool ever developed
It worked only in bacteria, so no biosafety review was needed

explanations.a: CRISPR-Cas9 absolutely requires a guide RNA; that guide is exactly what makes it easy to retarget.
explanations.b: Correct — unlike zinc-finger nucleases or TALENs, which required custom protein engineering for every new DNA target, CRISPR-Cas9 only needed a new, cheap synthetic guide RNA, drastically lowering cost and expertise barriers.
explanations.c: Zinc-finger nucleases and TALENs preceded CRISPR-Cas9 as genome-editing tools; CRISPR was not first.
explanations.d: CRISPR-Cas9 was rapidly applied in human cells, zebrafish, and plants, and was very much subject to biosafety review.

lessons.label: The Patent War and the Nobel

sections.heading: Two filings, one interference
sections.body: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier's team (via UC Berkeley and the University of Vienna) filed a provisional patent application in May 2012, describing CRISPR-Cas9 broadly. Feng Zhang's team at the Broad Institute filed later, in December 2012, but paid for the USPTO's 'Track One' prioritized examination and so received granted patents first — patents written specifically around CRISPR-Cas9 use in eukaryotic (plant and animal) cells. Broad's foundational patent, US 8,697,359, was granted in April 2014, while UC's application was still in ordinary examination. Note what did *not* cause this: both applications were filed before the America Invents Act's first-to-file provisions took effect on March 16, 2013, so priority between them was still governed by the older first-to-invent rules. That is exactly why UC's 2015 challenge at the Patent Office took the form of an interference proceeding — a fact-finding contest over who actually invented eukaryotic CRISPR editing first — rather than a simple comparison of filing dates. Under a pure first-to-file rule, UC's earlier May 2012 date would have settled the matter immediately.

sections.heading: No interference, then priority to Broad — then reopened
sections.body: In February 2017, the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) ruled there was 'no interference-in-fact': it found that a person skilled in the art would not have had a reasonable expectation that a system working in bacteria would also work in the more complex eukaryotic cell environment, so Broad's eukaryotic claims were patentably distinct from UC's broader claims and both sets of patents could coexist. The Federal Circuit affirmed that in September 2018. UC then pursued a second interference over the same eukaryotic territory, and in February 2022 the PTAB ruled again — this time awarding Broad priority of invention for CRISPR-Cas9 editing in eukaryotic cells. UC and Vienna appealed, and on 12 May 2025 the Federal Circuit vacated that 2022 decision and remanded the case to the PTAB. The appeals court held that the Board had applied the wrong legal standard for conception: it had effectively demanded that the Doudna-Charpentier team show their design would work in eukaryotic cells, when the correct test is whether the inventors held a definite and permanent idea of the invention that a skilled person could reduce to practice using routine methods. The Board, in other words, had collapsed conception into reduction to practice. As of 2026 the PTAB has not issued its decision on remand, so priority for the single-guide eukaryotic claims is genuinely unsettled.

sections.heading: The 2020 Nobel and the credit it couldn't fully settle
sections.body: In October 2020, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Doudna and Charpentier alone, 'for the development of a method for genome editing' — the first time two women shared a Nobel science prize without a male co-recipient. The award recognized the mechanistic discovery (the June 2012 in vitro paper) but sidestepped the harder question of who deserves credit for turning it into a genome-editing tool. Feng Zhang, George Church, and the Lithuanian biochemist Virginijus Siksnys (whose independent PNAS paper on dual-RNA-guided cleavage was submitted before Jinek and Charpentier's but published after) were left out, as was Francisco Mojica, whose foundational 2005 hypothesis the Nobel committee's own materials cited. The episode is now a standard case study in how scientific prizes compress a many-author, many-country discovery into a small, contestable list of names.

lessons.workedExample: A judge asks a student: 'If Doudna and Charpentier won the Nobel, does that mean their patent claim also won?' The precise answer is no — and the reason is more interesting than a simple yes or no. The Nobel recognized the June 2012 discovery of programmable dual-RNA-guided cleavage: a scientific-priority judgement made by a Swedish academy, and final the day it was announced. The patent dispute is a separate legal question — who can show, under US patent law, that they first conceived and reduced eukaryotic-cell editing to practice — decided by the PTAB and the Federal Circuit on lab notebooks, dated records, and doctrines like conception. Those tracks ran independently and on different clocks: Broad held the upper hand after the PTAB's 2022 priority ruling, but the Federal Circuit vacated that ruling in May 2025 and sent it back for reconsideration under the correct conception standard, so the legal question is still open while the Nobel has been settled since 2020. Scientific priority and patent priority are different questions, asked by different bodies, on different evidence.
lessons.judgeFraming: This pairing is a favorite judge probe because it tests whether a student conflates prestige with legal entitlement, or discovery with application. A strong answer keeps the two tracks separate: the Nobel rewards the foundational biochemical mechanism (dual-RNA-guided cleavage, June 2012), while the patent interference asks who first conceived and reduced a specific, commercially valuable application — eukaryotic-cell editing — to practice. A student who knows the patent track is still unresolved (vacated and remanded in May 2025) rather than settled in Broad's favour is showing they follow the story rather than a headline. Naming at least one scientist left out of the Nobel (Zhang, Church, Siksnys, or Mojica) and explaining why shows they understand that scientific credit is an ongoing negotiation, not a settled fact stamped by one prize.

questions.prompt: What did the PTAB's February 2017 'no interference-in-fact' ruling actually decide?

options.text: That UC Berkeley's patent claims were invalid entirely
That Broad's eukaryotic-cell claims were patentably distinct from UC's broader claims, since success in eukaryotic cells was not obviously predictable from success in bacteria
That Doudna and Charpentier had committed fraud in their patent filing
That CRISPR-Cas9 could not be patented at all

explanations.a: The ruling did not invalidate UC's claims; it found the two parties' claims covered different, non-overlapping territory.
explanations.b: Correct — the PTAB found no reasonable expectation that bacterial success would translate to eukaryotic cells, making Broad's eukaryotic claims distinct enough from UC's claims that both patent estates could stand.
explanations.c: No finding of fraud was made against either party in this proceeding.
explanations.d: The ruling was about which party's claims covered which application, not about patentability of CRISPR-Cas9 in general.

questions.prompt: The PTAB awarded Broad priority of invention for eukaryotic CRISPR-Cas9 editing in February 2022. What happened to that decision on appeal?

options.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed it, ending the dispute in Broad's favour
In May 2025 the Federal Circuit vacated it and remanded, holding that the PTAB had applied the wrong standard for conception
The Federal Circuit reversed it outright and awarded the eukaryotic patents to UC and Vienna
UC and Vienna declined to appeal, so the 2022 ruling became final

explanations.a: It was not affirmed — the Federal Circuit found a legal error in how the Board analysed conception and sent the case back.
explanations.b: Correct — on 12 May 2025 the Federal Circuit vacated the 2022 priority award and remanded. The Board had effectively required proof that the Doudna-Charpentier design would work in eukaryotic cells, collapsing conception into reduction to practice; the correct test is whether the inventors had a definite and permanent idea a skilled person could implement by routine methods.
explanations.c: The court did not decide priority itself. It corrected the legal standard and returned the fact-finding to the PTAB, which has not yet ruled on remand.
explanations.d: UC and Vienna did appeal, and the appeal succeeded in reopening the priority question.

questions.prompt: Match each figure to their role in the patent/Nobel story.

right.text: Sole recipients of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Broad Institute researcher whose team's eukaryotic-use patents were granted first, via prioritized examination, and who received no Nobel
Submitted an independent dual-RNA-cleavage paper before Jinek/Charpentier's but published after, and received no Nobel
Authored the foundational 2005 spacer-match hypothesis, cited by the Nobel committee but not awarded the prize

questions.explanation: Doudna and Charpentier alone received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Zhang's Broad team filed later but used Track One prioritized examination, so its eukaryotic patents issued first (April 2014); he was not a Nobel recipient, and the underlying priority contest is still unresolved on remand. Siksnys's independently submitted PNAS paper was published after Jinek and Charpentier's Science paper and he was excluded from the prize. Mojica's 2005 hypothesis was foundational and cited by the Nobel committee's own materials, yet he too was left off the prize.

questions.prompt: Broad filed seven months after UC yet was first to receive a granted patent, and the fight was then fought through an interference proceeding — a first-to-invent mechanism — even though the US was shifting to first-to-file. What explains both facts?

options.text: Broad paid for the USPTO's Track One prioritized examination, which speeds up examination but confers no priority; and because both applications predate the AIA's 16 March 2013 first-to-file cutover, priority between them was still decided under first-to-invent rules
The America Invents Act's first-to-file rules had just taken effect, and under them Broad's expedited grant date overrode UC's earlier filing date
The first-to-file transition applies only to individual inventors, not to institutions like UC and Broad, so the old rules governed
Interference proceedings were mandatory for all biotechnology patents regardless of when the applications were filed

explanations.a: Correct — two separate mechanisms. Track One buys faster examination, which is why Broad's patent issued in April 2014, but it does not move an applicant ahead in priority. And since UC filed in May 2012 and Broad in December 2012, both beat the AIA's March 2013 cutover, so the old first-to-invent regime applied — which is precisely why an interference (a contest over who invented first, not who filed first) was the available tool.
explanations.b: Backwards on two counts. The AIA's first-to-file provisions did not reach these applications at all, and had they applied they would have favoured UC's *earlier* May 2012 filing. A grant date never overrides a filing date.
explanations.c: The first-to-file transition applies regardless of whether the applicant is an individual or an institution. What made the old rules apply here was the filing dates, not the identity of the filers.
explanations.d: Interference is used specifically to resolve contested priority under first-to-invent rules; it was never a blanket requirement for biotechnology patents, and the AIA phased it out for later-filed applications.

lessons.label: He Jiankui and the Germline Line

sections.heading: The split before the crossing
sections.body: The debate over editing human embryos predates He Jiankui by years. At a 2015 meeting in Napa, California, scientists including Doudna and David Baltimore discussed whether heritable (germline) human editing should proceed. Weeks later, Edward Lanphier and coauthors published a call in Nature for a moratorium on clinical germline editing, arguing the technology was too immature and the ethical groundwork unlaid. George Church publicly dissented, arguing that a blanket moratorium could block legitimate, carefully governed research and that the harder question was how to regulate germline editing responsibly, not whether to ban discussion of it outright. That unresolved split was still open when He acted.

sections.heading: November 2018: the twins and what the editing actually did
sections.body: In November 2018, He Jiankui, then at Southern University of Science and Technology in Shenzhen, announced that he had edited human embryos to disrupt the CCR5 gene, aiming to confer HIV resistance, and that twin girls (given the pseudonyms Lulu and Nana) had been born from these edited embryos, with a third child born later. The scientific failures were severe: the edits were mosaic (not present in every cell, undermining any claimed protection), and none of the resulting alleles matched CCR5-Δ32, the naturally occurring deletion that actually confers HIV resistance in some populations — the girls carried novel, uncharacterized CCR5 variants of unknown function instead. The story broke before He's own announcement: MIT Technology Review reporter Antonio Regalado found He's filing in a Chinese clinical-trial registry and published it days ahead of the summit, undercutting any claim that the work had gone through normal scientific transparency or oversight. He then revealed the work at the Second International Summit on Human Genome Editing in Hong Kong, where the international scientific community's reaction was immediate condemnation.

sections.heading: Conviction and the still-open question
sections.body: In December 2019, a Shenzhen court convicted He and two collaborators of illegal medical practice, sentencing He to three years in prison and a fine reported around 3 million yuan (roughly $430,000), with a lifetime ban from reproductive medicine. The WHO convened an advisory committee on human genome editing governance, and the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) together with the UK's Royal Society issued reports establishing criteria before any future heritable editing could be considered responsible. None of these bodies declared heritable editing permanently forbidden — the live, unresolved question in the field is whether germline editing is off-limits in principle or simply premature given today's editing precision and oversight.

lessons.workedExample: A judge asks a student to explain, precisely, what went wrong scientifically (not just ethically) with He's experiment. The strongest answer separates two failures. First, mosaicism: because the editing was done at the single-cell embryo stage and Cas9 kept cutting after the first division, different cells in the resulting babies carry different edits or no edit at all — so even if the intended edit worked, not every cell would be protected. Second, the edits produced were not CCR5-Δ32, the specific 32-base-pair deletion known from population studies to disrupt the CCR5 receptor and block HIV entry; instead, sequencing showed novel indels of unverified function, meaning the girls may carry a mutation with unknown, potentially harmful consequences and no confirmed protective benefit.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe He Jiankui specifically because it is the case where 'this seems like a reasonable use of CRISPR' collapses on the actual science, not just the ethics. A student who only says 'it was unethical because it wasn't consented to properly' has skipped the harder, more testable claim: the edits themselves were scientifically inadequate — mosaic, off-target from the known protective variant, and performed without evidence they would even work as intended. Naming the mosaicism and the CCR5-Δ32 mismatch specifically shows a student can evaluate a genome-editing claim on its technical merits, not just its headline.

questions.prompt: Why did the CCR5 edits in Lulu and Nana likely fail to confer the intended HIV resistance?

options.text: CCR5 has no known connection to HIV infection
The edits were mosaic and did not match CCR5-Δ32, the specific naturally protective deletion
The embryos were not implanted successfully
CRISPR cannot target the CCR5 gene at all

explanations.a: CCR5 is well established as the co-receptor HIV uses to enter immune cells; CCR5-Δ32 carriers show natural resistance.
explanations.b: Correct — the resulting edits were present in only some cells (mosaicism) and produced novel variants, not the CCR5-Δ32 deletion known to disrupt HIV entry, so protection was not reliably established.
explanations.c: The embryos were successfully implanted and resulted in live births; implantation was not the failure point.
explanations.d: CRISPR was able to target and cut CCR5; the failure was in the precision and consistency of the resulting edit, not an inability to target the gene.

questions.prompt: What was George Church's position in the debate that followed the 2015 Lanphier et al. moratorium call?

options.text: He agreed a full, permanent ban on germline editing research and discussion was necessary
He argued a blanket moratorium could block legitimate governed research and that regulation, not prohibition of discussion, was the harder problem
He called for immediate clinical trials of germline editing in 2015
He had no public position on the moratorium debate

explanations.a: Church's dissent was specifically against a blanket moratorium, not in favor of one.
explanations.b: Correct — Church publicly argued against a total moratorium, favoring careful, responsible regulatory pathways over an outright ban on even discussing germline editing.
explanations.c: Church did not call for immediate clinical application in 2015; his argument was about not foreclosing responsible research and debate.
explanations.d: Church was a visible, named dissenting voice against the Lanphier et al. moratorium call.

questions.prompt: Order these events from earliest to latest.

items.text: Napa meeting and Lanphier et al.'s moratorium call in Nature
He Jiankui announces edited twins at the Hong Kong summit
Shenzhen court convicts He, sentencing him to three years in prison
WHO advisory committee and NASEM/Royal Society governance reports follow

questions.explanation: The Napa meeting and Lanphier et al.'s moratorium call came in 2015, He's announcement came in November 2018, his conviction and sentencing followed in December 2019, and the WHO and NASEM/Royal Society governance reports came after as the field worked to establish clearer oversight criteria.

questions.prompt: What is the 'live question' left open after He Jiankui's conviction and the subsequent governance reports?

options.text: Whether CRISPR can edit DNA at all
Whether heritable human genome editing is permanently forbidden in principle, or merely premature given current precision and oversight
Whether He Jiankui's conviction was legally valid
Whether somatic (non-heritable) gene therapy should be banned

explanations.a: CRISPR's basic ability to edit DNA was never in question by this point; the dispute concerns heritable human application specifically.
explanations.b: Correct — the WHO, NASEM, and Royal Society reports set criteria for future responsible research rather than declaring a permanent ban, leaving open whether germline editing could someday be judged ready.
explanations.c: The legal validity of the conviction under Chinese law was not the focus of the international scientific and ethical debate.
explanations.d: Somatic gene therapy (non-heritable, like Casgevy) is a separate, largely accepted category distinct from the germline controversy.

lessons.label: Does CRISPR Damage More Than We Thought?

sections.heading: A retraction: the mutations were the mice, not the editing
sections.body: In May 2017, Schaefer and colleagues reported in Nature Methods thousands of unexpected single-nucleotide variants and small indels in CRISPR-edited mice, alarming the field about off-target effects far beyond what standard prediction algorithms caught. But their design compared edited mice to unrelated control mice rather than to a shared genetic ancestor, so the 'unexpected mutations' were plausibly just normal background genetic variation between different mouse lines, not CRISPR off-target damage. Critics published rebuttals within weeks, and in March 2018 Nature Methods retracted the paper, with the retraction noting the observed variants could not be conclusively attributed to CRISPR-Cas9 — a reminder that a dramatic safety claim needs a properly matched control before it means anything.

sections.heading: On-target damage nobody was looking for
sections.body: The next scares held up better because they targeted a real blind spot: standard genotyping (PCR across the cut site, then short-read sequencing) only detects small indels near the cut and misses larger structural changes — a PCR amplicon typically spans well under a kilobase, so a multi-kilobase deletion that removes one of the primer-binding sites simply fails to amplify at all, reading as "no edit detected" rather than flagging a large rearrangement. In 2018, Kosicki, Tomberg, and Bradley used long-read sequencing and long-range PCR in mouse and human cells and found that DNA double-strand breaks from Cas9 frequently resolved into large kilobase-scale deletions and complex rearrangements at the very site being edited — damage invisible to the assays most labs were using. That same year, two separate Nature Medicine papers, from Haapaniemi and colleagues and from Ihry and colleagues, showed that CRISPR-induced double-strand breaks activate p53, the cell's DNA-damage checkpoint, meaning cells with a healthy, functioning p53 pathway tend to resist editing — so successfully edited cell populations can be inadvertently enriched for cells with impaired p53, a tumor-suppressor gene, raising a cancer-risk concern. The finding was serious enough that CRISPR-focused biotech stocks fell sharply within days of the reporting.

sections.heading: Chromothripsis, and the field's actual response
sections.body: In 2021, Leibowitz and colleagues in Nature Genetics went further, showing that Cas9-induced double-strand breaks can trigger chromothripsis — the catastrophic shattering and haphazard reassembly of a chromosome, a process previously associated mainly with cancer genomes. Rather than treating any one paper as a final verdict, the field responded methodologically: adopting long-read and whole-genome sequencing as standard safety assays instead of short-read PCR alone, shifting toward transient ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery — pre-assembled Cas9 protein plus guide RNA that degrades quickly, limiting the time double-strand breaks can accumulate — and increasing investment in nuclease-free editing approaches (base and prime editing) that avoid double-strand breaks altogether.

lessons.workedExample: A student cites the Schaefer et al. 2017 paper to argue CRISPR causes widespread unexpected mutation. A judge should be able to press on this and expect the student to know it was retracted — and why the retraction matters more than the original claim. The retraction wasn't a cover-up or a minor correction; it exposed a specific design flaw: the 'edited' and 'control' mice were not siblings from a shared genetic background, so the thousands of variants likely reflected ordinary strain-to-strain genetic variation, not anything CRISPR did. Citing a retracted paper as current evidence, without noting the retraction, signals a student hasn't traced their own source past the headline.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe CRISPR safety findings because this is where students most often cite the scariest-sounding paper without checking whether it held up. The Schaefer retraction versus the Kosicki, Haapaniemi/Ihry, and Leibowitz findings (which were not retracted and prompted real methodological change) is a clean test of whether a student evaluates evidence or just collects alarming headlines. The strongest answers also know the field's actual response — long-read sequencing, RNP delivery, nuclease-free editors — showing they understand science self-correcting through better assays rather than treating any single paper as the last word.

questions.prompt: Why was the Schaefer et al. 2017 Nature Methods paper retracted in 2018?

options.text: The authors admitted to fabricating the sequencing data
The edited and control mice lacked a shared genetic ancestor, so the observed variants likely reflected normal background strain variation rather than CRISPR-induced mutation
The mice used were the wrong species
A competing lab could not replicate the sequencing technology used

explanations.a: No fabrication was found; the issue was an experimental design flaw in the control comparison.
explanations.b: Correct — because the edited and control mice were not derived from a shared ancestor, the thousands of 'unexpected' variants were most plausibly ordinary genetic differences between mouse lines, not CRISPR off-target effects.
explanations.c: Both edited and control animals were mice; species was never in question.
explanations.d: The retraction was about interpretation of the comparison, not about the sequencing technology's validity.

questions.prompt: What did Kosicki, Tomberg, and Bradley (2018) find that standard short-read PCR-based genotyping was likely to miss?

options.text: Off-target cuts on entirely different chromosomes
Large kilobase-scale deletions and complex rearrangements occurring at the on-target cut site itself
Changes in gene expression levels unrelated to DNA sequence
Mosaic inheritance patterns across generations

explanations.a: Their finding concerned on-target damage at the intended cut site, not distant off-target cuts.
explanations.b: Correct — using long-read sequencing and long-range PCR, they found double-strand break repair frequently produced large deletions and complex rearrangements right at the targeted site, invisible to standard short-range genotyping.
explanations.c: The study examined DNA structural changes directly, not downstream expression effects.
explanations.d: This was a cell-line and animal-model finding about repair outcomes at the cut site, not a study of inheritance patterns.

questions.prompt: What safety concern did Haapaniemi et al. and Ihry et al. (both 2018, Nature Medicine) raise about p53?

options.text: p53 makes CRISPR editing impossible in all cell types
Functional p53 triggers a DNA-damage response that resists editing, so successfully edited cell populations may be inadvertently enriched for cells with impaired p53, a tumor suppressor
p53 repairs off-target cuts perfectly, eliminating any editing risk
p53 is only expressed in mouse cells, not human cells

explanations.a: Editing still occurs in cells with functional p53, just less efficiently; it is not made impossible.
explanations.b: Correct — because cells with intact p53 tend to resist successful editing, the surviving edited-cell population can be skewed toward cells with a weakened p53 pathway, raising concern about selecting for a cancer-associated vulnerability.
explanations.c: p53's role here is triggering damage response/cell-cycle arrest, not precise repair of the edit itself.
explanations.d: p53 is expressed and functions similarly across human and mouse cells; this was not a species-limited finding.

questions.prompt: Order these safety-related findings from earliest to latest.

items.text: Schaefer et al. report thousands of unexpected mutations in mice
Schaefer et al. paper retracted
Kosicki, Tomberg, and Bradley report large deletions/rearrangements; Haapaniemi et al. and Ihry et al. report p53-mediated selection
Leibowitz et al. report CRISPR-induced chromothripsis

questions.explanation: Schaefer et al.'s report appeared in May 2017 and was retracted in March 2018; the Kosicki et al. and the two p53 papers all appeared in 2018; Leibowitz et al.'s chromothripsis finding followed in 2021, showing the field's safety scrutiny deepened over time rather than resolving after any one paper.

lessons.label: Competing Camps and Unsettled Questions

sections.heading: Delivery and enzyme choice: no consensus winner
sections.body: Getting Cas9 into cells safely is its own contested engineering problem. Viral delivery (adeno-associated virus, AAV) gives sustained, efficient expression but that persistence is a liability: the longer Cas9 lingers in a cell, the more time it has to cut off-target sites, and AAV also triggers immune responses that can limit redosing. Delivering pre-assembled ribonucleoprotein (RNP) — Cas9 protein bound to its guide RNA, with no DNA or viral vector involved — clears from the cell within days, cutting off-target exposure window sharply, but it is harder to manufacture at scale and to target to specific tissues in the body. On the enzyme side, Cas12a (Cpf1) offers a different PAM requirement and cuts DNA leaving staggered rather than blunt ends, which can be an advantage for some editing strategies, but Cas9 remains far better characterized and more widely validated across cell types.

sections.heading: Cut-based editing versus the nuclease-free school
sections.body: The deepest methodological split is over whether double-strand breaks (DSBs) are an acceptable cost of editing at all. Standard Cas9 editing works by cutting both DNA strands and letting the cell's repair machinery introduce or fix a change — and the safety findings on large deletions, p53 activation, and chromothripsis all trace back to that break. Base editing and prime editing, developed largely in David Liu's lab, chemically rewrite individual bases or small sequences using a catalytically impaired Cas9 fused to other enzymes, without ever cutting both strands. Advocates argue this sidesteps the DSB-linked risks entirely; skeptics respond that 'DSB-free' does not automatically mean 'damage-free' — base and prime editors have their own off-target profile (unwanted bystander edits, RNA off-targets) that is still being characterized, so the claim that avoiding DSBs solves the safety problem outright is itself contested.

sections.heading: Preexisting immunity, and gene drives' containment debate
sections.body: A separate open question is whether the human immune system already limits CRISPR therapeutics before they even begin. Charlesworth and colleagues reported in 2019 that a majority of tested human donors carried preexisting antibodies against SpCas9 (from Streptococcus pyogenes) and SaCas9 (from Staphylococcus aureus) — both bacterial species common human pathogens — raising concern that repeat in vivo dosing could trigger a destructive immune reaction. Meanwhile in ecology, gene drives (CRISPR systems designed to spread an edit through a wild population faster than normal inheritance, proposed for uses like suppressing malaria-carrying mosquitoes) split researchers over containment. Kevin Esvelt, who helped develop the technology, has pushed for split-drive and daisy-chain designs that self-limit how far a drive can spread, arguing irreversible wild releases are too risky without them; Target Malaria, a research consortium, has moved toward staged field trials of gene-drive mosquitoes in Africa, arguing that regulatory review and community engagement — not indefinite containment — is the responsible path to a working malaria intervention.

lessons.workedExample: A judge asks a student defending a base-editing project: 'So base editing is safe because it doesn't cut both strands?' The strong answer resists the trap. Base and prime editors avoid the double-strand break entirely, so they sidestep the specific mechanisms behind large deletions, chromothripsis, and p53-mediated selection documented in Cas9 cutting studies. But that is not the same as being risk-free: base editors can produce unwanted 'bystander' edits at nearby bases within their editing window, and some variants have shown RNA-level off-target editing. The honest claim is narrower and more defensible: nuclease-free editors remove one well-documented category of risk, not risk altogether.
lessons.judgeFraming: This lesson exists because science-fair judges specifically listen for false binaries — 'CRISPR is dangerous' or 'the new method is safe' stated without qualification. A student who can lay out RNP versus viral delivery, or DSB-based versus nuclease-free editing, as genuine trade-offs with a real argument on each side (not a solved question with one correct camp) shows they can hold competing, well-evidenced positions at once. Naming Charlesworth's 2019 immunity finding or the Esvelt-versus-Target-Malaria containment debate by name signals the student engaged with the actual unsettled literature, not a simplified pro/con summary.

questions.prompt: What is the main safety trade-off between AAV viral delivery and RNP (ribonucleoprotein) delivery of Cas9?

options.text: AAV clears the cell within days, while RNP persists for months
AAV gives sustained expression but the persistence widens the off-target exposure window and can provoke immune responses, while RNP clears within days but is harder to manufacture and target
Both methods are functionally identical in persistence and immune response
RNP cannot deliver Cas9 to human cells at all

explanations.a: This reverses the actual persistence pattern — AAV is the longer-lasting delivery method, not RNP.
explanations.b: Correct — AAV's durability is a double-edged sword (more time for off-target cutting, immune responses limiting redosing), while RNP's rapid clearance limits exposure time but complicates manufacturing and tissue targeting.
explanations.c: The two methods differ substantially in persistence, which is precisely why each has a distinct risk profile.
explanations.d: RNP delivery of Cas9 into human cells is an established, actively used method in editing research and therapeutics.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest counterargument to the claim that base and prime editing are inherently safer than Cas9 cutting because they avoid double-strand breaks?

options.text: Base and prime editors cannot edit any gene that Cas9 can edit

Avoiding double-strand breaks removes DSB-linked risks like large deletions and chromothripsis, but base and prime editors have their own off-target profile (bystander edits, RNA off-targets) that is still being characterized
Base editors still cut both DNA strands, so the claim is simply false
Base and prime editing were never tested for off-target effects
There is no meaningful difference between the two editing approaches

explanations.a: Base and prime editors have a broad, growing range of applications; this is not the core safety counterargument.
explanations.b: Correct — sidestepping DSB-linked risk is real, but it does not mean risk-free; unwanted bystander edits and RNA-level off-targets are a documented, separate concern for these editors.
explanations.c: Base and prime editors are designed with catalytically impaired Cas9 that does not cut both strands; that is their defining mechanism.
explanations.d: Off-target profiling of base and prime editors is an active area of study, not something skipped entirely.
explanations.e: The two approaches differ mechanistically (blunt double-strand cutting versus chemical base rewriting), which is the whole basis of the safety debate.

questions.prompt: What did Charlesworth and colleagues (2019) report about preexisting human immunity to Cas9?
