options.text: No humans carry any preexisting immune response to Cas9 proteins
A majority of tested donors had preexisting antibodies against SpCas9 and SaCas9, both derived from common bacterial pathogens
Preexisting immunity only affects mice, not humans
Immunity to Cas9 makes gene editing permanently impossible in any patient

explanations.a: The study found the opposite: a high proportion of donors carried preexisting immune responses.
explanations.b: Correct — because SpCas9 and SaCas9 derive from Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus, common human pathogens, a majority of tested donors already carried antibodies against these Cas9 variants, raising concern for repeat in vivo dosing.
explanations.c: The finding was specifically about human donor serum and T cells, not mice.
explanations.d: The finding raises a dosing and delivery concern, not an absolute barrier; strategies like RNP delivery and alternative Cas orthologs are ways researchers are addressing it.

questions.prompt: Match each person or organization to their position in the gene-drive containment debate.

right.text: Advocates split-drive and daisy-chain designs that self-limit spread, arguing irreversible wild releases are too risky without them
A research consortium pursuing staged field trials of gene-drive mosquitoes in Africa, favoring regulatory review and community engagement over indefinite containment

questions.explanation: Esvelt, who helped develop gene-drive technology, has pushed for self-limiting containment designs given the risk of irreversible ecological spread, while Target Malaria has advanced toward staged, regulated field trials as the practical path toward a working malaria-control intervention.

lessons.label: Cost, Access, and Who Actually Gets Edited

sections.heading: A $2.2 million price tag for a disease concentrated where it can least be afforded
sections.body: Casgevy, approved in the US in December 2023, was the first CRISPR-based therapy to reach patients, editing a patient's own blood stem cells to reactivate fetal hemoglobin and treat sickle cell disease. Vertex Pharmaceuticals set its US wholesale acquisition price at roughly $2.2 million per patient — and total cost of care, including hospitalization, often runs higher. Sickle cell disease disproportionately affects people of sub-Saharan African descent, and its highest-burden populations live in sub-Saharan Africa itself, where total per-capita health spending often runs to only tens or low hundreds of dollars a year — a rounding error against Casgevy's $2.2 million single-patient list price. The therapy that exists is real; the population most affected by the disease is, for now, almost entirely priced out of it.

sections.heading: The infrastructure problem is not just the sticker price
sections.body: Even a donated or subsidized dose does not solve access on its own, because Casgevy's delivery requires infrastructure most health systems lack: a patient's blood stem cells must be collected (mobilized and harvested via apheresis), edited outside the body, and then the patient must undergo busulfan myeloablative conditioning — chemotherapy that wipes out existing bone marrow so the edited cells can engraft — followed by weeks of hospitalization to manage the resulting immune vulnerability. That level of transplant-capable hospital care, with specialized staff and monitoring, is scarce precisely in the regions with the highest sickle cell burden, meaning price reduction alone would not close the access gap without matching investment in treatment centers.

sections.heading: Patent thickets and the personalized-medicine dilemma
sections.body: Overlapping CRISPR patents — the Broad/UC estates described in this unit's patent lesson, plus delivery and cell-therapy patents layered on top — create a licensing thicket that raises costs and slows entry for any company or nonprofit trying to build a lower-cost version; advocates have pushed for humanitarian or non-exclusive licensing terms specifically for low-resource settings, an approach with mixed uptake so far. A separate, forward-looking access question emerged in 2025, when physicians at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia treated infant KJ Muldoon, who had a severe, life-threatening urea cycle disorder, with a base-editing therapy custom-designed for his specific mutation — a true n-of-1 treatment. Regulatory and reimbursement systems are built around clinical trials proving a treatment works across a population; a therapy engineered for exactly one patient's mutation raises the open question of whether, and how, such bespoke treatments can ever be formally approved and paid for at all.

lessons.workedExample: A judge asks a student proposing a low-cost CRISPR delivery method: 'If you cut the manufacturing cost, does that solve access for sickle cell patients in the highest-burden regions?' The strong answer says no, and explains why with the actual treatment pathway: even a free dose of edited cells requires busulfan myeloablative conditioning to clear existing bone marrow, followed by weeks of hospitalization to manage the resulting immune vulnerability — care that depends on transplant-capable hospital infrastructure, not just the drug product itself. A student who only addresses the $2.2 million price tag has identified one barrier; a student who also names the conditioning regimen and hospital-capacity requirement has identified the deeper one.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe cost and access specifically to see whether a student treats equity as a footnote or as a real engineering and policy constraint. The strongest answers go past the headline price tag ($2.2 million) to the two harder layers: the transplant infrastructure that even a free therapy would still require, and the regulatory mismatch exposed by KJ Muldoon's 2025 bespoke base-editing treatment, where a trial framework built to prove a therapy works across a population does not obviously fit a treatment engineered for one patient's mutation. Naming that specific tension shows the student understands access as an open scientific-policy question, not just a matter of charity pricing.

questions.prompt: Why does Casgevy's roughly $2.2 million US list price understate the real access problem for sickle cell disease?

options.text: Because sickle cell disease is rare worldwide, so few patients are affected regardless of price
Because delivery also requires busulfan myeloablative conditioning and weeks of transplant-capable hospital care, infrastructure scarce in the highest-burden regions
Because the price is expected to rise further after 2026
Because Casgevy has not yet received regulatory approval anywhere

explanations.a: Sickle cell disease has a large global burden, especially concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, not a rare condition overall.
explanations.b: Correct — even setting price aside, the treatment pathway requires stem-cell collection, myeloablative chemotherapy conditioning, and extended hospitalization in a transplant-capable facility, infrastructure that is scarce precisely where the disease burden is highest.
explanations.c: The lesson centers on the price as set at approval and the infrastructure gap, not projected future price changes.
explanations.d: Casgevy received US approval in December 2023 and has since been approved in additional jurisdictions; approval status is not the barrier described here.

questions.prompt: What regulatory tension does KJ Muldoon's 2025 personalized base-editing treatment illustrate?

options.text: That base editing cannot be used in infants for safety reasons
That clinical trial and approval frameworks are built to prove a treatment works across a population, which fits awkwardly with a therapy custom-designed for one patient's specific mutation
That urea cycle disorders cannot be treated with any form of gene editing
That the FDA had already approved a standard pathway for n-of-1 gene therapies before 2025

explanations.a: The treatment was in fact administered to an infant, showing base editing could be used in that setting under close medical supervision.
explanations.b: Correct — KJ Muldoon's therapy was engineered specifically for his individual mutation, an n-of-1 case, which sits uneasily inside approval and reimbursement systems designed around population-level trial evidence.
explanations.c: The treatment demonstrates that a urea cycle disorder was successfully targeted with a custom base-editing approach.
explanations.d: No established, standard regulatory pathway for n-of-1 gene therapies existed prior to this case; that absence is precisely the open question the case raises.

questions.prompt: How do overlapping CRISPR patents (the Broad and UC/Vienna estates plus delivery and cell-therapy patents) affect low-cost access efforts?

options.text: They have no effect, since basic CRISPR patents expired before Casgevy's approval
They create a licensing thicket that raises costs and slows entry for companies or nonprofits attempting lower-cost versions, motivating calls for humanitarian or non-exclusive licensing
They guarantee free licensing for any humanitarian use automatically
They apply only outside the United States, so US costs are unaffected

explanations.a: The CRISPR patent estates described in this unit's patent lesson remained active and contested well past Casgevy's 2023 approval.
explanations.b: Correct — layered, overlapping patents across gene-editing and cell-therapy methods raise licensing costs and complexity, which is why advocates specifically push for humanitarian or non-exclusive licensing terms for low-resource settings, with mixed success so far.
explanations.c: Humanitarian licensing is not automatic; it depends on specific negotiated terms that vary by patent holder and has seen only mixed uptake.
explanations.d: The estates cover use broadly, including in the US market where Casgevy itself is priced and sold.

questions.prompt: Order these access-related steps a sickle cell patient must go through, from first to last, once approved for Casgevy treatment.

items.text: Patient's blood stem cells are collected via apheresis
Stem cells are edited outside the body
Patient undergoes busulfan myeloablative conditioning to clear existing bone marrow
Edited cells are infused and patient is hospitalized for weeks during engraftment

questions.explanation: Stem cells must first be harvested from the patient, then edited outside the body, after which the patient undergoes conditioning chemotherapy to make room for the edited cells, and finally the edited cells are infused with an extended hospital stay required to manage the vulnerable period until the new cells engraft.

units.label: Editing in the World: Therapies, Crops, and Biosafety

lessons.label: Sickle Cell and Beta-Thalassemia: The First Approved CRISPR Therapy

sections.heading: Don't fix the gene, unsilence the backup
sections.body: Exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel, brand name Casgevy) does not repair the sickle mutation in HBB at all. It edits a different gene entirely: BCL11A, the transcription factor that shuts off fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production after infancy in favor of adult hemoglobin. CRISPR-Cas9 is used ex vivo, in the patient's own CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells, to cut a specific erythroid-lineage-specific enhancer region of BCL11A rather than the gene's coding sequence — a design that suppresses BCL11A only in red-blood-cell precursors, leaving its other essential roles (in the brain and immune system) untouched. With BCL11A silenced in erythroid cells, those cells revert to producing HbF, which does not polymerize the way sickle hemoglobin does and physically dilutes the sickled protein, addressing sickle-cell disease and beta-thalassemia with the same edit despite their different HBB mutations.

sections.heading: From Victoria Gray to two regulatory firsts
sections.body: Victoria Gray became the first person treated for sickle-cell disease in the US CRISPR trial in July 2019. The pivotal CLIMB-121 trial reported roughly 94% of evaluable patients (29 of 31) free of severe vaso-occlusive crises for at least 12 consecutive months; the companion CLIMB-111 trial in beta-thalassemia reported about 91% of patients (32 of 35) achieving transfusion independence. Casgevy became the world's first approved CRISPR-based medicine when the UK's MHRA authorized it in November 2023, followed by FDA approval on December 8, 2023 — the same day the FDA approved a second, older-technology therapy, lovotibeglogene autotemcel (lovo-cel, Lyfgenia), which uses a lentiviral vector to add a functional anti-sickling beta-globin gene rather than editing BCL11A.

sections.heading: The cost of the cure
sections.body: Both therapies require the same brutal prerequisite: myeloablative conditioning with busulfan chemotherapy to clear existing bone marrow so the edited stem cells can engraft. Busulfan carries a well-documented risk of infertility (it is genotoxic to gonadal stem cells, and fertility preservation counseling is now standard before treatment) and a smaller but real long-term risk of secondary malignancy from the conditioning regimen itself. So the therapy that cures the genetic disease still exposes patients to the older risks of transplant medicine — a tradeoff that has not been engineered away, only inherited from decades of stem-cell transplantation. There is a second cost that has nothing to do with biology: Vertex listed Casgevy at roughly $2.2 million per patient at its December 2023 approval, on top of the conditioning and months of hospitalization around the infusion. 'Standard care' for the patients weighing this decision means chronic blood transfusions or hydroxyurea, taken indefinitely, which manage symptoms without addressing the underlying HBB mutation — so the choice is a single high-risk, high-cost procedure with a shot at a functional cure against a lifetime of lower-risk, lower-cost management that never removes the disease.

lessons.workedExample: A 14-year-old with sickle-cell disease and her family are deciding between Casgevy and standard care. Casgevy will not touch the sickle allele in HBB — it will knock down BCL11A's erythroid enhancer so her bone marrow starts making fetal hemoglobin again, at levels the CLIMB-121 trial associated with a roughly 94% chance of no severe pain crises for a year afterward. Getting there requires harvesting her own CD34+ cells, wiping out her existing marrow with busulfan (with the associated infertility risk discussed and fertility preservation offered beforehand), and reinfusing the edited cells. The upside is a plausible functional cure; the downside is a rough regimen borrowed entirely from transplant medicine, not from CRISPR.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows Casgevy will ask why it edits BCL11A instead of just fixing the HBB sickle mutation directly, and a student who cannot answer has memorized the name of the drug rather than the strategy. The specific, defensible answer is that de-repressing fetal hemoglobin via an erythroid-restricted enhancer is a safer, better-precedented target than precisely correcting a single base in HBB across enough stem cells to matter — and a strong answer also flags that the conditioning regimen, not the edit, is still the therapy's biggest safety liability, which shows the student understands where the real risk in a 'cured by CRISPR' headline actually lives.

questions.prompt: What does the CRISPR edit in exa-cel (Casgevy) actually do?

options.text: Corrects the single-base sickle mutation directly in the HBB gene
Disrupts an erythroid-specific enhancer of BCL11A to de-repress fetal hemoglobin
Inserts a functional beta-globin gene using a lentiviral vector
Deletes the entire HBB gene to stop sickle hemoglobin production

explanations.a: That would be direct gene correction, which is not the exa-cel strategy — no editing of the HBB mutation itself occurs.
explanations.b: Correct — exa-cel disrupts the erythroid-lineage-specific enhancer of BCL11A in autologous CD34+ cells, which de-represses fetal hemoglobin (HbF) production without touching HBB.
explanations.c: This describes lovo-cel (Lyfgenia), the lentiviral gene-addition comparator approved the same day, not exa-cel.
explanations.d: Deleting HBB entirely would eliminate all adult hemoglobin production and is not the mechanism used.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of evaluable CLIMB-121 patients were free of severe vaso-occlusive crises for at least 12 months?

options.text: About 50%
About 70%
About 94%
100%, with zero exceptions reported

explanations.a: This understates the reported result substantially.
explanations.b: Still below the reported figure.
explanations.c: Correct — roughly 94% (29 of 31 evaluable patients) were free of severe vaso-occlusive crises for at least 12 consecutive months.
explanations.d: The trial reported 29 of 31 evaluable patients, not a perfect 100%.

questions.prompt: Match each regulatory or clinical milestone to its date.

left.text: Victoria Gray treated, first US sickle-cell patient

right.text: July 2019
November 2023
December 8, 2023

questions.explanation: Victoria Gray was treated in July 2019; the UK's MHRA authorized Casgevy as the world's first approved CRISPR medicine in November 2023; the FDA approved it in the US on December 8, 2023, the same day it approved the lentiviral comparator lovo-cel.

questions.prompt: What is the main unresolved safety cost of exa-cel treatment, independent of the CRISPR edit itself?

options.text: Off-target CRISPR cuts causing new mutations
Rejection of the edited cells by the immune system
Busulfan myeloablative conditioning, which carries infertility and secondary-malignancy risk
Loss of fetal hemoglobin production over time

explanations.a: Off-target effects are monitored but are not the therapy's dominant, well-documented risk — the conditioning regimen is.
explanations.b: The cells are autologous (the patient's own), so immune rejection of the edited product is not the central concern.
explanations.c: Correct — the busulfan conditioning required to clear existing marrow before edited-cell infusion carries known infertility risk and a smaller risk of secondary malignancy, inherited from standard transplant medicine rather than from the edit.
explanations.d: The trials reported durable HbF induction, not a decline over time, in evaluable patients.

lessons.label: Editing Inside the Body

sections.heading: NTLA-2001: the first systemic in vivo CRISPR trial
sections.body: Every edit discussed so far happens outside the body: cells are removed, edited in a dish, and reinfused. NTLA-2001, developed by Intellia Therapeutics for transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, was different — it was the first CRISPR therapy dosed directly into a living patient's bloodstream. A lipid nanoparticle (LNP) carries Cas9 mRNA and a guide RNA targeting the TTR gene; the LNP is taken up preferentially by hepatocytes in the liver, where the mRNA is translated, Cas9 finds and knocks out TTR, and the misfolding protein that causes ATTR amyloidosis stops being made. Gillmore et al. (NEJM, 2021) reported dose-dependent knockdown of serum TTR, with a mean reduction of roughly 87% at the highest tested dose of 0.3 mg/kg — a single infusion producing a durable, near-total loss of a disease-causing protein without ever touching the patient's cells outside the body.

sections.heading: A permanent edit for a common condition raises a different bar
sections.body: Verve Therapeutics took the same LNP-to-liver delivery approach but swapped Cas9 knockout for base editing, targeting PCSK9 with programs VERVE-101 and its successor VERVE-102. Disabling PCSK9 mimics naturally occurring loss-of-function variants known to permanently lower LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular risk — but high cholesterol is a common, manageable, largely preventable condition affecting a huge population, not a rare fatal disease with no alternative. That changes the risk calculus: an irreversible one-shot edit is easier to justify against a disease like ATTR amyloidosis, which is progressive and fatal, than against a condition already treatable with statins and other reversible drugs, which is why permanent in vivo editing for common chronic disease has drawn more caution than the same technology aimed at rare genetic disease.

sections.heading: Delivery, not biology, decided the order
sections.body: EDIT-101 (Editas Medicine) targeted CEP290-associated Leber congenital amaurosis by injecting an AAV5 vector carrying CRISPR components directly under the retina to correct a splice-site mutation in photoreceptor cells — and despite reporting a biological and functional signal in its BRILLIANCE trial, the program was discontinued in 2022 as Editas deprioritized it. Liver, eye, and blood became the first tissues reached by in vivo or ex vivo editing not because their diseases were biologically simplest, but because each solves the delivery problem differently: the liver's fenestrated blood vessels let LNPs reach hepatocytes efficiently, the eye is small, enclosed, and immune-privileged enough for direct local injection, and blood stem cells can simply be removed, edited outside the body, and put back — sidestepping in vivo delivery altogether.

lessons.workedExample: A biotech is choosing between two programs: an in vivo liver edit for a fatal, rare protein-misfolding disease versus an in vivo liver edit for high cholesterol in the general population. For the fatal disease, NTLA-2001's roughly 87% TTR knockdown at 0.3 mg/kg (Gillmore et al., 2021) is judged a good trade against a lethal, progressive illness with few alternatives. For cholesterol, Verve's PCSK9 base-editing approach (VERVE-101/102) offers a permanent fix but competes against reversible, decades-proven statins — so regulators and patients demand a much higher safety bar before accepting an irreversible edit, even though the delivery technology (LNP to hepatocytes) is nearly identical in both cases.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge will ask why in vivo CRISPR programs cluster in the liver, eye, and blood, and the answer a strong student gives is delivery, not disease biology — LNPs naturally accumulate in hepatocytes, the eye tolerates local injection into an immune-privileged compartment, and blood stem cells can be edited ex vivo entirely outside the delivery problem. A judge probing risk will also want the student to explain why a permanent PCSK9 edit for common high cholesterol is held to a stricter bar than a permanent TTR knockout for a rare fatal disease — irreversibility means the acceptable risk depends heavily on what the alternative treatment already is.

questions.prompt: What made NTLA-2001 a landmark trial?

options.text: It was the first ex vivo CRISPR edit of hematopoietic stem cells
It was the first systemic in vivo CRISPR therapy, dosed directly into the bloodstream
It was the first base-editing trial in humans
It was the first CRISPR trial to target a common chronic disease

explanations.a: Ex vivo hematopoietic stem cell editing (as in exa-cel) is a different and earlier-established approach.
explanations.b: Correct — NTLA-2001 delivered Cas9 mRNA and guide RNA via LNP directly into the patient's bloodstream, the first systemic in vivo CRISPR trial in humans.
explanations.c: NTLA-2001 used nuclease knockout, not base editing; VERVE-101 used base editing.
explanations.d: NTLA-2001 targeted ATTR amyloidosis, a rare disease, not a common chronic condition.

questions.prompt: Gillmore et al. (NEJM, 2021) reported approximately what mean reduction in serum TTR at the 0.3 mg/kg dose of NTLA-2001?

options.text: About 30%
About 50%
About 87%
About 99.9%

explanations.a: This is well below the reported figure at the highest dose.
explanations.b: This is closer to the reduction seen at a lower dose tested, not the highest dose.
explanations.c: Correct — the highest tested dose (0.3 mg/kg) was associated with a mean serum TTR reduction of roughly 87%.
explanations.d: The reported reduction was substantial but not this near-complete.

questions.prompt: Match each in vivo/ex vivo editing program to its target and delivery approach.

right.text: LNP-delivered Cas9 knockout of TTR in hepatocytes
LNP-delivered base editing of PCSK9 in hepatocytes
AAV5 subretinal delivery to correct a CEP290 splice mutation

questions.explanation: NTLA-2001 uses LNP-delivered Cas9 mRNA and guide RNA to knock out TTR in hepatocytes; VERVE-101/102 uses LNP-delivered base editing to disable PCSK9 in hepatocytes; EDIT-101 used AAV5 delivered subretinally to correct a CEP290 splice-site mutation in photoreceptors.

questions.prompt: Why does a permanent PCSK9 edit for high cholesterol face a stricter risk-benefit bar than a permanent TTR edit for ATTR amyloidosis?

options.text: PCSK9 editing uses an entirely untested delivery method
High cholesterol is common and already has reversible, effective treatments, while ATTR amyloidosis is rare, progressive, and often fatal
PCSK9 editing has shown no biological effect in any trial
TTR knockout is fully reversible, unlike PCSK9 editing

explanations.a: Both programs use essentially the same LNP-to-hepatocyte delivery platform.
explanations.b: Correct — an irreversible edit is easier to justify against a disease with few alternatives than against a widely prevalent, already-manageable condition with decades-proven reversible drugs like statins.
explanations.c: VERVE-101/102 have reported biological effects on LDL cholesterol; the concern is risk tolerance, not lack of efficacy.
explanations.d: Neither a nuclease knockout nor a base edit made in vivo is reversible; that is precisely why the population and alternative-treatment context matters so much.

lessons.label: Engineered Immune Cells and Cancer

sections.heading: Multiplex edits build an off-the-shelf T cell
sections.body: Standard CAR-T therapy uses a patient's own T cells, engineered to express a chimeric antigen receptor against a tumor marker — but manufacturing a custom product per patient is slow and expensive. Allogeneic, 'off-the-shelf' CAR-T instead starts with a healthy donor's T cells and edits out the two things that would cause rejection: TRAC, the gene encoding the constant region of the endogenous T-cell receptor (knocking it out prevents the donor cells from attacking the recipient's tissue, i.e., graft-versus-host disease), and B2M, which is required to display MHC class I on the cell surface (knocking it out helps the donor cells evade recognition and destruction by the recipient's own immune system). A third common edit disrupts PD-1 (PDCD1), the checkpoint receptor that drives T-cell exhaustion, to keep engineered cells functionally active longer inside the tumor.

sections.heading: From first-in-human safety to a named cure
sections.body: Stadtmauer et al. (Science, 2020) reported the first US first-in-human trial of CRISPR-multiplex-edited T cells, engineered with TRAC and PD-1 disruption plus a T-cell-receptor knock-in, given to patients with advanced cancers. The edited cells engrafted, persisted for months, and caused no severe adverse events tied to the editing itself — establishing that multiplexed CRISPR T-cell products were safe enough to move forward. In 2022, clinicians at Great Ormond Street Hospital treated Alyssa, a 13-year-old with relapsed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) who had exhausted other options, with base-edited allogeneic 'CAR7' T cells — donor cells edited at multiple loci (including knocking out the CD7 target antigen on the therapeutic cells themselves, to prevent fratricide, alongside TCR and other edits) — and she achieved remission.

sections.heading: Why base editing, specifically, for this product
sections.body: The CAR7 product needed several simultaneous edits in the same cell, and that is exactly where conventional nuclease-based multiplexing runs into trouble: each Cas9 cut is a double-strand break, and when several DSBs are made at once in one cell, the free ends from different cut sites can be mis-joined by the cell's repair machinery, producing chromosomal translocations. The frequency of these translocations scales with the number of simultaneous cuts — roughly, more pairs of open ends means more chances for a wrong pairing — so a four- or five-site multiplex nuclease edit carries meaningfully more genomic-rearrangement risk than a single cut. Base editors make their changes chemically, without cutting both DNA strands, so multiplexing many base edits in one cell does not create new translocation risk the way multiplexed nuclease cuts do — the specific technical reason base editing, not just CRISPR knockout, entered the clinic for products like CAR7.

lessons.workedExample: A cell-therapy company wants to manufacture allogeneic CAR-T cells with five edits at once: knock out TRAC, B2M, PD-1, the CD7 antigen (to prevent the CAR7 product attacking itself), and insert the CAR transgene. Using Cas9 nucleases at four separate knockout sites simultaneously creates four sets of double-strand-break ends floating in the same nucleus, and translocation risk rises with each additional simultaneous cut. Switching the four knockouts to base editors — which silence genes via premature stop codons or splice-site disruption without cutting both strands — removes that translocation risk entirely, which is exactly the design choice behind Alyssa's CAR7 T cells in 2022.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who understands multiplex gene editing will ask specifically why a project used base editors instead of standard CRISPR knockout for a multi-gene edit, and 'base editors are newer/better' is not an answer — the correct, specific answer is that simultaneous double-strand breaks at multiple loci raise translocation risk as more cut sites are open at once, and base editing avoids that failure mode by never cutting both DNA strands. A student who can connect that mechanism to a concrete clinical case, like Alyssa's CAR7 T cells, shows they understand why this particular editing tool was the right one for this particular multiplex product, not just that CRISPR was involved.

questions.prompt: Match each gene knockout in allogeneic CAR-T design to its purpose.

right.text: Prevents graft-versus-host disease by removing the donor's endogenous TCR
Reduces MHC class I surface display so the recipient's immune system is less likely to reject the donor cells
Reduces T-cell exhaustion, keeping engineered cells active longer

questions.explanation: TRAC knockout removes the endogenous T-cell receptor to prevent graft-versus-host disease; B2M knockout reduces MHC class I display to help evade immune rejection; PD-1 knockout disrupts a checkpoint receptor that otherwise drives T-cell exhaustion.

questions.prompt: What did Stadtmauer et al. (Science, 2020) establish?

options.text: The first cure of a solid tumor using CRISPR-edited T cells
That multiplex CRISPR-edited T cells could engraft, persist for months, and show acceptable safety in a first-in-human US trial
That base editing outperforms nuclease editing in every clinical measure
The first use of allogeneic donor T cells in any cancer therapy

explanations.a: The trial demonstrated safety and persistence, not a defined cure endpoint for a solid tumor.
explanations.b: Correct — this first-in-human US trial showed multiplex-edited (TRAC and PD-1 disrupted, TCR knocked in) T cells engrafted, persisted for months, and had acceptable safety.
explanations.c: The trial used nuclease-based multiplex editing, not base editing, and did not make this general comparison.
explanations.d: Allogeneic and engineered T-cell approaches predate this trial; its significance was demonstrating multiplex CRISPR editing specifically was safe in humans.

questions.prompt: Why does chromosomal translocation risk increase when multiple genes are knocked out simultaneously with Cas9 nucleases?

options.text: Cas9 becomes less accurate the more guide RNAs are used
Multiple simultaneous double-strand breaks create free DNA ends from different loci that can be mis-joined by repair machinery
Nuclease editing always damages the mitochondrial genome when multiplexed
The cell's proofreading enzymes are overwhelmed by RNA off-target binding

explanations.a: Per-guide accuracy is a separate issue from translocation risk, which is about repair of multiple simultaneous breaks.
explanations.b: Correct — each double-strand break generates two free DNA ends, and when several breaks exist at once, repair machinery can mistakenly join ends from different cut sites, producing translocations.
explanations.c: Translocation risk here concerns the nuclear genome, not mitochondrial DNA.
explanations.d: This describes a different concern (off-target guide binding), not the DSB-repair mechanism behind translocations.

questions.prompt: Alyssa's CAR7 T cells (Great Ormond Street, 2022) used base editing specifically because:

options.text: Base editors are cheaper to manufacture than Cas9 nucleases
The product required several simultaneous edits, and base editing avoids the translocation risk of multiple simultaneous double-strand breaks
Base editing was the only technology approved for pediatric leukemia
CD7 could only be disrupted by a base editor for biochemical reasons unrelated to safety

explanations.a: Cost was not the stated rationale; the choice was driven by safety at multiple simultaneous edit sites.
explanations.b: Correct — with several edits needed in one cell (TCR, CD7, others), base editing avoids the double-strand-break-driven translocation risk that scales with the number of simultaneous nuclease cuts.
explanations.c: There is no such blanket approval restriction by editing technology; the choice was a technical safety decision for this multiplex product.
explanations.d: CD7 disruption is achievable by either nuclease knockout or base editing; base editing was chosen for the multiplex safety profile, not a CD7-specific biochemical requirement.

lessons.label: Crops, Livestock, and Two Regulatory Philosophies

sections.heading: A decade of concrete edited organisms
sections.body: In April 2016, Yinong Yang's CRISPR-edited white button mushroom (Agaricus bisporus), knocked down in a polyphenol oxidase gene to resist browning, received a 'not regulated' letter from USDA APHIS — the first CRISPR-edited organism cleared for the US market, notable precisely because no foreign DNA was inserted. Calyxt's TALEN-edited high-oleic soybean followed as one of the first gene-edited food products commercially sold in the US, its oil marketed for a longer shelf life and no trans fats. In 2021, Japan's Sanatech Seed released the CRISPR-edited 'Sicilian Rouge High GABA' tomato — engineered by disrupting a regulatory domain of a GAD gene to raise GABA accumulation — becoming the first CRISPR-edited food crop sold at retail anywhere, including free seedlings distributed to home gardeners.

sections.heading: Livestock edits and a landmark transplant
sections.body: In 2022 the FDA issued a low-risk determination — a lighter-touch pathway than full new-animal-drug approval — for PRLR-SLICK cattle developed by Acceligen/Recombinetics, whose edited prolactin receptor gene produces a short, slick coat that improves heat tolerance in dairy cattle. Revivicor's GalSafe pigs, with the alpha-gal gene (GGTA1) knocked out, were FDA-cleared for both food use (people with alpha-gal meat allergy) and potential therapeutic and transplant applications. That second use became reality in January 2022, when surgeons at the University of Maryland transplanted a heart from a Revivicor pig carrying ten gene edits — knockouts preventing hyperacute rejection plus human transgene insertions for complement regulation — into patient David Bennett, the first pig-to-human heart xenotransplant.

sections.heading: One technology, two regulatory philosophies
sections.body: AquAdvantage salmon is the useful contrast case: it is transgenic, not gene-edited — an Atlantic salmon carrying a growth-hormone gene from Chinook salmon under a promoter borrowed from ocean pout, foreign DNA from two other species stitched in, approved by the FDA in 2015 as the first transgenic animal cleared for human consumption. The regulatory split this maps onto is explicit. In July 2018, the EU Court of Justice ruled that organisms produced by mutagenesis techniques including CRISPR fall under the EU's 2001 GMO Directive regardless of whether foreign DNA is present — a process-based rule that regulates how an organism was made. The US took the opposite approach: USDA's 2020 SECURE rule exempts plant edits that could plausibly have arisen through conventional breeding (small deletions, single-base changes) from full regulatory review — a product-based rule that regulates what the organism is, not the method used to make it.

lessons.workedExample: A company develops a CRISPR-edited tomato with a single-base change that boosts a natural compound, and separately a transgenic tomato with an inserted bacterial gene. Under the EU's process-based rule (2018 ECJ ruling), both would be classified as GMOs subject to the full GMO Directive, because both used a form of mutagenesis or transgenesis in their making, regardless of the size of the change. Under the US's product-based SECURE rule, the single-base CRISPR edit could qualify for exemption from full review because an equivalent change is plausible through conventional breeding, while the transgenic tomato with a foreign bacterial gene would not qualify, because no amount of conventional breeding could produce that result — the same two tomatoes land in different regulatory categories depending only on which system is judging them.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing regulatory literacy will ask why the same CRISPR-edited crop could be a regulated GMO in one country and an unregulated conventional-equivalent product in another, and the answer has to name the mechanism, not just the outcome: the EU's 2018 Court of Justice ruling regulates by process (how the organism was made), while the US SECURE rule regulates by product (whether the resulting trait could have arisen through conventional breeding). A student who can also place a specific approved organism — the non-browning mushroom, the GABA tomato, PRLR-SLICK cattle, or the contrast case of transgenic AquAdvantage salmon — on the right side of that line shows they understand the distinction is not academic; it changes what actually reaches a market.

questions.prompt: Order these approvals/releases chronologically, earliest first.

items.text: USDA 'not regulated' letter for the non-browning CRISPR mushroom
FDA approval of transgenic AquAdvantage salmon
Market release of Japan's GABA-enriched Sicilian Rouge tomato
Bennett pig-to-human heart xenotransplant

questions.explanation: AquAdvantage salmon was FDA-approved in 2015; the non-browning mushroom received its USDA letter in April 2016; the GABA tomato reached the Japanese retail market in 2021; the Bennett xenotransplant occurred in January 2022.

questions.prompt: Why is AquAdvantage salmon a useful contrast to the non-browning mushroom or the GABA tomato?

options.text: It is gene-edited using CRISPR rather than TALENs
It is transgenic, carrying inserted foreign DNA from two other species, rather than gene-edited with no foreign DNA added
It was never approved for sale anywhere
It was developed by the same company as the mushroom

explanations.a: AquAdvantage salmon was not edited with CRISPR or TALENs at all — it is a transgenic organism.
explanations.b: Correct — it carries a growth-hormone gene from Chinook salmon under a promoter from ocean pout, foreign DNA from two other species, contrasting with edits like the mushroom's or tomato's that add no foreign DNA.
explanations.c: It was FDA-approved in 2015 as the first transgenic animal cleared for human consumption.
explanations.d: These are unrelated products from different companies.

questions.prompt: The EU Court of Justice's 2018 ruling on mutagenesis-derived organisms is best described as:

options.text: Product-based: it regulates organisms according to whether the resulting trait could occur through conventional breeding
Process-based: it regulates organisms according to the method used to create them, regardless of the outcome
A full exemption of all CRISPR-edited crops from GMO law
Identical in effect to the US SECURE rule

explanations.a: This describes the US SECURE rule's philosophy, the opposite approach.
explanations.b: Correct — the ruling holds that organisms produced by mutagenesis techniques including CRISPR fall under the EU's GMO Directive because of how they were made, regardless of whether foreign DNA is present.
explanations.c: The ruling does the opposite: it brings CRISPR-edited organisms under GMO regulation.
explanations.d: The SECURE rule is product-based (outcome-focused) while the EU ruling is process-based; they reach different conclusions for the same organism.

questions.prompt: What did the FDA's 2022 low-risk determination for PRLR-SLICK cattle enable?

options.text: Full transgenic modification of cattle for pharmaceutical protein production
A lighter regulatory pathway (short of full new-animal-drug approval) for a heat-tolerance edit already found in some cattle breeds
A ban on all gene-edited livestock in the United States
Approval of PRLR-SLICK cattle specifically for xenotransplant donor use

explanations.a: PRLR-SLICK is a gene edit for a heat-tolerant coat trait, not a transgenic pharmaceutical-production platform.
explanations.b: Correct — the 2022 low-risk determination gave PRLR-SLICK cattle, edited for a slick heat-tolerant coat already present in some cattle populations, a lighter regulatory route than the full new-animal-drug process.
explanations.c: The determination enabled a pathway to market, not a ban.
explanations.d: Xenotransplant donor pigs (Revivicor/GalSafe) are a separate program from PRLR-SLICK cattle.

lessons.label: Editing as a Research Instrument: Screens and Models

sections.heading: Pooled knockout screens: thousands of experiments at once
sections.body: A genome-wide pooled CRISPR screen infects a large population of cells with a lentiviral library where each cell integrates one guide RNA targeting one gene, so the population collectively carries a knockout of every gene in the genome. The GeCKO library (Zhang lab) targets essentially the whole genome with roughly 6 guides per gene; the Brunello library (Broad Institute, Doench et al., 2016) is a refined design using about 4 optimized guides per gene, plus a set of non-targeting control guides that should show no growth effect. In a positive selection screen, cells are put under a selective pressure — a drug, a toxin, a virus — and guides that knock out genes conferring resistance become enriched over time, easy to spot by their rising abundance. In a negative selection (dropout) screen, no external pressure is applied; guides targeting essential genes simply disappear from the population as those cells die, revealing which genes cells cannot live without.

sections.heading: Reading out and trusting the result
sections.body: After selection, genomic DNA is extracted, the integrated guide sequences are PCR-amplified and sequenced by NGS, and guide abundance before versus after selection is compared as a log-fold-change. MAGeCK, a widely used analysis tool, ranks genes by how consistently their multiple guides shift in the same direction, using a robust rank-aggregation approach that resists being fooled by one lucky or unlucky guide. Two design parameters determine whether a screen result can be trusted: library coverage (cells transduced per guide, typically several hundred-fold, so that a guide is not lost to chance sampling) and multiplicity of infection (MOI), kept low, around 0.3, during viral delivery so that most transduced cells receive exactly one guide rather than several confounding edits at once. A working negative-selection screen should show known essential genes — ribosomal or spliceosome components — strongly depleted by the endpoint; if they are not, the screen did not apply enough selective pressure to trust its other results.

sections.heading: Beyond knockout: dosage, single-cell readout, and organisms
sections.body: CRISPRi and CRISPRa use a catalytically dead Cas9 (dCas9) fused to a repressor (KRAB) or activator (VP64/VPR) domain to turn a gene's expression down or up without cutting DNA at all, letting researchers screen for dosage effects and study genes too essential to survive full knockout. Perturb-seq goes further, pairing a pooled CRISPR perturbation with single-cell RNA sequencing so each individual cell's guide identity is linked to its own transcriptome, revealing not just whether a gene matters but the downstream expression program it controls. Outside pooled screens, targeted editing builds isogenic cell lines (identical genetic background except for one engineered variant), organoids, and mouse models that isolate a single gene's effect from all the natural variation a real population would carry.

lessons.workedExample: A lab wants to find genes required for a virus to infect human cells. They transduce cells with the Brunello library (about 4 guides/gene, roughly 77,000 guides total) at low MOI so each surviving cell carries one edit, maintaining several-hundred-fold coverage per guide. They expose the population to the virus: cells with a knockout in a gene the virus needs to enter survive and are enriched, while unedited cells die. Sequencing guide abundance before and after infection and running MAGeCK reveals which genes have guides consistently enriched across independent guides targeting the same gene — a hit driven by all 4 guides for one gene is trustworthy; a spike from a single guide out of 4, with the other 3 showing no effect, is more likely noise or an off-target artifact.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge evaluating a screening project will ask how the student knows a 'hit' gene is real rather than noise, and the specific, defensible answer names library design: multiple independent guides per gene should agree (which is what tools like MAGeCK test statistically), coverage needs to be high enough that a guide's disappearance reflects biology rather than random dropout, and MOI needs to be low enough that each cell's phenotype can be attributed to one edit. A student who can also point to essential-gene depletion as an internal positive control — 'if ribosomal genes weren't depleted in my dropout screen, my selection pressure or timepoint was wrong' — is demonstrating they understand screen validity, not just screen mechanics.

questions.prompt: In a negative selection (dropout) screen, what does it mean when guides targeting a particular gene become depleted over time?

options.text: That gene confers resistance to the selective pressure applied
That gene is likely essential for cell survival or fitness
The guide sequence failed to integrate into the genome
The gene is a non-targeting control

explanations.a: Conferring resistance under applied pressure describes enrichment in a positive selection screen, not depletion.
explanations.b: Correct — in a dropout screen, cells with essential genes knocked out die off, so guides targeting those genes disappear from the population over time.
explanations.c: Failed integration would show up as absence from the very start, not a decline over the course of the screen.
explanations.d: Non-targeting controls are expected to show no consistent enrichment or depletion, since they don't target any gene.

questions.prompt: Match each screening tool or technique to what it does.

right.text: Genome-wide pooled sgRNA library, about 4 guides per gene
Statistical tool ranking genes by consistent guide-level log-fold-change
Represses gene expression via a dead Cas9 fused to a repressor domain, without cutting DNA
Links each cell's CRISPR perturbation to its own single-cell transcriptome

questions.explanation: Brunello is a pooled genome-wide sgRNA library (about 4 guides/gene); MAGeCK statistically ranks genes by consistent log-fold-change across their guides; CRISPRi uses dCas9 fused to KRAB to repress transcription without cutting DNA; Perturb-seq couples pooled perturbations to single-cell RNA-seq readout.

questions.prompt: Why is low MOI (around 0.3) used during lentiviral guide delivery in a pooled screen?

options.text: It maximizes the number of guides each cell receives for stronger effects
It ensures most transduced cells receive exactly one guide, so a phenotype can be attributed to a single edit
It increases the total sequencing depth needed
It prevents essential genes from being included in the library

explanations.a: Low MOI intentionally limits guides per cell to mostly one, not many.
explanations.b: Correct — by Poisson statistics, a low MOI (~0.3) keeps most transduced cells receiving a single guide, so an observed phenotype can be confidently linked to one gene's edit rather than a confounded combination.
explanations.c: MOI governs guides-per-cell during infection, not the sequencing depth applied downstream.
explanations.d: MOI is unrelated to which genes are included in a library design.

questions.prompt: A dropout screen's endpoint shows that guides against known ribosomal and spliceosome genes are NOT depleted. What does this suggest?

options.text: The screen worked perfectly and ribosomal genes are non-essential
The screen likely did not apply enough selective pressure or run long enough to reach a trustworthy result
The library had too many guides per gene
The cells used were resistant to lentiviral transduction

explanations.a: Ribosomal and spliceosome genes are well-established essential genes; failing to see their depletion is a red flag, not a valid finding.
explanations.b: Correct — essential-gene depletion is a standard internal positive control; if it's absent, the screen likely lacked sufficient selection pressure or time to produce trustworthy dropout signal.
explanations.c: Guide count per gene affects statistical power, not whether essential genes show up as depleted at all.
explanations.d: Transduction resistance would show up as failed library representation from the start, not selectively at essential genes.

lessons.label: Biosafety, Biosecurity, and Doing This Responsibly

sections.heading: The oversight layer under every editing project
sections.body: Biosafety levels (BSL-1 through BSL-4) set the containment practices required for a given organism's risk, from an ordinary lab strain of E. coli (BSL-1) to agents requiring sealed suits and negative-pressure rooms (BSL-4). Any institution doing recombinant or synthetic nucleic acid work in the US is expected to have an Institutional Biosafety Committee (IBC) reviewing protocols before work starts, alongside ethics review for anything touching human subjects or animals. Some research crosses into dual-use research of concern (DURC): work with a legitimate scientific purpose that could be misapplied to cause harm. The clearest historical case is the 2011–2012 controversy over studies making H5N1 avian influenza transmissible between mammals, which the US National Science Advisory Board for Biosecurity (NSABB) initially recommended restricting from full publication — a rare instance of biosecurity concerns overriding open scientific publication norms.

sections.heading: Gene drives: editing that spreads itself
sections.body: A CRISPR-based gene drive copies itself into the matching chromosome during reproduction, pushing an edit through a wild population at far above the normal 50% Mendelian rate — potentially eliminating a disease-carrying mosquito population, for instance, but also raising an ecological reversibility problem: once a full drive is released and spreads through a wild population, it is extremely difficult to recall. Containment strategies exist specifically to manage this. Split drives keep the Cas9 enzyme and the guide RNA on separate, unlinked genetic loci so the drive only functions in lab crosses where both halves are combined, containing it to the laboratory. Daisy-chain drives, a design associated with Kevin Esvelt, use a chain of guide elements where each drives the next but not itself, so the drive loses potency over a few generations and is self-limiting and locally reversible rather than spreading indefinitely. Because a released drive doesn't respect national borders, field trials (such as Target Malaria's work on Anopheles gambiae suppression drives) raise questions of consent that cross jurisdictions, not just safety within one lab.

sections.heading: What a student team can actually do — and how to defend it
sections.body: A high-school team can legally and safely work with non-pathogenic BSL-1 organisms — standard lab strains of E. coli or yeast, or plant systems like Arabidopsis edited via Agrobacterium — inside a school lab or under a supervising institution's biosafety oversight, and this is exactly the territory most DIY-bio kits are built for. Anything involving human gene therapy, gene drives, select agents, or vertebrate animal work requires an institution with an IBC or IACUC and is not something a student team can undertake independently. When a judge asks 'should you have done this?', the strongest answer names the specific hazard the project could pose, the containment or oversight actually obtained (a teacher or PI's sign-off, working only with non-pathogenic organisms, no drive or germline component), and why the knowledge gained justified the residual risk — a concrete argument, not the slogan that science is inherently good.

lessons.workedExample: A student team wants to CRISPR-edit yeast to test a metabolic pathway hypothesis, using a commercial bacterial/yeast editing kit at school under a teacher's supervision. This sits squarely inside BSL-1, non-pathogenic organisms, no gene drive, no vertebrate animals, and no human-subject component — well within what a school lab can legitimately do, especially with the teacher acting as informal oversight. If the same team proposed building a gene drive in fruit flies to test population suppression, the ecological reversibility problem (a released drive is very hard to recall) and lack of institutional containment infrastructure (split-drive design, IBC review) would make the project impossible to defend outside a licensed research institution — the honest answer to 'can we do this' is no, not 'let's be careful.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'should you have done this?' is testing whether the student can reason about risk rather than recite a rule, so the strongest response names the actual containment level of the organism used (BSL-1 E. coli or yeast, no drive, no vertebrate work), states what oversight was actually obtained (teacher sign-off, following kit safety guidance), and explains in one sentence why the specific hazard was low enough to justify the specific knowledge gained. A student who cannot distinguish 'we used a harmless lab strain of yeast' from 'we could theoretically build a gene drive' has not internalized why gene drives specifically require split-drive or daisy-chain containment and institutional review that a garage kit cannot provide.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a split gene drive from a full, unconstrained gene drive?

options.text: A split drive uses base editing instead of nuclease cutting
A split drive separates Cas9 and the guide RNA onto unlinked loci, so it only functions when both are combined in a lab cross, containing it
A split drive can only be used in plants, never animals
A split drive spreads faster through a wild population than a full drive

explanations.a: The split/full distinction is about locus architecture (where Cas9 and guide RNA are located), not the type of editing enzyme.
explanations.b: Correct — keeping Cas9 and guide RNA on separate, unlinked loci means the drive only self-propagates when both halves are present together, which happens only in controlled lab crosses, containing the drive to the laboratory.
explanations.c: Split-drive designs are not restricted to plants; the concept applies broadly to sexually reproducing organisms.
explanations.d: A split drive is specifically designed to NOT spread in the wild, unlike a full drive.

questions.prompt: What makes daisy-chain drives (Esvelt) different from a standard full gene drive?

options.text: They use a chain of guide elements where each drives the next but not itself, causing the drive to lose potency and fade out over generations
They require no institutional oversight because they are inherently harmless
They spread with 100% efficiency indefinitely, unlike other drive designs
They can only be used on bacteria, not on sexually reproducing organisms

explanations.a: Correct — the chained structure means the drive is self-limiting, losing its driving capability after a handful of generations, making it more locally reversible than a standard full drive.
explanations.b: Daisy-chain drives still require institutional biosafety review; being self-limiting reduces but does not eliminate oversight needs.
explanations.c: The defining feature is the opposite: they fade out rather than persisting indefinitely.
explanations.d: Gene drives, including daisy-chain designs, are relevant to sexually reproducing organisms like insects, not bacteria.

questions.prompt: Dual-use research of concern (DURC) refers to research that:

options.text: Uses two different editing tools in the same experiment
Has a legitimate scientific purpose but could plausibly be misapplied to cause harm
Is automatically banned from all publication
Only applies to gene-drive research

explanations.a: DURC is about risk of misuse, not about how many tools or techniques are combined.
explanations.b: Correct — DURC describes research with a legitimate scientific purpose that could also be misapplied to pose a biosecurity threat, as with the H5N1 transmissibility studies debated by the NSABB.
explanations.c: DURC review can lead to restricted or redacted publication in specific cases, but it is not an automatic blanket ban.
explanations.d: DURC is a general biosecurity category that includes pathogen research (like H5N1 work) and is not limited to gene drives.

questions.prompt: A student team wants to know what they can legally do with a DIY-bio CRISPR kit at school. Which project fits within BSL-1, no-institution-required boundaries?

options.text: Editing a non-pathogenic lab strain of yeast to test a metabolic pathway, under teacher supervision
Building a gene drive in fruit flies to test population suppression
Editing human cells to test a gene therapy candidate
Editing a select agent pathogen to study virulence factors

explanations.a: Correct — a non-pathogenic BSL-1 organism like standard lab yeast, edited under teacher supervision with no drive or germline component, is exactly the territory DIY-bio kits and school labs are built for.
explanations.b: Gene drives require institutional containment infrastructure (split-drive design, IBC review) and ecological risk assessment far beyond a school lab's scope.
explanations.c: Human gene therapy work requires clinical-trial-level institutional and ethical oversight, not a student kit.
explanations.d: Select agents require specialized high-containment facilities and are explicitly outside what any unlicensed team, student or otherwise, can handle.

lessons.label: Reading and Drawing a Pedigree

sections.heading: Symbols and generations
sections.body: A pedigree is a standardized diagram of a family's phenotypes across generations, and the standardization matters: Bennett and colleagues published the nomenclature recommendations in 1995 (updated 2008 and again 2022) specifically so a pedigree drawn in one clinic could be read unambiguously in another. Squares are males, circles are females, and a diamond marks a person of undocumented sex. A fully shaded symbol means the person is affected by the trait under study; unfilled means unaffected; a small dot or half-shading can flag an asymptomatic carrier when that status comes from an actual test result rather than assumption. Generations stack in horizontal rows labeled top-to-bottom with Roman numerals (I is oldest); within a row, individuals are numbered left to right with Arabic numerals, so "II-3" unambiguously names the third person drawn in the second generation.

sections.heading: Unions, offspring, and special marks
sections.body: A horizontal line joining two people is a union; a vertical line drops from it to a horizontal sibship line their children hang from, in birth order. A doubled union line marks a consanguineous union — partners sharing a recent common ancestor — which matters because it raises the odds both carry the same rare recessive allele. Twins branch from one point below the sibship line; monozygotic twins get an added short bar connecting their two branches, dizygotic twins do not. A diagonal slash through a symbol marks a deceased individual, ideally with age or cause noted. A small filled triangle marks a pregnancy loss, stillbirth, or termination. An arrow (sometimes with "P") points to the proband — the affected individual whose presentation first brought the family to clinical attention — a detail that matters because a pedigree assembled starting from a proband carries ascertainment bias that a randomly sampled family does not.

sections.heading: What a pedigree does and does not establish
sections.body: A pedigree records reported phenotype and stated biological relationships — not genotype. Carrier status for an unaffected relative is inferred probabilistically from the surrounding pattern (the subject of a later lesson's Bayesian math), never read directly off the chart unless a test result is annotated. Because the data comes from interviews, it inherits every limit of self-report: relatives misremember or withhold diagnoses, an assumed father may not be the biological father, and reduced penetrance can make a true allele carrier look phenotypically "unaffected." A single small pedigree also rarely has enough informative individuals to prove a mode of inheritance outright — it narrows the hypotheses, which is exactly what the next lesson builds on.

lessons.workedExample: For a family-history assignment, a student interviews a grandmother, two parents, and four cousins about early-onset hearing loss across three generations. Generation I is the grandparents' union on one horizontal line; generation II hangs each parent-generation sibling off a sibship line; generation III holds the cousins. A grandparent who died of an unrelated cause gets a diagonal slash; identical-twin cousins get the connecting bar; the cousin whose hearing loss triggered the family's clinic visit gets the proband arrow. Two affected relatives are shaded solid; one whose status the family disputes is left unfilled with a note, because the pedigree should record what was actually reported, not what is guessed.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing pedigree work is checking whether a student can produce and read primary data without a lab, which is why notation precision matters more here than almost anywhere else in a genetics project — a mis-shaded symbol or skipped generation label makes every downstream inheritance claim unverifiable. The strongest tell is a student who volunteers the pedigree's limits unprompted, saying something like "this shows phenotype only, we didn't genotype anyone," rather than treating the diagram as proof of a mechanism.

questions.prompt: What does a fully shaded (filled) symbol on a pedigree represent?

options.text: An individual who has been genetically tested
An individual who is affected by the trait under study
An individual who is deceased
The proband

explanations.a: Testing status would be marked separately (e.g., a small dot), not by full shading, and most affected individuals are identified by phenotype, not a lab test.
explanations.b: Correct — full shading is the standard convention for an affected phenotype.
explanations.c: Deceased status is shown by a diagonal slash through the symbol, not by shading.
explanations.d: The proband is marked with an arrow, independent of whether the symbol is shaded.

questions.prompt: A double horizontal line connecting two partners in a union indicates:

options.text: A same-sex union
A consanguineous union (partners share a recent common ancestor)
A divorced couple
Twins

explanations.a: Sex is shown by the symbol shapes (square/circle), not by the union line style.
explanations.b: Correct — a doubled union line is the standard mark for consanguinity, which raises the odds partners share the same rare recessive allele.
explanations.c: A divorced or separated union is typically marked with a hash through the line, not a doubled line.
explanations.d: Twins branch from a point below a sibship line connecting children, not from the union line between parents.

questions.prompt: Match each pedigree mark to what it represents.

right.text: Deceased individual
Proband (first individual to bring the family to clinical attention)
Pregnancy loss, stillbirth, or termination
Individual of undocumented or unspecified sex

questions.explanation: Each mark has a fixed meaning under standardized pedigree nomenclature (Bennett et al., 1995): a slash records death, an arrow flags the proband, a triangle records a pregnancy that did not result in a living child, and a diamond is used when sex was not recorded.

questions.prompt: Which of the following can a pedigree, by itself, with no lab test results annotated, directly establish about an unaffected individual?

options.text: Their exact genotype at the disease locus
Whether they are a silent carrier of a recessive allele
Their reported phenotype and stated biological relationship to other family members
Their risk of passing the condition to a future child, with certainty

explanations.a: Genotype is never directly visible on a pedigree — it can only be inferred, or confirmed by an annotated test result.
explanations.b: Carrier status for an unaffected person is inferred from the surrounding pattern, not read directly off the diagram, unless a test result is noted.
explanations.c: Correct — a pedigree is fundamentally a record of reported phenotype and relationships; everything else is inferred from it.
explanations.d: Recurrence risk is a probability calculated from the pattern, never a certainty read directly off the chart.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building a pedigree from a family-history interview in the correct order.

items.text: Identify the proband and the reason the family came to attention
Interview relatives across at least three generations for phenotype and relationship information
Arrange individuals into horizontal generation rows labeled with Roman numerals
Draw union and sibship lines connecting partners and their offspring
Shade affected individuals and add special marks (deceased, twins, losses)

questions.explanation: You start from the proband because that defines the pedigree's purpose, gather raw phenotype and relationship data next, lay out the generational skeleton, connect the biological relationships, and only then annotate status and special events on top of the finished structure.

lessons.label: Autosomal Dominant and Recessive Patterns in Families

sections.heading: The dominant signature
sections.body: Autosomal dominant conditions produce a distinctive pedigree: vertical transmission, meaning the trait appears in every generation with no unaffected generation in between, because one copy of the pathogenic allele is enough. An affected child essentially always has an affected parent, unless the case is a fresh mutation. Males and females are affected in roughly equal numbers, and — critically — male-to-male transmission occurs (an affected father can have an affected son), which is the single cleanest fact that rules out X-linkage. Each child of an affected-by-unaffected mating carries a roughly 50% recurrence risk, a straight consequence of one heterozygous parent segregating the allele to half their gametes. Huntington disease (HTT, chromosome 4, a CAG-repeat expansion with onset typically in the 30s–50s) and achondroplasia (FGFR3; about 80% of cases arise as new mutations in otherwise unaffected parents) are the two textbook examples, and achondroplasia is a useful reminder that a dominant pedigree can still start with a single sporadic case.

sections.heading: The recessive signature
sections.body: Autosomal recessive conditions look almost opposite: horizontal clustering, where affected individuals bunch within one sibship rather than stringing down generations, because two unaffected carrier parents (each heterozygous, Aa) can each pass the allele on. Generations are typically skipped — grandparents and grandchildren both affected with an unaffected parent in between is a recessive-flavored pattern, not a dominant one. Two carrier parents have a 1-in-4 (25%) recurrence risk per pregnancy, and consanguineous unions show up more often in recessive pedigrees than in the general population, because related partners are more likely to share the same rare allele inherited from a common ancestor. Cystic fibrosis (CFTR, chromosome 7; ΔF508 is the single most common pathogenic allele) and sickle cell disease (HBB, chromosome 11; a single glutamic-acid-to-valine substitution at position 6 of beta-globin) are the standard examples.

sections.heading: From carrier frequency to a couple's risk
sections.body: Under Hardy-Weinberg, carrier frequency in a population is 2pq, where q is the frequency of the recessive allele. You can derive that carrier frequency instead of just quoting it: cystic fibrosis disease incidence (affected individuals, q²) runs about 1 in 2,500 births in Northern European populations, so q — the frequency of the recessive allele itself — is the square root of 1/2500, or about 1/50. Because q is small, p (the frequency of the normal allele) is close to 1, so the carrier term 2pq is well approximated by 2q: 2 × 1/50 = 1/25. That is where the familiar "1 in 25 carriers" figure comes from, and the same q² → q → 2pq chain works for any recessive condition once you know its birth incidence. That number lets you convert population genetics into a specific couple's risk without re-deriving Mendel's ratios from scratch: multiply each partner's probability of being a carrier by 1/4 (the recessive-ratio risk if both are carriers).

lessons.workedExample: A known CF carrier (confirmed by a prior test, so their carrier probability is 1) partners with someone from the general Northern European population, where carrier frequency is about 1/25. The couple's risk of having an affected child is: 1 (known carrier) × 1/25 (partner's carrier probability) × 1/4 (Mendelian risk if both are carriers) = 1/100. Note how this differs from two unrelated carriers of unknown status meeting in the general population, where you'd multiply 1/25 × 1/25 × 1/4 instead — a much smaller number, which is exactly why family history changes risk estimates so much.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe dominant-versus-recessive pattern recognition because it's the single most testable skill in a pedigree-based project — a student who can point to "no skipped generation, male-to-male transmission" or "unaffected carrier parents, sibship clustering" is reading the data, not reciting Mendel from memory. They push further into the carrier-frequency arithmetic specifically because plugging a real 2pq-derived number like 1/25 into a couple's risk calculation shows the student can connect population genetics to an individual pedigree, not just quote a memorized 3:1 ratio.

questions.prompt: Which pedigree feature is most diagnostic of autosomal dominant inheritance?

options.text: The trait clusters within a single sibship and skips generations
The trait appears in every generation with male-to-male transmission
Only males are ever affected
Affected individuals are more common in consanguineous unions

explanations.a: That clustering-and-skipping pattern is the recessive signature, not the dominant one.
explanations.b: Correct — vertical transmission across every generation, including father-to-son, is the clearest dominant signature and rules out X-linkage.
explanations.c: Autosomal dominant traits affect males and females roughly equally, unlike X-linked patterns.
explanations.d: Raised consanguinity is a recessive-pattern clue, since it increases the odds two related partners share the same rare allele.

questions.prompt: Two unaffected parents have a child affected with an autosomal recessive condition. What does this imply about the parents, and what is the recurrence risk for a future pregnancy?

options.text: Both parents are carriers (heterozygous); recurrence risk is 1/4
One parent must be affected but undiagnosed; recurrence risk is 1/2
The case must be a new mutation; recurrence risk is near zero
Both parents are carriers; recurrence risk is 1/2

explanations.a: Correct — two unaffected parents of an affected child are both obligate heterozygous carriers, and each pregnancy independently carries a 1/4 (25%) risk.
explanations.b: Recessive conditions require two copies of the allele; an unaffected heterozygous carrier is fully consistent with being unaffected.
explanations.c: A single affected child from two unaffected parents is the classic recessive signature, not evidence of a new mutation.
explanations.d: 1/2 is the dominant-pattern recurrence risk from one affected heterozygous parent, not the recessive two-carrier risk.

questions.prompt: A known CF carrier partners with someone from the general Northern European population (carrier frequency about 1/25). What is the couple's approximate risk of having a child with CF?

explanations.a: 1/4 would be the risk only if both partners were already known carriers.
explanations.b: 1/25 is the partner's carrier probability alone, before applying the 1/4 Mendelian factor.
explanations.c: Correct — 1 (known carrier) × 1/25 (partner's carrier probability) × 1/4 (recessive risk if both are carriers) = 1/100.
explanations.d: 1/2500 is the correct risk for two partners of unknown, general-population carrier status (1/25 × 1/25 × 1/4) — it under-counts this couple's risk because it ignores that one partner's carrier status is already confirmed, not just population-average.

questions.prompt: Match each condition to its inheritance pattern.

right.text: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive

questions.explanation: Huntington disease (HTT CAG expansion) and achondroplasia (FGFR3) both follow vertical, dominant transmission; cystic fibrosis (CFTR) and sickle cell disease (HBB) both require two pathogenic alleles and follow the horizontal, recessive pattern.

lessons.label: X-Linked, Y-Linked, and Mitochondrial Inheritance

sections.heading: X-linked recessive: hemizygous males, obligate-carrier mothers
sections.body: Males carry a single X, so they are hemizygous — one recessive allele on that X is enough to cause disease, with no second copy to mask it. Females need two copies to be affected, so X-linked recessive pedigrees show far more affected males than females. The clean diagnostic test is transmission: a father passes his Y, not his X, to every son, so male-to-male transmission never occurs; an affected father's daughters, in contrast, are all obligate carriers, since they must receive his affected X. This produces the classic "knight's move" pattern — an affected maternal uncle, an affected nephew, connected through unaffected carrier females rather than in an unbroken vertical line. Hemophilia A (F8, Xq28) and B (F9, Xq27) and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin gene, Xp21, one of the largest human genes at roughly 2.4 megabases) are the classic examples; hemophilia in European royalty descending from Queen Victoria is the textbook historical pedigree, later confirmed by DNA analysis of Romanov remains to be hemophilia B (Rogaev et al., 2009).

sections.heading: X-inactivation and X-linked dominant disease
sections.body: Mary Lyon's 1961 X-inactivation hypothesis explains why heterozygous carrier females are usually unaffected: one X per cell is randomly silenced early in embryogenesis, so on average about half of a carrier's cells express the normal allele. When inactivation skews heavily toward silencing the normal X (roughly beyond 75-80% in one direction), the result is a manifesting carrier with partial symptoms — an X-linked recessive carrier mother with mildly elevated creatine kinase, for instance. X-linked dominant conditions instead affect heterozygous females outright: Rett syndrome (MECP2, Xq28) is seen almost entirely in girls because the hemizygous male form is so severe it is usually lethal prenatally or in early infancy; X-linked hypophosphatemia (PHEX) affects both sexes, but an affected father transmits it to all his daughters and none of his sons.

sections.heading: Y-linked and mitochondrial: two purely unilineal patterns
sections.body: Y-linked (holandric) traits pass from father to every son and never to daughters, since only sons inherit the Y. Mitochondrial inheritance is the mirror image: mothers pass mtDNA to all their children, but fathers pass none, so mitochondrial pedigrees show strict maternal transmission to both sexes of offspring. Because each cell holds many mitochondria, an individual can carry a mix of mutant and normal mtDNA — heteroplasmy — and disease severity depends on a threshold effect, where a tissue only malfunctions once its mutant fraction crosses that tissue's energy-demand threshold. This explains the wildly variable severity of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) and MELAS within the same maternal lineage. A germline mitochondrial bottleneck during oogenesis sharply reduces the mtDNA copy number passed through primordial germ cells, which amplifies random shifts in heteroplasmy from one generation to the next.

lessons.workedExample: In a Duchenne muscular dystrophy pedigree, a woman whose brother is affected, and whose mother is confirmed (say, by carrier testing) to be a carrier, has a 50% chance of being a carrier herself, from her mother's 1/2 transmission — her own carrier status stays probable, not confirmed, unless a CK test or her own children's outcomes update it further. Note that with only one affected male and no confirmed maternal test, the mother is not automatically an obligate carrier: roughly a third of isolated DMD cases trace to a new mutation (in the mother's germline or the affected son himself) rather than an inherited allele, so obligate-carrier status usually requires either a second affected male relative (e.g., a maternal uncle) or a positive carrier test. If she is a carrier, each of her sons faces a 50% risk of DMD and each of her daughters faces a 50% chance of being a carrier; but unconditionally — before anyone knows whether she herself carries the allele — each son's risk is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 and each daughter's carrier chance is likewise 1/4. A creatine kinase blood test can flag manifesting carriers among the women in this family, since skewed X-inactivation occasionally produces mild muscle symptoms even in a heterozygous carrier.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges lean on X-linked versus autosomal recognition because "no male-to-male transmission" is the cleanest single discriminating test available on a pedigree, and a student who applies it correctly (rather than just noting "more males affected") shows real command of the mechanism.
