They probe heteroplasmy and the threshold effect specifically because it resolves a common point of confusion — why relatives who share the identical mitochondrial mutation can have dramatically different disease severity — and a student who can explain that without hand-waving has clearly gone past the vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Which observation on a pedigree rules out X-linked recessive inheritance in favor of autosomal dominant?

options.text: More males than females are affected
Male-to-male transmission (an affected father with an affected son)
All daughters of an affected father are carriers
The condition skips a generation

explanations.a: A male excess is consistent with X-linked recessive but does not by itself rule it out.
explanations.b: Correct — a father passes his Y, not his X, to sons, so male-to-male transmission is impossible for X-linked traits and points instead to an autosomal (or Y-linked) pattern.
explanations.c: That is expected under X-linked recessive inheritance, since every daughter of an affected father receives his affected X.
explanations.d: Skipped generations are more typical of recessive patterns generally and don't by themselves distinguish X-linked from autosomal.

questions.prompt: A woman's brother has Duchenne muscular dystrophy and their mother is confirmed a carrier. What is the woman's carrier status, and why?

options.text: She cannot be a carrier because she is unaffected
She has a 50% chance of being a carrier, from her mother's 1/2 transmission
She is definitely a carrier only if she also shows symptoms
Her carrier risk cannot be estimated without a test

explanations.a: X-linked recessive carrier females are typically unaffected precisely because X-inactivation averages out the mutant allele's effect across their cells.
explanations.b: Correct — since her mother is a heterozygous carrier, each child (son or daughter) has a 1/2 chance of inheriting the affected X.
explanations.c: Carrier status does not require symptoms; most carriers are asymptomatic due to X-inactivation.
explanations.d: Pedigree position alone gives a valid prior probability (1/2 here) even before any test is run.

questions.prompt: Within one maternal mitochondrial lineage carrying the same mtDNA mutation, relatives show very different disease severity. What best explains this?

options.text: Mitochondrial mutations are always fully penetrant, so severity differences must be misdiagnosis
Heteroplasmy varies between individuals, and a tissue's dysfunction depends on crossing that tissue's mutant-load threshold
Only males can be affected by mitochondrial disease
Mitochondrial DNA does not actually get inherited from the mother

explanations.a: Mitochondrial mutation severity is famously variable, not fixed, precisely because of heteroplasmy — this is not evidence of misdiagnosis.
explanations.b: Correct — different individuals (and different tissues within one individual) carry different mutant mtDNA fractions, and disease appears only once a tissue-specific threshold is crossed, which is why LHON and MELAS severity varies so much even within one family.
explanations.c: Both sexes can be affected by mitochondrial disease; only maternal transmission (not sex of offspring) is restricted.
explanations.d: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited maternally by both sons and daughters — that maternal transmission is the defining feature of the pattern.

questions.prompt: Match each inheritance pattern to its classic example.

right.text: Hemophilia A/B
Rett syndrome
MELAS
Non-syndromic infertility from AZF-region deletion

questions.explanation: Hemophilia follows classic X-linked recessive transmission with obligate-carrier daughters of affected fathers; Rett syndrome is X-linked dominant and seen almost entirely in females; MELAS is transmitted maternally through mtDNA with heteroplasmy-driven variable severity; Y-linked traits like AZF-region infertility pass only from father to son.

lessons.label: Penetrance, Expressivity, and Phenocopies

sections.heading: Penetrance: does the genotype show up at all?
sections.body: Penetrance is the proportion of people with a given genotype who show any phenotype at all — an all-or-nothing question, separate from how severe that phenotype is. Reduced (incomplete) penetrance means some genotype carriers show no detectable phenotype. BRCA1 pathogenic variants are a sharp example: a 2017 meta-analysis (Kuchenbaecker et al.) estimated carriers' cumulative breast-cancer risk at about 72% by age 80 — high, but well short of 100%, meaning a real fraction of mutation carriers will never develop breast cancer. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1, chromosome 17), by contrast, is close to fully penetrant by adulthood, so nearly every carrier eventually shows some sign, even if that sign is minor. Penetrance can also be age-dependent: Huntington disease is essentially fully penetrant, but only by old age, so a 30-year-old carrier can look pedigree-unaffected simply because they haven't reached typical onset yet.

sections.heading: Expressivity: given the phenotype, how severe is it?
sections.body: Variable expressivity describes carriers who all show the phenotype but at very different severities — the opposite axis from penetrance. Marfan syndrome (FBN1) is the classic case: within a single family carrying the identical mutation, one relative may have only tall stature and mild lens dislocation while another has life-threatening aortic dissection risk. NF1 shows the same spread — some carriers have only café-au-lait spots, others develop plexiform neurofibromas, scoliosis, or learning disabilities. Penetrance and expressivity are frequently confused but answer different questions: penetrance asks whether the trait shows at all, expressivity asks how bad it is once it does.

sections.heading: Sex-limited, sex-influenced, and phenocopies
sections.body: A sex-limited trait is only expressed in one sex, even though the genotype can be present (and transmitted) by either — male-limited precocious puberty (an activating LHCGR mutation, inherited as autosomal dominant) causes early puberty only in boys, though female carriers pass it on silently. A sex-influenced trait appears in both sexes but at different frequency or severity: hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE, C282Y homozygosity) is far more often clinically symptomatic in men, because women's cyclical menstrual iron loss delays or masks iron overload until after menopause. A phenocopy is a non-genetic condition that mimics an inherited one closely enough to distort a pedigree reading — an environmentally caused hearing loss (say, from an intrauterine infection) appearing in a family otherwise segregating a genetic deafness gene can make the pattern look inconsistent, when really one "case" simply isn't genetic at all.

lessons.workedExample: A student researching a family history finds that a grandmother had breast cancer and that the student's mother carries the same pathogenic BRCA1 variant, confirmed by genetic testing, but has never developed cancer at age 55. The student initially worries this breaks the dominant pattern their pedigree lesson taught them to expect. It doesn't: BRCA1's roughly 72%-by-age-80 penetrance means a meaningful fraction of carriers never develop the disease, and the mother could still develop cancer later, since penetrance for BRCA1-associated cancer keeps climbing with age. The correct conclusion is "reduced/age-dependent penetrance," not "this family doesn't really have a dominant mutation."
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe penetrance and expressivity because they are the most common source of a pedigree that looks "broken" in a real project — a student who sees an unaffected mutation carrier and concludes the mode of inheritance must be wrong has misread the data, while one who says "reduced penetrance" or "phenocopy" and explains why has correctly diagnosed the ambiguity instead of being fooled by it.

questions.prompt: A person carries a pathogenic BRCA1 variant but, at age 70, has never developed breast cancer. What concept best explains this, given BRCA1's roughly 72%-by-age-80 lifetime risk?

options.text: Variable expressivity
Reduced (incomplete) penetrance
A phenocopy
Sex-limited expression

explanations.a: Expressivity concerns severity among people who do show the phenotype; this person shows no phenotype at all, which is a penetrance question.
explanations.b: Correct — since BRCA1 penetrance is well under 100%, some carriers never develop the disease at all; that is the definition of reduced penetrance.
explanations.c: A phenocopy is an environmentally caused case that mimics the genetic disease; this scenario is about a real mutation carrier who stayed unaffected.
explanations.d: BRCA1-associated breast cancer risk applies to carriers regardless of sex-limited mechanisms like those seen in male-limited precocious puberty.

questions.prompt: Two relatives both carry the identical FBN1 mutation causing Marfan syndrome. One has only mild tall stature; the other has a life-threatening aortic dissection. This difference illustrates:

options.text: Reduced penetrance
Variable expressivity
A phenocopy
Locus heterogeneity

explanations.a: Both relatives show the phenotype (just at different severities), so penetrance — whether the phenotype shows at all — is not the issue here.
explanations.b: Correct — the same genotype producing a wide range of severities in different carriers is the definition of variable expressivity.
explanations.c: Both cases stem from the same real mutation, not an environmental mimic, so this is not a phenocopy.
explanations.d: Locus heterogeneity means different genes cause the same disease; here it's the identical mutation in the identical gene.

questions.prompt: Hereditary hemochromatosis (HFE, C282Y homozygosity) is a classic sex-influenced trait because:

options.text: Only men can inherit the HFE mutation
It appears in both sexes, but is more often clinically symptomatic in men, since menstrual iron loss delays symptom onset in women
It is transmitted only through the maternal line
It only affects women after menopause

explanations.a: HFE is autosomal, so both sexes can inherit and carry the mutation equally.
explanations.b: Correct — the genotype occurs equally in both sexes, but women's cyclical menstrual iron loss masks or delays iron-overload symptoms, so clinical hemochromatosis shows up more often, and earlier, in men.
explanations.c: HFE is an autosomal gene on chromosome 6, not maternally transmitted like mitochondrial disease.
explanations.d: The condition can present earlier in men than in women, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: Match each term to the example that illustrates it.

right.text: A BRCA1 carrier who never develops cancer
Marfan syndrome relatives with mild versus severe aortic involvement
Male-limited precocious puberty (LHCGR mutation)
Hearing loss from an intrauterine infection in a family segregating a deafness gene

questions.explanation: Reduced penetrance means a genotype carrier shows no phenotype (BRCA1); variable expressivity means the phenotype's severity differs among carriers (Marfan); a sex-limited trait shows only in one sex despite either sex carrying and transmitting it (male-limited precocious puberty); a phenocopy is a non-genetic mimic that can distort a pedigree reading (environmental hearing loss).

lessons.label: When the Simple Rules Break: Heterogeneity, Mosaicism, and De Novo Mutation

sections.heading: Locus and allelic heterogeneity
sections.body: Locus heterogeneity means the same clinical label can arise from mutations in entirely different genes. Retinitis pigmentosa is the extreme case: over 100 different genes (RHO and RPGR among the best known) can each independently cause the same progressive retinal degeneration, so two relatives diagnosed with "retinitis pigmentosa" need not share a causal variant at all. Non-syndromic hearing loss shows the same pattern — GJB2 (encoding connexin 26) is the single most common cause of recessive hereditary deafness, but dozens of other genes cause clinically indistinguishable hearing loss. Allelic heterogeneity is narrower: different mutations within the same gene, sometimes producing compound heterozygotes who carry two different pathogenic alleles at the same locus, one from each parent. A cystic fibrosis patient carrying ΔF508 on one CFTR allele and a distinct CFTR mutation on the other is still recessive disease — just not classic homozygosity, which can make a pedigree read oddly until you know to check for it.

sections.heading: Germline and somatic mosaicism
sections.body: Germline mosaicism occurs when a fraction of a parent's egg or sperm precursor cells carries a new mutation while the rest of that parent's body (and a standard blood test) looks entirely normal. This explains recurrence of an apparently sporadic dominant condition in a second child despite both parents testing negative: osteogenesis imperfecta (COL1A1/COL1A2) and Duchenne muscular dystrophy both have well-documented cases where germline mosaicism in a phenotypically normal parent produced a second affected child, with empirical recurrence-risk estimates around 6-7% quoted in genetic counseling for apparently sporadic dominant OI, rather than the near-zero risk a naive reading would suggest. Somatic mosaicism instead arises after fertilization, in only some body cells, producing patchy or segmental phenotypes — segmental neurofibromatosis confined to one body region, or McCune-Albright syndrome from a post-zygotic GNAS mutation, are classic examples.

sections.heading: De novo mutation rates and the paternal-age effect
sections.body: Whole-genome sequencing of parent-offspring trios has directly measured the human de novo mutation rate at roughly 60-80 new point mutations per genome per generation (trio-sequencing work such as Kong et al., 2012, using Icelandic families). Most of these trace to the paternal germline, because spermatogonial stem cells keep dividing throughout a man's life — roughly 23 divisions per year — copying DNA (and accumulating replication errors) at each round, while oocytes are largely arrested in meiosis from before a woman is even born. Kong et al. (2012) found the mutation count rises with paternal age at conception by roughly 1-2 extra mutations per year, meaning an older father transmits meaningfully more new mutations than a young one.

lessons.workedExample: A couple's first child has osteogenesis imperfecta with a mutation presumed to be a fresh dominant event, since neither parent shows any clinical signs and neither tests positive on a standard blood sample. When the couple asks about a second pregnancy, a genetic counselor still quotes an empirical recurrence risk around 6-7%, not near zero. The reasoning is germline mosaicism: one parent's blood may be entirely normal while a subset of their germ cells still carries the mutation, so the negative test does not rule out the possibility of another affected child.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe heterogeneity and mosaicism because these explain the real deviations from "textbook" pedigrees that trip up student projects: naming locus heterogeneity when two relatives share a diagnosis but not a variant, or citing germline mosaicism instead of concluding "the mutation must not be real" when an apparently sporadic dominant condition recurs, is the difference between a student who understands the mechanism and one who only memorized the clean cases.

questions.prompt: Two relatives are both diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa but genetic testing finds they carry mutations in two completely different genes. This is an example of:

options.text: Allelic heterogeneity
Locus heterogeneity
Germline mosaicism
A phenocopy

explanations.a: Allelic heterogeneity refers to different mutations within the same gene, not different genes altogether.
explanations.b: Correct — retinitis pigmentosa can arise from mutations in over 100 different genes, so a shared clinical label does not imply a shared causal gene.
explanations.c: Germline mosaicism concerns a parent's germ cells carrying a mutation absent from their soma, unrelated to this scenario.
explanations.d: Both relatives have genuine genetic causes of RP, just at different loci, so neither case is a non-genetic phenocopy.

questions.prompt: A couple's first child has an apparently sporadic dominant condition; both parents test negative on standard blood testing. A second child is later born affected. What best explains this recurrence?

options.text: The condition must actually be recessive, not dominant
Germline mosaicism in one parent, whose blood is normal but some germ cells carry the mutation
A calculation error — recurrence for a de novo dominant mutation is always exactly zero
The second child must have a completely unrelated condition

explanations.a: The condition's dominant biology is unchanged; the surprise is in transmission risk, not mode of inheritance.
explanations.b: Correct — germline mosaicism lets a phenotypically and blood-test normal parent still carry the mutation in a fraction of egg or sperm precursor cells, explaining recurrence.
explanations.c: Empirical recurrence risk for a genuinely de novo dominant mutation is low but not zero, precisely because germline mosaicism is possible and undetectable by standard blood testing.
explanations.d: Assuming an unrelated cause without evidence ignores the well-documented mosaicism explanation that fits this exact scenario.

questions.prompt: Trio-sequencing studies (e.g., Kong et al., 2012) found that most de novo point mutations trace to the paternal germline. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Sperm cells are larger than egg cells
Spermatogonial stem cells divide repeatedly throughout life, accumulating replication errors, while oocytes are largely meiotically arrested from before birth
Fathers are exposed to more environmental mutagens than mothers on average
Maternal mutations are repaired more efficiently by DNA repair enzymes

explanations.a: Cell size has no bearing on mutation accumulation; this is a distractor with no mechanistic basis.
explanations.b: Correct — ongoing spermatogonial divisions (roughly 23 per year) each carry a chance of a replication error, while oocytes are arrested for decades, which is why paternal age correlates with roughly 1-2 additional de novo mutations per year.
explanations.c: The paternal-age effect is attributed to replication-driven mutation from repeated cell division, not differential environmental exposure.
explanations.d: There is no established sex difference in DNA repair efficiency that explains this pattern; the division-count explanation is the established one.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to the example that illustrates it.

right.text: Retinitis pigmentosa caused by any of 100+ different genes
A CF patient with ΔF508 on one CFTR allele and a different CFTR mutation on the other
Recurrence of osteogenesis imperfecta in a second child despite both parents testing negative
McCune-Albright syndrome from a post-zygotic GNAS mutation affecting only some tissues

questions.explanation: Locus heterogeneity means different genes cause the same clinical picture (RP); allelic heterogeneity/compound heterozygosity means two different mutations in the same gene (CF); germline mosaicism explains recurrence despite negative parental testing (OI); somatic mosaicism produces a patchy, tissue-limited phenotype from a post-zygotic mutation (McCune-Albright).

lessons.label: Imprinting, Uniparental Disomy, and Repeat Expansion

sections.heading: Genomic imprinting: same region, opposite parent, opposite disease
sections.body: Genomic imprinting silences certain genes depending on which parent they came from, through DNA methylation marks laid down in the germline. The 15q11-q13 region is the clearest teaching case in human genetics: Prader-Willi syndrome (hypotonia, hyperphagia leading to obesity, intellectual disability) results from loss of the PATERNALLY contributed copy of this region, while Angelman syndrome (severe intellectual disability, ataxic movement, an unusually happy affect) results from loss of the MATERNALLY contributed copy of the exact same region — specifically loss of function of UBE3A, which is maternally expressed in neurons. Same chromosomal band, opposite parent of origin, two clinically distinct diseases — a direct demonstration that genotype location alone does not determine phenotype; parental origin matters too.

sections.heading: Three mechanisms, plus a second imprinted region
sections.body: Each of these disorders can arise through three distinct mechanisms: a straightforward deletion of the critical region on the parental chromosome that should have been active; uniparental disomy (UPD), where a child inherits both copies of chromosome 15 from a single parent and none from the other, so maternal UPD15 causes Prader-Willi (no active paternal copy present at all) and paternal UPD15 causes Angelman (no active maternal copy); or an imprinting-center defect, where the methylation mark fails to reset correctly despite the chromosome coming from the expected parent. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (overgrowth, macroglossia, omphalocele, elevated childhood tumor risk) is a second classic imprinting disorder, mapping to 11p15 with abnormal methylation at the H19/IGF2 and KCNQ1OT1 control regions.

sections.heading: Repeat expansion and anticipation
sections.body: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the 5' untranslated region of FMR1: fewer than 45 repeats is normal, 55-200 is a premutation, and more than 200 triggers hypermethylation that silences FMR1 entirely, causing full fragile X syndrome — the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. Premutation carriers are usually unaffected by fragile X syndrome itself but face distinct risks: FXTAS (fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome), mainly in older male premutation carriers, and FXPOI (fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency) in female premutation carriers. These repeats are unstable and expand almost exclusively during maternal transmission, so a premutation can expand into a full mutation from one generation to the next — producing anticipation, where severity increases or onset gets earlier in successive generations. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DMPK, a CTG repeat) shows the same maternal transmission bias, especially for its most severe, congenital form.

lessons.workedExample: A pedigree shows a maternal grandfather with mild learning difficulties and anxiety but no formal diagnosis (an FMR1 premutation carrier, in the 55-200 repeat range), his daughter who is unaffected but carries a larger repeat still in the premutation range, and her son who has full fragile X syndrome. This pattern is anticipation in action: because expansion from premutation to full mutation (over 200 repeats, triggering FMR1 silencing) happens almost exclusively during maternal transmission, the repeat grew large enough to cross the full-mutation threshold only when passed from the daughter to her son, explaining why the most severe presentation shows up two generations after the first mild signs.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe imprinting because Prader-Willi versus Angelman — the same 15q11-q13 region producing opposite diseases depending on parent of origin — is the cleanest test of whether a student understands that genotype location alone doesn't determine phenotype. They probe fragile X repeat thresholds specifically because citing the exact numeric cutoffs (45, 55, 200) instead of vague language ("a long repeat") is the difference between having read primary genetic criteria and having read a summary of them.

questions.prompt: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of function of which parental contribution to the 15q11-q13 region?

options.text: The paternal contribution
The maternal contribution
Either parent's contribution, with equal likelihood
Neither — Prader-Willi is unrelated to imprinting

explanations.a: Correct — Prader-Willi syndrome arises when the paternally contributed copy of 15q11-q13 is lost or silenced, whether by deletion, maternal UPD15, or an imprinting-center defect.
explanations.b: Loss of the maternal copy of this same region instead causes Angelman syndrome, the reciprocal disorder.
explanations.c: The parent of origin is specific and determines which of the two distinct syndromes results — it is not symmetric.
explanations.d: Prader-Willi is one of the two textbook examples of a human imprinting disorder.

questions.prompt: A child inherits both copies of chromosome 15 from their father and none from their mother (paternal uniparental disomy). Which syndrome results, and why?

options.text: Prader-Willi syndrome, because the active paternal copy is missing
Angelman syndrome, because the active maternal copy (needed for UBE3A expression) is missing
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, because 11p15 is duplicated
Fragile X syndrome, because FMR1 is silenced

explanations.a: This describes the opposite scenario — Prader-Willi results from maternal UPD15 (two maternal copies, missing the active paternal copy), not paternal UPD.
explanations.b: Correct — with both copies of chromosome 15 from the father, the maternally expressed UBE3A gene (normally active only on the maternal copy) has no active copy present at all, producing Angelman syndrome.
explanations.c: Beckwith-Wiedemann involves 11p15 methylation abnormalities, not chromosome 15 UPD.
explanations.d: Fragile X syndrome is caused by FMR1 CGG repeat expansion on the X chromosome, unrelated to chromosome 15 UPD.

questions.prompt: An FMR1 premutation carrier (55-200 CGG repeats) is generally unaffected by fragile X syndrome itself but is at elevated risk for:

options.text: FXTAS (in older carriers) or FXPOI (in female carriers)
Angelman syndrome
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
Duchenne muscular dystrophy

explanations.a: Correct — premutation carriers (55-200 repeats) are usually spared full fragile X syndrome but face FXTAS (tremor/ataxia, mainly older male carriers) or FXPOI (primary ovarian insufficiency, female carriers).
explanations.b: Angelman syndrome results from loss of the maternal 15q11-q13 contribution, an entirely separate mechanism from FMR1 repeat expansion.
explanations.c: Beckwith-Wiedemann maps to 11p15 methylation defects, unrelated to FMR1.
explanations.d: DMD is caused by dystrophin gene mutations on the X chromosome, unrelated to FMR1 repeat length.

questions.prompt: Match each FMR1 CGG repeat range to its consequence.

right.text: Normal; no fragile X-related risk
Premutation; risk of FXTAS or FXPOI, and risk of expanding further in offspring
Full mutation; FMR1 silenced by hypermethylation, causing fragile X syndrome

questions.explanation: Repeat length below 45 is stable and normal; 55-200 is a premutation that is generally unaffected by fragile X syndrome itself but carries FXTAS/FXPOI risk and instability on transmission; above 200 repeats triggers hypermethylation that silences FMR1 and causes full fragile X syndrome.

lessons.label: Recurrence Risk and Bayesian Pedigree Math

sections.heading: The four-column Bayes table
sections.body: Bayesian pedigree analysis combines a starting Mendelian expectation with new evidence to produce an updated risk, laid out as a table with one row per hypothesis and four columns. The prior is the probability of each hypothesis before any new evidence — typically a straight Mendelian ratio, like 1/2 for the daughter of a known carrier. The conditional probability is how likely the observed evidence would be under each hypothesis. The joint probability multiplies prior by conditional for each row. The posterior normalizes the joint probabilities so they sum to 1, by dividing each joint value by the sum of all joint values in the table — this posterior is the updated risk that actually answers the family's question.

sections.heading: Worked Duchenne muscular dystrophy example
sections.body: A woman with an affected maternal uncle has a prior carrier probability of 1/2, inherited from her obligate-carrier mother. She then has three sons, all unaffected. If she is a carrier, each son independently has a 1/2 chance of being unaffected, so the conditional probability of all three being unaffected is (1/2)^3 = 1/8. If she is not a carrier, all three sons being unaffected is certain, conditional = 1. The joint probabilities are: carrier = 1/2 × 1/8 = 1/16, non-carrier = 1/2 × 1 = 8/16. Summing gives 9/16, so the posterior carrier probability is (1/16) ÷ (9/16) = 1/9 — her three unaffected sons have pulled her risk down substantially, from an initial 1/2 to about 1/9.

sections.heading: Residual risk after a carrier screen
sections.body: The same table format handles population screening. Cystic fibrosis carrier frequency runs about 1/25 in the relevant population, so the prior for carrier is 1/25 and for non-carrier is 24/25. A carrier screening panel with 90% detection sensitivity, applied to someone with no family history, still misses 10% of true carriers, so the conditional probability of a negative result given carrier status is 0.10, and given non-carrier status is 1.0 (a true non-carrier is certain to test negative). The joint values are carrier = 1/25 × 0.10 = 0.004 and non-carrier = 24/25 × 1.0 = 0.96, summing to 0.964. The posterior carrier probability given a negative result is 0.004 ÷ 0.964 ≈ 1/241 — meaningfully lower than the 1/25 starting risk, but not zero, because the panel isn't perfect.

lessons.workedExample: A genetic counselor sees a pregnant patient from a population with a baseline CF carrier frequency of 1/25. She takes a carrier panel with 90% detection sensitivity and receives a negative result. Building the table: prior carrier = 1/25 (0.04), prior non-carrier = 24/25 (0.96); conditional (negative result) given carrier = 0.10, given non-carrier = 1.0; joint carrier = 0.04 × 0.10 = 0.004, joint non-carrier = 0.96 × 1.0 = 0.96; the two joints sum to 0.964. Posterior carrier probability = 0.004 ÷ 0.964 ≈ 0.00415, or roughly 1/241. The counselor reports this residual risk honestly, rather than telling the patient the negative screen rules out carrier status entirely.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe Bayesian pedigree math because reciting a carrier frequency or a Mendelian ratio from memory is not the same skill as building the four-column table and correctly normalizing it — a student who can walk a judge through prior, conditional, joint, and posterior for their own family's evidence (three unaffected sons, a negative screen) has demonstrated real command of conditional probability, arguably the single most differentiating math skill available in a genetics fair project.

questions.prompt: In a Bayes table for pedigree risk, what does the "prior" column represent?

options.text: The final, updated risk after all evidence is considered
The Mendelian-expectation probability of each hypothesis before any new evidence is added
The probability of the observed evidence given each hypothesis
A number that must always equal 1

explanations.a: That is the posterior, the last column of the table, not the prior.
explanations.b: Correct — the prior is the starting probability for each hypothesis, usually derived from Mendelian expectation, before incorporating new evidence.
explanations.c: That describes the conditional probability column, which comes after the prior in the table.
explanations.d: Individual priors need not equal 1; the priors across all hypotheses in the table should sum to 1, but no single prior is required to.

questions.prompt: A woman has a 1/2 prior probability of being a DMD carrier. If she is a carrier, what is the conditional probability that all three of her sons would be unaffected?

explanations.a: 1/2 is the chance for one son alone being unaffected, not all three together.
explanations.b: Correct — each son independently has a 1/2 chance of being unaffected if his mother is a carrier, so three unaffected sons in a row has conditional probability (1/2)^3 = 1/8.
explanations.c: 1/9 is the final posterior carrier probability after normalizing, not the conditional probability of this evidence.
explanations.d: A conditional probability of 1 would only apply to the non-carrier hypothesis, where unaffected sons are certain.

questions.prompt: Using the joint probabilities carrier = 1/16 and non-carrier = 8/16, what is the posterior probability that the woman is a DMD carrier?

explanations.a: 1/2 was her prior before the evidence of three unaffected sons was incorporated, not her updated posterior.
explanations.b: 1/8 is the conditional probability of the evidence given she is a carrier, not the normalized posterior.
explanations.d: 1/16 is the joint probability for the carrier row alone, before dividing by the sum of both joints.

questions.prompt: A patient from a population with 1/25 CF carrier frequency takes a screening panel with 90% detection sensitivity and tests negative. What is her approximate residual carrier risk?

options.text: 0 (the negative result rules out carrier status)
1/25 (unchanged, since the test result adds no information)

explanations.a: A 90%-sensitivity panel still misses 10% of true carriers, so a negative result cannot rule out carrier status entirely.
explanations.b: A negative result does lower her risk substantially from the 1/25 prior; treating it as uninformative ignores the test's 90% detection rate.
explanations.c: Correct — joint carrier = 1/25 × 0.10 = 0.004, joint non-carrier = 24/25 × 1.0 = 0.96, posterior = 0.004 ÷ 0.964 ≈ 1/241.
explanations.d: 1/10 does not follow from the Bayes calculation using this prior and this panel's detection rate.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building a Bayes table for pedigree risk in the correct order.

items.text: List each hypothesis and its prior probability from Mendelian expectation
Determine the conditional probability of the observed evidence under each hypothesis
Multiply prior by conditional for each hypothesis to get the joint probability
Divide each joint probability by the sum of all joint probabilities to get the posterior

questions.explanation: You start from the Mendelian prior, incorporate how likely the new evidence is under each hypothesis as a conditional, multiply the two together into a joint probability for each row, and finally normalize the joints into posteriors that sum to 1 and represent the updated risk.

units.label: Finding Disease Genes: Linkage, Sequencing, and Association

lessons.label: Linkage Analysis and the LOD Score

sections.heading: Recombination fraction as a ruler
sections.body: Two loci on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together unless a crossover separates them during meiosis. The recombination fraction, theta, is the proportion of meioses in which that separation happens — theta = 0 means the loci never separate (essentially the same spot, or perfectly linked), theta = 0.5 means they assort as independently as loci on different chromosomes. Because crossover frequency scales roughly with physical distance, theta doubles as a distance measure: 1% recombination is defined as 1 centimorgan (cM), a unit named for Thomas Hunt Morgan, whose early-1900s Drosophila crosses first showed recombination frequency could map gene order. To estimate theta in a human pedigree, you count informative meioses — transmissions where you can actually tell whether a recombination occurred, which requires a parent heterozygous at both loci — and divide the observed recombinants by that count.

sections.heading: The LOD score and where the thresholds come from
sections.body: Newton Morton formalized the standard test in 1955: the LOD score (logarithm of the odds) is log10 of the likelihood of the pedigree data at a given theta divided by the likelihood at theta = 0.5 (no linkage). Scores from multiple families sum, so a genome scan combines many small pedigrees. The field-standard cutoffs, LOD >= 3 to declare linkage and LOD <= -2 to exclude it, are not arbitrary round numbers — they are a Bayesian calculation. Before scanning, the prior odds that two randomly chosen loci are linked (given roughly 23 chromosome pairs, human genome) are about 1:50. A LOD of 3 is 1000:1 odds in favor of linkage from the data; multiplied by the 1:50 prior, the posterior odds land near 20:1, which works out to roughly a 5% chance the 'linkage' is a false positive — comparable to the intuition behind p < 0.05.

sections.heading: Parametric versus non-parametric mapping, and its limits
sections.body: Parametric (model-based) linkage requires specifying a mode of inheritance — dominant or recessive, penetrance, phenocopy rate — and is powerful when that model is right, which is why it succeeded for high-penetrance single-gene disorders: Huntington disease was localized to chromosome 4 in 1983, and the CFTR gene for cystic fibrosis was mapped by 1985. When the genetic model is unknown or the trait is complex, non-parametric methods like affected-sib-pair (ASP) analysis sidestep the guess: they test whether sibling pairs who both have the disease share a marker allele identical-by-descent more often than the 50% expected by chance. Both approaches share linkage's core limitation — statistical power comes from tracking recombination across a handful of large, informative meioses in a family, which works for rare, highly penetrant alleles but essentially fails for common variants of small effect, where no single family carries enough copies to generate a signal.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher studies a large three-generation family segregating an autosomal dominant retinal disease and genotypes a marker 4 cM from the presumed disease locus. Across the pedigree there are 16 informative meioses (parents heterozygous at both the marker and disease locus), and 1 of them shows recombination between the marker and the disease phenotype — a recombination fraction of 1/16 = 0.0625, close to the assumed map distance. Plugging that into the likelihood ratio versus theta = 0.5 across the family yields LOD = 3.2, clearing the LOD >= 3 threshold, so the marker is declared linked and the search for the gene narrows to the region flanking it. A single small nuclear family with only 6 informative meioses and zero observed recombinants would produce a maximal LOD around 1.8 — too few meioses to ever reach significance alone, which is why linkage studies pool multiple pedigrees.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees 'linkage analysis' on a poster is checking whether the student understands that a LOD score is a likelihood ratio with a specific, derivable threshold — not just 'a p-value for genes.' The tell of real understanding is being able to say why LOD 3 was chosen (the ~1:50 prior odds that make it behave like a 5% false-positive rate) and why the same approach cannot find a common variant of modest effect — that requires naming the constraint (too few informative meioses per family, and no family segregating a common allele shows a clean transmission pattern) rather than reciting 'linkage is for rare diseases.'

questions.prompt: A recombination fraction (theta) of 0.01 between two loci is, by definition, equivalent to what genetic map distance?

options.text: 1 centimorgan (cM)
1 megabase (Mb)
100 centimorgans
It cannot be converted to a distance without a physical map

explanations.a: Correct — 1% recombination is the definition of 1 cM, the genetic-distance unit built directly from theta.
explanations.b: A megabase is a physical distance measured in base pairs, not a recombination-derived genetic distance; the two are correlated but not interchangeable.
explanations.c: That would require theta = 1.0, which is not a valid recombination fraction (max is 0.5, independent assortment).
explanations.d: The genetic map (in cM) is defined directly from recombination fraction, with no physical map required.

questions.prompt: Why is a LOD score of 3 (not, say, 1 or 5) the conventional threshold for declaring linkage?

options.text: It is a round number chosen purely for tradition
Combined with the low prior odds (~1:50) that two random loci are linked, it yields posterior odds around 20:1, roughly a 5% false-positive rate
It corresponds exactly to theta = 0
It is the minimum score achievable with a single informative meiosis

explanations.a: Morton's 1955 derivation was a deliberate Bayesian calculation, not an arbitrary convention.
explanations.b: Correct — LOD 3 means 1000:1 odds favoring linkage from the data, and folding in the ~1:50 prior odds of any two loci being linked gives posterior odds near 20:1, about a 5% false-positive rate.
explanations.c: LOD score is a likelihood ratio at an estimated theta value, not a statement that theta equals zero.
explanations.d: A single informative meiosis contributes only a small fraction of a LOD unit; reaching LOD 3 requires many meioses, usually pooled across families.

questions.prompt: Match each linkage-mapping approach to its defining feature.

right.text: Requires specifying mode of inheritance and penetrance in advance
Tests excess identical-by-descent marker sharing between affected siblings
log10 of the likelihood ratio for linkage at theta versus theta = 0.5

questions.explanation: Parametric linkage needs a specified genetic model; affected-sib-pair analysis instead looks for above-chance IBD sharing at a marker among affected siblings, requiring no inheritance model; the LOD score is the log-likelihood-ratio statistic underlying both.

questions.prompt: Why does linkage analysis fail to detect common disease variants of small effect, even with large pedigrees?

options.text: Common variants recombine at a different rate than rare variants

Power comes from tracking recombination across informative meioses within families, and no single family or small pedigree set carries enough copies of a common, small-effect allele to produce a detectable transmission signal
LOD scores cannot be calculated for autosomal traits
Common variants are always located outside coding regions

explanations.a: Recombination rate depends on chromosomal position, not on whether the underlying allele is common or rare.
explanations.b: Correct — linkage's statistical power is built from countable informative meioses in pedigrees, which works for rare, highly penetrant alleles segregating cleanly in a family, but a common variant of small effect produces too weak and too diffuse a signal within any one family's transmissions.
explanations.c: LOD scores are calculated the same way regardless of chromosome type; the limitation is statistical power, not computability.
explanations.d: Variant location (coding vs. non-coding) is unrelated to why linkage struggles with common, small-effect alleles.

lessons.label: From Positional Cloning to Trio Exome Sequencing

sections.heading: The old road: from a linked marker to a named gene
sections.body: Before genome sequencing was affordable, finding a disease gene after linkage narrowed a region meant physically walking there. Positional cloning built a physical map of overlapping clones (cosmids, then yeast artificial chromosomes) across the linked interval, extended step by step through chromosome walking or, to cover ground faster, chromosome jumping, which skips ahead using large-insert clones instead of crawling through every overlap. Once the interval was tiled, researchers picked candidate genes by function or expression pattern and sequenced them in patients looking for mutations that segregated with disease. The cystic fibrosis gene, CFTR, is the textbook case: linkage placed it on chromosome 7 in 1985, and it took Lap-Chee Tsui, Francis Collins, and John Riordan's teams until 1989 to walk and jump to the actual gene and confirm the causal deltaF508 deletion. Huntington disease took even longer — linked to chromosome 4 in 1983, the gene (HTT) was not identified until 1993, a full decade of positional cloning on a single locus.

sections.heading: Trio sequencing collapses years into weeks
sections.body: Modern diagnosis of suspected genetic disease skips mapping entirely: sequence the affected child's exome or genome alongside both parents (a trio) and filter variants directly by inheritance logic. A de novo variant is present in the child but absent from both parents' sequence — the pattern expected for many severe, early-onset conditions that are not inherited. A homozygous recessive variant is present in a single copy in each carrier parent and both copies in the child; a compound heterozygous case carries two different damaging variants in the same gene, one from each parent. X-linked patterns are checked by inheritance from a carrier mother. Each candidate variant is then filtered against population allele-frequency databases like gnomAD (aggregating well over 100,000 exomes/genomes) — a variant too common in the general population to plausibly cause a rare severe disease is dropped.

sections.heading: Diagnostic yield, and what exome sequencing still misses
sections.body: Trio exome sequencing solves roughly 25-40% of previously undiagnosed rare-disease cases — a striking number given these are patients who already exhausted standard clinical workups, but still a minority, which is the field's open problem. Whole genome sequencing, sequencing all ~3 billion bases rather than just the ~1-2% that is protein-coding exome, adds detection of structural variants (large deletions, duplications, inversions), deep-intronic mutations that disrupt splicing far from any exon, and repeat expansions (the kind that cause Huntington disease and fragile X syndrome) — categories exome capture is poorly suited to detect because it only sequences exons and misses the intervening and flanking sequence entirely.

lessons.workedExample: A child presents with severe developmental delay and seizures of unknown cause; standard single-gene tests were negative. A clinical lab sequences the child's exome plus both unaffected parents. Filtering removes all variants present in gnomAD at greater than 0.1% frequency, then narrows to genes with any plausible developmental-disorder link. One variant survives: a missense change in a known neurodevelopmental gene, present in the child, absent in both parents — a de novo variant, the single strongest inheritance pattern for a severe, sporadic pediatric condition. This single trio comparison, completed in weeks, reproduces what would once have required years of linkage mapping across an extended family the size of the CFTR or Huntington pedigrees, and it only works because there is no large affected family to map in the first place.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing a genomics project ask 'why didn't you just use linkage mapping?' to check whether a student understands that trio sequencing solves a different problem than positional cloning did — it needs no large multigenerational pedigree, no assumed inheritance model, and no physical walk across a chromosome, because it reads the causal variant directly. The strong answer names the specific inheritance filter used (de novo, compound het, etc.) and the allele-frequency database that ruled out common variants, rather than vaguely citing 'we sequenced the DNA.'

questions.prompt: Order the classic positional-cloning workflow from a linked marker to a confirmed disease gene.

items.text: Linkage analysis narrows the disease locus to a chromosomal interval
Chromosome walking/jumping builds a physical map of overlapping clones across the interval
Candidate genes within the interval are selected by function or expression pattern
Candidate gene is sequenced in unrelated patients to confirm segregating mutations

questions.explanation: Positional cloning starts from a linkage-defined interval, physically tiles that interval via chromosome walking/jumping, picks plausible candidate genes within it, and finally confirms causality by finding disease-segregating mutations in unrelated patients — the workflow that took CFTR four years (1985-1989) and HTT a full decade (1983-1993).

questions.prompt: Match each trio-sequencing inheritance pattern to its defining genotype signature.

right.text: Present in the child, absent from both parents' sequence
Same variant, one copy in each carrier parent, both copies in the affected child
Two different damaging variants in the same gene, one inherited from each parent

questions.explanation: De novo variants appear in the child but neither parent; homozygous recessive means both copies of the same variant, one from each carrier parent; compound heterozygous means two distinct damaging variants in the same gene, contributed one from each parent.

questions.prompt: What does whole genome sequencing detect that whole exome sequencing typically misses?

options.text: Missense variants in protein-coding exons
Structural variants, deep-intronic splice-disrupting mutations, and repeat expansions
Nonsense variants that truncate a protein
De novo variants in general

explanations.a: Exome sequencing is specifically designed to capture coding-region missense variants; this is one of its strengths, not a blind spot.
explanations.b: Correct — because exome capture targets only the ~1-2% of the genome that is protein-coding, it largely misses large structural rearrangements, splice-disrupting variants deep in introns, and repeat expansions (as in Huntington disease or fragile X syndrome), all of which whole genome sequencing can detect.
explanations.c: Nonsense variants occur in coding exons and are well-captured by exome sequencing.
explanations.d: De novo variants can occur in coding regions and are readily detected by exome sequencing; the exome/genome distinction is about location in the genome, not inheritance pattern.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of previously undiagnosed rare-disease cases does trio exome/genome sequencing typically resolve?

options.text: About 25-40%
About 90-95%
Less than 1%
Exactly 50%, by definition of the trio design

explanations.a: Correct — diagnostic yield for trio sequencing in undiagnosed rare disease is typically cited around 25-40%, a meaningful minority given these patients already failed standard workups.
explanations.b: That figure vastly overstates yield; most trio-sequenced cases remain unsolved even after this test.
explanations.c: This understates the real, substantial diagnostic value trio sequencing provides.
explanations.d: There is no reason the yield would land at exactly 50%; it is an empirical figure from case series, not a designed property of the trio method.

lessons.label: The Candidate-Gene Study and Why It Failed

sections.heading: Anatomy of a hypothesis-driven single-SNP study
sections.body: For roughly two decades before genome-wide arrays became affordable, the standard approach to complex-disease genetics was the candidate-gene study: pick a gene with plausible biology (a neurotransmitter transporter for a psychiatric trait, an inflammation gene for an autoimmune one), genotype one or a handful of SNPs in it, and test for association with disease in a sample that was often small — frequently under 500 subjects total. Researchers had wide latitude in how they defined the phenotype and which subgroups to analyze, and the bar for a reportable result was an unadjusted p < 0.05 on that single test, with no requirement to replicate the finding in an independent sample before publishing.

sections.heading: Why low power guarantees inflated, unreplicable results
sections.body: A study with too few subjects to reliably detect a true small effect can still occasionally cross p < 0.05 purely by chance, or find a real but tiny effect whose estimated size is, by statistical necessity, inflated in that particular sample — a phenomenon called the winner's curse: among all the noisy estimates that happened to clear the threshold, the ones that do are disproportionately the ones where chance pushed the estimate up. Journals in this era rarely published null results, so the literature accumulated a lopsided record of 'significant' candidate-gene findings that looked impressive in aggregate but were never filtered by replication. One of the most cited examples, Caspi and colleagues' 2003 Science paper linking a serotonin-transporter promoter variant (5-HTTLPR) to depression risk after stressful life events, could not be reproduced in Risch and colleagues' 2009 JAMA meta-analysis of far larger, pooled samples.

sections.heading: The reckoning and the methodological lesson
sections.body: The clearest reckoning came in Border and colleagues' 2019 American Journal of Psychiatry study, which tested 18 of the most-published candidate genes for depression — including SLC6A4, DRD4, and APOE — in cohorts totaling more than 620,000 individuals, several orders of magnitude larger than any original candidate-gene study. None of the genes showed association stronger than chance, and their effect sizes were statistically indistinguishable from noise. This result, and others like it, forced a shift in the field's design norms: genome-wide (not single-gene) scanning to avoid selecting the SNP after seeing the data, pre-specified analysis plans, a far stricter significance threshold to account for testing many variants, and mandatory independent replication before a finding could be trusted — the design that became the genome-wide association study.

lessons.workedExample: A 2001 study genotypes one SNP in a dopamine-receptor gene in 150 cases with a psychiatric diagnosis and 150 controls, tests for association, and reports p = 0.03 with an odds ratio of 2.1 — a seemingly large effect. A well-powered 2015 GWAS meta-analysis of the same phenotype in over 100,000 subjects finds the true effect of that SNP, if it exists at all, has an odds ratio closer to 1.02. The original study was not fabricated or dishonest — with only 300 subjects it had very low power to detect a true small effect, so any result that cleared p < 0.05 was, by the winner's curse, almost certainly an overestimate, and a play of chance was nearly as likely an explanation as a real signal.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this history will ask a student citing an old candidate-gene finding whether it has been replicated in a large, pre-registered sample — because the candidate-gene era is the field's cautionary tale about small n, flexible analysis, and no replication requirement producing a literature that looked solid but collapsed under Border and colleagues' 2019 re-test. A strong answer names the winner's curse mechanism (low power inflates whatever clears the threshold) rather than just saying 'it wasn't replicated.'

questions.prompt: In the classic candidate-gene study design, what combination of features made false-positive findings especially likely?

options.text: Small samples (often under 500), flexible phenotype/subgroup definitions, unadjusted p < 0.05, and no replication requirement
Genome-wide scanning combined with a very strict significance threshold
Mandatory pre-registration of the single SNP to be tested
Testing only in twin pairs, which inflates statistical power

explanations.a: Correct — small samples, flexible analysis choices, a lenient unadjusted threshold, and no replication requirement together let chance findings look like real, publishable discoveries.
explanations.b: This describes the later GWAS design that replaced candidate-gene studies specifically to fix these problems; it is the opposite of the candidate-gene approach.
explanations.c: Candidate-gene studies notoriously lacked pre-registration, which is part of why researchers had flexibility in phenotype and subgroup definitions.
explanations.d: Candidate-gene studies were not restricted to twin designs, and using twins would not itself explain the inflated positive rate; the core issues were sample size and analytic flexibility.

questions.prompt: What is the 'winner's curse' in the context of underpowered genetic association studies?

options.text: The tendency for the first published finding on a gene to always be correct
The tendency for effect-size estimates that happen to clear a significance threshold in a low-power study to be systematically inflated compared to the true effect
A statistical penalty applied automatically by journals to small studies
The observation that larger studies always find larger effects than smaller ones

explanations.a: The winner's curse describes exactly the opposite pattern — early, small, 'winning' studies are the ones most likely to be wrong about effect size.
explanations.b: Correct — when power is low, only estimates pushed upward by chance clear the significance bar, so the reported effect sizes among 'significant' small studies are systematically inflated relative to the truth.
explanations.c: It is a statistical consequence of low power and thresholding, not an editorial penalty.
explanations.d: Larger, well-powered studies tend to find smaller, more accurate effect-size estimates than the inflated ones from small studies — the reverse of this claim.

questions.prompt: Border and colleagues' 2019 study tested 18 historically prominent candidate genes for depression (including SLC6A4, DRD4, and APOE) in a combined sample of over 620,000 people. What did they find?

options.text: All 18 genes replicated with even stronger effect sizes than originally reported
None of the 18 genes showed association stronger than chance; their effect sizes were indistinguishable from noise
Exactly half of the genes replicated
The study was underpowered to draw any conclusion

explanations.a: The opposite occurred — none of the genes showed a stronger or even comparable effect in the large, well-powered re-test.
explanations.b: Correct — despite decades of candidate-gene publications on these genes, none showed association with depression beyond what chance would produce in this vastly larger, better-powered sample.
explanations.c: No partial-replication pattern like this was found; essentially none of the 18 genes held up.
explanations.d: At over 620,000 individuals, this was one of the best-powered tests of these candidate genes ever conducted — power was not the limitation.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the methodological history of candidate-gene research on depression.

items.text: Caspi and colleagues (2003) report a 5-HTTLPR x stress interaction predicting depression
Risch and colleagues (2009) meta-analysis fails to replicate the interaction in larger pooled samples
Border and colleagues (2019) test 18 candidate genes in over 620,000 individuals and find no signal
The field shifts to genome-wide, pre-specified designs with mandatory replication

questions.explanation: The chronology runs from the original influential candidate-gene finding (2003), through a large meta-analysis failing to replicate it (2009), to a definitive large-scale rejection of the broader candidate-gene literature (2019), which cemented the field's move to genome-wide, pre-registered, replication-required study design.

lessons.label: GWAS Design: Arrays, LD Tagging, and Imputation

sections.heading: How half a million SNPs can stand in for the whole genome
sections.body: A genome-wide association study genotypes 500,000 to 1,000,000 SNPs on a microarray, far fewer than the roughly 10 million common variants in the genome — yet it works because nearby variants are correlated. Linkage disequilibrium (LD) is the non-random association of alleles at nearby loci, inherited together in blocks because recombination has not yet shuffled them apart. The HapMap Project (2002-2005) mapped this block structure across populations, showing that genotyping one tag SNP lets you statistically infer the alleles at every other SNP in its haplotype block, without genotyping them directly. Array design exploits this: a few hundred thousand well-chosen tags can proxy for most common variation genome-wide.

sections.heading: Imputation extends coverage, and quality filters bound trust
sections.body: Imputation statistically fills in the ungenotyped variants between tags, using a reference panel of densely sequenced genomes to learn the local haplotype structure and infer each sample's likely genotype at millions of additional positions. Reference panels have grown steadily denser and more diverse: HapMap, then the 1000 Genomes Project (roughly 2,500 genomes across populations, completed 2015), then larger resources like the Haplotype Reference Consortium and NHLBI's TOPMed program, which sequenced well over 100,000 genomes. Imputation can push a study from several hundred thousand genotyped SNPs to tens of millions of analyzed variants, but each imputed genotype carries an uncertainty estimate — commonly reported as an r-squared or INFO score — and variants below a quality cutoff (often r-squared < 0.3) are dropped before analysis, because a poorly imputed variant behaves like added noise, not signal.

sections.heading: Study design, QC, and the blind spots that remain
sections.body: A GWAS is run either as case-control (logistic regression on disease status) or on a continuous measurement (linear regression on a quantitative trait like height or LDL cholesterol), with age, sex, and ancestry included as covariates. Before any association test, samples go through quality control: call rate thresholds (excluding samples or SNPs with too much missing data), heterozygosity outlier checks (flagging likely sample contamination or inbreeding), sex checks (comparing genotypic sex on the X chromosome to reported sex to catch sample mix-ups), and minor allele frequency and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium filters applied to controls (a SNP wildly out of Hardy-Weinberg proportions usually signals a genotyping error rather than biology). Biobank-scale cohorts made all of this dramatically more powerful — UK Biobank alone genotyped roughly 500,000 participants recruited from 2006-2010. Even at that scale, array-plus-imputation GWAS has real blind spots: rare variants below about 0.1-1% frequency, insertions/deletions, and structural variation are poorly tagged by common SNPs and largely invisible to this design.

lessons.workedExample: A study genotypes 600,000 tag SNPs on 50,000 cases and 50,000 controls, then imputes against the TOPMed reference panel, expanding the analyzed set to roughly 20 million variants. After QC removes samples with call rates below 98%, sex-mismatched samples, and SNPs failing Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium in controls (p < 1e-6), and after dropping imputed variants with r-squared below 0.3, about 8 million well-imputed variants with minor allele frequency above 1% remain for logistic regression against case-control status, adjusting for the first ten ancestry principal components. A rare structural deletion known from other studies to affect the same phenotype does not appear anywhere in this result set — not because it doesn't matter, but because it falls in exactly the blind spot common-SNP arrays and LD-based imputation cannot see.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe GWAS methodology because it is easy to cite 'we ran a GWAS' without understanding that the array only genotypes a small fraction of the genome directly — the rest is inferred through LD and imputation, with an explicit quality filter deciding what gets trusted. A strong answer can explain why a tag SNP works as a proxy at all (LD blocks) and can name a specific QC step (Hardy-Weinberg filtering, call-rate thresholds) rather than treating quality control as an unspecified black box.

questions.prompt: Why can a GWAS array genotyping only ~500,000-1,000,000 SNPs capture information about millions of other variants?

options.text: Because linkage disequilibrium means nearby variants are correlated, so a genotyped tag SNP statistically proxies for its haplotype block
Because the array directly sequences the entire genome at low depth
Because rare variants are automatically included regardless of genotyping
Because imputation requires no reference data

explanations.a: Correct — LD means alleles at nearby loci are inherited together in blocks, so one genotyped tag SNP carries information about the rest of its block, which is what imputation exploits.
explanations.b: SNP arrays genotype only pre-selected positions; they do not sequence the genome at all.
explanations.c: Rare variants are precisely what tag-SNP arrays and LD-based imputation struggle to capture, not what they automatically include.
explanations.d: Imputation specifically requires a densely sequenced reference panel (e.g., 1000 Genomes, TOPMed) to learn haplotype structure before it can infer ungenotyped variants.

questions.prompt: Match each QC step to what it is designed to catch.

right.text: Samples or SNPs with excessive missing genotype data
Sample mix-ups, via mismatch between genotypic and reported sex
SNPs likely affected by genotyping error, flagged by unusual allele-frequency proportions

questions.explanation: Call-rate thresholds catch excessive missingness, sex checks compare X-chromosome genotype to reported sex to catch sample mix-ups, and a Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium filter in controls flags SNPs whose genotype proportions deviate from expectation, usually indicating a genotyping artifact rather than real biology.

questions.prompt: UK Biobank, a major driver of GWAS statistical power, genotyped approximately how many participants?

options.text: 50 million

explanations.a: This is far too small to be the scale that made UK Biobank a landmark GWAS resource.
explanations.b: Still far smaller than UK Biobank's actual cohort size.
explanations.c: Correct — UK Biobank recruited and genotyped roughly 500,000 participants (recruitment 2006-2010), one of the largest genotyped cohorts used for GWAS.
explanations.d: No single biobank has reached this scale; this overstates UK Biobank's size by roughly a hundredfold.

questions.prompt: Which category of genetic variation is a well-known blind spot for standard array-plus-imputation GWAS design?

options.text: Common SNPs with minor allele frequency above 5%
Rare variants, indels, and structural variation
SNPs located on autosomes
Variants within well-characterized LD blocks

explanations.a: Common SNPs are exactly what arrays and LD-based imputation are designed to capture well.
explanations.b: Correct — rare variants (below roughly 0.1-1% frequency), insertions/deletions, and structural variants are poorly tagged by common-SNP arrays and LD-based imputation, leaving them largely undetected.
explanations.c: Autosomal location is not itself a limiting factor; both autosomal and sex-chromosome common SNPs are well covered by standard arrays.
explanations.d: Variants inside well-characterized LD blocks are precisely the ones imputation handles well, since the reference panel captures that block structure.

lessons.label: Controlling Confounding: Population Structure, Relatedness, and Batch

sections.heading: When ancestry, not biology, drives the association
sections.body: If cases and controls differ in ancestry mix, any allele whose frequency happens to differ between those ancestral groups will look associated with disease, whether or not it has any biological connection to it. Hamer and Sirota's 2000 commentary offered the illustrative parable now known as the 'chopstick gene': in a hypothetical sample pooling Asian and European ancestry groups that differ both in chopstick-use rates and in unrelated allele frequencies, a study could find a statistically significant 'chopstick gene,' purely because ancestry confounds both variables at once. Real GWAS carry this same risk whenever recruitment, geography, or study site correlates with both ancestry and disease prevalence — population stratification was one of the first problems the field had to solve before GWAS results could be trusted.

sections.heading: The statistical toolkit for structure and relatedness
sections.body: Price and colleagues' 2006 EIGENSTRAT method established the standard fix: run principal component analysis (PCA) on genome-wide genotypes and include the top principal components as covariates in the association model, which absorbs the ancestry axes along which allele frequencies vary. A companion diagnostic, the genomic control inflation factor (lambda_GC), compares the observed median test statistic across the genome to what is expected under no association; a lambda meaningfully above 1.0 signals residual stratification (or, at very large sample sizes, real polygenic signal) that has not been fully corrected. When samples include related individuals or case-control ratios are imbalanced, linear/logistic mixed models such as BOLT-LMM, SAIGE, and REGENIE go further, modeling a genetic relatedness matrix directly so cryptic relatedness and imbalance no longer bias results the way naive regression would.

sections.heading: Family-based designs and batch effects
sections.body: Spielman and colleagues' 1993 transmission disequilibrium test (TDT) takes a structurally different approach: rather than comparing unrelated cases to unrelated controls, it asks whether heterozygous parents transmit a given allele to their affected child more often than the 50% expected by chance. Because the comparison happens entirely within families, ancestry differences between families cannot create a spurious result — the TDT is immune to population stratification by design, at the cost of needing parent-offspring trios rather than simple case-control samples. A separate, purely technical confound is batch effect: if cases and controls were genotyped on different array versions, at different sites, or at different times, systematic differences in signal intensity or calling can masquerade as case-control differences at specific SNPs, which is why processing cases and controls together (or explicitly modeling batch as a covariate) is a standard design requirement, not an afterthought.

lessons.workedExample: A study of a metabolic disease recruits cases mostly from a clinic in one region and controls mostly from a biobank recruited nationally, with the case cohort skewing toward one ancestry group by chance of geography. Without correction, dozens of SNPs known to differ in frequency across ancestry groups but with no plausible link to the disease reach genome-wide significance, and the genomic control lambda comes out at 1.15 — a red flag for uncorrected structure. Adding the first ten principal components from genome-wide genotypes as covariates and re-running the analysis drops lambda back to about 1.02, and the spurious ancestry-driven hits disappear, leaving only the handful of associations that replicate in an independent, ancestry-matched cohort.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how did you control for population structure?' is testing whether a student understands that an association can be entirely real statistically and entirely non-biological — the chopstick-gene problem. The strong answer names a specific control (ancestry principal components, a mixed model, or a family-based TDT design) and explains what it corrects for, rather than a generic 'we controlled for confounders.'

questions.prompt: The 'chopstick gene' parable illustrates which specific confounding problem in genetic association studies?

options.text: Population stratification, where ancestry differences between cases and controls create spurious associations at unrelated SNPs
Genotyping batch effects between array versions
The winner's curse in underpowered studies
Linkage disequilibrium decay with physical distance

explanations.a: Correct — the parable shows how a trait (chopstick use) correlated with ancestry, combined with ancestry-correlated but biologically unrelated allele frequencies, produces a spurious 'gene' association driven entirely by population stratification.
explanations.b: Batch effects are a distinct, purely technical confound from mismatched genotyping processing, not what this parable illustrates.
explanations.c: The winner's curse concerns inflated effect-size estimates from low-power studies, unrelated to ancestry confounding.
explanations.d: LD decay describes how correlation between loci weakens with distance; the parable is about ancestry confounding, not LD structure.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to what it does in a GWAS.

right.text: Absorbs ancestry axes of allele-frequency variation as regression covariates
Diagnostic comparing observed vs. expected test-statistic inflation across the genome
Models a genetic relatedness matrix to handle cryptic relatedness and case-control imbalance
Tests within-family allele transmission from heterozygous parents to affected offspring, immune to stratification by design

questions.explanation: PCA-derived ancestry covariates absorb structure directly in the regression; lambda_GC is a diagnostic for residual inflation; mixed models explicitly account for relatedness and imbalance; and the family-based TDT sidesteps stratification entirely by comparing transmitted vs. untransmitted alleles within families.

questions.prompt: Why is the transmission disequilibrium test (TDT) described as immune to population stratification 'by design'?

options.text: Because it uses a much larger sample size than case-control studies
Because it compares transmitted versus untransmitted alleles within the same family, so ancestry differences between families cannot create a spurious signal
Because it does not require any genotyping
Because it can only be applied to diseases with no genetic component

explanations.a: TDT sample sizes are not inherently larger than case-control studies; its immunity to stratification comes from its within-family design, not sample size.
explanations.b: Correct — because the comparison is always within a family (transmitted vs. untransmitted parental alleles), between-family ancestry differences have no opportunity to bias the result.
explanations.c: TDT still requires genotyping parents and affected offspring; the design difference is the comparison structure, not the absence of genotyping.
explanations.d: TDT is used specifically to study genetic transmission in diseases believed to have a genetic component; this option misdescribes its purpose entirely.

questions.prompt: A study finds that cases were genotyped in 2019 on one array version at Site A, while controls were genotyped in 2015 on a different array version at Site B. What kind of confound does this create?

options.text: A batch effect, where systematic technical differences between processing runs can masquerade as case-control differences at specific SNPs
Population stratification
The winner's curse
No confound, since genotype calls are deterministic regardless of array or timing

explanations.a: Correct — differences in array version, site, and processing time between the case and control groups are a classic batch effect, which can produce spurious SNP-level differences unrelated to disease biology.
explanations.b: Population stratification specifically concerns ancestry composition differences, not technical processing differences; this scenario as described is a technical, not ancestral, confound.
explanations.c: The winner's curse describes effect-size inflation from low power in already-significant findings, not a source of spurious association from processing differences.
explanations.d: Genotyping is not perfectly deterministic across array platforms, sites, and time; systematic technical variation is exactly why batch effects are a real, well-documented confound.

lessons.label: Rare-Variant and Gene-Burden Testing

sections.heading: Why single-variant tests run out of power
sections.body: A GWAS-style test on one SNP at a time depends on having enough carriers of the minor allele in both cases and controls to detect a frequency difference. Below roughly 0.1% allele frequency, almost no study, even a biobank-scale one, has enough carriers of any single rare variant to reach significance — a variant seen in three cases and one control tells you almost nothing statistically, no matter how large the surrounding cohort is. Rare variants are also individually far more numerous and heterogeneous than common ones; a single disease gene can harbor dozens of distinct rare loss-of-function variants across a population, each private to a handful of families, so testing each one separately wastes nearly all the statistical signal.

sections.heading: Aggregating variants inside a gene instead of testing them one at a time
sections.body: Gene-based burden tests solve this by collapsing all qualifying rare variants within a gene into a single count per person and testing whether that count differs between cases and controls — the approach Li and Leal formalized in 2008 as the combined multivariate and collapsing (CMC) method. A simple burden test assumes every qualifying variant pushes risk in the same direction, which fails when a gene contains both risk-increasing and protective rare variants that would cancel out in a summed count. Wu and colleagues' 2011 sequence kernel association test (SKAT) fixes this by allowing variants within a gene to have effects of different magnitude and direction, testing for excess variance in outcome explained by the gene's variants rather than a directional sum; Lee and colleagues' 2012 SKAT-O combines both approaches, adaptively weighting toward whichever performs better for a given gene's variant profile.

sections.heading: Filtering choices, significance thresholds, and a case study in reverse genetics
sections.body: The result of a burden test depends heavily on which variants are allowed into the collapsed count: loss-of-function-only filtering (nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice-disrupting variants) gives the cleanest biological interpretation but the fewest qualifying variants; adding predicted-deleterious missense variants (using scores like CADD, where a cutoff around 20 marks the top ~1% most damaging predicted variants, or REVEL for missense pathogenicity specifically) expands the count at the cost of noisier, less certain classification. Because a typical exome contains roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, exome-wide significance requires a Bonferroni-style threshold near p < 2.5 x 10^-6 (0.05 divided by 20,000), tighter than a single-test 0.05 but far looser than genome-wide GWAS thresholds. The signature success of this approach is PCSK9: Cohen and colleagues' 2005-2006 studies in the Dallas Heart Study cohort found that Black participants carrying rare PCSK9 nonsense mutations had roughly 28% lower LDL cholesterol and about an 88% reduction in coronary heart disease risk, while white participants carrying the more common PCSK9 missense variant R46L showed a smaller but still substantial effect (about 15% lower LDL, roughly 47% reduced coronary heart disease risk) — a finding from rare-variant analysis that directly motivated development of PCSK9-inhibitor drugs.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher studies a candidate gene for early-onset kidney disease across 4,000 exomes. No single rare variant in the gene appears in more than 2 people, so no single-variant test has any power. Collapsing all loss-of-function variants in the gene into a per-person carrier count and running a burden test finds 29 of 2,000 cases are carriers versus 2 of 2,000 controls, a strongly significant excess (p ~ 4.6 x 10^-7, clearing the 2.5 x 10^-6 exome-wide threshold).
