Re-running with a looser filter that also includes predicted-deleterious missense variants roughly quadruples the carrier count among cases (to 125) but pulls in far more noise among controls, pushing their carrier count up nearly forty-fold (to 75) — the added missense variants are so much less specific to disease that they weaken the p-value to roughly 4 x 10^-4, illustrating why the variant-filtering choice itself is a real analytic decision, not a formality.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about rare-variant analysis is checking whether a student understands that aggregation is a necessity, not a stylistic choice — single-variant tests are structurally powerless below about 0.1% frequency. The strong answer names a specific aggregation method (burden versus SKAT) and can explain the tradeoff in variant-filtering strictness (fewer, cleaner loss-of-function variants versus more, noisier predicted-deleterious ones), ideally grounding the stakes with the PCSK9 story, where a rare-variant finding became an actual drug target.

questions.prompt: Why do single-variant association tests have essentially no statistical power for variants below about 0.1% allele frequency?

options.text: Because rare variants cannot be sequenced accurately
Because too few carriers exist in even large cohorts to detect a frequency difference between cases and controls for any one variant
Because rare variants are never causal
Because imputation panels exclude all rare variants by policy

explanations.a: Modern sequencing can call rare variants accurately; the limitation is statistical, not technical.
explanations.b: Correct — with so few carriers of any single rare variant, even a large cohort cannot reliably distinguish a true frequency difference from chance at the single-variant level.
explanations.c: Rare variants are frequently causal (indeed often more penetrant than common variants); the issue is detection power, not causality.
explanations.d: Imputation quality for very rare variants is genuinely poor, but this is a separate technical limitation, not the core power argument for burden testing.

questions.prompt: How does SKAT differ from a simple burden/collapsing test?

options.text: SKAT can only be applied to common variants
SKAT allows variants within a gene to have effects of different magnitude and direction, while a simple burden test assumes all qualifying variants push risk the same way
SKAT requires no variant filtering at all
SKAT and burden tests are mathematically identical

explanations.a: SKAT was specifically developed for rare-variant gene-based testing, not common variants.
explanations.b: Correct — SKAT tests for excess variance in outcome explained by a gene's variants regardless of effect direction, which retains power when a gene has a mix of risk-increasing and protective variants that a directional sum would cancel out.
explanations.c: SKAT still requires a defined set of qualifying variants (e.g., by function or predicted deleteriousness); it does not skip filtering.
explanations.d: They test different statistical hypotheses; SKAT-O was developed specifically to combine both because neither dominates the other in all situations.

questions.prompt: In the PCSK9 case, what did Cohen and colleagues (2005-2006) find in Black participants of the Dallas Heart Study carrying rare PCSK9 nonsense mutations?

options.text: Markedly lower LDL cholesterol and roughly 88% reduced coronary heart disease risk
Markedly higher LDL cholesterol and increased coronary heart disease risk
No measurable difference in LDL cholesterol or coronary risk
Elevated blood pressure with no change in cholesterol

explanations.a: Correct — in the Dallas Heart Study cohort, Black participants carrying rare PCSK9 nonsense mutations had markedly lower LDL cholesterol and about 88% reduced coronary heart disease risk (white participants carrying the missense variant R46L showed a smaller but still substantial effect), a finding that directly motivated PCSK9-inhibitor drug development.
explanations.b: This reverses the actual finding; loss-of-function PCSK9 variants lower, not raise, LDL and coronary risk.
explanations.c: The effect was large and clearly measurable, which is precisely why it became a landmark rare-variant finding.
explanations.d: The finding concerned LDL cholesterol and coronary risk, not blood pressure.

questions.prompt: Given roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes tested, what is the approximate exome-wide significance threshold used to control for multiple testing in gene-based burden analysis?

explanations.a: This is the uncorrected single-test threshold and would produce massive false-positive rates across 20,000 gene tests.
explanations.b: This is the standard genome-wide significance threshold for single-SNP GWAS (correcting for roughly a million independent common variants), not the gene-based exome-wide threshold.
explanations.c: Correct — dividing 0.05 by roughly 20,000 genes gives an exome-wide Bonferroni threshold near 2.5 x 10^-6.
explanations.d: This threshold is far too lenient to correct for testing 20,000 genes.

lessons.label: Beyond Association: Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization

sections.heading: Genotype as nature's randomized trial
sections.body: Mendel's second law randomly assorts alleles at meiosis, independent of the lifestyle and environmental factors that plague observational epidemiology — so a genetic variant robustly associated with an exposure (say, a variant that raises LDL cholesterol) can be used as an instrumental variable to test whether that exposure causally affects an outcome (say, coronary disease), the logic behind Mendelian randomization (MR). Three assumptions have to hold for the instrument to be valid: relevance, the variant must be robustly associated with the exposure; independence, the variant must not be associated with confounders of the exposure-outcome relationship; and the exclusion restriction, the variant must affect the outcome only through the exposure, not through any other pathway. Most modern MR is two-sample MR, combining summary statistics from two separate GWAS — one for the exposure, one for the outcome — rather than requiring both measured in the same individuals.

sections.heading: Pleiotropy is the dominant threat, and how it is tested
sections.body: The exclusion-restriction assumption is the hardest to guarantee, because many genetic variants are pleiotropic — they influence more than one trait through independent biological pathways, which would let the instrument affect the outcome outside the exposure of interest, biasing the causal estimate. Several sensitivity analyses were built specifically to detect and correct this: Bowden and colleagues' 2015 MR-Egger regression allows the regression intercept to be non-zero, and a significant intercept flags directional pleiotropy across the instrument set; Bowden and colleagues' 2016 weighted-median estimator gives a consistent causal estimate even if up to half the instrument's genetic variants are invalid; and Verbanck and colleagues' 2018 MR-PRESSO detects individual outlier variants likely driven by pleiotropy and can re-estimate the causal effect after removing them. Consistency across these different methods, which make different assumptions about how pleiotropy behaves, is treated as evidence the causal estimate is not simply an artifact of one method's blind spot.

sections.heading: When MR overturns observational findings, and the gene-level analogue
sections.body: MR has directly contradicted strong observational correlations twice in cardiovascular disease: HDL cholesterol is strongly associated with lower coronary heart disease risk in cohort studies, but MR using variants like the endothelial lipase variant studied by Voight and colleagues (2012) found no reduction in coronary risk from genetically raised HDL, undermining HDL as a causal target. Similarly, MR studies of C-reactive protein (CRP) found CRP-raising variants carried no excess coronary risk despite CRP's strong observational correlation with heart disease, reclassifying CRP as a marker of inflammation rather than a cause of disease. By contrast, MR has repeatedly confirmed causality for LDL cholesterol, body mass index, and blood pressure on cardiovascular outcomes, consistent with clinical trial evidence (statins lowering LDL reduce events). The same instrumental logic applies at the level of a single gene through eQTL colocalization: rather than asking whether a trait-associated variant affects disease through an intermediate trait, colocalization analysis (formalized by Giambartolomei and colleagues in 2014) asks whether a GWAS signal and an expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) signal for a nearby gene share the same underlying causal variant, linking an anonymous association-scan hit to a specific candidate gene via shared genetic architecture.

lessons.workedExample: A cohort study finds that people with higher HDL cholesterol have substantially lower rates of coronary heart disease, prompting drug development targeting HDL-raising. A two-sample MR study instead uses genetic variants known to robustly raise HDL (satisfying relevance), checks that these variants are not correlated with known confounders like exercise or diet (supporting independence), and tests their association with coronary disease outcomes in an independent GWAS. The genetically predicted increase in HDL shows no corresponding drop in coronary risk, and MR-Egger's intercept is not significantly different from zero, arguing against a simple pleiotropy explanation for the null result. This mismatch between the observational correlation and the MR-derived causal estimate is exactly why several HDL-raising drugs that succeeded in raising HDL in clinical trials failed to reduce cardiovascular events — the MR result anticipated the trial failures.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing Mendelian randomization wants to see whether a student can name the actual failure mode being guarded against — pleiotropy violating the exclusion-restriction assumption — rather than reciting 'genes are randomized so it's like an RCT.' The strongest answers can point to a concrete case where MR overturned an observational finding (HDL or CRP) and name at least one sensitivity method (MR-Egger, weighted median, or MR-PRESSO) used to check whether the causal estimate survives when pleiotropy is allowed for.

questions.prompt: Match each Mendelian randomization instrumental-variable assumption to its meaning.

right.text: The variant is robustly associated with the exposure
The variant is not associated with confounders of the exposure-outcome relationship
The variant affects the outcome only through the exposure, not via any other pathway

questions.explanation: Relevance requires a strong variant-exposure association; independence requires the variant to be unrelated to confounders; exclusion restriction, the hardest to guarantee and the one pleiotropy threatens, requires the variant to affect the outcome solely through the exposure of interest.

questions.prompt: What is the dominant threat to Mendelian randomization's validity, and which assumption does it violate?

options.text: Small sample size, which violates the relevance assumption
Pleiotropy, where a variant affects the outcome through a pathway independent of the exposure, violating the exclusion restriction
Measurement error in the outcome, which violates independence
Population stratification, which violates relevance

explanations.a: Small sample size affects statistical power, not the validity of the causal assumptions themselves.
explanations.b: Correct — pleiotropy means the instrument influences the outcome through a route other than the exposure being studied, directly violating the exclusion restriction, which is why MR-Egger, weighted-median, and MR-PRESSO were developed specifically to detect and correct for it.
explanations.c: Outcome measurement error is a general study-quality concern, not the specific, dominant MR threat discussed here.
explanations.d: Population stratification is a confound relevant to GWAS generally, but the specific MR threat tied to the exclusion-restriction assumption is pleiotropy.

questions.prompt: What did Mendelian randomization studies find regarding HDL cholesterol and coronary heart disease risk, in contrast to observational cohort studies?

options.text: MR confirmed the same strong protective causal effect seen observationally
MR found no reduction in coronary risk from genetically raised HDL, despite the strong observational association
MR could not be applied to HDL at all
MR found HDL increases coronary risk

explanations.a: This is the opposite of what MR found; the causal estimate did not match the strong observational correlation.
explanations.b: Correct — despite HDL's strong inverse observational association with coronary disease, MR studies using HDL-raising variants (such as the endothelial lipase variant studied by Voight and colleagues, 2012) found no corresponding reduction in coronary risk, undermining HDL as a causal, druggable target.
explanations.c: MR was successfully applied to HDL and is one of the field's most cited examples of MR contradicting observational epidemiology.
explanations.d: MR found no significant effect in either direction on coronary risk from genetically raised HDL, not an increase in risk.

questions.prompt: eQTL colocalization analysis, the gene-level analogue of MR-style reasoning, tests whether:

options.text: A GWAS association signal and an eQTL signal for a nearby gene share the same underlying causal variant
Two unrelated diseases share any genetic variants at all
A gene's expression level is heritable
A drug target has been validated in a clinical trial

explanations.a: Correct — colocalization analysis (Giambartolomei and colleagues, 2014) tests whether a disease-association signal and a gene-expression (eQTL) signal at the same locus point to the same causal variant, linking an anonymous GWAS hit to a specific candidate gene.
explanations.b: Colocalization is about a single locus linking a trait signal to an expression signal, not a general cross-disease variant-sharing test.
explanations.c: Heritability of expression is a separate question (addressed by eQTL mapping itself), not what colocalization specifically tests.
explanations.d: Colocalization is a genetic-statistical analysis, not a clinical trial method; it can motivate a drug target hypothesis but does not itself validate one in trial.

lessons.label: Anatomy of a Manhattan Plot

sections.heading: Position on the x-axis, significance on the y-axis
sections.body: A Manhattan plot lays every tested SNP along its chromosome and physical position on the x-axis, and plots -log10 of its association p-value on the y-axis, so a stronger signal draws a taller point. Chromosomes alternate shading so the eye can find the skyline of "towers" rising out of the genomic background. The name comes from that skyline: a genome with a few sharp, isolated spikes against a flat baseline looks like the Manhattan skyline seen from the water. The format became the field's default visual after large early case-control studies, most notably the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium's 2007 study of seven common diseases, popularized it as the standard first figure in a GWAS paper — a single image a reader can scan for both the number and the strength of a study's discoveries before reading a word of text.

sections.heading: Where 5x10^-8 comes from
sections.body: The genome-wide significance line is not an arbitrary round number; it is a Bonferroni-style correction, 0.05 divided by roughly one million independent statistical tests, giving 5x10^-8. That million comes from estimates of the number of effectively independent common-variant blocks in the genome after accounting for linkage disequilibrium (LD) — Dudbridge and Gusnanto (2008) and Pe'er et al. (2008) both empirically derived numbers in that range from HapMap data, even though a modern imputed GWAS may test 5-10 million SNPs directly. The threshold does not scale up with the literal SNP count tested after imputation, because imputation adds millions of SNPs that are themselves correlated with already-tested neighbors through LD — they are not new independent hypotheses, just denser coverage of the same roughly one million independent chunks of genome.

sections.heading: Reading peak shape: skyscraper versus lone dot
sections.body: A real association peak is broad because LD drags many neighboring SNPs above the line together — a wide "skyscraper" of correlated, decaying significance around a core signal is the expected shape of true biology. A single significant dot with no elevated neighbors nearby is suspicious; it usually reflects a genotyping error, a poorly imputed variant (low imputation r-squared), or a batch artifact rather than a real biological association, since true causal signal should be shared across the SNPs in LD with it. It is also important not to equate tower height with biological importance: the tallest peak marks the best-powered signal — the product of allele frequency, effect size, and sample size — not necessarily the SNP with the largest true effect on the trait. A rare variant with a genuinely larger effect can sit far lower on the plot simply because the study lacked enough carriers to estimate its effect precisely, while a common, modest-effect variant reaches enormous statistical confidence purely from being measured in tens of thousands of people.

lessons.workedExample: A GWAS of 400,000 imputed SNPs across 60,000 participants produces a chr16 peak near FTO reaching -log10(p) = 25, spanning roughly 200 kb with dozens of SNPs above the 5x10^-8 line and a smooth decay in significance moving outward — classic LD-supported skyscraper. The same plot shows an isolated SNP on chr3 at -log10(p) = 9 with no neighboring SNP within 500 kb clearing even p < 1e-4. A careful reader checks that SNP's imputation quality score before trusting it; a low score (say, INFO < 0.3) explains the isolated spike without invoking new biology.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "why 5x10^-8 and not 0.05?" is testing whether a student understands multiple-testing correction as a real statistical necessity, not a rule memorized without reason — the strong answer names the roughly one-million-independent-test logic and explains why imputed SNP count does not move the goalposts. A judge who points at a single unsupported dot and asks "is this real?" is testing whether the student knows LD should produce a cluster of correlated significant SNPs around any genuine signal, and can name genotyping/imputation artifacts as the leading alternative explanation for a lone spike.

questions.prompt: The genome-wide significance threshold of 5x10^-8 is derived from approximately how many effectively independent tests?

options.text: About 1,000 independent tests
About 1 million independent tests
About 10 million independent tests, matching the number of imputed SNPs
Exactly the number of SNPs on the genotyping chip

explanations.a: A thousand independent tests would give a much less stringent threshold (0.05/1,000 = 5x10^-5), far looser than the standard used.
explanations.b: Correct — Dudbridge and Gusnanto (2008) and Pe'er et al. (2008) both estimated roughly one million effectively independent common-variant blocks in the genome (after accounting for LD), and 0.05 divided by that count gives approximately 5x10^-8.
explanations.c: Imputed SNP counts run into the millions, but those SNPs are correlated through LD, not independent — using the raw imputed count would over-correct.
explanations.d: Chip SNP counts (a few hundred thousand to a million probes) are a genotyping detail, not the basis for the correction, which is about independent genomic information, not probe count.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't the significance threshold get stricter as imputation adds millions more tested SNPs?

options.text: Imputed SNPs are excluded from Manhattan plots entirely
Imputed SNPs are correlated with already-tested neighbors via LD, so they add density, not new independent hypotheses
Imputation always reduces the total SNP count
The threshold is recalculated per study to match whatever number of SNPs was tested

explanations.a: Imputed SNPs are routinely plotted and are often where the strongest signals appear.
explanations.b: Correct — imputation fills in genotypes at SNPs that are statistically predicted from LD with genotyped SNPs, so they are not independent tests; the effective number of independent genomic units stays near one million regardless of how many SNPs are imputed.
explanations.c: Imputation increases, not decreases, the number of SNPs tested, often from a few hundred thousand genotyped SNPs to several million.
explanations.d: The 5x10^-8 convention is fixed and used across studies precisely because it reflects independent genomic units, not the literal per-study SNP count.

questions.prompt: A single SNP clears genome-wide significance with no neighboring SNPs elevated nearby. What should a careful reader suspect first?

options.text: A newly evolved allele with no LD partners anywhere in the genome
A genotyping or imputation artifact, such as low imputation quality
That this is definitely the strongest true effect in the study
A sign that the study is underpowered

explanations.a: LD partners exist for essentially every common variant in a population; a total absence of correlated neighbors is not a plausible biological explanation.
explanations.b: Correct — a true association should be echoed by nearby SNPs in LD; an isolated significant dot with no supporting shoulder is the classic signature of a genotyping error or poor imputation quality at that single site.
explanations.c: Peak height reflects statistical power (frequency, effect size, sample size), not truth by itself, and an isolated dot is actually less trustworthy than a supported peak.
explanations.d: An artifact can appear in a well-powered study; underpowering would tend to produce weaker signals everywhere, not one suspiciously isolated significant hit.

questions.prompt: Peak A is very tall (-log10 p = 40) but narrow; Peak B is moderately tall (-log10 p = 12) but spans a broad region with many correlated SNPs above the line. What can you conclude?

options.text: Peak A definitely has the larger true effect on the trait
Peak A is best-powered (frequency x effect size x sample size), which does not necessarily mean it has the largest effect size
Peak B must be an artifact because it is shorter
Both peaks are equally likely to be artifacts

explanations.a: Height reflects statistical power, which is a combination of allele frequency, effect size, and sample size — a common variant with a modest effect can out-power a rare variant with a larger effect.
explanations.b: Correct — tallest does not mean largest effect; it means the p-value is smallest, which can be driven by a common allele frequency and large sample size rather than a large effect.
explanations.c: A broad, LD-supported region is actually the expected shape of a real signal, not evidence of an artifact.
explanations.d: Peak B's broad LD support makes it look more like real biology than an isolated artifact; the two peaks are not equally suspicious.

lessons.label: QQ Plots, Genomic Inflation, and Polygenicity

sections.heading: Observed versus expected: reading the diagonal
sections.body: A quantile-quantile (QQ) plot for a GWAS sorts every SNP's -log10 p-value and plots it against the -log10 p-value expected under the null hypothesis of no association, if p-values were uniformly distributed. If nothing in the genome were associated with the trait, every point would sit on the y=x diagonal. A well-behaved GWAS hugs that diagonal closely across the bulk of the distribution and only lifts off late, in the extreme tail — the handful of SNPs with real association. That late lift-off, against an otherwise flat diagonal, is the signature of true, sparse (or moderately polygenic) signal sitting on top of a clean null.

sections.heading: Inflation across the whole curve: confounding, not signal
sections.body: If the observed points drift above the diagonal early, across low and moderate p-values rather than only in the extreme tail, that is genomic inflation, and it usually indicates a technical or design problem rather than biology: population stratification (ancestry differences between cases and controls that correlate with allele frequency genome-wide), cryptic relatedness (unaccounted-for family structure inflating shared genotype-phenotype correlations), or batch effects (genotyping plate or array differences correlated with case-control status). Devlin and Roeder (1999) introduced genomic control, using the inflation factor lambda_GC — the ratio of the observed median chi-square statistic to the expected median under the null — as a genome-wide summary; lambda_GC near 1.0 is expected under no confounding, and values well above 1.0 flag stratification or relatedness. Their original proposal even suggested dividing every SNP's chi-square statistic by lambda_GC as a blunt genome-wide correction, a practice later studies moved away from once it became clear that a single genome-wide factor could over-correct real polygenic signal along with true confounding.

sections.heading: The lambda_GC trap and LD score regression's fix
sections.body: Lambda_GC is not a clean confounding detector on its own, because it legitimately rises with sample size for genuinely polygenic traits: as N grows, even true small effects distributed across thousands of variants push the whole chi-square distribution upward, inflating lambda_GC without any confounding at all. This ambiguity — is the inflation stratification or is it real polygenicity? — motivated Bulik-Sullivan et al. (2015) to develop LD score regression (LDSC). LDSC regresses each SNP's chi-square statistic on its LD score (how much genetic variation it tags through linkage disequilibrium with neighbors); true polygenic signal should be stronger for SNPs that tag more variation, producing a regression slope, while confounding inflates all SNPs roughly uniformly regardless of LD score, showing up in the regression intercept. An intercept near 1.0 with an elevated slope indicates real polygenicity; an elevated intercept indicates stratification or other confounding. This decomposition is what let large biobank-scale studies — with lambda_GC values of 1.3 or higher purely from sample size and polygenicity — continue reporting results with confidence, since LDSC could confirm the intercept stayed near 1.0 even as the slope, and lambda_GC, climbed with N.

lessons.workedExample: Study X, N=20,000, pools participants from three loosely matched ancestry groups without adjusting for ancestry principal components: lambda_GC = 1.08 and the QQ plot shows the observed line drifting above the diagonal starting at moderate p-values (around p = 0.01) — a stratification signature. Study Y, N=250,000, a single well-matched ancestry cohort, gets lambda_GC = 1.15, higher than Study X, but its QQ plot hugs the diagonal until deep in the tail. Running LDSC on both: Study X's intercept is 1.06 (confounding present); Study Y's intercept is 1.01 with a strong positive slope (the higher lambda_GC is polygenicity, not confounding) — lambda_GC alone would have wrongly flagged Study Y as more confounded.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes lambda_GC specifically because it is a classic trap: a naive reader treats any lambda_GC above 1.0 as proof of a flawed study, when for a well-powered, truly polygenic trait, rising lambda_GC with sample size is expected and not a defect. A judge wants to hear that the student knows lambda_GC alone cannot separate confounding from polygenicity, and can name LD score regression's intercept-versus-slope decomposition as the tool that actually resolves the ambiguity — that distinction is the difference between reading a diagnostic plot and just pattern-matching a number.

questions.prompt: In a well-behaved GWAS QQ plot with real, sparse signal, where does the observed line lift off the diagonal?

options.text: Immediately at the lowest p-values, across the entire distribution
Only late, in the extreme tail of most significant SNPs
It never lifts off, even for a true signal
Randomly, with no relationship to significance

explanations.a: Lift-off across the entire distribution, not just the tail, is the signature of genome-wide inflation from confounding, not real sparse signal.
explanations.b: Correct — true association signal is concentrated in a small number of genuinely associated SNPs, so the observed line hugs the diagonal until only the most extreme, most significant SNPs pull away from it.
explanations.c: A genuine association study should show tail lift-off; total adherence to the diagonal everywhere would indicate no detected signal at all.
explanations.d: The pattern is systematic, not random — it directly reflects where true association concentrates in the p-value distribution.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a typical cause of genome-wide inflation (early, whole-curve lift-off in a QQ plot)?

options.text: Population stratification between cases and controls
Cryptic relatedness among participants
Genotyping batch effects correlated with case-control status
A single SNP with an unusually large true effect on the trait

explanations.a: Stratification is a canonical cause of genome-wide inflation, since ancestry differences correlate with allele frequency across the whole genome.
explanations.b: Unaccounted-for relatedness inflates shared genotype-phenotype correlations broadly, another canonical cause.
explanations.c: Batch effects correlated with case status can create spurious genome-wide association signal, another canonical cause.
explanations.d: Correct — a single large true effect would show up as a late tail lift-off for that one signal, not as inflation smeared across the entire distribution.

questions.prompt: Why can a rising lambda_GC with increasing sample size be misleading if interpreted as pure confounding?

options.text: Lambda_GC always decreases with sample size, so a rise is impossible
For truly polygenic traits, larger sample sizes legitimately push lambda_GC above 1.0 even with no confounding present
Lambda_GC is only defined for case-control studies, never quantitative traits
Lambda_GC cannot be computed for sample sizes above 100,000

explanations.a: Lambda_GC characteristically rises with sample size for polygenic traits, not decreases.
explanations.b: Correct — as sample size grows, even true small effects spread across many variants inflate the overall chi-square distribution, raising lambda_GC without any stratification or batch confounding.
explanations.c: Lambda_GC applies to any GWAS test statistic, quantitative or case-control.
explanations.d: There is no such sample-size ceiling; lambda_GC is routinely reported in studies with hundreds of thousands of participants.

questions.prompt: Match each LD score regression output to what it estimates.

right.text: Confounding (stratification, relatedness, batch effects) — should be near 1.0 if absent
Genuine polygenic signal, tracking how chi-square rises with each SNP's LD score

questions.explanation: Bulik-Sullivan et al. (2015) showed that regressing chi-square statistics on LD score separates the two sources of inflation: confounding inflates all SNPs roughly uniformly regardless of how much variation they tag, which shows up as an elevated intercept, while true polygenic signal is stronger for high-LD-score SNPs (which tag more of the genome's causal variants), which shows up as a positive slope.

lessons.label: Effect Size, Odds Ratios, and Variance Explained

sections.heading: Small effects are the norm, not the exception
sections.body: Most common-variant hits in a complex-disease GWAS carry odds ratios (OR) between about 1.05 and 1.20 per copy of the risk allele — a 5-20% increase in odds, not the doubling or tripling intuition might expect from a headline-making "gene for" a disease. TCF7L2's rs7903146, one of the strongest and most reproducible type 2 diabetes hits ever found, carries an OR near 1.4 per T allele, and it is considered unusually large for a common variant — most confirmed hits sit well below it. A p-value of 1e-40 measures how confidently the study can reject "no association," which is a function of sample size and allele frequency as much as effect size; it says nothing directly about how much of the trait's variance that SNP explains, and a genome-wide-significant hit routinely accounts for well under 1% of total variance in liability to disease.

sections.heading: Why big effects are rare: the frequency-effect trade-off
sections.body: Alleles with large effects on a disease-relevant trait tend to be rare in the population, because natural selection actively removes them — a purifying-selection force sometimes called negative selection. An allele that substantially raises disease risk or reduces reproductive fitness cannot drift up to high frequency without selection pushing back, so by the time a variant is common enough for a GWAS to detect reliably (typically minor allele frequency above 1-5%), it has almost by definition survived selection, which means its effect on fitness-relevant traits is usually small. This is the empirical basis of the "common disease, common variant" hypothesis that motivated GWAS design, in tension with the observation that some of the largest true effects on disease risk come from rare variants that only large-scale rare-variant or exome studies can find.

sections.heading: Reading the results table
sections.body: A GWAS results row typically reports: the lead SNP (rsID and chromosomal position), the effect allele and its frequency (EAF) in the study population, an effect size — either beta (for a quantitative trait, under an additive per-allele model) or an odds ratio (for case-control), its standard error, and the p-value. The additive per-allele model codes genotype as 0, 1, or 2 copies of the effect allele and assumes each copy adds the same increment to risk or trait value (log-additive on the OR scale) — simpler and much more common in practice than a genotypic model that estimates a separate effect for each of the three genotype classes. The effect allele must always be stated because beta and OR are directional: report the same association with the other allele as the "effect allele" and beta flips sign, while OR flips to its reciprocal (1/OR) — a table without a stated effect allele is unreadable, and misreading which allele an OR refers to is a classic reporting error worth catching.

lessons.workedExample: A results table lists rs7903146, effect allele T, EAF = 0.30, OR = 1.40, SE(log OR) = 0.02, p = 3e-120 for type 2 diabetes at the TCF7L2 locus. Despite the extraordinarily small p-value, converting this OR to the liability scale using a threshold model, given the trait's population prevalence and the allele's 30% frequency, yields a variance explained on the order of a few tenths of one percent of total liability — because variance explained scales with both effect size and 2p(1-p) (a term maximized at 50% frequency), and OR = 1.40 is a modest per-allele shift compared to the many other genetic and environmental contributors to diabetes risk. A student who reports "p = 3e-120, so this gene explains diabetes" has confused significance with magnitude.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge pushes on this distinction — tiny p-value versus tiny variance explained — because it is the single most common misinterpretation in a student GWAS project: treating statistical significance as a proxy for biological or clinical importance. The strong answer separates the two explicitly, names that p-value tracks confidence (driven by sample size and frequency) while variance explained tracks magnitude, and can explain why: large effects are selected against and stay rare, so the common variants a GWAS is well-powered to find are, almost by construction, small-effect ones.

questions.prompt: A typical common-variant GWAS hit for a complex disease has an odds ratio in roughly what range?

options.text: 1.05 to 1.20 per allele
2.0 to 5.0 per allele
10 to 20 per allele
Exactly 1.00, since GWAS only detects non-effects

explanations.a: Correct — most confirmed common-variant hits for complex disease fall in the OR 1.05-1.20 range; even a notably strong hit like TCF7L2 at OR ~1.4 is considered an outlier on the large end.
explanations.b: Effects of this size are rare for common variants and are more typical of highly penetrant rare-variant or Mendelian findings.
explanations.c: This magnitude would essentially be a Mendelian-disease-level effect, not what genome-wide-significant common-variant GWAS hits typically show.
explanations.d: By definition a genome-wide-significant hit has OR meaningfully different from 1.00; OR = 1.00 would mean no association at all.

questions.prompt: Why can a SNP with p = 1e-40 still explain well under 1% of a trait's variance?

options.text: P-values and variance explained measure the same thing, so this cannot happen
P-value reflects confidence against the null (driven by sample size and allele frequency), while variance explained reflects the magnitude of the effect — they are different quantities
It can only happen if the study made a calculation error
Small p-values always imply small effects by mathematical necessity

explanations.a: They are related but distinct: a very large sample size can make even a tiny true effect statistically overwhelming, without that effect explaining much of the trait's total variance.
explanations.b: Correct — p-value is a statement about how confidently you can reject no-association given the data (heavily influenced by N), while variance explained is a statement about effect magnitude; a large N can drive p toward zero for a genuinely small effect.
explanations.c: This pattern is expected and normal for common-variant GWAS hits, not an error.
explanations.d: There is no such necessity; in fact for well-powered studies, small true effects routinely produce extremely small p-values.

questions.prompt: Why do large-effect alleles tend to be rare in the population?

options.text: Large effects always arise from recent mutations that have not had time to spread
Natural selection removes alleles with substantial negative effects on fitness-relevant traits, keeping them rare
Large-effect alleles are physically larger and harder to inherit
GWAS genotyping arrays are biased against detecting large-effect alleles

explanations.a: Some large-effect alleles are old but kept rare by ongoing selection, not merely recent — age alone does not explain the frequency-effect relationship.
explanations.b: Correct — purifying selection pushes back against alleles that substantially raise disease risk or reduce fitness, so alleles with large effects rarely reach high population frequency; common variants have, in effect, survived selection and so tend to carry smaller effects.
explanations.c: Allele size (in base pairs) has no bearing on inheritance mechanics or effect size in this context.
explanations.d: Genotyping arrays are typically designed to include common variants; the scarcity of large-effect common hits is a population-genetic phenomenon, not an array-design artifact.

questions.prompt: A results table reports beta = -0.15 for SNP rs12345 with effect allele G. If the table instead reported the effect allele as A (the other allele), what would beta become?

options.text: -0.15, unchanged
+0.15, the sign flips
0.15 squared
It cannot be determined without new data

explanations.a: Beta is directional relative to the stated effect allele; switching which allele is counted flips the sign of the association.
explanations.b: Correct — beta (and OR) is defined per copy of the stated effect allele; flipping the effect allele to the complementary allele flips the sign of a beta (or inverts an OR to 1/OR), without requiring any new data.
explanations.c: Squaring is not the relevant transformation; flipping the effect allele produces the negative (or reciprocal, for OR) of the original value.
explanations.d: This is fully determined by the algebra of switching the reference allele — no new data collection is needed.

lessons.label: From Association Peak to Causal Gene

sections.heading: The lead SNP is usually a proxy, not a cause
sections.body: Because linkage disequilibrium correlates a SNP's genotype with dozens of physically nearby SNPs, the statistically strongest SNP in a peak — the "lead SNP" — is very often just the one that happened to be genotyped or imputed most precisely, not the one doing anything biologically. Statistical fine-mapping methods (such as FINEMAP or SuSiE) use the LD structure and effect-size pattern across a locus to shrink a broad peak down to a 95% credible set: the smallest set of variants that, together, has a 95% chance of containing the true causal variant. A credible set can still contain dozens of candidates when LD in the region is strong, meaning fine-mapping narrows the search but rarely finishes it on statistics alone.

sections.heading: The nearest-gene fallacy and the FTO cautionary tale
sections.body: The most common shortcut error is assuming the causal gene is whichever gene physically contains or sits nearest the lead SNP — the "nearest-gene" assumption. The canonical counter-example is the FTO locus: SNPs in FTO's introns (including rs9939609 and rs1421085) were among the earliest and most robust GWAS hits for obesity and BMI, and for years were described as "the FTO obesity gene." Smemo et al. (2014, Nature) showed the region instead makes long-range chromatin contact with the distant genes IRX3 and IRX5, and Claussnitzer et al. (2015, NEJM) traced the mechanism further: the risk variant rs1421085 disrupts a binding site for the repressor ARID5B, derepressing IRX3 and IRX5 and shifting adipocyte precursor cells away from energy-burning "beige fat" toward energy-storing white fat. The intronic location inside FTO was a red herring; FTO itself is not the functional gene at that locus.

sections.heading: Regulatory evidence: eQTLs, chromatin, and functional proof
sections.body: Because roughly 90% of GWAS hits (an estimate traced to Hindorff et al., 2009) fall in non-coding, intronic, or intergenic DNA rather than in protein-coding exons, connecting a peak to a gene almost always means gathering regulatory evidence rather than reading a changed amino acid. Expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) and splicing QTL (sQTL) colocalization — testing, with methods like coloc (Giambartolomei et al., 2014), whether the GWAS signal and a gene-expression signal in a relevant tissue (often drawn from the GTEx resource) share the same underlying causal variant — is the standard first pass. Chromatin conformation data (Hi-C) showing physical DNA looping, and enhancer annotations from projects like ENCODE or the Roadmap Epigenomics Project, add supporting evidence. None of this is proof on its own; the real burden of proof is functional follow-up — editing the candidate variant (often with CRISPR) in a disease-relevant cell type and showing the expected downstream change, as Claussnitzer's team did in human adipocyte precursors.

lessons.workedExample: At the FTO obesity locus, fine-mapping narrows dozens of intronic FTO SNPs in tight LD to a 95% credible set of roughly 89 candidates, all statistically near-indistinguishable by association strength alone. eQTL colocalization in adipose tissue flags IRX3 and IRX5 expression, not FTO expression, as correlated with the same signal. Chromatin contact data shows the FTO intronic region physically loops to the IRX3 promoter hundreds of kilobases away. Finally, CRISPR editing of the ARID5B motif at rs1421085 in human preadipocytes (Claussnitzer et al., 2015) directly changes IRX3/IRX5 expression and thermogenic capacity — the step that converts a statistical and regulatory hypothesis into a causal claim.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks "what is the causal gene?" specifically to catch the nearest-gene fallacy, the single most common shortcut in student GWAS projects — naming FTO as "the obesity gene" is the textbook wrong answer. A judge wants to hear the actual evidence chain: fine-mapping to a credible set, eQTL/sQTL colocalization in a relevant tissue, chromatin contact evidence, and ideally functional validation in a relevant cell type — and an acknowledgment that, since ~90% of hits are non-coding, this regulatory-evidence chain is the norm, not an exotic exception.

questions.prompt: Why is the lead SNP in a GWAS peak usually not assumed to be the causal variant itself?

options.text: Lead SNPs are always excluded from further study by convention
Linkage disequilibrium correlates it with many nearby SNPs, so it may just be the one most precisely genotyped or imputed rather than the functional one
Lead SNPs are chosen at random from the peak
The lead SNP is always located outside the gene entirely

explanations.a: Lead SNPs are actively studied further, including fine-mapping and functional follow-up, not excluded.
explanations.b: Correct — LD means many SNPs in a region carry nearly the same statistical signal, so the SNP that happens to show the strongest association is often simply well-measured rather than functionally special.
explanations.c: The lead SNP is the one with the strongest statistical association, not a random pick.
explanations.d: Lead SNPs can fall inside or outside genes; location alone does not determine lead-SNP status.

questions.prompt: At the FTO locus, what did later mechanistic work identify as the functionally relevant gene(s), rather than FTO itself?

options.text: IRX3 and IRX5
TCF7L2
ARID5B, acting as the target gene rather than a regulatory protein
No other gene — FTO itself was confirmed as fully causal

explanations.a: Correct — Smemo et al. (2014) and Claussnitzer et al. (2015) showed the obesity-associated FTO intronic variants act through long-range chromatin contacts on the distant genes IRX3 and IRX5, not on FTO.
explanations.b: TCF7L2 is a separate, unrelated locus associated with type 2 diabetes, not part of the FTO story.
explanations.c: ARID5B is the repressor protein whose binding site is disrupted by the risk variant — it is a regulatory factor in the mechanism, not the downstream target gene.
explanations.d: FTO itself was the nearest-gene assumption that the mechanistic work overturned; it is not the functionally implicated gene.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of GWAS hits fall in non-coding (intronic or intergenic) DNA rather than protein-coding exons?

options.text: About 10%
About 50%
About 90%
Essentially 0%; almost all hits change an amino acid

explanations.a: This underestimates the non-coding fraction substantially; coding hits are the small minority, not the near-totality implied here.
explanations.b: This is well below the actual figure; non-coding hits dominate far more than an even split.
explanations.c: Correct — Hindorff et al. (2009) traced roughly 90% of GWAS hits to intronic or intergenic regions, which is exactly why regulatory evidence (eQTLs, chromatin contact, enhancer annotation) rather than amino-acid change dominates the search for causal mechanism.
explanations.d: A small but real minority of GWAS hits are coding variants; the claim that essentially none are is incorrect.

questions.prompt: Order the typical steps in moving from a raw GWAS association peak to a functionally validated causal gene.

items.text: Identify the lead SNP and the broad LD-supported association peak
Statistical fine-mapping to a 95% credible set of candidate variants
eQTL/sQTL colocalization and chromatin-contact evidence pointing to candidate target gene(s)
Functional validation (e.g., CRISPR editing) in a disease-relevant cell type

questions.explanation: The pipeline moves from raw statistical discovery (the peak and its lead SNP) to statistical narrowing (fine-mapping to a credible set), to regulatory/genomic evidence connecting candidate variants to a likely target gene (eQTL colocalization, chromatin contact), and finally to direct functional proof in a relevant cell type — the step that actually establishes causality rather than correlation.

lessons.label: Replication, Winner's Curse, and Meta-Analysis

sections.heading: Why replication in an independent cohort is non-negotiable
sections.body: A GWAS hit clearing 5x10^-8 in a single discovery cohort is not treated as established until it clears a comparable threshold again in a separate, independent sample — the field's core norm since large early studies like the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium (2007) made independent replication standard practice. Replication protects against the many ways a single cohort can produce a false positive that survives even stringent multiple-testing correction: subtle population stratification the study's covariates did not fully capture, cryptic relatedness, batch effects tied to genotyping plates, or simple bad luck in a single sample. A hit that replicates in a cohort with different genotyping technology, different recruitment, and often a different population is far harder to explain away as a technical artifact.

sections.heading: Winner's curse: why discovery effects shrink
sections.body: Discovery-cohort effect-size estimates are systematically inflated, a phenomenon borrowed from auction theory — the term "winner's curse" originates with Capen, Clapp, and Campbell (1971), describing how the winning bid in an auction tends to overestimate an asset's true value. In GWAS, only SNPs whose observed effect estimate clears a strict significance threshold get reported as hits, and among SNPs near that threshold, the ones that clear it are disproportionately those where random sampling noise happened to push the estimate up, not down. Zöllner and Pritchard (2007) formalized this for GWAS effect-size estimation: the true effect is, on average, smaller than the discovery estimate, so an independent replication cohort — free of that same selection filter — should be expected to show a smaller, regressed-toward-the-mean effect size, not a discrepancy that signals the original finding was wrong.

sections.heading: Combining cohorts: meta-analysis and consortia
sections.body: Because any single cohort is underpowered for small common-variant effects, the field pools results across cohorts via meta-analysis rather than pooling raw genotypes. A fixed-effect meta-analysis assumes one true effect size shared across all cohorts and combines them by inverse-variance weighting; a random-effects model instead allows the true effect to vary between cohorts, adding an extra between-study variance term. The I-squared statistic (Higgins and Thompson, 2002) quantifies what fraction of total variation across cohorts reflects real heterogeneity rather than chance sampling noise; a high I-squared often signals that cohorts define the phenotype differently (self-reported versus clinically diagnosed diabetes, for instance) or draw from different ancestries or environments, and is a flag to inspect phenotype harmonization before trusting the pooled result. Large trait-specific consortia — GIANT for anthropometric traits like height and BMI, the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium (PGC) for conditions like schizophrenia and depression, and CARDIoGRAMplusC4D for coronary artery disease — pool summary statistics (not individual-level genotypes, for privacy and logistics) from hundreds of contributing cohorts to reach sample sizes in the hundreds of thousands to millions, the scale genuinely needed to detect OR 1.05-1.20 effects reliably.

lessons.workedExample: The PGC Schizophrenia Working Group (Ripke et al., 2014, Nature) meta-analyzed roughly 37,000 cases and 113,000 controls across dozens of cohorts and identified 108 genome-wide-significant loci, most with modest heterogeneity (low I-squared) because case definitions were harmonized across sites using comparable clinical criteria. A hypothetical single-site discovery SNP with OR = 1.15 in an initial N = 15,000 sample, when tested in an independent N = 40,000 replication cohort, drops to OR = 1.08 — consistent with winner's curse regression toward the true (smaller) effect, not evidence the original association was spurious, provided the replication p-value still clears a reasonable bar in the expected direction.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes replication and winner's curse because a student who reports only a discovery-cohort effect size, without checking whether it was independently replicated, has skipped the step that separates a candidate finding from an established one — and a student who sees a smaller effect in replication and panics that "the result didn't hold up" reveals they don't understand that shrinkage is the expected, textbook behavior of winner's curse, not a failure. A judge also listens for whether a student can explain what a high I-squared in a meta-analysis implies (usually phenotype definition or population differences), since blindly pooling heterogeneous cohorts without noticing is a common error.

questions.prompt: Why does the field require independent replication even after a SNP clears 5x10^-8 in a discovery cohort?

options.text: Because 5x10^-8 is not actually a strict threshold
Because a single cohort can produce false positives from stratification, relatedness, batch effects, or chance, that replication in a separate sample helps rule out
Because journals require a minimum of two papers per finding regardless of statistics
Because discovery cohorts never use genome-wide significance thresholds

explanations.a: 5x10^-8 is a stringent, deliberately conservative threshold; the issue is not its strictness but the other sources of error it cannot fully rule out.
explanations.b: Correct — technical and design confounders that survive even careful analysis in one cohort are far less likely to survive independently in a second cohort with different genotyping, recruitment, and often ancestry, which is why replication is the field's core validation norm.
explanations.c: The requirement is a scientific validation norm, not a publishing-count rule.
explanations.d: Discovery cohorts do apply genome-wide significance; that is exactly the threshold replication is meant to confirm holds up independently.

questions.prompt: A SNP shows OR = 1.20 in the discovery cohort and OR = 1.09 in an independent replication cohort, both in the same direction and both significant. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The replication disproves the original finding
This is winner's curse: discovery estimates are selected for being large enough to clear threshold, so a smaller, more accurate effect in replication is expected
One of the two studies must have made a genotyping error
The effect size should always be identical across cohorts if the finding is real

explanations.a: A same-direction, still-significant replication supports rather than disproves the finding; only the magnitude shrank, as expected.
explanations.b: Correct — winner's curse means discovery-cohort effects are systematically inflated because only SNPs whose noisy estimate cleared the threshold get reported; an independent cohort, not subject to that same selection filter, is expected to show a smaller, more accurate effect.
explanations.c: Effect-size shrinkage on replication is the expected statistical pattern, not evidence of an error in either study.
explanations.d: Sampling noise alone guarantees some difference in estimated effect size between any two finite cohorts, even for a real effect.

questions.prompt: A meta-analysis across ten cohorts finds a high I-squared statistic for a given SNP. What does that most directly suggest?

options.text: The SNP is definitely a false positive
A large fraction of the variation in effect estimates across cohorts reflects real heterogeneity rather than chance, prompting a look at phenotype definitions or population differences
The meta-analysis sample size is too small to compute I-squared reliably
The fixed-effect model must be used instead of random-effects

explanations.a: High heterogeneity is a flag to investigate, not proof of a false positive; the underlying signal can still be real in at least some cohorts.
explanations.b: Correct — the I-squared statistic (Higgins and Thompson, 2002) quantifies the proportion of cross-cohort variance attributable to true heterogeneity rather than sampling noise, and high values often trace back to differing phenotype definitions or differing populations across cohorts.
explanations.c: I-squared is computable regardless of sample size, though its precision improves with more cohorts; it is not undefined at small scale.
explanations.d: High heterogeneity is actually a reason to prefer a random-effects model, which allows for between-study variation, over a fixed-effect model.

questions.prompt: Match each consortium to the trait domain it is best known for.

right.text: Anthropometric traits (height, BMI)
Psychiatric traits (e.g., schizophrenia, depression)
Coronary artery disease

questions.explanation: GIANT (Genetic Investigation of ANthropometric Traits) pools cohorts for height, BMI, and related measures; the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium pools cohorts for psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia and depression; CARDIoGRAMplusC4D pools cohorts for coronary artery disease — each reaching sample sizes in the hundreds of thousands by combining summary statistics across many contributing studies.

lessons.label: Heritability and the Missing-Heritability Accounting

sections.heading: Three different numbers, all called "heritability"
sections.body: Height offers the clearest public ledger of a persistent puzzle in human genetics. Classical twin studies, comparing trait similarity between identical (monozygotic) and fraternal (dizygotic) twins, converge on a broad-sense heritability for adult height of roughly 0.8 — a large meta-analysis of twin studies by Silventoinen et al. (2003), pooling over 20,000 twin pairs across multiple countries, landed in that range. This is the family/twin estimate: it captures all genetic contribution to variance, common and rare, but relies on assumptions about twins' shared environments. A separate, more recent estimate uses only genotyped common SNPs directly: SNP-heritability, computed with methods like GCTA (Yang et al., 2010, using a genomic-relatedness-based restricted maximum-likelihood approach, GREML) or LD score regression, comes out at roughly 0.5 for height — capturing only the additive variance tagged by common variants on a genotyping array, a meaningfully smaller number than the twin estimate.

sections.heading: The gap between SNP-heritability and hits in hand
sections.body: A third number is smaller still: the variance explained by the SNPs that actually reach genome-wide significance in a given GWAS. Early height GWAS around 2008-2009, with tens of thousands of participants and on the order of 40-50 confirmed loci, collectively explained only about 5% of height's variance — a striking shortfall against both the ~0.8 twin estimate and the ~0.5 SNP-heritability estimate, a gap widely discussed as "missing heritability" in the years following the first wave of GWAS. That gap has narrowed substantially with scale rather than staying missing forever: Yengo et al. (2022, Nature), analyzing roughly 5.4 million individuals and identifying on the order of 12,000 near-independent loci, recovered variance explained approaching the common-SNP heritability ceiling — showing that much of the original "missing" heritability was simply undetected because early studies were underpowered for thousands of small-effect common variants, not because the variants did not exist.

sections.heading: Where the rest plausibly goes, and what heritability does not tell you
sections.body: Even after common-SNP heritability is fully accounted for, a further gap remains between SNP-heritability (~0.5) and twin heritability (~0.8) for height. Plausible contributors include rare variants not well-tagged by common-SNP genotyping arrays or imputation panels, imperfect LD tagging of causal variants (an array SNP correlated with, but not identical to, the true causal variant underestimates the variant's tagged contribution), gene-gene interaction (epistasis) and gene-environment interaction not captured by additive models, and the equal-environments assumption in twin designs — if identical twins actually share more environment than fraternal twins beyond genetics, classical twin heritability estimates can be inflated. Whatever the final accounting, a crucial and frequently missed interpretive point is that a heritability estimate is a population-level statistic describing how variance partitions in one population, in one environment, at one time — it says nothing about whether an individual's trait value is fixed or modifiable. Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a near fully genetically determined (highly "heritable" in the relevant sense) condition that is nonetheless fully manageable with a controlled diet, the standard textbook illustration that heritability and malleability are entirely separate axes.

lessons.workedExample: For height: twin studies put heritability near 0.8 (Silventoinen et al., 2003); GCTA-based SNP-heritability using common genotyped variants comes in near 0.5 (Yang et al., 2010, and later LD score regression estimates); the first wave of genome-wide-significant loci circa 2008-2009 explained only about 5% of variance despite the trait's high heritability. Fourteen years later, Yengo et al. (2022) scaled the discovery sample to 5.4 million people and roughly 12,000 loci, closing most of the gap between "hits in hand" and the ~0.5 SNP-heritability ceiling — demonstrating that the earlier 5% figure reflected study power, not a true absence of common-variant signal, while the remaining gap up to 0.8 still points toward rare variants, imperfect tagging, and non-additive effects.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes the twin-versus-SNP-versus-hits-explained distinction because conflating them is extremely common — a student who says "height is 80% heritable, but GWAS only found 5%, so GWAS must be broken" has missed that these are three different, non-competing quantities answering different questions, and that the 2008-era 5% figure was a snapshot of an underpowered early study, not a permanent ceiling, as later mega-scale GWAS demonstrated. A judge also specifically listens for the malleability trap: whether a student can state, unprompted, that a high heritability estimate (like PKU's) does not imply a trait is unchangeable — confusing the two is the single most consequential misreading of heritability data in public discussion of genetics.

questions.prompt: Match each height heritability estimate to its approximate value and source method.

left.text: Variance explained by first-wave (circa 2008-2009) genome-wide-significant loci

right.text: ~0.8, from MZ/DZ twin comparisons
~0.5, from common-SNP-based methods
~5%, from ~40-50 confirmed loci in early GWAS

questions.explanation: The three quantities form a descending ledger: twin studies (Silventoinen et al., 2003) give the broadest genetic estimate (~0.8); GCTA/LD score regression restrict to common genotyped SNPs (~0.5); and the earliest wave of genome-wide-significant hits, being underpowered relative to the true number of small-effect variants, explained only about 5% despite the trait's much higher underlying heritability.

questions.prompt: What did Yengo et al. (2022), scaling height GWAS to roughly 5.4 million individuals, demonstrate about the earlier ~5% variance-explained figure?

options.text: That the 5% figure was correct and represents a permanent ceiling on common-variant discovery
That the shortfall was largely a matter of statistical power — with enough sample size, common-variant discovery approached the SNP-heritability ceiling
That height has no meaningful genetic component after all
That twin studies had overestimated heritability by a factor of ten

explanations.a: The 5% figure was specific to early, underpowered studies with far fewer participants and loci; it was not a ceiling, as the later study demonstrated.
explanations.b: Correct — scaling to millions of participants and roughly 12,000 near-independent loci recovered variance explained approaching the ~0.5 common-SNP heritability estimate, showing the earlier gap largely reflected insufficient power to detect thousands of small-effect common variants, not their absence.
explanations.c: The much larger variance explained recovered at scale directly supports a substantial common-variant genetic contribution to height, the opposite of this claim.
explanations.d: Twin heritability (~0.8) and SNP-heritability (~0.5) remain distinct estimates for different reasons (e.g., rare variants, non-additive effects); nothing in the 2022 result overturns the twin estimate by an order of magnitude.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT typically offered as a plausible contributor to the remaining gap between SNP-heritability (~0.5) and twin heritability (~0.8) for height?

options.text: Rare variants not well-tagged by common-SNP arrays or imputation
Imperfect LD tagging between genotyped SNPs and true causal variants
Gene-gene and gene-environment interactions not captured by additive models
The fact that height is not influenced by genetics at all

explanations.a: Rare variants below the frequency or imputation quality thresholds used in standard SNP-heritability methods are a commonly cited contributor to the gap.
explanations.b: Causal variants imperfectly correlated with genotyped/imputed SNPs will have their contribution underestimated, a recognized contributor to the gap.
explanations.c: Non-additive genetic effects (epistasis) and gene-environment interactions are not captured by the additive models underlying standard heritability estimates, a recognized contributor.
explanations.d: Correct — this is false and contradicted by both the twin (~0.8) and SNP-heritability (~0.5) estimates, both of which indicate a very substantial genetic contribution to height variation.

questions.prompt: A student argues: "PKU is highly heritable, so it must be an unchangeable, untreatable condition." What is the flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: There is no flaw; high heritability does imply a trait cannot be modified

Heritability describes population-level variance partitioning, not whether an individual trait can be modified by environment or intervention — PKU is highly heritable yet fully manageable with dietary control
PKU is not actually a genetic condition
Heritability only applies to quantitative traits like height, never to diseases like PKU

explanations.a: This restates the flawed premise; heritability and modifiability are separate axes, and this is the exact misconception the question is testing.
explanations.b: Correct — PKU is close to fully genetically determined in the heritability sense, yet its severe symptoms are entirely preventable with a phenylalanine-restricted diet, making it the standard illustration that a high heritability estimate says nothing about whether a trait's expression can be changed by intervention.
explanations.c: PKU is a well-characterized single-gene metabolic disorder with a strong genetic basis; the flaw is not in calling it genetic but in equating that with unchangeable.
explanations.d: Heritability is a general statistical concept applicable to any trait with measurable variance, including disease conditions like PKU, not only continuous quantitative traits.

lessons.label: Huntington Disease: The First Genome-Wide Linkage Hunt

sections.heading: A kindred on Lake Maracaibo
sections.body: In 1979, neuropsychologist Nancy Wexler began traveling to villages on Lake Maracaibo, Venezuela, where an extraordinarily large kindred carried Huntington disease (HD) — a fatal, dominantly inherited neurodegenerative disorder causing progressive chorea, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms, usually starting in a person's 30s-40s. Over years of fieldwork, Wexler's team traced a pedigree spanning tens of thousands of individuals descended from a single 19th-century woman, and collected thousands of blood samples and detailed genealogies from the region. Because HD is dominant with near-complete penetrance, and because the Venezuelan kindred was so large and well-documented, it offered something no other human disease pedigree could: enough meiotic events to localize a gene using only anonymous DNA markers, with no idea what the gene did or what protein it made.

sections.heading: G8 and the first disease gene mapped blind
sections.body: In 1983, James Gusella and colleagues reported in Nature that a marker called G8 (locus D4S10), an anonymous restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP), co-segregated with HD in the Venezuelan pedigree and in US families, placing the HD gene near the tip of chromosome 4p. This was the first human disease gene ever localized purely by linkage to a random DNA marker, with no prior clue about chromosome, protein, or pathway — proof that reverse genetics (from map position to gene, rather than from known protein to gene) could work in humans. It also set an expectation, badly disappointed by the following decade: finding the marker did not mean finding the gene.

sections.heading: Ten years to IT15/HTT, and a test nobody was sure to want
sections.body: It took a full decade of chromosome walking and jumping before the Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group identified the gene itself in 1993: IT15 ("interesting transcript 15"), now called HTT, containing an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat. Repeat counts of 26 or fewer are normal; 27-35 is an 'intermediate' or mutable normal range — not disease-causing in the carrier, but unstable and prone to further expansion in the next generation, especially on paternal transmission, which is the mechanism behind anticipation (earlier, more severe onset in successive generations) and juvenile-onset HD; 36-39 shows reduced, age-dependent penetrance; 40 or more is fully penetrant, with longer repeats generally predicting earlier onset. The discovery made presymptomatic testing possible for at-risk relatives — but with no disease-modifying treatment available, genetic counselors built a cautious testing protocol (multiple counseling sessions, psychological screening, no unrequested results for minors). Uptake among at-risk adults has stayed low, commonly cited around 10-20%, revealing that a test's mere existence does not mean people want to know.

lessons.workedExample: A 28-year-old whose mother has HD is deciding whether to get tested before starting a family. Genetic counseling walks through the actual numbers: if she inherited the expanded allele, she has a 50% chance of passing it to each child, and a repeat count near 40 would predict full penetrance with no way to know the exact age of onset. If she does not test, she can still act on the 50/50 prior — but testing collapses that uncertainty into a near-certainty, for a disease with no treatment. This is exactly why real-world uptake sits closer to 10-20% than 100%: knowing does not equal wanting to know, especially absent an intervention that changes the outcome.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about HD because it is the cleanest case study for separating 'finding a gene' from 'helping a patient.' A student who only recites that HTT causes HD via CAG expansion is reciting a fact sheet. A student who can explain why linkage to an anonymous marker in 1983 was itself a methodological breakthrough, why ten more years were needed to get from map position to gene, and why a definitive test can still see low real-world uptake when no treatment follows, has grasped the actual arc of medical genetics: mapping is not diagnosis, and diagnosis is not the same thing as a cure.

questions.prompt: What made the 1983 Gusella et al. discovery of the G8 marker a methodological landmark, independent of Huntington disease itself?

options.text: It was the first time a disease gene was localized using linkage to an anonymous DNA marker, with no prior knowledge of the gene or protein
It was the first time a protein's amino acid sequence was used to find its gene
It proved Huntington disease was caused by a chromosomal deletion
It was the first study to sequence an entire human chromosome

explanations.a: Correct — G8 was an anonymous RFLP with no known function; linking it to HD showed reverse genetics (map first, identify gene later) could work in humans, without starting from a known protein.
explanations.b: That describes 'forward' biochemical genetics, the opposite of what made this discovery notable — no protein was known going in.
explanations.c: HD is caused by a CAG-repeat expansion within the HTT gene, not a chromosomal deletion.
explanations.d: Whole-chromosome sequencing did not exist in 1983; this was linkage mapping with a single polymorphic marker.

questions.prompt: A patient's HTT CAG repeat count comes back at 37. What does this mean under the ranges described in this lesson?

options.text: Normal, no increased risk
Reduced, age-dependent penetrance — may or may not develop HD
Fully penetrant — will develop HD if they live long enough
The result is uninterpretable without a second test

explanations.a: Normal is 26 or fewer repeats; 37 is well above that range.
explanations.b: Correct — 36-39 repeats falls in the reduced-penetrance range, meaning disease is possible but not certain.
explanations.c: Full penetrance is associated with 40 or more repeats, not 37.
explanations.d: CAG repeat sizing is a direct, interpretable molecular result; no second test is needed to place it in a penetrance range.

questions.prompt: Put these Huntington disease milestones in chronological order.

items.text: Wexler begins fieldwork with the Lake Maracaibo kindred
Gusella et al. link HD to the G8 marker on chromosome 4
The Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group identifies IT15/HTT and its CAG expansion

questions.explanation: Wexler's fieldwork began in 1979 and supplied the samples and pedigrees; Gusella's team used them to localize the gene to chromosome 4p in 1983; the gene itself, HTT, was not cloned until 1993 — a full decade later.

questions.prompt: Why does uptake of predictive HD testing among at-risk relatives stay relatively low (roughly 10-20%) despite the test being definitive?

options.text: The test is too expensive for most families to afford
There is no disease-modifying treatment, so a positive result changes psychological certainty without changing medical options
Most at-risk individuals are unaware the test exists
The test has a high false-positive rate

explanations.a: Cost is a barrier in many genetic tests, but the low-uptake pattern for HD testing is specifically discussed in the context of absent treatment, not price.
explanations.b: Correct — collapsing a 50/50 uncertainty into near-certainty is not obviously worth it when no intervention follows, which is why counseling protocols were built around this exact tradeoff.
explanations.c: The testing protocol and its low uptake are well documented precisely because at-risk individuals are informed of the option through genetic counseling.
explanations.d: CAG repeat sizing is a highly accurate molecular measurement, not a test prone to false positives.

lessons.label: Cystic Fibrosis: Positional Cloning and Thirty Years to a Drug

sections.heading: Finding a gene with no biochemical head start
sections.body: Cystic fibrosis (CF) causes thick mucus in the lungs and pancreas, but in the 1980s no one knew which protein was broken. Linkage analysis localized the CF locus to chromosome 7 in 1985 — a map position with no gene name attached. It then took Lap-Chee Tsui, Francis Collins, and John Riordan's teams four more years of positional cloning — chromosome walking (moving stepwise along the DNA from the linked marker) combined with chromosome jumping (leaping over long stretches to save time), a technique Collins had pioneered specifically because walking alone was too slow for large genomic distances — to reach and identify the actual gene in 1989. This was purely map-based: they had no idea the gene would encode an ion channel until they found it and worked out its sequence and predicted structure. The gene, CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator), turned out to encode a chloride channel — a functional category nobody had predicted for a disease previously understood only through its clinical effects on mucus and sweat.

sections.heading: One dominant deletion, thousands of others
sections.body: The single most common CF-causing mutation, a three-base-pair deletion removing a phenylalanine at position 508 (delta-F508, or F508del), accounts for roughly 70% of CF alleles worldwide, though that fraction varies by population (higher in northern Europe, lower elsewhere). F508del causes CFTR protein to misfold and get degraded before it ever reaches the cell membrane — a folding-and-trafficking defect, not a total loss of the protein's coding sequence. Since 1989, more than 2,000 additional CFTR variants have been catalogued, falling into distinct functional classes: some destroy the protein entirely, some (like F508del) block folding/trafficking, some make a channel that reaches the membrane but barely opens (gating defects), and some reduce channel conductance. That classification scheme mattered enormously for treatment, because different classes respond to different drugs.

sections.heading: From gene to mechanism-matched drug, at very different speeds
sections.body: It took over two decades to turn CFTR's identity into a therapy that treats the protein defect itself rather than just symptoms. Ivacaftor (Kalydeco), approved by the FDA in 2012, is a 'potentiator' that holds gating-class channels open longer — but it only helps the small slice of patients (a few percent) carrying gating mutations like G551D. The bigger breakthrough came in 2019: elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta), a triple combination correcting F508del folding and trafficking while potentiating the channel, extended meaningful benefit to roughly 90% of CF patients, since most carry at least one F508del allele. The 23-year gap between gene and gating-mutation drug, then a further 7 years to a drug reaching most patients, is the honest answer to 'find the gene, cure the disease': finding the gene was necessary but nowhere near sufficient.

lessons.workedExample: A newborn screen flags a baby with two CFTR variants: one F508del and one G551D. Because F508del is a folding/trafficking defect and G551D is a gating defect, the baby's CFTR protein has two different kinds of problems on its two alleles. Ivacaftor alone (aimed at gating defects) would only address the G551D-bearing protein and leave the F508del-bearing protein still misfolded and degraded. Trikafta's three-drug combination is designed for exactly this kind of case: correctors address the F508del folding problem, and the potentiator addresses gating on whichever allele reaches the membrane — which is why the field moved from single-mutation drugs to combination therapy as CFTR's variant classes became better understood.
