lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on CFTR because it is the sharpest classroom-friendly answer to a question every genetics-fair project eventually invites: 'so if the gene was cloned in 1989, why did it take 30 more years to get most patients a real drug?' A student who can name the mutation classes (misfolding vs. gating vs. absent protein) and explain why a gating-drug (ivacaftor) helps only a few percent while a folding-corrector combination (Trikafta) helps ~90% has understood that treatment design has to match a variant's actual molecular mechanism — not just its gene.

questions.prompt: What technique did Tsui, Collins, and Riordan use to get from the 1985 chromosome-7 map position to the identified CFTR gene in 1989, without any prior knowledge of its protein?

options.text: Whole-genome sequencing of multiple CF patients
Positional cloning via chromosome walking and jumping from a linked marker
CRISPR screening of lung tissue
Comparing CF patients' proteins to a known chloride-channel protein

explanations.a: Whole-genome sequencing did not exist as a practical tool in 1989; the gene was found through positional mapping, not sequencing whole genomes.
explanations.b: Correct — positional cloning combined chromosome walking (stepwise) with chromosome jumping (leaping over distance) to move from the 1985 linked marker on chromosome 7 to the gene itself, with no biochemical head start.
explanations.c: CRISPR-based screening did not exist in 1989.
explanations.d: The chloride-channel function of CFTR was discovered only after the gene was cloned and its sequence analyzed — it was not a starting assumption.

questions.prompt: Why does ivacaftor alone help only a small percentage of CF patients, while Trikafta helps roughly 90%?

options.text: Ivacaftor is a potentiator effective mainly for gating-class mutations, but most patients carry F508del, a folding/trafficking defect that Trikafta's correctors address
Ivacaftor is more expensive, so fewer patients can access it
Trikafta works on a different gene than ivacaftor
Ivacaftor was withdrawn from the market shortly after approval

explanations.a: Correct — ivacaftor helps channels that reach the membrane but barely open (gating defects, a few percent of patients); Trikafta adds correctors that fix F508del folding/trafficking, covering roughly 90% of patients who carry at least one F508del allele.
explanations.b: Cost is not the mechanism described here — the difference is which molecular defect each drug addresses.
explanations.c: Both drugs target CFTR; they differ in mechanism (potentiation vs. correction plus potentiation), not gene target.
explanations.d: Ivacaftor remains an approved, marketed drug for gating mutations; it was not withdrawn.

questions.prompt: Match each CFTR-related term to its correct description.

right.text: A deletion causing CFTR to misfold and be degraded before reaching the membrane; ~70% of CF alleles worldwide
A potentiator approved for gating-class mutations like G551D, helping a few percent of patients
A triple-combination drug covering ~90% of patients by correcting folding/trafficking plus potentiating the channel
The 1989 positional-cloning method used to find CFTR with no prior protein knowledge

questions.explanation: F508del is the dominant folding-defect deletion; ivacaftor is a gating-mutation potentiator with narrow reach; Trikafta combines correctors and a potentiator to cover most patients; chromosome walking/jumping was the positional-cloning method that found CFTR before its function was known.

questions.prompt: What does the roughly 30-year gap between cloning CFTR (four years after its 1985 chromosome-7 map position, identified in 1989) and Trikafta reaching ~90% of patients (2019) best illustrate?

options.text: Finding a disease gene is typically sufficient by itself to produce an effective drug within a few years
Identifying a gene is necessary but not sufficient — turning it into a mechanism-matched therapy requires understanding functional variant classes and years of drug development
CFTR mutations are too rare to justify drug development
Positional cloning is now considered an unreliable method

explanations.a: The CFTR story is the counterexample to this claim — even after the gene was mapped in 1985 and cloned in 1989, the gap to a broadly effective drug was decades, not years.
explanations.b: Correct — knowing the gene told researchers what protein was broken, but designing drugs required classifying how each mutation broke it (misfolding, gating, absence) and building distinct chemistry for each mechanism.
explanations.c: CF is one of the most common life-limiting recessive genetic diseases in populations of European descent, driving substantial drug-development investment.
explanations.d: Positional cloning successfully identified CFTR and remains a valid historical method; its reliability is not what the 30-year gap illustrates.

lessons.label: BRCA1/2, Patents, and Who Owns a Gene

sections.heading: Against prevailing doubt: a Mendelian form of breast cancer
sections.body: In 1990, geneticist Mary-Claire King published linkage evidence that early-onset breast cancer clustered in some families as a single dominant gene on chromosome 17q21 — at a time when most of the field assumed breast cancer was too common and too heterogeneous to have a major-gene Mendelian form worth searching for. King had spent nearly two decades collecting family pedigrees to make the case statistically undeniable. Her result reframed hereditary breast cancer as a locus problem, and triggered a cloning race. BRCA1 was cloned in 1994 by a team including Mark Skolnick, a scientist affiliated with Myriad Genetics; BRCA2, on a different chromosome, was cloned the following year, 1995, by a separate international collaboration. Together the two genes explain most, though far from all, of clearly hereditary breast and ovarian cancer. The clinical stakes were substantial: a pathogenic BRCA1 mutation confers roughly a 55-72% lifetime risk of breast cancer and roughly a 39-44% lifetime risk of ovarian cancer, with BRCA2 carriers facing somewhat lower but still sharply elevated risks for both — figures that made knowing one's carrier status, and who could test for it, a matter of real medical consequence, not just scientific interest.

sections.heading: A single company, a single price
sections.body: Myriad Genetics patented BRCA1 and BRCA2 and became the sole US provider of clinical BRCA testing for nearly two decades, pricing its BRACAnalysis test at roughly $3,000-4,000. Because Myriad held exclusive patent rights over the isolated gene sequences, no other US lab could legally offer full BRCA sequencing, which blocked second-opinion testing, competition-driven price drops, and — critically — blocked outside researchers from freely reanalyzing variants Myriad had already classified. Myriad also kept much of its own variant-classification data (which specific mutations were pathogenic versus benign) proprietary, a practice that became its own controversy separate from the patent fight.

sections.heading: The Supreme Court draws a line, and data gets freed
sections.body: In Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics (2013), the US Supreme Court ruled unanimously that a naturally occurring, isolated segment of genomic DNA is not patentable merely because it has been isolated from the body — but that complementary DNA (cDNA, synthesized without introns) is patent-eligible because it does not occur naturally in that exact form. The ruling opened BRCA testing to competitors and dropped prices substantially. In parallel, the fight over Myriad's withheld variant classifications spurred the open-data response: NCBI's ClinVar became a shared public repository for variant interpretations, and grassroots efforts including the Sharing Clinical Reports Project and the Free the Data movement pushed labs and patients to submit BRCA results publicly so that no single company's private database could be the last word on whether a variant was dangerous.

lessons.workedExample: Before 2013, a woman with a family history of breast cancer whose Myriad test found a 'variant of uncertain significance' had nowhere else to turn — Myriad's patent meant no competing lab could re-run BRCA1/2 sequencing, and Myriad's own classification database was not public, so an independent expert could not check the call. After AMP v. Myriad opened isolated-DNA testing to competitors, and as ClinVar accumulated public variant submissions from many labs and research groups, the same uncertain variant could increasingly be cross-checked against pooled data from thousands of other cases — turning one company's private judgment call into a comparison against a shared, growing evidence base.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises BRCA patents because it forces a student to separate the science (finding and cloning a gene) from the economics and law around it (who can test for it, at what price, using whose data). A strong answer distinguishes what the Supreme Court actually held — isolated genomic DNA is not patentable, cDNA is — from the looser claim 'genes can't be patented,' and connects the ruling to a concrete downstream effect: variant data moving from one company's locked database into public resources like ClinVar. That is the difference between reciting a court case and understanding what it changed for patients.

questions.prompt: What did the Supreme Court actually hold in Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics (2013)?

options.text: No human gene of any kind can ever be patented
Isolated naturally occurring genomic DNA is not patentable, but synthetically created cDNA is patent-eligible
Myriad's BRCA patents were valid and testing must remain exclusive to Myriad
Only diagnostic methods, not DNA sequences of any kind, can be patented

explanations.a: The ruling was narrower than a blanket ban — it distinguished isolated natural DNA from cDNA rather than banning all gene-related patents.
explanations.b: Correct — the Court held unanimously that merely isolating a naturally occurring DNA segment does not make it a patentable invention, while cDNA, which does not exist in that exact intron-free form in nature, remains eligible.
explanations.c: The ruling struck down Myriad's isolated-DNA claims, ending its testing exclusivity, not upholding it.
explanations.d: The case was specifically about DNA sequence patents (isolated genomic DNA vs. cDNA), not a general statement that no DNA sequence could ever be patented.

questions.prompt: Why was Mary-Claire King's 1990 linkage finding scientifically surprising to much of the field at the time?

options.text: It showed breast cancer had no genetic component at all
Most researchers assumed breast cancer was too common and heterogeneous to have a major single-gene Mendelian form worth searching for
It contradicted the existence of any environmental risk factors for breast cancer
It was the first study to use any DNA marker in cancer research

explanations.a: King's finding demonstrated the opposite — a clear dominant genetic locus in some families.
explanations.b: Correct — prevailing opinion doubted a common cancer like breast cancer would trace to a single major gene in a Mendelian pattern, which is exactly what King's linkage data against 17q21 challenged.
explanations.c: The finding was about a hereditary subset of cases and did not make claims about environmental risk factors.
explanations.d: Linkage analysis using DNA markers predates 1990 (e.g., the 1983 Huntington disease work); King's contribution was applying it successfully to breast cancer families.

questions.prompt: Put these BRCA-related events in chronological order.

items.text: Mary-Claire King links early-onset breast cancer to chromosome 17q21
BRCA1 is cloned by a team including Myriad-affiliated researcher Mark Skolnick
BRCA2 is cloned by a separate international collaboration
The Supreme Court rules on Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics

questions.explanation: King's linkage finding came in 1990, BRCA1 was cloned in 1994, BRCA2 followed in 1995, and the Supreme Court's ruling on gene patentability came nearly two decades later, in 2013.

questions.prompt: What role did ClinVar, the Sharing Clinical Reports Project, and the Free the Data movement play in the BRCA story?

options.text: They were Myriad-run initiatives to promote its patented test
They pushed variant-classification data into public, shared repositories, countering the practice of keeping BRCA variant interpretations proprietary
They were legal teams that argued the Myriad case before the Supreme Court
They developed the original chromosome 17 linkage map used by King

explanations.a: These were responses against, not initiatives by, Myriad's proprietary data practices.
explanations.b: Correct — they were part of the effort to move BRCA variant classifications out of any single company's private database and into shared public resources so independent experts could cross-check calls.
explanations.c: The Supreme Court case involved separate legal advocacy (the American Civil Liberties Union and the Association for Molecular Pathology, among others), not these data-sharing initiatives.
explanations.d: King's 1990 linkage work predates these data-sharing initiatives by roughly two decades and used family pedigree linkage analysis, not a public variant database.

lessons.label: The Replication Crisis and the Birth of GWAS

sections.heading: The candidate-gene era's collapse
sections.body: Through the 1990s and early 2000s, the dominant strategy for finding genes behind common diseases was the candidate-gene study: pick a gene with a biologically plausible story (say, a neurotransmitter receptor for a psychiatric trait), genotype a few hundred cases and controls at that one gene, and report an association. Hundreds of these studies were published, often with small sample sizes (a few hundred subjects) and no correction for the fact that researchers could try many genes and many statistical models before finding one 'hit.' When larger, independent samples tried to replicate these associations, most failed to hold up. The pattern was so consistent across psychiatry, cardiology, and other fields that it became known as part of a broader replication crisis in genetic association research, and it discredited the single-candidate-gene approach as fundamentally underpowered for the small effect sizes common variants actually have.

sections.heading: WTCCC: scale as the fix
sections.body: The response was to stop guessing which gene to test and instead test the whole genome, atheoretically, in samples large enough to survive strict correction for testing hundreds of thousands of markers at once. The Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium's 2007 Nature study was the landmark demonstration: roughly 14,000 cases split across seven common diseases (bipolar disorder, coronary artery disease, Crohn's disease, hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and type 2 diabetes), compared against roughly 3,000 shared controls, genotyped at about 500,000 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) genome-wide. Sharing one control set across seven disease studies was itself an economic innovation — controls are the expensive, reusable half of a case-control design, so pooling them let seven studies split one cost. The study delivered multiple robust, replicated hits per disease and functionally legitimized genome-wide association studies (GWAS) as the field's default design.

sections.heading: Norms that hardened afterward
sections.body: WTCCC's success, and the candidate-gene failures before it, hardened a set of norms that persist in GWAS today. Genome-wide significance was set at p < 5 x 10^-8, a Bonferroni-style correction for testing roughly a million independent common variants — a far stricter bar than the p < 0.05 that had waved through candidate-gene 'hits.' Independent replication in a separate sample became mandatory before a finding could be trusted, not optional. Consortium-style meta-analysis, pooling many cohorts to reach the huge sample sizes needed to detect small effects, became the standard operating structure rather than a single lab's dataset. Public posting of summary statistics and the creation of the GWAS Catalog made results checkable and reusable field-wide, and pre-specified analysis plans reduced the researcher-degrees-of-freedom problem that had let candidate-gene studies find whatever they were looking for.

lessons.workedExample: A 2003 candidate-gene study reports that a specific serotonin-related gene variant is associated with depression risk in 200 cases versus 200 controls, at p = 0.03. Post-WTCCC norms would flag several problems at once: 200-per-group is underpowered to detect a realistic common-variant effect size; p = 0.03 is nowhere near the 5 x 10^-8 genome-wide threshold that later became standard; and there is no independent replication sample. A modern GWAS-consortium study of the same trait, pooling tens of thousands of cases from many cohorts, tests all common variants genome-wide, applies the strict threshold, and only reports a hit that replicates in a held-out sample — which is why most individual candidate-gene depression 'findings' from that era failed to reappear in large modern GWAS.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on this history because it is the cleanest illustration of how a field enforces rigor on itself after a crisis, and it maps directly onto a science-fair project's own design choices: sample size, correction for multiple comparisons, and replication. A student who can explain why WTCCC's shared-control design was both a statistical and economic innovation, and why 5 x 10^-8 replaced p < 0.05 as the bar, is showing they understand that a 'significant' result from an underpowered, uncorrected, unreplicated study is close to meaningless — the exact lesson the candidate-gene era taught the hard way.

questions.prompt: What was the primary methodological weakness of the candidate-gene era of association studies?

options.text: They tested too many genes at once, making results uninterpretable
Small sample sizes and loose significance thresholds produced 'hits' that mostly failed to replicate in larger, independent samples
They used whole-genome sequencing instead of genotyping arrays
They only studied rare Mendelian diseases, not common ones

explanations.a: The opposite problem occurred — candidate-gene studies tested too few genes (often just one), chosen by guesswork, not too many.
explanations.b: Correct — small samples (often a few hundred subjects) combined with a p < 0.05 threshold and no correction for the many genes/models tried produced associations that mostly did not hold up under replication.
explanations.c: Whole-genome sequencing was not the technology in use; candidate-gene studies typically genotyped one pre-selected gene.
explanations.d: The candidate-gene approach was applied specifically to common, complex diseases (psychiatric, cardiovascular, etc.), not primarily rare Mendelian conditions.

questions.prompt: Why did WTCCC use one shared set of roughly 3,000 controls across all seven disease studies rather than separate controls for each disease?

options.text: Controls are the expensive, reusable part of a case-control design, so pooling them let seven studies split one cost
It was required by UK law at the time
Cases and controls needed to have the exact same disease to be comparable
Sharing controls increased the total number of SNPs that could be genotyped

explanations.a: Correct — this was an economic and logistical innovation: one well-characterized control panel could be reused across multiple case cohorts, dramatically cutting the cost of running seven large studies at once.
explanations.b: There was no such legal requirement; the shared-control design was a study-design choice, not a legal mandate.
explanations.c: Controls in a case-control design are unaffected individuals, not matched by having the same disease as any specific case group.
explanations.d: The number of SNPs genotyped (about 500,000) was a property of the genotyping array used, unrelated to whether controls were shared.

questions.prompt: Match each post-WTCCC norm to what it addressed.

right.text: Corrects for testing roughly a million independent common variants genome-wide, far stricter than p < 0.05
Ensures a finding is not a one-off statistical fluke in a single sample
Pools many cohorts to reach the large sample sizes needed to detect small common-variant effects
Makes results checkable and reusable across the whole field rather than locked in one lab's files

questions.explanation: Each norm targeted a specific candidate-gene-era failure: a strict genome-wide threshold replaced loose significance cutoffs, mandatory replication caught one-off flukes, consortium pooling supplied adequate statistical power, and public data sharing let the whole field check and reuse results.

questions.prompt: How many diseases and roughly how many cases did the 2007 WTCCC Nature study examine?

options.text: Seven diseases, roughly 14,000 cases total
One disease, roughly 14,000 cases
Seven diseases, roughly 500,000 cases total
Three diseases, roughly 3,000 cases total

explanations.a: Correct — the study spanned seven common diseases with roughly 14,000 cases total (about 2,000 per disease), compared against a shared pool of roughly 3,000 controls.
explanations.b: The landmark feature of the study was precisely that it spanned seven diseases at once using shared controls, not a single-disease design.
explanations.c: Roughly 500,000 refers to the number of SNPs genotyped per person, not the number of cases.
explanations.d: Three thousand describes the shared control group size, not the number of diseases or cases studied.

lessons.label: Missing Heritability and the Omnigenic Debate

sections.heading: Naming the gap
sections.body: Twin and family studies had long estimated that human height is roughly 80% heritable — most of the variation between people traces to genetic differences. But when early GWAS began reporting individually significant height-associated SNPs in the mid-to-late 2000s, those hits, added together, explained only a few percent of the trait's variance. Science journalist Brendan Maher's 2008 Nature feature gave this gap a durable name: 'missing heritability.' The puzzle was not whether height was heritable (twin studies were solid) but where the heritability was hiding, since genome-wide scans covering the vast majority of common variation were not finding it in significant hits.

sections.heading: Two competing explanations
sections.body: One camp argued the common-disease/common-variant hypothesis had simply been tested with too little power: real effects existed but were individually too small to cross strict genome-wide significance thresholds in the sample sizes then available. A rival camp, represented by geneticists Jon McClellan and Mary-Claire King (the same King who mapped BRCA1), argued instead for a rare-variant, genetic-heterogeneity model: that much of the missing heritability in complex disease reflects many different rare, large-effect variants scattered across families and individuals, rather than a tractable number of common variants. That rare-variant view found sharper statistical teeth in David Goldstein's group, whose 2010 PLoS Biology paper (Dickson, Wang, Krantz, Hakonarson, and Goldstein) proposed the synthetic-association critique: a common SNP might show a weak GWAS signal not because it does anything itself, but because it happens to sit near a genuinely causal rare variant, making the 'common variant hit' partly a statistical mirage pointing at something rarer and stronger nearby. The two camps disagreed about where researchers should spend limited sequencing budgets next.

sections.heading: GCTA settles part of it, and omnigenic reframes the rest
sections.body: In 2010, Jian Yang, Peter Visscher, and colleagues published a Nature Genetics study using a new method called GCTA (genome-wide complex trait analysis), which does not require any single SNP to be individually significant — instead it estimates the total variance explained by all common SNPs considered simultaneously. Applied to height, GCTA showed that common SNPs collectively captured roughly 45% of the heritability, far more than the few percent visible from significant hits alone, though still short of the ~80% from twin studies. This showed the heritability was not truly 'missing' so much as spread across many individually sub-threshold common variants that additive models could recover in bulk. In 2017, Evan Boyle, Yang Li, and Jonathan Pritchard proposed the omnigenic model in Cell, arguing that for complex traits, a small number of 'core' genes directly affecting the trait are joined by a much larger, diffuse 'periphery' of genes that influence the trait indirectly through trans-regulatory networks — meaning nearly any expressed gene in a relevant cell type could nudge the trait slightly. Critics have objected that the model is difficult to test directly, risks being unfalsifiable if 'periphery' can absorb any inconvenient result, and may blur past useful distinctions between genes with large biological importance and genes that are merely statistically associated.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher in 2009 has GWAS data on 5,000 people's height and finds 20 SNPs crossing genome-wide significance, together explaining about 3% of height variance — far short of the ~80% twin-study estimate. Running Yang et al.'s GCTA method on the same genotype data, without requiring any individual SNP to be significant, recovers roughly 45% of the heritability from the additive effects of common SNPs across the genome. This single reanalysis illustrates the core missing-heritability resolution: the heritability was not absent, it was distributed across thousands of common variants with effects too small to individually clear a strict significance bar, but recoverable when modeled in aggregate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about missing heritability because it is the field's best worked example of a hypothesis surviving a serious empirical challenge through better statistics rather than being abandoned. A strong answer distinguishes three separate things students often conflate: the original gap Maher named in 2008, the McClellan-King rare-variant/genetic-heterogeneity counter-hypothesis, Dickson and Goldstein's synthetic-association critique that reinforced it, and Yang et al.'s 2010 GCTA result that partly resolved the debate by showing common variants collectively explain much more than their individually significant subset. Naming the omnigenic model's actual falsifiability objection, not just describing it approvingly, shows the student understands this is a live, contested area — not settled textbook fact.

questions.prompt: What specifically did Brendan Maher's 2008 Nature feature call 'missing heritability'?

options.text: The fact that twin studies and GWAS-significant hits disagreed about how much of a trait's variance was genetic at all
The gap between the large heritability estimated from twin/family studies and the small fraction of variance explained by individually significant GWAS hits
The absence of any genetic component to height
Missing DNA samples from early GWAS cohorts

explanations.a: Twin studies and GWAS were not disagreeing about whether a trait was genetic — the puzzle was that significant hits could not account for the heritability twin studies had already established.
explanations.b: Correct — twin studies put height's heritability near 80%, but the individually significant SNPs from early GWAS explained only a few percent, and Maher's piece named that gap.
explanations.c: Height's genetic component was well established by twin studies; the puzzle was locating it in GWAS data, not its existence.
explanations.d: The term refers to a statistical/explanatory gap in variance, not literally missing physical samples.

questions.prompt: What is the synthetic-association critique raised by Dickson, Wang, Krantz, Hakonarson, and Goldstein (2010)?

options.text: A common SNP's weak GWAS signal may reflect its proximity to a genuinely causal rare variant, rather than the common SNP itself having an effect
GWAS results are entirely fabricated by researchers
Rare variants can never be detected by any genomic method
Common variants and rare variants always have identical effect sizes

explanations.a: Correct — the critique proposed that some apparent common-variant GWAS 'hits' could be statistical artifacts of linkage to a nearby rare, large-effect variant, rather than real effects of the common SNP itself.
explanations.b: The critique is a scientific hypothesis about linkage and signal interpretation, not an accusation of fabrication.
explanations.c: The critique assumes rare variants exist and can matter; it argues for looking harder for them, not that they are undetectable.
explanations.d: The rare-variant hypothesis specifically proposed that rare variants could have larger effects than common ones, not identical effect sizes.

questions.prompt: What did Yang, Visscher, and colleagues' 2010 GCTA analysis of height show?

options.text: Common SNPs, considered simultaneously rather than requiring individual significance, collectively explained roughly 45% of height's heritability
Height has no genetic component
Only rare variants contribute to height heritability
GWAS significance thresholds should be lowered to p < 0.05

explanations.a: Correct — GCTA modeled all common SNPs together without requiring individual significance, recovering about 45% of height's heritability, far more than the few percent visible from significant hits alone.
explanations.b: Twin studies and GCTA both support a strong genetic component to height; GCTA increased the explained fraction rather than eliminating it.
explanations.c: GCTA specifically analyzed common SNPs, showing they collectively mattered far more than previously credited — it did not conclude rare variants were the whole story.
explanations.d: GCTA did not argue for loosening genome-wide significance thresholds; it used a different statistical approach that did not depend on per-SNP significance at all.

questions.prompt: What is a substantive objection critics have raised against Boyle, Li, and Pritchard's 2017 omnigenic model?

options.text: It claims complex traits have no genetic basis
Its 'core gene' versus diffuse 'periphery' distinction is difficult to test directly and risks being unfalsifiable, since almost any result can be absorbed into 'periphery' effects
It was published in a journal with no peer review
It contradicts the existence of GWAS entirely

explanations.a: The omnigenic model assumes and builds on a strong genetic basis for complex traits; it does not deny genetic contribution.
explanations.b: Correct — because the periphery category is broad and loosely defined (nearly any expressed gene in a relevant cell type could qualify), critics argue the model can absorb almost any finding, making it hard to falsify or test with a sharp prediction.
explanations.c: The model was published in Cell, a major peer-reviewed journal; publication venue is not the basis of the substantive criticism.
explanations.d: The omnigenic model was proposed to explain GWAS results (why so many loci across the genome show small associations with a trait), not to contradict the GWAS method itself.

lessons.label: Eugenics, Consent, and the Field's Ethical Debts

sections.heading: Compulsory sterilization, blessed by the Supreme Court
sections.body: In the early 20th century, the American eugenics movement pushed dozens of US states to pass compulsory sterilization laws targeting people labeled 'feebleminded,' institutionalized, or otherwise deemed genetically unfit. In Buck v. Bell (1927), the Supreme Court upheld Virginia's sterilization law 8-1, with Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. writing that 'three generations of imbeciles are enough' about Carrie Buck, her mother, and her infant daughter — none of whom had been rigorously assessed. The ruling was never overturned. Over the following decades, an estimated 60,000-plus Americans were sterilized without meaningful consent, and Nazi Germany's own eugenic sterilization program explicitly cited US laws, including California's, as precedent and model when building its policy in the 1930s.

sections.heading: Samples taken, trust broken
sections.body: Medical mistrust rooted in real historical abuse shaped how genetics research is now regulated. The Tuskegee syphilis study, in which researchers withheld treatment from Black men for decades without informed consent, left a legacy of justified mistrust toward genetic and medical research in Black communities that researchers still have to actively address. In the 1990s, Arizona State University researchers collected diabetes-related blood samples from members of the Havasupai Tribe, then reused the same samples for studies of schizophrenia, inbreeding, and population migration that the tribe had never consented to and found culturally harmful — a case that reached settlement in 2010, with the tribe receiving $700,000 and the return of remaining samples. Separately, cells taken from Henrietta Lacks in 1951 without her knowledge or consent became the HeLa line, a foundational tool of biomedical research; when researchers published the HeLa genome sequence in 2013, they did so without consulting her surviving family, prompting public objection and a subsequent NIH agreement giving the family a voice in controlled-access approval for HeLa genomic data.

sections.heading: What changed, and what GINA still leaves open
sections.body: These episodes, among others, are why modern human genetics research runs through informed consent processes and Institutional Review Board (IRB) oversight, and why tribal and indigenous communities increasingly assert data sovereignty — the right to govern how their genetic data is collected, stored, and reused, as the Havasupai case made concrete. At the federal level, the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA), signed in 2008, prohibits health insurers and employers from using genetic information to discriminate. But GINA's protections are narrower than most people assume: it does not cover life insurance, disability insurance, or long-term-care insurance, and it exempts employers with fewer than 15 employees — gaps that remain live policy debates whenever direct-to-consumer genetic testing or research participation comes up.

lessons.workedExample: A university genetics lab wants to collect DNA from a Native American community to study a metabolic disease. Applying the lessons of Havasupai, the lab cannot simply obtain one broad consent form and later run unrelated studies (ancestry, psychiatric traits) on the same samples — the tribe's data sovereignty means separate, specific consent is needed for each distinct use, and the tribe may require ongoing say over storage, sharing, and destruction of samples after the study ends. A participant in this study should also understand GINA's limits: a finding of disease risk cannot be used against them by a health insurer or their employer, but it legally could affect their eligibility or premiums for a life insurance or long-term-care policy, since those are outside GINA's protection.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises this history because science-fair genetics projects routinely involve human data or samples, even informally, and the ethical debts of the field are not abstract — they produced the specific rules (IRB review, informed consent, GINA) a student project must actually follow. A strong answer names a concrete historical case (Buck v. Bell, Havasupai, or Henrietta Lacks) and connects it to a specific present-day safeguard it produced, then can also name a real gap that persists — GINA's exclusion of life and disability insurance — showing the student understands that consent and protection are still incomplete, not solved problems from the past.

questions.prompt: What did the Supreme Court hold in Buck v. Bell (1927)?

options.text: It struck down compulsory sterilization laws as unconstitutional
It upheld Virginia's compulsory sterilization law, with Holmes writing 'three generations of imbeciles are enough'
It required informed consent before any medical procedure
It banned the use of genetic information in employment decisions

explanations.a: The Court did the opposite — it upheld the law, an 8-1 decision that was never overturned.
explanations.b: Correct — Justice Holmes wrote the majority opinion upholding Virginia's sterilization law and used that phrase about Carrie Buck's family.
explanations.c: The ruling upheld a law authorizing sterilization without the kind of consent modern practice would require; it did not establish an informed-consent requirement.
explanations.d: That describes a purpose closer to GINA (2008), a federal law enacted more than 80 years after Buck v. Bell.

questions.prompt: What made the Havasupai Tribe's blood samples case (settled 2010) a research-ethics landmark?

options.text: Samples collected for a diabetes study were reused for schizophrenia, inbreeding, and migration research the tribe had not consented to
The tribe refused to allow any medical research on its members
It was the first case to establish informed consent in any medical research
The samples were destroyed before any research could be conducted

explanations.a: Correct — samples collected under a diabetes-research premise were repurposed for unrelated, culturally sensitive studies without the tribe's consent, which the tribe experienced as a violation and litigated to a 2010 settlement.
explanations.b: The tribe had agreed to specific diabetes-related research; the dispute was about undisclosed reuse beyond that scope, not a blanket refusal of research.
explanations.c: Informed consent as a research principle predates this case by decades (e.g., the Nuremberg Code, Belmont Report); Havasupai is notable for tribal data sovereignty and scope-of-consent, not originating informed consent itself.
explanations.d: The settlement included return of remaining samples to the tribe, not destruction before research occurred — research had already been conducted, which was the core grievance.

questions.prompt: Which of these does GINA (2008) explicitly NOT protect against genetic-information-based discrimination?

options.text: Health insurance underwriting decisions
Employment decisions at companies with 15 or more employees
Life insurance, disability insurance, and long-term-care insurance
Hiring decisions based on genetic test results at a covered employer

explanations.a: GINA does cover health insurance, prohibiting insurers from using genetic information in coverage or premium decisions.
explanations.b: GINA covers employment discrimination at employers with 15 or more employees; smaller employers are the exempted gap, not this one.
explanations.c: Correct — GINA's protections stop at health insurance and employment; life, disability, and long-term-care insurers remain legally permitted to use genetic information in many jurisdictions.
explanations.d: GINA does prohibit covered employers from using genetic test results in hiring and other employment decisions.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.

items.text: Buck v. Bell upholds compulsory sterilization
Cells are taken from Henrietta Lacks without her knowledge, becoming the HeLa line
GINA is signed into law
The Havasupai Tribe's lawsuit against Arizona State University is settled

questions.explanation: Buck v. Bell was decided in 1927; Henrietta Lacks's cells were taken in 1951; GINA was signed in 2008; the Havasupai settlement was reached in 2010 — spanning nearly a century of the field's evolving relationship to consent.

lessons.label: The Diversity Problem and the Ancestry Debate

sections.heading: Measuring the imbalance
sections.body: In 2016, Alice Popejoy and Stephanie Fullerton published an analysis in Nature, 'Genomics Is Failing on Diversity,' quantifying just how skewed GWAS participation had become: roughly 81% of GWAS participants were of European ancestry, even though people of European descent make up a much smaller share of the global population. Later updates to this tracking showed only partial improvement over subsequent years, with European ancestry still dominating despite growing recruitment efforts elsewhere. Because GWAS statistical power and downstream clinical tools are built from whichever populations are actually studied, this imbalance was never a purely academic accounting problem — it meant genomic medicine's toolkit was being built to fit one ancestral group far better than others.

sections.heading: Two concrete harms this produced
sections.body: Manrai and colleagues' 2016 NEJM study made the imbalance's clinical cost visible: several genetic variants that are common and benign in Black Americans had been misclassified as disease-causing for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, because the reference control populations used to judge variants as 'rare enough to be dangerous' had themselves been overwhelmingly European, so a variant merely uncommon among Europeans could look alarming even when it was unremarkable in a population that had not been adequately represented in those reference panels. The five highest-frequency misclassified variants accounted for the large majority of these misdiagnoses. Separately, Martin and colleagues' 2019 Nature Genetics study demonstrated that polygenic risk scores — trait predictions built by combining many small-effect variants from GWAS — lose most of their predictive accuracy when applied to ancestry groups other than the one the score was trained on, because allele frequencies, linkage patterns, and even which variants matter can differ meaningfully across ancestries. Both papers converted an abstract representation problem into demonstrated, patient-level consequences.

sections.heading: Responses, and an unresolved definitional fight
sections.body: Several major efforts now explicitly target this gap: H3Africa builds African-led genomic research capacity and cohorts across the continent; the All of Us Research Program, run by the US National Institutes of Health, aims to enroll a cohort that is majority non-European and historically underrepresented in research; and the Population Architecture using Genomics and Epidemiology (PAGE) study specifically pools diverse US cohorts to test whether findings from European-ancestry GWAS actually replicate elsewhere. Underneath these programs sits an unresolved methodological argument: should genomic studies classify participants by self-identified race, self-identified ethnicity, discrete continental-ancestry categories, or continuous genetic-similarity measures that avoid discrete labels altogether? Each choice carries different scientific and social tradeoffs, and the field has not converged on one answer.

lessons.workedExample: A clinical lab in the early 2010s flags a genetic variant in a Black American patient as likely causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, because the variant is rare in the lab's mostly-European reference database. Following the logic Manrai et al. later exposed, this classification conflates 'rare in our (mostly European) reference panel' with 'rare in general' — but the variant may in fact be common and harmless in populations of African ancestry, simply because those populations were underrepresented in the panel used to judge rarity. A patient could be told they carry a life-threatening cardiac mutation, face unnecessary interventions or anxiety, and pass that misclassification to relatives who are also tested — a direct clinical harm traced back to whose genomes built the reference data.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes ancestry and diversity because it is where an abstract methods critique becomes a documented patient-harm story, and because it directly tests whether a student can connect representation in a training dataset to a specific downstream failure mode. A strong answer names the actual mechanism in each case — reference-panel rarity misjudged as pathogenicity in Manrai et al., or a polygenic score's learned weights not transferring across populations with different allele frequencies and linkage patterns in Martin et al. — rather than gesturing vaguely at 'bias.' Naming the unresolved classification debate (race vs. ethnicity vs. continental ancestry vs. genetic similarity) shows the student knows this is a live argument, not a solved footnote.

questions.prompt: What did Popejoy and Fullerton's 2016 Nature analysis find about GWAS participant ancestry?

options.text: Roughly 81% of GWAS participants were of European ancestry
GWAS participants were evenly split across all major ancestry groups
Fewer than 10% of GWAS participants were of European ancestry
Ancestry data was not tracked in GWAS at the time

explanations.a: Correct — the analysis found roughly 81% of GWAS participants were of European ancestry, a large overrepresentation relative to that group's share of the global population.
explanations.b: The entire point of the analysis was to document a severe imbalance, not an even split.
explanations.c: This inverts the actual finding — European ancestry was dramatically overrepresented, not underrepresented.
explanations.d: Ancestry data was in fact tracked well enough for Popejoy and Fullerton to compile this quantitative analysis in the first place.

questions.prompt: According to Manrai et al. (2016), why were some benign variants misclassified as causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy specifically in Black American patients?

options.text: The variants were genuinely rare and dangerous only in Black Americans
Reference control panels used to judge variant rarity were overwhelmingly European, so variants uncommon in Europeans but actually common and benign in other populations looked alarming by comparison
The sequencing technology used produced more errors in samples from Black American patients
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy occurs only in Black Americans

explanations.a: The finding was the opposite — the variants were benign and common in the affected population, not genuinely dangerous.
explanations.b: Correct — pathogenicity classification depended on how rare a variant appeared in reference panels, and those panels' European skew made an ancestry-common, harmless variant look suspiciously rare and thus 'likely pathogenic.'
explanations.c: The misclassification was a statistical/reference-data problem, not a sequencing-error problem.
explanations.d: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy occurs across ancestries; the misclassification issue was specific to how certain variants were interpreted, not to the disease's occurrence being limited to one group.

questions.prompt: Why do polygenic risk scores, per Martin et al. (2019), lose accuracy when applied outside the ancestry group they were trained on?

options.text: Polygenic scores are only mathematically valid for one ancestry group by definition
Allele frequencies, linkage patterns, and which variants matter can differ meaningfully across ancestry groups, so weights learned in one population transfer poorly to another
Polygenic scores require a specific skin-color measurement to calculate
Non-European genomes contain fewer SNPs than European genomes
All genotyping arrays exclude non-European samples entirely

explanations.a: Polygenic scores are a statistical method applicable to any population in principle; the accuracy drop is an empirical transferability problem, not a definitional restriction.
explanations.b: Correct — differences in allele frequency and linkage disequilibrium patterns across ancestries mean the specific variant weights learned from a European-ancestry training GWAS do not map cleanly onto another population's genetic architecture.
explanations.c: Polygenic scores are computed from genotype data, not any visual or phenotypic proxy like skin color.
explanations.d: Genomes across ancestries have comparable numbers of SNPs; the issue is which variants carry predictive weight and how strongly, not a raw count difference.
explanations.e: Genotyping arrays can and do include non-European samples; the disparity is about how many such samples have historically been included in large GWAS training sets, not a technical exclusion.

questions.prompt: Match each initiative to its primary purpose.

right.text: Builds African-led genomic research capacity and cohorts across the continent
US NIH program aiming to enroll a cohort majority non-European and historically underrepresented in research
Pools diverse US cohorts to test whether European-ancestry GWAS findings replicate in other populations

questions.explanation: H3Africa focuses on building genomic research infrastructure within Africa; All of Us is a US national cohort explicitly targeting greater ancestral and demographic diversity; PAGE specifically tests replication of GWAS findings across diverse US populations.

lessons.label: Estimating Penetrance Without Fooling Yourself

sections.heading: Penetrance depends on who you asked
sections.body: Penetrance is the probability that a carrier of a genetic variant develops the associated disease, but that probability is not a fixed property of the variant alone — it is a property of the variant measured in a particular population, sampled in a particular way. For decades, BRCA1/BRCA2 penetrance estimates came almost entirely from clinic-referred, multiplex cancer families: households already flagged for genetic testing because several relatives had breast or ovarian cancer. That referral filter is not random. A family with one carrier and five cancer diagnoses is far more likely to walk into a genetics clinic than a family with one carrier and zero diagnoses, so early estimates — cumulative breast-cancer risk quoted as high as 80-85% — were built on a population pre-selected for dense disease history, and the true population-wide penetrance was systematically overstated.

sections.heading: Prospective cohorts correct the ascertainment bias
sections.body: Kuchenbaecker and colleagues (2017), pooling prospective data from the International BRCA1/2 Carrier Cohort Study and related registries, followed carriers forward in time rather than reconstructing risk backward from affected relatives. Their estimates — cumulative breast-cancer risk to age 80 of about 72% for BRCA1 carriers and about 69% for BRCA2 carriers — sit meaningfully below the older clinic-based figures, and risk still varied by birth cohort and by family history within the carrier group itself, confirming that even 'penetrance' is modulated by other genetic and environmental factors, not a single carrier-wide constant. When biobank studies later examined 'pathogenic' variants in people ascertained for reasons unrelated to a cancer family history — unselected population cohorts such as the UK Biobank, analyzed by Wright and colleagues (2019) and later biobank follow-ups — penetrance for many of the same variant classifications came out markedly lower still, because the biobank population lacks the disease-family filter entirely.

sections.heading: Kin-cohort methods and penetrance as a curve, not a number
sections.body: One method built specifically to correct ascertainment bias is the kin-cohort design: instead of studying probands (the person who triggered testing) directly, researchers survey the disease history of the proband's relatives and use segregation-analysis math to back out an unbiased penetrance estimate, since a relative's disease status was not itself the reason anyone entered the study. A related fix is proband exclusion — dropping the index case from risk calculations, since the proband was picked precisely because they were affected. Both approaches point at the same underlying truth: penetrance is really a cumulative-incidence curve across a lifetime, rising with age, not a single yes/no percentage, and any reported number is only meaningful attached to an age and an ascertainment method.

lessons.workedExample: A commercial lab reports a novel BRCA2 variant as '78% penetrant for breast cancer' citing a 2005 clinic-based paper. A genetic counselor pulls the paper and finds the cohort was ascertained through a hereditary-cancer clinic where every family had at least three affected members. She flags that this number cannot be handed to a patient found via unselected tumor-panel testing with no family history, because the clinic sample was pre-filtered for exactly the outcome being measured. She instead cites Kuchenbaecker et al. (2017)-style prospective-cohort figures as a better anchor, and notes that even those need adjustment for the patient's own family history before counseling.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'where did your risk number come from?' is testing whether the student understands ascertainment bias, the single most common way a genetics project quietly imports an inflated statistic. A student who can name the difference between a clinic-referred cohort and a prospective or biobank cohort — and explain why the referral filter itself biases the estimate — is demonstrating that they read past the headline percentage into the sampling design. A student who quotes '80% penetrant' without saying where the carriers came from has memorized a number, not understood a method.

questions.prompt: Why did early clinic-based BRCA1/BRCA2 penetrance estimates run higher than later prospective-cohort estimates like Kuchenbaecker et al. (2017)?

options.text: Clinic families were recruited because they already had dense cancer history, inflating the apparent penetrance
Older sequencing technology produced more false-positive variant calls
BRCA1/BRCA2 penetrance has genuinely declined over time due to environmental change
Clinic-based studies used larger sample sizes, which mathematically inflates risk estimates

explanations.a: Correct — referral to a hereditary-cancer clinic was driven by having multiple affected relatives, so clinic cohorts oversample carriers from disease-dense families, inflating penetrance relative to the general carrier population.
explanations.b: The bias is about who was sampled, not variant-calling accuracy; both eras used validated sequencing for known BRCA1/2 mutations.
explanations.c: There is no evidence of a true biological decline in penetrance; the gap is a sampling artifact, not a real trend.
explanations.d: Larger sample size does not systematically inflate an estimate; ascertainment bias (who is included) does, regardless of size.

questions.prompt: In Kuchenbaecker et al. (2017), the prospective-cohort cumulative breast-cancer risk to age 80 was approximately:

options.text: 72% for BRCA1, 69% for BRCA2
50% for BRCA1, 50% for BRCA2
95% for BRCA1, 90% for BRCA2
72% for BRCA2, 69% for BRCA1

explanations.a: Correct — the prospective cohort estimated roughly 72% cumulative risk to age 80 for BRCA1 carriers and roughly 69% for BRCA2 carriers, both below older clinic-based figures.
explanations.b: This understates both estimates; the prospective cohort still found substantially elevated lifetime risk, just lower than clinic-based figures.
explanations.c: This overstates the risk in the direction of the older, ascertainment-biased clinic estimates the prospective study corrected.
explanations.d: The genes are swapped — BRCA1 carried the slightly higher estimate (~72%), not BRCA2.

questions.prompt: Match each method or population to what it does about ascertainment bias in penetrance estimation.

right.text: Surveys relatives' disease history instead of the index case, using segregation analysis to back out an unbiased estimate
Drops the index case, who was selected because affected, from the risk calculation
Recruited via already having several affected relatives; inflates apparent penetrance
Ascertained without regard to disease/family history; tends to yield lower penetrance for the same variant class

questions.explanation: Kin-cohort and proband-exclusion are corrective methods that remove the selection filter mathematically; biobank cohorts avoid the filter by construction since recruitment did not depend on disease status; clinic-referred families are the biased source both methods were built to correct for.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to describe penetrance as a single percentage rather than a cumulative-incidence curve?

options.text: Because penetrance rises with age and a single number hides at what age that risk applies
Because penetrance is identical across all variants in a gene, so a curve is unnecessary
Because penetrance only applies to men, not women
Because cumulative-incidence curves are only used for infectious diseases

explanations.a: Correct — cumulative risk accumulates over a lifetime, so '72% by age 80' means something different from '72% by age 40'; a bare percentage without an age anchor is underspecified.
explanations.b: Penetrance varies substantially by specific variant and by modifying factors like family history, not just gene identity.
explanations.c: Penetrance applies across sexes for many conditions, though risk magnitude and cancer type can differ; this option misstates the concept.
explanations.d: Cumulative-incidence curves are a standard tool in any time-to-event analysis, including hereditary cancer risk, not just infectious disease.

lessons.label: Absolute Risk, Relative Risk, and How to Communicate Both

sections.heading: Three numbers, three meanings
sections.body: A relative risk (or risk ratio) compares the incidence in an exposed group to the incidence in an unexposed group: 'carriers get the disease three times as often as non-carriers.' An odds ratio, common in case-control genetic studies because it can be computed without knowing the true population incidence, compares the odds of exposure among cases to the odds among controls, and approximates relative risk only when the disease is rare. Absolute risk (or lifetime risk) is the actual probability a given person develops the disease over a stated period — the number that matters for a real decision. A variant with a relative risk of 3.0 sounds dramatic in isolation, but its meaning depends entirely on the baseline: tripling a common 10%-lifetime-risk disease reaches 30%, while tripling a rare 1-in-10,000 baseline reaches 3 in 10,000 — still a rare event in absolute terms.

sections.heading: Natural frequencies fix the comprehension gap
sections.body: Risk-communication research led by figures such as Gerd Gigerenzer has repeatedly shown that both patients and, troublingly, many practicing clinicians systematically misread relative-risk statements — overestimating the real-world impact of a '50% increased risk' headline when the underlying baseline is tiny. The fix that reliably improves comprehension is natural-frequency framing: instead of 'your risk increases by 50%,' say 'out of 1,000 people with your profile, about 15 will develop the condition instead of about 10.' Icon arrays — grids of 100 or 1,000 stick figures with the affected ones highlighted — exploit the same principle visually and are now standard in decision aids for BRCA and cardiovascular risk counseling because they let a viewer count the difference rather than multiply a fraction.

sections.heading: Number needed to screen, and the DTC labeling problem
sections.body: Number needed to screen extends the related number-needed-to-treat concept to a screening program: how many people must be screened to prevent (or detect) one additional adverse outcome, once test performance — sensitivity, specificity — and downstream treatment uptake are folded in on top of the treatment's own effect, which is why number needed to screen is typically larger than the number needed to treat for the same underlying intervention. Either figure makes a modest relative benefit concrete and comparable across interventions, and is far more useful for policy than a bare relative-risk reduction. Direct-to-consumer genetic testing has made the communication problem urgent at scale: services report variant-level 'increased risk' or 'elevated risk' labels built on relative-risk multipliers against thin, sometimes single-study baselines, and studies of DTC users find a persistent pattern of consumers treating a modest relative-risk label as if it were a near-certain diagnosis, then either over-reacting with unnecessary procedures or, when the number turns out small in absolute terms, distrusting genetics results generally.

lessons.workedExample: A DTC report tells a user their genotype carries a 'relative risk of 2.0' for a condition with a 2% lifetime population risk. Read as a bare multiplier, 2.0 sounds alarming. Converted to absolute and natural-frequency terms: baseline is 2 in 100 people; doubling gives 4 in 100 people with this genotype. A genetic counselor reframes the report as 'out of 100 people with your result, about 4 will develop this condition versus about 2 without it' and pairs it with an icon array of 100 figures, 4 shaded. The relative-risk number was accurate; the communication was the failure point, and it is fixed without touching the underlying statistic.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes risk communication specifically because it is where technically correct genetics becomes practically misleading, and because a student who can only state 'relative risk 2.0' hasn't shown they understand what that number does to a person's actual odds. The strong answer converts the relative figure into an absolute, baseline-anchored statement — ideally a natural-frequency framing like 'out of 100 people' — and can explain why the same relative risk means something very different against a rare baseline than a common one. That conversion is the whole skill being tested.

questions.prompt: A variant triples disease risk (relative risk = 3.0) against a baseline lifetime incidence of 1 in 10,000. What is the approximate absolute risk for a carrier?

options.text: About 3 in 10,000
About 30%
About 1 in 3
About 3 in 100

explanations.a: Correct — multiplying a 1-in-10,000 baseline by 3 gives roughly 3 in 10,000, still a rare absolute event despite the dramatic-sounding threefold relative risk.
explanations.b: 30% would result from tripling a 10% baseline, not a 1-in-10,000 baseline; this confuses the multiplier's effect across very different baselines.
explanations.c: This wildly overstates the risk; nothing about a threefold relative risk on a tiny baseline approaches 1-in-3 absolute odds.
explanations.d: This is off by two orders of magnitude from the correct calculation on a 1-in-10,000 baseline.

questions.prompt: Why does natural-frequency framing ('40 out of 1,000 people') improve risk comprehension compared to a percentage-increase statement ('a 25% increased risk')?

options.text: It anchors the risk to a concrete baseline count, so the reader does not have to infer or guess the denominator
It always produces a smaller-sounding number, which is more comforting to patients
It replaces the need for any baseline incidence data
It is mathematically a different, more accurate quantity than a percentage

explanations.a: Correct — natural-frequency framing gives both the affected count and the total explicitly, removing the ambiguous 'increase relative to what?' step that trips up relative-risk statements.
explanations.b: Natural frequencies are not chosen to minimize the number; the same underlying risk can look larger or smaller depending on framing, but the goal is accuracy, not comfort.
explanations.c: Natural-frequency framing requires baseline incidence data to construct — it displays that data explicitly rather than eliminating the need for it.
explanations.d: A well-constructed natural-frequency statement and an accurate percentage describe the same underlying risk; the difference is comprehension, not the underlying math.

questions.prompt: An odds ratio from a case-control study approximates relative risk well when:

options.text: The disease is rare in the population studied
The disease affects at least half the population
The study has a very large sample size, regardless of disease frequency
The variant has a large effect size

explanations.a: Correct — the rare-disease assumption is the standard justification: when incidence is low, odds and probability are numerically close, so the odds ratio closely approximates the relative risk.
explanations.b: A common disease is exactly where odds ratio and relative risk diverge most, not converge; this is the opposite of the correct condition.
explanations.c: Sample size affects the precision (confidence interval) of the estimate, not whether odds ratio approximates relative risk — that depends on disease frequency.
explanations.d: Effect size is unrelated to whether the rare-disease approximation holds; a large or small effect can occur at any baseline frequency.

questions.prompt: What does 'number needed to screen' represent?

options.text: How many people must be screened to prevent (or detect) one additional adverse outcome
The number of genetic variants a screening panel tests
The relative risk expressed as a whole number
The number of false positives generated per true positive

explanations.a: Correct — number needed to screen translates a risk reduction or detection rate into a concrete count of people who must undergo screening for one additional good outcome, making benefit tangible and comparable across interventions.
explanations.b: That describes panel size or test breadth, an unrelated concept from screening efficacy.
explanations.c: Number needed to screen is a derived clinical-utility statistic, not simply a relative risk rounded to an integer.
explanations.d: That describes a false-positive rate or positive predictive value, a different diagnostic-accuracy concept.

lessons.label: Building a Polygenic Score

sections.heading: From summary statistics to a single number
sections.body: A polygenic score (PGS or PRS) starts with GWAS summary statistics: for each variant tested against a trait, an estimated effect size (a beta or log-odds ratio) and a p-value for association. Building the score is conceptually simple — for a given person, count their risk-allele dosage at each included variant (0, 1, or 2 copies), multiply by that variant's effect-size weight, and sum across every included variant to produce one number per person. The hard engineering is entirely in deciding which variants to include and how to weight them, because a raw GWAS carries millions of correlated, partly redundant, partly noisy signals.

sections.heading: Handling linkage disequilibrium and choosing a threshold honestly
sections.body: Nearby variants are correlated through linkage disequilibrium (LD), so summing raw effect sizes across all of them double-counts the same underlying signal. Clumping-and-thresholding handles this by picking a p-value cutoff, then within each LD block keeping only the most significant variant and discarding (clumping) its correlated neighbors — simple and interpretable, but it throws away real signal sitting just below the threshold. Bayesian shrinkage methods such as LDpred2 and PRS-CS instead keep nearly all variants but shrink each effect-size estimate toward zero in proportion to its LD context and its statistical uncertainty, letting weak-but-real signals contribute a little rather than being cut entirely. The p-value threshold itself is a choice with real consequences: a lenient threshold captures more true polygenic signal but adds noise, and a threshold tuned by peeking at the same data used to build the score is a form of leakage, not a neutral analytic decision.

sections.heading: Train, validate, test — and the sample-overlap trap
sections.body: A defensible PGS pipeline keeps three cohorts strictly separate: the GWAS training cohort supplies the effect-size weights, an independent validation cohort tunes hyperparameters like the p-value threshold or shrinkage strength, and a held-out test cohort — touched exactly once, at the end — reports the final predictive accuracy. The classic inflation error is sample overlap: if any individuals appear in both the GWAS training data and the cohort used to evaluate the score, the score appears to predict better than it actually would in a truly independent population, because it is partly just recognizing itself. Finally, a raw summed score is not directly interpretable — it must be standardized (mean-centered and scaled) against an ancestry-matched reference panel so that a raw sum becomes a percentile or a z-score that means the same thing for every person scored against it.

lessons.workedExample: A team builds a type-2-diabetes PGS from a GWAS of 200,000 individuals. They naively include 50 people from that same GWAS in their 'validation' set to tune the p-value threshold, and the score appears to explain 12% of trait variance. A reviewer notices the overlap, the team rebuilds validation from a fully independent biobank subset with zero shared individuals, and the honest accuracy drops to 7% — the gap is entirely sample-overlap leakage, not a real improvement from retuning. The corrected pipeline also standardizes each test-cohort score against an ancestry-matched reference so a score of '+1.5 SD' means the same thing across every person's report.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about training/validation/test separation because sample-overlap leakage is the single most common way a polygenic-score result gets inflated, and it is invisible unless a student explicitly describes how their cohorts were split. A strong answer names clumping-and-thresholding or a shrinkage method by name, explains why LD forces a choice at all, and can state plainly that touching the test set more than once — or letting any individual appear in both training and evaluation — invalidates the reported accuracy. That is the difference between a score a judge can trust and one that was quietly tuned on its own answer key.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of building and evaluating a polygenic score correctly.

items.text: Obtain GWAS summary statistics (effect sizes, p-values) from a training cohort
Apply clumping-and-thresholding or a shrinkage method (e.g., LDpred2) to select and weight variants
Tune hyperparameters (like the p-value threshold) on an independent validation cohort
Report final predictive accuracy on a held-out test cohort touched only once

questions.explanation: The pipeline flows from training-cohort summary statistics, through variant selection/weighting that accounts for LD, to hyperparameter tuning on a separate validation set, ending with a single, final evaluation on a test cohort that was never used for training or tuning.

questions.prompt: Why does linkage disequilibrium (LD) create a problem for simply summing GWAS effect sizes across all variants?

options.text: Correlated nearby variants would have their shared signal double-counted if all were summed with their full effect sizes
LD causes GWAS p-values to be systematically miscalculated
LD only affects variants on the sex chromosomes
LD makes effect sizes impossible to estimate at all

explanations.a: Correct — variants in LD are statistically correlated because they are co-inherited, so summing raw effects across all of them counts the same underlying causal signal multiple times, inflating the score's apparent contribution from that region.
explanations.b: LD is a property of co-inheritance patterns, not a flaw in p-value calculation itself; p-values remain valid single-variant statistics.
explanations.c: LD occurs genome-wide across all chromosomes, not only sex chromosomes.
explanations.d: Effect sizes can be estimated despite LD; the problem is combining them naively across correlated variants, not estimating them individually.

questions.prompt: Match each PGS construction method to its core strategy.

right.text: Keep only the top variant per LD block above a p-value cutoff; discard correlated neighbors
Keep nearly all variants but shrink each effect size toward zero based on LD and estimation uncertainty

questions.explanation: Clumping-and-thresholding is a simple selection rule that discards redundant signal; Bayesian shrinkage methods retain more variants but down-weight them proportionally to LD context and uncertainty, generally capturing more true polygenic signal at the cost of more complex modeling.

questions.prompt: A validation cohort shares 200 individuals with the GWAS training cohort used to generate the score's weights. What is the likely consequence?

options.text: The score's reported predictive accuracy will be inflated relative to its true performance in an independent population
The score's accuracy will be unaffected, since 200 individuals is a small fraction of a large GWAS
The score will underestimate its true predictive accuracy
The overlap only affects ancestry standardization, not predictive accuracy

explanations.a: Correct — this is sample overlap, the classic inflation error: the score is partly evaluated on individuals it was trained on, so it appears more predictive than it would be on a truly independent sample, regardless of how small the overlap seems.
explanations.b: Even a modest overlap can measurably inflate accuracy estimates, and the direction of the bias is always toward overstatement, not negligibility, in principle — the flaw invalidates the comparison regardless of scale.
explanations.c: The bias runs the opposite direction — overlap inflates apparent accuracy, it does not deflate it.
explanations.d: Sample overlap directly corrupts the accuracy estimate itself; it is a separate issue from ancestry-matched standardization of the score's scale.

lessons.label: How Good Are Polygenic Scores, Really?

sections.heading: Khera et al. (2018) and the 'genomic equivalent of a monogenic mutation' claim
sections.body: Khera and colleagues (2018, Nature Genetics) built genome-wide polygenic scores for five common diseases — coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and breast cancer — most prominently coronary artery disease, and reported that roughly 8% of the population fell into a category with threefold or greater risk relative to the rest of the population — a risk stratum, they argued, comparable to carrying a rare monogenic mutation like familial hypercholesterolemia, but affecting far more people. The coronary-artery-disease score was validated in the UK Biobank cohort of roughly 288,000 genotyped individuals, giving the tail-risk estimates the statistical power that made the comparison credible in the first place. In the extreme tail of the score's distribution, relative risk reached roughly twentyfold. The framing generated real excitement and real pushback: critics noted that 'equivalent to a monogenic mutation' compares a population-level relative-risk category to an individual-level penetrance estimate, two different kinds of number, and that the eye-catching tail statistics describe a small slice of the population, not the score's typical, much weaker performance for everyone else.

sections.heading: Discrimination is usually modest, and incremental gains are small
sections.body: Outside the dramatic tail, the more representative summary statistic is the AUC (area under the ROC curve), which measures how well a score discriminates cases from controls across the whole distribution. For most common diseases, a polygenic score alone achieves an AUC in roughly the 0.6-0.65 range — better than a coin flip (0.5) but far short of a strong individual-level diagnostic tool (0.9+). Adding the polygenic score on top of established clinical risk factors (age, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking status) typically nudges the combined AUC up by only a few hundredths, not by a transformative margin. That gap between the headline population-stratification numbers and the modest individual-level discrimination is the recurring source of confusion in how these scores get reported.

sections.heading: Calibration, discrimination, and the population-versus-individual lesson
sections.body: Discrimination (can the score rank higher-risk people above lower-risk people, measured by AUC) and calibration (do the score's predicted probabilities match observed event rates) are separate properties, and a score can be well calibrated on average while still discriminating weakly for any one person. Compared against a simple, free clinical tool — family history — polygenic scores often perform comparably or only modestly better for many conditions, though the two capture somewhat different information and combine usefully. The central lesson researchers converged on: a polygenic score can be genuinely useful for stratifying a population into risk bands worth different screening intensity, while still being a weak, uncertain predictor for what happens to any specific individual.

lessons.workedExample: A clinic wants to decide whether a 45-year-old with no family history of heart disease should get an expensive imaging test. Their coronary-artery-disease PGS places them at the 92nd percentile. Read alone as 'top 8%, threefold+ risk,' this sounds like a strong signal for action. But the AUC for this score alone is about 0.6-0.65, meaning at the individual level the score is a soft nudge, not a diagnosis. The clinician combines the PGS with the patient's actual cholesterol, blood pressure, and smoking status — the incremental AUC gain from adding PGS to those factors is only a few hundredths — and treats the score as one modest input among several, not a standalone verdict.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on 'how good is your predictor, really?' because polygenic-score headlines (like '8% of people at threefold risk') are easy to repeat and easy to misapply to an individual. The strong answer distinguishes population-level stratification from individual-level discrimination, can cite an approximate AUC range for common-disease PGS, and explains that adding a score to established clinical risk factors typically produces only a small incremental gain — not a replacement for them. A student who conflates 'a threefold risk stratum exists in the population' with 'this score reliably predicts what happens to me' has missed the exact distinction the field spent years correcting.

questions.prompt: In Khera et al. (2018), what proportion of the population fell into the category with threefold or greater coronary-artery-disease risk from the genome-wide polygenic score?

options.text: About 8%
About 50%
About 1%
About 25%

explanations.a: Correct — Khera et al. (2018) reported roughly 8% of the population at threefold or greater relative risk, a stratum they compared in size and severity to rare monogenic-mutation carriers.
explanations.b: 50% would not represent a meaningfully elevated-risk minority; the entire point of the tail-risk framing was identifying a smaller, distinctly higher-risk group.
explanations.c: 1% understates the reported figure; the extreme ~20-fold relative risk applied to a smaller sliver, but the threefold-or-greater category was about 8%.
explanations.d: 25% overstates the reported proportion at threefold-or-greater risk.

questions.prompt: A polygenic score for a common disease has an AUC of about 0.62 when used alone. What does this indicate about its individual-level predictive power?

options.text: It discriminates cases from controls only modestly better than chance, well short of a strong individual diagnostic tool
It is essentially useless and provides no information
