It perfectly predicts disease status for any given person
It means 62% of carriers will develop the disease
It is equivalent to a monogenic mutation's penetrance

explanations.a: Correct — an AUC of 0.62 sits between chance (0.5) and a strong diagnostic (0.9+), meaning the score does discriminate somewhat but is a weak individual-level predictor on its own.
explanations.b: An AUC above 0.5 does carry real information, even if modest; it is not equivalent to no discrimination at all.
explanations.c: Perfect prediction would correspond to an AUC of 1.0, far above the described 0.62.
explanations.d: AUC is a discrimination statistic across the whole ranked distribution, not a direct probability of disease for carriers — this conflates AUC with absolute risk.
explanations.e: AUC (a population-level discrimination statistic) and penetrance (an individual carrier's disease probability) are different kinds of number, one of the exact confusions this lesson highlights.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between calibration and discrimination for a risk score?

options.text: Discrimination measures how well the score ranks higher- versus lower-risk people; calibration measures whether predicted probabilities match observed event rates
They are two names for the same statistical property
Calibration only applies to monogenic conditions, discrimination only to polygenic ones
Discrimination measures accuracy in one ancestry group, calibration measures accuracy across ancestry groups

explanations.a: Correct — discrimination (commonly measured by AUC) asks whether the score correctly orders people by risk, while calibration asks whether the score's stated probabilities actually match how often the outcome occurs; a score can do well on one and poorly on the other.
explanations.b: They are distinct statistical properties that can diverge — a well-calibrated score can still discriminate poorly for individuals, and vice versa.
explanations.c: Both concepts apply generally to any risk score, monogenic or polygenic; the terms are not restricted this way.
explanations.d: This describes portability across ancestry groups, a different concept covered elsewhere, not the calibration/discrimination distinction.

questions.prompt: What is the central lesson researchers draw from the gap between Khera et al.'s population-level tail statistics and the typical AUC for common-disease polygenic scores?

options.text: A score can usefully stratify a population into risk bands while remaining a weak predictor for any specific individual
Polygenic scores are scientifically invalid and should not be used at all
The tail statistics and the AUC measure exactly the same thing, so there is no real gap
Individual-level prediction is always more reliable than population-level stratification

explanations.a: Correct — this is the reconciling lesson: population-level stratification (identifying an 8% high-risk group) can be genuinely useful for screening policy even while the score's individual-level discrimination (AUC ~0.6-0.65) remains modest for any one person.
explanations.b: The scores have real, validated statistical properties; the issue is how they are communicated and applied, not that they are invalid.
explanations.c: Population-stratification statistics and individual-level AUC are different measurements that can diverge, which is precisely the source of public confusion this lesson addresses.
explanations.d: It is the opposite pattern here — population stratification is the stronger use case, while individual-level prediction is the weaker one for these scores.

lessons.label: Portability, Ancestry, and the Fairness Problem

sections.heading: Martin et al. (2019): a stark accuracy gap
sections.body: Martin and colleagues (2019, Nature Genetics), in a paper titled 'Clinical use of current polygenic risk scores may exacerbate health disparities,' quantified a problem the field had known about qualitatively but not measured cleanly: polygenic scores built from European-ancestry GWAS lose most of their predictive accuracy when applied to people of different ancestries. In individuals of African ancestry, accuracy fell to roughly a quarter to a half of what the same score achieved in European-ancestry individuals; South Asian and Hispanic/Latino populations showed intermediate losses, tracking roughly with genetic distance from the European training population. Because the overwhelming majority of GWAS participants to date have been of European ancestry, this is not a minor edge case — it is the default behavior of nearly every clinically discussed polygenic score.

sections.heading: Why portability fails: three compounding mechanisms
sections.body: The accuracy loss is not one problem but several stacking together. First, linkage disequilibrium patterns differ across populations with different demographic histories, so a tag variant that closely trails a true causal variant in Europeans may sit in a different LD block — or no meaningful LD block at all — in another population, breaking the statistical proxy the score relies on. Second, allele frequencies differ across ancestries, so a variant common enough to be well-powered in one GWAS may be rare and poorly estimated in another. Third, the true causal effect sizes themselves can differ across populations, driven by gene-environment interactions and by genetic background (epistasis), meaning even a perfectly identified causal variant is not guaranteed to carry the same effect size everywhere.

sections.heading: Mitigation and the deployment stakes
sections.body: Active fixes include multi-ancestry GWAS that deliberately recruit non-European cohorts to estimate effect sizes directly rather than extrapolating; PRS-CSx, a Bayesian method that jointly models multiple ancestry-specific GWAS and borrows statistical strength across them while allowing effect sizes to differ by population; and local-ancestry-aware scores, which use ancestry inferred at each genomic segment (relevant in admixed individuals) to apply the more appropriate population-specific weight variant by variant. Martin and colleagues' central warning was not just technical but a deployment argument: rolling out current, largely Europe-trained polygenic scores into clinics today would not merely fail to help non-European patients equally — it would actively widen existing health disparities, by giving clinicians a confidently-stated, unreliable number for exactly the patients least represented in the training data.

lessons.workedExample: A hospital pilots a coronary-artery-disease PGS built from a European-ancestry GWAS. For a European-ancestry patient, the score's reported percentile is reasonably informative. For a patient of West African ancestry, Martin et al.'s findings predict the same score type would explain only about a quarter to a half as much of the true risk variance — yet the report format shows an equally confident-looking percentile for both patients, with no visible caveat. A hospital that adopts the score uniformly is quietly delivering a less accurate tool to exactly the patients already underserved by other cardiovascular risk models, unless it either withholds the score for underrepresented ancestries or switches to a multi-ancestry method like PRS-CSx.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'does your score work the same for everyone?' is testing whether a student knows that polygenic-score accuracy is not ancestry-neutral by default — it is a direct, measured consequence of whose genomes trained the GWAS. The strong answer names Martin et al. (2019), states the rough magnitude of the accuracy drop in non-European populations, and can explain at least one mechanism (LD differences, allele-frequency differences, or effect-size heterogeneity) rather than gesturing vaguely at 'bias.' A student who proposes deploying a Europe-trained score without acknowledging this gap has skipped the field's central open problem.

questions.prompt: According to Martin et al. (2019), how does polygenic-score accuracy in individuals of African ancestry compare to accuracy in European-ancestry individuals, when the score is trained on European-ancestry GWAS data?

options.text: It falls to roughly a quarter to a half of the European-ancestry accuracy
It is essentially identical, since human genomes are highly similar overall
It is higher, because African populations have greater genetic diversity
It falls to zero, providing no information at all

explanations.a: Correct — Martin et al. (2019) found accuracy dropping to roughly a quarter to a half of the European-ancestry value in African-ancestry individuals, a substantial but not total loss of predictive power.
explanations.b: Despite overall genomic similarity across humans, the specific LD patterns and allele frequencies a GWAS-derived score relies on are population-specific enough to cause a large, measured accuracy gap.
explanations.c: Greater genetic diversity in African populations works against, not for, a Europe-trained score's portability — more diversity means the European-derived tag variants are less reliable proxies.
explanations.d: The accuracy loss is severe but not total; the score retains some predictive signal, just substantially reduced.

questions.prompt: Match each mechanism to why it reduces polygenic-score portability across ancestries.

right.text: A tag variant that closely trails the true causal variant in one population may not do so in another, breaking the statistical proxy
A variant well-powered (common) in the training population may be rare and poorly estimated in another
Gene-environment interaction or genetic background can make even a correctly identified causal variant carry a different-sized effect elsewhere

questions.explanation: LD differences break the tag-variant proxy relationship the score relies on; allele-frequency differences change how well each variant's effect was estimated in the original GWAS; and effect-size heterogeneity means even accurately identified causal variants are not guaranteed to transfer their effect magnitude across populations.

questions.prompt: PRS-CSx improves cross-ancestry portability primarily by:

options.text: Jointly modeling multiple ancestry-specific GWAS, borrowing statistical strength across them while letting effect sizes differ by population
Simply applying the European-derived score to every population without adjustment
Discarding all non-European GWAS data as unreliable
Increasing the p-value threshold used in clumping-and-thresholding

explanations.a: Correct — PRS-CSx is a Bayesian method that combines GWAS summary statistics from multiple ancestries, sharing information across them while allowing population-specific effect-size differences, improving accuracy beyond a single-ancestry score.
explanations.b: That describes the unmitigated portability problem itself, not a fix for it.
explanations.c: PRS-CSx does the opposite — it actively incorporates non-European GWAS data rather than discarding it.
explanations.d: Adjusting a p-value threshold is a clumping-and-thresholding parameter unrelated to PRS-CSx's cross-ancestry joint-modeling approach.

questions.prompt: Why did Martin et al. (2019) argue that clinical deployment of current polygenic scores could worsen health disparities, rather than simply being less helpful for some patients?

options.text: Because underrepresented-ancestry patients would receive a confidently-presented but substantially less accurate risk number, compounding existing gaps in care
Because polygenic scores are more expensive to run for non-European patients
Because non-European patients are excluded from receiving any score at all under current guidelines
Because the disparity only affects rare monogenic conditions, not common disease risk

explanations.a: Correct — the concern is that a score with degraded accuracy, if presented with the same apparent confidence as it has for European-ancestry patients, actively misleads clinical decisions for underrepresented patients rather than being neutrally less useful.
explanations.b: The concern in the paper is about accuracy and equity of information, not computational cost differences between populations.
explanations.c: The problem is the opposite — scores are typically still reported for all patients without adequately flagging the ancestry-driven accuracy gap, not withheld.
explanations.d: The portability problem specifically concerns polygenic (common, multi-variant) scores for common disease, the exact category this lesson addresses, not monogenic conditions.

lessons.label: Embryo Screening and the Limits of Prediction

sections.heading: What PGT-P sells versus what the math supports
sections.body: Polygenic embryo screening (PGT-P) is offered by commercial fertility-adjacent companies as a way to rank a set of IVF embryos by predicted future polygenic score — for disease risk, and in some marketing, for traits like height or cognitive ability — so prospective parents can choose which embryo to implant. The core mathematical constraint the marketing tends to understate is that full siblings, including embryos from the same IVF cycle, already share about half their genetic variance; selecting among roughly ten embryos from one couple is selecting from a narrow, highly related distribution, not from the wide range of variation seen across the general population that a GWAS effect size was estimated on.

sections.heading: Karavani et al. (2019) and Turley et al. (2021): modest gains, wide uncertainty
sections.body: Karavani and colleagues (2019, Cell) simulated embryo selection using real polygenic scores and found that selecting the top-scoring embryo out of a realistic sibling set of about ten yielded an average gain of roughly 2.5-3 IQ points over picking randomly — a real but small effect, and one accompanied by wide prediction intervals, meaning in many actual families the 'top-scoring' embryo would not have turned out to be the highest-trait sibling at all. Turley and colleagues (2021, New England Journal of Medicine) ran an analogous simulation for disease risk rather than a quantitative trait, modeling conditions like type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease, and reached a similarly modest conclusion: the expected absolute risk reduction from selecting among embryos using current polygenic scores is small, with substantial uncertainty around any individual case, and the authors argued absolute risk reduction — not a more dramatic-sounding relative-risk reduction — is the number that should be reported to prospective parents.

sections.heading: Pleiotropy, portability, and the professional response
sections.body: Two problems compound the modest-gain finding. Pleiotropy means a variant selected for lowering one disease's polygenic score may simultaneously raise the score for an unrelated trait or a different disease, so optimizing for one outcome risks unintended correlated selection elsewhere in the embryo's future phenotype — a tradeoff PGT-P reports generally do not surface. The ancestry-portability problem compounds the uncertainty further, since the underlying scores were built predominantly from European-ancestry GWAS and are markedly less accurate for other-ancestry embryos. Professional bodies including the American Society of Human Genetics (ASHG) and the European Society of Human Genetics (ESHG) have issued position statements characterizing PGT-P for polygenic traits as not clinically or scientifically justified given current evidence, and the underlying behavioral-genetics question — whether cognitive or educational-attainment polygenic scores should ever inform reproductive decisions — remains a live, unresolved controversy in the field, separate from the disease-risk use case.

lessons.workedExample: A couple undergoing IVF is offered PGT-P and told their top-ranked embryo (of nine viable ones) has a 'meaningfully lower' polygenic disease-risk profile than the others. Applying Turley et al. (2021)-style reasoning, they ask their genetic counselor for the absolute, not relative, risk reduction. The counselor explains that selecting the top-ranked embryo from a same-family set of nine, using current scores, is expected to lower absolute lifetime risk by a small amount with a wide margin of uncertainty — and that the same variants influencing the target disease's score may correlate with other, unreported traits due to pleiotropy. The couple decides the modest, uncertain gain does not justify treating the ranking as a meaningful selection criterion.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks about PGT-P is testing whether a student can separate a company's marketing claim from what a peer-reviewed simulation actually supports. The strong answer cites the approximate magnitude from Karavani et al. (2019) or Turley et al. (2021) — a few IQ points or a small absolute risk reduction across a same-family sibling set — and explains why full siblings' shared genetic variance caps the achievable gain regardless of scoring precision. It should also name pleiotropy or the ancestry-portability problem as an additional reason the technology's real-world benefit is smaller and murkier than advertised. A student who treats the top-ranked embryo as simply 'the best embryo' has missed the entire quantitative point.

questions.prompt: In Karavani et al. (2019), what was the approximate average IQ gain from selecting the top-scoring embryo out of a realistic sibling set of about ten, compared to random selection?

options.text: About 2.5-3 IQ points
About 15-20 IQ points
About 0 IQ points — no measurable effect
About 8-10 IQ points

explanations.a: Correct — Karavani et al. (2019) estimated an average gain of roughly 2.5-3 IQ points from selecting the top-scoring embryo among about ten siblings, a real but modest effect with wide prediction intervals.
explanations.b: This overstates the simulated effect by roughly an order of magnitude; the paper's headline finding was explicitly that gains this large were not supported.
explanations.c: The study found a small but nonzero average effect, not a complete absence of predicted gain.
explanations.d: This is still an overstatement of the modest, single-digit gain the simulation actually found.

questions.prompt: Why does selecting among full-sibling IVF embryos yield a smaller polygenic-score gain than the GWAS effect sizes alone might suggest?

options.text: Full siblings already share roughly half their genetic variance, so the range of trait variation available to select from is narrower than in the general population
IVF embryos have systematically different DNA repair mechanisms than naturally conceived embryos
GWAS effect sizes only apply to adults, not embryos
Polygenic scores cannot be computed at all from embryonic DNA

explanations.a: Correct — because full siblings share about half their genetic variance, the spread of polygenic scores across one family's embryo set is much narrower than the spread across the unrelated individuals a GWAS was trained on, capping the achievable gain from selection.
explanations.b: There is no established difference in DNA repair mechanisms between IVF and naturally conceived embryos that drives this effect; the limiting factor is shared sibling genetic variance.
explanations.c: GWAS-derived effect sizes are genotype-based and, in principle, apply at any developmental stage; the limitation here is about the sibling variance available to select among, not developmental timing.
explanations.d: Polygenic scores can technically be computed from embryonic biopsy DNA, which is the basis of PGT-P itself; the issue is what that score can usefully predict, not whether it can be computed.

questions.prompt: How does pleiotropy specifically complicate polygenic embryo selection for a single target disease?

options.text: A variant that lowers the score for the target disease may simultaneously raise risk for an unrelated trait or condition, an unintended correlated effect not shown in the report
Pleiotropy means the polygenic score cannot be computed for more than one disease at a time
Pleiotropy only affects monogenic conditions, not polygenic scores
Pleiotropy makes GWAS summary statistics impossible to obtain

explanations.a: Correct — pleiotropy means a given variant can influence multiple traits, so optimizing selection for one disease's score risks unintentionally shifting risk for other, unreported traits in a direction that was never evaluated.
explanations.b: Pleiotropy is about one variant affecting multiple traits, not a computational limit on how many scores can be calculated.
explanations.c: Pleiotropy is a general genetic phenomenon relevant to both monogenic and polygenic traits, not exclusive to monogenic conditions.
explanations.d: Pleiotropy describes a biological relationship between variants and traits; it does not prevent GWAS summary statistics from being generated.

questions.prompt: What was the position taken by professional bodies such as ASHG and ESHG regarding PGT-P for polygenic traits like height or cognitive ability?

options.text: It is not clinically or scientifically justified given current evidence
It should be mandatory for all IVF cycles
It is fully validated and ready for routine clinical deployment
It has no ethical concerns and only technical ones remain

explanations.a: Correct — ASHG and ESHG position statements have characterized polygenic embryo screening for traits as not clinically or scientifically justified given the current state of evidence, citing the modest and uncertain gains described in this lesson.
explanations.b: No major professional genetics body has called for mandatory use; the stated position runs in the opposite direction, urging caution.
explanations.c: The professional consensus explicitly rejects the claim that the technology is validated and ready for routine deployment.
explanations.d: Both scientific/technical limitations (modest gain, portability, pleiotropy) and ethical concerns have been raised together, not technical issues alone.

lessons.label: The ACMG/AMP Classification Framework

sections.heading: Five tiers, built from graded evidence codes
sections.body: Richards et al. (2015), the joint ACMG/AMP standards published in Genetics in Medicine, replaced ad hoc "this looks bad" variant calls with a shared rulebook. Every piece of evidence about a variant gets assigned to a named code at a strength level: for pathogenicity, PVS1 (very strong), PS1-PS4 (strong), PM1-PM6 (moderate), PP1-PP5 (supporting); for benignity, BA1 (stand-alone), BS1-BS4 (strong), BP1-BP7 (supporting). A curator collects whichever codes apply to a specific variant, then applies fixed combining rules — for example, one PVS1 plus one PS code, or two PS codes alone, both reach Pathogenic; one PVS1 with one PM reaches only Likely Pathogenic. The output is always one of five tiers: Pathogenic, Likely Pathogenic, Uncertain Significance (VUS), Likely Benign, or Benign. The system deliberately trades some sensitivity for reproducibility: two independent labs applying the same codes to the same variant should land on the same tier.

sections.heading: PVS1: the strongest single code, and why it isn't automatic
sections.body: PVS1 applies to a null variant — nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice-site, or a whole/partial exon deletion — in a gene where loss of function is an established disease mechanism (it does not apply in a gene that causes disease through gain-of-function or dominant-negative effects). Early practice treated any premature stop as full-strength PVS1, but not all truncations behave the same: a stop in the final exon may escape nonsense-mediated decay and produce a stable, partly functional protein. Abou Tayoun et al. (2018), the ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation (SVI) working group's PVS1 decision tree, formalized this by scoring exon position, NMD prediction, and whether skipping the affected exon preserves reading frame, downgrading PVS1 to Strong, Moderate, or even Supporting when the biology is less certain.

sections.heading: Putting numbers under the rules: the Bayesian reformulation
sections.body: Tavtigian et al. (2018) asked whether the 2015 combining rules were internally consistent, and modeled each evidence code as multiplying the prior odds of pathogenicity by a fixed factor — roughly 2.08x for Supporting, 4.33x for Moderate, 18.7x for Strong, and 350x for Very Strong. Taking logarithms turns multiplication into addition, giving point values (PVS1=8, PS=4, PM=2, PP=1) that sum to a total crossing fixed thresholds for each tier — and confirmed the 2015 rules were a reasonable approximation of a genuine Bayesian classifier. Tavtigian, Harrison, Boucher & Biesecker (2020) then refined this into a "naturally scaled" point system, and that refined version is now used directly by many ClinGen expert panels to combine evidence and to build gene-specific rule modifications.

lessons.workedExample: A student is classifying BRCA1 c.68_69delAG, a well-characterized Ashkenazi founder frameshift near the start of the gene. It is absent from gnomAD (PM2_Supporting) and a frameshift predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay well before the last exon, so full-strength PVS1 applies per the Abou Tayoun decision tree. Under the 2015 combining rules, PVS1 plus a single PM code (here PM2) reaches only Likely Pathogenic, since 1 Very Strong plus 1 Moderate falls short of the combinations required for Pathogenic. Under Tavtigian's points, though, PVS1 contributes 8 and PM2 contributes 2, for a total of 10 — at or above the Pathogenic threshold — so this is one of the documented cases where the Bayesian point system reaches Pathogenic while the original 2015 categorical rules cap the same evidence at Likely Pathogenic.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "walk me through why you called this Likely Pathogenic and not Pathogenic" is testing whether a student understands evidence strength as a graded system, not a gut call. A strong answer names the specific codes applied (which ones, at what strength) and states the combining rule that produced the tier; a weak answer says the variant "looked disruptive" or cites a single database hit with no code attached.

questions.prompt: PVS1 is the strongest pathogenic evidence code. To which situation does it apply?

options.text: Any missense variant predicted damaging by an in silico tool
A null variant (nonsense, frameshift, canonical splice-site, exon deletion) in a gene where loss of function is a known disease mechanism
Any variant absent from gnomAD
A variant seen in an affected relative

explanations.a: Missense predictions are in silico evidence, capped at Supporting strength (PP3), not PVS1.
explanations.b: Correct — PVS1 is reserved for null variants in genes where loss of function is the established mechanism, and does not apply in gain-of-function or dominant-negative genes.
explanations.c: Absence from population databases is PM2, a separate and much weaker code.
explanations.d: Segregation with disease in relatives is PP1/BS4 territory, not PVS1.

questions.prompt: According to Abou Tayoun et al. (2018), why might a premature stop codon receive less than full-strength PVS1?

options.text: Because stop codons are never pathogenic
Because a stop in the final exon may escape nonsense-mediated decay and produce a partly functional protein
Because PVS1 only applies to missense variants
Because ClinGen abolished PVS1 in 2018

explanations.a: Stop codons are frequently pathogenic; that is precisely why PVS1 exists.
explanations.b: Correct — the PVS1 decision tree downgrades strength when exon position, NMD escape, or exon-skipping rescue make a stable, partly functional protein plausible.
explanations.c: PVS1 applies to null variants (nonsense, frameshift, splice, exon deletion), not missense variants.
explanations.d: The 2018 paper refined how PVS1 is applied; it did not remove the code.

questions.prompt: Match each evidence-code prefix to its strength category in the ACMG/AMP framework.

right.text: Very strong pathogenic
Strong pathogenic
Stand-alone benign
Supporting benign

questions.explanation: PVS1 is the single very-strong pathogenic code; PS codes are strong pathogenic; BA1 is the stand-alone benign code (sufficient by itself); BP codes are supporting benign, the weakest benign tier.

questions.prompt: What did Tavtigian et al. (2018) demonstrate by modeling ACMG/AMP evidence as multiplying odds of pathogenicity?

options.text: That the 2015 combining rules were arbitrary and should be discarded
That each evidence strength level corresponds to a roughly fixed odds multiplier, and log-converting these gives additive point values consistent with the original rules
That only PVS1 evidence matters for classification
That population frequency is irrelevant to variant classification

explanations.a: The paper validated the rules as a reasonable approximation of a Bayesian classifier rather than discarding them.
explanations.b: Correct — Supporting/Moderate/Strong/Very Strong evidence corresponds to roughly 2.08x/4.33x/18.7x/350x odds multipliers; taking logs yields additive points (e.g., PVS1=8, PM=2) that reproduce the 2015 tiers.
explanations.c: The framework explicitly combines many code types, not PVS1 alone.
explanations.d: Population frequency (BA1/BS1/PM2) remains a core evidence category in both the 2015 rules and the point system.

lessons.label: Evidence Types in Practice

sections.heading: Population frequency: gnomAD and the max-credible-frequency calculation
sections.body: The Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD), pooling exome and genome data from over 800,000 individuals, is the default source for BA1: a variant above 5% frequency in any gnomAD subpopulation is stand-alone benign evidence, full stop, regardless of what else is known about it. But 5% is a blunt, disease-agnostic ceiling. Whiffin et al. (2017) formalized a sharper, disease-specific alternative: the maximum credible population allele frequency, calculated from disease prevalence, penetrance, and how much of the disease burden this one gene (and this one variant) plausibly explains. Worked through: a dominant disorder with 1-in-1,000 prevalence, where this variant is estimated to explain 25% of cases at 50% penetrance, yields a maximum credible frequency near 0.05% — so a variant actually observed at 2% in a gnomAD subpopulation is forty-fold too common to be causing that disorder, making the frequency alone strong-to-stand-alone benign evidence even though it sits well under the generic 5% BA1 cutoff. Ancestry matters here because a variant common in one subpopulation and rare in others still clears BA1/BS1 on whichever subpopulation it is common in.

sections.heading: In silico predictors: useful, capped, and not independent of each other
sections.body: REVEL (Ioannidis et al., 2016) is a meta-predictor trained to combine thirteen individual missense scores into one ensemble probability; CADD (Kircher et al., 2014) scores any variant type by how deleterious its genomic context looks; SpliceAI (Jaganathan et al., 2019) is a deep neural network predicting splice-altering effects from sequence alone; AlphaMissense (Cheng et al., 2023) repurposes AlphaFold's structural predictions to score missense pathogenicity genome-wide. All four are useful triage tools, but ACMG/AMP caps computational evidence at Supporting strength (PP3/BP4) by default — Pejaver et al. (2022) later calibrated specific thresholds per tool so a handful of well-validated predictors, used carefully, can reach Moderate. The critical practical rule: these tools share training data and underlying features, so running a variant through REVEL, CADD, and AlphaMissense and citing all three as separate PP3 hits is double-counting one correlated signal, not three independent lines of evidence — ClinGen guidance is to apply a single calibrated score.

sections.heading: Direct genetic evidence: segregation, de novo, hotspots, and case-control
sections.body: PP1 credits co-segregation of variant and disease within a family, formally via a LOD score; PS2 is much stronger and requires a confirmed de novo occurrence — the variant present in an affected child and absent in both parents on trio sequencing, with parentage (maternity and paternity) independently confirmed by markers, not merely assumed. PM1 applies when a variant falls in a well-established mutational hotspot or critical functional domain with little benign variation. PS4 draws on case-control data: the variant's frequency is significantly enriched in affected individuals relative to matched controls.

lessons.workedExample: A cardiology team finds a missense variant in MYH7 in a child with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Trio sequencing shows the variant in the child but neither parent, and independent marker-based testing confirms both parents are the child's biological parents with no family history of the condition — that combination earns PS2. The variant falls inside the myosin motor domain, a known mutational hotspot for HCM-causing substitutions (PM1), is absent from gnomAD (PM2), and scores 0.91 on REVEL, comfortably above the calibrated pathogenic threshold (PP3). The team correctly cites REVEL once, not REVEL-plus-CADD-plus-AlphaMissense as three separate supporting points, since the scores are not independent.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "which of these lines of evidence are actually independent?" is probing whether a student understands that ACMG evidence codes are not meant to be piled up uncritically — citing three correlated in silico tools as three separate supporting points, or double-counting a population frequency both as PM2 and as an in silico feature that used the same database, inflates a variant's apparent support without adding real information.

questions.prompt: A variant is observed at 2% frequency in a gnomAD subpopulation. For a rare dominant disorder whose maximum credible population allele frequency (Whiffin et al., 2017) works out to 0.05%, what does this imply?

options.text: The variant is too rare to interpret
The observed frequency is forty-fold higher than the disease can credibly tolerate, supporting a benign classification even though it is below the generic 5% BA1 threshold
The variant must be pathogenic because it is common
Frequency data are irrelevant once a maximum credible frequency has been calculated

explanations.a: 2% is common, not rare, relative to what a rare dominant disorder could plausibly tolerate.
explanations.b: Correct — disease-specific maximum credible frequency lets benign frequency evidence apply well below the generic 5% BA1 cutoff, because a truly disease-causing rare-disorder allele should not be this common.
explanations.c: Common frequency in a population argues against, not for, causing a rare disorder.
explanations.d: The calculation is only useful because it is compared against the observed frequency; it doesn't replace it.

questions.prompt: Why is it inappropriate to cite REVEL, CADD, and AlphaMissense scores as three separate PP3 supporting-evidence points for the same variant?

options.text: Because only CADD is a valid predictor
Because the tools share training data and features and are correlated, so stacking them double-counts one signal rather than combining independent evidence
Because in silico evidence can never be used at all
Because ACMG/AMP forbids the use of more than one software tool per variant

explanations.a: All four tools discussed are legitimate, calibrated predictors; the issue is independence, not validity.
explanations.b: Correct — because these predictors are built on overlapping features and training sets, ClinGen guidance is to apply one calibrated score rather than treat correlated tools as independent evidence.
explanations.c: In silico evidence is used routinely; it is capped at Supporting (or Moderate for calibrated tools per Pejaver et al., 2022), not excluded.
explanations.d: There's no blanket ban on running multiple tools for triage — the rule is about not citing correlated results as independent evidence lines.

questions.prompt: Match each evidence code to the type of data that supports it.

right.text: Confirmed de novo occurrence with verified parentage
Location in a mutational hotspot or critical functional domain
Significant enrichment in affected cases versus matched controls
Co-segregation with disease within a family (LOD score)

questions.explanation: PS2 requires a confirmed de novo variant with independently verified parentage; PM1 flags hotspot or functional-domain location; PS4 is case-control enrichment; PP1 is family segregation, formalized via LOD score.

questions.prompt: Order the steps required before a laboratory can assign PS2 (confirmed de novo) evidence to a variant.

items.text: Trio sequencing shows the variant present in the affected child but absent in both parents
Independent marker-based testing confirms both parents are the child's biological parents
No family history of the condition is confirmed
PS2 is assigned as strong pathogenic evidence

questions.explanation: PS2 requires first observing the apparent de novo occurrence on trio sequencing, then independently confirming parentage (ruling out a false de novo caused by a parentage error), then confirming there is no known family history, before the strong evidence code is applied.

lessons.label: The VUS Problem

sections.heading: Why most rare missense variants land in the middle
sections.body: A null variant gets PVS1 almost for free, because loss of function is a mechanistic given. A missense substitution has no such shortcut: whether swapping one amino acid for another actually breaks the protein has to be inferred from accumulated, individually weak evidence — a calibrated in silico score, absence from population databases, maybe a functional-domain location. Most unique missense variants identified in clinical sequencing are rare or private to one family, so the population, segregation, and functional data needed to push a call across the Likely Pathogenic or Likely Benign line simply doesn't exist yet at the time of testing. The result is structural, not a failure of any one lab: a large share of missense findings in clinical exome and panel testing resolve as Uncertain Significance, not because the variant is unusual, but because missense evidence takes more independent lines to accumulate than null-variant evidence does.

sections.heading: An uneven bucket: ancestry and reference-database composition
sections.body: BA1/BS1 frequency evidence and many calibrated in silico thresholds were built primarily from datasets historically dominated by individuals of European ancestry. A genuinely common, harmless variant in an underrepresented population can look falsely rare in gnomAD and falsely uncertain in ClinVar, simply because fewer matched genomes exist to prove it benign. On hereditary cancer panels, VUS rates run roughly 5-6% in patients of European ancestry but have been reported as high as 21% in patients of African ancestry — a gap driven by reference-database composition, not by any biological difference in variant pathogenicity.

sections.heading: What a VUS is (and is not) allowed to do
sections.body: By ACMG/AMP convention, a VUS carries no established disease association and must not drive a clinical management decision — no prophylactic surgery, no drug change, no altered surveillance — and must not be used for predictive or cascade testing in at-risk relatives, because a shared VUS tells a relative nothing about their actual risk. Mersch et al. (2018), a JAMA study of hereditary-cancer genetic testing, found that only a small minority of unique VUS were ever reclassified, but among those that were, the large majority moved down to benign or likely benign, versus a much smaller share moving up to pathogenic or likely pathogenic — when a VUS does resolve, it overwhelmingly resolves toward reassurance, not danger.

sections.heading: The documented cost of treating uncertainty as an answer
sections.body: That imbalance is exactly why over-calling a VUS causes real harm. Clinical-care studies tracking reclassification events have found cases where a VUS was acted on as if pathogenic — triggering intensified surveillance or prophylactic surgery — only for the variant to later be downgraded to benign, meaning the intervention addressed a risk that was never real. The strict rule against clinical action on an uncertain result exists specifically to prevent that outcome.

lessons.workedExample: A proband tests positive for a BRCA2 missense VUS. Her sister, unaffected, asks to be tested for "the family variant" to find out if she is at risk. A genetic counselor explains this is not appropriate predictive testing: because the variant's clinical significance is unknown, a positive result in the sister would not establish elevated risk, and a negative result would not establish safety — either result would only add confusion. The correct action is to offer testing on established pathogenic/likely pathogenic findings only, and to revisit the sister's options if and when the VUS is reclassified.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "what would you do if your gene of interest came back as a VUS in your model system or dataset" is testing whether a student understands that uncertainty is not a null result to discard or a positive result to act on — it is its own category with its own rules. A strong answer states plainly that a VUS cannot justify a clinical or predictive claim and explains why (no established disease association yet), rather than quietly treating an uncertain finding as supportive evidence for the student's hypothesis.

questions.prompt: Why do hereditary cancer panels report substantially higher VUS rates in patients of African ancestry (up to ~21%) than in patients of European ancestry (~5-6%)?

options.text: Because African-ancestry genomes contain intrinsically more disease-causing variants

Because reference and frequency databases like gnomAD and ClinVar have historically been dominated by European-ancestry data, making genuinely benign variants in underrepresented populations look falsely rare and uncertain
Because laboratories apply different ACMG/AMP rules by ancestry
Because VUS rates are unrelated to database composition and reflect true biological differences

explanations.a: There is no biological basis for one ancestry group carrying more disease-causing variants; the gap is a data-representation artifact.
explanations.b: Correct — with fewer matched genomes in reference databases, common, harmless variants in underrepresented populations can look rare enough to fail BA1/BS1, leaving them uncertain rather than resolved as benign.
explanations.c: The same ACMG/AMP rules apply regardless of ancestry; what differs is the completeness of the frequency evidence available to apply those rules.
explanations.d: The disparity is well attributed to reference-database composition, not to a true biological pathogenicity difference.

questions.prompt: In the Mersch et al. (2018) JAMA study, when a VUS was eventually reclassified, what was the predominant outcome?

options.text: Roughly equal numbers moved to pathogenic and to benign
The large majority moved down to benign or likely benign, versus a much smaller share moving up to pathogenic or likely pathogenic
Nearly all reclassified VUS moved up to pathogenic
Reclassification outcomes were not reported by direction

explanations.a: The outcomes were highly skewed, not roughly equal.
explanations.b: Correct — of the small share of VUS that were ever reclassified, the large majority were downgraded to benign/likely benign and only a much smaller share were upgraded to pathogenic/likely pathogenic.
explanations.c: The overwhelming majority moved toward benign, the opposite of this option.
explanations.d: The study specifically reported reclassification direction, not just that reclassification occurred.

questions.prompt: A clinician wants to test an unaffected relative to see if they carry the same VUS found in a proband, in order to reassure them about their cancer risk. Is this appropriate use of a VUS?

options.text: Yes, because a negative result would prove the relative is not at risk
No, because a VUS has no established disease association, so neither a positive nor a negative result in the relative would establish actual risk
Yes, because VUS results are treated identically to Likely Pathogenic results for cascade testing
No, because VUS testing is technically impossible in relatives

explanations.a: A negative result only shows the relative lacks that specific allele; it says nothing about their overall risk, and offers false reassurance if interpreted as clearance.
explanations.b: Correct — ACMG/AMP guidance is explicit that a VUS should not be used for predictive or cascade testing, since its clinical meaning is not yet established in either direction.
explanations.c: VUS and Likely Pathogenic are deliberately different tiers precisely because they carry different levels of actionable evidence.
explanations.d: The test is technically possible; the objection is about clinical appropriateness, not feasibility.

questions.prompt: What is the core reason a rare missense variant is more likely to end up classified as VUS than a rare nonsense (null) variant in the same gene?

options.text: Missense variants are always less damaging biologically

A null variant can claim PVS1 nearly automatically when loss of function is the disease mechanism, while a missense variant's effect must be inferred from multiple weaker, independently accumulated lines of evidence
Missense variants are not covered by the ACMG/AMP framework
Laboratories are required to classify all missense variants as VUS by policy

explanations.a: Missense variants vary widely in severity; some are fully benign and some are highly damaging — the classification difficulty is about evidence, not intrinsic severity.
explanations.b: Correct — PVS1 gives null variants a near-automatic strong evidence code in LOF-mechanism genes, while missense variants must accumulate several weaker codes (in silico, frequency, segregation, functional) to cross a classification threshold.
explanations.c: The ACMG/AMP framework explicitly includes missense-relevant codes such as PM1, PM5, PP2, and PP3.
explanations.d: There is no such blanket policy; missense variants are classified case-by-case on the evidence available.

lessons.label: Functional Assays and Multiplexed Assays of Variant Effect

sections.heading: From one variant at a time to thousands at once
sections.body: Classic functional assays test a single variant: clone it, express it, measure one readout, repeat for the next variant. That approach cannot keep pace with the millions of rare missense variants sequencing turns up. Multiplexed assays of variant effect (MAVEs) instead build a library covering nearly every possible substitution in a gene or domain and score them all in one pooled experiment. An early large-scale precursor was Kato et al. (2003), who used a yeast transactivation assay to functionally test roughly 2,314 TP53 substitutions in the DNA-binding domain, measured against a small panel of p53-responsive yeast reporter constructs. Matreyek et al. (2018) formalized the modern MAVE approach as VAMP-seq (variant abundance by massively parallel sequencing), sorting cells by fluorescence-tagged protein stability and deep-sequencing the pools to score 7,801 missense variants of PTEN and TPMT for intracellular abundance in one experiment.

sections.heading: Findlay et al. (2018): saturation genome editing of BRCA1
sections.body: Findlay et al. (2018), published in Nature, pushed this further with saturation genome editing (SGE): using CRISPR-Cas9 and homology-directed repair, the team installed nearly every possible single-nucleotide variant directly into the endogenous BRCA1 locus across 13 exons encoding the RING and BRCT domains, in haploid HAP1 cells. Haploid cells matter because there is no second, functional copy to mask a damaging variant's effect — cells carrying a variant that disables BRCA1 lose fitness and drop out of the population over several days of growth, detected by comparing variant frequencies before and after selection via deep sequencing. Function scores for nearly 4,000 SNVs came out cleanly bimodal — functional or non-functional — and matched existing ACMG classifications almost perfectly, resolving over 100 prior variants of uncertain significance. Related saturation approaches have since profiled PTEN, TP53, MSH2, and, more recently, BRCA2.

sections.heading: Calibrating an assay before it counts as evidence
sections.body: A functional score is not automatically strong evidence; it has to be calibrated. Brnich et al. (2019), the ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation working group's PS3/BS3 recommendations, formalized this using OddsPath: run the assay on a well-characterized truth set of already-classified pathogenic and benign variants, measure how cleanly the assay's scores separate the two groups, and convert that separation into an odds-of-pathogenicity value. Only then does the assay earn a specific PS3/BS3 evidence strength — Supporting, Moderate, Strong, or Very Strong — calibrated to how well it actually performs, not to how convincing the readout looks by eye. An assay validated on only a handful of controls, or without both pathogenic and benign representatives, cannot be assigned strong evidence regardless of how large the underlying screen is.

sections.heading: What a cell-line readout cannot tell you
sections.body: SGE in HAP1 cells measures one thing — cell fitness in one clonal cell line, over one selection window — as a proxy for BRCA1 function. It cannot capture tissue-specific splicing, age-dependent penetrance, or gene-environment interaction the way a real patient's decades-long disease course does, which is why calibration against real clinical outcomes, not just internal consistency, remains essential.

lessons.workedExample: A clinical lab has a BRCA1 missense VUS sitting in the RING domain. Consulting the Findlay et al. (2018) public function-score dataset, the variant clusters tightly with the non-functional (pathogenic-control) group rather than the functional (benign-control) group. Because the ClinGen SVI OddsPath calibration for this specific assay places non-functional scores at Strong evidence strength, the lab applies PS3_Strong. Combined with PM2 (absent from gnomAD) and PP3 (a calibrated REVEL score above threshold), the variant crosses from VUS to Likely Pathogenic — a reclassification made possible only because the assay had been calibrated against known controls first.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how do you know your assay's readout means what you think it means" is testing whether a student distinguishes a functional difference from calibrated evidence. The naive answer treats any visible difference between two conditions as proof of pathogenicity; the strong answer explains that the assay must first be run on variants of already-known status to establish what score threshold corresponds to which evidence strength, exactly as OddsPath calibration requires.

questions.prompt: Why did Findlay et al. (2018) use haploid HAP1 cells rather than a standard diploid cell line for BRCA1 saturation genome editing?

options.text: Haploid cells are easier to culture and cheaper, with no scientific bearing on the readout
In a haploid cell there is no second, functional BRCA1 copy to mask a damaging variant, so loss-of-function variants produce a clear fitness defect
Haploid cells cannot undergo CRISPR-Cas9 editing, so they were used as a negative control
HAP1 cells do not express BRCA1 at all

explanations.a: Culture convenience is not the scientific rationale; the haploid genotype is essential to the assay's logic.
explanations.b: Correct — with only one BRCA1 allele, a damaging variant cannot be masked by a second functional copy, so its effect on cell fitness (and thus its dropout from the population) is directly observable.
explanations.c: HAP1 cells are readily edited with CRISPR-Cas9 via homology-directed repair; that editability is what makes SGE possible.
explanations.d: HAP1 cells require functional BRCA1 for viability, which is exactly why loss-of-function variants cause the cells to drop out under selection.

questions.prompt: What does the OddsPath calibration described by Brnich et al. (2019) actually establish before a functional assay can contribute PS3/BS3 evidence?

options.text: That the assay was published in a high-impact journal
How cleanly the assay's scores separate a truth set of already-classified pathogenic and benign variants, converted into an odds-of-pathogenicity value that sets the evidence strength
That the assay was run at least 1,000 times
That the assay used CRISPR-Cas9 specifically

explanations.a: Journal prestige has no bearing on OddsPath calibration.
explanations.b: Correct — the assay is run on variants of known pathogenic and benign status, and how well it separates them determines the odds of pathogenicity, which maps to a specific evidence strength.
explanations.c: There is no fixed replicate-count rule; calibration depends on the composition and separation of the control set, not raw repetition count.
explanations.d: Calibration applies to any functional assay type, not specifically CRISPR-based ones.

questions.prompt: Match each gene to the multiplexed functional assay approach used to study it.

right.text: Saturation genome editing scoring cell fitness/dropout in haploid HAP1 cells (Findlay et al., 2018)
VAMP-seq scoring intracellular protein abundance (Matreyek et al., 2018)
Yeast transactivation assay scoring transcriptional activity (Kato et al., 2003)

questions.explanation: Findlay et al. used saturation genome editing and fitness dropout in HAP1 cells for BRCA1; Matreyek et al. used VAMP-seq protein-abundance sorting for PTEN (and TPMT); Kato et al. used a yeast-based transactivation assay for TP53.

questions.prompt: What is a genuine limitation of a saturation-genome-editing function score, even after proper OddsPath calibration?

options.text: It cannot be used as evidence at all under ACMG/AMP rules
It reflects one molecular readout in one clonal cell line under one selection condition, and cannot capture tissue-specific, age-dependent, or whole-organism aspects of the real disease
It only works for genes with fewer than 100 exons
It cannot distinguish missense variants from nonsense variants

explanations.a: Calibrated functional evidence is explicitly usable as PS3/BS3 evidence under ACMG/AMP rules.
explanations.b: Correct — a cell-line fitness or abundance readout is a proxy for one aspect of gene function, and does not capture the full, tissue-specific, age-dependent biology of a whole-organism disease.
explanations.c: The method's applicability isn't limited by exon count; it is limited by editability and by whether a selectable phenotype exists.
explanations.d: SGE can and does profile missense, nonsense, and splice-relevant variants alike within the edited region.

lessons.label: Databases, Conflicting Calls, and Gene-Disease Validity

sections.heading: ClinVar: a public archive, not a single verdict
sections.body: ClinVar, hosted by NCBI, is not itself an interpretation authority — it is a public archive where any clinical laboratory, clinic, or researcher can submit an interpretation with whatever evidence they choose to attach. A star system communicates how much confidence to place in an entry: 0 stars means no assertion criteria were provided; 1 star means a single submitter with criteria, or multiple submitters who disagree; 2 stars means multiple submitters agree; 3 stars means review by a ClinGen expert panel; 4 stars means the classification is enshrined in a practice guideline. Conflicts are common, but Harrison et al. (2017), a ClinGen pilot across four clinical laboratories, showed many are fixable: of 6,169 variants interpreted by at least two labs, 88.3% were already concordant, and among the 724 that were not, reassessing 242 of them with current criteria and shared internal data resolved 87.2% (211), lifting overall concordance to 91.7%. Most conflict, in other words, is stale review catching up to shared evidence, not irreconcilable scientific disagreement.

sections.heading: ClinGen variant curation expert panels
sections.body: ClinGen organizes gene- or disease-specific Variant Curation Expert Panels (VCEPs) that write formal rule specifications adapting the general ACMG/AMP codes to that gene's biology (adjusting PM1 hotspots, BA1/BS1 frequency thresholds, or PS3/BS3 calibration, as with the ATM and APC examples used elsewhere in this unit) and then apply them collectively to reach 3-star, ClinVar-endorsed consensus calls that supersede individual-lab submissions for that variant.

sections.heading: Gene-disease validity is a separate question from variant classification
sections.body: Before asking whether a specific variant is pathogenic, there is a prior question: does this gene even cause this disease? ClinGen's Gene-Disease Validity framework scores that relationship on a six-tier scale — Definitive, Strong, Moderate, Limited, Disputed, Refuted — independent of any one variant. ClinGen's Hereditary Hearing Loss expert panel has systematically evaluated hearing-loss genes and found that only roughly half reach Definitive status, with a substantial share landing at Limited, Disputed, or Refuted — meaning a meaningful share of genes sold on commercial hearing-loss panels carry thin evidence for causing the disease at all, independent of how any individual variant in them is classified.

sections.heading: OMIM, HGMD, LOVD, and the literature-propagated false-pathogenic claim
sections.body: OMIM catalogs gene-phenotype relationships narratively, without ACMG-style variant scoring; HGMD aggregates variants reported as disease-causing in the literature, historically without systematically re-checking each claim against current population data; LOVD quality varies widely because it is curated locus-by-locus by different individual groups. Bell et al. (2011), a large carrier-screening study, found HGMD-listed "disease-causing" variants occurring at frequencies — some above 5% in their cohort — flatly incompatible with the severe recessive phenotypes they were supposedly causing, a signature of an early, under-evidenced claim being cited and re-cited without anyone re-verifying it. Before quoting a variant's status, the practical routine is: check the ClinVar star rating and look for a VCEP review, cross-check the raw gnomAD frequency directly rather than trusting any single database's label, and check whether the underlying literature actually reports segregation or functional data — or just one early case report.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to write "this variant is a known pathogenic mutation, per HGMD" in a project. Following the routine, they instead look it up in ClinVar and find a 1-star entry with two labs disagreeing, no VCEP review. Checking gnomAD directly, the variant appears at 3% frequency in one subpopulation — far too common for the severe dominant disorder it was originally reported to cause in a single 1990s case report. The student correctly reports it as "a variant with a disputed, literature-propagated pathogenic claim that population frequency data argue against," rather than repeating the unverified HGMD label.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how did you verify that assertion, and how confident is the source" is testing whether a student treats a database hit as a citation to be checked, not a fact to be repeated. The strong answer names the star rating or VCEP status and shows a cross-check (e.g., gnomAD frequency) rather than citing a single database entry as if it were settled.

questions.prompt: What does a 3-star ClinVar review status specifically indicate?

options.text: A single lab submitted an interpretation without assertion criteria
The variant was reviewed and classified by a ClinGen expert panel (VCEP)
Two or more submitters agree but no expert panel has reviewed it
The classification is enshrined in an official practice guideline

explanations.a: That describes 0 stars, the lowest confidence tier.
explanations.b: Correct — 3 stars specifically means a ClinGen Variant Curation Expert Panel reviewed and classified the variant, which supersedes individual-lab submissions.
explanations.c: Multiple concordant submitters without expert review is the 2-star tier, not 3.
explanations.d: A practice-guideline-level classification is the 4-star tier, above expert panel review.

questions.prompt: In the Harrison et al. (2017) four-laboratory ClinVar pilot, what happened when 242 discordant variants were reassessed with current criteria and shared data?

options.text: None were resolved, confirming conflicts are permanent
87.2% (211) were resolved, raising overall concordance from 88.3% to 91.7%
All 724 originally discordant variants were reassessed and resolved
The labs stopped sharing data after the pilot due to poor results

explanations.a: The opposite occurred — most reassessed conflicts were resolved.
explanations.b: Correct — reassessing 242 of the 724 discordant variants resolved 211 (87.2%) of them, lifting overall concordance from 88.3% to 91.7%.
explanations.c: Only a subset (242 of 724) were reassessed in this pilot, not the full discordant set.
explanations.d: The pilot's success argued for more data sharing, not less; it was a ClinGen-supported initiative that continued.

questions.prompt: How does ClinGen's Gene-Disease Validity classification differ from ACMG/AMP variant classification?

options.text: They are the same framework applied at different scales
Gene-Disease Validity asks whether a gene causes a given disease at all (Definitive through Refuted), a prior question independent of any single variant's pathogenicity
Gene-Disease Validity only applies to genes with zero known pathogenic variants
Gene-Disease Validity replaced ACMG/AMP variant classification in 2015

explanations.a: They are related but distinct frameworks: one scores a gene-disease relationship, the other scores an individual variant.
explanations.b: Correct — Gene-Disease Validity is a six-tier scale (Definitive, Strong, Moderate, Limited, Disputed, Refuted) evaluating whether the gene itself is established as causing the disease, separate from classifying any particular variant in it.
explanations.c: It applies to any gene-disease claim under evaluation, regardless of how many pathogenic variants have been reported.
explanations.d: Both frameworks coexist; Gene-Disease Validity addresses a different question than variant-level ACMG/AMP classification.

questions.prompt: Match each resource to its defining characteristic.

right.text: Public archive of submitted variant interpretations with a star confidence system
Narrative catalog of gene-phenotype relationships, not variant-level ACMG scoring
Aggregates literature-reported disease variants, historically without systematic re-verification against population data
Locus-specific databases curated individually, with quality varying widely by curator

questions.explanation: ClinVar is the star-rated public archive of submitted interpretations; OMIM narratively catalogs gene-phenotype relationships; HGMD aggregates literature-reported variants without systematic re-verification, which is how Bell et al. (2011) found stale false-pathogenic claims; LOVD quality depends on the individual curator of each locus-specific database.

lessons.label: Secondary Findings, Reanalysis, and the Duty to Recontact

sections.heading: The ACMG secondary findings list, and why it started controversial
sections.body: When a patient's exome or genome is sequenced for one reason — say, an undiagnosed neurodevelopmental disorder — the data technically contains everything else in their genome too. ACMG's secondary findings (SF) list tells labs to actively look, in that data, for pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in a fixed set of genes tied to serious, medically actionable conditions, regardless of why the test was ordered. The current list, ACMG SF v3.2, covers 81 genes spanning hereditary breast/ovarian cancer (BRCA1/BRCA2), Lynch syndrome (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM), familial hypercholesterolemia (LDLR, APOB, PCSK9), long-QT syndrome (KCNQ1, KCNH2, SCN5A), and Marfan syndrome (FBN1), among others — chosen because finding the variant changes management: surveillance, prophylactic surgery, statins, or beta-blockers. The original 2013 list of 56 genes was mandatory with no opt-out at all, which proved contentious enough that ACMG revised the policy within about a year to let patients decline secondary findings as a block.

sections.heading: Autonomy versus benefit: the opt-out debate
sections.body: The core tension is patient autonomy — the right not to know, and to avoid anxiety, insurance-related worry, or unwanted information about future disease — against the clinical benefit of catching an actionable, serious condition before it manifests. Current consensus lets a patient opt out of the whole SF category, but not gene-by-gene, and real-world implementation is inconsistent: surveys of clinical labs have found some effectively run the policy as opt-in rather than true opt-out, quietly weakening the autonomy protection the policy was designed to guarantee.

sections.heading: Research sequencing and the pediatric question
sections.body: Clinical sequencing under ACMG guidance actively screens for SF genes; research sequencing generally carries no such obligation unless the study's own protocol specifies returning results, though newer frameworks argue researchers share some responsibility to recontact participants when reinterpretation changes a result's meaning. Pediatric return is its own fault line: the field has long discouraged returning predictive adult-onset results to children, to preserve their future right to decide for themselves — yet ACMG recommends returning adult-onset actionable SF even in pediatric patients, reasoning that early identification (for example, a childhood LDLR finding supporting early statin therapy) outweighs the deferred-autonomy cost. Critics counter that trading a child's future choice for early intervention isn't obviously the right trade for every gene on the list.

sections.heading: Reanalysis lifts yield; recontact duty stays unsettled
sections.body: Genomic knowledge keeps moving after the initial report: genes get newly linked to disease, variant classifications get updated, and analysis pipelines improve. Periodic reanalysis of previously undiagnosed exomes has been found to raise diagnostic yield by roughly 10-15% after a few years. But whose job it is to act on a changed classification remains genuinely unsettled — ACMG's recontact guidance describes a shared-responsibility model (the laboratory flags reinterpretation, the ordering clinician manages patient recontact) with an ethical rather than a firm legal duty in most jurisdictions.

lessons.workedExample: A child had exome sequencing four years ago for an undiagnosed neurodevelopmental condition; the report was negative, and the family had opted out of secondary findings. During routine periodic reanalysis, the lab finds that a variant flagged as VUS at the time has since been reclassified Likely Pathogenic in a gene newly linked to the child's phenotype. Under the shared-responsibility model, the laboratory is expected to flag the reinterpretation and notify the ordering clinic; the clinic is then expected to recontact the family. No law compels either step in most places, but professional guidance treats skipping them as an ethical lapse — the family finally gets a diagnosis four years after the original negative result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "why not just screen every gene for every patient automatically" is testing whether a student sees secondary findings and reanalysis as policy tradeoffs, not pure technical capability — cost, consent, patient autonomy, and workflow all constrain what "we could check for this" turns into "we should report this," and a strong answer names the specific tradeoff (autonomy vs. benefit, or deferred consent for children) rather than treating more genomic information as an unqualified good.

questions.prompt: Why did the original 2013 ACMG secondary findings policy (56 genes, no opt-out) prove controversial enough to be revised within about a year?

options.text: It required patients to pay extra for secondary findings analysis
It gave patients no way to decline receiving findings unrelated to why they were tested, conflicting with the principle of patient autonomy
It only covered pediatric patients
It required a second blood draw

explanations.a: Cost was not the central objection raised against the original policy.
explanations.b: Correct — mandating return of findings unrelated to the original testing indication, with no opt-out, was seen as overriding a patient's right not to know, prompting ACMG to add an opt-out.
explanations.c: The original list applied broadly, not only to pediatric patients; the pediatric question is a separate, ongoing debate.
explanations.d: Secondary findings are drawn from the same sequencing data already generated, requiring no additional sample.

questions.prompt: What is the central tension in the secondary-findings opt-out debate?

options.text: Whether sequencing technology is accurate enough to detect the variants at all
Patient autonomy (the right not to know, and to avoid unwanted information) versus the clinical benefit of catching an actionable condition early
Whether the 81 genes on the list cause any disease at all
Cost of sequencing versus cost of standard clinical care

explanations.a: Detection accuracy for these well-established genes is not the debated issue.
explanations.b: Correct — the policy balances a patient's right to decline unsolicited information against the clear clinical benefit of early detection for actionable conditions.
explanations.c: SF genes are selected specifically because they have established, actionable gene-disease relationships.
explanations.d: The debate centers on consent and benefit, not on the marginal cost of the analysis.

questions.prompt: What is the specific objection to ACMG's recommendation to return adult-onset actionable secondary findings in pediatric patients?

options.text: Children's DNA cannot be sequenced accurately
It trades away the child's future autonomy to decide for themselves whether to learn adult-onset predictive information, in exchange for earlier intervention
Pediatric patients are never included in the ACMG SF list
Adult-onset conditions cannot be detected by sequencing until adulthood

explanations.a: Sequencing accuracy in children is not the concern here.
explanations.b: Correct — the field's traditional norm defers predictive adult-onset testing until the child can consent; returning it earlier trades that future autonomy for the benefit of earlier management.
explanations.c: ACMG explicitly recommends returning applicable adult-onset SF findings in pediatric patients, with parental opt-out available.
explanations.d: The underlying variant is present and detectable from birth; only the disease's typical onset is in adulthood.

questions.prompt: Match each ACMG secondary-findings condition category to a gene it includes.

right.text: BRCA1/BRCA2
MLH1
LDLR
FBN1

questions.explanation: ACMG SF v3.2 includes BRCA1/BRCA2 for hereditary breast/ovarian cancer, MLH1 (among other mismatch-repair genes) for Lynch syndrome, LDLR for familial hypercholesterolemia, and FBN1 for Marfan syndrome.

units.label: Medical Genetics in Practice: Screening, Counseling, and Cases

lessons.label: Newborn Screening as a Population Program

sections.heading: Guthrie's Bacterial Assay and the PKU Case
sections.body: Robert Guthrie developed the bacterial inhibition assay in 1963: a spot of blood dried on filter paper is punched out and placed on a plate of Bacillus subtilis whose growth is normally blocked by a chemical inhibitor — bacterial growth resumes in proportion to how much phenylalanine is in the blood, giving a cheap, semi-quantitative readout from a single heel-prick. This let states screen every newborn for phenylketonuria (PKU), an autosomal recessive block in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase that, left untreated, causes severe intellectual disability within the first years of life. The case for screening rests on the fact that a phenylalanine-restricted diet started in the first weeks of life prevents that damage almost entirely — a rare case where a genetic diagnosis converts directly into a simple, effective intervention, which is why PKU became the template disease that justified population-wide newborn screening at all.

sections.heading: From One Spot to Dozens of Metabolites
sections.body: The dried blood spot outlived Guthrie's bacterial plate. Modern programs punch the same card but read it with tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), which fragments and weighs dozens of amino acids, acylcarnitines, and other metabolites from a single spot in minutes — enough to flag PKU alongside conditions like MCAD deficiency and maple syrup urine disease in one run. The US Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP), maintained by the Department of Health and Human Services, lists roughly 35 core conditions judged to benefit from early detection plus around 26 secondary conditions the same tests pick up incidentally. States choose their own panels on top of RUSP's recommendation, so coverage is not fully uniform nationally.

sections.heading: Screening Is Not Diagnosis
sections.body: A positive newborn screen is a flag, not a diagnosis — confirmatory testing always follows. Because missing a treatable disease is catastrophic and retesting is cheap, thresholds are set for high sensitivity, which mathematically guarantees many false positives: a family gets an urgent call, drives to a specialist, and waits days for a normal confirmatory result — real anxiety for what is usually a false alarm. James Wilson and Gunnar Jungner's 1968 WHO criteria still frame the tradeoff: screen only for conditions with an important, treatable, latent phase and an available treatment. That framework is under new strain as pilot programs — BabySeq in Boston and Genomics England's Newborn Genomes Programme — test whether whole-genome sequencing should supplement or replace the biochemical panel, since sequencing surfaces variants of uncertain significance and adult-onset risks a heel-prick spot never could.

lessons.workedExample: A newborn's day-3 heel-prick MS/MS screen shows phenylalanine at four times the cutoff. The state lab flags it within 24 hours; the family is called in for a confirmatory plasma amino acid panel while doctors start a low-phenylalanine formula as a precaution. The confirmatory test comes back elevated, and the child is diagnosed with classic PKU by two weeks of age — well inside the treatment window pediatricians target, since long-term IQ outcomes track closely with how early diet starts. A different family gets the same urgent call for a slightly elevated value that turns out to be transient, tied to the newborn's still-maturing liver enzymes; the confirmatory test is normal. Both calls were the correct behavior of a high-sensitivity threshold — one caught real disease in time, the other cost a family two anxious days for nothing.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask why newborn screening tolerates so many false positives because it tests whether a student understands sensitivity and specificity as a designed policy tradeoff, not a lab failure. A strong answer names the Wilson-Jungner logic — screen only when a treatable latent phase exists — and connects the high-sensitivity threshold to a cost asymmetry: missing PKU causes irreversible harm, while a false positive costs a stressful week and a repeat blood draw. A student who can also explain why sequencing-based newborn screening reopens this debate, since it generates variants of uncertain significance a heel-prick never produced, shows they grasp that the ethical tradeoff scales with the technology, not just the disease.

questions.prompt: What did Guthrie's original bacterial inhibition assay actually measure to detect PKU?

options.text: DNA sequence at the phenylalanine hydroxylase gene
How much bacterial growth resumed on a plate whose inhibitor is overcome by phenylalanine in the blood spot
The infant's blood glucose level
Antibody levels against phenylalanine

explanations.a: Guthrie's 1963 assay predates practical DNA sequencing; it read a metabolite level, not a gene sequence.
explanations.b: Correct — the assay measured bacterial growth resuming in proportion to blood phenylalanine, a biochemical proxy, not a direct genetic test.
explanations.c: Glucose was not the analyte; PKU screening targets phenylalanine, not blood sugar.
explanations.d: The assay used a growth-inhibition mechanism, not an antibody/immunoassay method.

questions.prompt: Why are newborn screening thresholds set for high sensitivity even though this generates many false positives?

options.text: Because false positives are cheaper for hospitals to bill
Because missing a treatable disease like PKU causes irreversible harm, while a false positive costs only anxiety and a repeat test
Because state law requires every test to catch 100% of cases with no exceptions
Because MS/MS cannot be tuned for specificity

explanations.a: Billing is not the rationale; the tradeoff is about harm avoided versus anxiety caused.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the Wilson-Jungner logic: since a missed diagnosis is catastrophic and irreversible while a false positive just costs a retest, thresholds are deliberately biased toward catching every true case.
explanations.c: No screening test achieves literal 100% sensitivity; the policy choice is to bias toward high sensitivity, not guarantee perfection.
explanations.d: MS/MS can be tuned, but the deliberate choice is to favor sensitivity over specificity, not a technical limitation.

questions.prompt: Match each newborn-screening element to what it does.

right.text: 1963 method reading phenylalanine from bacterial growth on a dried blood spot
Modern method that reads dozens of metabolites from one blood spot at once
1968 WHO framework for which conditions justify population screening
The US list of roughly 35 core plus ~26 secondary screened conditions

questions.explanation: Guthrie's assay was the original 1963 bacterial-growth method for phenylalanine; MS/MS replaced it with multiplexed metabolite detection; the Wilson-Jungner criteria set the 1968 policy logic for what belongs on a screening program; RUSP is the current US panel built on that logic.

questions.prompt: What is the central debate around adding genomic sequencing to newborn screening, as illustrated by BabySeq and Genomics England's Newborn Genomes Programme?

options.text: Sequencing is too slow to return results before symptoms appear
Sequencing generates variants of uncertain significance and adult-onset findings that a biochemical heel-prick panel never surfaced, reopening the Wilson-Jungner tradeoff at larger scale
Sequencing cannot detect PKU at all
Sequencing eliminates the need for any confirmatory testing

explanations.a: Turnaround time is not the core ethical debate described; the issue is what kinds of results sequencing produces.
