explanations.b: Correct — sequencing surfaces uncertain and adult-onset findings the biochemical panel was never designed to generate, forcing the same 'should we screen for this' question onto a much larger set of results.
explanations.c: Sequencing can in principle detect PKU-causing variants; the debate is about the broader results it also returns.
explanations.d: Confirmatory testing remains necessary; sequencing does not remove the screening-versus-diagnosis distinction.

lessons.label: Carrier Screening and Founder Populations

sections.heading: Why Some Populations Carry More of a Disease Allele
sections.body: A founder effect occurs when a population descends from a small ancestral group, so an allele one founder happened to carry can reach a much higher frequency than in the general population, purely from drift and reduced diversity — not selection for the allele itself. Ashkenazi Jewish populations, descending from a demographic bottleneck within the last several centuries, carry elevated carrier frequencies for Tay-Sachs disease (HEXA, roughly 1 in 30 versus roughly 1 in 300 in the general population), Canavan disease (ASPA), Gaucher disease type 1 (GBA, carrier frequency as high as roughly 1 in 15, the most common of the group), and the BRCA1 185delAG founder mutation, which alone accounts for a large share of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer risk in this population. French Canadians in Quebec, founded by a few thousand seventeenth-century settlers, carry their own distinct Tay-Sachs founder mutation — different from the Ashkenazi allele, a case of independent founder effects converging on the same disease — plus elevated tyrosinemia type I concentrated in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region, traceable to a small number of founding families. Finland's isolated settlement history and geographic isolation produced the 'Finnish disease heritage,' roughly forty recessive conditions enriched there and rare elsewhere, a textbook case of drift acting independently of any selective advantage.

sections.heading: Screening's Measured Effect: Tay-Sachs Since the 1970s
sections.body: Since carrier screening and counseling began in Ashkenazi Jewish communities in the early 1970s, Tay-Sachs births in that population have fallen by more than 90% — one of medical genetics' longest-running population success stories. Part of that program is Dor Yeshorim, founded in 1983 by Rabbi Josef Ekstein after losing four children to Tay-Sachs; it screens Orthodox Jewish teenagers anonymously before matchmaking begins and returns not individual carrier status but only a compatibility flag for two coded IDs, avoiding stigma or disclosure that could affect a person's marriage prospects.

sections.heading: Targeted Versus Pan-Ethnic Panels, and What Comes Next
sections.body: Targeted ethnic panels test a handful of conditions known to be elevated in a specific ancestry, which is cheap and high-yield but misses risk from ancestry a patient does not report or does not know about. Expanded pan-ethnic panels instead screen hundreds of genes regardless of stated ancestry, catching more but at higher cost and with more uncertain, low-frequency findings to interpret. Either way, a negative result never reaches zero — residual risk remains because panels do not include every possible disease-causing variant. A couple who both screen positive as carriers of the same recessive condition face real reproductive choices: preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disease (PGT-M) during IVF, donor gametes, prenatal diagnosis of a natural pregnancy, or continuing the pregnancy with delivery prepared at a center equipped for an affected newborn.

lessons.workedExample: A couple planning pregnancy, both of Ashkenazi Jewish descent on one side and unknown ancestry on the other, is offered a choice: a targeted Ashkenazi panel covering Tay-Sachs, Canavan, and Gaucher, or an expanded pan-ethnic panel covering several hundred recessive genes. They choose the expanded panel because of the unknown-ancestry parent. Results show the Ashkenazi partner is a Tay-Sachs carrier; the other partner screens negative for Tay-Sachs but the report also flags a residual risk, since no panel detects every possible HEXA variant. Because only one partner is a confirmed carrier, their own reproductive risk for Tay-Sachs specifically is low, but the counselor still discusses residual risk explicitly rather than treating the negative result as a guarantee.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes founder-population carrier screening to see whether a student can separate genetic drift from natural selection as the explanation for elevated allele frequency, since 'the population evolved resistance' is a common but wrong instinct. A strong answer names the bottleneck mechanism, cites a specific carrier frequency (Tay-Sachs at roughly 1 in 30 in Ashkenazi Jews versus 1 in 300 generally), and can explain why a screening program driven by community buy-in, like Dor Yeshorim's anonymous matching, achieved a measured population-level outcome rather than just individual test results — showing the student connects the population genetics to the public-health program built on top of it.

questions.prompt: What mechanism explains why Tay-Sachs carrier frequency is elevated in Ashkenazi Jewish populations?

options.text: Natural selection favored the Tay-Sachs allele because carriers had a survival advantage
A founder effect: descent from a small ancestral population let an allele one founder carried drift to unusually high frequency
The mutation rate at the HEXA gene is unusually high specifically in this population
Consanguineous marriage is required by religious law

explanations.a: Selection for a carrier advantage is not the established explanation used here; the lesson attributes the elevated frequency to founder effect and drift, not fitness benefit.
explanations.b: Correct — a founder effect from a demographic bottleneck lets drift raise an allele's frequency in a descendant population regardless of any selective advantage.
explanations.c: Elevated frequency reflects population history (founder effect), not a gene-specific elevated mutation rate.
explanations.d: Consanguinity is not a stated cause here; founder effect from population history is the mechanism described.

questions.prompt: Why does Dor Yeshorim return only an anonymous compatibility flag rather than each person's individual carrier status?

options.text: Because carrier status cannot be tested reliably
To avoid stigma or disclosure that could affect an individual's marriage prospects within the community
Because the test only works on couples, not individuals
Because Israeli law forbids disclosing genetic results

explanations.a: The test is reliable; the anonymous design is a social choice, not a technical limitation.
explanations.b: Correct — returning only a coded-ID compatibility result rather than individual carrier status avoids stigmatizing a carrier or affecting their prospects in matchmaking.
explanations.c: Each person is tested individually; it is the reporting format, not the testing itself, that is paired and anonymous.
explanations.d: This is a program design choice, not a description of a specific national law.

questions.prompt: Match each founder population to its associated elevated-frequency condition.

right.text: Tay-Sachs, Canavan, Gaucher, BRCA1 185delAG
Tyrosinemia type I and a distinct Tay-Sachs founder mutation
The 'Finnish disease heritage,' roughly 40 enriched recessive conditions

questions.explanation: Each population's distinct settlement bottleneck elevated a different set of recessive disease alleles: Ashkenazi Jewish populations for Tay-Sachs/Canavan/Gaucher/BRCA1 185delAG, Quebec's Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region for tyrosinemia I and its own Tay-Sachs allele, and Finland for its distinctive disease heritage.

questions.prompt: A couple both screen negative on a targeted ethnic carrier panel for a recessive disease. What should they understand about that result?

options.text: Their risk of having an affected child for that disease is now exactly zero
A negative result lowers risk but leaves residual risk, since no panel tests every possible disease-causing variant
The test must be repeated every year to remain valid
A negative result means they are not carriers of any recessive disease

explanations.a: Panels do not include every possible pathogenic variant, so residual risk is never truly zero.
explanations.b: Correct — carrier screening substantially lowers but does not eliminate risk, because rare or novel variants outside the panel's coverage are not detected.
explanations.c: Carrier status is based on inherited DNA and does not change over time, so annual retesting is not the issue.
explanations.d: A negative result is specific to the conditions tested on that panel, not a guarantee against all recessive disease.

lessons.label: Prenatal Testing and the NIPT Math

sections.heading: What NIPT Actually Measures
sections.body: Noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) sequences cell-free DNA (cfDNA) fragments circulating in maternal plasma, most of which comes from the mother but a fraction — the 'fetal fraction,' typically around 10% — comes from placental trophoblast cells and stands in for fetal DNA. Fetal fraction is lower with higher maternal BMI, since a larger maternal blood volume dilutes the placental contribution, and lower before roughly 10 weeks of gestation, before enough placental cfDNA has accumulated; most labs require a minimum fetal fraction to report a result at all. Critically, NIPT does not produce a fetal karyotype or directly visualize chromosomes. It counts how many sequencing reads map to each chromosome and flags a statistically significant excess or deficit — for trisomy 21, an over-representation of chromosome-21 reads relative to the expected proportion — which is counting statistics, not direct fetal cytogenetics.

sections.heading: Why the Same Test Has Wildly Different Reliability by Condition
sections.body: Even a test with very high sensitivity and specificity produces a positive predictive value (PPV) that depends heavily on how common the condition is in the population being tested — a direct consequence of Bayes' theorem. For trisomy 21, whose prevalence rises steeply with maternal age, NIPT's PPV in an older mother is around 90%: most positives are real. But for rare microdeletion syndromes such as 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, whose prevalence is far lower in the general population, PPV on the same assay falls well under 50%, often under 10% — because at low prevalence, the test's imperfect specificity generates more false positives than the tiny number of true cases can outweigh, even though the underlying assay performance has not changed.

sections.heading: Why a Positive Result Still Needs a Diagnostic Follow-Up
sections.body: Several biological sources make NIPT positive results wrong that a karyotype would catch. Confined placental mosaicism occurs when a chromosomal abnormality exists in placental cells but not in the fetus itself, since cfDNA reflects the placenta rather than the fetus directly. A vanishing twin — a co-twin that stopped developing early in pregnancy — can keep shedding abnormal cfDNA that gets misattributed to the surviving fetus. An occult maternal malignancy or maternal chromosomal mosaicism can shed its own abnormal cfDNA into the same plasma sample. Because of these pathways, a positive NIPT result is a screening flag, never a diagnosis — chorionic villus sampling (CVS) or amniocentesis, which directly sample placental or fetal cells for karyotype or microarray analysis, remain required to confirm any result before an irreversible decision is made.

lessons.workedExample: A 40-year-old patient's NIPT flags high risk for trisomy 21, using an assay with roughly 99% sensitivity and 99.9% specificity. Because trisomy 21 prevalence at her age is around 1 in 100, the resulting PPV computes to roughly 90% — about 9 in 10 patients with this exact result truly have an affected fetus, so her counselor recommends confirmatory CVS while noting the result is fairly likely to be confirmed. A 26-year-old patient on the same assay is flagged high risk for a 22q11.2 microdeletion. Despite similar assay sensitivity and specificity, the condition's much lower prevalence means PPV here is well under 50% — most patients who get this specific flag do not have an affected fetus. Her counselor explains that base rate explicitly and still recommends amniocentesis before any decision is made, since only the diagnostic test can resolve it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe NIPT's PPV math because many students conflate 'the test is 99% accurate' with 'a positive result means 99% chance of disease' — the base-rate fallacy that shows up across medical screening generally, not just prenatal testing. A strong answer names why the same assay yields a roughly 90% PPV for trisomy 21 in an older mother but well under 50% for a rare microdeletion like 22q11.2, ties that gap explicitly to disease prevalence rather than test quality, and states plainly that NIPT is a screen, not a diagnosis, requiring CVS or amniocentesis before any irreversible decision.

questions.prompt: What does NIPT directly measure to flag a chromosomal condition?

options.text: A direct microscopic image of fetal chromosomes
A statistical over- or under-representation of sequencing reads mapping to a given chromosome in maternal plasma cell-free DNA
Antibodies in maternal blood against fetal proteins
Fetal heart rate patterns

explanations.a: A karyotype visualizes chromosomes directly; NIPT does not — that is precisely why it is a screen, not a diagnostic test.
explanations.b: Correct — NIPT sequences maternal plasma cfDNA and counts reads per chromosome, flagging statistically significant deviations from the expected proportion.
explanations.c: NIPT is a DNA sequencing-based test, not an antibody-based immunoassay.
explanations.d: Heart rate monitoring is unrelated to cfDNA-based chromosomal screening.

questions.prompt: Why does NIPT's positive predictive value differ so much between trisomy 21 in an older mother and a rare microdeletion like 22q11.2, given similar assay sensitivity and specificity?

options.text: The lab uses a completely different, less accurate assay for microdeletions
Lower disease prevalence means a similarly imperfect test generates proportionally more false positives relative to true positives
Microdeletions cannot be detected by cell-free DNA at all
Older mothers have more fetal fraction, which is the real driver of PPV

explanations.a: The lesson attributes the PPV difference to prevalence, not to a fundamentally different or worse assay.
explanations.b: Correct — this is Bayes' theorem in practice: at low prevalence, even a highly specific test's false positives can outnumber the rare true positives, driving PPV down despite unchanged assay performance.
explanations.c: Microdeletions are detectable by cfDNA sequencing; the issue is reliability of a positive result (PPV), not detectability.
explanations.d: Fetal fraction affects overall test validity, but the PPV gap described is driven by prevalence differences between the two conditions, not fetal fraction.

questions.prompt: Match each false-positive source to its mechanism.

right.text: A chromosomal abnormality present in placental cells but not the fetus itself
A co-twin that stopped developing early keeps shedding abnormal cfDNA attributed to the surviving fetus
An occult maternal condition sheds its own abnormal cfDNA into the same plasma sample

questions.explanation: Each source produces a false-positive NIPT result through a different biological route not related to the fetus's actual chromosomes: confined placental mosaicism affects only the placenta, vanishing twin contributes cfDNA from a nonviable co-twin, and maternal malignancy or mosaicism contributes abnormal cfDNA from the mother herself.

questions.prompt: Why does a positive NIPT result require confirmation by CVS or amniocentesis rather than being treated as diagnostic?

options.text: Because NIPT is measuring placental or maternal-mixed cfDNA statistically, and several biological sources (confined placental mosaicism, vanishing twin, maternal malignancy) can produce a positive result without the fetus actually having the condition
Because NIPT results take too long to return
Because insurance requires a second test regardless of accuracy
Because NIPT cannot detect trisomy 21 at all

explanations.a: Correct — NIPT's plasma-based, statistical, placenta-derived approach creates real biological pathways to a false positive, so a diagnostic test sampling fetal or placental cells directly is required before an irreversible decision.
explanations.b: Turnaround time is not the reason confirmatory testing is required; it is about what the test can and cannot prove.
explanations.c: Insurance policy is not the underlying scientific reason described in this lesson.
explanations.d: NIPT is used specifically to screen for trisomy 21 and does so with high PPV in higher-prevalence groups; the issue is confirming a positive, not an inability to detect it.

lessons.label: Genetic Counseling, Consent, and Family Communication

sections.heading: The Structure of a Consultation
sections.body: A genetics consultation typically opens with a three-generation pedigree, capturing family history of the condition in question and clarifying the likely inheritance pattern; that structures a quantitative risk estimate — 50% for a child of an autosomal dominant carrier, 25% for a sibling of an autosomal recessive proband once both parents' carrier status is known. Pre-test counseling then covers what a test can and cannot answer, the range of possible results including uninformative or variant-of-uncertain-significance outcomes, and what each result would mean for decisions the patient actually faces, before informed consent is signed. Only then does testing proceed. Result disclosure is typically delivered in person with time built in for questions, and follow-up connects the patient to relevant specialists, support groups, or the option for at-risk relatives to pursue their own testing.

sections.heading: The Non-Directive Tradition and Its Critics
sections.body: Non-directive counseling — presenting information and options without steering a patient toward a decision — became the field's norm partly as a deliberate reaction to eugenics. Sheldon Reed coined the term 'genetic counseling' in 1947, explicitly distancing the new profession from the coercive sterilization and 'fitness' programs earlier eugenicists had run under a genetics banner. But strict non-directiveness draws real critique: to a patient facing a genuinely hard call who wants a professional's judgment rather than a list of probabilities, pure neutrality can feel like abandonment, and critics argue counselors already shape decisions through framing and question order even while claiming to stay neutral.

sections.heading: Predictive Testing, Minors, and Duty to Warn
sections.body: Predictive testing for untreatable adult-onset disease follows a protocol modeled on Huntington disease: multiple pre-test counseling sessions, a mandatory waiting period, and psychological evaluation before disclosure, because a predictive positive for a currently untreatable, highly penetrant condition carries different stakes than a diagnostic test in a symptomatic patient. Testing minors for that same category of disease is generally deferred until adulthood unless the condition is childhood-onset or a positive result would change childhood management, preserving the child's future right to decide for themselves. The duty-to-warn dilemma — a patient refusing to inform at-risk relatives of a shared genetic risk — has no clean legal answer in most US jurisdictions and is negotiated case by case. Long-term outcome studies, including of Huntington predictive testing, find most tested individuals, even those who learn they carry the mutation, adapt without lasting psychological harm, though a minority experience significant distress.

lessons.workedExample: A 30-year-old at 50% risk for Huntington disease, after her father's recent diagnosis, requests predictive testing. Under the standard protocol she completes at least two pre-test counseling sessions covering the CAG-repeat test's near-certainty, undergoes a required psychological evaluation given the elevated depression and suicide risk documented after a positive predictive result for an untreatable disease, and waits out a mandated interval before the blood draw. She tests positive. At six-month follow-up, outcome assessment finds she is not clinically depressed and has adjusted to the news, consistent with published data that most predictive-test recipients adapt over time; she is now using the result to plan long-term care and to decide how to inform her own children about their future testing options.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes non-directiveness and predictive-testing protocols in this lesson because a project touching genetic risk is judged partly on whether a student understands why counselors present options rather than tell a patient what to do, and why untreatable adult-onset conditions like Huntington disease get a heavier multi-session protocol most other genetic tests skip. Naming the eugenics-reaction origin of non-directiveness and the specific components of the Huntington protocol — waiting period, psychological evaluation — signals the student understands genetic counseling as a designed response to real historical and ethical stakes, not a generic 'be supportive' gesture.

questions.prompt: Order the typical stages of a genetics consultation.

items.text: Construct a three-generation pedigree and assess risk
Pre-test counseling and informed consent
Testing is performed
Result disclosure
Follow-up and referral

questions.explanation: A consultation moves from establishing family-history-based risk, through pre-test counseling and consent, to the test itself, then disclosure of the result, and finally follow-up support or referral.

questions.prompt: Why did the non-directive counseling norm emerge in genetic counseling's early history?

options.text: Insurance companies required it to limit liability
As a deliberate reaction against eugenics-era coercive programs that had used genetics to steer people's reproductive decisions
Because genetic tests were too unreliable to base advice on
Because patients preferred not to speak with a counselor at all

explanations.a: The lesson attributes non-directiveness to an ethical/historical reaction, not an insurance requirement.
explanations.b: Correct — Sheldon Reed's 1947 coining of 'genetic counseling' and the field's non-directive stance were shaped by an explicit break from eugenics-era coercion.
explanations.c: Test reliability is a separate issue from the ethical stance of not steering a patient's decision.
explanations.d: Non-directiveness describes how information is delivered during a consultation, not whether a consultation happens.

questions.prompt: Under standard practice, when is genetic testing of a minor for an adult-onset, currently untreatable condition generally recommended?

options.text: As early as possible, so parents can plan
Deferred until adulthood, unless the condition is childhood-onset or a result would change childhood management
Only if both parents are already confirmed carriers
Never, under any circumstance

explanations.a: Early testing for a currently untreatable adult-onset condition is generally not recommended, to preserve the child's future autonomy.
explanations.b: Correct — testing is deferred to protect the child's right to decide as an adult, unless early knowledge would change how the child is medically managed now.
explanations.c: Parental carrier confirmation does not override the standard deferral for untreatable adult-onset conditions in minors.
explanations.d: Testing minors is not an absolute never — it proceeds when the condition is childhood-onset or actionable in childhood.

questions.prompt: What do long-term outcome studies of predictive testing for Huntington disease generally find about tested individuals who learn they carry the mutation?

options.text: Nearly all develop severe, lasting psychological harm
Most adapt without lasting psychological harm, though a minority experience significant distress
They uniformly regret having been tested
Outcomes cannot be studied because too few people choose predictive testing

explanations.a: This overstates the finding; lasting severe harm is not the typical outcome described.
explanations.b: Correct — outcome data show most tested individuals, even those who test positive, adapt over time, though a minority do experience significant distress.
explanations.c: Uniform regret is not the finding; adaptation is the more common pattern.
explanations.d: Predictive testing has been studied longitudinally enough to generate this adaptation finding.

lessons.label: Pharmacogenomics at the Bedside

sections.heading: When HLA Type Predicts a Dangerous Immune Reaction
sections.body: HLA-B*57:01 and the HIV drug abacavir is the field's cleanest success story. Before genotype-guided prescribing, roughly 5-8% of patients started on abacavir developed a hypersensitivity reaction, occasionally fatal on re-exposure; the 2008 PREDICT-1 trial found that screening patients for HLA-B*57:01 before starting abacavir and excluding carriers essentially eliminated immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity reactions, compared with prescribing by clinical judgment alone — pre-treatment HLA-B*57:01 testing is now the standard of care, valued for an extremely reliable negative predictive value. HLA-B*15:02, common in Southeast Asian and Han Chinese populations, carries a strong association with carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, severe blistering skin reactions; a 2004 Taiwan case-control study first established the link tightly enough that regulators now recommend HLA-B*15:02 screening before starting carbamazepine in patients from at-risk ancestries, since the allele is rare in European-ancestry populations and the screening recommendation is targeted rather than universal.

sections.heading: When a Metabolizing Enzyme Changes Whether a Drug Works or Harms
sections.body: Other gene-drug pairs act through drug-activating or drug-clearing enzymes rather than immune recognition. CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles blunt activation of clopidogrel, a prodrug that needs CYP2C19 to become its active antiplatelet form, leaving poor metabolizers at higher risk of stent thrombosis after cardiac stenting. CYP2D6 converts codeine into its active metabolite, morphine; poor metabolizers get little pain relief from codeine, while ultrarapid metabolizers can generate dangerously high morphine levels from a standard dose — cases of infant morphine toxicity in breastfeeding infants of ultrarapid-metabolizer mothers prompted an FDA boxed warning against codeine in nursing mothers and in children. TPMT and NUDT15 variants slow clearance of thiopurine drugs used in leukemia and autoimmune disease treatment, and low enzyme activity without dose reduction causes severe, sometimes fatal, myelosuppression. DPYD variants similarly reduce clearance of the chemotherapy drug fluorouracil, and undetected deficiency has caused fatal toxicity at standard chemotherapy doses.

sections.heading: From Diplotype to Prescribing Action
sections.body: The Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) publishes guidelines that translate a patient's diplotype — the pair of alleles at a gene like CYP2D6 — into a metabolizer phenotype (poor, intermediate, normal, rapid, or ultrarapid) and then a specific prescribing action: avoid this drug, substitute this alternate, or adjust the dose by a stated amount, so a clinician does not have to interpret raw genotype data from scratch. Despite that infrastructure, pre-emptive panel testing — genotyping a patient before any prescription is written, banking the result for whatever drug comes later — remains contested, since evidence of improved outcomes is strongest for only a handful of gene-drug pairs and cost-effectiveness varies by health system, so most prescribing today still happens without it.

lessons.workedExample: A patient starting clopidogrel after coronary stent placement is genotyped and found to carry two CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles, a poor metabolizer. Following CPIC guidance, the cardiologist switches to prasugrel, an antiplatelet that does not depend on CYP2C19 activation, instead of prescribing standard-dose clopidogrel, which would leave the patient under-protected against stent thrombosis. The same clinic sees a patient of Southeast Asian ancestry about to start carbamazepine for a seizure disorder; per CPIC and FDA labeling guidance, HLA-B*15:02 is tested first, and only a negative result clears the prescription — a pre-emptive check built directly into the prescribing workflow rather than left to clinical judgment alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe pharmacogenomics because it is a direct, testable application connecting a genotype to a real clinical action with a named mechanism, not a vague 'genes affect drug response' claim. A strong answer distinguishes the two mechanism classes at work — HLA-restricted immune hypersensitivity (abacavir, carbamazepine) versus enzyme-mediated activation or clearance (CYP2C19/clopidogrel, CYP2D6/codeine, TPMT-NUDT15/thiopurines, DPYD/fluorouracil) — and can name CPIC as the body that operationalizes a diplotype into a specific prescribing decision, showing the student understands pharmacogenomics as an implemented clinical system, not just a genetics fact.

questions.prompt: What did the PREDICT-1 trial establish about HLA-B*57:01 screening before starting abacavir?

options.text: It had no measurable effect on hypersensitivity reaction rates
Screening and excluding carriers essentially eliminated immunologically confirmed hypersensitivity reactions
It only worked in patients under 18
It identified patients who needed a higher abacavir dose

explanations.a: The trial showed a clear, clinically meaningful effect, not a null result.
explanations.b: Correct — pre-treatment HLA-B*57:01 screening and exclusion of carriers essentially eliminated confirmed hypersensitivity reactions, making it standard of care.
explanations.c: The trial and resulting practice were not restricted to a pediatric population.
explanations.d: HLA-B*57:01 status is used to avoid the drug in carriers, not to adjust dosing.

questions.prompt: Match each gene to the drug whose effect or toxicity it governs.

right.text: Clopidogrel fails to activate, raising stent thrombosis risk
Codeine converts to dangerously high morphine levels
Thiopurine drugs (azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine) cause severe myelosuppression
Fluorouracil chemotherapy causes fatal toxicity at standard dose

questions.explanation: Each gene affects a different drug through activation or clearance: CYP2C19 loss-of-function blocks clopidogrel activation, CYP2D6 ultrarapid activity over-converts codeine to morphine, low TPMT/NUDT15 activity impairs thiopurine clearance causing myelosuppression, and DPYD deficiency impairs fluorouracil clearance causing toxicity.

questions.prompt: What does a CPIC guideline provide that raw genotype data alone does not?

options.text: A specific, published prescribing action tied to a metabolizer phenotype derived from the patient's diplotype
A guarantee that the patient will have no side effects from any drug
A full genome sequence for the patient
A legal requirement that all patients be genotyped before any prescription

explanations.a: Correct — CPIC translates a diplotype into a metabolizer phenotype and then a concrete prescribing action, so a clinician does not have to interpret raw genotype data themselves.
explanations.b: CPIC guidelines reduce specific known risks; they do not guarantee freedom from all possible side effects.
explanations.c: CPIC works with targeted gene results, not necessarily a full genome sequence.
explanations.d: Pre-emptive panel testing before every prescription remains contested and is not a universal legal mandate.

questions.prompt: Why does pre-emptive pharmacogenomic panel testing (genotyping before any prescription is written) remain contested?

options.text: Because it is technically impossible with current sequencing methods
Because outcome evidence is strongest for only a handful of gene-drug pairs and cost-effectiveness varies by health system
Because CPIC guidelines do not exist for any gene-drug pair
Because it is banned by federal law in the United States

explanations.a: The technology exists and is used; the debate is about evidence strength and cost-effectiveness, not feasibility.
explanations.b: Correct — the strongest outcome evidence covers only a subset of gene-drug pairs, and cost-effectiveness depends on the health system, which keeps pre-emptive testing from being universally adopted.
explanations.c: CPIC guidelines exist for numerous gene-drug pairs; that is not the source of the controversy.
explanations.d: There is no such federal ban; the contested aspect is evidence and cost, not legality.

lessons.label: Consumer Genomics, Privacy, and Forensic Genealogy

sections.heading: Arrays, Not Sequencing — and Why That Produces False Positives
sections.body: Direct-to-consumer (DTC) companies like 23andMe and AncestryDNA genotype customers with SNP arrays — chips that interrogate several hundred thousand to a million predetermined positions in the genome via probe hybridization — rather than sequencing every base the way a clinical whole-genome or whole-exome test does. That distinction matters for reliability: array calls at specific positions can be wrong, and a widely cited 2018 study by Tandy-Connor and colleagues found that roughly 40% of variants reported as pathogenic in raw DTC data did not hold up when retested with a clinical-grade confirmatory method. That false-positive rate is why clinicians now routinely recommend confirmatory testing before acting on any DTC 'pathogenic' finding, especially before a major medical decision such as prophylactic surgery.

sections.heading: A Regulatory Back-and-Forth
sections.body: In November 2013, the FDA sent 23andMe a warning letter ordering it to stop marketing health-related interpretations of its raw genotype data, citing unproven analytical and clinical validity — the company complied and sold only ancestry and raw data for about two years. The FDA authorized a Bloom syndrome carrier-status report in 2015, then in 2017 authorized a limited set of genetic health risk reports, including Parkinson's disease and late-onset Alzheimer's disease risk variants, and in 2018 authorized reporting of three specific Ashkenazi-founder BRCA1/BRCA2 variants — a narrow reinstatement, not a return to reporting on the full range of clinically significant variants a laboratory-based diagnostic panel would cover.

sections.heading: Relatives, Genealogy, and the Gaps in the Law
sections.body: Because DTC databases pool millions of genotypes, they routinely surface relative matches a customer never expected — half-siblings from donor conception, or a parent who turns out not to be a biological parent — misattributed-parentage discoveries that spread through families with no counseling built into the product. The same relative-matching principle powers investigative genetic genealogy: police used the public database GEDmatch to identify the Golden State Killer in April 2018 by finding distant cousins of crime-scene DNA and building a family tree down to the suspect, a technique since used in hundreds of cold cases; GEDmatch subsequently restricted law-enforcement searching to users who explicitly opt in. Legal protection lags the technology: the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA, 2008) bars discrimination in health insurance and employment but explicitly does not cover life, disability, or long-term-care insurance, and the October 2023 23andMe breach, which exposed data on millions of users through credential-stuffing attacks against reused passwords, underscored that consumer genetic data is also an ordinary cybersecurity liability, not just a health-privacy one.

lessons.workedExample: A customer orders a DTC ancestry-and-health kit, and the report flags a 'likely pathogenic' BRCA1 variant. Alarmed, they consider a prophylactic surgery decision based on the raw-data report alone. Given the roughly 40% false-positive rate Tandy-Connor and colleagues found in raw DTC pathogenic calls, a genetic counselor insists on confirmatory clinical-grade testing first — and in this case the confirmatory test comes back negative, sparing the patient a moot decision. Meanwhile, that same customer's 'relative matches' list surfaces an unexpected half-sibling, revealing a donor-conception origin nobody in the family had disclosed — a discovery the platform's relative-matching feature was never designed to provide counseling support for.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe DTC genomics because it is the genetics topic students are most likely to have personal experience with, and 'my 23andMe said...' is a common but scientifically loose claim at a fair. A strong answer names the array-versus-sequencing distinction and the roughly 40% false-positive figure from Tandy-Connor and colleagues to explain why raw DTC output is not clinical-grade, and can cite a concrete downstream case — the Golden State Killer identification via GEDmatch — to show they understand consumer genetic data has uses and consequences well beyond the health report a customer actually paid for.

questions.prompt: How do most direct-to-consumer genetic tests actually determine a customer's genotype?

options.text: Whole-genome sequencing that reads every base in the customer's DNA
A SNP array that interrogates several hundred thousand to a million predetermined positions via probe hybridization
Karyotyping under a microscope
RNA sequencing of a saliva sample

explanations.a: Most DTC companies use arrays, not whole-genome sequencing, which is more expensive and not standard for consumer kits.
explanations.b: Correct — DTC testing typically uses SNP genotyping arrays that check a fixed set of known positions rather than reading every base.
explanations.c: Karyotyping visualizes whole chromosomes under a microscope and is unrelated to DTC SNP-based reports.
explanations.d: DTC kits genotype DNA, not RNA, and are not RNA-sequencing based.

questions.prompt: What did the Tandy-Connor et al. (2018) study find about raw DTC data flagged as 'pathogenic'?

options.text: Roughly 40% of such variants did not hold up on clinical-grade confirmatory testing
Every flagged variant was independently confirmed as accurate
DTC companies had stopped reporting any health variants by that point
The false-positive rate was under 1%

explanations.a: Correct — roughly 40% of raw-data pathogenic calls failed clinical-grade confirmation, the basis for recommending confirmatory testing before acting on a DTC result.
explanations.b: The study's central finding was the opposite: a substantial false-positive rate, not universal confirmation.
explanations.c: The study concerns variants that were reported; it does not describe DTC companies halting health reporting entirely.
explanations.d: A sub-1% false-positive rate would not have driven the clinical recommendation for confirmatory testing described in this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a specific gap in GINA (the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act)?

options.text: It covers life, disability, and long-term-care insurance but not health insurance or employment
It bars discrimination in health insurance and employment but does not cover life, disability, or long-term-care insurance
It applies only to DTC companies, not clinical labs
It has no protections at all and is purely symbolic

explanations.a: This reverses GINA's actual coverage; it protects health insurance and employment, not the other insurance types.
explanations.b: Correct — GINA (2008) protects against genetic discrimination in health insurance and employment specifically, leaving life, disability, and long-term-care insurance uncovered.
explanations.c: GINA's protections are not limited to DTC-sourced data; the gap described is about which insurance types are covered, not which company generated the data.
explanations.d: GINA does provide enforceable protections in its covered domains; the issue is its scope, not its existence.

questions.prompt: Match each event to its year.

left.text: FDA warning letter halts 23andMe health reports
Golden State Killer identified via GEDmatch

questions.explanation: GINA was enacted in 2008, the FDA warning letter halting 23andMe's health reports came in November 2013, the Golden State Killer was identified through GEDmatch genealogy in April 2018, and the 23andMe credential-stuffing breach occurred in October 2023.

lessons.label: Counting Alleles: Frequencies, Not Just Genotypes

sections.heading: Allele frequency is what population genetics tracks
sections.body: A population geneticist's basic unit of description is not "how many people are AA, Aa, or aa" but the frequency of each allele in the shared gene pool. For a biallelic locus with N diploid individuals (2N alleles total), the frequency of allele A is p = (2*N_AA + N_Aa)/2N, and since there are only two alleles, q = 1 - p is automatically the frequency of a. Genotype frequency is a derived, mating-dependent readout: the same allele frequencies can produce very different genotype proportions depending on who mates with whom (assortative mating, inbreeding, population mixing), but the allele frequencies themselves are what carries forward, generation to generation, absent an evolutionary force acting on them. That is why every quantity in this segment — Hardy-Weinberg proportions, F-statistics, linkage disequilibrium — is built on p and q rather than on raw genotype counts.

sections.heading: A real locus worked both ways: MN blood group
sections.body: The MN blood group is the classroom-standard example because it is fully codominant — MM, MN, and NN are each directly visible on a blood typing panel, with no masked heterozygote to worry about. A typical European-ancestry sample shows genotype proportions near 29% MM, 50% MN, 21% NN. Converting to allele frequency: p(M) = (2*0.29 + 0.50)/2 = 0.54, q(N) = 1 - 0.54 = 0.46. Running the conversion the other direction — from allele frequency back to expected genotype proportions under random mating — reproduces almost exactly the observed 29/50/21 split, which is itself a preview of the Hardy-Weinberg check in the next lesson.

sections.heading: CCR5-delta32 and the sample-size caveat
sections.body: CCR5-delta32, a 32-base-pair deletion in the chemokine receptor gene CCR5 that confers resistance to HIV entry, sits at roughly 10% allele frequency in Northern European populations and falls to near zero in East Asian and sub-Saharan African populations — a geographic gradient sharp enough that the allele is used as a textbook marker of European ancestry. But a frequency is only as good as the sample it comes from. The standard error of an estimated allele frequency is approximately the square root of pq/2n; for p = 0.1 and a class-sized sample of n = 30 people (60 alleles), that works out to about 0.04 — a four-percentage-point margin on a ten-percent estimate, wide enough that a single misgenotyped person can swing q by nearly two points.

lessons.workedExample: A class genotypes 30 students at the CCR5 locus and finds 20 wild-type/wild-type, 8 wild-type/delta32, and 2 delta32/delta32. Allele frequency: q(delta32) = (2*2 + 8)/(2*30) = 12/60 = 0.20, and p(wild-type) = 0.80. That 20% classroom estimate is double the ~10% figure typically reported for Northern European populations. The gap is not necessarily an error — with n = 30, the standard error on q is roughly 0.05, so a true population value of 0.10 could plausibly, though not typically, produce a sample estimate this far off by chance (roughly a 1-in-100 event at this sample size). The lesson: report the count the frequency came from, not just the percentage, and treat any allele frequency from fewer than a few hundred people as an estimate with real uncertainty, not a fact.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe allele-frequency arithmetic because it is the single most common place a project quietly goes wrong: students report a percentage of "how many people had the trait" without ever converting genotype counts to an allele frequency, or they treat a frequency from 20 genotyped classmates as if it were a population constant. A student who can show the 2*N_AA + N_Aa arithmetic from raw counts, and who flags the sample-size caveat unprompted, has demonstrated the actual skill; one who just quotes a percentage from a paper has not.

questions.prompt: In a sample of 200 people genotyped at a biallelic locus, 98 are AA, 84 are Aa, and 18 are aa. What is q, the frequency of the a allele?

explanations.a: This is 18/200, the raw proportion of aa individuals — it undercounts a alleles because it ignores the a alleles carried by the 84 heterozygotes.
explanations.b: Correct: p = (2*98 + 84)/400 = 280/400 = 0.70, so q = 1 - 0.70 = 0.30. Every a allele is counted once per Aa individual and twice per aa individual, over 400 total alleles.
explanations.c: This is p, the frequency of the A allele, not q.
explanations.d: This is 84/200, the raw proportion of heterozygous individuals, not an allele frequency.

questions.prompt: Which statement about CCR5-delta32 allele frequency is accurate?

options.text: It is roughly 10% in Northern European populations and near zero in East Asian populations
It is uniformly close to 50% in every human population
It is highest in East Asian populations and absent in Europe
It cannot be estimated from genotype counts because the deletion has no detectable phenotype

explanations.a: Correct — this geographic gradient, roughly 10% in Northern Europe and near zero in East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, is well documented and used as a marker of ancestry.
explanations.b: The allele frequency varies sharply by geography; it is not uniform across populations.
explanations.c: The gradient runs the opposite direction: highest in Northern Europe, near zero in East Asia.
explanations.d: The deletion is readily genotyped by PCR regardless of phenotype, which is exactly how its frequency is measured.

questions.prompt: Why does a 30-person sample give a much less reliable allele frequency estimate than a 3,000-person sample?

options.text: Small samples always underestimate rare alleles
The standard error of an allele frequency estimate scales with 1/sqrt(n), so it shrinks as sample size grows
Genotyping technology is less accurate on small batches
Allele frequency is undefined for samples under 100 people

explanations.a: Small samples can over- or under-estimate a frequency by chance; there is no systematic bias toward underestimation.
explanations.b: Correct — the standard error is approximately sqrt(pq/2n), which shrinks as n grows, so larger samples pin down the true population frequency far more tightly.
explanations.c: Sample size affects statistical precision, not the accuracy of the genotyping assay itself.
explanations.d: Allele frequency can be computed from any sample size, including very small ones; it is simply less precise.

questions.prompt: Match each symbol or count to what it represents in allele-frequency arithmetic.

right.text: Frequency of the A allele
Frequency of the a allele, equal to 1 - p
Count of heterozygous individuals in the sample
Total number of alleles at the locus across the sample

questions.explanation: p is the frequency of allele A, q = 1 - p is the frequency of allele a, N_Aa is the observed count of heterozygotes, and 2N is the total allele count in a diploid sample of N individuals — the denominator in every allele-frequency calculation.

lessons.label: The Hardy-Weinberg Principle

sections.heading: Random union of gametes gives p^2 + 2pq + q^2
sections.body: If a population's gene pool holds allele A at frequency p and allele a at frequency q, and gametes combine at random to form the next generation, the probability an offspring draws A from both parents is p*p = p^2, the probability it draws A from one parent and a from the other is p*q + q*p = 2pq, and the probability it draws a from both is q^2. Those three terms are exactly the expansion of (p + q)^2 = p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1, which is why Hardy-Weinberg genotype proportions are sometimes just called "the binomial expansion applied to mating." The result rests on five explicit assumptions: no selection (all genotypes survive and reproduce equally), no mutation, no migration (no gene flow in or out), infinite population size (no genetic drift), and random mating with respect to the locus. Violate any one and the population can still deviate from p^2:2pq:q^2, which is precisely what makes HWE useful as a null model — the deviation is diagnostic.

sections.heading: The 1908 dinner-table dispute
sections.body: The principle's origin is an argument, not a derivation for its own sake. Statistician Udny Yule had objected that if brachydactyly (short fingers), a dominant Mendelian trait, did not sweep toward becoming the common form in three generations, Mendelian inheritance must be wrong — his intuition was that a dominant allele should mechanically drift toward a 3:1 phenotype ratio and then hold there. Geneticist Reginald Punnett couldn't rebut the math on the spot and took the problem to his Cambridge cricket teammate, the mathematician G. H. Hardy, who wrote up the algebra above in a short 1908 letter to Science under the title "Mendelian Proportions in a Mixed Population." Working independently in Germany the same year, physician Wilhelm Weinberg published an equivalent derivation — including the multi-allele and X-linked extensions Hardy didn't cover — which is why the result carries both names.

sections.heading: The non-obvious part: one generation is enough
sections.body: The genuinely surprising claim is not that equilibrium exists but how fast it arrives: starting from any arbitrary genotype distribution — even one wildly skewed, with almost no heterozygotes — a single generation of random mating restores p^2:2pq:q^2 proportions exactly, and the allele frequencies p and q themselves never change at all under the five assumptions, generation after generation. That answered Yule directly: a dominant allele's frequency does not drift upward just because it is dominant; dominance affects which genotype is visible, not which allele is more common. Equilibrium genotype proportions and constant allele frequency are two separate claims bundled into one principle, and separating them is usually where a first read gets confused.

lessons.workedExample: A founder population starts wildly out of equilibrium: 90 AA, 0 Aa, 10 aa (N = 100, no heterozygotes at all). Allele frequencies: p = (2*90 + 0)/200 = 0.90, q = (2*10 + 0)/200 = 0.10. Under random mating, the very next generation's expected genotype proportions are p^2 = 0.81 (AA), 2pq = 0.18 (Aa), q^2 = 0.01 (aa) — heterozygotes jump from 0% to 18% in one generation, even though p and q themselves (0.90 and 0.10) never moved. This is the step a lot of students miss: HWE restores genotype proportions in one generation, but it says nothing about the allele frequencies changing — those were already fixed by the founders and stay fixed absent selection, mutation, migration, or drift.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking a student to state the Hardy-Weinberg assumptions is testing whether the student understands HWE as a null hypothesis rather than a law of nature — every one of the five assumptions (no selection, no mutation, no migration, infinite size, random mating) is routinely violated by real populations, and knowing which assumption a given result violates is what turns a chi-square deviation into a biological claim instead of a shrug. A student who can also explain why one generation suffices to restore equilibrium proportions — and that allele frequency, not genotype frequency, is the quantity that stays constant — has separated two ideas that are easy to conflate.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the five Hardy-Weinberg assumptions?

options.text: No mutation
Random mating
Equal numbers of males and females
Infinite population size

explanations.a: No mutation is one of the five standard assumptions.
explanations.b: Random mating with respect to the locus is one of the five standard assumptions.
explanations.c: Correct — a 1:1 sex ratio is not one of the five HWE assumptions; HWE proportions can hold with skewed sex ratios as long as mating with respect to the locus is otherwise random and the other four assumptions hold.
explanations.d: Infinite population size (i.e., no genetic drift) is one of the five standard assumptions.

questions.prompt: Udny Yule's original objection, which prompted Hardy's 1908 letter, was that:

options.text: A dominant trait like brachydactyly should mechanically increase toward becoming the common phenotype over generations
Recessive alleles should disappear from a population within a few generations
Genotype and allele frequencies should always be equal
Mendelian inheritance could not explain continuous traits like height

explanations.a: Correct — Yule argued that because brachydactyly is dominant, it should trend toward becoming the common form, and its failure to do so seemed to him like evidence against Mendelian inheritance.
explanations.b: Yule's objection was about a dominant trait becoming common, not about recessive alleles disappearing.
explanations.c: This confuses two different quantities but was not Yule's stated objection.
explanations.d: The dispute concerned a specific discrete Mendelian trait (brachydactyly), not continuous traits.

questions.prompt: A population starts with genotype proportions 100% Aa (all heterozygotes) and then mates randomly for one generation. What happens to p and to the genotype proportions?

options.text: Both p and the genotype proportions stay exactly the same
p stays at 0.5, but genotype proportions shift to 0.25 AA : 0.50 Aa : 0.25 aa
p changes to 1.0 as A becomes fixed
Genotype proportions stay 100% Aa, but p drifts toward 0

explanations.a: Genotype proportions do change in the first generation of random mating, from 100% Aa toward Hardy-Weinberg proportions; only allele frequency stays fixed.
explanations.b: Correct — p = q = 0.5 in the starting population and remains 0.5 under random mating (no force is acting on the allele frequency), but genotype proportions move immediately to p^2:2pq:q^2 = 0.25:0.50:0.25.
explanations.c: Nothing in random mating alone drives an allele to fixation; that requires selection or drift.
explanations.d: Allele frequency stays constant under HWE assumptions; it is genotype proportions, not allele frequency, that shift here.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the 1908 history of the Hardy-Weinberg principle.

items.text: Udny Yule argues that a dominant trait should mechanically increase toward becoming the common phenotype
Reginald Punnett cannot resolve Yule's objection and brings the problem to G. H. Hardy
Hardy publishes the p^2 + 2pq + q^2 algebra in a letter to Science
Wilhelm Weinberg independently publishes an equivalent derivation in Germany the same year

questions.explanation: Yule's objection to Punnett came first; Punnett, unable to resolve it, brought the problem to Hardy; Hardy then published the equilibrium algebra in his 1908 Science letter; Weinberg's independent German-language derivation appeared the same year, which is why the principle carries both names.

lessons.label: Testing HWE and Reading Its Failures

sections.heading: The chi-square goodness-of-fit test
sections.body: Testing whether an observed genotype distribution matches Hardy-Weinberg expectations is a standard chi-square goodness-of-fit test. From the sample's allele frequencies p and q, compute expected counts N*p^2, N*2pq, and N*q^2 for the three genotype classes, then sum (observed - expected)^2 / expected across all three classes. Because p and q were themselves estimated from the same data (one degree of freedom is spent fitting p), and three genotype classes minus one fitted parameter minus one (for the constraint that proportions sum to 1) leaves exactly 1 degree of freedom for a biallelic locus. A chi-square statistic above about 3.84 corresponds to p < 0.05 on 1 df, the conventional cutoff for flagging a locus as out of equilibrium.

sections.heading: Where chi-square breaks: rare alleles and the exact test
sections.body: Chi-square is an asymptotic approximation, and it degrades badly when any expected genotype count is small — which happens automatically whenever the minor allele is rare, since the homozygous-minor class (q^2) shrinks fastest. In that regime chi-square systematically over-rejects, flagging loci as violating HWE that are actually fine. Wigginton, Cutler, and Abecasis addressed this in a widely cited 2005 paper by deriving a computationally efficient exact test that directly evaluates the probability of the observed heterozygote count against every possible genotype configuration consistent with the observed allele counts, without relying on the chi-square approximation at all. Their exact test is now the standard tool anywhere minor allele frequency is low, which in genome-wide data is most loci.

sections.heading: HWE testing as genotyping QC, not biology
sections.body: In genome-wide association studies, an HWE test is run at essentially every SNP as a quality-control filter, applied to controls only (cases are deliberately excluded from the filter because a true disease-associated variant can legitimately deviate from HWE among affected individuals). The field's standard working threshold flags and typically drops any SNP with an HWE p-value below 1e-6 in controls. The working assumption behind that threshold is that a single SNP failing HWE in a large, presumably randomly mating control sample is far more likely to reflect genotyping error — a poorly clustering cluster plot, a probe that cross-hybridizes to a paralogous region, or a copy-number variant masquerading as a SNP — than a real biological signal, since true biological deviations (selection, population structure, inbreeding) tend to show up across many loci at once, not as an isolated single-SNP spike.

lessons.workedExample: A GWAS control sample of 5,000 people is genotyped at a SNP with observed counts 4,050 AA, 100 Aa, and 850 aa. Allele frequency: q = (2*850 + 100)/10,000 = 1,800/10,000 = 0.18, p = 0.82. Expected HWE counts: N*p^2 = 5,000*0.6724 = 3,362 AA, N*2pq = 5,000*0.2952 = 1,476 Aa, N*q^2 = 5,000*0.0324 = 162 aa. The observed heterozygote count (100) is drastically below the expected 1,476 — a massive heterozygote deficit that chi-square would flag with an enormous statistic, p far below 1e-6. Because the minor allele here isn't rare (q = 0.18, so chi-square is reasonably trustworthy) and the deficit is so extreme, the QC pipeline drops this SNP as a near-certain genotyping artifact — most plausibly two genotype clusters (Aa and aa) that a calling algorithm merged — rather than investigating it as biology.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "how did you test for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, and what would a failure mean?" is checking whether the student understands HWE testing as a diagnostic for data quality, not a search for evolution in action. The sharp answer distinguishes the ordinary chi-square case from the low-minor-allele-frequency case where an exact test like Wigginton-Cutler-Abecasis is required, and states the field's default interpretive move: a single-SNP HWE failure in controls is treated as genotyping error until many loci show the same pattern. A student who says "we found one SNP that failed and concluded natural selection was acting on it" has the causal arrow backwards for GWAS-scale data.

questions.prompt: How many degrees of freedom does the standard chi-square HWE test use for a biallelic locus, and why?

options.text: 2, because there are two alleles
1, because three genotype categories minus one fitted allele-frequency parameter minus the constraint that proportions sum to 1 leaves one
3, one for each genotype class
0, because allele frequency is assumed known in advance

explanations.a: Degrees of freedom in this test come from the genotype categories and fitted parameters, not directly from the allele count.
explanations.b: Correct — with three genotype classes, one degree of freedom is used fitting p from the data, and one more is used by the constraint that the three proportions sum to 1, leaving exactly 1 df.
explanations.c: Each genotype class contributes to the test statistic, but degrees of freedom are reduced by fitted parameters and the sum-to-1 constraint.
explanations.d: Allele frequency is estimated from the same sample being tested, not assumed known, and that estimation itself costs a degree of freedom.

questions.prompt: Why does the standard chi-square HWE test perform poorly for a locus with a rare minor allele?

options.text: Rare alleles violate the random-mating assumption
The expected count in the homozygous-minor-allele genotype class becomes very small, and chi-square's approximation breaks down, causing over-rejection
Rare alleles cannot be genotyped accurately by any platform
Chi-square requires exactly two genotype classes to be valid

explanations.a: Allele rarity has nothing to do with whether mating is random; it is a statistical, not biological, issue for the test.
explanations.b: Correct — as minor allele frequency drops, the q^2 expected count shrinks fastest, and chi-square's asymptotic approximation is unreliable with small expected counts, systematically over-rejecting true HWE.
explanations.c: Genotyping accuracy is a separate technical issue from the statistical validity of the chi-square approximation.
explanations.d: Chi-square is applied to all three genotype classes at a biallelic locus, not restricted to two.

questions.prompt: In GWAS quality control, why is the HWE filter typically applied to controls only, and dropped when p < 1e-6?

options.text: Because cases are always genotyped on a different platform than controls

Because a true disease-associated variant can legitimately deviate from HWE among affected cases, so applying the filter there would remove real signal, while an HWE failure among presumably randomly mating controls most often reflects genotyping error at that SNP
Because HWE cannot mathematically be computed in case samples
Because controls always have larger sample sizes than cases

explanations.a: Platform differences are a separate QC concern; they are not the reason HWE filtering is restricted to controls.
explanations.b: Correct — a real disease variant may deviate from HWE specifically among affected individuals, so filtering cases would discard true signal, whereas a control-only failure is interpreted as a likely genotyping artifact at that SNP.
explanations.c: HWE proportions can be computed for any genotyped sample, including cases; the issue is interpretive, not computational.
explanations.d: Sample size is unrelated to why the filter is scoped to controls; the rationale is about avoiding removal of true disease signal.

questions.prompt: The exact test developed by Wigginton, Cutler, and Abecasis (2005) improves on chi-square primarily by:

options.text: Directly evaluating the probability of the observed heterozygote count against all genotype configurations consistent with the observed allele counts, without relying on the chi-square approximation
Increasing the significance threshold to make the test more conservative
Requiring a larger minimum sample size before any test can run
Replacing allele frequency estimation with a fixed population-wide value

explanations.a: Correct — the exact test computes probabilities directly from the discrete distribution of possible genotype configurations rather than relying on chi-square's large-sample approximation, which is what makes it reliable for rare alleles.
explanations.b: The exact test changes the underlying probability calculation, not just the significance cutoff.
explanations.c: The exact test is specifically useful at smaller expected counts, not gated behind a larger minimum sample size.
explanations.d: The exact test still uses sample allele frequencies; it does not substitute a fixed external value.

lessons.label: Structure, Inbreeding and the Wahlund Effect

sections.heading: Pooling subpopulations mimics inbreeding: the Wahlund effect
sections.body: Swedish geneticist Sten Wahlund showed in 1928 that pooling samples from two or more subpopulations with different allele frequencies, then treating the pool as one population, always produces a deficit of heterozygotes relative to Hardy-Weinberg expectations, even if every subpopulation is internally in perfect equilibrium. The mechanism is that expected heterozygosity is a nonlinear (concave) function of allele frequency, 2pq, so averaging 2pq across subpopulations always gives a smaller number than computing 2pq from the averaged allele frequency — the pooled p^2 and q^2 both get inflated at the expense of the pooled 2pq. A textbook case: two demes each fixed near p = 0.9 and p = 0.1 respectively, both internally in HWE with essentially normal heterozygosity, will show a large apparent heterozygote deficit once combined into a single sample, purely as a sampling artifact of unrecognized structure.

sections.heading: The same signature, a different cause: inbreeding
sections.body: Real inbreeding — mating between relatives — produces the exact same statistical signature, a heterozygote deficit relative to Hardy-Weinberg expectations, because related parents are more likely to transmit identical-by-descent copies of the same allele. At a single locus, a heterozygote deficit from cryptic population structure (Wahlund) and a heterozygote deficit from true inbreeding are mathematically indistinguishable — both show up as an excess of homozygotes over p^2 + q^2. The only way to tell them apart is to genotype many loci simultaneously: structure produces a correlated deficit driven by the same underlying subpopulation split at every locus (and shows up as detectable allele-frequency differentiation, F_ST, between subgroups), while true inbreeding produces long, physically contiguous stretches of homozygosity within a single individual's genome that structure alone does not create.

sections.heading: F as a heterozygote deficit, and Wright's hierarchy
sections.body: The inbreeding coefficient F is defined directly from the deficit: F = 1 - H_obs/H_exp, where H_obs is observed heterozygosity and H_exp is Hardy-Weinberg-expected heterozygosity (2pq); F = 0 means no deficit, F approaching 1 means almost no heterozygotes survive. Sewall Wright extended this into a three-level hierarchy of related statistics: F_IS (deficit of an Individual relative to its Subpopulation, i.e., local inbreeding), F_ST (differentiation of a Subpopulation relative to the Total population, i.e., structure), and F_IT (deficit of an Individual relative to the Total population, combining both effects), related by (1 - F_IT) = (1 - F_IS)(1 - F_ST). Modern sequencing data lets researchers measure the individual-level component directly as runs of homozygosity (ROH) — long stretches with no heterozygous genotypes — a genomic measure of realized inbreeding that catches unrecorded or distant relatedness that a written pedigree misses entirely.

lessons.workedExample: Two isolated island populations of a beetle are each internally in HWE: island A has p(A) = 0.9 (H_exp = 2*0.9*0.1 = 0.18), island B has p(A) = 0.1 (H_exp = 2*0.1*0.9 = 0.18) — both show 18% expected heterozygosity. A researcher who doesn't know about the two islands pools all the beetles into one sample: average p = 0.5, so a naive Hardy-Weinberg calculation on the pooled data expects H = 2*0.5*0.5 = 0.50, but the actual pooled heterozygosity is still just the average of the two islands' true values, 0.18 — a huge apparent deficit (F = 1 - 0.18/0.50 = 0.64) that has nothing to do with inbreeding at all. Only genotyping several unlinked loci and finding the same island-vs-island split at each one reveals the true cause as structure, not relatedness.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the Wahlund effect and F because they are a trap that catches students who compute one heterozygosity number from a mixed sample and jump straight to "this population is inbred." The concept a judge wants to hear is that a single-locus heterozygote deficit is ambiguous by construction — it could be cryptic subpopulation structure, could be true inbreeding, and looks identical either way at one locus — and that the disambiguating move is always to check whether the deficit is consistent across many independent loci (structure) or concentrated in long homozygous runs within individuals (inbreeding). Naming F_IS, F_ST, and F_IT correctly, and stating the identity linking them, signals the student has gone past the single-locus headline number.

questions.prompt: Why does pooling two internally-HWE subpopulations with different allele frequencies produce an apparent heterozygote deficit?

options.text: Because heterozygosity (2pq) is a concave function of p, so averaging 2pq across subpopulations is always less than computing 2pq from the pooled average p
Because mating between the two subpopulations physically destroys heterozygous genotypes
Because pooling always reduces the total sample size
Because allele frequencies cannot be averaged mathematically

explanations.a: Correct — this is the mathematical core of the Wahlund effect: 2pq's concavity means the average of two 2pq values is always less than or equal to 2 times the product of the averaged p and q, so pooling structured subpopulations mechanically deflates observed heterozygosity relative to the naive expectation.
explanations.b: The effect is a statistical artifact of averaging, not a physical process destroying genotypes.
explanations.c: Pooling increases total sample size; the effect is about allele-frequency structure, not sample size.
explanations.d: Allele frequencies can be averaged; the issue is that 2pq computed from the average differs from the average of 2pq.

questions.prompt: At a single locus, how can a researcher distinguish a heterozygote deficit caused by cryptic population structure from one caused by true inbreeding?

options.text: They cannot be distinguished at all, under any circumstances

They cannot be distinguished from a single locus alone; structure shows a correlated deficit across many loci (with detectable F_ST between subgroups), while inbreeding shows long runs of homozygosity within an individual's genome
Structure only affects dominant traits, while inbreeding only affects recessive traits
Inbreeding always produces a lower F value than structure

explanations.a: They can be distinguished, just not from a single locus in isolation — multiple loci and genome-wide patterns resolve the ambiguity.
explanations.b: Correct — a single locus's deficit is ambiguous between the two causes; many loci showing a consistent structure signature (F_ST) point to subpopulation mixing, while contiguous runs of homozygosity within one genome point to real relatedness.
explanations.c: Dominance has no bearing on distinguishing these two causes of a heterozygote deficit.
explanations.d: F values from either cause can be large or small; the magnitude of F alone does not identify the cause.

questions.prompt: A population has H_exp = 0.40 and H_obs = 0.28. What is F?

explanations.a: 0.12 is H_exp - H_obs, not the normalized deficit F = 1 - H_obs/H_exp.
explanations.c: 0.70 is H_obs/H_exp, which is 1 - F, not F itself.
explanations.d: This inverts the ratio incorrectly; F is defined as 1 minus the observed-to-expected heterozygosity ratio.

questions.prompt: Match each F-statistic to what it measures in Wright's hierarchy.

right.text: Heterozygote deficit of an Individual relative to its own Subpopulation (local inbreeding)
Allele-frequency differentiation of a Subpopulation relative to the Total population (structure)
Heterozygote deficit of an Individual relative to the Total population, combining both local inbreeding and structure

questions.explanation: F_IS captures inbreeding within a subpopulation, F_ST captures differentiation between subpopulations (the structure component), and F_IT captures the combined deficit of an individual relative to the whole population, related by (1 - F_IT) = (1 - F_IS)(1 - F_ST).

lessons.label: Effective Population Size

sections.heading: Ne is a modeling stand-in, not a headcount
sections.body: Effective population size, Ne, is defined as the size of an idealized Wright-Fisher population — one with random mating, non-overlapping generations, equal sex ratio, and Poisson-distributed offspring number — that would experience genetic drift at the same rate as the real, messier population under study. Real populations violate every one of those idealizations (unequal sex ratio, some individuals leaving far more offspring than others, fluctuating census size year to year), and Ne is the number that absorbs all that mess into one comparable quantity. Two flavors matter for different questions: inbreeding Ne measures the rate at which unrelated individuals become related (relevant to heterozygosity loss and inbreeding coefficients), and variance Ne measures the rate at which allele frequencies drift generation to generation (relevant to how fast drift outpaces selection). They usually track together but are not identical, and which one a paper reports depends on what it is trying to predict.

sections.heading: Why Ne is almost always smaller than census size N
sections.body: Two structural facts drag Ne below the census count N. First, fluctuating population size is averaged with the harmonic mean, not the arithmetic mean, across generations — and the harmonic mean is dominated by the smallest value in the series, so a single severe bottleneck generation depresses long-run Ne far more than an arithmetic average would suggest, even if the population rebounds quickly afterward. Second, unequal reproductive contribution by the two sexes shrinks Ne through Ne = 4*Nm*Nf/(Nm + Nf): if one sex is far rarer than the other (a harem-breeding species, or a species with a handful of dominant males), Ne collapses toward roughly four times the rarer sex's count rather than tracking the total. Empirically, meta-analyses of wild populations across taxa find Ne/N ratios clustering around 0.1 — effective size is typically only about a tenth of the number of individuals you could count in the field.

sections.heading: The long-term human Ne of about 10,000
sections.body: Applying these ideas to our own species, multiple independent lines of evidence — genome-wide levels of neutral genetic diversity, the pattern of coalescence times across the genome, and comparisons to other great apes with far higher genetic diversity despite comparable or smaller modern census sizes — converge on a long-term effective human population size of roughly 10,000 individuals, sustained over most of the species' history despite a much larger true census size. That figure of ~10,000 is not a claim about how many humans existed at any one moment; it is a Wright-Fisher-equivalent number that anchors mutation-rate calibration, coalescent dating of shared ancestry, and bottleneck timing estimates used throughout population genomics — it recurs as a reference point across nearly every dated claim in this segment.

lessons.workedExample: A conservation program tracks a fish population whose census size fluctuates: 1,000 in year one, 1,000 in year two, then a drought crashes it to 50 in year three, followed by recovery to 1,000 in year four. The arithmetic mean census size across the four years is (1,000+1,000+50+1,000)/4 = 762.5. But the harmonic-mean effective size is 4/(1/1000 + 1/1000 + 1/50 + 1/1000) = 4/(0.001+0.001+0.02+0.001) = 4/0.023 = about 174 — less than a quarter of the arithmetic mean, because the single crash year dominates the harmonic-mean calculation. The population's long-term capacity to retain genetic diversity is set by that ~174 figure, not by the more optimistic 762.5, which is exactly why a single bad year can leave a lasting genetic footprint that recovery in headcount alone does not erase.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about effective population size is testing whether a student understands why the number of animals you can count in the field is the wrong number to plug into a drift or inbreeding calculation. The strong answer names the harmonic-mean sensitivity to bottlenecks and the unequal-sex-ratio formula as the two concrete reasons Ne undershoots N, and can cite the empirical Ne/N ratio of roughly 0.1 as a sanity check rather than treating census size and effective size as interchangeable. A student who conflates the two has missed the entire point of defining Ne in the first place.

questions.prompt: Effective population size (Ne) is best defined as:

options.text: The exact number of individuals counted in a field census
The size of an idealized Wright-Fisher population that would experience genetic drift at the same rate as the real population under study
The number of individuals that survive to reproductive age each year
The total number of alleles present at a single locus

explanations.a: Census size is the field headcount; Ne is a distinct, usually smaller, modeling quantity.
explanations.b: Correct — Ne is defined by matching drift rate to an idealized Wright-Fisher population, which absorbs real-world deviations like unequal sex ratio and fluctuating size into one comparable number.
explanations.c: Survival to reproductive age is one contributor to reproductive variance, but it is not itself the definition of Ne.
explanations.d: Allele count at a locus is unrelated to the definition of effective population size.

questions.prompt: Why is the harmonic mean, rather than the arithmetic mean, used to average fluctuating census sizes across generations when estimating Ne?

options.text: The harmonic mean is easier to compute

The harmonic mean is disproportionately pulled down by the smallest value in the series, capturing how a single severe bottleneck generation dominates long-run drift even if the population later recovers
The harmonic mean always equals the arithmetic mean for population data
The harmonic mean ignores bottleneck years entirely

explanations.a: Ease of computation is not the reason; the harmonic mean is chosen because it correctly reflects the biology of drift under fluctuating size.
explanations.b: Correct — because the harmonic mean is dominated by small values, a single bottleneck generation depresses the long-run Ne far more than a simple arithmetic average would, matching how a genetic bottleneck's effects on diversity outlast a quick census recovery.
explanations.c: The two means are equal only when all values in the series are identical; with fluctuation they diverge, often sharply.
explanations.d: The harmonic mean is dominated by bottleneck years, not indifferent to them.
