questions.prompt: A species has 900 breeding females and 10 breeding males in a given generation. Using Ne = 4*Nm*Nf/(Nm+Nf), what is Ne, and how does it compare to the total census size of 910?

options.text: Ne = 39.6, far below the census size of 910, because the rare sex (males) limits effective size
Ne = 910, identical to the census size
Ne = 4,500, larger than the census size
Ne = 900, equal to the number of females alone

explanations.a: Correct — Ne = 4*10*900/(10+900) = 36,000/910 = about 39.6, dramatically below the 910 census total, illustrating how a scarce sex collapses effective size even when the other sex is abundant.
explanations.b: Equal sex ratio would give Ne close to census size, but the extreme skew here (10 males vs. 900 females) drags Ne far below 910.
explanations.c: This value is far too high; the formula's denominator (Nm+Nf) prevents Ne from exceeding roughly 4 times the rarer sex's count.
explanations.d: Ne is not simply the count of the more abundant sex; both sexes and their imbalance enter the formula.

questions.prompt: The long-term effective population size of humans, roughly 10,000, is best understood as:

options.text: A literal historical headcount of how many humans existed at one specific moment
A Wright-Fisher-equivalent figure inferred from genetic diversity and coalescence patterns, used to calibrate mutation rates and date shared ancestry, distinct from any true historical census size
The current global human population divided by ten
A number that applies only to a single isolated founding population and not to the species as a whole

explanations.a: Ne is not a census headcount at any single time point; it is a modeling quantity inferred from genetic patterns.
explanations.b: Correct — the ~10,000 figure comes from genome-wide diversity and coalescent evidence and serves as a calibration anchor for mutation-rate and divergence-time estimates across population genomics, not a literal historical count.
explanations.c: This is not how the figure is derived or defined; it has no relationship to today's global population number.
explanations.d: The figure is a long-term, species-wide effective size estimate, not restricted to a single founding group.

lessons.label: Linkage Disequilibrium: The Second Fundamental Quantity

sections.heading: D, D', and r^2
sections.body: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium describes a single locus in isolation; linkage disequilibrium (LD) describes whether two loci's alleles are associated with each other more than chance predicts. The raw measure is D = p_AB - p_A*p_B, the observed frequency of the two-locus AB haplotype minus what independence would predict from the single-locus frequencies alone. D = 0 means the loci are in linkage equilibrium, alleles at one locus give no information about the other. D is awkward to compare across loci because its maximum possible magnitude depends on the individual allele frequencies, so two normalized versions are used instead: D', which rescales D by its theoretical maximum (D' = 1 means no historical recombination has separated the two alleles, regardless of how strong the correlation looks), and r^2, the squared correlation coefficient between the two loci's alleles, which is what matters practically for tagging one SNP with another in genotyping and association studies.

sections.heading: LD decays with recombination distance and time
sections.body: Linkage disequilibrium breaks down over generations as recombination shuffles haplotypes, and the expected decay follows approximately r^2 ~ 1/(1 + 4*Ne*c), where c is the recombination fraction between the two loci and Ne is effective population size — so LD persists longer at physically closer loci (smaller c) and in populations with smaller Ne (fewer recombination events accumulated per unit time, and less allele-frequency diversity to erode correlations). This decay is not smooth along a chromosome: recombination is concentrated in narrow recombination hotspots rather than spread uniformly, which carves the genome into haplotype blocks — stretches of tens of kilobases within which LD stays high and few distinct haplotypes are observed, punctuated by hotspots where LD collapses sharply from one block to the next.

sections.heading: LD range as a fingerprint of population history
sections.body: Because LD decay depends on Ne and on the number of generations since alleles first co-occurred, populations that passed through a bottleneck carry LD over much longer physical distances than populations that did not, since a bottleneck both shrinks Ne (slowing decay) and reduces haplotype diversity to a smaller founding set. Reich and colleagues demonstrated this directly in a 2001 genome-wide LD survey, finding useful LD in a US population of north-European descent typically extending out to roughly 60 kilobases — markedly farther than in a Nigerian population sample, where LD fell off over a distance on the order of a few kilobases. That gap is a genetic signature of the out-of-Africa bottleneck: the ancestors of non-African populations passed through a small founding group as they left Africa, and that founding event both shrank Ne and left every descendant haplotype dragging a longer stretch of correlated ancestry behind it than African populations, which never passed through so severe a bottleneck, retain.

lessons.workedExample: A genotyping array designer wants to tag a disease-associated SNP that is expensive to assay directly, using a cheaper nearby SNP instead. In a European-ancestry reference panel, the two SNPs are 40 kb apart and show r^2 = 0.85 — high enough that genotyping the proxy SNP predicts the target SNP's genotype in the vast majority of individuals, so the array design substitutes the proxy and saves cost. The same pair of SNPs, assayed in a Nigerian reference panel, shows r^2 = 0.15 at that same 40 kb distance, because LD decays over much shorter physical distances in the ancestrally larger, non-bottlenecked African population; the same tagging strategy would fail there, silently under-capturing the disease signal. This is exactly why GWAS panels designed on European LD patterns transfer poorly to African-ancestry cohorts.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe linkage disequilibrium because it is the concept that separates "I know Hardy-Weinberg" from "I understand population genomics," and because the African-versus-European LD-range contrast is a compact, checkable fact that reveals whether a student actually understands the out-of-Africa bottleneck mechanistically or is just repeating the phrase. The strong answer connects the r^2 ~ 1/(1+4*Ne*c) decay formula to why a founding bottleneck (lower Ne, fewer generations of accumulated recombination since the founding event) produces the longer LD blocks seen in non-African genomes, rather than treating the 60 kb versus few-kb figures as an isolated trivia fact.

questions.prompt: D = 0 between two loci means:

options.text: The two loci are physically adjacent on the chromosome
The observed two-locus haplotype frequency exactly matches what independent (unlinked) single-locus allele frequencies would predict — the loci are in linkage equilibrium
Both loci are fixed for the same allele
The population is not in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium

explanations.a: Physical distance affects the rate of LD decay but is not what D = 0 itself indicates.
explanations.b: Correct — D = p_AB - p_A*p_B, so D = 0 means the observed haplotype frequency equals the product of the individual allele frequencies, exactly what statistical independence between the two loci predicts.
explanations.c: Fixation at both loci is a separate condition and does not by itself determine D.
explanations.d: Linkage disequilibrium and Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium are different concepts — one describes two-locus haplotype association, the other single-locus genotype proportions.

questions.prompt: According to the approximate decay relationship r^2 ~ 1/(1 + 4*Ne*c), which pair of loci is expected to retain the highest LD?

options.text: Loci far apart (large c) in a population with large Ne
Loci close together (small c) in a population with small Ne
Loci close together (small c) in a population with large Ne
LD is unaffected by either c or Ne

explanations.a: Large c and large Ne both push r^2 toward zero in the formula, giving the lowest, not highest, LD.
explanations.b: Correct — small c (physically close loci) and small Ne (fewer accumulated recombination events, less haplotype diversity to erode correlation) both keep the denominator small, maximizing r^2.
explanations.c: Large Ne accelerates LD decay even at close physical distance, lowering r^2 relative to the small-Ne case.
explanations.d: Both c and Ne appear directly in the denominator of the decay formula and strongly affect r^2.

questions.prompt: Reich and colleagues (2001) found useful linkage disequilibrium extending to roughly 60 kb in a US population of north-European descent but markedly less far — on the order of a few kb — in a Nigerian sample. What does this contrast reveal about population history?

options.text: European populations have a higher mutation rate than African populations

The non-African population passed through an out-of-Africa founding bottleneck that shrank effective population size and reduced haplotype diversity, slowing LD decay relative to the larger, non-bottlenecked ancestral African population
Recombination hotspots are entirely absent from the European genome
The Nigerian sample must have been genotyped on lower-resolution technology

explanations.a: The contrast reflects effective population size and demographic history (a bottleneck), not differences in mutation rate.
explanations.b: Correct — the out-of-Africa bottleneck reduced Ne and haplotype diversity in non-African ancestors, and by the decay formula a smaller Ne means slower LD decay, producing the longer LD blocks observed in the European-ancestry sample.
explanations.c: Recombination hotspots exist in all human populations; their presence does not explain the population-level LD-range difference.
explanations.d: The contrast is a well-established demographic and population-genetic finding, not a technical artifact of genotyping resolution.

questions.prompt: Why is r^2, rather than raw D, the standard metric for choosing a proxy SNP in genotyping array design?

options.text: r^2 is a normalized correlation measure comparable across loci with different allele frequencies and directly reflects how well one SNP's genotype predicts another's
r^2 is always numerically identical to D
D cannot be computed for any real dataset
r^2 ignores allele frequency entirely, making it simpler to compute

explanations.a: Correct — raw D's maximum possible magnitude depends on the two loci's individual allele frequencies, making it hard to compare across SNP pairs, while r^2 is a normalized correlation that directly quantifies predictive power for tagging purposes.
explanations.b: r^2 is derived from D but is a distinct, normalized quantity; the two are not numerically identical in general.
explanations.c: D is a standard, computable quantity — it is simply less convenient than r^2 for cross-locus comparison.
explanations.d: r^2 is computed from allele and haplotype frequencies, not independent of them; it is chosen for normalization, not for ignoring frequency.

lessons.label: Genetic Drift and the Wright-Fisher Model

sections.heading: Sampling 2N gametes, generation after generation
sections.body: The Wright-Fisher model, developed independently by Sewall Wright and Ronald Fisher in the 1930s, treats each new generation as a random draw of 2N gametes from the current allele pool of a diploid population of size N. If an allele sits at frequency p, the number of copies drawn next generation follows a binomial distribution, and the variance of the frequency change per generation works out to pq/2N. That single formula is the whole model: drift is not a directional push but sampling error, and its magnitude scales inversely with population size. A population of N = 20 has a variance 100 times larger than one of N = 2000, so the same starting frequency can swing wildly in the small population while barely wobbling in the large one over the same number of generations.

sections.heading: Three numbers that follow from binomial sampling
sections.body: Three consequences fall directly out of this sampling process, all first worked out rigorously by Motoo Kimura in the 1950s-60s. First, the probability that a neutral allele eventually fixes equals its current frequency in the population — a new mutation, present as a single copy, therefore has a fixation probability of exactly 1/(2N). Second, conditional on fixing, the mean time to fixation of a neutral allele is approximately 4Ne generations, where Ne is the effective population size (often smaller than the census size N because of unequal sex ratios, variance in offspring number, or population bottlenecks). Unequal sex ratio alone shows the gap: Wright's formula gives Ne = 4*Nm*Nf/(Nm+Nf), so a census of N = 50 split as 10 males and 40 females yields Ne = 4*10*40/50 = 32, not 50 — fewer breeding males means more sampling noise than the census size alone would suggest. Third, heterozygosity decays each generation by a factor of roughly 1/(2Ne), so small populations lose genetic variation measurably faster than large ones, independent of any selective pressure.

sections.heading: Drift has no direction
sections.body: Simulating trajectories at N = 20 versus N = 2000 makes the key conceptual point visible: at N = 20, replicate runs starting at p = 0.5 fan out fast, with many hitting 0 or 1 (fixation or loss) within a few dozen generations. At N = 2000, replicate trajectories from the same starting point stay clustered near 0.5 for far longer, because the per-generation variance pq/2N is 100-fold smaller. Neither population is being pushed toward high or low frequency — drift is symmetric and undirected, it just makes noise, and small populations have proportionally more noise relative to signal.

lessons.workedExample: A conservation team is tracking a rare coat-color allele at frequency p = 0.3 in two isolated island populations, one with Ne = 25 and one with Ne = 2500. Using Var(Δp) = pq/2N, the small island has a per-generation variance of (0.3)(0.7)/50 = 0.0042, versus (0.3)(0.7)/5000 = 0.000042 for the large one — a 100-fold difference. Over 50 generations, simulations show the small island's allele frequency has a real chance of drifting to fixation or loss even with zero selection, while the large island's frequency stays close to 0.3. The team correctly concludes that the small island's allele trajectory says nothing about fitness — it is a sample-size artifact, not evidence of an advantage or disadvantage.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe genetic drift because it is the null hypothesis every selection claim must be measured against, and the giveaway phrase is 'this allele became more common, so it must have been favored.' A student who understands drift responds by asking about population size: with a small Ne, an allele can rise or fall by chance alone, and 4Ne generations to fixation is a specific, testable timescale a judge can compare against the observed data. The strongest answers name pq/2N and explain why a bottlenecked or founder population is the setting where drift, not selection, is the more parsimonious explanation for an unexpected frequency shift.

questions.prompt: In the Wright-Fisher model, the variance of the per-generation change in allele frequency p is given by:

options.text: pq/2N
4Nemu
s*p*q

explanations.a: Correct — binomial sampling of 2N gametes each generation gives Var(Δp) = pq/2N, the core result of the Wright-Fisher model.
explanations.b: This has the population size in the wrong place; variance from sampling decreases, not increases, with N.
explanations.c: 4Nemu is the mutation-drift equilibrium parameter theta, not the per-generation sampling variance.
explanations.d: s*p*q resembles the selection term in the one-locus recursion, not the drift variance, which has no selection coefficient at all.

questions.prompt: A brand-new neutral mutation appears as a single copy in a diploid population of size N = 500. What is its probability of eventually fixing?

options.text: It cannot fix without selection

explanations.a: This uses N instead of 2N; the relevant denominator is the total number of gene copies, 2N.
explanations.b: Correct — a neutral allele's fixation probability equals its current frequency, and a single new copy out of 2N = 1000 total copies has frequency 1/1000.
explanations.c: 1/2 would only apply if the allele already sat at 50% frequency, not for a brand-new single-copy mutant.
explanations.d: Neutral alleles can and do fix by drift alone; selection is not required for fixation.

questions.prompt: Comparing populations of N = 20 and N = 2000 starting at the same allele frequency, simulated trajectories show that the small population:

options.text: Trends systematically toward higher allele frequency
Fans out faster and more often hits fixation or loss, with no directional bias
Stays closer to the starting frequency than the large population
Experiences stronger selection than the large population

explanations.a: Drift has no inherent direction; it is undirected sampling noise, not a trend toward higher frequency.
explanations.b: Correct — the 100-fold larger variance (pq/2N) at N = 20 makes trajectories fan out and hit the boundaries (0 or 1) much sooner, symmetrically in either direction.
explanations.c: The opposite is true — the small population's trajectories spread out faster because sampling variance is larger.
explanations.d: The Wright-Fisher model as described here has no selection term at all; the difference is purely a sample-size effect.

questions.prompt: Match each drift-related quantity to its approximate value or description under the Wright-Fisher model.

left.text: Fixation probability of a neutral allele
Mean time to fixation of a neutral allele that does fix

right.text: Equal to its current frequency (1/2N for a new mutant)
Approximately 4Ne generations
Approximately 1/(2Ne) per generation

questions.explanation: These three results all follow from Kimura's diffusion-approximation treatment of binomial sampling: fixation probability equals current frequency, mean fixation time for a fixing neutral allele is about 4Ne generations, and heterozygosity is lost at roughly 1/(2Ne) per generation.

lessons.label: Mutation: The Source of Everything

sections.heading: Measuring the human mutation rate directly
sections.body: Every other force in this unit reshuffles existing variation; only mutation creates new alleles, so its rate sets the raw material budget for all of evolution. Kong et al. (2012) measured this directly by whole-genome sequencing 78 Icelandic parent-offspring trios, comparing each child's genome to both parents' to catch mutations that arose fresh in the germline. With an average father's age of 29.7 at conception, they estimated a de novo rate of about 1.2x10^-8 mutations per base pair per generation, translating to roughly 60-70 new single-nucleotide mutations in each newborn's genome out of about 3.2 billion base pairs — a tiny per-base rate that adds up across a genome-sized target.

sections.heading: Why fathers matter more with every passing year
sections.body: The Kong et al. (2012) trios revealed a striking asymmetry: most new mutations trace to the father, not the mother, because sperm-producing cells keep dividing throughout a man's life while the pool of egg cells is largely fixed before birth, so each additional replication cycle in spermatogenesis is another chance to copy a base wrong. The study estimated that paternal mutations increase by roughly one to two extra mutations per year of the father's age, with the total mutation count roughly doubling every 16.5 years — meaning a child of an older father starts life carrying a measurably larger mutational load than a sibling born when the father was younger.

sections.heading: From mutation rate to standing diversity
sections.body: Population genetics connects this input rate to the variation actually observed today through mutation-drift equilibrium. Under the infinite-sites assumption — that every new mutation hits a brand-new site, never recreating one already present — drift constantly removes variation (losing heterozygosity at about 1/(2Ne) per generation, as the previous lesson showed) while mutation constantly replaces it. At steady state, the expected nucleotide diversity is theta = 4*Ne*mu, where mu is the per-site mutation rate. Plugging in a human mu near 1.2x10^-8 per generation and estimates of human effective population size in the tens of thousands gives a predicted theta on the order of 0.001 — matching the empirically observed nucleotide diversity pi of roughly 0.001, or about one difference per kilobase between two random human chromosomes. That match is one of the cleanest confirmations that drift and mutation, not selection, set the baseline level of genome-wide diversity. The match is not perfectly settled, though: pedigree-based rates like Kong et al.'s 1.2x10^-8 run noticeably lower than older phylogenetic, fossil-calibrated substitution-rate estimates of roughly 2-2.5x10^-8, a real gap population geneticists still call the mutation rate paradox and continue to investigate.

lessons.workedExample: A genetic counselor is asked why a child conceived by a 45-year-old father is estimated to carry more de novo mutations than one conceived by a 25-year-old father from the same couple. Using the Kong et al. (2012) finding of roughly one to two additional mutations per year of paternal age, the 20-year gap predicts on the order of 20-40 extra de novo mutations, consistent with the doubling-every-16.5-years pattern the study reported. The counselor explains this is not because older sperm are damaged by the environment, but because spermatogonial stem cells have divided many more times by age 45, and each division is another opportunity for an uncorrected replication error to become a permanent germline mutation.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe mutation rate because it is the one force students often treat as a vague background fact rather than a measured number with a source. The strong answer names Kong et al. (2012), the trio-sequencing method that isolated de novo events from inherited variants, and the specific rate (about 1.2x10^-8 per base per generation) rather than saying 'mutations happen randomly.' A judge testing depth will ask why fathers contribute more mutations than mothers — the answer must invoke the biology of continuous spermatogenesis versus a fixed oocyte pool, not just restate that older parents have more mutations.

questions.prompt: Kong et al. (2012) estimated the human de novo mutation rate, using whole-genome sequencing of parent-offspring trios, at approximately:

options.text: 1.2 x 10^-8 mutations per base pair per generation
1.2 x 10^-4 mutations per base pair per generation
1 mutation per genome per generation
1.2 x 10^-8 mutations per base pair per year

explanations.a: Correct — this is the rate Kong et al. (2012) measured from 78 Icelandic trios, corresponding to roughly 60-70 new mutations across the genome per generation.
explanations.b: This rate is four orders of magnitude too high; at this rate the genome would accumulate hundreds of thousands of mutations per generation.
explanations.c: The actual figure is far higher than one mutation per genome — closer to 60-70 across the roughly 3.2-billion-base genome.
explanations.d: The rate is per generation, not per year; generations in the study spanned decades, not a single year.

questions.prompt: Why did Kong et al. (2012) find that most de novo mutations trace to the father rather than the mother?

options.text: Sperm cells are exposed to more environmental radiation than egg cells
Spermatogonial stem cells divide continuously throughout life, giving more replication cycles per mutation opportunity, while the egg-cell pool is largely fixed before birth
Maternal mutations are repaired more efficiently by DNA repair enzymes
The Y chromosome mutates faster than autosomes

explanations.a: The study attributed the paternal bias to replication-driven errors during ongoing spermatogenesis, not to differential environmental exposure.
explanations.b: Correct — continuous spermatogenesis means more cell divisions (and thus more chances for replication errors) accumulate with paternal age, unlike the largely non-dividing oocyte pool.
explanations.c: The asymmetry is about mutation opportunity (cell division count), not a difference in repair efficiency between the sexes.
explanations.d: The finding concerns genome-wide autosomal mutation counts from trio sequencing, not a Y-chromosome-specific effect.

questions.prompt: Under mutation-drift equilibrium, theta = 4*Ne*mu predicts human nucleotide diversity (pi) close to the observed value when reasonable estimates of Ne and mu are used. What is the approximate observed pi for humans?

options.text: About 0.1 (one difference per 10 bases)
About 0.001 (one difference per kilobase)
About 0.5 (one difference every other base)
Essentially zero, since humans are genetically identical

explanations.a: This diversity level is far too high for humans; a value near 0.1 would imply extreme heterozygosity not observed in real genomes.
explanations.b: Correct — human pi is approximately 0.001, meaning two random human chromosomes differ at roughly one site per thousand bases, matching the theta = 4*Ne*mu prediction using human Ne and mu.
explanations.c: A pi of 0.5 would mean humans differ at half of all bases, wildly inconsistent with known human genetic similarity.
explanations.d: Humans are not genetically identical; measurable diversity exists, just at the low level of about one difference per kilobase.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps that connect a measured per-base mutation rate to the observed level of standing human genetic diversity.

items.text: Sequence parent-offspring trios to directly count de novo mutations and estimate mu
Recognize that under the infinite-sites assumption, each new mutation creates variation at a brand-new site
Combine mu with effective population size Ne via theta = 4*Ne*mu to predict equilibrium diversity
Compare the predicted theta to the empirically observed nucleotide diversity pi (~0.001)

questions.explanation: The logical chain starts with measuring mu empirically (trio sequencing), then invokes the infinite-sites assumption to justify treating each mutation as a new variant, then combines mu with Ne in the theta = 4*Ne*mu formula, and finally checks that prediction against the observed pi — the step that confirms mutation-drift equilibrium explains human diversity.

lessons.label: Selection in a Population-Genetic Frame

sections.heading: Relative fitness, s, and h
sections.body: Population genetics does not track survival or reproduction in absolute terms; it tracks relative fitness, the reproductive output of one genotype compared to another, normalized so the fittest genotype equals 1. For a single locus with alleles A and a, the three genotype fitnesses are typically written 1, 1-hs, and 1-s for AA, Aa, and aa, where s is the selection coefficient (the fitness disadvantage of the aa homozygote) and h is the dominance coefficient describing how much of that disadvantage shows up in the heterozygote — h = 0.5 for additive effects, h near 0 for a recessive deleterious allele, h near 1 for a dominant one. This framework, formalized by Fisher, Wright, and J.B.S. Haldane in the 1920s-30s, turns natural selection into an algebraic recursion: each generation, allele frequency updates according to the average fitness contributed by each genotype, weighted by Hardy-Weinberg proportions.

sections.heading: The logistic sweep
sections.body: Iterating the one-locus recursion for a favored allele under directional selection produces a characteristic S-shaped, logistic trajectory: frequency change is slow while the allele is rare (few copies to select on), accelerates through intermediate frequencies where selection has maximal leverage, then slows again as the allele approaches fixation and few disadvantaged genotypes remain to be removed. The time such a sweep takes scales with both the strength of selection and the population size, following approximately (2/s)*ln(2N) generations — a stronger s shortens the sweep, while a larger N lengthens it slightly because the allele starts from a smaller initial frequency (1/(2N)) and there is more distance to travel from rare to common.

sections.heading: Haldane's 1927 result: selection is a coin flip weighted by 2s
sections.body: The most counterintuitive result in this lesson is Haldane's (1927) finding that a single new beneficial mutation, even one that is strongly favored, usually does not fix — its fixation probability is only about 2s. A mutation with a 1% fitness advantage (s = 0.01) therefore fixes only about 2% of the time and is lost to drift roughly 98% of the time, because in its first few generations as one or a few copies, it is still vulnerable to the same binomial sampling that governs neutral alleles. Selection only reliably wins once an allele has drifted up to a substantial number of copies; a new beneficial mutation must survive that initial gauntlet of drift before its fitness advantage can consistently express itself.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher studying antibiotic resistance in a bacterial population estimates a resistance allele confers a 4% fitness advantage (s = 0.04) in the presence of the drug, in a population where the allele starts as a single new mutation among 2N = 2,000,000 gene copies. Using Haldane's approximation, the fixation probability is about 2s = 0.08, so even this strongly beneficial mutation is lost roughly 92% of the time it arises, and repeated independent mutation events are needed before one survives drift's early gauntlet and sweeps. Once a lineage does survive, the sweep to near-fixation is predicted to take on the order of (2/0.04)*ln(2,000,000) generations, illustrating why resistance can appear to emerge abruptly after many silent failed attempts.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe selection at the population-genetic level because students often describe it as deterministic — 'the beneficial allele wins.' Haldane's 2s result is the specific fact that dismantles that intuition: it forces a student to explain that even a clearly advantageous mutation is usually lost to drift while rare, and that fixation is a probability, not a guarantee. A judge asking 'why hasn't this beneficial variant already fixed in your population if it's so advantageous?' is testing whether the student can invoke the stochastic loss of early copies rather than assuming selection acts like a light switch.

questions.prompt: In the standard one-locus selection model with genotype fitnesses 1, 1-hs, 1-s for AA, Aa, aa, what does the dominance coefficient h control?

options.text: The overall strength of selection against the aa homozygote
How much of the aa homozygote's fitness disadvantage is expressed in the Aa heterozygote
The mutation rate from A to a
The effective population size

explanations.a: The overall strength of selection against aa is s, not h; h instead governs the heterozygote's fitness.
explanations.b: Correct — h scales how much of the homozygote disadvantage (s) shows up in the heterozygote's fitness (1-hs), ranging from additive (h=0.5) to fully recessive (h=0) to fully dominant (h=1).
explanations.c: Dominance and mutation rate are separate parameters; h has nothing to do with how often A mutates to a.
explanations.d: Effective population size is a demographic parameter (Ne), unrelated to the dominance relationship between alleles.

questions.prompt: According to Haldane's (1927) result, a new beneficial mutation with selection coefficient s = 0.01 (a 1% fitness advantage) has an approximate fixation probability of:

options.text: About 50%, since it is beneficial
About 2%
About 99%
Exactly 1/(2N), the same as a neutral allele

explanations.a: Being beneficial does not guarantee a high fixation probability; a new mutation still starts as a single vulnerable copy subject to drift.
explanations.b: Correct — Haldane's approximation gives fixation probability of about 2s, so s = 0.01 yields roughly 0.02, or 2%.
explanations.c: 99% dramatically overstates how reliably a weakly beneficial new mutation escapes early loss by drift.
explanations.d: 1/(2N) is the neutral fixation probability; a beneficial allele's fixation probability (2s) is higher than neutral but still usually small for weak selection.

questions.prompt: The shape of an allele frequency trajectory under directional selection, from rare to fixed, is best described as:

options.text: Linear, with a constant rate of increase
Logistic (S-shaped): slow while rare, fast at intermediate frequency, slow again near fixation
Immediate jump from rare to fixed in one generation
Oscillating indefinitely around the starting frequency

explanations.a: A constant linear rate does not match the recursion's behavior, which changes speed depending on genotype frequencies.
explanations.b: Correct — the one-locus recursion produces a logistic curve because selection has the least genotypes to act on when the allele is rare or nearly fixed, and the most leverage at intermediate frequency.
explanations.c: Selection changes frequency gradually across many generations, governed by s and N, not instantaneously.
explanations.d: Directional selection pushes frequency toward fixation or loss; sustained oscillation is a signature of balancing selection, not directional selection.

questions.prompt: Approximately how many generations does a sweep to fixation take for a favored allele with selection coefficient s in a population of size N?

options.text: 4Ne generations regardless of s
1/(2N) generations
s*N generations

explanations.a: Correct — this approximation reflects that stronger selection (larger s) shortens the sweep, while larger N lengthens it slightly because the allele starts from a smaller initial frequency.
explanations.b: 4Ne generations is the mean fixation time for a neutral allele, not a selected one; selection typically fixes an allele much faster than drift alone.
explanations.c: 1/(2N) is a probability (the neutral fixation probability for a new mutant), not a timescale in generations.
explanations.d: s*N would grow without bound as N increases and does not match the logarithmic dependence on population size seen in real sweep dynamics.

lessons.label: Balancing Selection and Why Variation Persists

sections.heading: Heterozygote advantage: the HbS case
sections.body: Directional selection erases variation by driving one allele to fixation, but balancing selection actively maintains two or more alleles at intermediate frequency. The clearest textbook case is the sickle-cell allele HbS, first linked to malaria resistance by Allison (1954): heterozygotes (HbA/HbS) suffer little sickling but gain strong resistance to Plasmodium falciparum malaria, while HbS/HbS homozygotes suffer severe, often fatal sickle-cell disease, and HbA/HbA homozygotes remain fully vulnerable to malaria mortality. With fitness of AA = 1-s1 (the malaria cost) and SS = 1-s2 (the disease cost) and the heterozygote at fitness 1, the two opposing homozygote costs push the allele toward a stable interior equilibrium rather than fixation or loss. That equilibrium frequency works out to q* = s1/(s1+s2): the stronger the malaria pressure (larger s1) relative to the disease cost (s2), the higher the stable HbS frequency, which is exactly why HbS reaches its highest frequencies, sometimes over 15%, in historically malaria-endemic regions of sub-Saharan Africa.

sections.heading: Frequency-dependent selection: an advantage that shrinks as it spreads
sections.body: A second balancing mechanism is negative frequency-dependent selection, where a genotype's fitness advantage depends on being rare rather than being intrinsically superior. Hori's (1993) study of scale-eating cichlid fish in Lake Tanganyika is a clean example: the fish have a genetically determined mouth asymmetry, left-jawed or right-jawed, and each morph attacks prey fish from the side its mouth favors. Whichever morph is currently rare catches prey off guard more often, so its population share rises — until it becomes common, prey grow wary of that side, and the advantage flips to the other morph, producing oscillation around roughly equal frequencies rather than fixation of either form.

sections.heading: MHC/HLA and the genomic signature of balancing selection
sections.body: The most extreme documented case is the MHC/HLA gene family, which presents pathogen fragments to the immune system; more alleles let an individual recognize a wider range of pathogens, so rare or heterozygous variants are repeatedly favored. Klein and colleagues showed some HLA allele lineages are trans-species polymorphisms, meaning specific allelic lineages are shared by descent between humans and chimpanzees — the polymorphism has persisted through millions of years and a full speciation event, far longer than any neutral allele's expected lifespan. Genomically, long-term balancing selection leaves a recognizable fingerprint: an excess of intermediate-frequency variants (a positive Tajima's D) and elevated nucleotide diversity clustered right around the target locus, sharply contrasting with the diversity trough a selective sweep leaves behind.

lessons.workedExample: A student models the HbS/HbA system with a malaria-driven fitness cost to HbA/HbA of s1 = 0.15 and a sickle-cell-disease cost to HbS/HbS of s2 = 0.90 (roughly reflecting historical child mortality without modern treatment). Using q* = s1/(s1+s2) = 0.15/(0.15+0.90) ≈ 0.143, the model predicts an equilibrium HbS allele frequency near 14%, consistent with frequencies reported in high-malaria-burden regions of West Africa. The student then checks that this is a stable equilibrium by noting that if HbS frequency temporarily overshoots 14%, more SS homozygotes appear and drag the population average fitness down until frequency falls back, and if it undershoots, more AA homozygotes die of malaria and pull the frequency back up.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe balancing selection because it is the direct counterexample to the intuition, correctly built from the earlier directional-selection lesson, that selection always erases variation. A judge will ask why the malaria-resistance allele hasn't simply fixed if it's so beneficial — the strong answer names the heterozygote-advantage mechanism and the equilibrium formula, showing the allele is trapped at an interior frequency by two opposing homozygote costs, not by weak selection. Naming the genomic signature (elevated diversity, intermediate-frequency excess) also lets a student explain how researchers detect balancing selection at a locus without already knowing its phenotype.

questions.prompt: In the HbS/HbA malaria system, the HbA/HbS heterozygote has the highest relative fitness because:

options.text: It has no sickle hemoglobin at all
It gains substantial resistance to malaria while avoiding the severe disease seen in HbS/HbS homozygotes
It is immune to all mosquito-borne diseases
It has a higher mutation rate than either homozygote

explanations.a: Heterozygotes do carry one HbS copy; the advantage comes from having both alleles, not from lacking HbS entirely.
explanations.b: Correct — the heterozygote combines malaria resistance from the HbS allele with avoidance of the severe sickling disease that HbS/HbS homozygotes suffer, giving it the highest fitness of the three genotypes under malaria pressure.
explanations.c: The resistance is specifically to Plasmodium falciparum malaria, not a general immunity to all mosquito-borne diseases.
explanations.d: Mutation rate is unrelated to this fitness advantage; the mechanism is about survival and reproduction, not mutation.

questions.prompt: Given fitness costs s1 (against the AA homozygote) and s2 (against the aa homozygote) under heterozygote advantage, the stable equilibrium frequency of the a allele is:

explanations.a: Correct — the equilibrium frequency of the minor allele under heterozygote advantage is s1/(s1+s2), where s1 is the cost to the other homozygote (AA); a stronger cost to AA pushes the a-allele equilibrium frequency higher.
explanations.b: This formula is swapped — it gives the equilibrium frequency of the A allele (1-q*), not of a.
explanations.c: Multiplying the two selection coefficients has no basis in the standard derivation of the heterozygote-advantage equilibrium.
explanations.d: This expression is not derived from the fitness recursion and can even produce a negative or nonsensical frequency for typical s1 and s2 values.

questions.prompt: In Hori's (1993) study of scale-eating cichlid fish, why does the rare mouth-asymmetry morph (left- or right-jawed) have a fitness advantage?

options.text: The rare morph is intrinsically stronger and better at swimming
Prey fish become wary of whichever side attacks them more often, so the currently rare morph catches prey off guard more successfully
The rare morph has a higher mutation rate
The common morph cannot reproduce

explanations.a: The advantage is not about intrinsic strength; both morphs are otherwise equivalent, differing only in mouth-side asymmetry and its frequency.
explanations.b: Correct — this is negative frequency-dependent selection: prey vigilance adapts to whichever attack side is currently common, so the rarer morph benefits from surprise, and the advantage flips as frequencies shift.
explanations.c: Mutation rate plays no role in this mechanism; the advantage is purely about predation success relative to prey wariness.
explanations.d: The common morph still reproduces; it simply has a lower feeding success rate while common, not zero fitness.

questions.prompt: The genomic signature that distinguishes long-term balancing selection from a recent selective sweep is:

options.text: A sharp trough in diversity right at the selected site, like a sweep
An excess of intermediate-frequency variants and elevated diversity clustered around the target locus
Complete fixation of a single allele across the whole population
No detectable difference from genome-wide background diversity

explanations.a: A diversity trough is the signature of a selective sweep (directional selection), which removes linked variation — the opposite of what balancing selection produces.
explanations.b: Correct — balancing selection maintains multiple alleles at intermediate frequency for a long time, producing a local excess of intermediate-frequency variants and elevated diversity around the locus, as seen at HLA/MHC.
explanations.c: Fixation of a single allele is the outcome of directional selection or drift, not balancing selection, which by definition maintains multiple alleles.
explanations.d: Balancing selection leaves a detectable, distinctive elevation in diversity and allele-frequency spectrum shape relative to the genomic background, unlike neutral regions.

lessons.label: Migration, Gene Flow and Population Connectivity

sections.heading: The island model and Nm
sections.body: Wright's (1931) island model treats a species as many subpopulations, each of effective size N, exchanging migrants with a shared common pool at some fraction m per generation. The key composite parameter is Nm, the absolute number of migrants entering a subpopulation each generation — not the migration rate alone, since a low rate m in a large population can move just as many actual individuals as a high rate in a small one. Under this model, migration homogenizes allele frequencies across subpopulations while drift within each subpopulation pulls them apart, and the balance between those two opposing forces settles into an equilibrium level of population differentiation.

sections.heading: F_ST, the one-migrant rule, and its fragile assumptions
sections.body: That equilibrium differentiation is captured by Wright's F_ST statistic, and under the island model it works out to approximately F_ST ≈ 1/(1+4Nm). This equation yields Wright's well-known one-migrant-per-generation rule of thumb: when Nm = 1, F_ST settles near 0.2, low enough that subpopulations stay genetically cohesive rather than diverging into separate gene pools, even though most individuals never migrate at all. The rule is popular precisely because it is so simple, but it rests on fragile assumptions that real populations routinely violate: an island model requires all subpopulations to be the same size, migration to be random and equally likely between any pair of subpopulations, and neutrality at the locus in question — violate any of these (unequal subpopulation sizes, geographic structure, or selection acting against migrant alleles) and the Nm = 1 threshold no longer reliably predicts cohesion.

sections.heading: Stepping-stones, clines, and a confound selection shares with migration
sections.body: The island model's biggest simplification is that any two subpopulations exchange migrants equally regardless of distance, which fails badly for species spread across real geography. Kimura and Weiss (1964) proposed the stepping-stone model instead, where migration happens mainly between geographically adjacent subpopulations, producing isolation by distance: genetic differentiation grows systematically with geographic distance rather than staying uniform, an effect Wright had already described qualitatively in 1943. A subtle trap follows from this: a smooth geographic cline in allele frequency looks identical whether it arises from gradual gene flow between distance-limited demes with no selection, or from a spatially varying selection gradient (an environmental factor that favors different alleles in different places) acting on an otherwise well-mixed population — distinguishing the two requires additional evidence, such as testing whether the cline tracks an environmental variable or comparing it against clines at neutral loci.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher studies two frog subpopulations, each with Ne = 500, connected by an estimated migration rate m = 0.002 per generation. Nm = 500 x 0.002 = 1, right at Wright's threshold, predicting F_ST ≈ 1/(1+4x1) = 0.2 — moderate differentiation but not full isolation. If the researcher instead finds F_ST = 0.5 at a particular locus, far higher than the neutral island-model prediction, that locus is a candidate for local selection reducing effective gene flow there specifically, since migration and drift alone (as modeled) would not produce such strong differentiation at that Nm. This is exactly the logic genome scans use to flag outlier loci as candidates for local adaptation against a neutral migration-drift background.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe migration because students often conflate migration rate with migrant number, and the fix is precise: Nm, not m alone, determines differentiation, so the same rate means something different in a population of 50 versus 50,000. A judge presenting a smooth allele-frequency cline across a species range is testing whether the student names both candidate explanations — isolation by distance from stepping-stone gene flow, and a selection gradient — and proposes a way to tell them apart, rather than assuming a cline automatically proves either adaptation or connectivity.

questions.prompt: In Wright's island model, why is the composite parameter Nm (not m alone) the key quantity for predicting population differentiation?

options.text: Because Nm gives the absolute number of migrants exchanged per generation, which is what actually opposes drift regardless of subpopulation size
Because N and m always take the same numeric value
Because m alone has no effect on allele frequencies
Because Nm measures the mutation rate at migrant loci

explanations.a: Correct — a low migration rate in a large population can move as many actual migrants as a high rate in a small one, so it is the absolute migrant number, Nm, that counterbalances drift and determines equilibrium differentiation.
explanations.b: N and m are independent parameters (population size and migration rate) with no requirement to be numerically equal.
explanations.c: The migration rate m does affect frequencies, but its effect scales with population size N, which is why the product matters more than m in isolation.
explanations.d: Nm is a migration/drift parameter and has nothing to do with mutation rate.

questions.prompt: Under the island model, Wright's approximation for equilibrium F_ST is F_ST ≈ 1/(1+4Nm). What F_ST does this predict when Nm = 1 (Wright's one-migrant-per-generation rule)?

options.text: F_ST ≈ 0

explanations.a: F_ST = 0 would mean no differentiation at all, but the formula with Nm = 1 gives a nonzero value.
explanations.b: Correct — plugging Nm = 1 into 1/(1+4x1) gives 1/5 = 0.2, Wright's benchmark for subpopulations that remain genetically cohesive despite limited migration.
explanations.c: 0.8 would indicate strong differentiation, which corresponds to a much lower Nm (far less migration) than Nm = 1.
explanations.d: F_ST = 1.0 would mean complete fixation of different alleles in each subpopulation (total isolation), the opposite of what one migrant per generation produces.

questions.prompt: Which assumption of the basic island model is most directly relaxed by the stepping-stone model of Kimura and Weiss (1964)?

options.text: That all subpopulations are the same effective size
That migration occurs mainly between geographically adjacent subpopulations rather than equally among all pairs
That mutation is the only source of new variation
That fitness is equal across all genotypes

explanations.a: Equal subpopulation size is a separate island-model assumption not specifically addressed by the stepping-stone model.
explanations.b: Correct — the stepping-stone model replaces the island model's assumption of equal migration between any pair of subpopulations with migration limited mainly to geographic neighbors, producing isolation by distance.
explanations.c: Mutation as a variation source is a separate topic from the geographic structure of migration that the stepping-stone model addresses.
explanations.d: Equal fitness across genotypes concerns selection, not the geographic structure of migration that distinguishes stepping-stone from island models.

questions.prompt: A smooth cline in allele frequency across a species' geographic range could be produced by:

options.text: Only gradual gene flow between geographically limited demes, never by selection
Only a spatially varying selection gradient, never by gene flow
Either gradual, distance-limited gene flow (isolation by distance) or a spatially varying selection gradient — the two look similar and require additional evidence to distinguish
Only genetic drift acting identically in every subpopulation

explanations.a: Selection can also produce a smooth cline if an environmental factor varies gradually across the range, so gene flow is not the only possible cause.
explanations.b: Gene flow limited by geographic distance (isolation by distance) can also produce a smooth cline without any selection at all, so selection is not the only possible cause.
explanations.c: Correct — both mechanisms can produce visually similar clines, so distinguishing them requires further evidence, such as whether the cline tracks an environmental variable or whether it appears at neutral comparison loci.
explanations.d: Drift acting identically everywhere would not produce a systematic geographic gradient; it produces random, undirected local fluctuation, not a smooth cline.

lessons.label: Nearly Neutral: When Drift Beats Selection

sections.heading: Ohta's threshold: the same mutation, two fates
sections.body: The strict neutral theory treats mutations as either neutral (s = 0) or under strong selection, but Ohta (1973) argued most mutations occupy a middle ground: slightly deleterious, with a real but small fitness cost. Her key insight was that whether such a mutation behaves as effectively neutral or as truly deleterious depends not on s alone but on the product Nes — a mutation with |s| below roughly 1/(2Ne) is effectively invisible to selection, because drift's sampling noise overwhelms such a weak fitness signal, while the identical mutation with the identical s becomes efficiently purged once Ne is large enough to push |s| above that threshold. The same variant, unchanged in its biochemical effect, is selectively neutral in a small population and selectively removed in a large one — population size, not mutation identity, decides its fate.

sections.heading: Drift load and the danger for small populations
sections.body: This threshold has a direct consequence for populations that shrink: as Ne falls, the range of |s| values that count as effectively neutral widens, so mildly deleterious mutations that a larger population would have purged instead drift to appreciable frequency or even fixation, accumulating as drift load. In the most severe cases this becomes a self-reinforcing spiral termed mutational meltdown (Lynch et al., 1995): a shrinking population accumulates deleterious mutations faster than selection can remove them, the resulting fitness decline further reduces population size and thus Ne, which widens the nearly-neutral zone further, accelerating decline toward extinction. This is why conservation genetics treats effective population size, not census count, as the number that predicts a population's genetic health.

sections.heading: Why Ne, not N, and what it means for growing human populations
sections.body: Effective population size is almost always smaller than the census count because Ne depends on how evenly individuals contribute offspring, not how many individuals exist: unequal sex ratios, high variance in reproductive success, and historical bottlenecks all reduce Ne relative to N by shrinking the pool of genetic contributors, and Ne is closer to the harmonic mean of population size over time, so a single sharp bottleneck can permanently depress Ne even after census numbers rebound. Human populations show a related but distinct pattern: Keinan and Clark (2012) documented that recent explosive population growth has left an excess of rare variants, including deleterious ones, because purifying selection has not yet had time to remove them even though current Ne is large — growth outruns selection's ability to keep pace, a transient mutation-selection disequilibrium rather than a permanently small nearly-neutral zone.

lessons.workedExample: A wildlife geneticist compares two populations of an endangered fox: one stable at Ne = 5,000 and one recently bottlenecked to Ne = 50. A slightly deleterious mutation with s = -0.0005 has |Nes| = 2.5 in the large population (above the effectively-neutral threshold of roughly Nes < 1, so selection efficiently removes it) but |Nes| = 0.025 in the bottlenecked population (well below threshold, so it drifts as if neutral and can rise toward fixation). The geneticist concludes the bottlenecked population is accumulating a measurable drift load of mildly harmful variants that the larger population would have purged, and flags the risk of a mutational-meltdown spiral if the population does not recover Ne quickly.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the nearly neutral theory because it resolves an apparent contradiction students often stumble on: how can the 'same' mutation be neutral in one study and deleterious in another? The strong answer names Ohta (1973) and the |s| versus 1/(2Ne) threshold, showing that effective population size — not the mutation's biochemistry — determines whether selection can 'see' it. A judge working with an endangered-species or human-genetics project will specifically ask why Ne, not census size, is the relevant number, and the student should be able to name a factor (unequal reproductive variance, a historical bottleneck) that separates the two.

questions.prompt: According to Ohta's (1973) nearly neutral theory, a mutation with selection coefficient s behaves as effectively neutral when:

options.text: s is exactly zero
|s| is below roughly 1/(2Ne)
|s| is above roughly 1/(2Ne)
The mutation occurs in a coding region

explanations.a: Strict neutrality (s=0) is the classical neutral theory's condition; Ohta's contribution was showing that mutations with small but nonzero s can also behave as effectively neutral.
explanations.b: Correct — when |s| falls below roughly 1/(2Ne), drift's sampling noise overwhelms the weak selective signal, so the mutation behaves as if neutral even though it has a real (small) fitness cost.
explanations.c: Above this threshold, selection dominates over drift and can efficiently remove or favor the mutation — the opposite of effectively neutral behavior.
explanations.d: Coding versus noncoding location is unrelated to the Ne-and-s-based threshold that defines the nearly neutral zone.

questions.prompt: A specific mutation with s = -0.001 is effectively neutral in a population with Ne = 200 but is efficiently purged by selection in a population with Ne = 200,000. What explains this difference?

options.text: The mutation's fitness effect s physically changes between the two populations
The same s falls below the 1/(2Ne) threshold in the small population but above it in the large population, shifting whether drift or selection dominates
Mutation rate differs between the two populations
The large population has a higher migration rate

explanations.a: The biochemical fitness effect s of the mutation does not change; what changes is whether selection can 'see' that fixed effect against the background of drift.
explanations.b: Correct — |Nes| = 0.2 in the small population (well below 1, effectively neutral) versus |Nes| = 200 in the large one (far above 1, strongly selected), so the same s produces opposite fates depending on Ne.
explanations.c: Mutation rate is not part of the nearly neutral threshold calculation, which concerns Ne and s only.
explanations.d: Migration rate is not invoked in this scenario or in Ohta's nearly neutral framework as the explanation for this contrast.

questions.prompt: Why does conservation genetics treat effective population size (Ne) rather than census size (N) as the number that predicts genetic health?

options.text: Because Ne and N are always numerically identical, so it doesn't matter which is used
Because Ne accounts for factors like unequal reproductive variance and historical bottlenecks that reduce the effective pool of genetic contributors below the census count
Because census size cannot be measured in wild populations
Because Ne only applies to bacteria, not to vertebrates

explanations.a: Ne is almost always smaller than N, not identical to it, which is precisely why the distinction matters.
explanations.b: Correct — unequal sex ratios, variance in offspring number, and bottlenecks (Ne tracking closer to the harmonic mean over time) all shrink Ne relative to N, and it is Ne that governs how efficiently selection can act against drift.
explanations.c: Census size can be estimated by direct counts or mark-recapture; the issue is that it is not the number that determines selection's efficiency, not that it is unmeasurable.
explanations.d: Effective population size is a general population-genetic concept applicable to any sexually or asexually reproducing population, including vertebrates.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the mutational meltdown spiral described by Lynch and colleagues (1995) for a shrinking population.

items.text: Population size (and thus Ne) declines
The nearly-neutral zone (|s| below 1/(2Ne)) widens, so more mildly deleterious mutations escape selection
Deleterious mutations accumulate faster than selection can remove them, lowering average fitness
Reduced fitness further shrinks the population, restarting the cycle at a smaller size

questions.explanation: Mutational meltdown is a feedback loop: a population decline shrinks Ne, which widens the nearly-neutral zone and lets more deleterious mutations drift to appreciable frequency, which lowers fitness and shrinks the population further, restarting the cycle at an even smaller Ne.

units.label: Genome-Wide Data and the Population-Genomics Toolkit

lessons.label: Arrays, Sequencing and Ascertainment Bias

sections.heading: Three ways to get genotypes, three different costs
sections.body: A SNP genotyping array (Illumina and Affymetrix chips are the workhorses) reads a few hundred thousand to a few million pre-chosen positions in the genome for a few dollars a sample — cheap enough for biobanks of hundreds of thousands of people, but blind to any variant not printed on the chip. Whole-genome sequencing reads everything, but coverage (how many times, on average, each base is read) trades directly against cost: high-coverage sequencing at 30x gives confident individual genotype calls, while low-coverage sequencing at roughly 1x reads most of the genome only zero or one times per sample, so a single sample's raw reads cannot reliably call a heterozygote. Population projects often choose low-coverage sequencing across many samples over high-coverage sequencing of a few, because population-level allele frequencies can be recovered accurately even when no single genotype is confidently known — accuracy is pooled across the sample rather than concentrated in each individual.

sections.heading: Ascertainment bias: the array was designed on someone
sections.body: Early SNP arrays, including the chips behind much of the HapMap and early GWAS era, were designed using SNPs discovered mostly by sequencing a handful of individuals of European ancestry. Any variant common in African or Indigenous American populations but rare or absent in that discovery panel was underrepresented on the chip, even though African populations carry the deepest human genetic diversity, having diversified longest since modern humans first appear in the fossil record in Africa. The result is ascertainment bias: array-derived allele-frequency spectra are skewed toward intermediate frequencies, the site-frequency spectrum looks artificially depleted of rare variants outside the discovery population, apparent diversity in African samples is deflated relative to reality, and downstream statistics computed on biased sites — F_ST between populations, PCA axes separating them — inherit the distortion. A population that looks unremarkable on a biased array can look like an outlier once unbiased whole-genome data is used instead.

sections.heading: The low-coverage fix: work with likelihoods, not hard calls
sections.body: At 1x coverage, forcing each site into a hard genotype call (0, 1, or 2 copies of the alternate allele) throws away real uncertainty and introduces bias, because a single observed read looks identical whether it came from a true homozygote or a heterozygote that happened to be sampled once. The standard fix, implemented in the widely used ANGSD toolkit, is to carry genotype likelihoods — the probability of each possible genotype given the observed reads and their base-quality scores — through every downstream analysis (allele-frequency estimation, PCA, F_ST) instead of collapsing to a single called genotype per site. This lets low-coverage sequencing of many individuals produce population-level estimates as accurate as far more expensive high-coverage calling, provided the analysis pipeline is built to consume likelihoods rather than hard genotypes.

lessons.workedExample: A team genotypes 200 rural Peruvian samples on a commercial array originally designed from a European discovery panel, then compares heterozygosity to a European reference set genotyped on the same chip. The Peruvian samples come back with lower heterozygosity — a result the team is tempted to report as evidence of a historical bottleneck. But because the chip's SNPs were ascertained in Europeans, only variants already common in Europe were printed on it; a variant common in Andean populations but never seen in the discovery panel was never a candidate for inclusion. Switching to 1x low-coverage whole-genome sequencing analyzed with genotype likelihoods (ANGSD) instead of the array recovers the full site-frequency spectrum for both groups and the apparent heterozygosity gap shrinks sharply — the original result was largely an artifact of where the chip was designed, not a biological difference.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a diversity or divergence comparison built on SNP-array data should immediately ask where the array's SNPs were discovered, because ascertainment bias is invisible in the output — F_ST, heterozygosity, and PCA all run without error on biased input and produce a confident-looking, wrong number. A student who names the discovery-panel problem and explains why low-coverage sequencing with genotype likelihoods sidesteps it (rather than just citing coverage depth as a number) is showing they understand that the tool shapes what can be seen, not just how precisely.

questions.prompt: Why does using a SNP array originally designed from a European discovery panel tend to deflate measured diversity in African samples?

options.text: African samples are biologically less diverse than European samples
The array's SNPs were chosen because they were common in the discovery panel, so variants common only outside that panel were never printed on the chip
African DNA degrades faster during array hybridization
Arrays cannot read GC-rich regions, which are more common in African genomes

explanations.a: The opposite is true — African populations carry the deepest diversity of any human population group, since modern humans have the longest history there; the array result is an artifact, not biology.
explanations.b: Correct — SNPs discovered mostly in European samples are enriched for variants common in Europe, so the chip is blind to a share of the variation that is actually common in other populations, deflating their apparent diversity.
explanations.c: Array hybridization chemistry does not differ by ancestry in this way; this is not the mechanism of ascertainment bias.
explanations.d: GC content is not the driver of ascertainment bias — discovery-panel composition is.

questions.prompt: Why can a 1x low-coverage sequencing project still produce accurate population-level allele frequencies, even though no single sample's genotype is confidently known?

options.text: Because low coverage always overestimates true allele frequency
Because genotype uncertainty at each site is preserved as a likelihood and pooled across many individuals, rather than forced into a single hard call per person
Because 1x coverage is actually equivalent to 30x coverage for any statistic
Because low-coverage reads are automatically re-sequenced until 30x is reached

explanations.a: Low coverage does not systematically overestimate frequency; the risk is bias from forcing hard calls, not a directional inflation.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the genotype-likelihood approach implemented in ANGSD: carry per-site uncertainty forward and let allele-frequency estimation pool information across the sample rather than trusting any one individual's call.
explanations.c: 1x and 30x are not equivalent for individual-level questions (like heterozygosity of one person); they can be comparably useful only for population-level allele frequencies when likelihoods are used.
explanations.d: Low-coverage projects deliberately stay at low coverage across many samples rather than re-sequencing to high coverage; that trade-off is the whole point of the design.

questions.prompt: Match each data-generation approach to its defining property.

right.text: Cheap per sample but limited to a pre-chosen, potentially ascertainment-biased set of sites
Reads most of the genome only 0-1 times per sample; needs genotype likelihoods, not hard calls, for reliable population inference
Confident individual-level genotype calls at high per-sample cost

questions.explanation: Arrays are cheap but constrained to their designed SNP set (and its discovery-panel bias); low-coverage sequencing is cheap per genome but individually uncertain, requiring likelihood-based tools like ANGSD; high-coverage sequencing is expensive but gives trustworthy individual genotypes.

questions.prompt: Which downstream population-genomic statistics are vulnerable to distortion from SNP-array ascertainment bias?

options.text: None — F_ST and PCA are computed the same way regardless of the input SNP set
Only PCA, because F_ST is always computed from whole-genome sequencing
Both F_ST and PCA, because both are computed directly from the (potentially biased) set of genotyped sites
Only mitochondrial DNA analyses, since arrays do not genotype autosomal SNPs

explanations.a: Both statistics run without error on biased input, but 'runs without error' is not the same as 'gives the true answer' — the bias in the input propagates through.
explanations.b: F_ST is routinely computed from array data in practice, not exclusively from sequencing; it is just as exposed to ascertainment bias as PCA.
explanations.c: Correct — both F_ST and PCA are built directly from whichever sites were genotyped, so a biased SNP set skews both a population's apparent divergence from others and its position on PCA axes.
explanations.d: Arrays do genotype autosomal SNPs; this option misdescribes what arrays measure.

lessons.label: Reference Panels, Imputation and Who Is In Them

sections.heading: The panels the field actually runs on
sections.body: Almost every population-genomic and imputation analysis leans on a small set of shared reference resources. The 1000 Genomes Project's phase 3 release sequenced 2,504 individuals from 26 populations across five continental groups, giving a catalog of over 88 million variants on phased haplotypes. The Human Genome Diversity Project (HGDP) sampled a smaller number of individuals but from a far broader, more anthropologically deliberate set of populations, including many small, isolated groups absent from 1000 Genomes. The Simons Genome Diversity Project (SGDP), published by Mallick and colleagues in 2016, sequenced 300 high-coverage genomes from 142 populations chosen specifically to maximize worldwide diversity. For clinical-scale imputation, the Haplotype Reference Consortium (HRC) and the newer, larger TOPMed panel (built from tens of thousands of deeply sequenced genomes, heavily weighted toward US biobank cohorts) are the working standards.

sections.heading: How imputation actually works
sections.body: Imputation fills in genotypes a study never directly measured — typically the millions of sites an array missed — by matching each study individual's genotyped SNPs against the haplotypes in a reference panel and inferring the alleles at intervening positions from whichever reference haplotype shares the longest matching stretch. This works because of linkage disequilibrium: nearby alleles are co-inherited on the same chromosome often enough that a short observed haplotype reliably predicts its neighbors, provided the reference panel actually contains a haplotype like the study individual's. Tools such as IMPUTE, Minimac, and Beagle implement this via a hidden Markov model over the panel's haplotypes.

sections.heading: Why panel composition is a scientific limit, not a footnote
sections.body: Imputation accuracy depends entirely on whether the reference panel contains haplotypes that resemble the person being imputed. Accuracy collapses for low minor-allele-frequency variants, because a rare allele has fewer reference copies to match against and a higher chance the panel simply lacks a carrier at all. It collapses even harder for individuals from ancestries thinly represented in the panel: 1000 Genomes and HRC are heavily weighted toward European and East Asian samples, so African, Indigenous American, and Oceanian individuals — despite carrying more real genetic diversity per person in the African case — get systematically worse imputation, because the panel has fewer matching haplotypes to draw from. This is not a fixable engineering detail; it is a direct consequence of who was sequenced when the panel was built, and it means published results (disease-variant discovery, polygenic scores) built on poorly imputed ancestries are less reliable for exactly the populations least represented in the resource.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher imputes array data from a Nigerian cohort and a British cohort against the same reference panel dominated by European haplotypes (much like early HRC composition). At common variants, both cohorts impute well. But at a variant with 2% frequency that is common only in West African populations, the panel — sparse in African haplotypes — has few or no matching reference chromosomes, so imputation accuracy for that variant collapses specifically in the Nigerian cohort while remaining fine in the British one. A downstream disease-association scan built on this imputed data will be systematically underpowered to detect real African-specific variants, not because the biology differs, but because the reference panel was never built to represent that haplotype diversity in the first place.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes reference-panel composition because it is the single most common hidden confound in any project that imputes genotypes: a student who reports imputed variants without checking which populations built the panel is trusting a tool whose accuracy is not uniform across their sample. The strong answer names a specific panel (1000 Genomes, HRC, TOPMed), states who it over- or under-represents, and connects that directly to why low-frequency or under-represented-ancestry variants come out less reliable — showing the limitation is understood as a property of the data resource, not a bug to be waved away.

questions.prompt: Match each reference resource to its defining scale or composition.

right.text: 2,504 individuals, 26 populations, phased haplotypes
300 high-coverage genomes from 142 populations chosen for worldwide diversity
Tens of thousands of deep genomes, heavily weighted toward US biobank cohorts

questions.explanation: 1000 Genomes phase 3 sequenced 2,504 individuals from 26 populations; SGDP (Mallick et al. 2016) sequenced 300 genomes from 142 populations chosen for diversity rather than sample size; TOPMed is a much larger, deep-coverage panel built mostly from US biobank cohorts.

questions.prompt: Imputation infers an unmeasured genotype primarily by relying on which population-genetic phenomenon?

options.text: Linkage disequilibrium, so a matching nearby haplotype predicts the unmeasured allele
Convergent evolution across unrelated populations
Random mating alone, independent of any reference panel
Mitochondrial inheritance patterns

explanations.a: Correct — imputation matches a study individual's genotyped SNPs to reference haplotypes and infers unmeasured alleles from whichever haplotype shares the longest matching stretch, which only works because of linkage disequilibrium between nearby sites.
explanations.b: Convergent evolution is unrelated to how imputation works.
explanations.c: Imputation is meaningless without a reference panel; it is not derived from random mating alone.
explanations.d: Mitochondrial inheritance is irrelevant to autosomal imputation via haplotype matching.

questions.prompt: Why does imputation accuracy collapse for individuals from ancestries thinly represented in the reference panel?

options.text: Because their DNA is chemically harder to sequence
Because the panel has fewer or no haplotypes resembling theirs to match against
Because imputation software applies a fixed penalty to non-European samples
Because their genomes contain more sequencing errors on average

explanations.a: There is no chemical sequencing difference by ancestry; the issue is panel composition, not lab chemistry.
explanations.b: Correct — imputation quality depends on the panel containing haplotypes similar to the individual being imputed; thin representation means fewer matches and worse inference, independent of underlying biology.
explanations.c: Imputation algorithms have no ancestry-aware penalty built in; the degraded accuracy is an emergent consequence of panel composition, not a coded rule.
explanations.d: This is not a sequencing-error phenomenon; it is a reference-matching phenomenon.

questions.prompt: A variant present at 2% frequency only in a population poorly represented in the reference panel will most likely be imputed with:

options.text: Higher accuracy than a common variant, since rare variants are easier to detect
The same accuracy as any common variant, since panel size does not matter for imputation
Lower accuracy, because low minor-allele-frequency variants already impute poorly, compounded by sparse reference coverage of that ancestry
Perfect accuracy, because imputation always defaults to the most common allele

explanations.a: Rare variants are harder, not easier, to impute accurately — fewer reference carriers means less information to match against.
explanations.b: Panel size and composition matter enormously for imputation accuracy; this option contradicts the core mechanism.
explanations.c: Correct — low-frequency variants already have fewer reference copies to match, and if that population is also thinly represented, the compounding effect drives accuracy down sharply.
explanations.d: Imputation does not default to the common allele in a way that yields 'perfect' accuracy; that would simply be wrong for anyone actually carrying the rare variant.

lessons.label: Population-Genomic Quality Control

sections.heading: Filtering samples and sites before any structure analysis
sections.body: Before a dataset is fit for PCA, ADMIXTURE, or any structure inference, it passes through a standard quality-control pipeline. Sample call-rate and variant call-rate thresholds (commonly requiring genotypes present at 95-98% or more of sites, and sites genotyped in 95-98% or more of samples) remove individuals and variants with too much missing data, since a genotyping failure is not random with respect to sample or site and can masquerade as a genetic signal. A minor-allele-frequency (MAF) filter, typically dropping variants below 1-5% frequency, removes sites where genotyping error rates are large relative to the true signal and where a handful of miscalls can swing an allele frequency estimate substantially.

sections.heading: LD pruning and relatedness: removing correlated and duplicated signal
sections.body: PCA and ADMIXTURE assume, implicitly, that each variant contributes independent information; variants in strong linkage disequilibrium (LD) with each other violate that assumption and let one underlying genomic region dominate an axis that should reflect genome-wide ancestry. The fix is LD pruning — sliding a window across the genome (a common choice is 50 SNPs, stepping 5 at a time) and dropping one member of any pair correlated above a threshold such as r-squared of 0.2 — before running PCA or ADMIXTURE. Relatedness is a second, distinct problem: close relatives share far more of their genome than random population members, so an unfiltered pair of siblings or a parent-child pair can visibly distort a PCA plot or ADMIXTURE's inferred cluster proportions.
