Kinship-based tools such as KING estimate relatedness directly from genotype data using a kinship coefficient; the standard cutoff of 0.0884 flags any pair as second-degree relatives or closer (half-siblings, grandparent-grandchild, avuncular pairs) or nearer, and one member of each such pair is dropped.

sections.heading: Excluding known problem regions
sections.body: A handful of genomic regions carry unusually long-range LD or unusual population-frequency structure that is real but not informative about genome-wide ancestry, and standard practice excludes them before PCA or ADMIXTURE. The MHC region on chromosome 6 has extraordinarily long haplotype blocks maintained by balancing selection on immune genes; a well-known inversion polymorphism on chromosome 8 spans megabases and creates a strong, LD-driven cluster that reflects inversion genotype, not ancestry. Left in, either region alone can generate a spurious PC axis. Perhaps the most important lesson is procedural, not statistical: a genotyping batch effect — one lab plate or sequencing run processed on a different day, machine, or protocol — can produce a systematic difference in call rate or allele calling between batches that lines up with a sample metadata variable (like collection site), producing a clean, reproducible, entirely artifactual PCA axis that looks exactly like real population structure until someone checks whether it correlates with batch instead of geography.

lessons.workedExample: A team runs PCA on a cohort collected at two hospitals, unaware that samples from hospital A were genotyped on one array lot and hospital B on a different lot processed months later. PC1 separates the two hospitals cleanly, with a smooth gradient and tight clusters — it looks like textbook population structure. But when the team checks which cases and controls are enriched at each PC1 extreme, the split maps perfectly onto hospital of origin, not onto any known geographic or ancestry variable, and a follow-up check shows differential missingness (variant call rate) between the two batches. The batch effect, not ancestry, generated PC1; the fix is enforcing a uniform call-rate threshold across both batches, re-checking whether the axis survives, and if it does not, treating it as a QC failure rather than a discovery.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about QC because a beautiful PCA or ADMIXTURE plot is cheap to produce and easy to over-trust — LD pruning, relatedness filtering, and problem-region exclusion are exactly the unglamorous steps a rushed project skips, and skipping them is the single most common way a clean-looking cluster turns out to be a batch effect or a MHC/inversion artifact rather than biology. A strong answer names a specific filter (an r-squared threshold, a KING kinship cutoff, MHC exclusion) and explains what artifact it prevents, showing the student understands QC as a set of targeted defenses against known failure modes, not a rote checklist.

questions.prompt: Order these steps as they should occur in a standard pipeline before running PCA or ADMIXTURE.

items.text: Apply sample and variant call-rate thresholds, and a MAF filter
Filter related individuals using a kinship-coefficient cutoff (e.g., KING at 0.0884)
LD-prune remaining variants (e.g., r-squared below 0.2 in sliding windows) and exclude long-range-LD regions like the MHC
Run PCA / ADMIXTURE on the filtered, pruned dataset

questions.explanation: Basic call-rate and MAF filtering removes low-quality data first; relatedness filtering removes individuals who would distort the sample independent of any variant-level issue; LD pruning and region exclusion address correlated/anomalous signal among the remaining variants; only after all of this is the dataset suitable to feed into PCA or ADMIXTURE.

questions.prompt: A KING kinship coefficient of 0.10 between two samples in a cohort most likely indicates:

options.text: The two samples are unrelated
The two samples are second-degree relatives (e.g., half-siblings or grandparent-grandchild) or closer, and at least one should typically be dropped
A genotyping batch effect, not a real relatedness signal
The two samples come from different continental populations

explanations.a: Unrelated pairs have kinship coefficients near zero, well below 0.0884; 0.10 is well above that cutoff.
explanations.b: Correct — the standard KING cutoff of 0.0884 flags second-degree-or-closer relatives, and a value of 0.10 falls in that range, so standard practice drops one member of the pair before structure analysis.
explanations.c: Kinship coefficients measure genome sharing consistent with pedigree relatedness; a batch effect would show up as a call-rate or PCA artifact, not specifically as an elevated pairwise kinship estimate.
explanations.d: Distinct continental populations do not produce elevated kinship coefficients between random pairs of individuals; kinship reflects recent shared ancestry (a specific family relationship), not broad population membership.

questions.prompt: Why are the MHC region and the chromosome 8 inversion routinely excluded before PCA or ADMIXTURE, even though the LD there is real, not an artifact?

options.text: Because sequencing technology cannot read those regions accurately
Because their unusually long-range LD lets a single region dominate a PC or cluster axis, making it reflect that one locus rather than genome-wide ancestry
Because those regions are always monomorphic and therefore uninformative
Because they are located on the sex chromosomes and must be analyzed separately by definition

explanations.a: This is not a sequencing-technology limitation; both regions can be sequenced and genotyped normally.
explanations.b: Correct — real, unusually long-range LD (from balancing selection at the MHC, and from suppressed recombination across the chromosome 8 inversion) means a small region can generate an entire PC axis or cluster split driven by that locus alone, not by genome-wide relatedness.
explanations.c: Both regions are highly polymorphic, not monomorphic — that is part of why their LD structure is so distinctive.
explanations.d: The MHC is on chromosome 6 and the inversion discussed is on chromosome 8; neither is a sex chromosome.

questions.prompt: A PCA plot shows a clean, tight separation between two sample groups that turns out to correlate perfectly with which sequencing lab processed the samples, not with any geographic variable. What does this illustrate?

options.text: That PCA cannot detect real population structure
That a genotyping batch effect can produce an axis that looks exactly like real population structure, which is why QC checks should include testing whether a PC correlates with batch
That the two labs sampled genetically distinct human subspecies
That MAF filtering was set too permissively

explanations.a: PCA works correctly as a statistical method here; the problem is what signal it is picking up, not a flaw in PCA itself.
explanations.b: Correct — this is exactly the batch-effect failure mode: a systematic call-rate or calling difference between processing batches can align with sample metadata and generate a clean, reproducible, but entirely artifactual structure axis.
explanations.c: Humans do not have genetically distinct subspecies; this explanation is biologically incorrect regardless of the batch confound.
explanations.d: A permissive MAF filter would let more noisy low-frequency variants through, but the described scenario is specifically about a batch effect, not variant frequency choice.

lessons.label: Ancient DNA as a Data Type

sections.heading: Damage is the proof, not just the problem
sections.body: DNA extracted from remains hundreds to tens of thousands of years old is degraded in a specific, chemically predictable way, and that damage pattern is what authenticates a sample as genuinely ancient rather than modern contamination. Depurination — spontaneous loss of purine bases — leaves the sugar-phosphate backbone prone to breaking, so ancient DNA fragments are short, typically well under 100 base pairs. Cytosine bases near the fragment's exposed 5-prime ends deaminate to uracil over time, which sequencers read as thymine, producing a signature excess of cytosine-to-thymine substitutions concentrated at fragment ends. A real ancient sample shows this pattern; a modern contaminant does not, so authentication tools plot the damage curve and refuse to treat a sample as ancient without it. Uracil-DNA-glycosylase (UDG) treatment removes damaged uracil bases before library preparation, trading away some of that authenticating signal in exchange for longer, less error-prone reads — a genuine tradeoff between confidence in authenticity and data quality.

sections.heading: Where the DNA actually survives, and how much contamination there is
sections.body: Pinhasi and colleagues (2015) showed that the dense otic-capsule portion of the petrous bone, which encases the inner ear, yields dramatically more endogenous ancient DNA than other skeletal elements — up to roughly two orders of magnitude more than typical bone — because its density protects DNA from microbial and environmental degradation. That single finding reshaped sampling strategy across the field, with the petrous bone becoming the default target wherever preserved. Because modern human DNA from excavators, curators, and lab handling is everywhere, every ancient sample is screened for contamination: comparing the sample's mitochondrial DNA against a consensus sequence flags a mixed (contaminated) versus a clean signal, and in male individuals, X-chromosome heterozygosity is a second, independent check, since a male should carry only one X and any apparent heterozygosity there signals modern DNA contamination mixed in.

sections.heading: Capture, pseudo-haploid calls, and why aDNA can't just be merged with modern data
sections.body: Because ancient DNA is scarce and degraded, most studies don't shotgun-sequence the whole genome; instead they use in-solution capture — commonly the 1240k panel, which enriches for roughly 1.2 million previously identified informative SNPs — to pull out just the sites needed for population analysis from a sea of fragmented, largely non-human DNA. At the resulting low coverage, most sites are covered once, so instead of calling a full diploid genotype, analyses use pseudo-haploid calls: one random read is drawn per site to represent that individual's allele there. Merging ancient and modern data naively is a mistake for two compounding reasons: reference bias, where reads carrying the reference allele map more easily than reads carrying a divergent (often damage-altered) allele, systematically skews allele calls toward the reference; and unremoved damage substitutions masquerade as real genetic variants. Both must be explicitly corrected (damage-aware genotype callers, reference-bias-aware mapping) before ancient and modern genotypes can be analyzed side by side.

lessons.workedExample: A lab receives a 4,000-year-old skeleton with well-preserved long bones and a petrous bone fragment. Sampling the femur first yields almost no usable DNA — mostly soil bacteria. Following Pinhasi et al. (2015), the team switches to the petrous bone and recovers roughly 50-fold more endogenous human DNA from the same extraction protocol. They run 1240k capture, get average coverage around 0.5x per targeted site, and call pseudo-haploid genotypes rather than diploid ones. Before comparing this ancient individual to a modern reference panel on the same PCA, they check the fragment-length distribution and the cytosine-to-thymine damage curve (confirming authenticity), estimate contamination from mitochondrial consensus mismatch and, since the individual is male, X-chromosome heterozygosity (both low, confirming a clean sample), and finally apply a reference-bias correction before merging — skipping any one of these steps could put an artifact, not the ancient individual's real ancestry, on the plot.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about ancient DNA authentication because the damage pattern is the field's built-in lie detector: a sample that is not actually ancient, or that is badly contaminated with modern DNA, will fail the cytosine-to-thymine damage check or the mitochondrial/X-heterozygosity contamination estimate, and a student who can name these specific checks (rather than saying 'we made sure it was old') demonstrates they understand that ancient DNA claims are falsifiable and are routinely, publicly checked before anyone trusts the downstream population-genetic conclusion.

questions.prompt: What damage signature is used to authenticate a DNA sample as genuinely ancient rather than modern contamination?

options.text: An excess of cytosine-to-thymine substitutions concentrated at fragment 5-prime ends, alongside short (well under 100 bp) fragment lengths
An excess of guanine-to-adenine substitutions spread evenly across each read
Unusually long, intact fragments exceeding 1,000 base pairs
A complete absence of any base substitutions relative to the reference genome

explanations.a: Correct — deamination of cytosine to uracil (read as thymine) concentrated near fragment ends, combined with depurination-driven fragmentation to short reads, is the diagnostic damage pattern of ancient DNA.
explanations.b: The characteristic substitution is cytosine-to-thymine at fragment ends, not a uniformly distributed guanine-to-adenine pattern.
explanations.c: Ancient DNA is characteristically short and fragmented, not long and intact; long intact fragments would suggest modern contamination.
explanations.d: A complete absence of substitutions would actually be suspicious — it is the presence of the specific damage pattern that authenticates a sample, not the absence of any variation.

questions.prompt: According to Pinhasi et al. (2015), which skeletal element gives the best endogenous ancient DNA yield, and why?

options.text: The femur, because it is the largest bone and yields the most material
The dense otic-capsule portion of the petrous bone, because its density protects DNA from microbial and environmental degradation
Tooth enamel, because it contains no DNA-degrading enzymes
Rib bones, because they are usually the best preserved macroscopically

explanations.a: Bone size does not predict DNA yield; the femur is a common but often poor source compared to the petrous bone.
explanations.b: Correct — Pinhasi et al. (2015) showed the dense otic-capsule region of the petrous bone yields dramatically more endogenous DNA than other skeletal elements, because its density shields DNA from degradation.
explanations.c: Tooth cementum can also preserve DNA reasonably well, but the finding specifically highlighted is about the petrous bone, not enamel being enzyme-free.
explanations.d: Macroscopic preservation (how intact a bone looks) does not reliably predict endogenous DNA content; the petrous bone's advantage is about internal density, not outward appearance.

questions.prompt: Match each ancient-DNA quality check to what it is used to detect.

left.text: Cytosine-to-thymine damage curve at fragment ends
X-chromosome heterozygosity in a male individual

right.text: Whether the sample is genuinely ancient versus modern contamination
Whether the sample is a mixture of the target individual and modern contaminating DNA (mitochondrial evidence)
Whether modern DNA is contaminating a male sample (since a male should have only one X)

questions.explanation: The damage curve authenticates antiquity itself; mitochondrial consensus mismatch flags contamination by comparing observed reads to a single expected sequence; X-heterozygosity in males is a second, independent contamination check because a true single-X genotype cannot appear heterozygous unless contaminating DNA is mixed in.

questions.prompt: Why can't ancient DNA genotypes simply be pooled with modern genotypes on the same PCA without correction?

options.text: Because ancient DNA uses a different genetic code
Because reference bias (reference-allele reads mapping more easily) and unremoved damage substitutions can both distort ancient genotype calls relative to modern ones unless explicitly corrected
Because ancient individuals cannot be represented on a PCA at all
Because PCA requires diploid genotype calls and no other genotype format is permitted

explanations.a: All humans, ancient or modern, share the same genetic code; this is not the source of the incompatibility.
explanations.b: Correct — reference bias skews mapping toward the reference allele, and leftover damage-driven substitutions can be mistaken for real variants, so both must be corrected before ancient and modern calls are comparable.
explanations.c: Ancient individuals are routinely projected onto PCA built from modern reference panels; the issue is doing so without correcting for these biases, not an inherent impossibility.
explanations.d: Pseudo-haploid (single-read) calls, not full diploid genotypes, are standard for low-coverage ancient samples, and PCA methods exist that accommodate this; the format itself is not the barrier.

lessons.label: Simulation: Building the Null

sections.heading: Two directions of simulation, two different jobs
sections.body: Coalescent simulation runs backward in time: starting from a sample of present-day chromosomes, it randomly merges (coalesces) lineages into shared ancestors according to population size and history, tracing genealogies back to a common ancestor without ever simulating the individuals who did not contribute descendants to the sample. Tools built on this model — Hudson's original ms and the modern, tree-sequence-based msprime — are fast precisely because they skip everyone whose lineage went extinct, making them the standard choice for simulating neutral variation under a demographic history (population sizes, splits, migration, bottlenecks) to ask what genetic diversity should look like if no selection acted. Forward simulation runs the other direction, generating each generation from the last, individual by individual, tracking who mates, who dies, and what mutations arise and rise or fall in frequency. This is slower and more memory-intensive, but it is the only approach that can model selection, linkage between selected and neutral sites, and complex non-neutral dynamics realistically; SLiM is the dominant modern tool for this, letting researchers script arbitrary selection, mating systems, and spatial structure.

sections.heading: The professional habit: no selection claim without a fitted neutral null
sections.body: A core norm in population genomics is that no claim of selection, or of a specific demographic event (a bottleneck, an admixture pulse, a split time), is publishable without comparing the observed statistic against a simulated null distribution generated under a demographic model independently fitted to the same data. The reasoning is that demographic history alone — bottlenecks, population growth, migration — can produce exactly the same signatures (reduced diversity, skewed site-frequency spectra, elevated F_ST at some loci) that selection produces, so an unusual value at one locus means nothing until it is shown to be unusual even after the genome-wide demographic backdrop is accounted for. In practice this means: fit a demographic model to genome-wide neutral variation, simulate many replicate genomes under that fitted model, and ask whether the locus of interest falls outside the resulting null distribution.

sections.heading: Fitting the model and scaling the simulation
sections.body: Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) is the standard way to fit demographic parameters when the true likelihood of an observed genome under a demographic model is computationally intractable: simulate many datasets across a range of candidate parameter values, compare each simulated dataset to the real data using summary statistics, and retain the parameter values whose simulations most closely resemble reality, building up an approximate posterior distribution without ever writing down the exact likelihood. The other bottleneck simulation faces at scale is simply data volume — a naive simulator recording every mutation in every individual for millions of samples is intractable. Tree sequences, the data structure underlying msprime and adopted by SLiM, solve this by recording only the genealogical relationships (the ancestral recombination graph) rather than every genotype, letting mutations be overlaid afterward; this compresses what would be enormous genotype matrices into a structure that makes million-sample, whole-chromosome simulation and analysis computationally tractable.

lessons.workedExample: A team finds a gene with unusually low diversity and an excess of rare alleles in a population's genome and wants to claim positive selection swept through it recently. Before publishing that claim, they use ABC to fit a demographic model (population size history, including a known historical bottleneck) to genome-wide neutral sites, then run msprime to simulate thousands of replicate neutral regions under that fitted bottleneck model. If the bottleneck alone regularly produces regions with diversity and site-frequency-spectrum skew as extreme as the candidate gene, the selection claim doesn't hold — the pattern is within the range demographic history alone explains. Only if the candidate gene falls clearly outside that simulated null distribution do they proceed to model the specific selective sweep, at which point a forward simulator like SLiM (which can jointly model selection and linkage, unlike the backward-only coalescent) becomes the right tool to test whether a plausible selection coefficient reproduces the observed pattern.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what's your null model?' because population genetics has a well-known failure mode where a demographic event and natural selection produce statistically indistinguishable signatures at a single locus, and a student who reports 'this region has low diversity, so it was selected' without a demography-matched null is making an unfalsifiable claim. The strong answer names the specific null-building workflow — fit demography (often via ABC), simulate a neutral null under it (coalescent, via msprime), and only then ask if the observed locus is an outlier — showing they understand that an unusual number means nothing until compared to what unselected history alone would produce.

questions.prompt: What is the essential difference between coalescent (backward-in-time) simulation and forward simulation?

options.text: Coalescent simulation traces sampled lineages back to shared ancestors and skips lineages that left no descendants, while forward simulation builds each generation individual by individual and can model selection and linkage directly
Coalescent simulation can model selection but forward simulation cannot
The two methods produce identical output and differ only in programming language
Forward simulation is always faster because it processes fewer generations

explanations.a: Correct — the coalescent's backward efficiency comes from only tracing ancestry that actually contributed to the sample, while forward simulation must track every individual each generation but can therefore represent selection and linkage realistically.
explanations.b: This has it backwards — forward simulators like SLiM are the standard choice for modeling selection realistically, precisely because the coalescent is a neutral-genealogy model.
explanations.c: The two approaches make different tradeoffs and are suited to different questions; they are not interchangeable or identical in output.
explanations.d: Forward simulation is generally slower and more memory-intensive than coalescent simulation, not faster, because it must simulate every individual each generation rather than skip non-contributing lineages.

questions.prompt: Why can't an unusually low-diversity genomic region be taken as evidence of positive selection without further work?

options.text: Because low diversity is always a sequencing artifact

Because demographic history alone (bottlenecks, population growth, migration) can produce the same reduced-diversity signature, so the region must be compared to a demography-matched neutral null before selection can be claimed
Because diversity cannot be measured accurately at any single locus
Because selection never reduces diversity

explanations.a: Low diversity is a real, measurable population-genetic signature, not necessarily an artifact.
explanations.b: Correct — this is exactly why a fitted demographic null is required: a bottleneck can mimic a selective sweep's diversity signature genome-wide, so only a locus that stands out even against that null supports a selection claim.
explanations.c: Locus-level diversity can be measured; the issue is not measurement precision but interpretation without a proper null.
explanations.d: Selection, particularly a selective sweep, characteristically does reduce diversity near the selected site — that is exactly why it can be confused with a demographic signature.

questions.prompt: What problem does approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) solve in fitting a demographic model?

options.text: It avoids simulation entirely by computing an exact likelihood
It fits demographic parameters by comparing many simulated datasets to real data via summary statistics, when the exact likelihood is computationally intractable
It replaces the need for any neutral null model
It is used only for forward simulation, never for coalescent-based demographic inference

explanations.a: ABC is used precisely because an exact likelihood is not tractable to compute; it relies on simulation, not likelihood formulas.
explanations.b: Correct — ABC simulates across a range of candidate parameters, compares simulated to real summary statistics, and retains parameter values that best reproduce the real data, approximating a posterior without an exact likelihood.
explanations.c: ABC is a tool for fitting the demographic model that then generates the neutral null, not a replacement for having a null at all.
explanations.d: ABC is commonly used to fit demographic models that feed coalescent simulations (e.g., msprime), not exclusively forward simulation.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or data structure to its primary role in the population-genomic simulation workflow.

right.text: Fast coalescent (backward) simulation of neutral variation under a demographic model
Forward simulation with selection, linkage, and complex mating/spatial structure
Data structure recording only genealogical relationships, making million-sample simulation tractable

questions.explanation: msprime is the modern coalescent simulator for fast, large-scale neutral simulation; SLiM is the standard forward simulator for modeling selection and linkage explicitly; tree sequences are the underlying data structure that avoids storing full genotype matrices, enabling simulation and analysis at massive sample sizes.

lessons.label: Sampling, Consent and Who Gets Sequenced

sections.heading: What a 'population' in a dataset actually is
sections.body: Every reference panel or study cohort labels its samples with a population name, but that label is almost always a self-identified cultural, linguistic, or national category collected by a questionnaire, not a genetically defined cluster. Genetic ancestry is continuous and shaped by migration and admixture, so a person can self-identify with one group while carrying measurable ancestry from several; treating the label as if it perfectly partitions genetic variation builds an assumption into the data before any analysis begins. Compounding this, most population-genomic sampling is convenience sampling: researchers recruit through accessible institutions (universities, hospitals, existing biobanks), so panels are disproportionately built from populations near research infrastructure and from people willing and able to participate under a given consent process. Every downstream cluster plot, F_ST estimate, or admixture proportion inherits whichever populations happened to be convenient to sample, not a representative cross-section of human diversity.

sections.heading: When consent breaks down: Havasupai
sections.body: Between 1990 and 1994, researchers at Arizona State University collected blood samples from around 400 Havasupai tribal members, with participants told the samples would be used to study diabetes. The samples were later used for additional studies — including schizophrenia, inbreeding, and population-migration research — that participants had not consented to and that touched on topics considered culturally sensitive within the tribe. The Havasupai Tribe sued in 2004; the case ended in an out-of-court settlement in April 2010, with the university paying compensation, funding a clinic and school, and returning the samples. Because it settled rather than going to verdict, it set no binding legal precedent, but it became the field's central cautionary case for what specific, purpose-limited informed consent has to mean in genetic research, and it directly shaped subsequent research-ethics frameworks and consent-form design.

sections.heading: Whose remains, whose rules: sovereignty in modern and ancient DNA
sections.body: Two frameworks now govern who gets a say over genetic data drawn from a community. For living Indigenous communities, the CARE Principles (Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics) assert that a community, not just an individual sample donor, has an ongoing say over how its genetic data is used — a direct response to cases like Havasupai. For ancient remains, the tension is sharper because the people whose DNA is analyzed cannot consent at all. Alpaslan-Roodenberg and colleagues (2021), representing researchers from 24 countries, proposed five globally applicable guidelines for ancient-DNA research — following local regulations, planning studies in advance, minimizing damage to remains, making data available for re-examination, and consulting relevant stakeholders — though the guidelines drew public criticism from other researchers for not weighting Indigenous community authority as heavily as North American frameworks developed under NAGPRA (the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act) do. The clearest resolution case is Kennewick Man: Rasmussen and colleagues (2015) sequenced the roughly 8,500-year-old skeleton's genome and showed it was more closely related to modern Native Americans, including the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, than to any other population, ending a legal dispute and leading to repatriation of the remains — now referred to as the Ancient One — to regional tribes under NAGPRA.

lessons.workedExample: A study wants to characterize 'Andean population structure' and recruits 150 volunteers from a single university clinic in a regional capital. The resulting sample is a convenience sample: overrepresenting people with access to that clinic (urban, likely more admixed) and underrepresenting rural highland communities that are harder to reach and less connected to that institution. A PCA built on this sample will show whatever structure exists among clinic-goers, and a naive reader could mistake that for 'the' population structure of the region. A more defensible design would explicitly report recruitment method and its likely biases, seek community-level engagement (following CARE-style principles) with specific highland communities before sampling there, and use genuinely specific informed consent — naming the exact analyses planned — rather than the broad, reusable consent language that led directly to the Havasupai dispute when samples were repurposed for studies participants never agreed to.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks how a study defined its 'population' and obtained consent because these are the two places where a plausible-sounding genomics project can quietly encode bias or violate trust without any coding error at all — convenience sampling shapes every cluster plot downstream, and reused or vague consent has a real, litigated history (Havasupai) with a real, documented harm. A strong answer distinguishes self-identified label from genetic ancestry, names the sampling method's likely bias, and states what specific consent was obtained for — showing the student understands that who is in the data, and under what agreement, is itself a scientific and ethical claim, not just paperwork.

questions.prompt: In the Havasupai case, what specifically went wrong with consent?

options.text: No consent was ever obtained from any participant
Samples collected under consent for diabetes research were later used for other studies (including schizophrenia and migration research) that participants had not agreed to
The tribe was paid for their samples but never told what they would be used for
The study was conducted entirely without university oversight

explanations.a: Consent was obtained for a specific purpose (diabetes research); the problem was that samples were later reused beyond that purpose.
explanations.b: Correct — the samples, collected roughly 1990-1994 with consent framed around diabetes, were used for additional studies participants had not agreed to, leading to a 2004 lawsuit and a 2010 settlement.
explanations.c: The core issue documented in the case was purpose-limited consent being exceeded, not simply a lack of disclosure about payment.
explanations.d: The research was conducted through Arizona State University; the dispute was about the scope of consent, not an absence of institutional involvement.

questions.prompt: Why does convenience sampling in population genomics affect the science, not just the ethics, of a study?

options.text: It doesn't — sampling method has no effect on statistical results as long as sample size is large enough

Because whichever populations happen to be sampled shape every downstream statistic (PCA, F_ST, admixture proportions), so a non-representative sample produces a non-representative — but confident-looking — picture of population structure
Because convenience samples always have higher sequencing error rates
Because only self-identified labels, never genetic ancestry, are affected by sampling method

explanations.a: Sample size does not fix a biased sampling frame; a large but non-representative sample still misrepresents the populations it fails to include.
explanations.b: Correct — every structure statistic is computed from whoever is in the dataset, so convenience sampling (recruiting near research infrastructure, from willing participants) shapes the apparent genetic landscape independent of any lab error.
explanations.c: Sampling method (who is recruited) is unrelated to sequencing error rate, which is a technical property of the assay.
explanations.d: Genetic ancestry estimates are computed from whoever is sampled, so they are just as shaped by sampling bias as self-identified labels are.

questions.prompt: Match each case, framework, or guideline to what it addresses.

right.text: Community-level authority over genetic data use for living Indigenous communities
Five globally applicable proposed guidelines for ancient-DNA research ethics
Genomic evidence linking Kennewick Man (the Ancient One) to modern Native American tribes, leading to repatriation

questions.explanation: CARE (Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics) addresses ongoing community authority over data from living groups; Alpaslan-Roodenberg et al. (2021) proposed five global guidelines for ancient-DNA research, drawing both support and criticism; Rasmussen et al. (2015) sequenced Kennewick Man's genome, showing close relatedness to modern Native Americans (including the Colville tribes) and enabling repatriation under NAGPRA.

questions.prompt: Why is the label attached to a sample in a reference panel (e.g., 'Yoruba' or 'British') not the same thing as a genetically defined cluster?

options.text: Because the labels are randomly assigned by the sequencing machine
Because the label is typically a self-identified cultural, linguistic, or national category, while genetic ancestry is continuous and shaped by migration and admixture
Because reference panels never record any population label at all
Because genetic ancestry is entirely determined by national citizenship

explanations.a: Labels come from participant self-report during recruitment, not from any output of the sequencing process.
explanations.b: Correct — a self-identified label is a social/cultural category, while the underlying genetic ancestry it is meant to proxy is continuous and admixed, so treating the label as a clean genetic partition builds in an unwarranted assumption.
explanations.c: Reference panels like 1000 Genomes and HGDP explicitly do record population labels; the issue is what those labels do and don't capture, not their absence.
explanations.d: Genetic ancestry reflects biological descent and migration history, not legal citizenship status.

lessons.label: Measuring Differentiation: F_ST and Friends

sections.heading: Wright's F_ST: variance among groups, not a distance between people
sections.body: Sewall Wright introduced F_ST in the 1940s as one of three F-statistics (F_IS, F_IT, F_ST) partitioning heterozygosity across levels of population structure. F_ST specifically is the proportion of total allele-frequency variance attributable to differences among subpopulations, relative to the variance expected if the whole species mated as one panmictic unit: F_ST = (H_T - H_S)/H_T, where H_T is expected heterozygosity treating the total sample as randomly mating and H_S is the average expected heterozygosity within subpopulations. Its two siblings measure related but distinct things: F_IS is the inbreeding of an individual relative to its own subpopulation (excess homozygosity from non-random mating within the group), while F_IT is that same inbreeding measured relative to the total pooled population, folding in both within-subpopulation mating patterns and the subdivision F_ST itself. A high F_ST means subpopulations have drifted or been isolated enough that their allele frequencies diverge; a low F_ST means alleles are distributed similarly everywhere. F_ST is a population-level summary of allele-frequency variance across many loci - it says nothing about how different any two individuals are, since within-population variation swamps between-population variation at nearly every single locus in humans.

sections.heading: Two estimators, two different behaviors: Weir-Cockerham vs Hudson
sections.body: True allele frequencies are never observed, only genotypes from finite samples, so F_ST must be estimated, and the estimator matters. Weir and Cockerham (1984) built an ANOVA-style estimator correcting for finite sample size, becoming the field's default for decades and shipping in tools like vcftools and PLINK. Bhatia et al. (2013) showed a ratio-of-averages estimator built on the earlier Hudson, Slatkin and Maddison (1992) formulation behaves more predictably when populations differ in sample size or when variants are rare, because the Weir-Cockerham estimator can be badly biased by unequal sample sizes and low minor-allele-frequency sites, where a handful of sampling errors dominates the ratio. Two papers reporting 'F_ST' on the same data can therefore disagree meaningfully, and the fix is checking which estimator was used and whether variants were MAF-filtered.

sections.heading: Anchoring the numbers in real human data
sections.body: Genome-wide F_ST among the three classic continental groupings (sub-Saharan African, European, East Asian) sits around 0.10-0.15 - roughly 10-15% of allele-frequency variance pooled across many loci is explained by continental group membership. That range is typically estimated from large reference panels such as the 1000 Genomes Project or the Human Genome Diversity Project (HGDP), pooling results across many thousands of genome-wide variants rather than reading it off any single locus. Within a single continent, differentiation drops sharply: F_ST among European countries is typically under 0.01, and neighboring populations can be nearly indistinguishable at genome scale. Both figures describe variance in frequencies across loci - they do not mean any one person's genome is '10-15% different,' since at any single SNP most variation is shared across groups.

lessons.workedExample: A student computes F_ST between two simulated populations of 20 individuals each, gets F_ST = 0.18, and reports 'these populations are 18% genetically different.' A reviewer should push back: F_ST = 0.18 means 18% of total allele-frequency variance is explained by which population a sample came from - not that any two individuals differ by 18%, nor that the populations share only 82% of their alleles. With n=20, the Weir-Cockerham correction also matters: at low sample size and moderate allele frequency, sampling noise inflates raw estimates, so the student should report the estimator used and a bootstrap confidence interval across loci, not a single point value treated as ground truth.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'what does your F_ST number actually mean?' because F_ST is the most commonly misreported population-genetics statistic in student projects - it gets glossed as 'percent genetically different,' which is wrong and invites the fair's most cutting follow-up. A strong answer distinguishes variance-explained from individual dissimilarity, names which estimator was used (Weir-Cockerham or Hudson) and why it matters at the student's sample size or MAF range, and can state what a 'high' versus 'low' value looks like in real data (0.10-0.15 across continents, under 0.01 within Europe) rather than treating any nonzero F_ST as automatically meaningful.

questions.prompt: An analysis reports F_ST = 0.12 between two populations. What does that most accurately mean?

options.text: 12% of allele-frequency variance across loci is attributable to population membership
Individuals from the two populations differ at 12% of their genome
The two populations share only 88% of their alleles
Any two random individuals from different populations are 12% more genetically different than two from the same population

explanations.a: Correct - F_ST is the proportion of total allele-frequency variance, pooled across many loci, explained by which subpopulation a sample belongs to.
explanations.b: F_ST is not a per-genome difference measure between individuals; within-population variation dominates at almost every single locus.
explanations.c: F_ST does not describe the fraction of alleles shared or unshared between populations.
explanations.d: F_ST is a population-level variance statistic, not an individual pairwise dissimilarity score.

questions.prompt: Why might the Weir-Cockerham (1984) and Hudson (Bhatia et al. 2013) F_ST estimators give meaningfully different values on the same dataset?

options.text: They estimate different biological quantities entirely
The Weir-Cockerham estimator can be biased by unequal sample sizes and low-MAF variants, where the Hudson estimator is more robust
Hudson's estimator only works on non-human species
Weir-Cockerham requires whole-genome sequencing while Hudson requires SNP arrays

explanations.a: Both estimate the same underlying quantity, Wright's F_ST - they can just diverge numerically under certain data conditions.
explanations.b: Correct - Bhatia et al. (2013) showed the Hudson (ratio-of-averages) estimator is more stable than Weir-Cockerham when sample sizes are unequal or variants are rare.
explanations.c: Both estimators are general-purpose and apply to any species with genotype data.
explanations.d: The choice of estimator is independent of sequencing versus array platform.

questions.prompt: Match each statement about F_ST estimators to the correct description.

right.text: ANOVA-style correction for finite sample size; historic default implemented in PLINK and vcftools
Ratio-of-averages form, more robust to unequal sample sizes and low-MAF variants
Estimate the same underlying quantity, Wright's F_ST, but can diverge on real data

questions.explanation: Weir-Cockerham is the classic ANOVA-style, finite-sample-corrected estimator; the Hudson estimator is a ratio-of-averages form shown by Bhatia et al. (2013) to be more robust under unequal sample size or low MAF; both target the same population quantity but can give different numbers on the same data.

questions.prompt: Order the conceptual steps in computing Wright's F_ST from genotype data.

items.text: Genotype individuals across subpopulations at many loci
Compute expected heterozygosity within each subpopulation (H_S)
Compute expected heterozygosity assuming the total sample is one randomly mating population (H_T)
Compute F_ST = (H_T - H_S)/H_T, averaged across loci

questions.explanation: You first need genotype data across subpopulations, then compute within-subpopulation heterozygosity (H_S) and total-pooled heterozygosity (H_T), and only then combine them into the F_ST ratio.

lessons.label: PCA on Genotype Data

sections.heading: What a principal component actually summarizes
sections.body: Principal component analysis (PCA) on genotype data starts from a matrix of individuals by SNPs, where each entry is a genotype dosage (0, 1, or 2 copies of an allele), centered and often scaled by expected binomial variance. PCA finds the orthogonal axes (eigenvectors) capturing the most covariance in that matrix across individuals - in practice, the top axes track which SNPs' allele frequencies co-vary across which samples. A PC is not a group label; it is a continuous coordinate. Patterson, Price and Reich (2006) formalized the connection to population genetics, showing the top eigenvalues of the genetic covariance matrix correspond to the effective number of underlying populations, testable with a Tracy-Widom significance test from random matrix theory - a PC that fails this test is likely capturing noise, not structure.

sections.heading: EIGENSTRAT and 'genes mirror geography'
sections.body: That 2006 paper's method, EIGENSTRAT, was built to correct population stratification in genome-wide association studies: uncorrected, allele-frequency differences between subtly structured cases and controls generate spurious associations, so EIGENSTRAT regresses out the top significant PCs before testing. The clearest demonstration that PCA captures real geography came from Novembre et al. (2008), who ran PCA on roughly 1,387 European individuals from the POPRES panel and found plotting PC1 against PC2, then rotating it, reproduced a recognizable map of Europe - individuals landing roughly where geography would place them, with a resolution fine enough to distinguish neighboring countries. That result, 'genes mirror geography,' is the canonical demonstration that PCA axes can track continuous isolation-by-distance, not discrete ancestral populations.

sections.heading: Classic artifacts that hijack a PC
sections.body: A single inversion polymorphism or region of long-range linkage disequilibrium - classic offenders include the chromosome 8p23 and 17q21 inversions and the MHC region on chromosome 6 - can dominate a PC entirely, because tightly linked SNPs move together and swamp genome-wide signal; the fix is excluding known high-LD regions before running PCA. A single outlier family or set of close relatives can also hijack a whole axis, since PCA is sensitive to any strong covariance source, related or not. Projecting new samples onto PCs computed from a reference panel, rather than including them in the original computation, causes shrinkage toward the origin, understating differentiation. And because PCA has no notion of 'true' population, axes can encode the sampling design itself - which cohort was sequenced on which batch - as easily as real ancestry.

lessons.workedExample: A team runs PCA on 500 genotyped volunteers and finds PC1 perfectly separates 12 individuals from the rest. Excited, they call it a new ancestry cluster - but closer inspection shows those 12 are three extended families (siblings and first cousins) recruited from the same two households, and removing known high-LD regions plus keeping only one representative per family collapses PC1 into noise. Before interpreting a PC as ancestry, check whether it survives (1) excluding long-range LD regions like the MHC and known inversions, (2) removing close relatives or restricting to one per family, and (3) confirming the eigenvalue clears a Tracy-Widom significance threshold, rather than assuming any visible separation is population structure.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on PCA because a scatter plot with two visually separated blobs looks like proof of population structure whether or not it is. A strong defense names the specific artifact checked - inversions and long-range LD excluded, relatives removed or restricted, an eigenvalue significance test applied - because those are exactly the failure modes that produce a convincing-looking PC1/PC2 plot from noise, one family, or a batch effect. Citing Novembre et al.'s 'genes mirror geography' result also shows the student understands a PC as a continuous, interpretable geographic gradient rather than a certificate of discrete ancestry groups.

questions.prompt: What does the top principal component of a genotype PCA most directly represent?

options.text: A discrete label assigning each individual to one ancestral group
A continuous axis capturing the largest source of allele-frequency covariance across individuals
The individual with the most heterozygous genotype
A direct measurement of geographic distance between sampling sites

explanations.a: PCA produces continuous coordinates, not group labels; assigning discrete labels is a separate, later interpretive step.
explanations.b: Correct - the top PC is the orthogonal axis capturing the most covariance in allele frequencies across the sampled individuals.
explanations.c: Heterozygosity per individual is a different summary statistic, not what a PC axis represents.
explanations.d: PCA is computed purely from genotype covariance; any resemblance to geography (as in Novembre et al. 2008) is an empirical finding, not a built-in guarantee.

questions.prompt: What did Novembre et al. (2008) find when running PCA on roughly 1,387 European individuals from the POPRES panel?

options.text: PC1 and PC2, once plotted and rotated, reproduced a recognizable map of Europe
Europeans formed a single indistinguishable genetic cluster with no internal structure
PCA failed entirely on European samples due to insufficient differentiation
Only non-European continental groups showed any PCA structure

explanations.a: Correct - this 'genes mirror geography' result is the canonical demonstration that PCA can track continuous isolation-by-distance at fine geographic resolution.
explanations.b: The paper's key finding was the opposite: fine-grained, geography-tracking structure was detectable.
explanations.c: PCA succeeded in resolving structure within Europe, despite the low F_ST values described in the prior lesson.
explanations.d: The paper specifically demonstrated fine structure within Europe, not just at the continental level.

questions.prompt: Match each PCA artifact to its cause.

left.text: A PC dominated by one region of the genome
A PC that separates a small cluster of individuals
New samples appear less differentiated than they truly are
A PC that tracks which lab processed the samples

right.text: An inversion or long-range LD block (e.g., 8p23, 17q21, the MHC) swamping genome-wide signal
Close relatives (siblings, cousins) generating strong covariance unrelated to population ancestry
Shrinkage from projecting samples onto PCs computed without them
PCs encoding the sampling design rather than biology

questions.explanation: Long-range LD/inversions, close relatives, projection shrinkage, and sampling-design confounds are the four classic PCA artifacts that can be mistaken for genuine ancestry structure.

questions.prompt: What was EIGENSTRAT, introduced alongside Patterson, Price and Reich's (2006) PCA framework, designed to do?

options.text: Sequence whole genomes faster
Correct for population stratification in GWAS by regressing out significant top PCs before association testing
Assign discrete ancestral cluster labels using Bayesian MCMC
Estimate F_ST between continental groups

explanations.a: EIGENSTRAT is an analysis method for correcting stratification, not a sequencing technology.
explanations.b: Correct - EIGENSTRAT uses the top significant PCs (identified via the Tracy-Widom test) to correct for stratification that would otherwise create spurious GWAS associations.
explanations.c: That describes STRUCTURE's Bayesian mixed-membership model, a different tool covered in a later lesson.
explanations.d: F_ST estimation is a separate statistic covered in the prior lesson, not what EIGENSTRAT computes.

lessons.label: Model-Based Clustering: STRUCTURE and ADMIXTURE

sections.heading: A mixed-membership model of ancestry
sections.body: Pritchard, Stephens and Donnelly (2000) introduced a Bayesian mixed-membership model for population structure: each individual's genome is treated as a mixture of K ancestral populations, and the model jointly estimates each population's allele frequencies and each individual's admixture proportions (q, summing to 1 across K) from unlinked marker genotypes, using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) implemented in the STRUCTURE software. The model can also run in a no-admixture mode assigning individuals wholly to one cluster, but the admixture version - allowing fractional membership - became the default because human populations rarely fit clean discrete boxes. STRUCTURE's Bayesian MCMC is thorough but slow, often impractical on the hundreds of thousands of SNPs and tens of thousands of samples modern arrays and biobanks produce.

sections.heading: ADMIXTURE's speed, and the myth of a single true K
sections.body: Alexander, Novembre and Lange (2009) built ADMIXTURE to fit the identical K-population mixture likelihood by maximum likelihood using a fast block-relaxation algorithm rather than MCMC sampling, running orders of magnitude faster and scaling to genome-wide SNP data with results closely matching STRUCTURE on the same input. Neither tool tells you K in advance; ADMIXTURE reports a cross-validation (CV) error for each K tested, and users conventionally pick the K with the lowest CV error. But CV error curves are often flat across a range of K, several K values can be near-equally supported, and each successive K typically just splits an existing cluster into finer real structure rather than revealing one 'true' number of ancestral populations - so K is a modeling choice tuned to the question, not a biological constant to be discovered.

sections.heading: When a bar plot lies without anyone lying
sections.body: Lawson, van Dorp and Falush (2018) showed something unsettling: simulating data with straightforward serial-founder bottleneck history and unbalanced sample sizes across groups - with zero actual admixture built in - reliably produced ADMIXTURE bar plots that looked like plausible real-world admixture, complete with shared colored segments a naive reader would call evidence of mixture. The model must explain each individual's allele frequencies using only K cluster profiles, and when true history is a tree with bottlenecks rather than clean discrete founding populations, or one group is oversampled relative to another, the best-fitting mixture proportions can mimic admixture that never happened. The lesson: a bar plot is the output of a model under stated assumptions, not a direct observation, and needs corroboration.

lessons.workedExample: A team runs ADMIXTURE at K=2 through K=6 on 250 samples from three regions (150 from Region A, 50 each from B and C) and picks K=3 because CV error is lowest there, then reports Region A individuals show 20% 'Region C ancestry' as evidence of historical migration. Before accepting that, they should rerun with balanced sampling (subsampling Region A to 50), check whether the pattern replicates across multiple random seeds and the neighboring K=2 and K=4 solutions, and note that Lawson et al. (2018) showed exactly this setup - oversampling one group plus ordinary bottleneck history - can produce mixed-color bars with no real admixture at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe admixture bar plots hard because they are the most visually persuasive and most over-interpreted output in population genetics - a bar of mixed colors looks like direct evidence of migration even when it isn't. A strong answer treats K as a chosen modeling parameter, justified by a CV-error sweep rather than asserted, checks that sample sizes across groups are balanced, and can cite Lawson, van Dorp and Falush's (2018) result that sampling imbalance and simple bottleneck history alone generate convincing-looking admixture patterns - meaning a bar plot is a model output to be corroborated, never treated as raw observation.

questions.prompt: What is the core difference between STRUCTURE (Pritchard, Stephens and Donnelly 2000) and ADMIXTURE (Alexander, Novembre and Lange 2009)?

options.text: They fit the same K-population mixture model, but STRUCTURE uses Bayesian MCMC while ADMIXTURE uses fast maximum-likelihood optimization
STRUCTURE assumes no admixture is possible, while ADMIXTURE always assumes full admixture
ADMIXTURE only works on animal genomes, not human genomes
STRUCTURE analyzes haplotypes while ADMIXTURE analyzes single markers only

explanations.a: Correct - both fit the identical mixed-membership likelihood; ADMIXTURE simply replaces slow MCMC with a fast block-relaxation maximum-likelihood algorithm, giving near-identical results much faster.
explanations.b: STRUCTURE's admixture mode allows fractional membership; a no-admixture mode also exists, but the models are not opposites in the way described.
explanations.c: ADMIXTURE is a general-purpose tool applicable to any species with genotype data, including humans.
explanations.d: Both tools primarily use unlinked marker genotypes, not full haplotype information; that distinction belongs to a different class of methods (covered in a later lesson).

questions.prompt: Why is picking the K with the lowest cross-validation (CV) error not the same as finding the 'true' number of ancestral populations?

options.text: CV error is unrelated to K in any way
CV error curves are often flat across a range of K, and each additional K often just splits existing structure finer rather than revealing one true value
CV error can only be computed for K=1
ADMIXTURE does not report CV error at all

explanations.a: CV error is specifically computed as a function of K and is the conventional criterion for choosing it.
explanations.b: Correct - because several K values can be near-equally supported and successive K often reveals finer real substructure rather than a single correct count, K is treated as a modeling choice, not a discoverable constant.
explanations.c: CV error is computed across the full range of K values tested, not just K=1.
explanations.d: ADMIXTURE explicitly reports CV error per K as its standard model-selection output.

questions.prompt: What did Lawson, van Dorp and Falush (2018) demonstrate about ADMIXTURE bar plots?

options.text: Bar plots are always accurate regardless of sampling design
Sampling imbalance and ordinary bottleneck history alone, with zero true admixture, can produce plausible-looking mixed-color bar plots
ADMIXTURE cannot run on simulated data
Bar plots only fail when K is set too low

explanations.a: The paper's point was the opposite: bar plots can mislead even without any modeling errors.
explanations.b: Correct - this is the paper's central, unsettling finding: a model output can look like real admixture purely from bottleneck demography and unbalanced sampling.
explanations.c: The demonstration relied specifically on simulated data with known, controlled (zero) admixture.
explanations.d: The artifact was shown across a range of K choices, not only at low K.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for responsibly running and interpreting an ADMIXTURE analysis.

items.text: Balance sample sizes across groups before running the analysis
Run ADMIXTURE across a sweep of K values
Select K by comparing cross-validation error across the sweep, including neighboring K values
Replicate with multiple random seeds and interpret the bar plot as a model output, not a raw observation

questions.explanation: Balanced sampling should be established before running the model; then a K sweep is run; CV error across that sweep (including neighboring K) guides model selection; and finally, seed replication and cautious interpretation guard against the Lawson et al. (2018) artifact.

lessons.label: f-Statistics: Testing Admixture Directly

sections.heading: f3: a near-diagnostic admixture test
sections.body: f3(X; A, B) tests whether population X is a mixture of lineages related to source populations A and B by measuring the product of allele-frequency differences (X-A)(X-B) averaged across the genome. If X is unadmixed and simply related to A and B by a normal population tree, this statistic is positive; if X is truly a mixture of two divergent lineages, drift specific to A and B pulls allele frequencies in opposite directions at many sites, driving the statistic significantly negative. Patterson et al. (2012), formalizing f-statistics for the Reich lab's admixture toolkit, showed a significantly negative f3 (Z-score below about -3) is strong, hard-to-fake evidence of admixture - one of the few population-genetic signals that is nearly diagnostic rather than merely suggestive, though a non-negative f3 does not rule out admixture, since it can fail to detect subtle or symmetric mixtures.

sections.heading: f4 and the D-statistic: testing whether four populations form a clean tree
sections.body: f4(A, B; C, D) and the closely related D-statistic (the 'ABBA-BABA' test) ask whether four populations relate as a clean, unadmixed tree. Counting sites where the derived allele is shared unexpectedly between B and C ('ABBA') versus between A and C ('BABA') - both non-sister-pair sharing patterns expected from incomplete lineage sorting alone - a true tree with no gene flow predicts these two counts to be equal, so D should be zero; a significant deviation (read off a Z-score, typically |Z| > 3) indicates gene flow between one of A or B and one of C or D. This four-population test of 'treeness' became widely known for testing Neanderthal gene flow into non-African modern humans, and is now standard for testing any specific gene-flow hypothesis without requiring a specified admixture proportion.

sections.heading: qpAdm and qpGraph: structured hypothesis tests
sections.body: Beyond single tests, qpAdm fits a target population's admixture proportions as a weighted mixture of specified reference ('left') populations, using a larger panel of outgroups ('right' populations) to constrain the fit without requiring a full tree. qpGraph goes further, fitting an entire admixture graph - nodes, split times, and admixture edges with weights - to a full matrix of f-statistics simultaneously, flagging a model as inadequate when it cannot reproduce the observed statistics within error. qpGraph, from Patterson et al. (2012), and qpAdm, introduced a few years later in the supplementary methods of Haak et al. (2015), both turn f-statistics into structured hypothesis tests rather than one-off numbers.

sections.heading: The assumption that breaks everything: clean outgroups
sections.body: All of these tests assume the reference and outgroup populations are themselves unadmixed with the lineages under test - violated silently whenever there is unmodeled gene flow into a supposed outgroup, biasing every downstream f3, f4, qpAdm, and qpGraph result. The other classic failure is an unsampled 'ghost' population: real admixture from a lineage nobody sequenced gets misattributed to whichever sampled population is genetically closest, producing a confidently wrong proportion or graph edge. An f-statistic result is only as good as the population set it was tested against.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher tests f3(Sardinian; Early_European_Farmer, Anatolian_Neolithic) and gets a strongly negative Z-score of -12, concluding Sardinians descend from a mixture of those two related lineages - a defensible read, since f3 that negative essentially cannot arise from any unadmixed tree relationship. They then run qpAdm treating Sardinians as a two-way mixture of those same sources against a panel of eight outgroups, getting estimated proportions of roughly 65%/35% with a good model fit (p>0.05). Before publishing, they should still ask whether any outgroup itself received undocumented gene flow from a population related to the sources, since that alone could distort the fitted proportions without failing the model's own fit statistic.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on f-statistics because a negative f3 or a significant D-statistic feels like unambiguous proof of admixture, and it usually is a strong signal - but only conditional on every reference and outgroup population actually being what the analysis assumes: unadmixed with the groups under test. A strong answer reports the actual Z-score rather than just 'significant,' names which populations served as sources versus outgroups, and can explain how an unmodeled ghost population or undetected gene flow into an outgroup would silently bias the result - showing the student understands these are conditional tests, not raw facts about history.

questions.prompt: A researcher computes f3(X; A, B) and finds it significantly negative (Z < -3). What is the strongest supported conclusion?

options.text: X shows near-diagnostic evidence of being an admixture of lineages related to A and B
X is definitely unrelated to both A and B
A and B are admixed with each other
The result is inconclusive and requires no further interpretation

explanations.a: Correct - Patterson et al. (2012) showed a significantly negative f3 is strong, near-diagnostic evidence that X descends from admixture between lineages related to A and B.
explanations.b: A significant negative f3 indicates the opposite: a specific relationship (admixture) linking X to both A and B.
explanations.c: The test f3(X; A, B) asks about X's relationship to A and B, not about a relationship between A and B themselves.
explanations.d: A significantly negative f3 is one of the more interpretable, near-diagnostic signals in this toolkit, not an inconclusive one.

questions.prompt: What does a significant D-statistic (ABBA-BABA test) on four populations (A, B; C, D) indicate?

options.text: That A and B are identical populations
That the four populations do not fit a clean tree with no gene flow - implying gene flow between one of A/B and one of C/D
That C and D must be the same age
That mutation rates differ between A and B

explanations.a: The test compares site-pattern counts across four distinct populations; it does not test whether A and B are identical.
explanations.b: Correct - unequal ABBA and BABA site counts indicate the four populations violate simple treeness, pointing to gene flow between a member of the (A,B) pair and a member of the (C,D) pair.
explanations.c: The test is about shared derived alleles indicating gene flow, not about divergence dates.
explanations.d: The test assumes similar mutation processes; it is not designed to detect mutation-rate differences.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or statistic to its primary purpose.

right.text: Tests whether X is admixed between lineages related to A and B; significantly negative is near-diagnostic
Tests whether four populations form a clean, unadmixed tree ('treeness')
Fits a target's admixture proportions as a mixture of specified sources, using outgroups to constrain the fit
Fits an entire admixture graph - nodes, split times, admixture edges - to a full matrix of f-statistics

questions.explanation: f3 is the admixture-detection test on one population; f4/D tests four-population treeness; qpAdm fits proportions against a specified source/outgroup set; qpGraph fits a full admixture graph to all the f-statistics at once.

questions.prompt: Why can an unmodeled 'ghost' population silently break f3, f4, qpAdm, and qpGraph results?

options.text: Because ghost populations always increase sample size, which these tests cannot handle
Because real admixture from an unsampled lineage gets misattributed to whichever sampled population is genetically closest, biasing the fitted proportions or graph
Because these tests require at least one extinct population to run at all
Because ghost populations only affect Y-chromosome analyses

explanations.a: Ghost populations are unsampled, not an issue of sample size in the analyzed panel.
explanations.b: Correct - these methods can only work with the populations they are given, so gene flow from an unsampled lineage gets folded into the nearest sampled proxy, producing a confidently wrong result.
explanations.c: These tests run on any specified set of sampled populations; an extinct/ghost lineage is not a requirement.
explanations.d: The ghost-population problem applies to genome-wide autosomal analyses generally, not a specific chromosome type.

lessons.label: Haplotypes, IBD and Dating Admixture

sections.heading: Why keeping variants in order buys extra resolution
sections.body: Allele-frequency methods like F_ST or PCA summarize how common each variant is in each group, discarding the order variants appear along a chromosome; haplotype-based methods keep that order and resolve far finer structure as a result. ChromoPainter (Lawson et al. 2012) models each individual's genome as a mosaic 'painted' from chunks copied from every other sampled haplotype, using a copying model related to the Li and Stephens framework, and tallies how much each individual's genome is best explained by each other individual or group, producing a coancestry matrix. fineSTRUCTURE then clusters individuals hierarchically from that matrix. Because linked variants inherited together carry information about specific shared history, not just marginal frequency, this approach distinguished 17 genetically distinct clusters within Great Britain in the People of the British Isles project (Leslie et al. 2015), at a resolution PCA and F_ST could not reach.

sections.heading: Identical-by-descent segments as a molecular clock
sections.body: The raw signal behind these methods is identical-by-descent (IBD): a haplotype segment two individuals both inherited, unbroken, from a shared ancestor. Every generation, recombination has a chance to break a shared segment, so segment length shrinks with time since the common ancestor - a useful rule of thumb is that expected segment length is about 50/g centimorgans (cM) after g generations, since recombination occurs at roughly 1 cM per megabase per generation on each of the two lineages leading back to the shared ancestor, and a segment survives intact only as long as no recombination event falls inside it on either lineage. Long, multi-tens-of-centimorgan shared segments point to recent shared ancestry, within a handful of generations, while short segments accumulate from ancient shared ancestry, giving IBD length a built-in molecular clock.

sections.heading: GLOBETROTTER: dating admixture from chunk-length decay
sections.body: Hellenthal et al. (2014), in 'A Genetic Atlas of Human Admixture History,' combined ChromoPainter's copying profiles with a new tool, GLOBETROTTER, to detect and date admixture events across roughly 95 worldwide populations. GLOBETROTTER examines how the length of ancestry-informative haplotype chunks decays with genetic distance from a putative source, fits that decay to an exponential curve - the same recombination logic as the IBD clock - and estimates both a date and whether the data fit a single admixture pulse or multiple events better. The paper dated dozens of historical admixture events across the globe purely from present-day haplotype decay, without any ancient DNA.

sections.heading: RFMix: ancestry per segment, not per genome
sections.body: RFMix and similar local-ancestry inference tools take an admixed individual's genome and, using reference panels for each ancestral source, assign an ancestry label to each segment of each haplotype along the chromosome rather than one genome-wide proportion. That segment-level map enables admixture mapping: testing whether local ancestry at a given position correlates with a disease or trait across an admixed cohort, common in African-American and Latino genetic studies, which can localize a causal variant using far fewer markers than a standard genome-wide association study needs.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher finds an individual carries a 40 cM IBD segment shared with a reference Iberian panel. Using the ~50/g cM rule, 40 cM implies g = 50/40 = 1.25, so a little over one generation back - an extremely recent shared ancestor (parent or grandparent level), not a centuries-old population-level admixture event. By contrast, GLOBETROTTER applied to that same individual's whole genome finds the average length of Iberian-associated chunks decaying with a time constant consistent with roughly 15 generations (420-450 years assuming 28-30 years per generation), suggesting the bulk of that ancestry entered the population historically, while the one long 40 cM segment is a separate, much more recent event layered on top - a distinction only haplotype length, not allele frequency, could reveal.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe haplotype methods because they are the tool that actually answers 'when' and 'how granular,' questions allele-frequency methods like F_ST or plain PCA cannot touch. A strong answer explains why keeping variants in their chromosomal order, not just their frequency, is what buys the extra resolution and dating power, can state the segment-length-to-generations relationship (roughly 50/g cM) to justify a specific date rather than a vague 'long ago,' and knows the difference between a genome-wide proportion (ADMIXTURE) and a per-segment local-ancestry call (RFMix), since conflating the two is a common, checkpoint-losing error.

questions.prompt: Why can haplotype-based methods like ChromoPainter/fineSTRUCTURE resolve finer population structure than allele-frequency methods like F_ST or PCA?

options.text: They use more SNPs than any other method
They preserve the order variants appear along a chromosome, capturing linked-variant history that marginal allele frequency discards
They only work on non-human species
They ignore recombination entirely

explanations.a: The number of SNPs is not the distinguishing factor; it is what information is kept about them.
explanations.b: Correct - keeping variants in chromosomal order lets these methods use linked-variant (haplotype) history, which marginal allele-frequency summaries like F_ST or standard PCA discard.
explanations.c: ChromoPainter and fineSTRUCTURE are general-purpose and were demonstrated extensively on human data, including the People of the British Isles project.
explanations.d: Recombination is central to these methods - it is literally what breaks haplotypes into the 'chunks' ChromoPainter models.

questions.prompt: Using the approximation that expected IBD segment length is about 50/g centimorgans after g generations, roughly how many generations back is the common ancestor for a shared 10 cM segment?

options.text: About 2 generations
About 5 generations
About 20 generations
About 100 generations

explanations.a: 2 generations would predict a much longer expected segment (50/2 = 25 cM), not 10 cM.
explanations.b: Correct - solving 50/g = 10 gives g = 5 generations, a moderately recent shared ancestor.
explanations.c: 20 generations would predict a much shorter expected segment (50/20 = 2.5 cM), not 10 cM.
explanations.d: 100 generations would predict a segment near 0.5 cM, far shorter than 10 cM.

questions.prompt: What did Hellenthal et al. (2014) accomplish with GLOBETROTTER in 'A Genetic Atlas of Human Admixture History'?

options.text: They sequenced ancient DNA from 95 archaeological sites to date admixture events
They detected and dated admixture events across roughly 95 worldwide populations using present-day haplotype chunk-length decay, without ancient DNA
They proved that no historical admixture has ever occurred in human populations
They replaced F_ST as the standard estimator of population differentiation

explanations.a: The method used present-day genotype data and haplotype decay, not ancient DNA sequencing.
explanations.b: Correct - GLOBETROTTER fit the decay of ancestry-linked haplotype chunk length with genetic distance to date admixture events across roughly 95 populations, entirely from modern samples.
explanations.c: The paper's entire contribution was dating dozens of real historical admixture events, not disproving admixture.
explanations.d: GLOBETROTTER is an admixture-dating tool, unrelated to F_ST estimation.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or concept to its function.

right.text: Fine-scale hierarchical clustering from a haplotype copying/coancestry matrix
Dates admixture events from the decay of ancestry-linked haplotype chunk length with genetic distance
Assigns local ancestry per genomic segment, enabling admixture mapping of disease loci
Acts as a molecular clock: roughly 50/g centimorgans after g generations

questions.explanation: ChromoPainter/fineSTRUCTURE clusters via haplotype copying; GLOBETROTTER dates admixture from chunk decay; RFMix gives per-segment local ancestry for admixture mapping; IBD segment length itself serves as the underlying molecular clock both later tools build on.

lessons.label: Ancestry Is Not Race

sections.heading: Clines look like clusters when sampling has gaps
sections.body: Human genetic variation across geography is mostly continuous - a cline shaped by isolation by distance, where genetic similarity fades gradually with geographic distance rather than jumping at sharp boundaries. But sample discretely, grabbing individuals from Nigeria, France, and Japan while skipping everywhere between, and a clustering algorithm like STRUCTURE will return crisp, well-separated clusters, because it has no data from the gaps to reveal the underlying gradient. Serre and Pääbo (2004) argued exactly this: that widely cited discrete clusters, including Rosenberg et al.'s 2002 finding of major continental clusters, largely reflect sampling scheme rather than a true discontinuity in human variation. A second, related fact compounds this: cluster identity and any individual's assigned membership are functions of which reference populations are included - add or remove a population from the panel, and the clusters can shift.

sections.heading: Lewontin (1972) and Edwards (2003): both right, not contradictory
sections.body: Richard Lewontin's 1972 apportionment of classical genetic markers across major racial groupings found about 85% of total genetic variation lies within populations, roughly 8-10% among populations within a race, and only about 6-7% between the major races - leading him to argue racial classification captures almost none of human genetic variation and has no taxonomic significance. A.W.F.
