If instead the tips showed long, nearly star-like branches converging to a single recent burst of coalescence, that would instead flag exponential recent growth, not a bottleneck — the two demographic histories pull the same statistic (tree shape) in opposite directions, so shape alone, read carefully, distinguishes them.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what does your gene tree's shape actually tell you about population history?' because it tests whether a student understands the coalescent is a statistical model, not just a diagram. A student who can explain that rate scales as k(k-1)/2, that the last two lineages eat roughly half the expected tree depth, and that star-shaped trees flag growth while short compressed trees flag bottlenecks has grasped why coalescent theory is the mathematical bridge between an observed DNA tree and an inferred demographic story — rather than treating the tree as decoration attached to a phylogeny.

questions.prompt: In Kingman's coalescent, with k lineages remaining, the waiting time to the next coalescence event is exponentially distributed with what rate (in units of 2Ne generations)?

options.text: k
2Ne/k

explanations.a: The rate is not linear in k; it comes from counting pairs of lineages, which grows quadratically, not linearly.
explanations.b: Correct — there are k(k-1)/2 distinct pairs among k lineages, and any pair can coalesce, so the total rate is the pair count, k(k-1)/2, in units of 2Ne generations.
explanations.c: This inverts the relationship; the rate does not scale with Ne directly, Ne is absorbed into the time unit (2Ne generations).
explanations.d: This underestimates the rate by ignoring that all pairs, not just one lineage, can coalesce.

questions.prompt: Why does the expected time to the most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) grow only modestly as sample size n increases, approaching about 4Ne generations?

options.text: Because most of the expected tree depth is concentrated in the final coalescence of the last two lineages, which happens regardless of n
Because larger samples always coalesce faster in every generation
Because Ne shrinks as more lineages are sampled
Because sample size has no effect on any coalescent time

explanations.a: Correct — the last two lineages alone contribute an expected 2Ne generations (about half the ~4Ne total), and adding more early lineages barely changes this because those extra lineages coalesce quickly while many remain.
explanations.b: Larger samples increase the coalescence rate only while many lineages remain; the rate drops sharply as lineages become few, which is exactly why depth saturates.
explanations.c: Ne is a population-level parameter and does not change because of how many individuals a researcher happens to sample.
explanations.d: Sample size does affect early coalescence rates, it is only the total expected depth that saturates near 4Ne, not that n has zero effect.

questions.prompt: Match each demographic history to the genealogical/genetic signature it produces.

right.text: Star-like tree, long external branches, excess rare variants, negative Tajima's D
Overall shortened tree, forced near-simultaneous coalescences, reduced diversity

questions.explanation: Growth means the population was smaller in the ancient past, so deep coalescence is fast and recent lineages linger — a star tree with many rare variants. A bottleneck compresses many lineages through a narrow window of low Ne, shortening the tree and reducing diversity.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of a large sample's total expected tree depth (TMRCA) is spent waiting for the very last coalescence event, when only two lineages remain?

options.text: About 5%
About half
Essentially all of it
None — the last coalescence happens instantly

explanations.a: This drastically underestimates the disproportionate weight of the final step in the coalescent process.
explanations.b: Correct — the final two-lineage step has expected duration 2Ne generations, while total expected TMRCA is about 4Ne generations for a large sample, so the last step is about half the total depth.
explanations.c: Earlier coalescences among many lineages also contribute time, just each step contributes less as k grows, so it is not essentially all of the depth.
explanations.d: The final coalescence has rate 1 (in 2Ne units), the lowest rate of any step, so it takes the longest expected time of any single step, not zero.

lessons.label: Building Trees from Sequences

sections.heading: Distance methods: fast, but assumption-laden
sections.body: The cheapest way to build a tree is to compute pairwise genetic distances between sequences and cluster them. UPGMA (unweighted pair group method with arithmetic mean) clusters the closest pair, averages distances to the rest, and repeats — but it silently assumes an ultrametric tree, meaning every tip is equidistant from the root, which is exactly the molecular-clock assumption of a constant substitution rate across all lineages. When rates vary (a common reality), UPGMA can recover the wrong topology outright. Naoki Saitou and Masatoshi Nei's 1987 neighbor-joining algorithm fixed this by minimizing total branch length across the whole tree at each step rather than assuming equal tip depths, making it consistent even when lineages evolve at different rates and it remains a standard fast method for large datasets.

sections.heading: Parsimony's trap: long-branch attraction
sections.body: Maximum parsimony picks the tree requiring the fewest total substitutions to explain the data. It seems logical (Occam's razor for trees), but Joseph Felsenstein showed in 1978 that when two lineages both evolve fast (long branches) while related lineages evolve slowly, parsimony can be positively misleading: convergent changes on the two long branches look like shared derived similarity, pulling them together on the tree regardless of their true relationship. This long-branch attraction is not a matter of insufficient data — adding more sequence only makes parsimony more confidently wrong. It is the textbook argument for preferring model-based methods that explicitly account for multiple hits at the same site.

sections.heading: Likelihood, Bayesian inference, and how confident is confident
sections.body: Maximum likelihood evaluates trees under an explicit substitution model — from Jukes-Cantor's simplest case (JC69: equal rates between all four bases) to Kimura's two-parameter model (K80: separate transition/transversion rates) to the general time-reversible model (GTR, allowing six distinct rate classes) usually combined with a gamma distribution to model rate heterogeneity across sites. Bayesian methods (MrBayes, BEAST) use Markov chain Monte Carlo to sample the posterior distribution of trees directly, yielding a posterior probability per node. Crucially, a bootstrap proportion (Felsenstein 1985: resample sites with replacement, rebuild the tree, repeat hundreds of times, and count how often a clade recurs) and a Bayesian posterior probability are not the same currency — posteriors are consistently higher than bootstrap values for comparable support, partly because bootstrapping is a conservative resampling test of the data while posterior probability is the model-conditioned probability the clade is true given the priors, so a 95% posterior is not equivalent evidence to 95% bootstrap support.

lessons.workedExample: A student builds a tree of four species from a gene alignment and gets different topologies from UPGMA versus neighbor-joining. Checking pairwise distances, one lineage (a fast-evolving outgroup) has roughly double the substitutions per site of the others. UPGMA, forcing equal tip depths, distorts the tree to compensate and misplaces that lineage; neighbor-joining, which does not assume a clock, recovers the topology matching known taxonomy. The student then runs maximum likelihood under GTR+gamma and gets the same topology as neighbor-joining, with a bootstrap support of 68% at the contested node — a real but modest number, correctly reported as 'moderate support,' not treated as proof.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe tree-building method choice because a wrong method can produce a confidently wrong answer that looks identical to a right one on the page. A student who says 'I used neighbor-joining because rates weren't clock-like across my taxa' or 'I checked for long-branch attraction by adding a slower outgroup' shows they understand the assumptions baked into each algorithm. A student who reports '94% bootstrap' and '0.94 posterior probability' as interchangeable evidence reveals they do not understand that these two numbers are computed by fundamentally different logic and are not on the same scale.

questions.prompt: What key assumption does UPGMA make that neighbor-joining (Saitou and Nei, 1987) does not require?

options.text: That the alignment contains no gaps
That the tree is ultrametric — all tips equidistant from the root, i.e., a constant substitution rate (molecular clock)
That all sequences are the same length
That there are at least four taxa

explanations.a: Gap handling is an alignment issue, not what distinguishes these two clustering methods.
explanations.b: Correct — UPGMA clusters assuming equal evolutionary rates across all lineages (ultrametricity); neighbor-joining instead minimizes total branch length and tolerates unequal rates.
explanations.c: Sequence length equality is an alignment prerequisite for both methods, not a distinguishing assumption.
explanations.d: Both methods can technically run on more than three taxa; four is not a special threshold that separates them.

questions.prompt: Long-branch attraction (Felsenstein, 1978) causes maximum parsimony to be misled because:

options.text: Convergent substitutions on two fast-evolving lineages look like shared derived similarity, pulling those lineages together regardless of true relationship
Parsimony cannot handle more than two taxa at once
Fast-evolving lineages always have fewer available sites to analyze
Parsimony requires a pre-specified substitution model that is usually wrong

explanations.a: Correct — parsimony counts total changes needed, and when two long branches independently acquire the same changes by chance, parsimony reads that convergence as evidence of shared ancestry, grouping them incorrectly.
explanations.b: Parsimony works across any number of taxa; the problem is specific to branch-length heterogeneity, not taxon count.
explanations.c: Fast-evolving lineages have the same number of sites as any other; the issue is substitution saturation, not site count.
explanations.d: Parsimony's appeal is precisely that it does not require an explicit substitution model — that is what makes it vulnerable to multiple-hit artifacts a model-based method would correct for.

questions.prompt: Why are Bayesian posterior probabilities typically higher than bootstrap proportions for the same clade?

options.text: They measure the same underlying quantity, so any difference is a computational bug

Bootstrap resampling of sites is a comparatively conservative test of the data, while posterior probability is the model-conditioned probability the clade is true given the priors — different currencies that are not numerically equivalent
Posterior probabilities are always computed from a larger dataset
Bootstrap values ignore branch lengths entirely, which mechanically lowers them

explanations.a: They are not the same quantity by construction — one resamples data, the other integrates over a model-based posterior — so the systematic gap is expected, not a bug.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the well-documented pattern: posterior probabilities tend to run higher and more liberal than bootstrap support for comparable nodes, so equal-looking numbers (e.g., 95% each) are not equally strong evidence.
explanations.c: Both are typically computed from the same alignment; dataset size is not what drives the systematic difference.
explanations.d: Bootstrap support is about topology recovery frequency, not branch lengths directly, and this is not the source of the gap between the two measures.

questions.prompt: Order these substitution models from fewest to most free parameters governing base-substitution rates.

items.text: JC69 (Jukes-Cantor: equal rates between all bases)
K80 (Kimura two-parameter: separate transition/transversion rates)
GTR (general time-reversible: six distinct rate classes)

questions.explanation: JC69 has a single rate parameter (all substitutions equally likely), K80 adds a second parameter separating transitions from transversions, and GTR generalizes further to six independent rate classes among the four bases, making it the most parameter-rich of the three.

lessons.label: Gene Trees Are Not Species Trees

sections.heading: Ancestral polymorphism outlives speciation
sections.body: A species tree describes when lineages of populations split. A gene tree describes when two copies of one locus find their common ancestor — and because the coalescent process is stochastic, that ancestor can predate the population split by a long margin, especially when successive speciation events happen close together in time. When an ancestral population carries standing polymorphism at a locus, and then splits into two daughter lineages in quick succession, a given allele copy can fail to sort by the time of the second split. This is incomplete lineage sorting (ILS): the gene tree at that locus can group two species together that are not each other's closest relatives on the species tree.

sections.heading: The human-chimp-gorilla case, and the anomaly zone
sections.body: The classic demonstration is the human-chimpanzee-gorilla trichotomy. Genome-wide surveys, including the 2012 gorilla genome paper by Aylwyn Scally and colleagues, found that only about 70% of the genome supports the true species tree grouping humans and chimpanzees as closest relatives; roughly 15% instead groups humans with gorillas, and another 15% groups chimpanzees with gorillas — about 30% of the genome, in total, backs a topology that conflicts with the accepted species tree. This is a direct consequence of the short time between the gorilla-hominine split and the human-chimp split. Push the internal branches short enough and rare enough, and you enter what Degnan and Rosenberg formalized in 2006 as the anomaly zone: a regime where the single most probable gene tree topology is not the species tree at all, meaning majority-vote across loci would pick the wrong answer even with infinite data at each locus.

sections.heading: Recovering the species tree, and separating ILS from introgression
sections.body: Because no single gene tree (and not even the modal gene tree, in the anomaly zone) reliably equals the species tree, modern phylogenomics fits the multispecies coalescent explicitly: methods like ASTRAL (statistically consistent tree quartet-based summary) and StarBEAST (joint Bayesian estimation of gene trees and species tree together) combine signal across hundreds to thousands of independent loci to estimate the species tree despite widespread ILS. A separate, harder problem is that gene flow (introgression) after a split can produce the exact same discordant topology as ILS by pure chance. The two are told apart not by topology counts, which look identical, but by pattern-based statistics — the D-statistic (ABBA-BABA test) checks whether discordant site patterns are asymmetric across the genome in a way ILS alone predicts should be symmetric — and by branch-length asymmetry, since introgressed segments tend to show shorter coalescence times (younger divergence) than ILS-driven discordance of the same topology.

lessons.workedExample: A team sequences 500 loci across humans, chimpanzees, and gorillas and tabulates topology counts: about 350 loci support (human, chimp), 75 support (human, gorilla), and 75 support (chimp, gorilla) — matching the roughly 70/15/15 genome-wide split reported for this trio. On its own, this pattern is exactly what ILS predicts from a short internal branch between the gorilla split and the human-chimp split, no gene flow required. To check whether any of the minority topologies instead reflect ancient introgression rather than pure ILS, the team computes a D-statistic on the discordant site patterns: a significant deviation from zero would flag asymmetric gene flow, while a value near zero is consistent with ILS alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing gene trees versus species trees is testing whether a student can hold two ideas apart that look identical on a slide: a tree of alleles and a tree of populations. The tell is whether a student can explain why a minority gene-tree topology is not automatically evidence of hybridization — ILS alone produces discordance whenever speciation events are closely spaced — and can name a concrete way to tell ILS apart from introgression (a D-statistic, branch-length asymmetry) rather than treating 'some genes disagree with the species tree' as itself surprising or diagnostic of anything specific.

questions.prompt: Roughly what fraction of the human genome supports a gene-tree topology that conflicts with the accepted (human, chimp) species tree, per the 2012 gorilla genome analysis?

options.text: About 1%
About 30%
About 70%
Essentially 0%, gene trees always match the species tree

explanations.a: This drastically understates how common ILS-driven discordance is in this closely spaced trichotomy.
explanations.b: Correct — about 70% of the genome supports (human, chimp), while roughly 15% supports (human, gorilla) and 15% supports (chimp, gorilla), so about 30% overall conflicts with the species tree.
explanations.c: 70% is the fraction supporting the correct species-tree topology, not the fraction conflicting with it.
explanations.d: Gene trees frequently disagree with the species tree under ILS; zero discordance would be the surprising outcome here.

questions.prompt: What defines the 'anomaly zone' as formalized by Degnan and Rosenberg (2006)?

options.text: A region of a tree where sequencing errors are common
A parameter regime where the single most probable gene tree topology is not the true species tree topology
Any case where two species hybridize
A statistical artifact caused only by small sample sizes

explanations.a: The anomaly zone is a property of coalescent probabilities under short branches, not a description of sequencing quality.
explanations.b: Correct — with sufficiently short, closely spaced internal branches, the most probable gene tree can differ from the species tree, so even a majority-vote across infinite loci would recover the wrong topology.
explanations.c: Hybridization (introgression) is a separate phenomenon that can also cause discordance, but the anomaly zone specifically describes ILS probabilities under short branches, not gene flow.
explanations.d: The anomaly zone is a property of branch lengths and coalescent probabilities, not of how much data you collect — more loci do not fix it.

questions.prompt: Why can't topology counts alone distinguish incomplete lineage sorting from introgression when both produce the same discordant gene-tree topology?

options.text: Because both processes can generate the identical minority topology by chance; researchers instead look at asymmetry in site patterns (D-statistic) or branch-length/divergence-time differences
Because topology counts are never reliable for any purpose
Because introgression never produces discordant topologies
Because ILS only ever produces the true species tree topology

explanations.a: Correct — a discordant topology looks the same whether it arose from ancestral polymorphism sorting differently (ILS) or from post-split gene flow, so distinguishing them requires additional signal like the D-statistic's asymmetry test or coalescence-time (branch-length) differences.
explanations.b: Topology counts are informative for detecting discordance overall; the limitation is specifically in attributing the cause of a given discordant topology.
explanations.c: Introgression is a major cause of discordant topologies, often producing patterns very similar to ILS.
explanations.d: ILS is exactly the process that produces minority discordant topologies, not just the true species tree.

questions.prompt: Match each method or statistic to what it is used for.

right.text: Statistically consistent species-tree estimation from gene-tree quartets across many loci
Joint Bayesian co-estimation of gene trees and the species tree
Testing for asymmetric site-pattern signal indicating introgression rather than ILS alone

questions.explanation: ASTRAL summarizes many independent gene trees via quartets to estimate the species tree under the multispecies coalescent; StarBEAST jointly estimates gene trees and the species tree in one Bayesian framework; the D-statistic tests whether discordant site patterns are asymmetric in a way pure ILS would not predict, flagging introgression.

lessons.label: Molecular Clocks: Strict, Relaxed and Calibrated

sections.heading: A clock built from hemoglobin, and a clock put on trial
sections.body: Emile Zuckerkandl and Linus Pauling, comparing hemoglobin sequences across species between 1962 and 1965, noticed that amino-acid differences accumulated roughly in proportion to time since two lineages diverged — the molecular clock hypothesis: substitutions accrue at a roughly constant rate, so genetic distance becomes a proxy for elapsed time. The idea was tested hard almost immediately. Vincent Sarich and Allan Wilson, in 1967, used immunological cross-reactivity of blood albumin (micro-complement fixation, a distance proxy) to estimate that humans and chimpanzees split only around 5 million years ago. This directly contradicted the paleontological consensus of the time, which placed the split at 15 to 30 million years ago, largely anchored on fossils of Ramapithecus, then interpreted as an early hominid ancestor.

sections.heading: How the dispute resolved
sections.body: For roughly a decade this was a real fight between fields: paleontologists trusted the fossil-anchored deep split, molecular biologists trusted the clock. The resolution came from the fossil side, not the molecular side — through the late 1970s and 1980s, more complete Ramapithecus material (and comparison to Sivapithecus) showed it was not a hominid ancestor at all but instead related to the orangutan lineage, so it no longer constrained the human-chimp split to be ancient. Once that anchor was removed, the paleontological and molecular estimates converged toward a much younger split, now generally placed around 6 to 8 million years ago — close to the range the molecular clock had proposed all along, an outcome now taught as a case study in a converging line of evidence overturning an entrenched interpretation.

sections.heading: Strict versus relaxed clocks, and why the rate itself is contested
sections.body: A strict clock assumes one substitution rate across every branch of the tree — convenient, but often violated by real biology, where rate varies with generation time, metabolic rate, and population size. The uncorrelated relaxed clock (formalized by Alexei Drummond and colleagues in 2006) instead lets each branch draw its own rate from a shared statistical distribution, accommodating rate variation without assuming any particular pattern of rate inheritance between neighboring branches. Either way, the clock still needs to be set with a calibration — a fossil-dated node, or, for rapidly evolving organisms sampled over time, tip dating using the sampling dates themselves. Even with calibration nailed down, the human mutation-rate estimate itself is disputed: pedigree-based studies (sequencing parent-offspring trios directly) give roughly 1.2×10⁻⁸ mutations per base pair per generation, while classical phylogenetic estimates (calibrated against fossil divergence dates) give roughly 2.5×10⁻⁸ — almost exactly double. Because age estimates are inversely proportional to rate, this single twofold discrepancy roughly doubles or halves every date computed from it, including landmark dates like the human-Neanderthal split or the out-of-Africa migration.

lessons.workedExample: A team estimates the human-chimpanzee divergence date two ways. Using the pedigree mutation rate (~1.2×10⁻⁸ per site per generation) with a 29-year generation time, they get a divergence around 10-13 million years ago. Using the older phylogenetic rate (~2.5×10⁻⁸), the same sequence divergence data yields a date roughly half as old, around 5-6 million years — much closer to current consensus. This is not a rounding error: it is the direct arithmetic consequence of dividing the same observed genetic distance by two different rate estimates, and it is why any paper reporting a molecular date must state which mutation rate it used before the number means anything.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how did you calibrate your molecular clock, and which mutation rate did you use?' because a date with no stated rate and calibration is not a date at all — it is an unlabeled ratio. A student who can explain that the pedigree and phylogenetic mutation-rate estimates differ by roughly a factor of two, and that this factor propagates directly into any age estimate built on it, shows they understand the clock is a model with a load-bearing assumption, not a fact read directly off DNA. The Sarich-Wilson story is the concrete cautionary tale: a molecular estimate can be right while the field's fossil-based anchor is wrong, and only re-examining the fossil evidence itself resolved the dispute.

questions.prompt: Sarich and Wilson's 1967 albumin-based estimate of the human-chimpanzee split (~5 million years ago) conflicted with paleontological estimates of 15-30 million years ago anchored on what fossil?

options.text: Australopithecus afarensis
Ramapithecus
Neanderthal remains
Denisovan remains

explanations.a: Australopithecus afarensis (e.g., 'Lucy') was discovered later and dates to roughly 3-4 million years ago; it was not the fossil anchoring the older split estimate.
explanations.b: Correct — Ramapithecus was interpreted at the time as an early hominid ancestor, anchoring the human-chimp split at 15-30 million years ago; it was later reclassified as related to orangutans, removing that anchor.
explanations.c: Neanderthal remains bear on a much later divergence (within the Homo lineage), not the human-chimp split debate.
explanations.d: Denisovan remains, like Neanderthal, are relevant to recent hominin divergences, not the ancient human-chimp split dispute.

questions.prompt: How did the Sarich-Wilson versus paleontological dispute over the human-chimp split ultimately resolve?

options.text: The molecular clock hypothesis was abandoned entirely
Ramapithecus was reclassified as related to orangutans rather than hominids, removing the old anchor, and the dispute converged toward the younger molecular-style estimate
Both estimates were shown to be equally wrong and replaced by radiocarbon dating
The paleontological estimate of 15-30 million years was confirmed correct

explanations.a: The clock hypothesis was refined (e.g., into relaxed-clock models) but not abandoned; it remains central to molecular dating.
explanations.b: Correct — reinterpreting Ramapithecus as an orangutan relative removed the fossil constraint forcing an ancient split, and the consensus converged near 6-8 million years, close to the molecular estimate.
explanations.c: Radiocarbon dating is far too short-ranged (tens of thousands of years) to date a multi-million-year-old divergence like this.
explanations.d: The older estimate was not confirmed; it was specifically the fossil interpretation underlying that estimate that was overturned.

questions.prompt: The pedigree-based human mutation rate (~1.2×10⁻⁸ per base per generation) differs from the classical phylogenetic estimate (~2.5×10⁻⁸) by roughly what factor, and what is the consequence for dates derived from it?

options.text: About 10-fold; dates derived from it are essentially unusable
About 2-fold; using one rate instead of the other roughly doubles or halves any date computed from that rate
Less than 5%; the discrepancy is negligible for dating purposes
The two rates are actually identical once rounding is accounted for

explanations.a: A 10-fold gap overstates the discrepancy; the two estimates differ by roughly a factor of two, not an order of magnitude.
explanations.b: Correct — since age is inversely proportional to rate, a roughly twofold difference in mutation rate (1.2 vs 2.5 ×10⁻⁸) directly translates into dates differing by roughly a factor of two.
explanations.c: A near-twofold difference is far from negligible; it changes major dated events (like out-of-Africa timing) substantially.
explanations.d: The two values (1.2×10⁻⁸ and 2.5×10⁻⁸) are meaningfully different, not the same number under rounding.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an uncorrelated relaxed clock (Drummond et al., 2006) from a strict clock?

options.text: The relaxed clock forces every branch to share exactly the same substitution rate
The relaxed clock lets each branch draw its own rate from a shared statistical distribution, accommodating rate variation across the tree
The relaxed clock eliminates the need for any calibration point
The relaxed clock only applies to fossil calibration, never to tip dating

explanations.a: That description is the strict clock, not the relaxed clock; forcing one shared rate across all branches is exactly what the relaxed model relaxes.
explanations.b: Correct — the uncorrelated relaxed clock allows branch-specific rates drawn from a common distribution, capturing real biological rate variation (e.g., from generation time or metabolic rate) without a strict single-rate assumption.
explanations.c: Calibration (fossil or tip dating) is still required to convert relative substitution amounts into absolute time under either a strict or relaxed clock.
explanations.d: Relaxed clocks are used with both fossil calibration and tip dating; the method is not restricted to one calibration type.

lessons.label: Inferring Population Size Through Time

sections.heading: Reading a whole demographic history from one genome
sections.body: A striking 2011 result from Heng Li and Richard Durbin showed that a single diploid genome contains enough information to reconstruct effective population size (Ne) over roughly the last million years. Their method, PSMC (pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent), exploits the fact that the two copies of a chromosome an individual inherited recombine with each other's ancestors at different points along the genome, so the time to their most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) varies from one genomic segment to the next. Stretches of high heterozygosity imply deep TMRCA (segments that coalesce recently have had less time to accumulate differences); the distribution of these local TMRCAs along the genome, inferred via a hidden Markov model over recombination breakpoints, is then converted into a trajectory of Ne through time, since coalescence rate at each epoch depends directly on the Ne of that epoch.

sections.heading: Extending resolution: more samples, more information
sections.body: PSMC's resolution using a single genome degrades at both ends of the timescale — recently, because too few recombination events have occurred to give a fine-grained signal. MSMC (Schiffels and Durbin, 2014) extends the same sequential-coalescent framework to multiple haplotypes at once, using coalescence among several samples to sharpen resolution into more recent millennia. SMC++ (Terhorst, Kamm, and Song, 2017) pushes further by combining coalescent information with the site-frequency spectrum (SFS) and works directly on unphased genotype data from many unrelated individuals, letting it resolve much more recent history than single-genome PSMC while avoiding the need for costly haplotype phasing. A separate family of methods skips genealogies altogether: SFS-based tools like dadi, moments, and fastsimcoal2 fit explicit, hypothesis-driven multi-population demographic models (specific bottleneck sizes, split times, migration rates) directly to the observed frequency spectrum via likelihood or simulation, trading the flexibility of a free-form trajectory for the interpretability of a named model.

sections.heading: The out-of-Africa signal, and where these methods break
sections.body: Applied to human genomes, these methods converge on a sharp Ne crash associated with the out-of-Africa migration, generally dated to roughly 50,000 to 80,000 years ago, with effective population size falling to as low as a few thousand individuals in non-African lineages — a genetic bottleneck consistent with a small founding group leaving the ancestral African population. Two hard limits recur across this whole toolkit. First, PSMC in particular loses power in approximately the last 10,000 years: too little time has passed for enough recombination events to accumulate the signal the method depends on, so recent history (agriculture-era population booms, for instance) is largely invisible to it. Second, and more subtly, population structure can mimic a size change: if a sample's ancestors were actually two partially-isolated subpopulations that later merged, the resulting genealogy looks statistically like a single population that went through a bottleneck, even though total Ne never truly shrank — a confound formally explored by researchers like Lounès Chikhi and colleagues.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher runs PSMC on a single non-African human genome and gets a Ne trajectory showing a large ancestral population, then a sharp decline to roughly a few thousand around 60,000 years ago, then flat, uninformative signal from about 10,000 years ago to the present. They cannot use this to say anything about, e.g., agricultural-era population growth in the last 10,000 years — that is exactly the window PSMC cannot resolve. To extend the picture, they add several more genomes and run SMC++, which sharpens the recent end and reveals renewed post-bottleneck growth. But before concluding the ancestral 'large population' segment reflects one continuously large population, they must also ask whether it could instead reflect ancient population structure (two or more semi-isolated groups) later merging — since that scenario produces a very similar signature to a single large ancestral Ne.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what can your method not tell you?' because these tools are named, dateable, and each has documented blind spots — treating a PSMC plot as an unqualified population history is the tell of a student who ran the software without reading past the output figure. A strong answer names the specific limit relevant to the claim: PSMC cannot resolve the last ~10,000 years, so no claim about recent growth can rest on it, and any inferred ancient bottleneck must be checked against the alternative explanation that population structure, not a true Ne crash, produced the same genealogical signature.

questions.prompt: PSMC (Li and Durbin, 2011) infers effective population size through time from what signal within a single diploid genome?

options.text: The total number of protein-coding genes
The distribution of local time-to-most-recent-common-ancestor (TMRCA) between the two chromosome copies, varying along the genome due to recombination
The GC content of the genome
The number of chromosomes

explanations.a: Gene count has no direct relationship to coalescent time or effective population size inference.
explanations.b: Correct — recombination breaks the genome into segments with different local TMRCAs between the two inherited copies; PSMC uses a hidden Markov model to infer this TMRCA distribution and convert it into a Ne trajectory, since coalescence rate depends on Ne.
explanations.c: GC content reflects base composition and mutational/selective processes, not coalescent timing.
explanations.d: Chromosome number is a fixed karyotype feature, unrelated to demographic history inference.

questions.prompt: Roughly when do PSMC/MSMC/SMC++ analyses place the out-of-Africa bottleneck, and to roughly what effective population size?

options.text: About 500,000 years ago, falling to about 500,000 individuals
About 50,000-80,000 years ago, falling to as low as a few thousand individuals
About 5,000 years ago, falling to about 1 million individuals
There is no detectable out-of-Africa bottleneck in these analyses

explanations.a: This timing is far too old and the population size far too large for the documented out-of-Africa signal.
explanations.b: Correct — these methods converge on a sharp Ne decline around 50,000-80,000 years ago associated with the out-of-Africa migration, with effective size dropping to as low as a few thousand in non-African lineages.
explanations.c: This timing is too recent (within PSMC's blind zone) and the population figure far too large to match the documented bottleneck.
explanations.d: A clear bottleneck signal is one of the most robust and widely replicated findings from applying these methods to human genomes.

questions.prompt: Match each method to its key distinguishing capability.

right.text: Infers a Ne trajectory from a single diploid genome, but loses power in roughly the last 10,000 years
Combines coalescent and site-frequency-spectrum information from many unphased genomes to sharpen recent resolution
Fits explicit, named multi-population demographic models (bottleneck sizes, split times, migration rates) to the observed frequency spectrum

questions.explanation: PSMC needs only one genome but cannot resolve recent millennia; SMC++ combines coalescent and SFS signal across many unphased individuals to push resolution into recent history; SFS-based tools like dadi, moments, and fastsimcoal2 instead fit specific, interpretable multi-population models directly to allele-frequency data.

questions.prompt: Why can population structure (e.g., two semi-isolated subpopulations that later merge) produce a PSMC signature that mimics a true population bottleneck?

options.text: Because structure changes the mutation rate directly
Because reduced gene flow between subpopulations changes coalescence rates in a way that resembles reduced Ne, even though total population size never actually shrank
Because PSMC cannot be run on structured populations at all
Because structure only affects the Y chromosome, which PSMC does not use

explanations.a: Population structure does not alter the underlying mutation rate; the confound operates through coalescence rate, not mutation rate.
explanations.b: Correct — limited gene flow between semi-isolated groups slows coalescence between lineages in different subpopulations, producing a genealogical signature statistically similar to a genuine Ne decline, even without any true reduction in total population size.
explanations.c: PSMC can be run on structured populations; the issue is that its output can be misinterpreted, not that the method fails to execute.
explanations.d: PSMC works on autosomal diploid genome data generally, not specifically the Y chromosome, and the structure confound is a genome-wide coalescent effect.

lessons.label: Ancestral Recombination Graphs and Tree Sequences

sections.heading: One genome, many trees
sections.body: A single gene tree captures the genealogy at one non-recombining locus, but a real chromosome recombines, so different stretches of it descend through different genealogies. The ancestral recombination graph (ARG) is the full generalization: rather than one tree, it is a sequence of correlated local trees along the genome, linked by recombination events that swap which ancestor a segment traces back through. Move along the chromosome and the local tree topology and branch lengths change at each historical recombination breakpoint, while staying highly correlated with its neighbors, since most of the genealogy is shared between adjacent segments. The ARG is, in principle, the complete genealogical record of a sample — every coalescence and every recombination event that produced the observed genomes.

sections.heading: From intractable ideal to usable tool
sections.body: For a long time the ARG was a beautiful theoretical object nobody could actually estimate at scale: the space of possible ARGs consistent with real data is enormous, and early samplers were computationally prohibitive beyond a handful of genomes. ARGweaver (Rasmussen and colleagues, 2014) made genome-wide ARG sampling practical via a discretized, hidden-Markov-model-based MCMC approach, though still limited to modest sample sizes. Relate (Speidel and colleagues, 2019) scaled genealogy estimation to thousands of samples by building local trees efficiently and reweighting branch lengths afterward with a separate coalescent-based re-estimation step. tsinfer (Kelleher and colleagues, 2019) separated the problem further, reconstructing the sharing pattern of ancestral haplotypes (topology) without initially estimating time, with tsdate then dating the resulting nodes. Kelleher and colleagues applied tsinfer to real data at thousand-sample scale (the 1000 Genomes Project and the Simons Genome Diversity Project) and, separately, used simulation to show the approach scales to datasets of over a million genomes — a scale inconceivable with earlier ARG methods.

sections.heading: Tree sequences make it tractable, and where it still breaks
sections.body: The scaling breakthrough was as much about data structure as algorithm: the tskit tree-sequence encoding (Kelleher, Etheridge, and McVean's earlier succinct tree sequence work) stores the many correlated local trees not as separate objects but as a compact record of the edges that differ between adjacent trees, exploiting the fact that neighboring trees share most of their structure — this makes both storage and computation scale far better than genome size times sample size would suggest, which is what makes million-genome analysis tractable at all. What these ARG-based methods deliver once fitted: estimated ages for individual genetic variants, allele-frequency trajectories through time, locus-specific estimates of effective population size, and signals of selective sweeps from unusually young, unusually widespread haplotypes. Where they remain fragile: genotype error propagates directly into false recombination signal and distorted local trees; unphased data (not knowing which alleles sit on the same chromosome copy) makes topology inference substantially harder; and low-coverage or ancient DNA, which combines both problems with missing data, remains the hardest regime for all of these methods to handle reliably.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants to estimate the age of a disease-associated variant and check whether it shows signs of a recent selective sweep. They run tsinfer on a large modern cohort to infer the tree-sequence topology, then tsdate to assign ages to nodes, placing the variant's origin at a specific number of generations ago based on the local tree structure around it. The surrounding haplotype is unusually long and shared across many unrelated carriers — a signature consistent with a recent sweep, since a young, positively selected variant has not had time to accumulate recombination breakpoints that would shorten shared haplotype blocks. Before trusting the sweep signal, the team checks genotype quality at that locus specifically, since a genotyping error there could fabricate the same 'young, unusually shared haplotype' appearance without any real selection.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing ARG methods is testing whether a student understands genealogy inference has moved past 'one tree per study' into an object that changes along the genome, and whether the student knows both what that unlocks (variant dating, sweep detection, local Ne, at genome-wide and now population-wide scale via tskit) and where it is still shaky. The tell of real understanding is naming genotype error and unphased or ancient data specifically as failure modes, rather than treating an inferred ARG or its downstream variant-age estimate as ground truth just because it came from a named, published tool.

questions.prompt: What is an ancestral recombination graph (ARG), as distinct from a single gene tree?

options.text: A single tree that averages genealogical signal across the whole genome
A sequence of correlated local trees along the genome, linked by historical recombination events
A tree built only from mitochondrial DNA
A statistical test for detecting recombination hotspots only

explanations.a: An ARG does not average into one tree; it explicitly preserves how the genealogy differs from segment to segment.
explanations.b: Correct — because recombination causes different genomic segments to descend through different genealogies, the ARG represents the whole chromosome as a sequence of local trees, each linked to its neighbors by recombination breakpoints.
explanations.c: Mitochondrial DNA does not recombine (in the standard model), so it produces a single gene tree, not the kind of recombining structure an ARG describes.
explanations.d: An ARG is a genealogical structure, not merely a hotspot-detection statistic, though recombination events are part of what defines it.

questions.prompt: Match each method to what made it a scaling step forward for genealogy/ARG inference.

right.text: Made genome-wide ARG sampling practical via a discretized HMM-based MCMC approach, for modest sample sizes
Scaled genealogy estimation to thousands of samples by building trees efficiently, then re-estimating branch lengths
Split topology inference from dating; applied to real data at thousand-sample scale, and shown via simulation to scale to datasets of over a million genomes

questions.explanation: ARGweaver pioneered practical genome-wide ARG sampling via MCMC but was limited to smaller sample sizes; Relate scaled to thousands of genomes by decoupling tree-building from branch-length re-estimation; tsinfer/tsdate separated topology inference from dating entirely, applied to real data at thousand-sample scale and shown by simulation to scale to over a million genomes.

questions.prompt: What makes the tskit tree-sequence encoding scale to million-genome datasets, where earlier ARG representations could not?

options.text: It stores only the first and last tree in the genome, discarding the rest
It compactly encodes correlated local trees by recording only the edges that differ between adjacent trees, exploiting how much structure neighboring trees share
It avoids storing any genealogical information at all, only allele frequencies
It requires converting all data to a single averaged tree before storage

explanations.a: Discarding intermediate trees would lose the genealogical detail (variant ages, local Ne, sweep signals) the format is specifically designed to preserve.
explanations.b: Correct — because adjacent local trees along a recombining genome share most of their structure, tskit stores the differences between them rather than each tree independently, giving large storage and computational savings at genome scale.
explanations.c: Tree sequences retain full genealogical (topology and branch-length) information, not just allele frequencies, which is what supports variant-age and selection analyses downstream.
explanations.d: Averaging into a single tree is precisely what an ARG/tree-sequence approach avoids, since it would discard the segment-to-segment genealogical variation that is the whole point of the structure.

questions.prompt: Which two data conditions are named as making ARG-based inference (variant dating, sweep detection, local Ne) especially fragile?

options.text: High sequencing depth and large sample size
Genotype error and unphased or ancient/low-coverage data
Using too many samples from a single population
Working only with modern, high-quality genomes

explanations.a: High depth and large sample size generally help, rather than hinder, ARG-based inference; they are not the named failure modes.
explanations.b: Correct — genotype errors propagate into false recombination signal and distorted local trees, unphased data makes topology inference substantially harder, and ancient or low-coverage DNA combines both problems with missing data, making it the hardest regime.
explanations.c: Sample size from a single population is not identified as a fragility; the named issues are data-quality problems (errors, phasing, coverage/age), not sample composition.
explanations.d: Modern, high-quality genomes are the easier case for these methods, not a source of fragility; the difficulty lies specifically with error-prone, unphased, or ancient data.

units.label: Selection Signatures and Applied Population Genomics

lessons.label: Scanning the Genome for Selection: Frequency-Spectrum Tests

sections.heading: Tajima's D: comparing two ways to count diversity
sections.body: In 1989 Fumio Tajima proposed a test built on a simple mismatch: there are two independent ways to estimate the population mutation parameter theta from a sample of DNA sequences. Nucleotide diversity, pi, is the average number of pairwise differences between all sequences in the sample. Watterson's theta (1975) instead counts the total number of segregating sites and scales it by a factor that depends on sample size. Under neutral evolution with a constant population size, pi and Watterson's theta should converge on the same estimate, because both are just different summaries of the same underlying coalescent tree. Tajima's D is the standardized difference, pi minus Watterson's theta, divided by its standard deviation. A locus recently swept by positive selection loses most of its variation and then rebuilds it from new, low-frequency mutations, which inflates the number of segregating sites relative to pairwise diversity, producing a negative D. Population expansion produces the same negative-D signature genome-wide, which is the key confound below. Positive D, an excess of intermediate-frequency variants relative to rare ones, points to balancing selection or a recent population bottleneck, both of which discard rare variants and leave common ones overrepresented.

sections.heading: Polarizing the spectrum: Fu and Li, and Fay and Wu
sections.body: Tajima's D cannot tell you which allele is ancestral and which is derived, so it cannot distinguish rare-derived from rare-ancestral variants. Fu and Li's D (1993) refines this by using an outgroup species, often chimpanzee for human data, to polarize each site and count singletons (variants seen in only one sample copy) separately from the rest of the site-frequency spectrum. Fay and Wu's H (2000) pushes further, specifically hunting for an excess of high-frequency derived alleles, the signature left when a beneficial mutation drags nearby derived variants close to fixation. A classic hard sweep produces a distinctive two-part signature: negative Tajima's D near the selected site from the rare-variant excess, plus a negative, unusual H statistic driven by derived alleles pushed to high frequency.

sections.heading: The demography confound and why scans use outliers
sections.body: The central problem for every frequency-spectrum test is that demographic history, population growth, bottlenecks, and migration shift these statistics across the entire genome, not just at selected loci. A population that expanded after an out-of-Africa bottleneck will show genome-wide negative Tajima's D even with zero selection anywhere, because a growing population accumulates an excess of young, rare mutations everywhere. This is why practical selection scans rarely trust a single locus's raw D value. Instead they compute the statistic in windows across the whole genome and flag windows in the extreme tail, the outlier approach, on the logic that demography affects everywhere roughly equally while selection is locus-specific. A more rigorous alternative fits an explicit demographic null model, estimated from genome-wide data assumed to be selectively neutral, and tests each locus against that fitted null rather than against a generic outlier threshold.

lessons.workedExample: A team sequences a 50 kb region around a candidate immune gene in 100 individuals and finds Tajima's D = -2.1, well below the genome-wide average of -0.3 for that population. Read alone, -2.1 looks like a slam-dunk sweep signal. But this population is known from prior demographic work to have expanded roughly tenfold in the last 5,000 years, and genome-wide windows already average -0.3 to -0.5 from that expansion alone. The correct move is not to report -2.1 as proof of selection, but to ask where this locus sits relative to the empirical genome-wide distribution under this population's known demography — if -2.1 is within the range expansion alone produces elsewhere in the genome, the signal is not distinguishable from background demographic noise, and only a locus in the extreme outlier tail, or one corroborated by an independent haplotype-based test, supports a selection claim.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a project report a single negative Tajima's D value and call it 'evidence of selection' will ask what the genome-wide baseline looks like for that population, because that is precisely the confound the statistic cannot resolve on its own. A student who understands the test explains that demography shifts D everywhere and that a real claim needs either an outlier comparison against the rest of the genome or a fitted demographic null — not a bare threshold like 'D below -2 means selection.' Naming Tajima (1989) and the pi-versus-Watterson's-theta logic, and knowing that Fay and Wu's H needs an outgroup to polarize ancestral versus derived state, is what separates a student who ran vetted software from one who understands what the number measures.

questions.prompt: Tajima's D is calculated as the standardized difference between which two quantities?

options.text: Nucleotide diversity (pi) and Watterson's theta
The number of synonymous and nonsynonymous substitutions
Allele frequency in two different populations
The observed and expected heterozygosity under Hardy-Weinberg

explanations.a: Correct — Tajima's D standardizes the difference between pairwise nucleotide diversity (pi) and Watterson's theta, two estimators of the same neutral parameter that diverge under selection or demographic change.
explanations.b: That comparison (dN/dS) is a different test entirely, used to detect selection on protein-coding change across species, not within-population frequency-spectrum shape.
explanations.c: Comparing frequencies between populations describes differentiation statistics like FST or XP-EHH, not Tajima's D, which is computed within a single population sample.
explanations.d: Hardy-Weinberg deviation tests for things like inbreeding or assortative mating, not the frequency-spectrum shape that Tajima's D captures.

questions.prompt: A strongly negative Tajima's D at a locus most directly suggests an excess of which kind of variant?

options.text: Rare, low-frequency variants
Intermediate-frequency variants
Fixed differences between species
Heterozygous sites only

explanations.a: Correct — a recent sweep or population expansion rebuilds diversity from many new low-frequency mutations, inflating the segregating-site count relative to pairwise diversity and pushing D negative.
explanations.b: An excess of intermediate-frequency variants produces positive D, the signature of balancing selection or a bottleneck, the opposite pattern.
explanations.c: Fixed differences between species are a between-species measure and are not what within-population frequency-spectrum statistics like Tajima's D capture.
explanations.d: Tajima's D is computed from the site-frequency spectrum of segregating sites, not from a simple count of heterozygous genotypes.

questions.prompt: Why do Fu and Li's D and Fay and Wu's H require an outgroup species?

options.text: To polarize each site as ancestral versus derived
To increase the total sample size
To calibrate the mutation rate
To correct for sequencing error only

explanations.a: Correct — an outgroup, such as chimpanzee for human data, lets these tests determine which allele at each site is ancestral and which is derived, which Tajima's D alone cannot do.
explanations.b: The outgroup sequence is used for polarization, not folded into the within-species sample size.
explanations.c: Mutation rate calibration is a separate step in molecular-clock analyses, not the reason these frequency-spectrum tests use an outgroup.
explanations.d: Sequencing error correction is a data-quality step; the outgroup's role here is specifically to assign ancestral/derived states, not to filter errors.

questions.prompt: Why do genome scans typically flag selection candidates as statistical outliers rather than trusting a single locus's raw Tajima's D value?

options.text: Because demographic history shifts these statistics genome-wide, not just at selected sites
Because Tajima's D cannot be computed for more than one locus at a time
Because outlier scans are required by journal formatting standards
Because raw D values are always positive under neutrality

explanations.a: Correct — population expansions, bottlenecks, and migration shift the frequency spectrum across the whole genome, so a single locus's raw value is confounded with demography unless compared to the rest of the genome or an explicit demographic null.
explanations.b: Tajima's D is routinely computed in windows across an entire genome; that is exactly how outlier scans are built.
explanations.c: This is a methodological choice driven by the demography confound, not a formatting convention.
explanations.d: Raw D values fluctuate around zero under strict neutrality and constant population size; they are not systematically positive.

lessons.label: Haplotype and Differentiation Scans

sections.heading: EHH and iHS: reading the length of a haplotype
sections.body: A beneficial allele that rises in frequency fast does not give recombination much time to chop up the stretch of chromosome it started on, so it drags a long, unusually homozygous block of linked variation up with it, a pattern called a selective sweep. Sabeti and colleagues (2002) formalized this as extended haplotype homozygosity, EHH: the probability that two randomly chosen chromosomes carrying a given allele are identical across a growing distance from a core site. A neutral allele's EHH decays quickly with distance as recombination and mutation erode the haplotype; a recently selected allele's EHH decays much more slowly. Voight and colleagues (2006) turned this into the integrated haplotype score, iHS, which compares the area under the EHH decay curve for the ancestral versus the derived allele at a site, standardized genome-wide into a z-score. A large negative iHS flags a derived allele sitting on an unusually long haplotype relative to its ancestral counterpart, evidence of a sweep still in progress, not yet fixed. Because recombination needs time to break haplotypes down, iHS loses power for sweeps older than roughly the last 30,000 years or so, and for alleles already fixed, since it needs both allelic states present in the sample to compare.

sections.heading: Comparing populations: XP-EHH and the population branch statistic
sections.body: iHS is a within-population test and goes blind once an allele fixes. Sabeti and colleagues (2007) addressed this with XP-EHH, cross-population EHH, which compares haplotype homozygosity for the same site between two populations rather than between two alleles in one population. A site swept to fixation in one population but still segregating in another produces a strong XP-EHH signal, recovering exactly the fixed-sweep cases iHS misses. Yi and colleagues (2010), studying high-altitude adaptation in Tibetans at EPAS1, introduced the population branch statistic, PBS, which uses pairwise FST among three populations, typically the population of interest plus two reference populations, to estimate how much allele-frequency change has occurred specifically on the branch leading to the focal population since it split from the others. A large PBS at EPAS1 in Tibetans, contrasted against Han Chinese and a more distant reference, was part of the evidence for unusually strong, geographically localized selection on that locus.

sections.heading: SDS: watching selection in the very recent past
sections.body: All the tests above lose sensitivity as sweeps age past tens of thousands of years, because haplotype and frequency-spectrum signals eventually re-equilibrate. Field and colleagues (2016) built the singleton density score, SDS, from full-genome sequencing data in the UK10K project, using the density of singleton mutations, variants seen only once, around a site as a proxy for very recent local genealogical branch length. Recent selection shortens branches near a favored allele, thinning out singletons nearby. Because singleton density decays on the scale of a human generation, SDS can detect selection acting within roughly the last two to three thousand years, a resolution no haplotype test reaches, and the original study used it to catch ongoing selection on height, lactase persistence, and pigmentation in Britain.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to know whether a pigmentation-associated allele was selected recently in a single population versus long ago and shared across populations. iHS on the focal population alone comes back non-significant, which could mean no selection, or could mean the sweep is already fixed (iHS needs both alleles present to compare). Running XP-EHH against a population that never fixed the allele reveals a strong signal, showing the sweep did happen but completed long enough ago in the focal population that only the fixed allele remains there. Adding SDS from recent whole-genome sequences shows no ongoing singleton depletion near the site today, indicating the sweep is finished, not still in progress. Together the three tests reconstruct a timeline — iHS blind because of fixation, XP-EHH catching the completed fixation, SDS confirming the action is now in the past — that no single statistic could deliver alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes haplotype statistics by asking what timescale a given test can actually resolve, because picking the wrong test for the hypothesis is the most common misuse in student projects. A student who says 'iHS came back flat so there was no selection' has missed that iHS goes blind once an allele nears fixation; the judge wants to hear 'iHS is powered for incomplete sweeps within roughly the last 30,000 years, so a flat iHS with a fixed allele calls for XP-EHH instead, and SDS if the question is whether selection is still acting today.' Matching the statistic's detectable window to the specific claim being made is exactly the kind of precision that separates a defensible selection claim from a plausible-sounding one.

questions.prompt: What does extended haplotype homozygosity (EHH), as defined by Sabeti and colleagues (2002), measure?

options.text: The probability that two chromosomes carrying a given allele remain identical with increasing distance from a core site
The total number of SNPs in a genomic region
The mutation rate at a candidate locus
The allele frequency difference between two populations

explanations.a: Correct — EHH tracks how far, on average, a haplotype carrying a focal allele stays identical by descent as distance from the core site increases; recently selected alleles decay more slowly than neutral ones.
explanations.b: SNP counts describe variant density, not haplotype identity, and are not what EHH quantifies.
explanations.c: Mutation rate is a separate molecular parameter; EHH is about recombination-driven haplotype breakdown, not mutation.
explanations.d: Comparing allele frequency between populations describes FST-type statistics, not EHH, which within Sabeti et al. (2002) is computed within a population.

questions.prompt: Why does iHS lose power to detect selection once a beneficial allele has reached fixation?

options.text: It compares EHH decay between the ancestral and derived alleles, and fixation removes the ancestral allele from the sample
Fixed alleles cannot be sequenced
iHS only works on mitochondrial DNA
Fixation always erases the haplotype signal within one generation

explanations.a: Correct — iHS is built by contrasting the ancestral and derived allele's EHH decay at a site; once the derived allele is fixed there is no ancestral-allele haplotype left to compare it against.
explanations.b: Fixed alleles sequence normally; the limitation is statistical (no comparison group), not technical.
explanations.c: iHS is applied to nuclear autosomal data in standard use, not restricted to mitochondrial DNA.
explanations.d: Haplotype breakdown from recombination takes many generations; fixation itself does not instantly erase the surrounding haplotype structure.

questions.prompt: Which statistic was specifically designed to recover sweep signals that iHS misses because the selected allele has already fixed in one population?

options.text: XP-EHH
Watterson's theta
Tajima's D
Fu and Li's D

explanations.a: Correct — Sabeti and colleagues (2007) built XP-EHH to compare haplotype homozygosity between two populations, catching sites fixed in one population while still segregating in another, exactly the case iHS cannot see.
explanations.b: Watterson's theta is an estimator of the neutral mutation parameter from segregating-site counts, not a haplotype-fixation test.
explanations.c: Tajima's D is a within-population frequency-spectrum statistic and, like iHS, is not built to compare a fixed allele across populations.
explanations.d: Fu and Li's D also relies on within-population segregating variation and an outgroup for polarization, not cross-population haplotype comparison.

questions.prompt: Match each selection-scan statistic to the researcher(s) and year who introduced it.

right.text: Sabeti et al. (2002)
Voight et al. (2006)
Yi et al. (2010)
Field et al. (2016)

questions.explanation: EHH was formalized by Sabeti et al. (2002); iHS, which standardizes EHH decay into a within-population score, by Voight et al. (2006); the population branch statistic, used in the Tibetan EPAS1 high-altitude adaptation study, by Yi et al. (2010); and the singleton density score, built from UK10K sequencing to detect selection within the last few thousand years, by Field et al. (2016).

lessons.label: Case Study: Lactase Persistence

sections.heading: A single intron variant switching off an infant gene's shutdown
sections.body: In nearly all mammals, and in most humans worldwide, expression of the LCT gene, which produces the lactase enzyme that digests milk sugar, shuts down after weaning. Enattah and colleagues (2002) mapped the cause of lifelong lactase persistence in Finnish families to a single C-to-T substitution 13,910 base pairs upstream of LCT, sitting in an intron of the neighboring gene MCM6. That variant acts as a regulatory element that keeps LCT switched on into adulthood, and it explained lactase persistence in essentially all the Finnish subjects who had it. The discovery mattered beyond digestion: it demonstrated that a change in a nearby regulatory sequence, not a change in the enzyme's coding sequence itself, could be a target of strong recent selection.

sections.heading: Bersaglieri and one of the strongest signals in the human genome
sections.body: Bersaglieri and colleagues (2004) scanned 101 SNPs across a 3.2 megabase region around LCT in European-ancestry samples and found the persistence-associated haplotype extending largely undisrupted for more than a megabase, with extended haplotype homozygosity values that stood out even against other known selected loci. Estimated selection coefficients across different populations and methods have ranged roughly from about 0.01 up to 0.19, with Bersaglieri's own maximum-likelihood estimates clustering toward the high end, around 0.09 to 0.19, and the sweep dated to have accelerated somewhere between roughly 2,000 and 20,000 years ago. That combination of haplotype length, age, and selection strength made LCT one of the most cited examples of recent strong positive selection in the human genome, taught alongside skin pigmentation loci as a textbook sweep.

sections.heading: Independent origins, and a complication about what actually drove it
sections.body: Tishkoff and colleagues (2007) sequenced LCT regulatory regions in East African pastoralist populations and found lactase persistence there was not explained by the European -13910 variant at all, but instead associated with an independent variant, -14010 G-to-C, on a distinct haplotype background, showing signs of an equally strong, separately originated sweep. Finding the same functional outcome, lifelong lactase expression, arising from different mutations in unlinked populations is convergent adaptation, and it is stronger evidence that milk digestion mattered to fitness than either signal alone. The obvious story, that the allele rose because dairying started and milk drinkers gained a nutritional edge, ran into trouble when Evershed and colleagues (2022) combined ancient pottery lipid residues with ancient DNA across thousands of years of European prehistory and showed dairying was already widespread for millennia before the lactase-persistence allele began its rapid rise. That timing gap has pushed researchers toward alternative pressures, such as milk's usefulness as a clean, pathogen-free liquid during famine or gut-infection episodes, rather than routine milk drinking itself, as the actual driver of one of the best-known sweeps in humans.

lessons.workedExample: A student claims the LCT sweep proves 'humans evolved to drink milk once farming started,' citing Bersaglieri (2004) as if the story ends there. A stronger project treats the sweep as an open question: it notes Enattah et al. (2002) located the causal variant in an MCM6 intron rather than in LCT's coding sequence, it uses Bersaglieri (2004) for the sweep's strength and rough age window, it brings in Tishkoff et al. (2007) to show East Africans reached the same trait through the independent -14010 variant, and then uses Evershed et al. (2022) to note that dairying predates the allele's rise by a wide margin — meaning the simple 'milk drinking caused the selection' story cannot be the whole explanation, and famine or pathogen-related pressures are now live alternatives. Citing all four sources in that order shows the sweep is well-documented but its ultimate cause is still contested, not settled.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who knows this literature will push on the causal story specifically, because the LCT sweep is famous enough that students often repeat the milk-drinking narrative without knowing it has been complicated. A student who can explain that Evershed et al. (2022) found dairying long predating the allele's frequency rise, and that this reopens rather than closes the question of what drove selection, demonstrates they engaged with the primary literature rather than a simplified textbook summary. Naming the East African -14010 variant from Tishkoff et al. (2007) as convergent, independent evolution of the same trait is the strongest single move available, since independent origins are the clearest possible evidence that a trait was genuinely under selection rather than a coincidental drift signal.

questions.prompt: Where is the -13910 C-to-T variant that Enattah and colleagues (2002) linked to European lactase persistence located?

options.text: In the LCT protein-coding sequence itself
In an intron of the neighboring MCM6 gene, acting as a regulatory element for LCT
On the mitochondrial genome
In the promoter of the DUFFY gene

explanations.a: The variant does not alter the lactase enzyme's amino acid sequence; it lies outside LCT's coding region entirely.
explanations.b: Correct — the variant sits within an intron of MCM6, a neighboring gene, and functions as a regulatory element that keeps LCT switched on into adulthood.
explanations.c: LCT and MCM6 are both nuclear, autosomal genes; this variant has nothing to do with mitochondrial DNA.
explanations.d: The Duffy gene is unrelated to lactase persistence; it is relevant to malaria resistance, covered in a separate case study.

questions.prompt: What did Tishkoff and colleagues (2007) find about lactase persistence in East African pastoralist populations?

options.text: They carry the same -13910 variant found in Europeans, inherited from a shared ancestral population
They lack lactase persistence entirely, despite a history of pastoralism
They show an independent variant, -14010, on a distinct haplotype, indicating convergent evolution
They show no evidence of selection at the LCT region at all

explanations.a: Tishkoff et al. found the East African signal was not explained by the European -13910 variant; it involved a different mutation on a different haplotype background.
explanations.b: The opposite is true — pastoralist groups showed strong signs of lactase persistence, associated with their own regulatory variant.
explanations.c: Correct — the -14010 variant, on an independent haplotype, showed its own strong recent-selection signature, a case of convergent adaptation to the same functional outcome as the European sweep.
explanations.d: The East African samples showed clear evidence of a strong, independently originated selective sweep at the LCT regulatory region.

questions.prompt: What did Evershed and colleagues (2022) show that complicates the simple 'milk drinking drove the sweep' explanation for European lactase persistence?

options.text: That the lactase-persistence allele was already common before dairying began
That dairying was already widespread for millennia before the lactase-persistence allele's frequency rose sharply
That no ancient Europeans ever consumed dairy products
That the -13910 variant has no effect on LCT expression

explanations.a: The finding runs the other direction: dairying came first, and the allele's rise lagged behind it by a substantial margin.
explanations.b: Correct — combining ancient pottery lipid residues with ancient DNA, Evershed and colleagues showed widespread dairying long predated the allele's rapid rise, undercutting the idea that milk consumption alone straightforwardly drove the sweep.
explanations.c: Pottery lipid residue evidence indicates the opposite — dairy products were widely used across ancient Europe well before the allele became common.
explanations.d: The regulatory function of -13910 established by Enattah et al. (2002) is not what this study addressed or challenged.

questions.prompt: Order these lactase-persistence findings by publication year, earliest first.

items.text: Enattah et al. locate the -13910 MCM6 variant
Bersaglieri et al. measure the extended haplotype and selection strength
Tishkoff et al. find the independent -14010 East African variant
Evershed et al. show dairying predates the allele's rise

questions.explanation: Enattah et al. (2002) first identified the causal European regulatory variant; Bersaglieri et al. (2004) then characterized the strength and extent of the sweep; Tishkoff et al. (2007) found the independent East African variant; and Evershed et al. (2022) most recently used combined archaeological and ancient-DNA evidence to challenge the timing of the milk-drinking explanation.

lessons.label: Case Study: Malaria and the Cost of Adaptation

sections.heading: Allison's discovery and the heterozygote-advantage equilibrium
sections.body: Anthony Allison's 1954 fieldwork in East Africa showed that carriers of one copy of the sickle-cell hemoglobin allele, HbS, suffered substantially less severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria than people with two copies of the normal HbA allele, while people with two copies of HbS developed sickle-cell disease, historically fatal in childhood without modern treatment. This is heterozygote advantage: the AS heterozygote outcompetes both homozygotes, AA (vulnerable to malaria) and SS (vulnerable to sickle-cell disease), on fitness. Because the two homozygous genotypes carry separate fitness costs, the allele does not sweep to fixation or disappear; it settles at a stable equilibrium frequency set by the ratio of those two costs, which is why HbS reaches its highest frequencies, sometimes exceeding 15 to 20 percent, specifically in historically malaria-endemic parts of sub-Saharan Africa, and is rare or absent in populations without a history of falciparum exposure.

sections.heading: The same pressure, several unrelated genetic answers
sections.body: Malaria resistance is not a one-gene story. HbC, a different beta-globin variant, reaches high frequency in parts of West Africa and confers milder protection with a smaller fitness cost than HbS, and the two alleles are found in overlapping but distinguishable geographic distributions. G6PD deficiency, caused by variants including the A- allele common in sub-Saharan Africa and the Mediterranean variant common around the Mediterranean basin and parts of Asia, reduces the parasite's ability to thrive inside red blood cells with abnormal oxidative metabolism, and both variants show classic selection-scan signatures at their respective loci. Alpha-thalassemia, caused by deletions reducing alpha-globin production, is common across malaria-endemic regions of Africa, the Mediterranean, and Southeast Asia and independently reduces malaria severity through altered red-cell physiology. Each of these variants arose from a different mutational mechanism in a different gene, yet each reached elevated frequency specifically where P. falciparum has been historically endemic.

sections.heading: Duffy-null: a different pathogen, a sweep near fixation
sections.body: Plasmodium vivax malaria, a distinct species from P. falciparum, requires the Duffy antigen receptor on red blood cells to invade them. A promoter variant that silences Duffy antigen expression on red cells, the Duffy-null allele, is at or near fixation across most of sub-Saharan Africa, essentially eliminating P. vivax as a threat in those populations while leaving other blood cell types, where the Duffy antigen still functions, largely unaffected. Because it approaches fixation, Duffy-null shows the sweep signatures suited to XP-EHH rather than within-population iHS, illustrating the timescale-matching lesson from the haplotype-scan lesson directly. Taken together, HbS, HbC, G6PD variants, alpha-thalassemia, and Duffy-null represent at least five independent genetic solutions converging on malaria resistance, and that repeated, independent convergence across unrelated genes and mechanisms is far stronger evidence that malaria has been an unusually strong selective force on humans than any single locus could provide alone.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to argue malaria selection is well-documented, not a one-off anecdote. Citing HbS alone, with Allison's 1954 heterozygote-advantage result, is a starting point but is a single data point. A stronger argument lays out that HbC arose independently in West Africa with a different cost-benefit profile than HbS, that G6PD deficiency evolved via at least two separate variants (A- and Mediterranean) in different geographic regions, that alpha-thalassemia deletions do the same through yet another mechanism, and that Duffy-null approaches fixation across sub-Saharan Africa against a different Plasmodium species entirely.
