Five unrelated genes, five unrelated mutational mechanisms, one convergent outcome, geographically overlapping with historical malaria endemicity — that pattern of independent convergence is the actual evidence, not any single alelle's frequency by itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this case study by asking why heterozygote advantage does not simply let the beneficial allele sweep to fixation the way a sweep at LCT or Duffy-null does, because that distinction, a stable balanced polymorphism versus a directional sweep, is the single most important idea the case study teaches. A student who can explain that HbS persists at an equilibrium frequency set by the relative costs of the AA and SS homozygotes, rather than fixing, has understood balancing selection as a distinct process from a hard sweep. Naming multiple independent malaria-resistance genes, not just sickle-cell, signals the student grasps that convergent, repeated origins of a trait are the strongest available evidence for selection, a theme that recurs across this whole unit.

questions.prompt: Why does the HbS allele settle at a stable intermediate frequency rather than sweeping to fixation in malaria-endemic populations?

options.text: Because the AS heterozygote has higher fitness than both the AA and SS homozygotes, so neither homozygous genotype is favored
Because HbS cannot be detected by natural selection
Because malaria only affects heterozygotes
Because the mutation rate at this locus is unusually high

explanations.a: Correct — this is heterozygote advantage: AS carriers avoid both severe malaria (an AA risk) and sickle-cell disease (an SS risk), so the population settles at an equilibrium frequency set by the relative costs of the two homozygous genotypes rather than fixing the allele.
explanations.b: HbS is one of the most extensively documented targets of natural selection in humans, first characterized by Allison in 1954.
explanations.c: Malaria affects all genotypes; AA individuals are the most vulnerable to severe disease, not immune to it.
explanations.d: The equilibrium frequency is a selection-balance outcome, not a mutation-rate effect; mutation rate is not the relevant driver here.

questions.prompt: Which pathogen does the near-fixed Duffy-null allele in sub-Saharan Africa specifically confer resistance to?

options.text: Plasmodium vivax
Plasmodium falciparum
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Influenza virus

explanations.a: Correct — Duffy-null silences the Duffy antigen receptor that Plasmodium vivax requires to invade red blood cells, effectively eliminating vivax malaria risk where the allele is near-fixed.
explanations.b: P. falciparum invasion does not depend on the Duffy antigen; HbS, HbC, G6PD variants, and alpha-thalassemia are the resistance mechanisms relevant to falciparum.
explanations.c: Tuberculosis resistance is not the selective pressure associated with the Duffy-null variant.
explanations.d: Influenza is unrelated to Duffy antigen biology; this variant's selective history is specific to Plasmodium vivax.

questions.prompt: Why do researchers treat the existence of HbS, HbC, G6PD deficiency variants, alpha-thalassemia, AND Duffy-null together as unusually strong evidence for malaria's role as a selective force?

options.text: Because they are all the same mutation inherited from a common ancestor
Because they represent independent origins, in different genes, converging on the same functional outcome of malaria resistance
Because only one of the five variants has actually been confirmed to affect malaria risk
Because they all produce identical clinical symptoms

explanations.a: These are distinct mutations in different genes (beta-globin, G6PD, alpha-globin, the Duffy promoter), not a single shared ancestral variant.
explanations.b: Correct — independent convergence on the same adaptive outcome through unrelated genes and mechanisms is much harder to explain by chance or coincidental drift than any single locus's frequency alone.
explanations.c: All five have documented, independent evidence tying them to malaria resistance, not just one.
explanations.d: Their clinical profiles differ substantially, from asymptomatic carriers to sickle-cell disease in HbS homozygotes; the unifying feature is the resistance outcome, not identical symptoms.

questions.prompt: Match each malaria-resistance variant to its geographic association or mechanism.

right.text: Documented by Allison (1954) via heterozygote protection against P. falciparum
Reaches high frequency in parts of West Africa with milder protection than HbS
Common variant in sub-Saharan Africa reducing parasite oxidative fitness in red cells
Near fixation across sub-Saharan Africa, blocking P. vivax invasion

questions.explanation: HbS's protective heterozygote effect against P. falciparum was Allison's original 1954 finding; HbC is a distinct, milder-protection variant concentrated in West Africa; the G6PD A- allele is a sub-Saharan African variant reducing parasite fitness through altered red-cell oxidative metabolism; and Duffy-null is near fixation across sub-Saharan Africa, blocking P. vivax invasion specifically.

lessons.label: The Sweeps Debate: How Much Adaptation, and What Kind?

sections.heading: Hard sweeps, soft sweeps, and polygenic shifts
sections.body: The classic sweep model, the one behind Tajima's D, iHS, and EHH, assumes a single new beneficial mutation arises, is rare, and then rises to high frequency dragging one haplotype background with it: a hard sweep. Hermisson and Pennings (2005) formalized an alternative, the soft sweep, where selection instead acts on an allele that was already present as standing genetic variation at some low frequency before conditions changed, or on a mutation that arises repeatedly on different haplotype backgrounds (recurrent mutation). Because a soft sweep starts from multiple independent copies on different haplotypes rather than one, it leaves a much weaker, more diffuse haplotype signature, and classic hard-sweep tests like iHS can miss it. Pritchard, Pickrell, and Coop (2010) pushed the picture further with polygenic adaptation: for traits controlled by many loci, such as height, natural selection may act by nudging allele frequencies at hundreds of loci by small amounts each, with no single locus reaching a detectable sweep signature at all, the total phenotypic shift built from many nearly invisible pieces rather than one strong signal.

sections.heading: Hernandez and colleagues: fewer classic sweeps than expected
sections.body: Hernandez and colleagues (2011), publishing in Science, used population genomic data to test how common classic hard sweeps actually were across the recent human genome, and reported that clear evidence for hard, complete sweeps was substantially rarer than earlier candidate-gene studies had suggested. That result reframed the field's expectations: rather than the genome being dotted with dramatic LCT-style sweeps, most recent human adaptation may look more like the soft-sweep and polygenic modes, harder to detect with any single classic statistic, which is part of why the toolkit in this unit includes several complementary tests rather than one definitive one.

sections.heading: Background selection: a sweep look-alike with no beneficial mutation
sections.body: Charlesworth, Morgan, and Charlesworth (1993) described background selection: continuous removal of deleterious mutations by purifying selection reduces diversity at linked neutral sites nearby, because a chromosome carrying a harmful mutation, and everything linked to it, gets purged from the population together. In regions of low recombination, where a lot of sequence is linked to any given deleterious mutation, this produces a trough in diversity that can look very similar to a positive selective sweep, even though no beneficial mutation was ever involved. This is the central confound for every method in this unit: both positive selection and background selection reduce local diversity and can distort the frequency spectrum, so a diversity trough alone is not proof of adaptive selection. Because of this, a full accounting of diversity variation along the genome, sometimes called linked selection broadly, has to model background selection's expected effect from local recombination rate and gene density before attributing any remaining trough to positive selection specifically.

lessons.workedExample: A team finds a low-diversity region near a gene and initially claims a hard sweep. Checking local recombination rate, they find the region sits in a gene-dense, low-recombination stretch of the genome, exactly where Charlesworth et al.'s (1993) background-selection model predicts diversity troughs from ordinary purifying selection on deleterious mutations, with no adaptive story required. They also run iHS and find no elevated haplotype-length signal, which argues against a recent hard sweep specifically. Rather than abandon the region, they reconsider it as a possible soft sweep or polygenic signal, per Hermisson and Pennings (2005) and Pritchard, Pickrell, and Coop (2010), and note that Hernandez et al. (2011) found classic hard sweeps to be less common than once assumed anyway, making a background-selection or polygenic explanation more parsimonious than an undetected hard sweep.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this lesson by asking what ELSE could explain a diversity trough besides positive selection, because background selection is the single most common blind spot in student selection-scan projects: it produces a sweep-shaped signature from purifying selection on deleterious mutations, with no adaptive story at all. A student who checks local recombination rate and gene density before claiming a sweep, and who can distinguish a hard sweep (one new mutation, strong haplotype signal) from a soft sweep (standing variation or recurrent mutation, weaker signal) from polygenic adaptation (many small shifts, no single-locus signal), shows they understand that 'low diversity here' is a starting observation, not a conclusion.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a soft sweep from a classic hard sweep, per Hermisson and Pennings (2005)?

options.text: A soft sweep begins from standing genetic variation or recurrent mutation on multiple haplotype backgrounds, rather than a single new mutation
A soft sweep only occurs in asexual organisms
A soft sweep always produces a stronger iHS signal than a hard sweep
A soft sweep cannot reach fixation
A soft sweep requires an outgroup species to detect

explanations.a: Correct — soft sweeps start from an allele already segregating as standing variation, or from a mutation recurring on different haplotypes, so multiple haplotype backgrounds rise together rather than one, weakening the classic sweep signature.
explanations.b: Soft sweeps are described in sexually reproducing populations, including humans; the concept is not restricted to asexual organisms.
explanations.c: The opposite is generally true — because multiple haplotype backgrounds are involved, soft sweeps typically produce a weaker, more diffuse haplotype signal than hard sweeps, which is why classic tests like iHS can miss them.
explanations.d: A soft sweep, like a hard sweep, can still drive an allele to fixation; the difference is in the starting haplotype diversity, not the endpoint.
explanations.e: Outgroup polarization is relevant to frequency-spectrum tests like Fay and Wu's H, not to the definition of a soft sweep.

questions.prompt: What did Hernandez and colleagues (2011) report about classic hard sweeps in recent human evolution?

options.text: That clear evidence for them was less common than earlier candidate-gene studies had suggested
That every human gene shows evidence of a hard sweep
That hard sweeps are impossible to detect with any statistical method
That hard sweeps only occur in non-coding DNA

explanations.a: Correct — their Science paper found substantially less genomic evidence for classic complete hard sweeps than earlier work had implied, reframing expectations toward soft-sweep and polygenic modes of adaptation.
explanations.b: The finding was the opposite of ubiquitous evidence; hard sweeps turned out to be rarer than expected across the genome.
explanations.c: Hard sweeps remain detectable by methods like iHS and EHH when they occur; the finding was about their frequency, not detectability in principle.
explanations.d: The study's finding concerned the rate of hard sweeps generally, not a restriction to non-coding regions.

questions.prompt: How can background selection, described by Charlesworth, Morgan, and Charlesworth (1993), mimic the signature of a positive selective sweep?

options.text: By purging deleterious mutations along with linked neutral variation, reducing local diversity with no beneficial mutation involved
By increasing the mutation rate at nearby loci
By causing a beneficial allele to fix faster than normal
By eliminating the need for an outgroup in frequency-spectrum tests

explanations.a: Correct — continuous removal of chromosomes carrying deleterious mutations also removes the neutral variation linked to them, producing a diversity trough that looks like a sweep even without any beneficial mutation, especially in low-recombination regions.
explanations.b: Background selection is about selective removal of existing deleterious variants, not an increase in mutation rate.
explanations.c: Background selection does not involve a beneficial allele fixing at all; it is purifying selection against harmful mutations.
explanations.d: Background selection is a population-genetic process affecting diversity patterns; it has no bearing on whether an outgroup is needed for polarization in frequency-spectrum tests.

questions.prompt: For a highly polygenic trait like height, why might Pritchard, Pickrell, and Coop's (2010) model of polygenic adaptation produce no detectable single-locus sweep signature at all?

options.text: Because selection can act by shifting allele frequencies slightly at hundreds of loci rather than driving any one locus to a strong signal
Because height is not a heritable trait
Because polygenic traits are never under selection
Because iHS cannot be computed for any trait with more than one associated locus

explanations.a: Correct — under polygenic adaptation, a phenotypic shift can be built from small, coordinated frequency changes across many loci, none of which individually produces a detectable classic sweep signature.
explanations.b: Height is highly heritable and influenced by many loci; that heritability is exactly what makes polygenic selection on it plausible.
explanations.c: The polygenic adaptation model is specifically a proposed mechanism by which selection does act on such traits, just distributed rather than concentrated.
explanations.d: iHS can be computed at any individual locus regardless of how many loci a trait involves; the issue is that no single locus shows enough signal to be detected, not a technical limitation of the statistic.

lessons.label: Pathogen Population Genomics in Real Time

sections.heading: A molecular clock fast enough to watch tick
sections.body: Everything earlier in this unit reconstructs selection that happened thousands to tens of thousands of years ago from present-day patterns. SARS-CoV-2 flipped that: its substitution rate has been estimated at roughly 8 x 10^-4 substitutions per site per year, which for its roughly 30,000-base genome works out to on the order of two new mutations fixed in a lineage per month. That is fast enough that researchers could track viral evolution essentially in real time during the pandemic rather than inferring it after the fact. Platforms built for this purpose, most visibly Nextstrain, pulled in genomes shared through GISAID, the global sequence-sharing database researchers used throughout the pandemic, and built continuously updated phylogenetic trees showing which lineages were spreading, where, and how fast, days or weeks after samples were collected rather than years.

sections.heading: Naming lineages and modeling the epidemic from the tree
sections.body: The Pango nomenclature system assigned systematic lineage names, such as B.1.1.7, later designated the Alpha variant by the World Health Organization, to genetically distinct, epidemiologically relevant branches of the SARS-CoV-2 tree as they emerged. Beyond just tracking which lineage was which, researchers fit explicit population-genetic models to the sequence data: Bayesian skyline models reconstruct how effective population size, and by extension something like transmission intensity, changed over time from the shape of a sampled phylogeny, while birth-death models treat transmission and detection as a stochastic branching process, letting researchers estimate the effective reproduction number, the average number of new infections caused by each existing case, directly from genomic data. The same phylogenetic trees also let researchers count how many separate times a lineage was introduced into a given country or region, since each independent introduction shows up as its own distinct entry point on the tree rather than a single expanding cluster.

sections.heading: Built on precedent: Ebola and seasonal influenza
sections.body: None of this machinery was invented from scratch during COVID-19. Real-time genomic surveillance of an outbreak was pioneered during the 2014-2016 West African Ebola epidemic, when sequencing teams working close to outbreak sites generated and shared viral genomes fast enough to inform contact tracing and outbreak response as the epidemic was still unfolding, establishing that rapid field sequencing during a live outbreak was logistically achievable. Seasonal influenza surveillance supplied the other half of the precedent: for decades, laboratories worldwide have tracked antigenic drift, the gradual accumulation of mutations in the virus's surface proteins that lets it evade prior immunity, and used that phylogenetic and antigenic data to select which strains go into each year's updated vaccine formulation. SARS-CoV-2 genomic epidemiology combined the outbreak-response urgency of the Ebola precedent with the strain-tracking, vaccine-relevant framework long used for influenza.

lessons.workedExample: A public health team sees a new SARS-CoV-2 lineage rising in case counts in one city and needs to know whether it arrived once and then spread locally, or was introduced many separate times from travel. Building a Nextstrain tree from genomes sampled in that city alongside genomes from elsewhere, they look for how the local sequences are distributed across the tree: if the local sequences form one tight, exclusive cluster descending from a single ancestral sequence, that supports a single introduction followed by local transmission; if local sequences instead appear scattered across many separate branches, each nested among genomes from different other regions, that supports many independent introductions. A birth-death model fit to the single-cluster scenario can then estimate the effective reproduction number for that local outbreak directly from how quickly the cluster's branches accumulate, without needing traditional epidemiological case-count data at all.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this material by asking how a phylogenetic tree alone, without traditional epidemiological surveys, can estimate something like the reproduction number or the number of separate outbreak introductions, because that is the specific inferential leap genomic epidemiology makes and a student needs to explain it rather than just say 'Nextstrain showed it.' A strong answer names birth-death models as the mechanism connecting tree shape to transmission parameters, and Bayesian skyline models as the mechanism connecting tree shape to effective population size over time, and can explain why a fast-mutating virus like SARS-CoV-2, at roughly 8 x 10^-4 substitutions per site per year, makes this kind of real-time inference feasible where a slow-mutating organism would not provide enough resolution over a short outbreak.

questions.prompt: Roughly what substitution rate has been estimated for SARS-CoV-2, and why does it matter for genomic surveillance?

options.text: Roughly 8 x 10^-4 substitutions per site per year, fast enough to track viral spread in near real time
Roughly 8 x 10^-4 substitutions per site per century, too slow to be useful during an outbreak
Exactly zero, since RNA viruses do not mutate
A rate identical to the human nuclear genome's mutation rate

explanations.a: Correct — at roughly 8 x 10^-4 substitutions per site per year, SARS-CoV-2 accumulates enough distinguishable mutations within weeks to months that researchers could reconstruct transmission chains and lineage spread essentially as the pandemic unfolded.
explanations.b: The rate is per year, not per century; a per-century rate that slow would indeed be far too slow for outbreak-timescale tracking, which is precisely why the actual per-year rate matters.
explanations.c: RNA viruses, including SARS-CoV-2, mutate readily; that ongoing mutation is exactly what genomic surveillance tracks.
explanations.d: The human nuclear mutation rate per generation is vastly lower per year than a fast-evolving RNA virus's substitution rate; the two are not comparable in this way.

questions.prompt: What does a birth-death phylogenetic model estimate from viral sequence data?

options.text: The effective reproduction number, by treating transmission and detection as a branching process
The exact date a virus first infected a human
The color of the pathogen under a microscope
The vaccine's manufacturing cost

explanations.a: Correct — birth-death models treat each transmission event and detection/sampling event as part of a stochastic branching process, letting researchers estimate the effective reproduction number directly from the shape of a phylogenetic tree built from sampled genomes.
explanations.b: Estimating a precise origin date is a different, related inference (root-to-tip dating) and not the specific quantity birth-death models are used for here.
explanations.c: Phylogenetic models work from genetic sequence data, not physical or visual properties of the pathogen.
explanations.d: Vaccine manufacturing cost is an economic quantity unrelated to phylodynamic modeling of sequence data.

questions.prompt: Which historical outbreak first demonstrated that real-time genomic sequencing could be logistically achieved close to an active outbreak to inform response?

options.text: The 2014-2016 West African Ebola epidemic
The 1918 influenza pandemic
The Black Death in medieval Europe
The 2003 SARS-CoV-1 outbreak

explanations.a: Correct — during the 2014-2016 West African Ebola epidemic, sequencing teams working near outbreak sites generated and shared viral genomes quickly enough to inform contact tracing and response in real time, establishing the field precedent later scaled up for SARS-CoV-2.
explanations.b: The 1918 pandemic long predates genomic sequencing technology entirely; there was no real-time sequencing capability at that time.
explanations.c: The Black Death predates any form of genomic sequencing by centuries and is studied today only through later ancient-pathogen-DNA techniques, not real-time surveillance.
explanations.d: SARS-CoV-1 in 2003 was sequenced and studied, but it is the Ebola 2014-2016 response that is specifically credited with pioneering real-time field-based genomic surveillance informing live outbreak response.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it refers to in pathogen genomic epidemiology.

right.text: A systematic lineage-naming system, e.g. B.1.1.7 (Alpha)
The global database used to share pandemic-era viral genomes
A model reconstructing effective population size over time from a phylogeny
Gradual surface-protein mutation that drives annual influenza vaccine strain updates

questions.explanation: Pango assigns systematic lineage names like B.1.1.7 (Alpha); GISAID is the shared global genome database that powered pandemic-era genomic surveillance; the Bayesian skyline model reconstructs effective population size trajectories from a phylogeny's branching pattern; and antigenic drift is the gradual mutation of influenza surface proteins that necessitates yearly vaccine strain updates.

lessons.label: Conservation and Agricultural Genomics

sections.heading: Genetic load, purging, and why small populations can spiral
sections.body: Every population carries genetic load, a burden of mildly and severely deleterious mutations kept at low frequency by selection-mutation balance. In a large population, recombination and selection efficiently keep most of these rare and mostly hidden in heterozygous form. In a small population, genetic drift overwhelms weak selection, so deleterious alleles can drift to higher frequency and become homozygous more often, producing inbreeding depression: reduced fertility, survival, and disease resistance. Sometimes small populations purge, purifying selection removes severely deleterious recessive alleles faster once they are frequently exposed as homozygotes, but purging works reliably only for the most severely harmful variants and is unreliable for mildly deleterious ones, which is why small population size is rarely a self-correcting problem. The Isle Royale wolf population is a well-documented collapse case: an isolated island population, founded by very few individuals, accumulated inbreeding-related skeletal deformities and fertility problems over decades of isolation, and the population crashed toward extirpation before a deliberate reintroduction of new wolves in 2018 restored genetic diversity.

sections.heading: Genetic rescue and an exception that complicates the rule
sections.body: The Florida panther is the standard genetic-rescue success story: by the 1990s, fewer than 30 individuals remained, showing classic inbreeding signs including kinked tails, heart defects, and low sperm quality. In 1995, wildlife managers introduced eight female pumas from Texas, and the population interbred with descendants of five of the eight, sharply reducing homozygosity while later work confirmed the historic Florida panther's distinct genetic ancestry was diluted, not erased; three decades later the population has grown roughly tenfold with fewer inbreeding-related defects. But small population size does not always predict high genetic load. Robinson and colleagues (2022) sequenced the vaquita, a porpoise down to roughly ten individuals in its only habitat in the Gulf of California, and found unexpectedly low deleterious genetic load, because the species had already been naturally small and rare for a very long evolutionary history, giving purifying selection ample time to purge its most severely harmful variants long before the population's recent bycatch-driven crash. Simulations from that long-small demographic history estimated a low inbreeding load and suggested the vaquita's extinction risk is currently driven overwhelmingly by ongoing bycatch mortality, not by an unavoidable genetic collapse, provided that mortality is reduced.

sections.heading: Domestication signatures and applying the same statistics to breeding
sections.body: Human-directed selection during domestication leaves the same sweep signatures this unit's tools detect in wild populations. The maize gene tb1 carries a regulatory mutation, selected during domestication from its wild ancestor teosinte, that suppresses lateral branching and produces the single, dominant stalk characteristic of modern corn. A mutation near the chicken TSHR gene is strongly associated with domestication across nearly all modern chicken breeds, linked to changes in reproduction and metabolism useful in captivity. Dogs show an expanded copy number of the AMY2B gene relative to wolves, boosting starch-digesting amylase and reflecting adaptation to a starch-rich, human-associated diet during domestication. Modern breeding programs now apply the same population-genomic toolkit deliberately: marker-assisted selection uses a known causal or tightly linked marker to select breeding stock directly, while genomic prediction fits statistical models across thousands of markers genome-wide to estimate an individual's breeding value for a complex trait before it is even phenotyped, the same underlying logic used to reconstruct wild selective sweeps, now run forward to engineer one on purpose.

lessons.workedExample: A conservation geneticist is asked whether a shrinking population of 50 animals needs genetic rescue, that is, introducing individuals from another population to restore diversity. Following the Florida panther precedent, the naive answer is always yes for a population that small. But the vaquita case, per Robinson et al. (2022), shows small census size does not automatically mean high genetic load: a species with a long history of natural rarity may have already purged its worst deleterious variants over thousands of generations, unlike the Florida panther, which crashed suddenly from a much larger historical population and had no time to purge before inbreeding depression set in. The geneticist would need to reconstruct the population's demographic history, not just count current individuals, to know whether this population resembles the panther's sudden-crash profile, needing intervention, or the vaquita's long-small profile, where the bigger threat may be an external mortality source rather than genetic load itself.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this material by asking whether a small population automatically needs genetic rescue, because the reflexive answer, small population equals doomed by inbreeding, is exactly what the vaquita case overturns. A student who can explain that a population's demographic history, specifically whether it crashed suddenly from a large ancestral size like the Florida panther, or has been naturally small for a long evolutionary history like the vaquita, determines its actual genetic load, is demonstrating real understanding rather than a rule of thumb. Being able to name a domestication signature, such as maize tb1 or dog AMY2B copy number, and explain that breeders now use marker-assisted selection or genomic prediction to do deliberately what natural selection did to these genes, ties the wild and applied halves of the unit together.

questions.prompt: What did Robinson and colleagues (2022) find that complicates the assumption that a tiny population, like the roughly ten remaining vaquitas, must carry a heavy burden of deleterious genetic load?

options.text: The vaquita's long history of natural small population size gave purifying selection time to purge severely deleterious variants, leaving unexpectedly low genetic load
The vaquita has no detectable DNA left to sequence
The vaquita's population has already recovered to historical levels
Vaquitas do not experience inbreeding depression under any circumstances

explanations.a: Correct — because the vaquita has been naturally rare for a long evolutionary history, not recently crashed from a much larger population, purifying selection had ample time to purge its most severely deleterious variants, leaving lower genetic load than its tiny current census size would suggest.
explanations.b: The study relied on genomic sequencing of the vaquita, so DNA was clearly available and analyzed.
explanations.c: The vaquita remains critically endangered at around ten individuals; the finding was about genetic load, not a population recovery.
explanations.d: The study modeled a low, not zero, inbreeding load; it did not claim vaquitas are immune to inbreeding depression, only that the risk from genetic load specifically is lower than expected.

questions.prompt: In the 1995 Florida panther genetic rescue, roughly how many Texas cougars were introduced, and what was the outcome?

options.text: Eight Texas cougars were introduced, and descendants of five of them interbred with the Florida population, reducing inbreeding signs
Eight Texas cougars were introduced but none successfully interbred with the Florida population
Fifty Texas cougars were introduced, fully replacing the original Florida panther population
No cougars were introduced; the recovery was due to captive breeding alone

explanations.a: Correct — eight female Texas cougars were released in 1995, and descendants from five of them interbred with Florida panthers, reducing homozygosity and inbreeding-related defects over subsequent decades.
explanations.b: Interbreeding did occur with five of the eight introduced cougars, which is the basis of the population's later recovery.
explanations.c: Only eight animals were introduced, a small genetic infusion, not a wholesale replacement of the existing population.
explanations.d: The recovery is specifically attributed to the introduced Texas cougars' genetic contribution via interbreeding with wild Florida panthers, not captive breeding.

questions.prompt: The tb1 regulatory mutation selected during maize domestication primarily affects which trait?

options.text: Suppression of lateral branching, producing a single dominant stalk
Resistance to Plasmodium falciparum
Coat color in domestic dogs
Starch-digesting amylase copy number

explanations.a: Correct — the tb1 mutation, selected from teosinte during maize domestication, suppresses lateral branching, giving domesticated corn its characteristic single dominant stalk rather than the bushier teosinte growth form.
explanations.b: Malaria resistance is unrelated to maize domestication; that is the subject of the earlier malaria case-study lesson.
explanations.c: Coat color genetics is a separate domestication story in dogs, not related to the maize tb1 locus.
explanations.d: Amylase copy number expansion is the dog domestication signature (AMY2B), a different gene and species than maize tb1.

questions.prompt: Match each domestication signature to the species and trait it affects.

right.text: Maize: suppresses lateral branching for a single dominant stalk
Chicken: associated with domestication-linked reproduction and metabolism changes
Dog: boosts starch-digesting amylase for a starch-rich diet

questions.explanation: tb1 is the maize domestication locus suppressing lateral branching; TSHR carries a mutation strongly associated with domestication across nearly all chicken breeds, tied to reproductive and metabolic changes; and AMY2B copy number expansion in dogs, relative to wolves, boosts starch digestion, reflecting adaptation to a human-associated, starch-rich diet.

units.label: The Transcriptome: What Expression Actually Is

lessons.label: Expression Is a Steady State, Not a Rate

sections.heading: A bathtub, not a speedometer
sections.body: When a gene shows up as 'more expressed' in an RNA-seq snapshot, it is tempting to read that as 'transcribed faster.' But the number you measure — transcript abundance at one moment — is a balance, not a rate. Abundance is set by the ratio of two independent processes: how fast RNA polymerase II makes new copies (synthesis) and how fast those copies are degraded by exonucleases and the RNA decay machinery. Like water level in a bathtub with the tap and drain both open, a rising level can mean the tap opened wider or the drain narrowed — you cannot tell which from the water level alone. A gene's steady-state abundance is literally synthesis rate divided by degradation rate; two genes transcribed at the identical rate can sit at wildly different steady-state levels if their transcripts decay at different speeds.

sections.heading: Schwanhausser 2011: the numbers that make this concrete
sections.body: Schwanhausser and colleagues (2011, Nature) measured synthesis and degradation across roughly 5,000 genes in mouse NIH3T3 fibroblasts, combining pulsed SILAC (stable-isotope protein labeling) with a kinetic model fit to genome-wide mRNA and protein abundance measurements — not the metabolic RNA labeling described below, which is a separate, more direct technique for isolating newly made transcripts. Their headline medians: mRNA half-life around 9 hours, protein half-life around 46 hours — proteins persist roughly five times longer than the transcripts that encode them. Critically, half-lives varied over two orders of magnitude gene to gene, so a 10-fold difference in decay rate between two genes is common, not exceptional. That variation means a fold-change on an RNA-seq plot can mean something completely different for a fast-decaying immediate-early gene (half-life under an hour) than for a stable housekeeping transcript (half-life of many hours). The immediate-early gene FOS is a textbook case: its mRNA half-life is well under an hour, so it can spike and clear within a single signaling event, in sharp contrast to a stable metabolic housekeeping transcript that changes abundance far more sluggishly for the same shift in transcription rate.

sections.heading: Metabolic labeling: the assay that separates the two
sections.body: To actually split synthesis from degradation instead of inferring it, labs use metabolic RNA labeling. Cells are fed a modified nucleoside — classically 4-thiouridine (4sU) — that gets incorporated only into RNA transcribed during the labeling window. Newly made transcripts can then be biochemically separated (thiol-biotin pulldown) or, in the newer SLAM-seq method (Herzog et al., 2017), chemically converted so the label appears as a T-to-C mismatch readable directly from standard sequencing, no physical separation needed. Comparing labeled ('new') to unlabeled ('old') RNA over a time course yields independent synthesis and decay rates per gene — the only way to know whether an expression change came from the tap or the drain.

lessons.workedExample: Two genes both rise 2-fold in RNA-seq between control and treatment. Gene A is an immediate-early transcription-factor gene with a 1-hour half-life; Gene B is a stable metabolic enzyme with a 20-hour half-life. For Gene A, a 2-fold abundance jump within an hour is almost certainly a burst of new transcription, since decay is fast enough to have already cleared roughly half of the 'old' molecules. For Gene B, the same 2-fold rise cannot be explained by a change in degradation alone: with a 20-hour half-life, the decay rate is only about 0.035/hour, so even halting degradation completely for the entire hour would add back at most about 3.5% of the pool, nowhere near a doubling. That makes a fast, large rise in a stable transcript like this stronger evidence of a big synthesis increase than the same rise would be in a fast-decaying transcript, since Gene B needs no help from reduced decay to explain the jump. A student who ran 4sU pulse-labeling would see this immediately: both Gene A's and Gene B's new-RNA fraction spike, confirming synthesis increased in each case.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'is that gene transcribed more, or just degraded less?' is testing whether a student understands that a single RNA-seq timepoint cannot distinguish the two — only knows the abundance ratio. The strong answer names the confound directly and points to a way to resolve it (metabolic labeling, a time course of decay after a transcription blocker), rather than restating 'the gene was upregulated' as if that phrase explained a mechanism. This also flags whether a student can reason quantitatively about half-life: a fast, large abundance rise is evidence of a synthesis increase for any half-life, but the case gets stronger, not weaker, for a long-lived transcript, since decay changes can only ever shift a small fraction of a slowly-turning-over pool within a short window.

questions.prompt: Steady-state mRNA abundance is best described as:

options.text: The rate at which RNA polymerase transcribes that gene
The balance between synthesis rate and degradation rate
The total number of exons in the gene's longest isoform
A fixed property of the gene that does not change between cell states

explanations.a: Transcription rate is only one of the two inputs; abundance also depends on how fast transcripts are degraded.
explanations.b: Correct — abundance at any snapshot reflects the ratio of synthesis to degradation, like water level reflecting tap versus drain.
explanations.c: Exon count affects splicing complexity, not steady-state abundance directly.
explanations.d: Abundance changes constantly as synthesis and degradation rates shift with cell state; it is not fixed.

questions.prompt: In Schwanhausser et al. (2011), the median mRNA half-life measured across mouse fibroblasts was roughly:

options.text: 9 minutes
9 hours
9 days
46 hours

explanations.a: 9 minutes is far too short for the measured median; individual unstable transcripts can approach this but the median does not.
explanations.b: Correct — the study's median mRNA half-life was about 9 hours, roughly five times shorter than the median protein half-life.
explanations.c: 9 days overstates mRNA stability by two orders of magnitude relative to the reported median.
explanations.d: 46 hours was the reported median protein half-life in the same study, not the mRNA half-life.

questions.prompt: What does metabolic labeling with 4sU (or SLAM-seq) let a researcher measure that ordinary RNA-seq cannot?

options.text: The exact chromosomal location of the gene
Whether a transcript is protein-coding or non-coding
Separate synthesis and degradation rates, by distinguishing newly made from pre-existing transcripts
The 3D folding structure of the transcript

explanations.a: Gene location is read from the reference genome, not from labeling chemistry.
explanations.b: Coding potential is inferred from sequence/ORF analysis, unrelated to metabolic labeling.
explanations.c: Correct — 4sU marks only transcripts made during the labeling window, so comparing labeled ('new') to total RNA yields independent synthesis and decay rates.
explanations.d: RNA structure requires different methods (e.g., SHAPE-seq), not metabolic labeling.

questions.prompt: A gene with a 20-hour mRNA half-life shows a 2-fold abundance increase measured 1 hour after treatment. What is the most defensible interpretation?

options.text: This is almost certainly driven by a large increase in synthesis, since a change in degradation alone could shift the pool by only a few percent over one hour
Given the long half-life, only a small fraction of the pool turns over in an hour, so a modest change in degradation could easily explain the rise without any change in synthesis
The result is impossible and must be a technical error
Long half-life transcripts cannot change abundance at all

explanations.a: Correct — with a 20-hour half-life the decay rate is only about 0.035/hour, so even eliminating degradation entirely for the hour would raise abundance by at most about 3.5%; a 2-fold rise this fast requires a large increase in synthesis.
explanations.b: Incorrect — the same fact (little of a stable pool turns over in an hour) caps degradation's maximum contribution at a few percent, so it cannot come close to explaining a 2-fold rise; synthesis must have increased.
explanations.c: Nothing about this result is technically implausible; it simply requires careful interpretation.
explanations.d: Stable transcripts absolutely can change abundance, just more slowly relative to their half-life.

lessons.label: RNA Species and Why rRNA Eats Your Run

sections.heading: Total RNA is mostly one thing, and it isn't mRNA
sections.body: Pull all the RNA out of a cell and the result is not a balanced mix of everything happening transcriptionally — it is overwhelmingly ribosomal RNA. Across mammalian cell types, ribosomal RNA (the 28S, 18S, 5.8S, and 5S rRNAs that build the ribosome) makes up roughly 80-90% of total cellular RNA by mass. Messenger RNA, the transcript class most gene-expression studies actually want, is a minority player at only about 1-5%. Transfer RNA (tRNA) contributes a further meaningful slice, and the rest is split among small nuclear RNA (snRNA, part of the spliceosome), small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA, guides rRNA modification), long non-coding RNA (lncRNA), and microRNA (miRNA). The reason rRNA dominates is simply throughput: a cell needs enormous numbers of ribosomes running continuously, so it devotes a correspondingly enormous fraction of its transcriptional and RNA-polymerase-I output to building them.

sections.heading: Library prep is a decision about what you'll be blind to
sections.body: Because rRNA so thoroughly swamps everything else, sequencing 'total RNA' without any enrichment step means the overwhelming majority of your sequencing reads — and your money — go to re-reading the same handful of ribosomal sequences over and over, not to the transcripts you care about. Every RNA-seq library prep protocol is therefore built around a choice of what to keep or remove. Poly(A) selection uses oligo-dT beads to capture only transcripts with a poly(A) tail, which enriches for mature mRNA and many lncRNAs but silently excludes histone mRNAs, most non-coding RNA, and unprocessed transcripts that lack a tail. rRNA depletion (chemical probes like RiboZero/RiboMinus, or enzymatic depletion) instead removes the rRNA species directly by hybridization or targeted digestion, keeping everything else — including non-polyadenylated transcripts poly(A) selection would have thrown away. Neither method captures small RNAs like miRNA, which need their own size-selected library prep entirely.

sections.heading: Reading the QC number: percent reads mapping to rRNA
sections.body: Because the stakes of getting this wrong are so high, a standard RNA-seq QC report includes the percentage of sequenced reads that map back to rRNA sequences. For a properly poly(A)-selected or rRNA-depleted library, that number should be low, typically under about 5-10%. A run where 50% or more of reads map to rRNA signals a failed or absent depletion step — the library effectively reverted to sequencing total RNA, and a large fraction of the sequencing budget was wasted reading ribosomal sequence instead of the transcripts the experiment was designed to measure. Recognizing that number, and knowing it means a technical failure rather than a biological result, is a basic first checkpoint before trusting any RNA-seq dataset.

lessons.workedExample: A lab runs RNA-seq on 24 samples at 20 million reads each, expecting to compare mRNA levels across treatment groups. The QC report comes back showing an average of 68% of reads mapping to rRNA. Doing the arithmetic, that means only about 6.4 million of the 20 million reads per sample actually carry information about non-ribosomal transcripts — roughly a third of the intended depth, spread thin because the depletion kit failed on this batch. Comparing this to a properly prepped run at 4% rRNA reads (19.2 million usable reads per sample) shows the practical cost: the failed run has effectively wasted roughly two-thirds of its sequencing budget re-reading the same ribosomal sequences, and any low-abundance transcript comparison in that dataset will be underpowered even though the raw read count 'looks' the same on paper.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'what fraction of your reads were rRNA?' is checking whether a student understands that raw read count is not the same as usable information, and that RNA-seq quality depends on a specific enrichment step working correctly. A student who can state the expected range (typically under about 5-10% for a working prep) and explain what a high number implies — wasted sequencing budget from a failed depletion, not a biological finding — demonstrates they understand library prep as a deliberate choice with a checkable consequence, not a black-box step before 'the real analysis.'

questions.prompt: In total cellular RNA extracted without any enrichment step, which RNA species dominates by mass?

options.text: Messenger RNA (mRNA)
Ribosomal RNA (rRNA)
MicroRNA (miRNA)
Long non-coding RNA (lncRNA)

explanations.a: mRNA is typically only about 1-5% of total RNA, far from dominant.
explanations.b: Correct — rRNA makes up roughly 80-90% of total cellular RNA, reflecting the cell's constant need to build ribosomes.
explanations.c: miRNAs are a tiny fraction of total RNA mass and require dedicated small-RNA library preps to even detect well.
explanations.d: lncRNAs are generally low-abundance and make up a small share of total RNA.

questions.prompt: Match each library preparation approach to what it captures or misses.

right.text: Enriches mature polyadenylated mRNA but excludes histone mRNAs and non-polyadenylated transcripts
Removes ribosomal RNA directly, retaining non-polyadenylated transcripts poly(A) selection would miss
Size-selects for very short transcripts like miRNA, which standard mRNA preps do not capture

questions.explanation: Poly(A) selection captures tailed mature mRNA but misses untailed transcripts (like histone mRNAs); rRNA depletion instead removes rRNA specifically and keeps non-polyadenylated RNA; small-RNA preps use size selection to capture short species like miRNA that other methods lose.

questions.prompt: A QC report shows 55% of reads in an RNA-seq run mapping to rRNA. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The cells had unusually high rRNA gene expression as a biological finding
The rRNA depletion or poly(A) selection step failed, wasting most of the sequencing budget on ribosomal sequence
This is within the expected range for a well-prepped library
The sequencer malfunctioned and produced random reads

explanations.a: rRNA transcription level is not what this metric reflects; it reflects whether the library enrichment step worked, not a biological rRNA expression change.
explanations.b: Correct — a working prep should keep rRNA reads under roughly 5-10%; 55% signals the enrichment step effectively failed.
explanations.c: This is far above the expected range (roughly under 5-10%) for a properly enriched library.
explanations.d: High rRNA mapping reflects a specific, diagnosable library-prep failure, not generic sequencer malfunction.

questions.prompt: Why can't a standard poly(A)-selected mRNA library also be used to quantify miRNA levels?

options.text: miRNAs lack a poly(A) tail and are far too short to be captured by standard mRNA library size selection
miRNAs are not made of RNA
miRNAs are only found in plant cells
Poly(A) selection specifically destroys miRNA molecules

explanations.a: Correct — miRNAs are unpolyadenylated and only about 22 nucleotides, so they are invisible to poly(A) capture and excluded by standard library size-selection steps; they need a dedicated small-RNA prep.
explanations.b: miRNAs are single-stranded RNA molecules, just very short ones.
explanations.c: miRNAs are found broadly across animals, plants, and some viruses, not only plants.
explanations.d: Poly(A) selection does not destroy miRNA; it simply never captures it in the first place since miRNA lacks the poly(A) tail the beads bind.

lessons.label: Isoforms, Splicing, and the Gene-Level Trap

sections.heading: One gene, many transcripts
sections.body: A 'gene' is a locus, not a single molecule. Most human genes produce several distinct mature mRNAs — isoforms — generated by alternative splicing (including or excluding particular exons), alternative transcription-start-site usage (starting transcription at a different point), and alternative 3'UTR usage (cleaving and polyadenylating at a different site, which changes which microRNA and RNA-binding-protein sites the 3' end carries). Because these isoforms can encode different protein sequences, or the same protein with a different regulatory tail, two isoforms of the same gene can be regulated in opposite directions by the same cellular signal — one going up while the other goes down — while their combined total stays essentially flat.

sections.heading: How common alternative splicing actually is
sections.body: This is not a rare edge case. Two landmark 2008 studies quantified it directly using high-throughput mRNA sequencing: Pan and colleagues (2008, Nature Genetics) estimated that roughly 95% of human multi-exon genes undergo alternative splicing, and Wang and colleagues (2008, Nature) independently estimated a comparably high figure, around 92-94%, surveying alternative isoform regulation across a panel of human tissues. Together those figures reframed splicing from a biochemical curiosity into the default state of the human transcriptome — the overwhelming majority of genes with more than one exon are not producing a single fixed product. A multi-exon gene producing only one isoform is closer to the exception than the rule. Annotation catalogs reflect the same scale: GENCODE, the reference gene-model project, annotates several transcript isoforms per multi-exon human gene on average, not one, which is why any pipeline that collapses a gene to a single representative transcript is already discarding information the annotation itself records.

sections.heading: The gene-level trap, and why it's still the default
sections.body: A differential-expression analysis run at the gene level sums (or otherwise aggregates) reads across all of a gene's isoforms into one number. That summation is a trap when an isoform switch is the real biology: if isoform A rises and isoform B falls by a similar magnitude, the gene-level total shows no significant change at all, hiding a functionally important switch (for instance, a shift toward a protein isoform with a different activity, even though 'the gene' looks unchanged). Despite this known blind spot, gene-level summarization remains the default first pass in most pipelines for two practical reasons: statistical power (isoform-level counts split already-limited reads across more categories, weakening each test) and annotation error (isoform-level quantification depends on accurately assigning reads to specific transcript models, and reference annotations, especially for less-studied genes, still contain incomplete or incorrect isoform structures). Isoform-level tools exist and matter, but they trade some power and reliability for resolution. The PKM example is a protein-activity switch, but isoform choice can matter even when no protein is ever made: a splice event that introduces a premature stop codon can route a transcript into nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), so an isoform switch can silently convert a stable, translated mRNA into an unstable, degraded one — a second, independent reason gene-level totals can miss the real story.

lessons.workedExample: The PKM gene encodes pyruvate kinase, a glycolysis enzyme, and produces two isoforms — PKM1 and PKM2 — through mutually exclusive inclusion of one of two adjacent exons. Many cancer cells shift splicing toward PKM2, a form linked to the altered metabolism (aerobic glycolysis) that fast-growing tumor cells rely on; David and colleagues (2010, Nature) showed specific hnRNP splicing factors drive this switch. If a student ran gene-level RNA-seq comparing tumor to normal tissue and only looked at total PKM expression, they might see little or no change, because PKM1 transcript falls roughly as much as PKM2 rises. Only an isoform-aware analysis — counting reads that specifically span the exon-exon junctions unique to each isoform — reveals the switch that gene-level counting erased.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'did you check isoforms, or just the gene total?' is testing whether a student knows that 'this gene didn't change' is a claim about a specific level of summarization, not a settled biological fact. The strong answer explains that a flat gene-level result can hide an isoform switch with real functional consequences, names why (splicing affects the overwhelming majority of multi-exon genes), and can justify why they nonetheless used gene-level analysis by default if they did — citing statistical power or annotation reliability, not just 'that's what the software does.'

questions.prompt: According to Pan et al. (2008, Nature Genetics) and Wang et al. (2008, Nature), roughly what fraction of human multi-exon genes undergo alternative splicing producing more than one isoform?

options.text: About 5-10%
About 40-50%
About 92-95%
Essentially 100%, with no exceptions

explanations.a: This drastically understates the finding; alternative splicing is the norm, not a rare event, for multi-exon genes.
explanations.b: Both studies reported a much higher fraction than this middle estimate.
explanations.c: Correct — Pan et al. independently estimated roughly 95% and Wang et al. estimated around 92-94% of multi-exon genes showing alternative splicing across human tissues.
explanations.d: The reported figures were very high but not literally universal; a small minority of multi-exon genes were not detected as alternatively spliced in these studies.

questions.prompt: Why can a gene-level differential-expression analysis show 'no change' for a gene that is actually undergoing an important isoform switch?

options.text: Gene-level analysis only counts reads from one randomly chosen isoform
Gene-level counts sum reads across all isoforms, so one isoform rising while another falls by a similar amount can cancel out in the total
Isoform switches never affect total read count
Gene-level analysis is always wrong and should never be used

explanations.a: Gene-level counting aggregates across all isoforms, not just one; the issue is summation, not random selection.
explanations.b: Correct — because gene-level counts are a sum, an isoform switch (one up, one down) can produce a flat total even though the underlying biology changed substantially.
explanations.c: The point is precisely that switches can leave the total roughly stable while individual isoforms move sharply.
explanations.d: Gene-level analysis remains the practical default for good reasons (power, annotation reliability); it has a known blind spot, but that does not make it categorically wrong to use.

questions.prompt: In the PKM gene example, what did David et al. (2010, Nature) show?

options.text: That PKM1 and PKM2 are produced from entirely separate genes on different chromosomes
That specific hnRNP splicing factors drive a shift toward the PKM2 isoform in cancer cells
That PKM has no role in glycolysis
That PKM2 is never expressed in normal tissue

explanations.a: PKM1 and PKM2 come from the same PKM gene locus via mutually exclusive exon inclusion, not separate genes.
explanations.b: Correct — the study identified hnRNP proteins as the splicing factors promoting the switch toward PKM2 associated with cancer-cell metabolism.
explanations.c: PKM encodes pyruvate kinase, a core glycolytic enzyme; the study is specifically about its metabolic role.
explanations.d: PKM2 is expressed in various proliferating normal tissues too, not exclusively in cancer.

questions.prompt: Despite the gene-level trap, why do most RNA-seq pipelines still default to gene-level summarization rather than isoform-level quantification?

options.text: Because isoform-level analysis is impossible with any current technology
Because splitting reads across isoforms reduces statistical power per category, and isoform assignment depends on reference annotations that can be incomplete or wrong
Because gene-level analysis is more biologically accurate in every case
Because isoforms do not affect protein function

explanations.a: Isoform-level quantification tools exist and are used; they are not impossible, just a tradeoff.
explanations.b: Correct — isoform-level counting divides limited reads across more categories (hurting power) and relies on annotation accuracy that is imperfect, especially for less-studied genes.
explanations.c: Gene-level analysis is a practical default, not a claim of superior biological accuracy; it can hide real isoform-level biology.
explanations.d: Isoforms frequently do affect protein sequence and function, which is exactly why the gene-level trap matters.

lessons.label: Non-coding RNA as Measured Signal

sections.heading: The genome is not mostly protein-coding genes
sections.body: GENCODE, the reference gene-annotation project, catalogues roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes in the human genome — a number that has held fairly steady for two decades. What has grown enormously is the annotation alongside it: a comparable count of long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) genes, loci that produce transcripts over 200 nucleotides that are not translated into protein. Add tens of thousands of microRNA (miRNA) and circular RNA (circRNA) loci and the honest picture is that protein-coding genes are only one class of transcriptional output among several roughly similarly sized ones. Each of these classes has different physical properties, and those properties dictate which library-prep method can even see them.

sections.heading: Three biotypes, three different assay demands
sections.body: Long non-coding RNAs are typically low in abundance compared to protein-coding transcripts, are poorly conserved across species (making cross-species comparison hard), and are frequently retained in the nucleus rather than exported to the cytoplasm like mRNA — some, like NEAT1, lack a poly(A) tail entirely and are invisible to standard oligo-dT selection, requiring rRNA-depletion-based total-RNA protocols instead. MicroRNAs are a different problem altogether: mature miRNAs are only about 22 nucleotides long, shorter than the adapters used in a standard mRNA library prep, and they carry no poly(A) tail — a conventional poly(A)-selected library will simply never capture them. Profiling miRNA requires a dedicated small-RNA library prep with size selection and specialized adapters. Circular RNAs (circRNAs), formed when a downstream splice donor joins back to an upstream splice acceptor (back-splicing), have no free 5' or 3' ends at all, making them both invisible to poly(A) selection and resistant to standard exonuclease digestion — a property researchers exploit deliberately, using RNase R treatment to degrade linear RNA and enrich for circRNA before sequencing, then identifying them by reads spanning the unusual back-splice junction.

sections.heading: An open, argued question: how much of this is functional?
sections.body: Detecting a transcript is not the same as proving it does something. The scale of non-coding transcription revealed by projects like ENCODE reignited a genuinely unresolved dispute: are the tens of thousands of annotated lncRNAs mostly functional regulatory molecules, or is much of this 'transcriptional noise' — RNA polymerase producing low-fidelity, non-functional transcripts as a byproduct of pervasive, loosely controlled transcription across the genome? Well-characterized cases (XIST silencing an X chromosome, MALAT1 in nuclear speckles) prove some lncRNAs matter enormously, but they are a minority of the total annotated set with that level of functional evidence. This argument — how much of the transcriptome is functional versus incidental — is exactly the kind of competing-claims dispute worth digging into in the landmark studies covering ENCODE.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to profile both lncRNA and miRNA changes in the same tumor samples, and plans to run one standard poly(A)-selected mRNA-seq library and just 'look for the non-coding RNAs in the data.' This fails on both counts: many of the lncRNAs of interest, like NEAT1, are non-polyadenylated and simply will not appear in a poly(A)-selected library at all, and mature miRNAs at ~22 nucleotides are shorter than the library insert size and lack a poly(A) tail, so they are excluded before sequencing even begins. The workable design instead splits the sample: a total-RNA, rRNA-depleted library captures both polyadenylated and non-polyadenylated lncRNAs, while a separate small-RNA library with size selection and miRNA-specific adapters captures the mature miRNAs — two different preps for two different biotypes, run from the same starting material.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how did you capture the non-coding RNA you're claiming to have measured?' is checking whether a student understands that 'non-coding RNA' is not one assay away — it is several distinct molecule classes with incompatible physical requirements (tail presence, length, structure) that no single standard mRNA-seq protocol satisfies at once. Naming the specific biotype and its matching prep (small-RNA kit for miRNA, rRNA depletion for non-polyadenylated lncRNA, RNase R enrichment for circRNA) shows real understanding; claiming a generic 'RNA-seq' run captured all of them does not.

questions.prompt: GENCODE annotates roughly 20,000 human protein-coding genes. How does the count of annotated lncRNA genes compare?

options.text: It is a comparable number, roughly similar in scale
There are essentially zero annotated lncRNA genes
lncRNA genes outnumber protein-coding genes by about 100-fold
Only about 50 lncRNA genes have ever been annotated

explanations.a: Correct — GENCODE annotates a comparable count of lncRNA genes alongside the roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, making non-coding loci a similarly large class.
explanations.b: lncRNA annotation has grown substantially and is far from zero.
explanations.c: This overstates the ratio; the counts are comparable in order of magnitude, not 100-fold apart.
explanations.d: Only a handful of lncRNAs (like XIST or MALAT1) are well-studied individually, but the total annotated count is far larger than 50.

questions.prompt: Match each RNA biotype to the property that makes it hard to capture with a standard poly(A)-selected mRNA library.

right.text: Only ~22 nucleotides long, shorter than standard library inserts, and lacks a poly(A) tail
Circular with no free ends, so it has no poly(A) tail and no standard 5'/3' terminus
Retained in the nucleus and lacks a poly(A) tail, so oligo-dT selection cannot capture it

questions.explanation: miRNA is too short and untailed for standard prep; circRNA's circular structure gives it no ends for poly(A) or standard adapter ligation; non-polyadenylated lncRNAs like NEAT1 lack the tail oligo-dT beads bind to, so they require total-RNA/rRNA-depletion protocols instead.

questions.prompt: Why is RNase R treatment used before sequencing circRNA?

options.text: It adds a poly(A) tail to circRNAs so they can be captured by oligo-dT beads
It degrades linear RNA (which has free ends the exonuclease can act on) while circRNA, lacking free ends, resists degradation and becomes enriched
It converts circRNA into protein-coding mRNA
It is required to detect protein-coding genes, unrelated to circRNA

explanations.a: RNase R is an exonuclease treatment, not a tailing enzyme; it does not add poly(A) tails.
explanations.b: Correct — RNase R degrades RNA from free ends inward, so linear transcripts are destroyed while circRNA's lack of free ends leaves it intact and relatively enriched.
explanations.c: RNase R does not alter the coding status of a transcript; it selectively degrades based on molecular structure.
explanations.d: RNase R enrichment is specifically a circRNA technique, not a general protein-coding gene detection step.

questions.prompt: The dispute over whether most annotated lncRNAs are functional regulators versus 'transcriptional noise' from pervasive transcription is best described as:

options.text: A settled question, since ENCODE definitively proved all annotated transcripts are functional
An open, actively argued question in the field, with well-characterized functional examples existing alongside many transcripts of unknown functional status
Irrelevant, since lncRNAs cannot be detected by sequencing at all
Resolved in favor of 'none of it is functional'

explanations.a: Detecting a transcript by sequencing does not by itself prove functionality; this remains contested rather than settled by detection alone.
explanations.b: Correct — some lncRNAs (like XIST) have strong functional evidence, but this is a minority of the total annotated set, and how much of the rest is functional versus incidental transcription is a genuine live debate.
explanations.c: lncRNAs are routinely detected by sequencing (with the right library prep), so detectability is not the issue in this dispute.
explanations.d: Some lncRNAs have well-established, non-trivial biological functions, so a blanket 'none functional' claim is not correct either.

lessons.label: Regulation: Why Two Cells with One Genome Differ

sections.heading: Same DNA, different output — what's upstream of a hit
sections.body: A liver cell and a neuron carry the identical genome, yet their transcriptomes barely overlap. A differential-expression 'hit' — a gene whose RNA-seq abundance differs sharply between two conditions — is a downstream readout, and a science-fair-level treatment should be able to point to what causal layer could explain it, without needing full molecular-biology depth. At the DNA level, every gene has a promoter (the site immediately upstream where RNA polymerase II and general transcription factors assemble) plus, often, one or more enhancers — regulatory DNA elements that can sit tens or hundreds of thousands of base pairs away from the gene they control. Enhancers reach their target promoter through chromatin looping: the intervening DNA folds so the physically distant enhancer is brought into direct contact with the promoter, forming a loop often stabilized by architectural proteins. A gene 'off' in one cell type and 'on' in another frequently traces back to whether the right enhancer-promoter loop is engaged in that cell.

sections.heading: Whether a transcription factor can even reach the DNA
sections.body: A transcription factor (TF) recognizes and binds a specific short DNA sequence — its binding motif — but only if that DNA is physically accessible; DNA wound tightly around nucleosomes in closed chromatin is largely off-limits to TF binding. This is why chromatin accessibility is measured as its own assay, most commonly ATAC-seq (Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using sequencing), which uses a hyperactive transposase to cut and tag open chromatin regions, revealing where the genome is 'unlocked' in a given cell type. Overlaying a differential-expression hit with ATAC-seq peaks near that gene, and scanning those open regions for known TF binding motifs, is the standard way to generate a candidate explanation: 'this gene turned on because its enhancer became accessible and a specific TF's motif sits right in that open region.'

sections.heading: Regulation doesn't stop at transcription
sections.body: Even after a transcript is made, RNA-level control can still explain an expression difference without any change in transcription at all. Sequence elements in the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) — such as AU-rich elements — recruit RNA-binding proteins that accelerate or protect a transcript from degradation, directly setting its half-life. MicroRNAs add another RNA-level layer: a miRNA with a seed sequence complementary to a site in a transcript's 3'UTR recruits the RNA-induced silencing complex, typically destabilizing the transcript or blocking its translation. A differential-expression hit, in other words, could be explained anywhere along this stack — enhancer accessibility, TF binding, or post-transcriptional stability control — and naming which layer you actually have evidence for (versus which you are merely speculating about) is the difference between a hypothesis and a claim.

lessons.workedExample: A student finds Gene X is 8-fold higher in cell type B than cell type A by RNA-seq. Checking ATAC-seq data from both cell types, they see a chromatin region 40 kb upstream of Gene X that is accessible in cell type B but closed in cell type A, and that region contains a canonical binding motif for a transcription factor known to be highly expressed specifically in cell type B. This builds a coherent, testable causal story: TF motif present, region accessible in the cell type where the gene is on, TF itself expressed there — an enhancer-driven explanation, though still a hypothesis pending direct evidence like a reporter assay or CRISPR interference at that site, not confirmed fact from correlation alone. An alternative student instead finds no accessibility difference at all, but discovers Gene X's 3'UTR contains a seed match for a miRNA that is expressed only in cell type A — pointing to post-transcriptional decay, not enhancer activity, as the more likely explanation for the same expression difference.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why is this gene different between your two conditions?' is testing whether a student can locate their hit within the actual regulatory stack instead of answering with a circular restatement ('it's regulated differently'). The strong answer names a specific layer — chromatin accessibility and TF binding at an enhancer, or RNA-level stability control via a 3'UTR element or miRNA — and is honest about whether they have direct evidence for that layer (an ATAC-seq peak, a motif match, a stability assay) or are only proposing it as the most plausible candidate given available data.

questions.prompt: Order the causal steps by which an enhancer can turn on a distant gene.

items.text: The enhancer region becomes accessible (open chromatin, detectable by ATAC-seq)
A transcription factor binds its motif within the now-accessible enhancer
Chromatin looping brings the enhancer into physical contact with the gene's promoter
RNA polymerase II is recruited to the promoter and transcription increases

questions.explanation: Accessibility must open the region before a TF can bind its motif there; the bound enhancer then engages the promoter through chromatin looping; only once that loop is formed does polymerase recruitment and increased transcription follow at the target gene.

questions.prompt: What does ATAC-seq directly measure?

options.text: The abundance of mature mRNA transcripts
Which regions of chromatin are accessible (open) versus tightly packaged
The rate of protein degradation
The sequence of a gene's coding exons

explanations.a: Transcript abundance is measured by RNA-seq, a separate assay from chromatin accessibility.
explanations.b: Correct — ATAC-seq uses a transposase to tag open chromatin, revealing which regulatory regions are accessible in a given cell type.
explanations.c: Protein degradation rate is a proteomics-level measurement, unrelated to chromatin accessibility.
explanations.d: Exon sequence comes from DNA or RNA sequencing/annotation, not from an accessibility assay.

questions.prompt: Match each regulatory mechanism to the level at which it acts.

right.text: DNA-level: brings distant regulatory DNA into contact with a gene's promoter
RNA-level: recruits proteins that set transcript stability/half-life
RNA-level: recruits a silencing complex that destabilizes or blocks translation of the target transcript

questions.explanation: Enhancer looping is a DNA/chromatin-level mechanism that controls transcription itself; AU-rich elements and miRNA targeting both act after transcription, at the RNA level, controlling how long a transcript survives or whether it gets translated.

questions.prompt: A student finds no difference in chromatin accessibility near Gene X between two cell types, but Gene X's RNA level still differs sharply. Which explanation is still consistent with this data?

options.text: The gene must not actually be differentially expressed
Post-transcriptional control, such as a 3'UTR stability element or miRNA targeting, could account for the difference without any transcriptional or accessibility change
ATAC-seq is a measurement of RNA stability, so this result already explains the difference
Chromatin accessibility is irrelevant to gene regulation

explanations.a: The RNA-seq result itself already established the expression difference; the question is about explaining it, not doubting it.
explanations.b: Correct — RNA-level mechanisms (stability elements, miRNA targeting) act after transcription and can fully account for an expression difference even when chromatin accessibility near the gene is unchanged.
explanations.c: ATAC-seq measures chromatin accessibility, not RNA stability; a null accessibility result does not by itself explain the RNA-level difference.
explanations.d: Accessibility is highly relevant in general; this scenario specifically shows why it isn't the explanation in this particular case, not that it never matters.

lessons.label: What a Read Count Actually Measures

sections.heading: A fixed budget, not an absolute yardstick
sections.body: A sequencer does not measure how many molecules of a transcript exist in a cell. It produces a fixed total number of reads per sample — the library size, typically tens of millions — and each individual read is effectively drawn at random from the pool of RNA fragments present, in proportion to how abundant that fragment's source transcript is. Statistically this is a multinomial sampling process: a fixed number of draws distributed across many categories (genes) according to their underlying probabilities. The consequence is that a read count is never an absolute quantity — it is a share of a fixed pie. Two samples with different total read counts, or the same sample compared to itself with a different sequencing depth, are not directly comparable as raw counts, because the pie itself is a different size.

sections.heading: Length matters because sequencing is fragment-based
sections.body: Standard RNA-seq protocols fragment RNA into short pieces before sequencing, and every fragment has roughly the same chance of being captured and read regardless of which end of a transcript it came from. That means a longer transcript simply generates more fragments, and therefore accumulates more reads, than a shorter transcript present at the identical molecule count. A 6,000-nucleotide transcript and a 600-nucleotide transcript expressed at exactly the same number of copies per cell will not show the same raw read count — the longer one will show roughly ten times more reads, purely from geometry, not biology. This length bias is exactly why normalized units like FPKM, RPKM, and TPM divide by transcript length before comparing genes to each other.

sections.heading: Compositionality: one gene's rise is every other gene's fall
sections.body: Because the sequencing budget per sample is fixed, expression data are compositional — every gene's read count is a proportion of that fixed total, not an independent measurement. This has a sharp, counterintuitive consequence: if one gene's true expression explodes, it consumes a larger share of the fixed read budget, which mathematically depresses the apparent read count of every other gene even if their true molecule counts never changed at all. This is the core reason simple 'reads per sample' comparisons can manufacture false differential-expression hits across the board, and it is precisely the problem that composition-aware normalization methods — DESeq2's median-of-ratios, edgeR's TMM (trimmed mean of M-values, Robinson & Oshlack, 2010) — are built to correct, by estimating a size factor that accounts for shifts in the overall composition rather than just the raw total read count.

lessons.workedExample: A sample is sequenced to a fixed depth of 10 million reads. In a control condition, one gene, Gene Z, makes up 5% of reads (500,000 reads), with the rest of the transcriptome sharing the remaining 9.5 million. In a treated condition, Gene Z's true expression rises sharply and now consumes 40% of the fixed 10-million-read budget (4 million reads) — a real biological change.
