But because the budget is fixed, every other gene's share of the pie has shrunk, even for genes whose true molecule count in the cell never changed: a gene that truly stayed flat at 200,000 molecules-worth of signal might now show only 120,000 reads, simply because Gene Z is eating a much larger slice. A naive comparison of raw read counts would flag that flat gene as 'downregulated,' when the honest description is that the whole composition shifted around one dominant, genuinely upregulated gene.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'is a read count an absolute measurement?' is testing whether a student understands that RNA-seq output is relative and compositional by construction, not a direct molecule count. The strong answer explains that the fixed total-reads-per-sample budget makes every gene's count a share of that total, so one gene's real change can mathematically move every other gene's apparent count — and can name why normalization exists at all, rather than treating it as a mysterious preprocessing step to run before 'the real analysis.'

questions.prompt: Why is an RNA-seq read count best described as a 'multinomial sample from a fixed budget' rather than an absolute molecule count?

options.text: Because the sequencer directly counts every RNA molecule in the cell with no sampling involved

Because each sample is sequenced to a fixed total number of reads, and each read is effectively drawn from the transcript pool in proportion to abundance, making counts relative shares of that fixed total
Because RNA degrades randomly during sequencing
Because only protein-coding genes are counted

explanations.a: The sequencer samples a fixed number of reads from the RNA pool; it does not exhaustively count every molecule present.
explanations.b: Correct — a fixed library size means every gene's count is drawn from (and constrained by) that same fixed total, making counts relative proportions, not absolute quantities.
explanations.c: Random degradation is a separate technical noise source, not the reason counts are compositional.
explanations.d: This sampling logic applies to any RNA species captured by the library, not specifically protein-coding genes.

questions.prompt: Two transcripts are present at the exact same number of molecules per cell, but one is 6,000 nucleotides long and the other is 600 nucleotides long. What happens to their raw read counts?

options.text: They will be roughly equal, since molecule count is identical
The longer transcript will show roughly ten times more reads, because fragment-based sequencing generates proportionally more fragments from longer transcripts
The shorter transcript will show more reads because it sequences faster
Read count is unrelated to transcript length

explanations.a: Equal molecule counts do not produce equal read counts once fragmentation is involved; length still matters.
explanations.b: Correct — because fragmentation makes read count scale with the number of fragments a transcript generates, a transcript ten times longer accumulates roughly ten times more reads at the same molecule count.
explanations.c: Sequencing speed is not what drives this difference; fragment count from length is.
explanations.d: Length is a major, well-documented driver of raw read count, which is exactly why length-normalized units like TPM exist.

questions.prompt: In a sample sequenced to a fixed 10 million reads, Gene Z's true expression rises from 5% to 40% of all reads between two conditions. What happens to the raw read count of a different gene whose true molecule count never changed?

options.text: It stays exactly the same, since its own biology didn't change
It can appear to decrease, because Gene Z's larger share of the fixed total read budget leaves proportionally fewer reads for every other gene
It always increases to compensate
Read counts for unrelated genes are mathematically independent of any other gene's expression

explanations.a: Because the total read budget is fixed, another gene's real change can still shift this gene's apparent count even without any biological change of its own.
explanations.b: Correct — compositionality means every gene's read count is a share of the same fixed total, so a large real increase in one gene mathematically depresses the apparent share of every other gene.
explanations.c: There is no compensatory increase; the effect goes the other direction, toward apparent depression.
explanations.d: This is the key misconception the lesson corrects — counts from a fixed-depth run are not independent across genes, precisely because they share one fixed total.

questions.prompt: Composition-aware normalization methods like DESeq2's median-of-ratios or edgeR's TMM exist primarily to correct for:

options.text: Errors in the reference genome sequence
Shifts in overall sample composition (e.g., one or a few genes dominating the read budget) that distort simple total-read-count comparisons
PCR machine calibration drift
Differences in sequencing adapter chemistry

explanations.a: Reference genome errors are a separate annotation/alignment issue, not what these normalization methods target.
explanations.b: Correct — these methods estimate size factors that account for compositional shifts (like one dominant gene skewing the whole distribution), rather than relying on the raw total read count alone.
explanations.c: This is not a hardware calibration correction; it is a statistical correction for compositional distortion.
explanations.d: Adapter chemistry differences are a library-prep technical issue, not the compositionality problem these methods solve.

lessons.label: mRNA vs Protein: the Correlation Problem

sections.heading: The number that should worry every RNA-seq claim
sections.body: The whole premise of transcriptomics as a proxy for cell biology rests on an assumption: more mRNA roughly means more protein, the actual functional molecule doing the work. That assumption is weaker than most people expect. In the same 2011 Nature study that measured synthesis and degradation rates across roughly 5,000 mouse fibroblast genes, Schwanhausser and colleagues also directly compared mRNA abundance to protein abundance gene-by-gene, and found mRNA levels explained only about 40% of the variance in protein levels (R-squared around 0.41). In plain terms: knowing how much of a gene's mRNA is present tells you well under half of what you'd need to know to predict how much protein is actually there.

sections.heading: Three reasons the correlation isn't tighter
sections.body: Translation efficiency varies enormously gene to gene — how many ribosomes load onto a given transcript and how productively they translate it depends on features like upstream open reading frames, RNA secondary structure near the start codon, and codon usage, so two transcripts at identical abundance can yield very different amounts of protein. Protein turnover compounds this: as established by the same half-life data, proteins persist roughly five times longer than their mRNAs on average, and degradation rates vary by gene, so a stable transcript encoding a rapidly-degraded protein and an unstable transcript encoding a long-lived protein can land at very different relative levels than their mRNA ratio alone would predict. Measurement noise adds a third layer — both RNA-seq and mass-spectrometry-based proteomics carry substantial technical variance, and any noise in either measurement mechanically drags down an observed correlation between them, independent of the true biology.

sections.heading: A later reanalysis, and what it changes
sections.body: Li, Bickel, and Biggin (2014) revisited this question and argued that once measurement error in both the RNA and protein assays is properly accounted for, the true biological correlation between mRNA and protein is substantially higher than the raw R-squared of about 0.4 — some estimates rising toward 0.8 or higher. That reanalysis matters, but it does not overturn the practical lesson: a meaningful chunk of protein-level variation remains genuinely explained by translation efficiency and turnover, not just noise, and no analysis claims mRNA and protein levels are interchangeable. The practical rule stands — if a study's actual question is about protein abundance, activity, or function (an enzyme's catalytic output, an antibody target's surface density, a disease-relevant aggregate), RNA-seq is measuring the wrong molecule, and a transcript-level finding needs an independent protein-level check before it supports a protein-level claim.

lessons.workedExample: A student finds a gene's mRNA rises 5-fold after a drug treatment and concludes the corresponding enzyme's activity in the cell increased 5-fold. This skips the entire chain the lesson lays out: translation efficiency for that transcript could be unchanged or even reduced under the drug (fewer ribosomes loading per transcript), and the enzyme's own turnover rate could accelerate under the same treatment, degrading protein as fast as it's made. A defensible version of the same claim runs a Western blot or targeted mass-spectrometry measurement of the actual protein, or better, a direct enzymatic activity assay, alongside the RNA-seq result — reporting 'mRNA rose 5-fold; protein rose 1.3-fold by Western blot' is a real, checkable finding, while 'mRNA rose 5-fold, so the protein and its activity must have too' is an unearned leap the R-squared of about 0.4 directly warns against.
lessons.judgeFraming: When a judge asks 'did you check protein?' after an RNA-seq result, they are testing whether a student understands that mRNA level is a proxy with a known, quantified ceiling — not interchangeable with the functional molecule most biological claims are actually about. The strong answer either shows an independent protein-level measurement (Western blot, mass spec, an activity assay) backing the RNA-seq finding, or explicitly scopes the claim to 'transcript level changed' without extending it to protein abundance or function. A student who cannot explain why mRNA and protein levels diverge — translation efficiency, differential turnover, measurement noise — has not actually grappled with what their RNA-seq data can and cannot support.

questions.prompt: In Schwanhausser et al. (2011), roughly what fraction of protein-level variance across genes was explained by mRNA abundance (R-squared)?

options.text: About 40%
About 95%
About 5%
Exactly 100%, mRNA and protein levels were interchangeable

explanations.a: Correct — the reported R-squared was about 0.41, meaning mRNA abundance explained roughly 40% of protein-level variance across the measured genes.
explanations.b: This overstates the correlation far beyond what the study reported.
explanations.c: This understates the correlation; some real relationship existed, just far from complete.
explanations.d: The entire point of the finding is that mRNA and protein levels are not interchangeable; a large share of protein variance is left unexplained by mRNA alone.

questions.prompt: Match each factor to how it weakens the mRNA-to-protein correlation.

right.text: Transcripts at equal abundance can be translated into very different amounts of protein depending on features like ribosome loading and codon usage
Genes with equally abundant mRNA can accumulate very different protein levels if their proteins are degraded at different rates
Technical variance in both RNA-seq and proteomics assays mechanically attenuates the observed correlation, independent of true biology

questions.explanation: Translation efficiency changes how much protein a given amount of mRNA yields; protein turnover changes how much protein accumulates and persists independent of mRNA; measurement noise in either assay lowers the observed correlation even when the underlying biological relationship is tighter.

questions.prompt: What did Li, Bickel, and Biggin (2014) argue in their reanalysis of mRNA-protein correlation?

options.text: That mRNA and protein levels are completely unrelated
That accounting for measurement error in both assays, the true biological correlation is substantially higher than the raw R-squared of about 0.4
That protein levels cannot be measured at all
That the original Schwanhausser dataset was fabricated

explanations.a: Their argument was the opposite direction — correcting for noise, they found a stronger relationship, not none at all.
explanations.b: Correct — they argued the raw correlation underestimates the true biological relationship once measurement error in the RNA and protein assays is accounted for.
explanations.c: Protein levels are measurable by established methods like mass spectrometry and Western blotting; the reanalysis worked with real measured protein data.
explanations.d: The reanalysis was a statistical reinterpretation of the same type of data, not an allegation of fabrication.

questions.prompt: A study's real question is whether an enzyme's catalytic activity changed after treatment. Why would RNA-seq alone be an insufficient assay to answer this?

options.text: RNA-seq measures transcript abundance, which explains only part of protein-level variance and says nothing directly about enzymatic activity, which also depends on protein modification and folding
RNA-seq cannot detect any gene related to enzymes
Enzyme activity and mRNA level are mathematically identical by definition
RNA-seq only works on non-coding RNA

explanations.a: Correct — mRNA level is an incomplete proxy for protein abundance (roughly 40% of variance explained), and protein abundance itself is still one step removed from catalytic activity, which also depends on post-translational state; RNA-seq alone cannot support an activity claim.
explanations.b: RNA-seq can detect transcripts from enzyme-encoding genes just like any other gene; detection is not the limitation here.
explanations.c: This is precisely the assumption the correlation problem disproves; they are related but far from identical.
explanations.d: RNA-seq (with appropriate library prep) captures mRNA from protein-coding genes routinely; it is not restricted to non-coding RNA.

units.label: From Sample to Library: RNA Handling and Prep

lessons.label: Getting Intact RNA Out of a Sample

sections.heading: RNases are everywhere and never sleep
sections.body: Ribonucleases are small, extremely stable enzymes that survive autoclaving and boiling, need no cofactor to cut RNA, and coat human skin, saliva, and dust. A single unprotected fingerprint on a tube can seed enough RNase to reduce a sample to fragments within minutes. This is why RNA work leans so heavily on technique rather than kit chemistry: gloves changed often, dedicated RNase-free pipette tips and surfaces, DEPC-treated (diethyl pyrocarbonate-inactivated) water, and speed. The two standard ways to stop degradation at the moment of collection are snap-freezing in liquid nitrogen, which halts enzymatic activity by dropping temperature almost instantly, and RNAlater, a high-salt stabilization reagent that diffuses into intact tissue and denatures RNases in place without freezing — useful for field or classroom collection where a liquid-nitrogen dewar is not available, though it penetrates slowly and works best on small pieces of tissue.

sections.heading: Two extraction chemistries, different tradeoffs
sections.body: TRIzol and related phenol-chloroform methods, built on the single-step guanidinium thiocyanate-phenol-chloroform protocol Chomczynski and Sacchi published in 1987, lyse cells and denature RNases in one step, then separate RNA into the aqueous phase by phase partitioning. It gives high yield and, notably, keeps small RNAs (microRNAs, other short regulatory species) that silica-column kits often lose. Silica-column kits such as the RNeasy family instead bind RNA to a silica membrane under chaotropic salt and ethanol, wash away protein and salt, and elute — cleaner, faster, and safer for a classroom (no phenol-chloroform waste stream), but a standard column's binding chemistry discards RNA under roughly 200 nucleotides, so it systematically loses microRNAs unless a small-RNA-specific kit is used. Both methods co-purify genomic DNA unless it is actively removed, so an on-column or in-solution DNase I digestion step is not optional for expression work — residual gDNA inflates apparent expression of intron-less or single-exon genes and distorts low-abundance transcript counts.

sections.heading: The sample can change before you even touch it
sections.body: Delay and handling stress alter the transcriptome before extraction begins. Immediate-early genes such as Fos and Jun switch on within minutes of tissue handling or hypoxia, so a specimen left on the bench is no longer measuring baseline biology. Single-cell work faces a sharper version: the warm enzymatic digestion used to dissociate tissue into single cells itself triggers a stress-response signature — van den Brink and colleagues (2017) showed dissociation induces Fos, Jun, and heat-shock genes like Hspa1b across dissociated cell types, which is why cold or fast dissociation protocols exist specifically to suppress this artifact.

lessons.workedExample: A team wants baseline gene expression from mouse liver but the animal facility is a 20-minute walk from the lab bench. If they carry the freshly dissected liver in a tube on ice and extract RNA an hour later, immediate-early genes like Fos will already be elevated from the stress of dissection and transport, contaminating their 'baseline' with a handling artifact. The fix is to mince and drop the tissue directly into liquid nitrogen or an RNAlater tube at the bench where it is collected, within seconds, then extract later from the stabilized sample — separating the biological question (baseline expression) from the logistics of getting the tissue to a bench.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing sample handling wants to know whether a student understands that RNA quality is decided at the moment of collection, not at the extraction bench. The tell is whether a student can name a specific stabilization method (snap-freezing or RNAlater) and explain what it prevents — RNase activity and, for dissociated or delayed samples, stress-gene induction — rather than assuming any kit will rescue a poorly handled sample. A student who says 'we used an RNA extraction kit' without addressing collection-to-freezing time has skipped the step that determines whether their downstream data reflects biology or handling artifact.

questions.prompt: Why is RNase contamination such a persistent risk during RNA extraction?

options.text: RNases require a specific cofactor that is hard to avoid introducing
RNases are small, heat-stable, cofactor-free enzymes present on skin and dust, so they survive routine sterilization
RNases only become active at freezing temperatures
RNases are destroyed by autoclaving, so contamination only comes from unautoclaved plasticware

explanations.a: RNases need no cofactor to function, which is exactly why they are so hard to inactivate or exclude.
explanations.b: Correct — their small size, stability, and lack of cofactor requirement mean they survive autoclaving and boiling and are ubiquitous on skin and dust, so RNase-free technique matters more than any single kit choice.
explanations.c: RNases are active across a wide temperature range; freezing is used to suppress, not trigger, their activity.
explanations.d: RNases survive autoclaving, which is precisely why RNase-free technique (gloves, dedicated surfaces) is needed beyond standard sterilization.

questions.prompt: Match each extraction consideration to the method it favors.

left.text: Best retention of microRNAs and other short RNAs
Requires an added enzymatic step to remove co-purifying genomic DNA

right.text: TRIzol / phenol-chloroform extraction
Standard silica-column kit
Both methods equally

questions.explanation: TRIzol-based phenol-chloroform extraction retains small RNAs that a standard silica column's ~200-nucleotide cutoff discards; silica columns avoid organic-solvent waste; but genomic DNA co-purifies with RNA in both chemistries, so a DNase digestion step is needed regardless of which method is used.

questions.prompt: A researcher extracts RNA from a sample with a standard silica-column kit and skips the DNase treatment step to save time. What is the most likely consequence for expression quantification?

options.text: No effect, since silica columns already exclude all genomic DNA
Apparent expression of intron-less or single-exon genes may be inflated by residual genomic DNA
Only microRNA measurements are affected
The sample will fail extraction entirely

explanations.a: Silica columns do not fully exclude genomic DNA; it co-purifies unless actively digested away.
explanations.b: Correct — residual genomic DNA is indistinguishable from mRNA at intron-less or single-exon loci during quantification, so skipping DNase treatment inflates apparent expression at those genes.
explanations.c: Genomic DNA carryover affects DNA-based signal at any locus lacking introns to distinguish it from mRNA, not specifically microRNA measurements.
explanations.d: Extraction proceeds normally without DNase treatment; the problem is downstream data interpretation, not extraction failure.

questions.prompt: According to van den Brink and colleagues (2017), what artifact does warm enzymatic dissociation introduce in single-cell RNA sequencing?

options.text: A uniform reduction in all gene expression across every cell type
Induction of stress-response genes such as Fos, Jun, and Hspa1b
Complete loss of ribosomal RNA
An increase in genomic DNA contamination

explanations.a: The effect is not a uniform reduction but a specific induction of stress-related genes.
explanations.b: Correct — van den Brink et al. (2017) showed that warm enzymatic tissue dissociation induces a stress-response signature, including Fos, Jun, and heat-shock genes like Hspa1b, across dissociated cell types.
explanations.c: The dissociation artifact is a transcriptional stress response, not a loss of ribosomal RNA.
explanations.d: Dissociation stress is a gene-expression artifact from handling, unrelated to genomic DNA carryover during extraction.

lessons.label: RIN, Bioanalyzer Traces, and the QC Gate

sections.heading: Reading an electropherogram
sections.body: Instruments like the Agilent Bioanalyzer or TapeStation run total RNA through a microfluidic capillary and report fluorescence versus migration time as an electropherogram, rather than a stained gel image. Intact eukaryotic total RNA produces two dominant, sharp peaks: the 18S and 28S ribosomal RNA subunits, with 28S migrating slower because it is roughly twice the length of 18S. Because there are proportionally more 28S than 18S bases, intact RNA gives a 28S:18S area ratio near 2. As RNA degrades, both peaks broaden and shrink while a smear of shorter fragments builds up underneath and between them — the shape of that smear, not just the two peaks, is the actual QC signal a trained eye or algorithm reads.

sections.heading: The RIN scale and the conventional gates
sections.body: Before 2006, labs judged degradation almost entirely from that 28S:18S ratio, which Schroeder and colleagues showed was inconsistent and could not be compared across instruments or labs. Their 2006 paper introduced the RNA Integrity Number (RIN): a machine-learning algorithm trained on a large library of Bioanalyzer traces that scores integrity from 1 (fully degraded) to 10 (fully intact) using the whole trace — peak heights, the fast region before 18S, and the degradation-associated baseline rise — not the ratio alone. Sequencing cores built downstream gates on top of that number: RIN 7 or higher is the conventional cutoff for standard poly(A)-selected RNA-seq libraries, while more demanding applications — full-length isoform assembly, precise splice-junction calling — commonly require RIN 8 or higher, because those analyses depend on reads spanning intact, uninterrupted transcripts.

sections.heading: When RIN itself breaks: FFPE and 3' bias
sections.body: Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue — the standard for clinical archives — chemically crosslinks and uniformly fragments RNA during fixation, so even a perfectly usable FFPE sample often scores a RIN of 2-3; RIN was built for fresh-frozen degradation patterns and misreads FFPE's uniform fragmentation as failure. The field instead uses DV200, the percentage of fragments longer than 200 nucleotides, with roughly 30% or higher considered workable for library prep. Whatever the cause, degradation has a specific downstream signature: because poly(A)-primed reverse transcription starts at the 3' end and cannot read through a break, a fragmented transcript only yields reads near its 3' end, producing 3' coverage bias and, since longer transcripts accumulate more internal breaks than short ones, a systematic underrepresentation of long genes relative to short ones in the resulting counts.

lessons.workedExample: A core facility runs two samples: fresh-frozen mouse brain (RIN 9.1) and an archived FFPE tumor block. The FFPE sample returns RIN 2.4 on the same scale, which looks like catastrophic degradation, but its DV200 is 42% — comfortably usable by FFPE standards. Sequencing both, the lab notices the FFPE library's coverage piles up almost entirely in the last few hundred bases of each transcript's 3' end, while the fresh-frozen library shows even coverage across gene bodies. A student comparing raw counts between the two without accounting for this would mistake the 3'-biased coverage loss in long FFPE transcripts for a real biological difference in gene length distribution between conditions.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about RNA QC wants to see that a student treats RIN as diagnostic, not just a pass/fail gate to clear. The strong answer explains what the number is built from (the shape of the whole electropherogram, not just the 28S:18S ratio) and what a low score predicts downstream — 3' coverage bias and length-dependent undercounting — rather than reciting 'RIN above 7 is good.' It is an even stronger answer if the student knows RIN's gate breaks down for FFPE and that DV200 exists precisely because RIN assumes a degradation pattern FFPE tissue does not follow.

questions.prompt: In an intact total RNA electropherogram, why does the 28S rRNA peak show roughly twice the area of the 18S peak?

options.text: The 28S subunit is roughly twice the length of the 18S subunit
28S rRNA is present in twice as many copies per ribosome
18S rRNA degrades twice as fast during extraction
The Bioanalyzer detector is calibrated to weight 28S signal higher

explanations.a: Correct — 28S rRNA is roughly double the length of 18S, so intact RNA carries proportionally more mass (and fluorescent stain) in the 28S band, giving a ~2:1 ratio.
explanations.b: Each ribosome contains one 28S and one 18S subunit; the ratio comes from length, not copy number.
explanations.c: This describes a degradation effect, not the basis of the ~2:1 ratio seen in intact RNA.
explanations.d: The instrument reports raw fluorescence proportional to nucleic acid mass; it is not weighted toward either peak.

questions.prompt: What did Schroeder et al. (2006) identify as the key limitation of using the 28S:18S ratio alone to judge RNA quality?

options.text: It could not be measured on a Bioanalyzer at all
It was inconsistent and not comparable across instruments and labs
It only worked for FFPE samples
It required a gel rather than a microfluidic run

explanations.a: The ratio was measurable on the Bioanalyzer; the problem was its unreliability, not the measurement itself.
explanations.b: Correct — Schroeder and colleagues showed the ratio alone was inconsistent and not comparable across labs and instruments, motivating an algorithm (RIN) that uses the whole electropherogram trace instead.
explanations.c: The ratio's inconsistency was a general fresh-tissue problem; FFPE's issues with RIN are a separate, later point.
explanations.d: The ratio was already computed from Bioanalyzer microfluidic traces; the issue was statistical, not the platform.

questions.prompt: Match each QC scenario to its appropriate metric or gate.

left.text: Full-length isoform assembly / precise splice-junction analysis

right.text: RIN of 7 or higher
RIN of 8 or higher
DV200 around 30% or higher

questions.explanation: Standard poly(A) RNA-seq conventionally gates at RIN 7+; demanding applications like isoform assembly, which need long uninterrupted transcript reads, gate at RIN 8+; FFPE tissue is fragmented in a way RIN misreads as failure, so DV200 (percent of fragments over 200 nt) is used instead, with roughly 30%+ considered workable.

questions.prompt: A degraded RNA sample is sequenced anyway. What effect is expected on the resulting read coverage and gene-level counts?

options.text: Even coverage across gene bodies with no systematic bias
3' coverage bias, with longer transcripts undercounted relative to shorter ones
5' coverage bias, with shorter transcripts undercounted
No effect on quantification, only on library yield

explanations.a: Degradation specifically disrupts even coverage; poly(A)-primed synthesis cannot read through a broken transcript to reach the 5' end.
explanations.b: Correct — since reverse transcription primes from the 3' poly(A) tail and cannot proceed past a break, fragmented transcripts yield reads concentrated near the 3' end, and because longer transcripts accumulate more internal breaks, they are disproportionately undercounted.
explanations.c: The bias runs the opposite direction: coverage concentrates at the 3' end, not the 5' end, because synthesis starts from the poly(A) tail.
explanations.d: Degradation changes not just yield but the shape of coverage and relative gene counts, particularly for long transcripts.

lessons.label: Poly(A) Selection vs rRNA Depletion

sections.heading: Oligo-dT capture: cheap, clean, and blind to a lot of the transcriptome
sections.body: Ribosomal RNA makes up roughly 80-90% of total cellular RNA, so any RNA-seq library needs a step that removes it before the remaining fraction is worth sequencing. Oligo-dT selection does this by binding beads coated with strings of deoxythymidine to the poly(A) tail that most mature eukaryotic mRNAs carry, pulling those transcripts out and discarding everything without a tail — an efficient, low-cost, well-established method. But it is blind to any RNA that never gets a poly(A) tail: replication-dependent histone mRNAs, which end in a stem-loop instead of a poly(A) tail; most long non-coding RNAs (many lncRNAs, such as NEAT1, are non-polyadenylated); nascent, still-being-transcribed pre-mRNA; and essentially all bacterial mRNA, since prokaryotes do not stably polyadenylate transcripts the way eukaryotes do. Oligo-dT also punishes degraded RNA specifically — if a transcript has already broken, only the fragment still attached to the poly(A) tail gets captured, so the rest of the molecule is lost and 3' bias gets worse.

sections.heading: rRNA depletion: keeps everything, costs more reads
sections.body: The alternative is to target rRNA directly rather than fish for mRNA. Modern kits typically hybridize DNA oligo probes to rRNA sequences and then digest the resulting RNA:DNA hybrids with RNase H (the successor approach to the original bead-based probe-hybridization-and-pulldown method sold as Ribo-Zero). Because depletion does not depend on a poly(A) tail, it retains histone mRNAs, non-polyadenylated lncRNAs, nascent transcripts, and works on bacterial samples and degraded or FFPE tissue where oligo-dT would fail outright. The cost is that depletion is never complete: some residual rRNA survives every kit, and because rRNA is such a large fraction of the input, even a small residual percentage consumes a real slice of sequencing depth that would otherwise go to the transcripts under study — and the probe sets themselves add cost.

sections.heading: Choosing by sample and question
sections.body: The decision rule follows from those tradeoffs: for fresh, high-integrity eukaryotic samples where the question is mRNA expression, oligo-dT selection is the default — cheaper and cleaner. For degraded or FFPE tissue, for questions that require non-polyadenylated species (lncRNA biology, histone gene regulation, nascent transcription), or for any non-eukaryotic or mixed-organism sample (bacteria, host-pathogen studies), rRNA depletion is required. Whole blood needs a further step: reticulocyte-derived globin transcripts (HBA1/2, HBB) can dominate blood RNA so heavily that they crowd out sequencing depth for every other gene, so blood protocols add a targeted globin-depletion step (such as globin-blocking oligos) on top of standard rRNA depletion.

lessons.workedExample: A team studying histone gene regulation during the cell cycle in cultured cells sequences their RNA using standard oligo-dT poly(A) selection because it was cheaper and available in the shared facility's standard protocol. Their library shows almost no reads mapping to the replication-dependent histone genes they care about, even though qPCR on the same RNA confirms the transcripts are present. The library prep, not the biology, caused the dropout: replication-dependent histone mRNAs lack poly(A) tails, so oligo-dT beads never captured them. Switching to an rRNA-depletion protocol on the next batch recovers histone transcript coverage because depletion does not depend on a poly(A) tail to select what gets sequenced.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why did you choose poly(A) selection or rRNA depletion?' is testing whether a student picked the method to fit the biological question or just used whatever the sequencing core defaults to. The strong answer names a specific RNA class relevant to their study (histone mRNA, a candidate lncRNA, bacterial transcripts, or a degraded/FFPE sample) and explains why that class would or would not survive oligo-dT capture — showing the student understands the method is a biological filter, not a neutral cleanup step, and that the wrong choice can silently erase the exact signal they were trying to measure.

questions.prompt: Why does oligo-dT selection fail to capture replication-dependent histone mRNAs?

options.text: Histone mRNAs are too short to bind oligo-dT beads
Histone mRNAs end in a stem-loop structure rather than a poly(A) tail
Histone mRNAs are degraded before extraction in nearly all samples
Oligo-dT beads specifically exclude nuclear-encoded transcripts

explanations.a: Length is not the issue; the beads select based on the presence of a poly(A) tail, which histone mRNAs lack.
explanations.b: Correct — replication-dependent histone mRNAs terminate in a stem-loop instead of a poly(A) tail, so oligo-dT beads, which bind poly(A) tails, never capture them.
explanations.c: This is a chemistry limitation of the capture method, not a statement about typical sample degradation.
explanations.d: Oligo-dT selection is indifferent to nuclear versus other origin; it selects strictly by the presence of a poly(A) tail.

questions.prompt: A researcher wants to sequence RNA from a mixed host-bacteria infection sample to capture bacterial transcripts. Which library prep strategy should they use?

options.text: Oligo-dT poly(A) selection, since it is cheaper
rRNA depletion, since bacterial mRNA is not reliably polyadenylated
Either method works equally well for bacterial transcripts
Neither method is compatible with mixed-organism samples

explanations.a: Oligo-dT selection would capture host mRNA but miss nearly all bacterial mRNA, since bacteria do not stably polyadenylate transcripts.
explanations.b: Correct — because bacterial mRNA lacks a stable poly(A) tail, only rRNA depletion (which does not depend on a poly(A) tail) will retain bacterial transcripts alongside host mRNA.
explanations.c: The two methods differ sharply here; oligo-dT would silently drop nearly all bacterial signal.
explanations.d: rRNA depletion is specifically compatible with mixed and non-eukaryotic samples; it is the appropriate choice, not an exclusion.

questions.prompt: Why do whole-blood RNA-seq protocols typically add a globin-depletion step beyond standard rRNA depletion?

options.text: Globin transcripts are non-polyadenylated and would otherwise be lost
Globin transcripts (HBA1/2, HBB) can dominate blood RNA and crowd out sequencing depth for other genes
Globin mRNA degrades faster than other transcripts and must be removed to protect RIN
Globin depletion is required to remove residual genomic DNA

explanations.a: Globin mRNA is polyadenylated like other eukaryotic mRNA; the issue is its overwhelming abundance, not its tail status.
explanations.b: Correct — globin transcripts from reticulocytes can make up a very large share of blood mRNA, so without targeted depletion they consume sequencing depth that should go to other genes.
explanations.c: Globin depletion addresses transcript abundance, not degradation rate or RIN.
explanations.d: Globin depletion targets specific mRNA transcripts, not genomic DNA contamination, which is handled by DNase treatment.

questions.prompt: Match each sample or question to the more appropriate library prep method.

left.text: Fresh, high-RIN eukaryotic sample, standard mRNA expression question
Study focused on non-polyadenylated lncRNA biology

right.text: Oligo-dT poly(A) selection
rRNA depletion

questions.explanation: Fresh, intact eukaryotic mRNA studies default to cheaper, cleaner poly(A) selection; degraded/FFPE samples and questions requiring non-polyadenylated species both require rRNA depletion, since depletion does not depend on transcript integrity or a poly(A) tail to retain a molecule.

lessons.label: Building the Library: Fragmentation, RT, Strandedness

sections.heading: Fragmentation and a bias baked in at the very first primer
sections.body: Sequencing platforms like Illumina read short fragments, so intact mRNA (typically 1-3 kb) must first be chopped into pieces around 200-300 bp, usually by heat with divalent cations or by enzymatic shearing. First-strand cDNA synthesis then primes off these fragments with random hexamers — short six-base primers meant to bind everywhere with equal likelihood. They do not. Hansen, Brenner, and Dudoit (2010) showed random hexamer priming has strong sequence-composition preferences, so certain hexamer sequences anneal more efficiently than others, producing a nonuniform, reproducible bias in where reads start along a transcript — a bias baked into the data before amplification or sequencing ever happens, and one every RNA-seq analyst has to know is a feature of the chemistry, not a biological signal.

sections.heading: Reverse transcription and the dUTP strand-marking trick
sections.body: A reverse transcriptase enzyme extends those hexamer primers into first-strand cDNA, complementary to the original RNA. Second-strand synthesis then copies that first strand into double-stranded cDNA — and this is where strand-of-origin information is normally lost, since a double-stranded fragment looks identical regardless of which original strand carried the RNA. The dUTP method (established by Parkhomchuk and colleagues and by Levin and colleagues, both in 2009-2010) fixes this: second-strand synthesis substitutes dUTP for dTTP, marking that strand chemically. Before PCR amplification, an enzyme (uracil-DNA glycosylase, UNG/USER) degrades the dUTP-marked strand, so only the original first strand amplifies — meaning every read in the final library can be traced back to the strand it came from. This is what makes a library 'strand-specific' or 'stranded.'

sections.heading: Adapters, PCR duplicates, and UMIs
sections.body: After second-strand synthesis, sequencing adapters are ligated to fragment ends, giving each fragment the flow-cell-binding sequence and sample index the sequencer needs, and the library is then PCR-amplified to reach the quantity required for sequencing. More PCR cycles mean more copies of the same original molecule, and those copies are read as separate reads unless something distinguishes them from genuinely independent molecules — inflating apparent expression, especially for high-abundance transcripts and low-input samples where more cycles are needed. Unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), short random barcodes ligated onto each original molecule before amplification, solve this: reads sharing both a UMI and a mapping position came from one original molecule via PCR, and can be collapsed to a single count, while reads with different UMIs at the same position are genuinely independent — a concept formalized by Kivioja and colleagues (2012).

lessons.workedExample: A student sequences an unstranded library across a genomic region where a long non-coding RNA sits antisense to a protein-coding gene, overlapping it on the opposite strand. Without strand information, reads from the antisense lncRNA cannot be distinguished from reads on the sense strand of the coding gene, so most pipelines either discard the ambiguous reads or wrongly attribute them to the coding gene, inflating its apparent expression and hiding the lncRNA entirely. Rerunning the same region with a dUTP-based stranded library resolves the ambiguity immediately: every read is tagged to its strand of origin, correctly splitting counts between the coding gene and its antisense neighbor.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about library prep wants to see that a student can trace where a specific bias enters — hexamer priming at first-strand synthesis, duplicate inflation from PCR — rather than treating 'library prep' as an opaque kit step. The strongest answers connect a bench step to its downstream consequence: naming that unstranded libraries cannot resolve overlapping or antisense genes, or that a low-input sample needing more PCR cycles will show more duplicate inflation unless UMIs were used. That connection is what separates a student who ran a protocol from one who understands why each step exists.

questions.prompt: Order these RNA-seq library construction steps as they occur on the bench.

items.text: Fragment RNA into ~200-300 bp pieces
Prime with random hexamers and synthesize first-strand cDNA
Synthesize second strand (dUTP method, for stranded libraries)
Ligate sequencing adapters
PCR-amplify the library

questions.explanation: RNA is fragmented first, then reverse-transcribed into first-strand cDNA using random hexamer priming, then converted to double-stranded cDNA via second-strand synthesis (with dUTP marking if the protocol is strand-specific), then adapters are ligated onto the fragment ends, and finally the whole library is PCR-amplified for sequencing.

questions.prompt: What did Hansen, Brenner, and Dudoit (2010) demonstrate about random hexamer priming in RNA-seq library prep?

options.text: It binds every possible six-base sequence with exactly equal affinity
It has sequence-composition preferences that create a nonuniform, reproducible bias in read start positions
It only works on rRNA-depleted samples
It eliminates the need for adapter ligation

explanations.a: The opposite of their finding — hexamer binding is not uniform across sequences.
explanations.b: Correct — Hansen, Brenner, and Dudoit (2010) showed random hexamers anneal preferentially to certain sequences, producing a reproducible bias in where reads start along a transcript.
explanations.c: Hexamer priming bias occurs regardless of whether the library used poly(A) selection or rRNA depletion; it is a reverse-transcription step, unrelated to rRNA removal chemistry.
explanations.d: Hexamer priming happens during reverse transcription, well before adapter ligation, and does not replace it.

questions.prompt: In the dUTP second-strand synthesis method for making a strand-specific library, what happens to the dUTP-marked strand before PCR amplification?

options.text: It is preferentially amplified over the unmarked strand
It is enzymatically degraded, so only the original first strand amplifies
It is ligated to a second set of adapters
It is used as the template for random hexamer priming a second time

explanations.a: The dUTP-marked strand is destroyed, not preferentially amplified.
explanations.b: Correct — an enzyme (UNG/USER) degrades the dUTP-containing second strand before PCR, so only the original first strand is amplified, preserving which strand each read came from.
explanations.c: Adapter ligation is a separate step and does not selectively target the dUTP-marked strand.
explanations.d: Hexamer priming happens earlier, during first-strand synthesis, not as a treatment applied to the marked second strand.

questions.prompt: A low-input sample requires extra PCR cycles to yield enough library for sequencing. What problem does this create, and what technique addresses it?

options.text: Increased PCR duplicates inflating apparent expression; addressed by UMIs that tag original molecules before amplification
Loss of strand information; addressed by the dUTP method
3' coverage bias; addressed by using more input RNA
Ribosomal RNA contamination; addressed by rRNA depletion

explanations.a: Correct — more PCR cycles produce more copies of the same original molecule, which read as separate reads unless UMIs (unique molecular identifiers) ligated before amplification allow duplicates sharing a UMI and position to be collapsed to one count.
explanations.b: Strand information is preserved or lost based on the second-strand synthesis chemistry (e.g., dUTP), not the number of PCR cycles.
explanations.c: 3' coverage bias comes from RNA degradation and poly(A)-primed synthesis, not from PCR cycle number.
explanations.d: Ribosomal RNA content is determined by the depletion or selection step, not by PCR amplification cycles.

lessons.label: Spike-ins and Absolute Quantification

sections.heading: ERCC controls: known amounts spanning a million-fold range
sections.body: The External RNA Controls Consortium (ERCC) developed a set of 92 synthetic, polyadenylated RNA transcripts, traceable back to NIST-certified DNA plasmids, sold as premixed kits and added to a sample at the library-prep stage in exactly known relative concentrations. The 92 controls are organized into four subgroups of 23, together spanning six orders of magnitude — roughly a millionfold range — in concentration. Because the input amount of every ERCC transcript is known in advance, a lab can sequence a spiked sample and plot observed read counts against expected concentration on a log-log scale: a straight, tight line across the full range demonstrates good dynamic range and linearity, the lowest concentration still reliably distinguished from background defines the limit of detection, and the scatter around that line — run to run, replicate to replicate — is a direct, empirical measurement of the assay's technical noise, independent of any biological variability in the actual sample.

sections.heading: SIRVs: testing isoform-level accuracy, not just detection
sections.body: ERCC transcripts are deliberately simple, single-exon sequences, so they test whether a pipeline can detect and count RNA accurately but say nothing about whether it can correctly assemble or quantify alternative isoforms. Lexogen's Spike-In RNA Variants (SIRVs) fill that gap: synthetic transcripts built to mimic real transcriptome complexity, with genes producing six to eighteen overlapping isoforms through alternative splicing, transcription start sites, and transcription end sites, at known relative and absolute concentrations. Because the true isoform structure and abundance are known in advance, SIRVs let a lab measure how much error an aligner or assembler introduces when trying to resolve overlapping, similar transcripts — a much harder and more realistic test than ERCC's single-exon controls provide.

sections.heading: Why spike-ins rescue you from a broken assumption
sections.body: Standard RNA-seq normalization methods assume that most genes are not differentially expressed between conditions, and scale libraries to make that assumption hold. That assumption fails when a condition causes a genuine global shift in transcription. Nie and colleagues (2012) showed that MYC acts as a near-universal amplifier of already-active genes rather than a specific on/off switch, so high-MYC cells show broadly elevated transcription across most active genes at once. Standard normalization, seeing 'most genes changed,' will renormalize that real global increase away and report little or no change — the opposite of the truth. Spike-ins solve this because they are added at a fixed amount independent of the cell's own transcriptional output, giving an external anchor unaffected by any biological shift, so spike-in-based normalization can detect and correctly scale a genuine global change that internal, gene-based normalization cannot see. The tradeoff: spike-ins are added after extraction, so they cannot correct for differences in extraction efficiency or degradation that happened before they were added, and their simple, largely unspliced composition does not perfectly mimic the length and sequence biases that affect real, complex endogenous mRNA during library prep.

lessons.workedExample: A lab compares gene expression in control versus MYC-overexpressing lymphocytes. Standard normalization (scaling each library so the bulk of genes look unchanged) finds almost no significant differentially expressed genes, which seems to contradict clear phenotypic differences between the two conditions. Because they included ERCC spike-ins added at identical amounts to every sample before library prep, they can instead scale each library to the spike-in signal rather than to the sample's own transcriptome. Re-normalized this way, the data reveals a broad, genuine increase in transcription across most active genes in the MYC-overexpressing cells — consistent with Nie et al.'s (2012) finding that MYC amplifies already-active genes globally, a signal that gene-based normalization had erased.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about spike-in controls wants to know whether a student understands they exist to break a specific, usually invisible assumption — that most genes don't change — rather than being generic 'quality control.' The strong answer names that assumption, explains why a genuine global shift (the MYC example is the canonical one) breaks standard normalization, and can also state the honest limitation: spike-ins are added after extraction, so they cannot rescue a sample where degradation or extraction bias happened upstream of the spike-in step. A student who calls spike-ins a cure-all for RNA-seq accuracy hasn't understood what they can and cannot control for.

questions.prompt: The 92 ERCC spike-in transcripts are organized to span approximately what range of concentration?

options.text: Roughly tenfold (one order of magnitude)
Roughly a millionfold (six orders of magnitude)
Roughly a hundredfold (two orders of magnitude)
A fixed, single concentration for all 92 transcripts

explanations.a: A tenfold range would be far too narrow to test the dynamic range RNA-seq experiments actually require.
explanations.b: Correct — the 92 ERCC controls are organized into four subgroups of 23, together spanning roughly six orders of magnitude, about a millionfold range, in concentration.
explanations.c: A hundredfold range understates the actual span by several orders of magnitude.
explanations.d: The controls are specifically designed at varying, known concentrations, not a single fixed concentration — that variation is what allows measuring dynamic range.

questions.prompt: Why do SIRV spike-in controls test something ERCC controls cannot?

options.text: SIRVs are radioactively labeled while ERCC controls are not
SIRVs include genes with multiple overlapping isoforms, testing isoform-level quantification accuracy that single-exon ERCC transcripts cannot
SIRVs are cheaper to manufacture than ERCC controls
SIRVs only work with rRNA-depleted libraries

explanations.a: Neither control type relies on radioactive labeling; both are synthetic RNA sequenced like any other transcript.
explanations.b: Correct — ERCC transcripts are simple, single-exon sequences that only test detection and dynamic range, while SIRVs include genes with six to eighteen overlapping isoforms, letting labs measure error in isoform-level assembly and quantification.
explanations.c: Manufacturing cost is not the distinguishing feature discussed; isoform complexity is.
explanations.d: SIRVs are not restricted to a particular library prep chemistry; the distinction is about isoform complexity, not depletion method.

questions.prompt: Why does standard gene-based RNA-seq normalization fail to detect the global transcriptional amplification Nie et al. (2012) described for MYC?

options.text: Standard normalization assumes most genes are unchanged, so a genuine broad increase gets scaled away rather than detected
Standard normalization cannot process any sample with more than 10,000 genes
MYC-overexpressing samples cannot be sequenced with standard library prep
Gene-based normalization only works for single-exon transcripts

explanations.a: Correct — standard normalization scales libraries under the assumption that most genes are not differentially expressed, so a real, broad increase across most active genes looks like 'no change' once that assumption forces the data back into balance.
explanations.b: Gene count is not the limiting factor in this failure mode; the assumption about typical differential expression is.
explanations.c: MYC-overexpressing samples sequence normally; the problem is in downstream normalization and analysis, not sequencing itself.
explanations.d: This limitation applies to gene-level expression comparisons generally, not specifically to single-exon transcripts.

questions.prompt: What is a known limitation of spike-in controls like ERCC and SIRV?

options.text: They are added after RNA extraction, so they cannot correct for extraction efficiency or degradation that occurred before they were added
They can only be used with poly(A) selection, never rRNA depletion
They eliminate the need for any biological replicates
They can only be used on bacterial samples

explanations.a: Correct — because spike-ins are added after RNA extraction, they cannot control for or correct differences in extraction efficiency or degradation that happened upstream, and their simple composition does not perfectly mimic the biases affecting real endogenous mRNA.
explanations.b: Spike-ins are compatible with either library prep strategy; the limitation is about the extraction timing, not depletion chemistry.
explanations.c: Spike-ins measure technical noise and enable normalization; they do not remove the need for biological replicates to capture biological variability.
explanations.d: Spike-ins like ERCC and SIRV are used broadly across eukaryotic and other RNA-seq experiments, not restricted to bacterial samples.

lessons.label: RT-qPCR: the Targeted Workhorse and Its Rules

sections.heading: Reading the curve: Cq, exponential phase, and efficiency
sections.body: Real-time PCR (RT-qPCR when it starts from RNA) monitors fluorescence every cycle as a target amplicon doubles, and reports the quantification cycle (Cq, also called Ct) — the cycle number where fluorescence crosses a fixed threshold above background, during the exponential phase where amplification is most reliable. A standard curve, built from serial dilutions of a known template, plots Cq against the log of starting concentration; because a perfectly efficient reaction doubles product every cycle, and log2(10) is 3.32, a slope of -3.32 corresponds to 100% amplification efficiency. In practice, labs accept slopes corresponding to roughly 90-110% efficiency (about -3.1 to -3.6) — outside that band, downstream comparisons between samples become unreliable because the assumption of consistent doubling per cycle no longer holds evenly across the concentration range.

sections.heading: Relative quantification and the reference-gene trap
sections.body: The most common way to compare expression between two conditions is the 2^-ΔΔCt method, formalized by Livak and Schmittgen (2001): subtract a reference gene's Cq from the target gene's Cq in each sample (ΔCq), then subtract the control condition's ΔCq from the treatment's ΔCq (ΔΔCq), and take 2 raised to the negative of that value as the fold change — a calculation that assumes near-100% efficiency for both target and reference. The method lives or dies on the reference gene being genuinely stable. GAPDH and ACTB (beta-actin) are the traditional defaults, but they are not universally constant — their expression shifts with treatment, tissue, and cell-cycle state, which is exactly why Vandesompele and colleagues (2002) built geNorm, a tool for empirically testing candidate reference genes' stability in a specific experiment rather than assuming a textbook housekeeping gene will hold.

sections.heading: Controls, melt curves, and reporting standards
sections.body: Because qPCR is sensitive enough to amplify contamination as readily as signal, several controls are standard: a no-template control (water instead of sample) catches reagent contamination or primer-dimer formation, and a no-RT control (the RNA sample run without reverse transcriptase) catches genomic DNA contamination, since only DNA — not RNA — would amplify without a reverse-transcription step. A post-run melt curve, which ramps temperature while monitoring fluorescence, should show one sharp peak at the amplicon's melting temperature; multiple or broad peaks flag nonspecific product or primer dimers. Bustin and colleagues (2009) formalized all of this into the MIQE guidelines (Minimum Information for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments) in Clinical Chemistry, specifying what must be reported — efficiency, controls, reference-gene validation — precisely because qPCR's simplicity makes it easy to run badly and still get a confident-looking number. Its most common role in a genomics project is validation: after RNA-seq flags candidate differentially expressed genes across the whole transcriptome, RT-qPCR checks specific hits on independent samples, trading genome-wide scope for cheaper, more precise, per-gene confirmation.

lessons.workedExample: A student's RNA-seq analysis flags a candidate gene as 3-fold upregulated after treatment. To validate it by RT-qPCR, they run a standard curve for their target primers and get a slope of -3.1, corresponding to about 110% efficiency — inside the acceptable range, so they proceed. They picked ACTB as their reference gene without testing it, and after treatment, ACTB's own Cq shifts by nearly a full cycle between conditions. Using the 2^-ΔΔCt method with that unstable reference gene produces a fold-change estimate that partly reflects ACTB's own drift, not just the target gene. Running a geNorm-style stability check across a small panel of candidate reference genes and switching to a more stable one restores a fold-change estimate that matches the RNA-seq result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about RT-qPCR validation wants to see that a student understands the method has embedded assumptions that can silently produce a confident, wrong number: near-100% efficiency, a genuinely stable reference gene, and specificity confirmed by a clean melt curve and proper controls. The strongest answer names which assumption they checked and how — reporting their standard curve slope, naming their no-RT and no-template controls, or explaining why they tested rather than assumed a stable reference gene — rather than simply stating 'we ran qPCR to confirm it,' which tells a judge nothing about whether the confirmation itself can be trusted.

questions.prompt: A standard curve for a qPCR assay has a slope of -3.32. What does this indicate?

options.text: The reaction has roughly 100% amplification efficiency
The reaction has failed and should be discarded
The target gene is not expressed
The reference gene is unstable across conditions

explanations.a: Correct — because log2(10) equals 3.32, a slope of -3.32 corresponds to the amplicon doubling every cycle, i.e., roughly 100% efficiency.
explanations.b: A slope near -3.32 is the target value for a well-behaved reaction, not a failure signal.
explanations.c: The slope describes amplification efficiency across a dilution series, not whether a target is expressed in a particular sample.
explanations.d: Reference-gene stability is assessed separately (e.g., with geNorm), not from the standard-curve slope of a single assay.

questions.prompt: In the 2^-ΔΔCt method (Livak and Schmittgen, 2001), why does using an unstable reference gene distort the resulting fold-change estimate?

options.text: The method does not use a reference gene at all
ΔCq is calculated by subtracting the reference gene's Cq from the target's, so any real shift in the reference gene's own expression gets folded into the target's apparent fold change
Unstable reference genes only affect the no-template control
The method automatically corrects for reference-gene instability

explanations.a: The method's core step, ΔCq, is explicitly defined relative to a reference gene's Cq.
explanations.b: Correct — because ΔCq subtracts the reference gene's Cq from the target gene's Cq, any real change in the reference gene between conditions is subtracted into the target's calculated fold change, producing a distorted result.
explanations.c: The no-template control tests for reagent contamination, unrelated to reference-gene expression stability.
explanations.d: The 2^-ΔΔCt method has no built-in correction for reference-gene instability; that is exactly why empirical stability testing (e.g., geNorm) matters.

questions.prompt: Match each RT-qPCR control or readout to what it detects.

left.text: No-RT control (RNA run without reverse transcriptase)
A melt curve with multiple or broad peaks

right.text: Reagent contamination or primer-dimer formation
Genomic DNA contamination in the RNA sample
Nonspecific amplification product or primer dimers

questions.explanation: A no-template control catches contamination in reagents or primer-dimer formation, since no real template is present to amplify; a no-RT control catches genomic DNA contamination, since only DNA (not RNA without reverse transcription) could amplify; and a melt curve with multiple or broad peaks flags nonspecific product or primer dimers rather than a single clean amplicon.

questions.prompt: Why do Bustin et al. (2009) argue the MIQE guidelines are necessary for qPCR specifically?

options.text: Because qPCR's simplicity makes it easy to run poorly and still produce a confident-looking number, so reporting standards (efficiency, controls, reference-gene validation) are needed for reproducibility
Because qPCR machines require annual government certification
Because qPCR cannot be used for relative quantification without MIQE
Because qPCR is only valid for bacterial samples under MIQE

explanations.a: Correct — Bustin and colleagues introduced MIQE because qPCR's technical simplicity lets a poorly controlled or poorly analyzed experiment still yield a confident numeric result, so standardized reporting of efficiency, controls, and reference-gene validation is needed to make results trustworthy and reproducible.
explanations.b: MIQE is a scientific reporting standard for publications, not a hardware certification requirement.
explanations.c: The 2^-ΔΔCt relative quantification method predates and is independent of the MIQE reporting framework.
explanations.d: MIQE applies broadly to qPCR reporting across sample types, not specifically or exclusively to bacterial samples.

lessons.label: Designing the Run: Depth, Replicates, Read Length

sections.heading: How many reads do you actually need?
sections.body: Sequencing depth is a budget question disguised as a biology question. For a standard bulk gene-level differential expression (DE) experiment, roughly 10-20 million mapped reads per sample is the bare minimum to reliably detect and quantify moderately-to-highly expressed genes, because gene-level counts pool reads across every exon of a transcript. Isoform-level work — distinguishing which exon a read supports, or assembling a novel transcript no annotation predicted — needs far more coverage per base, so labs push to 30-60 million reads or more, and pair the reads (paired-end, both ends of each fragment sequenced) so a read pair can span and confirm a splice junction from two directions instead of one. ENCODE's RNA-seq standards, the most cited depth guideline in the field, set a firmer floor near 30 million reads for general-purpose expression profiling and higher for isoform-resolution work — labs sequencing near the 10-20 million minimum are trading off below that recommended standard, precisely because the question you're asking sets the depth you need, not the other way around.

sections.heading: Replicates beat depth: Liu, Zhou & White (2014)
sections.body: Given a fixed sequencing budget, should you sequence 3 samples deeper or 6 samples shallower? Liu, Zhou & White (2014) answered this directly by simulating RNA-seq experiments across a range of depths and replicate counts and counting how many true DE genes each design recovered. Their result: adding biological replicates increased detection power more than adding sequencing depth, once depth passed a modest threshold (roughly 10 million reads). A design with more replicates at moderate depth consistently outperformed fewer replicates sequenced twice as deep. This is now the standard justification for n≥3 biological replicates per condition as a floor, not a nicety — with n=2 you cannot estimate within-group variance in a way that generalizes, and most DE tools (DESeq2, edgeR) either refuse to run or produce untrustworthy p-values.

sections.heading: Biological vs. technical replicates, and budgeting lanes
sections.body: A technical replicate — resequencing the same RNA library, or re-preparing a library from the same RNA extraction — mostly re-measures Illumina's own sequencing noise, which is already low and well-characterized; it tells you almost nothing about whether an effect will reproduce in another animal, plant, or patient. A biological replicate — an independent organism, culture dish, or tissue sample per condition — captures the variance that actually matters: individual variability. So if a grant funds one flow cell's worth of reads, splitting it three ways across biological replicates per condition is worth far more than spending it all deepening one sample. A practical budget: fix a target reads-per-sample from the depth table above, divide the flow cell's total output by that number, and that quotient is the maximum sample count — spend it on replicates and conditions, not on redundant depth.

lessons.workedExample: A lab has one NovaSeq lane yielding about 400 million read pairs and wants to compare drug-treated vs. control cells for gene-level DE. At 30 million reads/sample — ENCODE's recommended floor for general-purpose profiling — they can afford about 13 samples, roughly n=6 per condition, well above the n≥3 floor, with headroom to catch weaker effects. If they instead chased isoform-level resolution at 50 million reads/sample, the same lane affords only 8 samples (n=4 per condition) — still above the floor, but with much less power per Liu, Zhou & White's finding that replicates, not depth, drive detection. The right call depends on the question: gene-level DE favors the first split; a novel-isoform hunt justifies the second.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how many replicates did you run, and why?' because the answer instantly reveals whether a student understands that RNA-seq variance comes from biology, not from the sequencer. A student who says 'n=3 per condition because two replicates can't estimate variance, and I'd rather have replicates than more depth' is citing the actual statistical logic (and implicitly the Liu, Zhou & White finding) rather than a rule memorized without reason. A student who ran n=1 per condition, or confused resequencing the same sample with a biological replicate, has a result that cannot support a DE claim regardless of how clean the rest of the pipeline is.

questions.prompt: Given a fixed sequencing budget, Liu, Zhou & White (2014) found that detection power for DE genes is generally increased more by:

options.text: Sequencing fewer samples much more deeply
Adding biological replicates rather than adding depth, once depth passes a modest threshold
Using single-end reads instead of paired-end reads
Resequencing the same library as a technical replicate

explanations.a: Their simulation showed the opposite past a modest depth threshold — extra depth gave diminishing returns compared to extra replicates.
explanations.b: Correct — once depth passed roughly 10 million reads, adding biological replicates recovered more true DE genes than adding further depth.
explanations.c: Read pairing affects junction-spanning resolution, not the replicates-vs-depth tradeoff this study addressed.
explanations.d: Technical replicates were not the variable in this comparison, and they don't capture the biological variance that limits DE detection anyway.

questions.prompt: Why is a technical replicate (resequencing the same RNA library) a poor substitute for a biological replicate in a DE experiment?

options.text: It is more expensive than a biological replicate
It mostly re-measures Illumina sequencing noise, not the individual-to-individual variability a DE test needs to estimate
It cannot be sequenced on the same flow cell
It always produces fewer mapped reads

explanations.a: Cost isn't the core issue — the statistical content of the measurement is.
explanations.b: Correct — Illumina sequencing noise is already low and well-characterized, so re-measuring it tells you little about whether an effect generalizes across organisms or samples.
explanations.c: There's no such restriction; the issue is what variance the replicate captures, not flow-cell logistics.
explanations.d: Read count isn't systematically different for a technical replicate; the problem is what the replicate measures, not its yield.

questions.prompt: A student wants to detect novel splice isoforms, not just gene-level expression changes. Which design choice does this most directly justify?

options.text: Dropping to n=2 replicates to afford more depth
Higher depth (30-60M+ reads) and paired-end reads, so a read pair can span and confirm a junction
Using only technical replicates to save budget
Single-end reads at 10 million reads per sample

explanations.a: n=2 falls below the replicate floor regardless of the question being asked, and depth alone doesn't compensate for lost replication.
explanations.b: Correct — isoform-level and novel-transcript work needs deeper coverage per base and paired ends to confirm junctions from both directions.
explanations.c: Technical replicates don't add the coverage or junction-spanning information isoform detection needs.
explanations.d: This depth and read type match gene-level DE, not isoform-resolution work.

questions.prompt: Match each sequencing design element to what it primarily buys you.

right.text: Resolution to detect isoforms and novel transcripts
Statistical power to detect true DE genes across individuals
Confirmation of a splice junction from both fragment ends
Re-measurement of sequencer noise, not biological variance

questions.explanation: Depth buys per-base resolution for isoforms; biological replicates buy the statistical power DE testing depends on; paired-end reads let a fragment's two ends jointly confirm a junction; a technical replicate mainly re-measures the sequencer's own low, well-characterized noise.

lessons.label: Raw Reads and Quality Control

sections.heading: FASTQ: sequence plus a confidence score for every base
sections.body: A sequencer doesn't output clean DNA letters — it outputs a FASTQ file, four lines per read: an identifier line starting with '@', the called sequence (A/C/G/T/N), a '+' separator, and a line of ASCII characters encoding a Phred quality score per base. Phred score Q relates to error probability by Q = -10·log10(p): Q20 means a 1-in-100 chance that base is wrong, Q30 means 1-in-1000. Illumina platforms typically report Phred+33 encoding, where the ASCII character's numeric value minus 33 gives Q. A 150 bp read with Q30 across the board is trustworthy; a read that decays to Q15 near the 3' end (common — synthesis errors accumulate as a sequencing cycle runs longer) is not, and that decay is exactly what quality control is built to catch before it contaminates every downstream step.

sections.heading: FastQC: the modules that actually matter for RNA
sections.body: FastQC runs a fixed battery of checks, but for RNA-seq four modules carry the diagnostic weight. Per-base sequence quality shows the Q-score decay curve described above — a healthy run is flat and high, then droops gently at the 3' end. Adapter content flags when library-prep adapter sequence (the short synthetic oligo used to prime sequencing) appears within reads, which happens when the cDNA fragment was shorter than the read length and sequencing ran off the end into pure adapter. Overrepresented sequences flags any single sequence dominating the pool — in RNA-seq this is diagnostic rather than cosmetic: a burst of one rRNA sequence means the ribosomal-RNA depletion or poly-A selection step failed, and a burst of adapter dimer means fragment sizing failed. Sequence duplication levels shows how often the same read recurs; RNA-seq legitimately has high duplication because a handful of genes (actin, ribosomal protein genes) are so highly expressed that many independent fragments coincidentally map to the same start site — unlike DNA-seq, high duplication here is not automatically a red flag.

sections.heading: Trimming, MultiQC, and the numbers that separate salvageable from failed
sections.body: Adapter/quality trimming (Trimmomatic, fastp, cutadapt) removes adapter contamination and low-quality tails before alignment. Trim too aggressively, though, and you shorten reads below what a spliced aligner needs to confidently place a read spanning a junction, or you strip real biological signal that just happened to have a noisier basecall — trimming should target adapter sequence and clear quality collapse, not chase a slightly-lower-than-ideal average. MultiQC (Ewels et al. 2016) aggregates every sample's FastQC report into one dashboard, which matters because a single sample's numbers mean little in isolation — you need the batch to spot the one outlier. The numbers that separate salvageable from failed: alignment rate above roughly 80% for a good human/mouse library (below ~70% suggests contamination or the wrong reference), rRNA fraction that should be a low single-digit percentage after depletion, and duplication that's expected to be high for expression data but should track similarly across samples in the same experiment — a duplication spike unique to one sample flags degraded input RNA.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs FastQC on 6 samples and MultiQC flags one outlier: 45% adapter content, 22% rRNA, and a final alignment rate of 61%, while the other five sit at <2% adapter, <3% rRNA, and >85% alignment. The adapter content points to over-fragmented or under-sized cDNA inserts in that one library prep; the elevated rRNA points to a failed depletion step for that same sample. Rather than discarding the whole experiment, the student re-trims that sample with a stricter adapter-removal pass, reruns FastQC to confirm adapter content drops, and flags the sample's rRNA fraction as a caveat in downstream analysis — while treating the other five as clean and salvaging the run instead of resequencing everything.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes QC numbers because they're the fastest way to tell if a student trusts their pipeline blindly or actually looked at it. Naming a concrete threshold — 'alignment rate was 85%, well above the ~80% floor I'd expect for human RNA-seq' — shows the student knows what a healthy run looks like and checked. A student who can't say whether their rRNA fraction or duplication level was normal, or who trimmed every sample uniformly without checking whether trimming was even needed, has run a pipeline without knowing what it produced.

questions.prompt: A base has a Phred quality score of Q20. What is the approximate probability that base was called incorrectly?

options.text: 1 in 10
1 in 20

explanations.a: That error rate corresponds to Q10, not Q20.
explanations.b: Correct — Q = -10·log10(p), so Q20 gives p = 10^(-20/10) = 0.01, or 1 in 100.
explanations.c: That's the error rate for Q30, one order of magnitude better than Q20.
explanations.d: This isn't how the Phred formula maps score to probability.

questions.prompt: FastQC's overrepresented-sequences module flags a single sequence dominating an RNA-seq library. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: The sample is simply from a highly active tissue and no action is needed
Failed rRNA depletion/poly-A selection, or adapter dimer from failed fragment sizing
The sequencer's Phred scoring malfunctioned
The library has too many biological replicates

explanations.a: High expression of many genes doesn't produce a single dominating sequence the way a failed depletion or sizing step does.
explanations.b: Correct — in RNA-seq, a single overrepresented sequence typically diagnoses a failed rRNA-depletion/poly-A step or adapter dimer from fragment-sizing failure.
explanations.c: Overrepresentation is about sequence content, not the quality-score encoding.
explanations.d: Replicate count is a study-design choice unrelated to what one library's sequence content shows.

questions.prompt: Why is high sequence duplication in RNA-seq NOT automatically treated as a red flag, unlike in DNA-seq?

options.text: FastQC does not compute duplication for RNA-seq libraries
A handful of very highly expressed genes legitimately generate many independent fragments that map to the same start site
RNA-seq reads are always shorter, so duplicates are undercounted
Duplication only matters after alignment, not in FastQC

explanations.a: FastQC does compute a duplication-level module for any FASTQ input, RNA-seq included.
explanations.b: Correct — genes like actin or ribosomal proteins are expressed so highly that many biologically independent fragments coincidentally share a start site, producing legitimate high duplication.
explanations.c: Read length isn't the reason duplication runs high in RNA-seq; expression skew is.
explanations.d: FastQC's duplication module runs on raw reads before alignment.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of trimming reads too aggressively before alignment?

options.text: It increases the rRNA fraction
It can shorten reads below what a spliced aligner needs to confidently place a junction-spanning read, and can strip real signal
It always lowers the Phred score of remaining bases
It converts paired-end reads into single-end reads

explanations.a: Trimming affects read length and adapter content, not the biological rRNA fraction of the library.
explanations.b: Correct — over-trimming can leave reads too short to confidently span a splice junction, and can discard bases that were biologically real, just noisier.
explanations.c: Trimming removes low-quality bases; it doesn't change the Phred score of the bases that remain.
