explanations.d: Trimming operates within each read independently and does not merge or split a read pair's mate structure.

lessons.label: Splice-Aware Alignment to the Genome

sections.heading: Why a DNA aligner breaks on RNA reads
sections.body: A DNA aligner like BWA assumes a read is a contiguous stretch of the genome, tolerating small mismatches and short indels but not a large gap. RNA reads violate that assumption constantly: after splicing, a mature mRNA stitches together exons that can sit tens of thousands of bases apart in the genome, with introns removed entirely. A 100 bp RNA-seq read straddling an exon-exon junction has its first 40 bases matching one genomic location and its last 60 matching a location 8,000 bases downstream — to a DNA aligner that looks like a read with a massive, un-alignable gap, and it either gets discarded or forced into a bad, mismatch-heavy placement. Roughly a third of reads from a typical library span a junction somewhere, so ignoring this isn't a rare-edge-case problem — it silently kills a large chunk of the data.

sections.heading: How STAR and HISAT2 solve it
sections.body: Splice-aware aligners solve this by allowing a read to be split across two or more genomic locations connected by a large gap that corresponds to a real or plausible intron, then reporting that gap as a supported junction. STAR (Dobin et al. 2013) uses a maximal mappable seed search — extending each read as far as it uniquely matches, then re-seeding the unmatched remainder — which lets it find junctions de novo without needing them pre-annotated, and made it fast enough to become the field's default for well-resourced projects (it trades speed for a large in-memory genome index, tens of GB of RAM for a human genome). HISAT2 (Kim et al. 2015, updated 2019) instead builds a hierarchical index — a global FM-index of the genome plus many small local indexes around known and predicted splice sites — trading some of STAR's raw junction-discovery power for a dramatically smaller memory footprint, making it practical on a laptop. Both aligners output a junctions file alongside the alignment, listing every splice site the reads supported and how many reads crossed it, which is itself useful data — novel junctions absent from the reference annotation are candidate new isoforms.

sections.heading: Mapping rates, multimapping, and genome vs. transcriptome alignment
sections.body: For a good-quality human RNA-seq library, ENCODE-style QC expects north of 80% of reads to map uniquely to one genomic location; a rate meaningfully below that points to contamination, degraded RNA, or a mismatched reference genome build. The reads that don't map uniquely are mostly multimappers — reads equally consistent with two or more locations, which happens constantly for paralogous genes (near-duplicate genes from gene-family expansion) and repetitive elements. A multimapping read can't be assigned to one gene with confidence, so counting tools either discard it, split its weight fractionally across candidate loci, or assign it to a merged locus — and each choice biases counts for gene families differently, which is why paralog-heavy genes deserve extra scrutiny. Aligning to the genome plus an annotation (STAR/HISAT2's approach) can discover novel junctions and genes absent from the annotation, at the cost of needing the whole genome indexed; aligning only to a transcriptome (a curated set of known transcript sequences) is faster and simpler but is blind to anything not already annotated — it can only ever confirm what's already known to exist.

lessons.workedExample: A student aligns 20 million paired-end human RNA-seq reads with STAR against the reference genome plus a GENCODE annotation. The report shows 84% uniquely mapped, 9% mapped to multiple loci, and 7% unmapped. The 9% multimapping rate is unremarkable — it largely reflects genes with close paralogues (like histone gene clusters) and repetitive elements genome-wide. But if that number had come back at 35%, the student would suspect a lower-complexity library (e.g., PCR over-amplification collapsing diversity) or contamination with a repeat-rich sequence. The junctions file additionally reports 1,200 splice junctions not present in the GENCODE annotation, each junction supported by at least 3 independent reads — a modest but real signal worth flagging as candidate novel splicing, not proof of a new isoform on its own.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what aligner did you use, and why not just BWA?' is testing whether a student understands that RNA reads are not contiguous genomic sequence — the correct answer names the exon-junction problem directly, not just 'because that's what the tutorial used.' Pressing further on the uniquely-mapped percentage and what a low number would mean tests whether the student treated the alignment rate as a real QC gate or just moved past it to get to counts. A student who can explain why a multimapping read from a paralogous gene family can't simply be assigned to one gene has grasped a real limitation of the method, not just its happy path.

questions.prompt: Why does a standard DNA aligner (e.g., BWA) fail on many RNA-seq reads?

options.text: RNA reads contain more sequencing errors than DNA reads
A read spanning an exon-exon junction requires a large gap in the alignment that corresponds to a removed intron, which DNA aligners aren't built to allow
DNA aligners cannot process paired-end reads
RNA reads are always shorter than the minimum length DNA aligners accept

explanations.a: The failure isn't about error rate; RNA and DNA reads from the same platform have comparable base-call error profiles.
explanations.b: Correct — a junction-spanning read's two halves can map tens of thousands of bases apart on the genome because the intron between them was spliced out, which a DNA aligner treats as an un-alignable gap.
explanations.c: Paired-end support is unrelated to the splicing issue; the problem is within-read gaps, not pairing.
explanations.d: Read length is a library-prep choice, not the cause of the junction-alignment failure.

questions.prompt: What is the key architectural difference between how STAR and HISAT2 find splice junctions?

options.text: STAR uses a maximal mappable seed search with a large genome index; HISAT2 uses a hierarchical index (global FM-index plus small local indexes) for a much smaller memory footprint
STAR only works on mouse genomes; HISAT2 only works on human genomes
HISAT2 cannot report novel junctions absent from the annotation
STAR aligns only to the transcriptome, never to the genome

explanations.a: Correct — STAR's seed-and-extend approach needs a large in-memory index but can find junctions de novo; HISAT2's hierarchical indexing trades some of that discovery power for a much smaller memory footprint.
explanations.b: Both aligners are species-agnostic; the difference is indexing strategy, not organism restriction.
explanations.c: HISAT2 can identify novel junctions too, just via a different, more memory-efficient indexing strategy than STAR's.
explanations.d: STAR aligns to the genome (plus annotation), which is exactly what enables it to discover novel junctions.

questions.prompt: A read maps equally well to two paralogous genes and is called a multimapper. What is the core problem this creates for gene counting?

options.text: The read must be discarded from the FASTQ file entirely before counting can begin
The read cannot be assigned to one gene with confidence, so different counting choices (discard, fractional split, merge) bias paralog-family counts differently
It proves the sample was contaminated with another species
It means the read failed Phred quality filtering

explanations.a: Discarding is only one of several counting-tool choices, not a required step before counting starts.
explanations.b: Correct — because the read is genuinely ambiguous, however the counting tool handles it (discard, split, merge) systematically biases counts for paralog-heavy gene families.
explanations.c: Multimapping to paralogues is a normal genome-structure phenomenon, not a sign of cross-species contamination.
explanations.d: Multimapping is about placement ambiguity in the genome, unrelated to base-call quality scores.

questions.prompt: What can genome-plus-annotation alignment discover that transcriptome-only alignment cannot?

options.text: Higher Phred quality scores for each read
Novel junctions and genes not already present in the reference annotation
Faster processing time per sample
Lower memory usage

explanations.a: Alignment target doesn't change a read's intrinsic quality scores.
explanations.b: Correct — because it uses the whole genome, not just known transcripts, genome-plus-annotation alignment can find splice junctions and loci absent from the existing annotation; transcriptome-only alignment can only confirm what's already known.
explanations.c: Genome alignment is typically slower and more resource-intensive than transcriptome-only alignment, not faster.
explanations.d: Genome alignment requires indexing the whole genome, which uses more memory, not less.

lessons.label: Pseudoalignment and Transcript-Level Quantification

sections.heading: Skipping base-level alignment entirely
sections.body: Full spliced alignment (STAR, HISAT2) figures out the exact genomic coordinate and CIGAR string for every base of every read — powerful, but computationally heavy: it can take hours per sample and demands a large indexed genome. kallisto (Bray, Pimentel, Melsted & Pachter, 2016) introduced pseudoalignment: instead of asking 'exactly where does this read align, base by base,' it asks only 'which transcripts is this read compatible with?' It does this by breaking each read into k-mers (short fixed-length subsequences) and looking each one up in a hash index built from the transcriptome's k-mer content, quickly narrowing each read to the set of transcripts that share its k-mers. No base-by-base alignment, no CIGAR string, no genome coordinate — just a compatibility class per read. salmon (Patro, Duggal, Love, Irizarry & Kingsford, 2017) takes a related but distinct approach, using a lightweight mapping procedure and a richer statistical model of fragment generation, but shares kallisto's core move of skipping full alignment in favor of transcript-level compatibility. The payoff is speed: both tools quantify a typical sample in minutes on a laptop rather than the hour-plus and large-memory footprint full alignment needs — often reported as orders of magnitude faster.

sections.heading: Resolving ambiguity with the EM algorithm, and correcting bias
sections.body: Most reads are compatible with more than one transcript — isoforms of the same gene share most of their exons, so a read from a shared exon can't be assigned to one isoform by k-mer compatibility alone. kallisto and salmon resolve this with an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm: starting from a guess at each transcript's abundance, it computes the probability each ambiguous read belongs to each compatible transcript given current abundance estimates (the E-step), then re-estimates abundances from those probabilistically-assigned reads (the M-step), iterating until the estimates converge. This lets a read from a shared exon still contribute correctly to two isoforms' relative abundances instead of being thrown out or forced onto one arbitrarily. Both tools also correct for known biases in library prep: GC bias (regions of extreme GC content are amplified unevenly by PCR) and positional bias (coverage often isn't flat along a transcript — 3' bias from poly-A priming is common), fitting empirical bias models from the data itself rather than assuming reads are drawn uniformly at random.

sections.heading: From transcripts to genes with tximport, and where full alignment is still required
sections.body: Because most downstream DE tools (DESeq2, edgeR) expect gene-level counts, tximport (Soneson, Love & Robinson, 2015) rolls transcript-level abundance estimates from kallisto or salmon up to the gene level, summing the transcript estimates for each gene while preserving the more accurate transcript-level EM resolution underneath — shown to give better gene-level inference than counting at the gene level from scratch. But pseudoalignment isn't a universal replacement for full alignment. It can only quantify transcripts already present in its reference index, so it's blind to novel, unannotated transcripts or fusion genes. It reports no genomic coordinates, so it can't feed variant calling, which needs to know exactly where a read sits on the genome. And it has no real junction-QC output the way STAR's junctions file does, since it never determines which specific bases crossed which intron. For known-annotation gene expression and transcript-level quantification, pseudoalignment is now the standard, faster tool; for discovery work, full spliced alignment is still required.

lessons.workedExample: A lab quantifying 24 human RNA-seq samples against a known transcriptome runs salmon on each in about 4 minutes per sample on a standard laptop, versus an estimated hour-plus each with STAR on a compute cluster. For a gene with three annotated isoforms sharing a common first exon, salmon's EM algorithm assigns reads from that shared exon probabilistically across all three isoforms based on how much unique-exon evidence supports each one, then tximport sums the three isoform estimates into one gene-level count fed to DESeq2. When the lab later suspects a fusion transcript between two genes near a translocation breakpoint, they switch to STAR for that specific question, because salmon's transcriptome index has no entry for a sequence that doesn't exist in the reference.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why kallisto/salmon instead of STAR?' to check whether a student picked the fast tool blindly or understood the actual tradeoff: speed and transcript-level resolution via pseudoalignment and EM, at the cost of being unable to discover anything outside the reference transcriptome. A strong answer names the EM step and explains why it's needed (shared exons make reads ambiguous between isoforms), and can say in one sentence why the lab would still need STAR for a novel-transcript or variant-calling question. A student who calls pseudoalignment 'basically the same as alignment but faster' has missed that it answers a genuinely different question — compatibility, not coordinate.

questions.prompt: What question does pseudoalignment (kallisto, salmon) answer for each read, instead of a full base-level alignment?

options.text: Exactly which genomic coordinate and CIGAR string the read matches
Which transcripts the read is compatible with, based on shared k-mers
Whether the read passed Phred quality filtering
Which sequencing lane the read originated from

explanations.a: That base-by-base coordinate answer is exactly what full alignment (STAR/HISAT2) provides and pseudoalignment skips.
explanations.b: Correct — pseudoalignment narrows each read to a compatibility class of transcripts sharing its k-mers, without computing a base-level alignment.
explanations.c: Quality filtering happens upstream in QC/trimming, not as part of pseudoalignment's core question.
explanations.d: Lane of origin is metadata unrelated to what pseudoalignment computes about a read.

questions.prompt: Why do kallisto and salmon use an EM algorithm during quantification?

options.text: To correct sequencer hardware calibration errors
To probabilistically assign reads that are compatible with multiple isoforms (e.g., from a shared exon) to the transcripts they most likely came from
To convert paired-end reads into single-end reads
To trim adapter sequence from raw reads

explanations.a: EM here operates on abundance estimation, not sequencer hardware.
explanations.b: Correct — because isoforms of a gene share exons, many reads are compatible with more than one transcript, and EM iteratively estimates abundances and reassigns ambiguous reads until convergence.
explanations.c: Read pairing is a library-prep property untouched by the EM quantification step.
explanations.d: Adapter trimming is a separate upstream QC step, not part of EM-based quantification.

questions.prompt: What does tximport (Soneson, Love & Robinson, 2015) do?

options.text: Performs the initial pseudoalignment of raw reads to a transcriptome
Rolls transcript-level abundance estimates from kallisto/salmon up to gene-level counts for tools like DESeq2
Runs FastQC on raw FASTQ files
Calls genetic variants from aligned reads

explanations.a: Pseudoalignment itself is performed by kallisto or salmon, upstream of tximport.
explanations.b: Correct — tximport sums transcript-level estimates into gene-level counts, preserving the more accurate transcript-level EM resolution for downstream DE tools.
explanations.c: FastQC is a separate raw-read QC tool unrelated to tximport's role.
explanations.d: Variant calling requires genomic coordinates from full alignment, which pseudoalignment-based workflows don't produce.

questions.prompt: A researcher needs to detect a fusion transcript not present in any reference annotation. Why is salmon alone insufficient for this task?

options.text: Salmon can only process paired-end reads
Salmon can only quantify transcripts already present in its reference index, so it's blind to sequences absent from that index
Salmon does not correct for GC or positional bias
Salmon requires more RAM than STAR

explanations.a: Read pairing isn't the limiting factor for fusion detection.
explanations.b: Correct — pseudoalignment tools quantify against a fixed transcriptome index and have no mechanism to identify a novel sequence, like a fusion junction, that isn't already in that index.
explanations.c: Salmon does model and correct GC and positional bias; that isn't the limitation here.
explanations.d: Salmon's memory footprint is typically smaller than full genome aligners, not larger — and memory isn't the reason it misses fusions.

lessons.label: Counting Reads and the Annotation You Chose

sections.heading: From aligned reads to a per-gene count
sections.body: Once reads are aligned to the genome (say, by STAR), someone still has to decide which gene each aligned read belongs to — that's the job of a counting tool, most commonly featureCounts (Liao, Smyth & Shi, 2014) or HTSeq-count (Anders, Pyl & Huber, 2015). Both take an alignment file and a GTF (Gene Transfer Format) annotation describing where every gene's exons sit, then overlap each read's genomic position against those exon coordinates. The simple case — a read falls cleanly inside one gene's exon and nowhere else — is unambiguous. The hard cases are what actually distinguish the tools: a read overlapping two genes' exons at once (common when genes sit close together or overlap on opposite strands), or a read falling in an intron or intergenic region with no annotated feature at all. featureCounts by default discards reads overlapping more than one feature (ambiguous) and reads with no feature overlap at all; HTSeq-count offers several explicit modes (union, intersection-strict, intersection-nonempty) that handle partial-overlap cases differently, and the choice of mode changes the count for genes with overlapping neighbors.

sections.heading: Two labs, same FASTQs, different annotation, different answer
sections.body: The GTF file itself is not one fixed truth — GENCODE, RefSeq, and Ensembl are three actively maintained annotation sources that disagree on gene boundaries, which transcripts count as real, and how many genes exist at all, because each project makes different curation calls about weak evidence (a single EST match, a low-confidence prediction) and updates on a different schedule. GENCODE tends toward a more comprehensive, inclusive gene set including many lncRNAs and predicted transcripts; RefSeq is more conservative, favoring transcripts with strong experimental support. This isn't a cosmetic difference: reprocessing the identical FASTQ files with GENCODE v44 versus an older RefSeq build can shift which genes even exist in the count matrix, change exon boundaries enough to reclassify reads from 'unambiguous' to 'ambiguous' near gene edges, and produce a measurably different DE gene list from the same raw data — a result documented repeatedly when labs have compared pipelines run on identical reads with different annotation choices.

sections.heading: Where counts leak: unannotated and overlapping genes
sections.body: Two systematic leaks are worth knowing by name. First, any transcribed region absent from the chosen GTF — a novel lncRNA, an alternative promoter, a gene simply missing from that annotation's version — contributes reads that counting tools discard as 'no feature,' silently lowering the total usable read count and making that biology invisible no matter how real the signal is. Second, overlapping genes (antisense pairs, nested genes, genes sharing a locus on opposite strands) force a real choice: count the read for both genes, neither, or resolve by strand information if the library prep preserved strandedness (a stranded protocol lets you tell which strand a read came from, resolving many overlaps that an unstranded protocol cannot). A GTF version mismatch between alignment and counting steps, or a mismatch between the genome build used to align and the GTF used to count, produces coordinate errors that silently misassign or drop reads rather than throwing a visible error — which is why documenting the exact annotation version used is not bookkeeping, it's part of the result.

lessons.workedExample: A student processes the same 20M-read FASTQ file twice with featureCounts: once against GENCODE v44 and once against an older RefSeq annotation. The GENCODE run reports counts for 2,000 more genes (many lncRNAs RefSeq doesn't include) and, near a locus where two genes overlap on opposite strands, assigns 340 reads to one gene under GENCODE's boundaries versus splitting those same reads between two genes under RefSeq's slightly different exon coordinates. The DE gene list downstream differs by several dozen genes between the two runs — not because the biology changed, but because the annotation choice did. The student reports the exact GTF version and source used, because 'GENCODE v44, primary assembly' is not the same experiment as 'RefSeq GRCh38.p14 annotation.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'what annotation and version did you use?' is checking whether a student understands that a GTF is a choice, not a fixed ground truth — an answer that names the source and version demonstrates that, while 'I used the standard one' does not. Pressing on how the tool handled a read overlapping two genes tests whether the student engaged with the counting tool's actual decision rules or treated it as a black box. The strongest answers connect the two: naming a specific gene or region where switching annotation actually changed a result, which proves the student reprocessed rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: By default, how does featureCounts typically handle a read that overlaps exons from two different genes?

options.text: It assigns the read fully to both genes
It discards the read as ambiguous
It always assigns the read to the longer gene
It randomly assigns the read to one of the two genes

explanations.a: Double-counting a multi-gene-overlapping read isn't featureCounts' default behavior.
explanations.b: Correct — featureCounts' default discards reads overlapping more than one feature as ambiguous, rather than guessing an assignment.
explanations.c: Gene length isn't the default tiebreaker featureCounts uses for overlap ambiguity.
explanations.d: The default is a deterministic discard, not a random assignment.

questions.prompt: Why can reprocessing the identical FASTQ files with GENCODE versus RefSeq annotation produce a different DE gene list?

options.text: GENCODE and RefSeq use different Phred quality encodings
The two annotation sources disagree on gene boundaries and which transcripts count as real, changing which reads are ambiguous or unassigned
RefSeq annotations can only be used with HTSeq-count, not featureCounts
GENCODE requires a different sequencing platform

explanations.a: Phred encoding is a property of the raw FASTQ file, unrelated to which GTF annotation is used downstream.
explanations.b: Correct — differing curation calls about gene boundaries and transcript confidence between GENCODE and RefSeq change which reads are unambiguous, ambiguous, or unassigned, shifting the resulting counts and DE list.
explanations.c: Both featureCounts and HTSeq-count accept a GTF from any source; there's no such restriction.
explanations.d: Annotation choice is independent of the sequencing platform used to generate the reads.

questions.prompt: A gene exists biologically but is absent from the GTF file used for counting. What happens to reads from that gene?

options.text: They are automatically added as a new gene entry in the output
They are discarded as 'no feature,' silently lowering usable read count and hiding that biology
They are counted toward the nearest annotated gene regardless of distance
The counting tool throws a fatal error and stops

explanations.a: Counting tools work from the GTF as given; they don't discover or add new gene entries on their own.
explanations.b: Correct — reads with no overlapping annotated feature are discarded as 'no feature,' which silently makes that gene's expression invisible in the count matrix.
explanations.c: Standard counting tools don't reassign reads to the nearest gene by proximity when there's no direct overlap.
explanations.d: This is a silent, not a fatal, failure mode — the pipeline completes without flagging the missing biology.

questions.prompt: Match each scenario to the counting/annotation issue it illustrates.

left.text: A read overlaps exons from two genes on opposite strands
A real lncRNA is absent from the chosen GTF
Alignment used one genome build, counting used a GTF from a different build
The library prep preserved strand information

right.text: Can help resolve which of two overlapping genes a read truly belongs to
Contributes reads that get discarded as 'no feature,' hiding real biology
Produces coordinate mismatches that silently misassign or drop reads
A case counting tools must explicitly decide how to resolve (assign, discard, or split)

questions.explanation: Overlapping-gene reads force an explicit ambiguity decision by the counting tool; an unannotated gene's reads leak out as 'no feature'; a genome-build/GTF mismatch causes silent coordinate errors; and strand-preserving library prep can resolve overlaps that an unstranded protocol cannot.

lessons.label: Units: Counts, CPM, RPKM/FPKM, and TPM

sections.heading: Raw counts and the two things that distort them
sections.body: A raw count — the number of reads (or fragments) a counting tool assigned to a gene — is the ground-truth output of the pipeline, but it's distorted by two factors that have nothing to do with true expression: sequencing depth (a sample sequenced to 40 million reads will show roughly double the counts of an identical sample at 20 million, for every gene, with no biological difference) and gene length (a 6 kb transcript accumulates more reads than a 1 kb transcript expressed at the identical molar level, simply because a longer transcript offers more positions for a fragment to start from). Counts-per-million (CPM) fixes only the first problem: divide each gene's count by the sample's total mapped reads (in millions), so CPM = count / (total mapped reads / 10^6). CPM makes samples comparable to each other for the same gene, but does nothing about gene length, so it's unsuitable for comparing two different genes' expression within one sample.

sections.heading: RPKM/FPKM and TPM: same idea, opposite order of operations
sections.body: RPKM (Reads Per Kilobase per Million mapped reads) and its paired-end sibling FPKM (Fragments Per Kilobase per Million) fix both problems by dividing by library size first, then by gene length: RPKM = (reads mapped to gene / (total mapped reads / 10^6)) / (gene length in kb). TPM (Transcripts Per Million) computes the same two corrections in the opposite order — divide each gene's count by its length first (giving reads-per-kilobase, RPK), sum those RPK values across all genes in the sample, then divide every gene's RPK by that per-sample sum and multiply by 10^6. That reordering has a mathematically guaranteed consequence: TPM values in any sample always sum to exactly 10^6, by construction, because the normalizing denominator is built from the same sample's own gene-length-corrected values. RPKM/FPKM have no such property — the sum of RPKM across genes in a sample varies from sample to sample depending on that sample's specific expression distribution, because the length correction happens after the library-size correction rather than feeding into it.

sections.heading: Why that difference matters, and the rule DE tools enforce
sections.body: Wagner, Kin & Lynch (2012) made this the center of their argument against RPKM/FPKM for cross-sample comparison: because RPKM's per-sample total isn't fixed, the same true proportion of a transcriptome devoted to one gene can produce different RPKM values in two samples whose overall expression distributions differ — for instance, if one sample has a few extremely highly-expressed genes soaking up a large share of total reads, every other gene's RPKM in that sample gets compressed relative to a sample without that skew, even if that gene's true relative abundance didn't change. TPM's fixed-sum property makes it far more directly comparable across samples for exactly this reason, which is why TPM has largely displaced RPKM/FPKM for visualization and cross-sample comparison. But there's a rule underneath all of this that students most often break: every normalized unit — CPM, RPKM/FPKM, TPM — is for human-facing visualization and rough cross-sample comparison, never for feeding into a DE tool. DESeq2 and edgeR require raw integer counts as input because their statistical models (negative binomial distributions) explicitly model count noise and perform their own internal normalization (like DESeq2's median-of-ratios); feeding them pre-normalized, non-integer values breaks that model and invalidates the p-values it produces.

lessons.workedExample: A gene has 1,000 raw reads in Sample A (20 million total mapped reads) and 1,000 raw reads in Sample B (40 million total mapped reads), both for a 2 kb transcript. Raw counts look identical, but CPM tells the real story: Sample A's CPM is 1,000 / 20 = 50; Sample B's CPM is 1,000 / 40 = 25 — the gene's relative expression is actually half as high in B despite matching raw counts, because B was sequenced twice as deep. Converting to RPKM divides each by the 2 kb gene length (in kb), giving 25 and 12.5 respectively — same relative relationship, but the RPKM values for this gene can't be safely compared to a different gene's RPKM sum across the whole sample, whereas TPM values for every gene in Sample A will still sum to exactly 1,000,000, and likewise for Sample B, regardless of how skewed either sample's expression distribution is.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why TPM and not RPKM for your heatmap, and what did you feed DESeq2?' is running two checks at once: whether the student understands that TPM's fixed per-sample sum is what makes it more comparable across samples (the Wagner, Kin & Lynch argument), and whether the student knows DE testing needs raw counts, not normalized values. A student who normalized their counts to TPM and then fed those TPM values directly into DESeq2 has invalidated their own statistics without realizing it — this is the single most common technical error in student RNA-seq projects, and catching it is a fast way to separate a student who understands the pipeline from one who followed a tutorial's commands without knowing what each step required as input.

questions.prompt: What mathematical property is guaranteed for TPM values within any single sample, but NOT for RPKM/FPKM values?

options.text: TPM values are always integers
TPM values across all genes in a sample always sum to exactly 10^6
TPM values are always higher than the corresponding RPKM values
TPM requires paired-end reads while RPKM does not

explanations.a: TPM values are typically fractional, not integers, since they're a normalized ratio.
explanations.b: Correct — because TPM normalizes by gene length before summing across genes to build its denominator, every sample's TPM values sum to exactly 10^6 by construction; RPKM's per-sample sum varies because its length correction happens after the library-size correction.
explanations.c: There's no fixed magnitude relationship guaranteed between TPM and RPKM for a given gene.
explanations.d: Both TPM and RPKM/FPKM can be computed from single-end or paired-end data (FPKM is simply the paired-end/fragment-based variant); read pairing isn't what distinguishes them mathematically.

questions.prompt: Per Wagner, Kin & Lynch (2012), why does RPKM's lack of a fixed per-sample sum undermine cross-sample comparison?

options.text: RPKM cannot be computed for genes shorter than 1 kb
A sample with a few extremely highly-expressed genes compresses every other gene's RPKM relative to a sample without that skew, even without a true change in relative abundance
RPKM values are always negative for lowly expressed genes
RPKM cannot be computed from raw counts at all

explanations.a: RPKM's formula works for any gene length; there's no such minimum-length restriction.
explanations.b: Correct — because the per-sample RPKM total isn't fixed, differing overall expression skew between samples distorts one gene's RPKM comparison across those samples, which is the core of Wagner, Kin & Lynch's argument.
explanations.c: RPKM values are non-negative ratios; they don't go negative for low expression, they just approach zero.
explanations.d: RPKM is derived directly from raw counts via the library-size and gene-length corrections.

questions.prompt: A student normalizes their gene counts to TPM and feeds the TPM matrix directly into DESeq2 for differential expression testing. What is wrong with this?

options.text: Nothing — TPM is the preferred input for DESeq2
DESeq2's statistical model expects raw integer counts and performs its own internal normalization; feeding it pre-normalized, non-integer values breaks that model
TPM values are always too small for DESeq2 to process
DESeq2 can only accept RPKM, not TPM

explanations.a: This is backwards — DESeq2 requires raw counts, not TPM, as input.
explanations.b: Correct — DESeq2 and edgeR model raw count noise with a negative binomial distribution and normalize internally (e.g., median-of-ratios); pre-normalized TPM values break that modeling assumption and invalidate the resulting p-values.
explanations.c: The issue is the statistical model's assumptions, not the numeric magnitude of TPM values.
explanations.d: DESeq2 doesn't require RPKM either — it requires raw integer counts, regardless of which normalized unit the student might otherwise compute.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to compute TPM for a gene, from first to last.

items.text: Divide the gene's raw read count by its length in kilobases, giving reads-per-kilobase (RPK)
Sum the RPK values across every gene in the sample
Divide each gene's RPK by that per-sample RPK sum
Multiply the result by 10^6

questions.explanation: TPM first corrects for gene length (RPK), then sums those length-corrected values across the whole sample, then scales each gene's RPK by that sum and by 10^6 — this order-of-operations is exactly what guarantees TPM sums to 10^6 in every sample, unlike RPKM/FPKM which normalizes by library size before gene length.

units.label: Differential Expression: Models, Correction, and Calling Hits

lessons.label: Normalisation: Why Raw Counts Lie

sections.heading: Deeper sequencing is not the only thing that changes a count
sections.body: The obvious fix for comparing samples sequenced to different depths is dividing each gene's count by total library size — counts per million. That corrects for depth, but it silently assumes every sample's RNA is distributed the same way across genes, and RNA-seq breaks that assumption constantly. If one gene is a massive outlier — a classic case is hemoglobin in a blood sample, or a single amplicon-like transcript that balloons to 40% of reads in one condition — it eats a huge share of the fixed read budget, so every other gene's CPM drops even though nothing about them changed biologically. The same distortion shows up in global transcriptional amplification, where an oncogene like MYC drives a genome-wide increase in transcription (documented in 2012 work from Richard Young's lab — Lin et al. and Lovén et al. (the latter with David Levens), Cell 2012): total RNA output rises, so library-size scaling makes thousands of unchanged genes look artificially down because the denominator inflated.

sections.heading: Composition-robust size factors: DESeq2's median of ratios
sections.body: DESeq2 (Love, Huber & Anders, 2014) fixes this with median-of-ratios normalisation, inherited from earlier DESeq work by Anders and Huber (2010). For each gene, compute a pseudo-reference as the geometric mean of its counts across all samples, then take the ratio of each sample's count to that reference. A per-sample size factor is the median of all those gene-wise ratios. Using the median instead of the total is the key move: it is robust to the handful of genes that are wildly different between conditions, because the median only shifts if more than half the genes shift together — which is exactly the 'most genes are not differentially expressed' assumption baked into the method.

sections.heading: TMM and when even that assumption breaks
sections.body: edgeR's TMM — trimmed mean of M-values (Robinson & Oshlack, 2010) — solves the same problem differently: it trims the most extreme log-fold-change and high-intensity genes (default 30% and 5% trimmed from each tail) and averages what remains, weighted by precision. Both methods rest on the same premise: the majority of genes are not changing, so the bulk of the distribution can anchor the scale factor. That premise genuinely fails in specific experiments — global chromatin state changes, whole-transcriptome shutdown in a stress response, or a knockout of a global regulator can shift most genes at once. In those cases the only honest fix is spike-in controls (e.g. the ERCC RNA set) added at a fixed, known amount before library prep, giving an external ruler that composition shifts cannot distort.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher compares liver tissue before and after a drug that strongly induces one detox gene, which balloons from 0.5% to 15% of total reads in treated samples. Naive CPM normalisation divides every other gene's count by an inflated total in the treated sample, making thousands of genuinely unchanged genes appear systematically down-regulated. Running DESeq2's median-of-ratios instead: the per-gene ratios to the geometric-mean reference are unaffected for the ~95% of genes that didn't move, so the median size factor reflects true sequencing depth, not the one gene's takeover, and the false global down-shift disappears.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how did you normalise your counts?' is checking whether a student understands that normalisation encodes an assumption, not just a formula. 'I divided by total reads' signals CPM with no defense against composition shifts. Naming DESeq2's median-of-ratios or edgeR's TMM, and being able to say what happens if the majority-unchanged assumption is violated (spike-ins), shows the student knows normalisation is a modeling choice with a stated failure mode — not a mechanical preprocessing step to click through.

questions.prompt: Why can simple counts-per-million (CPM) normalisation distort results when one gene dominates the read budget in one sample?

options.text: CPM cannot be computed when any gene has a high count
Dividing by total library size means one inflated gene shrinks the apparent expression of every other gene in that sample
CPM only works for single-end reads
CPM removes the dominant gene from the dataset automatically

explanations.a: CPM is still computable; the problem is not a computational failure but a statistical distortion.
explanations.b: Correct — total library size is the denominator, so one gene eating a large fraction of reads deflates every other gene's CPM even though those genes didn't change biologically.
explanations.c: CPM normalisation is agnostic to read layout; that is not the source of the distortion.
explanations.d: CPM does not remove or filter any gene; it rescales all of them using the same flawed denominator.

questions.prompt: What core assumption do both DESeq2's median-of-ratios and edgeR's TMM rely on to compute a composition-robust size factor?

options.text: All genes must have identical expression across samples
Most genes are not differentially expressed between the conditions being compared
Samples must be sequenced to exactly equal depth
Only protein-coding genes are included in the count matrix

explanations.a: That would make differential expression impossible to detect at all; the methods only require most, not all, genes to be stable.
explanations.b: Correct — both methods anchor their scale factor on the bulk of genes assumed unchanged, using the median (DESeq2) or a trimmed, weighted mean (TMM) to stay robust to the genes that do change.
explanations.c: Normalisation exists precisely because sequencing depth varies between samples; equal depth is not required.
explanations.d: Neither method restricts itself to protein-coding genes by definition.

questions.prompt: In an experiment where a global regulator knockout shifts the expression of most genes in the genome at once, what is the recommended fix when normalisation's core assumption fails?

options.text: Switch from DESeq2 to edgeR, since the assumption differs between them
Use spike-in controls added at a known fixed amount as an external reference
Increase sequencing depth until the problem disappears
Remove the knockout samples from the analysis

explanations.a: Both DESeq2 and edgeR rely on the same 'most genes unchanged' premise; switching between them does not fix a violated assumption.
explanations.b: Correct — spike-ins like the ERCC set are added at a known amount before library prep, giving a composition-independent ruler when the majority of endogenous genes are moving together.
explanations.c: Deeper sequencing improves precision but does not fix a systematic compositional bias in the size factor.
explanations.d: Removing the very samples of interest defeats the point of the experiment rather than fixing the normalisation.

questions.prompt: Match each normalisation approach to its defining mechanism.

right.text: Divides by total library size only
Median of per-gene ratios to a geometric-mean reference sample
Trims extreme log-fold-change and intensity genes, then weights the rest
Known fixed RNA amount added before library prep, independent of endogenous composition

questions.explanation: CPM only rescales by total reads; median-of-ratios (DESeq2, Love, Huber & Anders 2014) uses the median gene-wise ratio to a geometric-mean pseudo-reference; TMM (Robinson & Oshlack 2010) trims extreme genes before averaging; spike-ins provide an external, composition-independent anchor when the majority-unchanged assumption itself fails.

lessons.label: Overdispersion and the Negative Binomial

sections.heading: Why Poisson is the wrong model for real replicates
sections.body: If RNA-seq counts came only from the randomness of sequencing a fixed pool of molecules — pulling reads like balls from an urn — the Poisson distribution would be the correct model, and its defining property is that variance equals the mean. Technical replicates (the same RNA library sequenced twice) do in fact look close to Poisson. But biological replicates — different mice, different flasks of cells, different students' bacterial cultures — show variance that is consistently larger than the mean, often by a factor of several-fold at typical expression levels. This extra spread is overdispersion, and it is not measurement error to be cleaned up; it is real biological variability in transcription between individuals, and any model that ignores it will report false confidence.

sections.heading: The negative binomial adds a dispersion parameter
sections.body: The negative binomial (NB) distribution generalizes the Poisson by adding a second parameter, dispersion (often written alpha or phi), where variance = mean + alpha × mean². When alpha is zero, NB collapses back to Poisson; as alpha grows, the distribution's tails widen to match the extra biological noise. Concretely, for a gene with mean count 100 and a typical RNA-seq dispersion of alpha = 0.01, variance = 100 + 0.01 × 100² = 200 — double what Poisson alone would predict for that same mean, and the gap only widens as expression level climbs since the alpha × mean² term grows quadratically. DESeq2 and edgeR both model counts as NB for exactly this reason — it is the standard workhorse for overdispersed count data, used far beyond genomics (insurance claims, ecological abundance counts). The idea of stabilizing per-gene dispersion by borrowing information across genes traces back to empirical-Bayes moderation methods like Robinson & Smyth's 'Moderated statistical tests for assessing differences in tag abundance' (Bioinformatics, 2007), which predates and underlies edgeR's shrinkage approach. The catch is that estimating a dispersion accurately, per gene, from only a handful of samples is a genuinely hard statistical problem.

sections.heading: Why n = 3 needs help, and how shrinkage supplies it
sections.body: With three replicates per condition, a per-gene dispersion estimated from only that gene's own data is extremely noisy — the sample size is simply too small to pin down a variance parameter reliably, so raw per-gene estimates bounce wildly and would produce an unstable, unreliable test. DESeq2's and edgeR's shared solution is empirical-Bayes shrinkage: fit a trend of dispersion versus mean expression across all ~20,000 genes in the dataset, then pull each gene's noisy individual estimate toward that fitted curve, weighted by how much data supports it. This borrows statistical strength across genes — genes at similar expression levels tend to have similar dispersion, so the trend estimated from thousands of genes stabilizes what three replicates alone cannot.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs an RNA-seq experiment with n=3 wild-type and n=3 mutant yeast cultures. For a mid-expression gene, the raw within-group variance computed from just those three replicates happens to be unusually low by chance, giving a tiny per-gene dispersion estimate. If used directly, that artificially small dispersion would make the test overconfident and could produce a false-positive p-value. DESeq2 instead looks at the fitted mean-dispersion trend built from all genes at similar expression, sees that genes at this expression level typically show a higher dispersion, and shrinks the gene's estimate upward toward that trend — trading a small amount of bias for a large reduction in variance, and preventing the false-positive call.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why not just use a t-test on your counts?' is probing whether the student knows count data violates the equal-variance assumptions behind ordinary tests, and specifically that variance grows with the mean in a gene-count-dependent way. The strong answer names the negative binomial, states that variance = mean + alpha × mean² captures biological overdispersion that Poisson misses, and explains that with only 3 replicates per gene, shrinking the dispersion estimate toward a trend fit across thousands of genes is what makes the test trustworthy at all — not a technicality, but the reason small-n RNA-seq works statistically.

questions.prompt: What defines the Poisson distribution, and why does it fail to describe biological replicates in RNA-seq?

options.text: Poisson requires variance to equal the mean, but biological replicates show variance consistently exceeding the mean
Poisson only applies to continuous data, and RNA-seq counts are discrete
Poisson cannot be computed for genes with zero counts
Poisson requires exactly two replicates per condition

explanations.a: Correct — Poisson's defining property is variance = mean, which describes technical sequencing noise well but underestimates the true spread seen across independent biological samples.
explanations.b: Poisson is specifically a discrete distribution, well suited to count data in principle; the problem is its variance assumption, not data type.
explanations.c: Poisson handles zero counts naturally as part of its distribution.
explanations.d: Poisson has no replicate-count requirement; the issue is its variance structure, not sample size directly.

questions.prompt: In the negative binomial variance formula, variance = mean + alpha × mean², what happens as the dispersion parameter alpha approaches zero?

options.text: The distribution becomes undefined
The distribution collapses toward the Poisson, since variance approaches the mean
The mean itself becomes zero
Variance becomes infinite

explanations.a: The formula remains well-defined at alpha = 0; it simply reduces to a familiar special case.
explanations.b: Correct — with alpha = 0, variance = mean, which is exactly the Poisson property, showing NB is a strict generalization of Poisson.
explanations.c: Alpha controls dispersion, not the mean parameter; the mean is independent of alpha.
explanations.d: Smaller alpha shrinks the extra variance term rather than inflating it toward infinity.

questions.prompt: Why is a per-gene dispersion estimated from only 3 replicates considered unreliable on its own?

options.text: Because 3 replicates is too small a sample to reliably pin down a variance-type parameter for that one gene
Because DESeq2 cannot process fewer than 10 replicates
Because dispersion can only be estimated from paired samples
Because three replicates always produce identical counts

explanations.a: Correct — variance-type parameters need many data points to estimate stably, and 3 values per gene simply do not carry enough information, so raw estimates swing wildly gene to gene.
explanations.b: DESeq2 runs on any replicate count including n=2 or n=3; the issue is estimate reliability, not a hard software limit.
explanations.c: Dispersion estimation does not require paired designs; it is a per-gene variance property within a group.
explanations.d: Real replicates vary; they are not expected to be identical.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of empirical-Bayes dispersion shrinkage as used by DESeq2 and edgeR.

items.text: Estimate a rough per-gene dispersion from that gene's own replicate counts
Fit a trend of dispersion versus mean expression across all genes in the dataset
Shrink each gene's noisy individual estimate toward the fitted trend
Use the shrunk, stabilized dispersion in the negative binomial test for that gene

questions.explanation: The pipeline starts with a noisy per-gene estimate, borrows strength by fitting a genome-wide mean-dispersion trend, pulls each gene's estimate toward that trend, and only then uses the stabilized value in the final NB-based significance test.

lessons.label: DESeq2, edgeR, and limma-voom Compared

sections.heading: Two schools: model the counts, or transform and reuse linear models
sections.body: DESeq2 (Love, Huber & Anders, 2014) and edgeR both work directly on raw counts, fitting a negative binomial generalized linear model per gene with shrunk dispersion estimates, then testing coefficients with a Wald test (DESeq2's default), edgeR's GLM-based likelihood-ratio or quasi-likelihood F-test (glmLRT/glmQLFTest), or, for simple two-group designs, edgeR's classic exactTest — a separate, non-GLM conditional exact test on NB-distributed counts (analogous to Fisher's exact test) that uses common/tagwise dispersion and involves no design matrix or tested coefficient at all. limma-voom (Law, Chen, Shi & Smyth, 2014) takes a different route: it transforms counts to log-CPM, then estimates the mean-variance relationship of that transformed data directly with a smoothed curve, and converts that curve into a precision weight for every single observation. Those weights get fed into limma's existing linear-model-and-empirical-Bayes machinery — originally built for microarray intensities — so voom's real contribution is making a mature, well-tested linear-model framework valid for count data, rather than building a new count model from scratch.

sections.heading: Where they agree and where small samples pull them apart
sections.body: Benchmark comparisons — notably Soneson & Delorenzi (2013), which evaluated multiple DE tools across simulated and real datasets — found DESeq(2) and edgeR broadly agree on the genes they call, especially at moderate-to-large sample sizes and clear effect sizes; their overlap is typically strong at the top of a ranked gene list. Differences emerge at small n. edgeR's classic exact test and DESeq2's Wald test can behave slightly differently in FDR control at very small sample sizes (n=2–3 per group) because dispersion estimation is inherently harder there. limma-voom, being built on linear models with long-established moderated t-statistics, has generally been reported to control false discovery rate conservatively and perform competitively even at small n, though it can lose some power relative to NB-based methods when counts are very low, since the log-transform-and-weight approach handles the noisiest, lowest-count genes less gracefully than a model built for counts natively.

sections.heading: Justifying a choice, not just naming a tool
sections.body: None of the three is universally 'best' — the honest framing for a judge is that they encode different tradeoffs. DESeq2 is often chosen for its conservative, well-documented defaults and built-in shrinkage estimators (size factors and log-fold-change shrinkage). edgeR offers more manual control over the GLM and dispersion-fitting process. limma-voom is attractive when a study has many samples, complex designs, or when reusing limma's mature duplicateCorrelation and batch-handling tools matters. A defensible answer names which tool was used, states one concrete reason tied to the study's sample size or design, and — ideally — reports that results were checked for overlap with a second method, since agreement between two independently-built statistical approaches is itself evidence the call is not a modeling artifact.

lessons.workedExample: A team has RNA-seq from 3 control and 3 treated zebrafish, a small, simple two-group design. They run both DESeq2 and limma-voom on the same count matrix. DESeq2's Wald test returns 340 genes at padj < 0.05; limma-voom returns 290, with 260 of those genes overlapping DESeq2's list. Rather than picking whichever list is longer, the team reports the overlapping 260 as their high-confidence core set, notes the non-overlapping genes are concentrated at low counts (exactly where the two methods' assumptions diverge most), and states in their methods section that they used DESeq2 as primary given its native count model at low n, cross-validated against limma-voom.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why DESeq2 and not edgeR or limma-voom?' is testing whether the tool choice was a default click or a decision. The weak answer is 'it's what the tutorial used.' The strong answer ties the choice to the study's own sample size and design — e.g. 'we had only 3 replicates per group, so we wanted a method built natively for count data with dispersion shrinkage rather than a log-transform approach' — and bonus points for having cross-checked against a second tool, since convergent results from two different statistical frameworks is stronger evidence than either tool's p-value alone.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental difference in how limma-voom handles RNA-seq counts compared to DESeq2 and edgeR?

options.text: limma-voom transforms counts to log-CPM and derives precision weights, then reuses linear-model machinery, rather than modeling raw counts with a negative binomial
limma-voom ignores sample size entirely
limma-voom only works on microarray data, not RNA-seq
limma-voom requires spike-in controls to run at all

explanations.a: Correct — voom (Law et al., 2014) estimates the mean-variance trend of log-CPM data and turns it into observation-level weights fed into limma's existing linear-model and empirical-Bayes framework, in contrast to DESeq2/edgeR's direct negative-binomial modeling of counts.
explanations.b: Precision weighting is explicitly how voom accounts for the variance structure that differs across samples and genes.
explanations.c: voom was specifically built to extend limma's microarray-era linear-model tools to make them valid for RNA-seq count data.
explanations.d: voom runs on standard RNA-seq count matrices; spike-ins are a separate normalisation tool, not a voom requirement.

questions.prompt: According to benchmark comparisons like Soneson & Delorenzi (2013), how do DESeq2/edgeR-style tools generally compare to each other at moderate-to-large sample sizes?

options.text: They produce almost entirely non-overlapping gene lists
They broadly agree, with strong overlap especially among top-ranked genes
One always finds zero significant genes
They cannot be compared because they use incompatible input formats

explanations.a: Benchmark work found the opposite — substantial concordance, not near-total disagreement, at reasonable sample sizes.
explanations.b: Correct — Soneson & Delorenzi (2013) and similar comparisons found DESeq(2) and edgeR broadly agree, particularly at the top of ranked gene lists, with differences concentrated at small n and low counts.
explanations.c: Both tools reliably detect real differential expression when it is present at adequate sample sizes.
explanations.d: Both take the same gene-by-sample count matrix as input, making direct comparison straightforward.

questions.prompt: A student wants to justify their choice of DESeq2 over limma-voom for a n=3-per-group experiment to a science-fair judge. Which statement is the strongest justification?

options.text: "DESeq2 was the first result when I searched for RNA-seq tools"
"DESeq2 models raw counts natively with a negative binomial and shrinkage, which fits our small replicate count better than a log-transform-based approach"
"DESeq2 always finds more significant genes than other tools"
"limma-voom cannot be installed alongside DESeq2"

explanations.a: This states no methodological reasoning and would not satisfy a judge probing the decision.
explanations.b: Correct — this ties the tool choice to a concrete property of the study design (small n) and a real methodological distinction (native count modeling with shrinkage vs. transform-then-linear-model).
explanations.c: Finding more significant genes is not inherently better — it could reflect looser FDR control rather than a real advantage.
explanations.d: Both tools are standard Bioconductor packages and can coexist in the same R environment; this claim is false and irrelevant to methodology.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to its core testing approach.

right.text: Negative binomial GLM per gene, tested with a Wald test
Negative binomial GLM per gene, tested with likelihood-ratio or quasi-likelihood F-test (or, for simple two-group designs, its non-GLM classic exact test)
Log-CPM transform with mean-variance precision weights fed into linear-model empirical Bayes

questions.explanation: DESeq2 defaults to a Wald test on NB GLM coefficients; edgeR fits its own NB GLM and tests it with a likelihood-ratio or quasi-likelihood F-test, or, for simple two-group designs, uses its classic exactTest — a separate non-GLM conditional exact test on NB counts with no design matrix or coefficient involved; limma-voom (Law et al., 2014) converts counts to weighted log-CPM values and runs them through limma's linear-model and empirical-Bayes machinery.

lessons.label: Design Matrices, Covariates, and Batch Effects

sections.heading: Writing the model tells the software what to hold constant
sections.body: A differential expression design formula like ~ batch + condition is not decoration — it tells DESeq2 or edgeR exactly which variables to statistically account for before testing the one you care about. All terms in the formula are fit jointly by the negative binomial GLM's maximum-likelihood estimation — including batch anywhere in the formula (~ batch + condition) adjusts the condition coefficient for batch-associated variation, regardless of term order. The convention is to list the variable of interest last, because that determines which coefficient results() and plotMA report by default in DESeq2 — not because order changes what gets adjusted for. Paired designs (the same patient's tumor and normal tissue, or a before/after sample from the same animal) use ~ patient + condition, treating each patient as their own baseline and dramatically increasing power because individual-to-individual variability — often the largest source of noise in human studies — is factored out entirely rather than left in the error term.

sections.heading: The unfixable case: confounding
sections.body: This only works if batch and condition are not perfectly aligned. If every control sample was processed on Monday and every treated sample was processed on Tuesday, batch and condition are perfectly confounded — the model cannot distinguish 'a Tuesday effect' from 'a treatment effect' because every Tuesday sample is also a treated sample. No statistical method, however sophisticated, can un-confound variables that were never varied independently in the data; this has to be prevented at the design stage, not fixed at the analysis stage. The cheap, practical prevention is randomizing sample processing order — mixing conditions across extraction days, library-prep batches, and sequencing lanes so batch and condition are statistically independent, which costs nothing but a bit of planning.

sections.heading: Removing unwanted variation after the fact — carefully
sections.body: When batch is known but not perfectly confounded, ComBat (Johnson, Li & Rabinovic, 2007) removes it directly: it uses an empirical Bayes framework to estimate batch-specific location and scale parameters per gene and adjusts each gene's values to remove them, originally built for microarray data but widely applied to RNA-seq-derived expression values. When the source of unwanted variation is unknown or unmeasured — a hidden batch nobody logged, a subtle processing-date drift — surrogate variable analysis (Leek & Storey, 2007) estimates hidden 'surrogate variables' directly from the expression data itself and includes them in the model as covariates. Both approaches carry a real risk: if the unwanted-variation estimate accidentally captures some of the true biological signal (which happens when batch and condition are partially, not perfectly, correlated), removing it strips out real differential expression along with the noise — so the correction should always be checked against a PCA or correlation plot to confirm it targeted batch structure, not the biology under study.

lessons.workedExample: A lab collects RNA from 12 mice: 6 control, 6 drug-treated, processed in two batches of 6 because the freezer only holds so many samples at once. If they extracted all 6 controls in batch 1 and all 6 treated in batch 2, condition and batch are perfectly confounded — unfixable after the fact. Instead they split each batch into 3 control + 3 treated. Now the design formula ~ batch + condition can legitimately estimate and subtract batch effects (freezer-thaw timing, reagent lot) before testing condition, and a PCA of the corrected data should show samples separating by condition, not by batch, confirming the correction worked without erasing the treatment signal.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'how did you control for batch effects?' is checking whether a student understands that batch is a design problem, not just a modeling checkbox. The fatal answer is describing a perfectly confounded design and then claiming a statistical correction fixed it — that reveals the student doesn't know confounding is mathematically unrecoverable. The strong answer describes randomizing processing order across conditions at the design stage, then names a specific covariate-adjustment approach (design formula, ComBat, or SVA) as a secondary layer, and can explain how they checked the correction didn't remove real biological signal.

questions.prompt: In the design formula ~ batch + condition, does the order of batch and condition determine whether batch gets adjusted for?

options.text: No — all terms are fit jointly by the GLM, so including batch anywhere in the formula adjusts condition for it; order instead determines which coefficient DESeq2 reports by default
Yes — listing batch first tells the model to estimate and remove batch-associated variation before testing condition
It forces the software to ignore condition entirely
It doubles the required sample size

explanations.a: Correct — the negative binomial GLM fits every term in the formula jointly via maximum likelihood, so condition's coefficient is already adjusted for batch as long as batch is in the formula at all; term order instead controls which coefficient results()/plotMA reports by default.
explanations.b: This describes sequential removal, but DESeq2/edgeR fit all formula terms jointly, not in the listed order — order does not change what gets adjusted for.
explanations.c: condition remains the tested variable regardless of term order.
explanations.d: Adding a covariate term does not change the required sample size by itself.

questions.prompt: If every control sample was processed on Monday and every treated sample on Tuesday, what can be done to recover an unbiased condition effect after data collection?

options.text: Apply ComBat to remove the day effect, and the condition effect will be recoverable
Nothing — batch and condition are perfectly confounded and no statistical method can separate them after the fact
Run surrogate variable analysis to estimate and subtract the hidden day variable
Increase the number of replicates within each day

explanations.a: ComBat needs batch and condition to vary somewhat independently across samples to distinguish their effects; with perfect confounding, it has no way to tell them apart.
explanations.b: Correct — when every sample of one condition falls in one batch and every sample of the other condition falls in another, there is no data pattern that lets any method separate 'day' from 'treatment'; this must be prevented by design, not fixed by analysis.
explanations.c: SVA has the same fundamental limitation as ComBat here: it cannot separate two variables that never varied independently in the data.
explanations.d: More replicates within the same confounded structure does not create the independent variation needed to separate batch from condition.

questions.prompt: What is the key risk of applying ComBat or SVA-style corrections when batch and condition are partially (not perfectly) correlated?

options.text: The correction may remove some real biological signal along with the batch noise
The correction will always increase the number of significant genes
The correction requires deleting half the samples
The correction only works on paired designs

explanations.a: Correct — if the estimated unwanted-variation signature overlaps with true condition-related variation, subtracting it removes real biology, which is why the correction should be validated against PCA or correlation plots.
explanations.b: The effect on gene counts could go either direction; there is no guarantee of an increase.
explanations.c: Neither ComBat nor SVA requires discarding samples.
explanations.d: Both approaches apply to unpaired as well as paired designs; they are not restricted to paired data.

questions.prompt: Match each tool or practice to what it does about unwanted variation.

right.text: Prevents confounding at the design stage, before any data exists
Adjusts for a known, recorded batch variable using empirical Bayes location/scale estimates
Estimates hidden, unmeasured sources of variation directly from the expression data

questions.explanation: Randomization is a design-stage prevention that costs nothing but planning; ComBat corrects for a batch variable the experimenter already recorded; SVA is for the case where the source of unwanted variation was never logged and must be inferred from the data itself.

lessons.label: Reading Volcano and MA Plots at Working Depth

sections.heading: Two axes, two failure modes
sections.body: A volcano plot puts log2 fold change on the x-axis and -log10(p-value) on the y-axis, and it is tempting to just eyeball 'dots far from the center' as hits. But each axis alone is biased in a specific, predictable direction. Ranking by p-value alone favors high-expression genes: those genes have lower relative sampling noise (variance shrinks as mean count grows in the negative binomial model), so even a small, biologically trivial fold change can reach significance. Ranking by fold change alone favors low-count genes: a gene that goes from 2 reads to 8 reads is a 4-fold change but is almost certainly just Poisson-level noise on tiny numbers, not a real biological shift. Neither axis is trustworthy in isolation — a defensible hit list needs both a fold-change threshold and a significance threshold together.

sections.heading: Shrinking the noise out of fold-change estimates
sections.body: Because low-count genes produce wildly unstable, inflated fold-change estimates, DESeq2 offers lfcShrink using the apeglm estimator (Zhu, Ibrahim & Love, 2019), an adaptive Bayesian shrinkage prior that pulls fold-change estimates toward zero in proportion to how much uncertainty surrounds them. Genes with few reads and huge estimated fold changes get pulled hardest; genes with many reads and well-supported effects are barely touched. On a raw (unshrunk) volcano plot, low-count genes show up as a horizontal fan of extreme fold-change values spreading out at low significance — apeglm-shrunk plots visibly compress that fan, leaving a volcano shape driven by genes with real evidence rather than genes with small denominators.

sections.heading: Thresholds are conventions, and the MA plot as a QC tool
sections.body: The common cutoffs — |log2 fold change| > 1 (a 2-fold change) and adjusted p-value < 0.05 — are field conventions, not derived truths; there is nothing statistically special about exactly 2-fold or exactly 5%, and a study with a subtler biological effect (say, a 1.3-fold transcription factor response) can reasonably justify a lower fold-change bar if it states that choice explicitly. The MA plot — log2 fold change on the y-axis, mean expression (log scale) on the x-axis — is the standard diagnostic for normalisation problems: after a correct normalisation, the bulk of points should form a horizontal band centered near zero across the expression range, because most genes shouldn't be changing. If that band is systematically shifted up or down, or tilts across the expression range, it is a visual signature that size factors were miscalculated or the majority-unchanged assumption was violated.

lessons.workedExample: A student generates a volcano plot from a small pilot RNA-seq run and notices dozens of points at the far right and left edges — huge fold changes — but all clustered near the bottom (low significance). Investigating, these turn out to be genes with 1-3 raw counts in most samples: any single extra read doubles or triples the estimate. After running DESeq2's lfcShrink with apeglm, those same genes collapse toward the plot's center, while a smaller cluster of genes with hundreds of reads and consistent, moderate fold changes remains visible and significant — the shrunk plot now tells a cleaner story that matches what the underlying count data actually supports.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge pointing at a volcano plot and asking 'why did you pick these thresholds?' is testing whether a student understands the plot as a statistical object with known failure modes, not a picture to admire. The weak answer treats fold-change > 2 and p < 0.05 as universal laws. The strong answer explains that raw fold-change estimates are noisiest at low counts, names shrinkage (apeglm) as the fix, and can point to an MA plot to show the normalisation itself was sound before any hits were called — demonstrating the student checked their pipeline rather than trusting default plot output.

questions.prompt: Why does ranking genes by p-value alone tend to favor high-expression genes?

options.text: High-expression genes are always biologically more important
Sampling noise shrinks relative to the mean as expression increases, so even small fold changes can reach statistical significance
p-values cannot be computed for low-expression genes
High-expression genes are excluded from multiple-testing correction

explanations.a: Biological importance is not determined by expression level; this is a statistical artifact, not a biological rule.
explanations.b: Correct — under the negative binomial model, variance grows more slowly than the square of the mean at high expression, so relative noise shrinks and small, potentially trivial fold changes become statistically detectable.
explanations.c: p-values are computable for low-expression genes too; the issue is a bias in what reaches significance, not a computability failure.
explanations.d: Multiple-testing correction is applied uniformly across all tested genes regardless of expression level.

questions.prompt: What does DESeq2's lfcShrink with the apeglm estimator (Zhu et al., 2019) do to fold-change estimates?

options.text: It deletes all low-count genes from the results table
It pulls fold-change estimates toward zero in proportion to their uncertainty, shrinking noisy low-count estimates the most
It doubles every gene's reported fold change
It converts fold changes into raw read counts

explanations.a: Low-count genes remain in the results; their fold-change estimates are adjusted, not the genes removed.
explanations.b: Correct — apeglm applies an adaptive Bayesian shrinkage prior, pulling poorly-supported (typically low-count) fold-change estimates toward zero while leaving well-supported estimates largely unchanged.
explanations.c: Shrinkage moves estimates toward zero, the opposite of doubling them.
explanations.d: Fold change and raw counts are different quantities; shrinkage operates on the fold-change estimate itself.

questions.prompt: On an MA plot after correct normalisation, what should the bulk of points look like?

options.text: A horizontal band centered near zero fold change across the range of mean expression
A diagonal line rising steadily from left to right
All points clustered at the highest expression values only
A vertical band at zero mean expression

explanations.a: Correct — since most genes are assumed not differentially expressed, a properly normalised MA plot shows the bulk of genes hugging fold change = 0 across the full expression range; systematic shifts or tilts flag a normalisation problem.
explanations.b: A rising diagonal would suggest expression-dependent bias, exactly the kind of pattern that signals a normalisation failure rather than a healthy result.
explanations.c: Genes span a wide range of mean expression; clustering only at the high end would indicate a data or plotting problem, not a healthy MA plot.
explanations.d: Mean expression spans a wide range on the x-axis; a vertical band at zero would be a nonsensical shape for this plot type.

questions.prompt: What is the best characterization of the common thresholds |log2 fold change| > 1 and padj < 0.05?

options.text: Field conventions, not statistically derived truths, and can be justified differently for a given study's expected effect size
Mathematically required by the negative binomial distribution
The only thresholds accepted by DESeq2 and edgeR
Guaranteed to produce zero false positives

explanations.a: Correct — these are widely used defaults, not values with special statistical status; a study with subtler expected effects can justify a different fold-change bar if that choice is stated explicitly.
explanations.b: Nothing in the negative binomial model mandates these specific numeric cutoffs.
explanations.c: Both tools report continuous fold-change and p-value statistics; the thresholds applied afterward are an analyst's choice, not a software restriction.
explanations.d: padj < 0.05 explicitly allows for an expected rate of false discoveries among the hits, not zero false positives.

lessons.label: Multiple Testing at Transcriptome Scale

sections.heading: Twenty thousand coin flips
sections.body: A typical human RNA-seq dataset tests roughly 20,000 genes simultaneously, one hypothesis test each. Even if none of them are truly differentially expressed, a raw p < 0.05 threshold is expected to falsely call about 5% of them significant purely by chance — that is what a p-value threshold means, a false-positive rate under the null. Five percent of 20,000 is roughly 1,000 genes: a large, convincing-looking list that is entirely noise. Bonferroni correction, which divides the significance threshold by the number of tests (0.05/20,000 ≈ 0.0000025), controls the probability of even one false positive across the whole experiment — the family-wise error rate — but at transcriptome scale that is punishingly conservative, discarding real signal to guard against a single false call in 20,000 tests.

sections.heading: Benjamini-Hochberg: a different promise
sections.body: The standard fix is the Benjamini-Hochberg (1995) procedure, which controls the false discovery rate (FDR) instead of the family-wise error rate. FDR is a completely different quantity: rather than bounding the chance of any false positive at all, it bounds the expected proportion of false positives among the genes you call significant. Practically, BH sorts all p-values from smallest to largest, compares each to a rank-dependent threshold (rank/total tests × alpha), and finds the largest rank where the p-value still falls under that line — every gene at or below that rank is called. This adapts to how many genes actually look real in the data, rather than punishing every test equally regardless of how many true signals exist.

sections.heading: What 'FDR 5% on 300 genes' actually claims, and two sanity checks
sections.body: A results table showing 300 genes at padj (BH-adjusted p-value) < 0.05 is claiming that on average about 5% of that list — roughly 15 genes — are expected to be false positives, not that there is a 5% chance any single gene is wrong, and not that the whole list has only a 5% chance of containing an error.
