Independent filtering (built into DESeq2's results() function) legitimately improves power: genes with very low mean counts are filtered out before the FDR correction is even applied, because they have so little statistical power that including them only adds to the total-test denominator without ever being called significant — removing them tightens BH's threshold for everyone else. A separate diagnostic, the raw p-value histogram, checks whether the test was calibrated at all: it should show a flat distribution across most p-values with a spike near zero (the true positives); a hump in the middle or a skew elsewhere signals a broken model — wrong normalisation, unaccounted batch effect, or misspecified design — that should be fixed before trusting any FDR number from that run.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher tests 20,000 genes and gets a raw p-value histogram that looks roughly uniform from 0.1 to 1.0 with a clear spike below 0.05 — a well-calibrated test. Applying BH at alpha=0.05 yields 300 genes with padj < 0.05. They correctly report this as: approximately 15 of these 300 genes (5% of 300) are expected to be false discoveries, so the list as a whole is a strong but not perfect candidate set, appropriate for follow-up validation rather than being treated as 300 individually proven facts. If they had instead seen a histogram that was flat everywhere with no spike near zero, that would signal no genes are truly differentially expressed, or that the model itself was miscalibrated — a result that should be investigated before any FDR number is trusted.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'what does your FDR of 5% actually mean' is testing for the single most common statistical misunderstanding in student genomics projects — treating FDR like a per-gene error rate instead of a list-wide expectation. The correct answer states the number of expected false positives in the reported list (5% of the list size, not 5% of all tested genes), and a strong answer adds that they checked the raw p-value histogram for a sensible shape before trusting the correction at all — showing the student understands FDR control assumes a properly calibrated test in the first place.

questions.prompt: Testing 20,000 genes at a raw (uncorrected) p < 0.05 threshold, roughly how many genes would be expected to appear significant purely by chance if none were truly differentially expressed?

options.text: About 5 genes
About 1,000 genes
About 20 genes
Zero genes

explanations.a: 5 genes would only be about 0.025% of 20,000, far below what a 5% false-positive rate produces.
explanations.b: Correct — 5% of 20,000 tests is about 1,000 genes, illustrating why raw p-value thresholds are unusable at transcriptome scale without correction.
explanations.c: 20 genes would represent only 0.1% of the tests, far less than the 5% rate implied by an uncorrected p < 0.05 cutoff.
explanations.d: A raw p < 0.05 threshold by definition allows a nonzero false-positive rate under the null; zero false positives is not the expectation.

questions.prompt: What is the key conceptual difference between Bonferroni correction and the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure?

options.text: Bonferroni controls the chance of any false positive across all tests; BH controls the expected proportion of false positives among genes called significant
They are mathematically identical procedures with different names
BH is only valid for fewer than 100 tests
Bonferroni is less conservative than BH in every case

explanations.a: Correct — Bonferroni bounds family-wise error rate (probability of even one false positive across the whole experiment), while BH (1995) bounds false discovery rate (expected proportion of false positives among calls made), a fundamentally different and less punishing quantity at large scale.
explanations.b: The two procedures use different math and produce different, generally non-identical, sets of significant genes.
explanations.c: BH scales well and is the standard choice specifically at large-scale settings like transcriptome-wide testing with thousands of genes.
explanations.d: Bonferroni is the more conservative of the two at transcriptome scale, not the less conservative one.

questions.prompt: A results table shows 300 genes at BH-adjusted p (padj) < 0.05. What does this most precisely claim?

options.text: Every one of the 300 genes has only a 5% chance of being a false positive
About 5% of the 300 genes, roughly 15, are expected to be false discoveries
There is a 5% chance the entire list contains any error at all
Exactly 15 specific genes in the list are known to be false positives

explanations.a: This restates the family-wise or per-comparison interpretation, which is not what FDR control provides; FDR is a list-wide expected proportion, not a per-gene probability.
explanations.b: Correct — FDR = 5% on a 300-gene list means the expected count of false positives among those 300 is about 5% of 300, roughly 15 genes, though which specific genes are false is unknown.
explanations.c: This describes family-wise error control (like Bonferroni), a different and stricter guarantee than FDR provides.
explanations.d: FDR gives an expected count, not a way to identify which specific genes are the false positives.

questions.prompt: Why does independent filtering of low-count genes (before FDR correction) legitimately increase statistical power rather than being a form of cherry-picking?

options.text: It removes genes with almost no power to ever be called significant, shrinking the total-test denominator and tightening the BH threshold for the remaining genes
It removes genes based on how large their fold change turned out to be
It removes genes based on their p-value being too small
It is only done after FDR correction is already complete

explanations.a: Correct — filtering is based on mean count/expression, a criterion independent of the test statistic itself, so it removes genes that could never realistically reach significance and reduces the multiple-testing burden on genes that could.
explanations.b: Filtering by fold change would bias the results by using the same information the significance test is trying to assess, which is not what independent filtering does.
explanations.c: Filtering by p-value would directly bias FDR control by using the test outcome to decide what to keep, violating the independence the method requires.
explanations.d: Independent filtering is applied before the FDR correction step, which is precisely why it can legitimately change the correction's threshold.

lessons.label: Heatmaps and Clustering Without Fooling Yourself

sections.heading: Row z-scores make a heatmap readable, and choices reshape the dendrogram
sections.body: A raw expression heatmap is nearly useless because different genes sit at wildly different absolute scales — a highly expressed gene's raw values would visually swamp a lowly expressed one even if both show the same relative pattern. Row z-scoring fixes this: for each gene (row), subtract its mean across samples and divide by its standard deviation, so every gene is plotted on the same relative scale, showing 'higher or lower than this gene's own average' rather than absolute magnitude. The clustering dendrogram drawn alongside a heatmap is not a single fixed truth — it depends on two explicit choices: the distance metric (Euclidean distance versus 1-minus-correlation give measurably different groupings, especially when overall magnitude differs between samples) and the linkage method (average, complete, or Ward's linkage each merge clusters differently). Changing either can visibly reshuffle which samples appear to cluster together, so a dendrogram should be reported with its metric and linkage stated, not treated as an objective fact about the data.

sections.heading: The double-dipping trap
sections.body: The most common heatmap error in student projects is double dipping: selecting the top N differentially expressed genes from a DESeq2/edgeR run — genes that were specifically chosen because they differ between groups — and then plotting a heatmap of just those genes and presenting the resulting clean group separation as independent evidence that the groups are different. It cannot be independent evidence, because the gene selection step already used the group labels to pick the genes; the heatmap is guaranteed to show separation by construction, the same way sorting a coin flip dataset by outcome and then noting the two piles look different tells you nothing new. This is a form of circular reasoning, not a second confirmation of the DE result.

sections.heading: PCA and correlation heatmaps as pre-registered, honest QC
sections.body: The fix is to run clustering diagnostics before selecting any differentially expressed genes, using all genes (or the most variable genes, chosen without reference to group labels) rather than a DE-selected subset. Principal component analysis (PCA) of samples, plotting PC1 vs PC2, is the standard first look: if replicates within a condition cluster tightly and separate cleanly from the other condition along an early PC, that is genuine, label-independent evidence the experimental effect is a dominant source of variance in the data. If instead samples cluster by processing batch or by an unplanned factor like RNA extraction date, that is caught here — before it can bias any downstream DE call. A sample-to-sample correlation heatmap (all genes, no DE filtering) serves the same honest-QC role, flagging outlier samples that correlate poorly with their replicates and should be investigated before, not after, hits are called.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs DESeq2 on 6 control vs 6 treated samples, gets 400 significant genes, makes a heatmap of just those 400 genes, and shows a judge a beautiful two-block pattern as 'proof the treatment worked.' A judge points out this is circular — the genes were chosen because they separate the groups. The stronger version of the project instead opens with a PCA plot built from all ~15,000 expressed genes (no DE filtering), showing the 6 control and 6 treated samples separating cleanly along PC1, which explains, say, 45% of total variance — establishing that treatment is a real, dominant driver of transcriptome-wide variation before any DE gene list is even generated, and only then presents the 400-gene heatmap as a detailed look at which genes drive that separation.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a heatmap of top DE genes cleanly separating two groups and asks 'is this independent evidence, or did you select these genes because they separate?' is testing for exactly the double-dipping error. The strong answer distinguishes the honest QC step (PCA or a correlation heatmap on all genes, done before any gene selection) from the illustrative step (a heatmap of the top hits, which is expected to look clean by construction and is not itself proof of anything). A student who cannot make this distinction is presenting circular reasoning as validation.

questions.prompt: What does row z-scoring accomplish in an expression heatmap?

options.text: It removes all genes with low expression from the plot
It rescales each gene to its own mean and standard deviation, so genes at very different absolute expression levels become visually comparable
It reorders samples alphabetically
It converts counts into p-values

explanations.a: Z-scoring does not filter genes; it rescales the values that are plotted.
explanations.b: Correct — subtracting each gene's mean and dividing by its standard deviation puts every row on the same relative scale, so a highly expressed gene and a lowly expressed gene with the same relative pattern look visually similar rather than one swamping the other.
explanations.c: Z-scoring operates on values within each gene's row, not on sample ordering.
explanations.d: Z-scoring is a rescaling of expression values, unrelated to statistical testing or p-value computation.

questions.prompt: Why might two heatmaps of the exact same data, made with different distance metrics or linkage methods, show visibly different dendrograms?

options.text: Because the dendrogram is not a single objective fact about the data — the choice of distance metric (e.g. Euclidean vs. correlation-based) and linkage method (e.g. average vs. complete vs. Ward's) both shape which samples merge together
Because one of the two heatmaps must contain a data-entry error
Because dendrograms are randomly generated each time
Because only one distance metric exists for clustering

explanations.a: Correct — distance metric and linkage method are both analyst choices that measurably affect clustering results, which is why they should be reported alongside any dendrogram.
explanations.b: Different results from different methodological choices do not imply an error; both dendrograms can be legitimately correct under their respective settings.
explanations.c: Clustering algorithms are deterministic given the metric and linkage choice, not random.
explanations.d: Multiple distance metrics exist (Euclidean, correlation-based, and others), and the choice between them is exactly what can change the result.

questions.prompt: A student selects the top 300 genes from a DESeq2 differential expression result, makes a heatmap of just those genes, and presents the resulting clean separation between groups as independent proof the groups differ. What is the flaw in this reasoning?

options.text: There is no flaw; this is standard, valid confirmatory evidence
This is double dipping — the genes were already selected using the group labels, so the heatmap is guaranteed to show separation by construction, not as new evidence
Heatmaps cannot display more than 50 genes at once
DESeq2 output cannot be visualized as a heatmap

explanations.a: This is exactly the double-dipping error; it is not valid independent evidence because gene selection already used the group labels.
explanations.b: Correct — because the genes were chosen for differing between groups, a heatmap of only those genes will separate the groups regardless of whether the underlying effect is real or noise; it is circular, not confirmatory.
explanations.c: Heatmap size is not the issue being described; the issue is a logical/statistical circularity in gene selection.
explanations.d: DESeq2 results are routinely visualized as heatmaps; the problem is which genes are chosen for the plot, not the visualization method itself.

questions.prompt: Order these steps to avoid the double-dipping trap when using clustering as evidence for a real experimental effect.

items.text: Run PCA or a correlation heatmap using all genes (or all variable genes chosen without reference to group labels)
Confirm replicates cluster together and separate by the intended experimental factor, not by batch or an unplanned variable
Run the differential expression test and select the top significant genes
Present a heatmap of the top DE genes as an illustration of which genes drive the separation, not as independent proof of it

questions.explanation: The honest sequence establishes label-independent evidence first (all-gene PCA or correlation heatmap), confirms the effect is a real driver of variance before any gene selection happens, then runs DE testing, and only presents the DE-gene heatmap as an illustrative detail rather than proof — since proof already came from the label-independent QC step.

lessons.label: Before Sequencing: Northerns, Differential Display, SAGE

sections.heading: One gene, one blot: the Northern
sections.body: Alwine, Kemp & Stark (1977) adapted Southern's DNA-blotting method to RNA: total or poly-A RNA is run on a gel, transferred to a membrane, and probed with a labeled sequence complementary to one transcript. The Northern blot answers exactly one question well — is this specific gene expressed, and roughly how much, in this sample versus that one — and it does so with a built-in size check, since transcript length shows up as band position. Its limit is the same as its strength: you need to already suspect a gene to design a probe for it. A Northern cannot tell you what changed across a whole transcriptome; it can only confirm or deny a hypothesis about a candidate you already named.

sections.heading: Casting a wider net without sequencing: differential display
sections.body: Liang & Pardee (1992) proposed differential display RT-PCR: reverse-transcribe mRNA with anchored oligo-dT primers, amplify with short arbitrary primers, and run the products side by side on a sequencing gel for two or more conditions. Bands present in one lane and absent in another flag candidate differentially expressed transcripts, which can then be cut out, cloned, and identified. This was the first practical way to survey an unknown fraction of the transcriptome for differences without picking genes in advance — genuinely hypothesis-generating. Its weaknesses were real: the short (roughly 10-nucleotide) arbitrary primers amplify unpredictably, many bands turn out to be artifacts or the same gene amplified twice — false-positive rates where most picked bands fail to validate on follow-up are well documented for the method — and it is a relative, gel-based readout, not a count.

sections.heading: Digital counting arrives: SAGE
sections.body: Velculescu, Zhang, Vogelstein & Kinzler (1995) introduced Serial Analysis of Gene Expression: a short sequence tag (originally 9 bp) taken from a defined position in each transcript is enough to identify the gene it came from, so tags are concatenated into long strings, cloned, and sequenced in bulk. Counting how many times each tag appears converts expression into a discrete, digital number rather than a hybridization intensity — the same logic RNA-seq would later scale up enormously. SAGE could, in principle, detect any expressed transcript, known or not, and its counts were directly comparable across experiments. What it lacked was throughput: Sanger sequencing thousands of tags per library was slow and costly, which is exactly the constraint next-generation sequencing removed a decade later.

lessons.workedExample: A 1990s lab wants to find genes turned on when a fibroblast is serum-starved versus serum-stimulated. If they already suspect cyclin D1 is involved, a Northern blot with a cyclin D1 probe is the fast, cheap, and definitive test — but it says nothing about anything else in the cell. If they have no candidate gene at all, differential display RT-PCR run on both conditions in parallel lanes can surface a handful of unexpected bands to chase down, at the cost of chasing false positives too. If they want an actual quantitative census of the whole transcriptome — every gene, with a count, comparable to a future experiment — SAGE is the only one of the three built for that, though building and sequencing the tag library takes far longer than either alternative.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees 'we used a Northern blot' or 'we ran differential display' wants to know whether the student picked the tool that matched their actual question — confirmatory versus discovery versus quantitative census — not just whichever method appeared in a protocol they found. Naming SAGE's tag-counting logic and explaining why it foreshadows RNA-seq (digital counts, no probe needed) also signals the student understands why the field moved away from hybridization-based methods at all, rather than treating microarrays and RNA-seq as arbitrary upgrades.

questions.prompt: What is the core limitation of a Northern blot for studying gene expression?

options.text: It cannot detect any RNA at all, only DNA
It requires a probe for a specific transcript, so you must already know which gene to look for
It only works on bacterial RNA
It gives no information about transcript size

explanations.a: Northern blots (Alwine, Kemp & Stark, 1977) specifically detect RNA, adapting Southern's DNA method.
explanations.b: Correct — a Northern blot probes for one known sequence at a time, so it can confirm or quantify a candidate gene but cannot survey unknown transcripts.
explanations.c: Northern blotting works on RNA from any organism with poly-A or total RNA that can be gel-separated.
explanations.d: Transcript size is actually one thing a Northern blot reveals well, via band position on the gel.

questions.prompt: What made differential display (Liang & Pardee, 1992) different from a Northern blot?

options.text: It could survey an unknown set of transcripts for differences across conditions without picking genes in advance
It gave exact digital counts of every transcript
It required no PCR amplification
It could only be used on a single known gene

explanations.a: Correct — arbitrary-primer RT-PCR compared band patterns across conditions, flagging candidate differentially expressed genes without prior hypotheses.
explanations.b: Differential display was gel-based and relative, not a digital count — that came later with SAGE and then RNA-seq.
explanations.c: Differential display depends on RT-PCR with arbitrary short primers to amplify products.
explanations.d: That describes a Northern blot's limitation, which differential display was designed to overcome.

questions.prompt: SAGE (Velculescu, Zhang, Vogelstein & Kinzler, 1995) converted gene expression measurement into what kind of readout?

options.text: A hybridization intensity on a gel
A discrete, digital tag count from sequencing
A visual band presence/absence call
A fluorescence ratio between two dyes

explanations.a: That describes Northern blotting or later two-colour microarrays, not SAGE.
explanations.b: Correct — SAGE concatenated short sequence tags and counted how often each appeared, producing discrete counts comparable to later RNA-seq counts.
explanations.c: Presence/absence band calls describe differential display, not SAGE's quantitative tag counting.
explanations.d: Two-dye fluorescence ratios describe cDNA microarrays, a later and different technology.

questions.prompt: Order these expression-profiling methods by publication date, earliest first.

items.text: Northern blot (Alwine, Kemp & Stark)
Differential display (Liang & Pardee)
SAGE (Velculescu, Zhang, Vogelstein & Kinzler)

questions.explanation: The Northern blot was published in 1977, differential display in 1992, and SAGE in 1995 — an eighteen-year arc from single-gene hybridization to genome-scale digital tag counting, well before next-generation sequencing existed.

lessons.label: The Microarray Era and Its Promise

sections.heading: Two platforms, one idea: probe the whole transcriptome at once
sections.body: Schena, Shalon, Davis & Brown (1995, Science) built the prototype: a glass slide spotted with complementary DNA for 45 Arabidopsis genes, hybridized against two samples each labeled with a different fluorescent dye, so the ratio of red to green at each spot gave a relative expression level for that gene in one sample versus the other. Affymetrix took a different manufacturing route, using photolithography — the same chip-fabrication technology as semiconductors — to synthesize short oligonucleotide probes directly on a chip, one base at a time, at fixed positions, so a single GeneChip could carry probes for tens of thousands of genes. Both approaches shared the same core trade: expression profiling stopped being one gene at a time and became a whole transcriptome read out in a single hybridization.

sections.heading: The demonstrations that made expression profiling famous
sections.body: Golub et al. (1999, Science) showed that expression profiles alone, with no prior knowledge of leukemia biology, could distinguish acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) from acute myeloid leukemia (AML) — proof that a transcriptome could serve as a diagnostic signature. Perou et al. (2000) and Sorlie et al. (2001) used microarrays to define 'intrinsic' molecular subtypes of breast cancer (luminal, basal-like, HER2-enriched, and others) that did not map cleanly onto older histological categories and reproduced across independent patient cohorts. Van 't Veer et al. (2002, Nature) took the next step toward the clinic: a 70-gene signature that predicted distant metastasis in early breast cancer better than standard clinical criteria, which was later commercialized as the MammaPrint test.

sections.heading: The catch: you can only see what you printed
sections.body: Every microarray is a fixed-probe technology — the genes or oligonucleotides on the chip are chosen and manufactured in advance, so a novel transcript, an unannotated splice variant, or a gene from an organism without a reference genome is invisible no matter how highly it is expressed. Cross-hybridization is a second structural problem: similar sequences (paralogs, splice isoforms, repetitive regions) can bind the same probe, blurring which gene actually produced the signal. Fluorescence intensity also saturates at both ends — very low-abundance transcripts sit in the noise floor and very high-abundance ones saturate the detector — compressing the dynamic range compared to a true count. These are not implementation bugs; they are consequences of measuring expression by hybridization to a predetermined probe set.

lessons.workedExample: A 2001 lab wants to know which genes distinguish two breast tumor subtypes. Using an Affymetrix GeneChip, they get a reproducible expression profile across thousands of pre-selected genes in hours — exactly the kind of large-scale comparison that let Perou and Sorlie define intrinsic subtypes. But if the relevant biological difference involves a newly-spliced isoform or a gene absent from the chip's design (common for less-studied species or genes discovered after the chip was manufactured), the array simply cannot see it, no matter how real the difference is. A student replicating this kind of study today needs to state which platform (two-colour cDNA versus Affymetrix oligonucleotide) and to recognize that a 'no difference detected' result on an array cannot rule out a real difference in an unprinted transcript.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about microarray results wants to hear the student name the fixed-probe constraint unprompted: an array can only report on genes chosen in advance, so a null result is not the same as an absence of biological effect. Naming a specific demonstration — Golub's ALL/AML classification, or the intrinsic breast-cancer subtypes from Perou and Sorlie — shows the student understands what the technology proved was possible, while explaining cross-hybridization or dynamic-range compression shows they understand why arrays were eventually supplanted rather than simply improved.

questions.prompt: Match each microarray platform to its defining manufacturing/detection method.

right.text: Spotted cDNA on glass, two-dye fluorescence ratio between two samples
Short oligonucleotides synthesized in place via photolithography

questions.explanation: Schena et al.'s prototype spotted cDNA for 45 Arabidopsis genes and compared two dye-labeled samples on one slide; Affymetrix instead synthesized short oligo probes directly on a chip using photolithography, the same technique used to fabricate semiconductors.

questions.prompt: What did Golub et al. (1999) demonstrate using microarray expression profiles?

options.text: That ALL and AML leukemias could be distinguished from expression data alone, without prior disease knowledge
That microarrays could sequence novel transcripts
That the 70-gene MammaPrint signature predicted metastasis
That cross-hybridization eliminates all measurement noise

explanations.a: Correct — Golub et al. (1999, Science) showed expression profiles alone could classify ALL versus AML, establishing that a transcriptome could serve as a diagnostic signature.
explanations.b: Microarrays cannot detect novel transcripts at all; they only report on pre-selected probes.
explanations.c: The 70-gene metastasis signature was van 't Veer et al. (2002), a separate study on breast cancer, not leukemia.
explanations.d: Cross-hybridization is a source of noise and ambiguity on arrays, not something arrays eliminate.

questions.prompt: Why can a microarray never detect a completely novel, unannotated transcript?

options.text: Because fluorescence dyes cannot bind to novel sequences
Because the probes on the array are chosen and manufactured in advance, so anything not printed is invisible
Because novel transcripts are always too short to hybridize
Because photolithography cannot synthesize oligonucleotides longer than 5 bases

explanations.a: Dye chemistry is unrelated to the limitation — the issue is which sequences have a matching probe on the chip.
explanations.b: Correct — microarrays are a fixed-probe technology; a gene, splice variant, or organism's transcript absent from the chip's design cannot be measured no matter its expression level.
explanations.c: Transcript length is not the barrier; the barrier is whether a complementary probe exists on the array at all.
explanations.d: Affymetrix oligo probes were typically around 25 bases, well beyond the technology's length limits; this is not the constraint.

questions.prompt: The van 't Veer et al. (2002) 70-gene signature became the basis for which commercial test?

options.text: MammaPrint
23andMe
GeneChip
SAGE-Dx

explanations.a: Correct — the 70-gene prognostic signature from van 't Veer et al. (2002) predicting distant metastasis in early breast cancer was later commercialized as MammaPrint.
explanations.b: 23andMe is a consumer genotyping company unrelated to this expression-signature work.
explanations.c: GeneChip is the Affymetrix microarray platform itself, not a diagnostic test derived from a specific gene signature.
explanations.d: SAGE-Dx is not a real product connected to this study; it invents a name from an unrelated method (SAGE).

lessons.label: The Reproducibility Reckoning

sections.heading: Signatures that performed no better than chance
sections.body: Michiels, Koscielny & Hill (2005, The Lancet) reanalyzed seven published cancer microarray studies that each claimed a gene-expression signature could predict patient outcome. Using proper resampling — repeatedly re-drawing training and validation sets rather than trusting a single split — they found that the list of genes selected as 'the' signature, and the accuracy attributed to it, was highly unstable across resamples: for most of the seven studies, the reported prognostic performance could not be reliably reproduced, and several signatures were statistically indistinguishable from chance once the original single split was replaced with proper validation. The core problem was small sample sizes relative to the huge number of genes tested, combined with selecting the 'best' gene list on the same data used to evaluate it.

sections.heading: Ioannidis et al. and the reproducibility floor
sections.body: Ioannidis, Allison and colleagues (2009, Nature Genetics) tried something more direct: take 18 published microarray studies and attempt to fully reproduce their reported results using the papers' own described methods and, where available, deposited data. They could fully reproduce the results of only 2 of the 18. The failures were not exotic — missing raw data, undocumented pre-processing steps, unspecified software versions, and simple transcription or labeling errors in supplementary tables. The finding mattered less as an indictment of any one lab than as evidence that the average published microarray paper of that era did not contain enough information for an independent group to check it, which is a precondition for a result counting as established science.

sections.heading: The institutional fix: standards, deposition, cross-platform checks
sections.body: The field's response predates both reanalyses in one case and follows them in others. Brazma et al. (2001) had already proposed MIAME (Minimum Information About a Microarray Experiment), a checklist specifying what a paper must report — raw data, normalization method, array design, experimental factors — for a microarray result to be independently interpretable. Journals and funders increasingly required deposition of raw data in public repositories such as GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) as a condition of publication, directly targeting the missing-data failure mode Ioannidis documented. Separately, the MAQC (MicroArray Quality Control) consortium's 2006 study tested the same RNA samples across multiple microarray platforms and labs to establish how much of the disagreement between platforms was technical noise versus real biology, giving the field a shared baseline for what 'reproducible' should even look like.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a 2004-style study of 40 patients measures 20,000 genes and reports a 15-gene signature that perfectly separates good from poor outcomes in that cohort. Michiels' method would resample the 40 patients into many different training/validation splits and check whether the same 15 genes, and the same accuracy, kept showing up. If a different resample yields a completely different gene list with similar claimed accuracy, that is the signature of overfitting to noise in a small sample — exactly what Michiels found in most of the seven studies reanalyzed. A student designing a similar analysis today should report whether their gene selection was stable under resampling and whether their raw data and code are deposited (MIAME-compliant, GEO-archived) so someone else could attempt the Ioannidis test on their own result.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing reproducibility wants a student to distinguish 'my result held up on the data I had' from 'my result would survive someone else re-running it' — the exact gap Michiels and Ioannidis exposed at scale. Naming MIAME and GEO deposition as concrete practices, not vague gestures at 'open science,' shows the student understands reproducibility as an engineering requirement (specify normalization, deposit raw data, report resampling stability) rather than a virtue to claim in a discussion section.

questions.prompt: What did Michiels, Koscielny & Hill (2005) find when they reanalyzed seven published cancer gene-expression signatures using proper resampling?

options.text: All seven signatures were confirmed with even higher accuracy than originally reported
For most of the seven, the selected gene list and reported accuracy were unstable, and performance was often no better than chance
The signatures worked perfectly but only in male patients
Resampling was mathematically impossible to apply to microarray data

explanations.a: The opposite occurred — resampling exposed instability, not confirmation, in most of the studies.
explanations.b: Correct — repeated resampling showed the gene lists and claimed accuracy were highly unstable, with several signatures statistically indistinguishable from chance.
explanations.c: No such sex-specific finding was part of this reanalysis; this invents a result not in the study.
explanations.d: Resampling (repeatedly re-splitting data into training/validation sets) is precisely the technique Michiels applied and found feasible.

questions.prompt: In Ioannidis et al. (2009), how many of the 18 published microarray studies could be fully reproduced using the papers' own described methods?

options.text: 2 of 18
0 of 18

explanations.a: Full reproducibility was the exception, not the norm, in this analysis.
explanations.b: This overstates the reproducibility rate found; the true figure was far lower.
explanations.c: Correct — only 2 of the 18 studies could be fully reproduced; the rest failed due to missing data, undocumented processing steps, or errors in reported tables.
explanations.d: Two studies were reproducible, so zero understates the (still troubling) result.

questions.prompt: Match each institutional response to what it directly addresses.

right.text: A reporting checklist specifying what must be described for a microarray result to be independently interpretable
Making raw data publicly archived as a condition of publication
Testing the same samples across platforms/labs to establish a technical-noise baseline

questions.explanation: MIAME defined a minimum reporting standard; GEO deposition made raw data itself available, directly targeting the missing-data failures Ioannidis documented; the MAQC consortium's cross-platform, cross-lab study established how much platform disagreement was technical noise versus real biology.

questions.prompt: Order these reproducibility-related events chronologically, earliest first.

items.text: Brazma et al. propose MIAME reporting standards
Michiels, Koscielny & Hill reanalyze seven cancer signatures
MAQC consortium publishes cross-platform concordance study
Ioannidis et al. attempt to reproduce 18 microarray studies

questions.explanation: MIAME was proposed in 2001, Michiels' reanalysis appeared in 2005, the MAQC consortium's concordance study followed in 2006, and Ioannidis et al.'s direct reproduction attempt was published in 2009 — a widening institutional and empirical response over the decade.

lessons.label: The Duke Scandal and Forensic Bioinformatics

sections.heading: A signature that promised to pick your chemotherapy
sections.body: Potti and Nevins (2006, Nature Medicine) published microarray-based 'chemosensitivity signatures': gene-expression patterns derived from cancer cell lines' sensitivity to specific chemotherapy drugs, claimed to predict which drug an individual patient's tumor would respond to. The promise was enormous — instead of trial-and-error chemotherapy, a patient's tumor expression profile would route them directly to the drug most likely to work. Duke moved fast on the strength of these results, opening clinical trials that assigned real patients to treatment arms based on the signatures' predictions.

sections.heading: Baggerly and Coombes take the data apart
sections.body: Biostatisticians Baggerly & Coombes attempted to validate the signatures independently and could not reproduce them. Their 2009 paper in the Annals of Applied Statistics, 'Deriving Chemosensitivity from Cell Lines: Forensic Bioinformatics and Reproducible Research in High-Throughput Biology,' laid out what they called forensic bioinformatics: working backward from a paper's figures and any available data to infer what the analysis must actually have done. Across five case studies they found simple, concrete errors — gene lists that were off by one row from a spreadsheet misalignment, and sample labels (sensitive versus resistant) that had been reversed, so a signature trained to predict drug response was in some cases trained on the opposite of what it claimed. The paper had first been rejected by a biomedical journal before appearing in a statistics journal in September 2009; Duke suspended the trials the following month pending an internal investigation.

sections.heading: The fallout and the lesson institutionalized
sections.body: The suspended 2010 trials were not quickly resolved — the investigation reopened repeatedly as further problems surfaced, including discrepancies in Potti's stated credentials, and by 2011 several of the underlying papers were retracted. The episode became a central case study for the Institute of Medicine's 2012 report, 'Evolution of Translational Omics: Lessons Learned and the Path Forward,' which used it to argue for mandatory data and code availability, independent validation, and a formal 'lock-down' of any omics-based test before it is used to assign patients to treatment in a trial. The throughline both Baggerly and the IOM drew was the same: reproducible code and archived data are not paperwork bolted onto real science after the fact — checking whether an off-by-one error or a label swap exists is itself a scientific control, and without it a result cannot be trusted regardless of how impressive the headline finding looks.

lessons.workedExample: Imagine a signature paper reports that gene X is upregulated in drug-resistant samples, and a reviewer wants to check this without re-running any wet-lab experiment. Forensic bioinformatics means downloading whatever raw data and code the authors deposited, re-deriving the reported gene list or classification from scratch, and comparing it to the paper's figures line by line. Baggerly and Coombes did exactly this on the Duke signatures and found that in one dataset, the 'sensitive' and 'resistant' labels were simply swapped relative to what the underlying assay files indicated — meaning the published predictive direction was backward. No new experiment was needed to catch this; the error was detectable purely from the paper's own deposited data, which is precisely why data availability functions as a check rather than a formality.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about validating someone else's results wants to hear that a student understands checking is itself a method, not an afterthought — Baggerly and Coombes caught a reversed-label error that put real patients on a trial with the wrong drug assignment, using nothing but the authors' own deposited data. A student who says 'we made our code and raw data available so this could be checked' is naming the actual control the Duke scandal proved necessary; a student who treats data-sharing as a compliance checkbox has missed why the field now requires it.

questions.prompt: What specific kinds of errors did Baggerly & Coombes (2009) document in the Potti/Nevins chemosensitivity signatures?

options.text: Gene lists off by one row and reversed sample labels (sensitive/resistant swapped)
The cell lines used were contaminated with mycoplasma
The microarray chips themselves were manufactured incorrectly
The patients enrolled in the trials did not actually have cancer

explanations.a: Correct — their forensic reanalysis found concrete errors like spreadsheet misalignments producing off-by-one gene lists and outright reversed sensitive/resistant sample labels.
explanations.b: Mycoplasma contamination is a real but different lab-quality issue, not what Baggerly and Coombes' forensic reanalysis identified.
explanations.c: The problem was in data handling and analysis, not in chip manufacturing.
explanations.d: This misstates the finding; the issue was analytical/data errors, not patient eligibility.

questions.prompt: What does 'forensic bioinformatics,' as Baggerly & Coombes used the term, mean?

options.text: Using DNA evidence to solve crimes
Working backward from a paper's figures and available data to infer what the analysis must actually have done
A machine-learning method for classifying gene expression
A type of microarray manufacturing process

explanations.a: This is unrelated forensic science, not the bioinformatics reanalysis technique described in the paper.
explanations.b: Correct — forensic bioinformatics reconstructs the actual analytical steps from a paper's reported figures and any deposited data, checking whether they hold up.
explanations.c: It is a method of scrutiny/reanalysis, not a classification algorithm itself.
explanations.d: It has nothing to do with chip manufacturing; it concerns auditing data analysis after the fact.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the Duke chemosensitivity scandal, earliest first.

items.text: Potti and Nevins publish chemosensitivity signatures in Nature Medicine
Baggerly & Coombes publish their forensic reanalysis in the Annals of Applied Statistics
Duke suspends the clinical trials pending investigation
Underlying papers are retracted

questions.explanation: The signatures were published in 2006, Baggerly and Coombes' reanalysis appeared in September 2009, Duke suspended the trials the following month (October 2009, with further suspensions into 2010), and retractions followed in 2011 as the investigation deepened.

questions.prompt: The 2012 Institute of Medicine report used the Duke case to argue primarily for:

options.text: Banning microarray technology from clinical use entirely
Mandatory data/code availability and independent validation before an omics-based test guides patient treatment in a trial
Requiring all cancer researchers to have medical degrees
Eliminating the use of statistics in biomedical research

explanations.a: The report did not call for banning the technology, but for stronger validation practices around how it is used.
explanations.b: Correct — 'Evolution of Translational Omics' (2012) argued for reproducible data/code and independent validation as preconditions for using omics-based tests to assign patients to treatment.
explanations.c: Credentialing requirements were not the report's focus; data and validation practices were.
explanations.d: The scandal underscored the need for more rigorous statistical checking, not less.

lessons.label: RNA-seq Takes Over

sections.heading: The first transcriptome-wide sequencing papers
sections.body: Nagalakshmi et al. (2008, Science) sequenced the yeast transcriptome directly, mapping reads back to the genome to reveal transcript boundaries, splicing, and expression levels without ever designing a probe. Mortazavi et al. (2008, Nature Methods) applied the same deep-sequencing logic to a mammalian system, the mouse transcriptome, and introduced RPKM (reads per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads) — a normalization that made expression comparable across genes of different lengths and across sequencing runs of different depth, solving a problem hybridization arrays never had to face because they measured intensity, not read counts. Lister et al. (2008, Cell) applied deep sequencing genome-wide in Arabidopsis, producing the first single-base-resolution map of the plant methylome via bisulfite sequencing and layering transcription data (mRNA-seq and small RNA-seq) alongside it, part of the same wave establishing that sequencing, not hybridization, could resolve an epigenome base by base.

sections.heading: What sequencing actually won on
sections.body: RNA-seq's real advantages over arrays were specific, not just 'more modern': a far wider dynamic range, since a rare transcript is simply a read that shows up a few times rather than a signal buried under the noise floor of a fixed detector — RNA-seq read counts routinely span five or more orders of magnitude, versus roughly two to three orders for a microarray before background noise and probe saturation flatten the signal at both ends; detection of novel and non-model-organism transcripts, since sequencing needs no pre-designed probe and works on any organism, even one without a reference genome; and isoform-level resolution, since reads spanning splice junctions can distinguish alternative transcripts that a single array probe would blur together. None of this required guessing what to look for in advance — the entire transcriptome, known or not, was in the data.

sections.heading: Where arrays held their ground, and the cross-platform check
sections.body: For years after RNA-seq's debut, arrays remained genuinely competitive on cost per sample and on a track record of established reproducibility that a newer technology had not yet built. The SEQC/MAQC-III consortium's 2014 study (Nature Biotechnology), an FDA-coordinated effort spanning multiple sequencing centers and countries, tested reference RNA samples across multiple sequencing platforms and sites and found that relative expression measurements were accurate and reproducible across labs and platforms when appropriate filters were applied — though transcript-level and absolute quantification remained harder. That result gave RNA-seq the same kind of cross-platform validation the 2006 MAQC study had given arrays, and it is a large part of why RNA-seq displaced arrays as the default rather than simply coexisting as a niche alternative.

lessons.workedExample: A 2009 lab studying a non-model insect species has no microarray designed for it — arrays require a reference gene list to print probes against, and none exists. RNA-seq sidesteps this entirely: reads are sequenced directly from the insect's mRNA and either mapped to a related genome or assembled de novo, and Mortazavi's RPKM normalization lets the resulting expression levels be compared meaningfully across transcripts of different lengths. The same lab studying a well-characterized model organism in 2009, where a mature, cheap, well-validated array already exists, might reasonably stick with the array for a straightforward differential-expression question — the RNA-seq advantage is real but was not yet decisive on cost or established reproducibility for every use case.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking 'why RNA-seq instead of a microarray' wants specifics, not a vague 'it's more modern' — the honest answer names dynamic range, novel/non-model transcript detection, and isoform resolution as the actual mechanisms of advantage, while acknowledging that for well-studied organisms and simple comparisons, arrays stayed cost-competitive for years and had cross-platform validation (MAQC) before RNA-seq had its own (SEQC/MAQC-III, 2014). A student who can state both sides shows they understand a technology transition as a tradeoff resolved by evidence, not an inevitability.

questions.prompt: What problem did RPKM, introduced by Mortazavi et al. (2008), solve?

options.text: It made expression comparable across genes of different lengths and across runs of different sequencing depth
It eliminated the need for a reference genome entirely
It converted RNA-seq data into a two-colour fluorescence ratio
It removed all sequencing errors from raw reads

explanations.a: Correct — reads per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads normalizes for both transcript length and total sequencing depth, making counts comparable within and across experiments.
explanations.b: RPKM is a normalization of mapped read counts; reads still generally need to be mapped to some reference or assembly.
explanations.c: Fluorescence ratios are a microarray concept; RPKM is a read-count normalization specific to sequencing data.
explanations.d: RPKM does not correct sequencing errors; it normalizes already-mapped read counts for length and depth.

questions.prompt: Why can RNA-seq detect a transcript from a species with no reference genome, while a microarray cannot?

options.text: RNA-seq requires no pre-designed probe; it reads whatever sequence is present, while an array can only detect what its printed probes match
RNA-seq uses fluorescent dyes that bind any organism's RNA
Microarrays cannot process RNA from any organism except humans
RNA-seq does not actually require any RNA extraction step

explanations.a: Correct — sequencing reads out whatever RNA is present directly, so it can, in principle, capture novel or non-model transcripts, unlike a fixed-probe array.
explanations.b: Dye chemistry is not the relevant distinction; the key difference is fixed-probe design versus unbiased sequencing.
explanations.c: Microarrays can be designed for other organisms, but only if probes are specifically designed for that species' known genes.
explanations.d: RNA-seq still requires RNA extraction and library preparation before sequencing.

questions.prompt: What did the SEQC/MAQC-III consortium's 2014 study establish about RNA-seq?

options.text: That RNA-seq could never be reproduced across different labs
That relative expression measurements were accurate and reproducible across platforms and labs with appropriate filters, though transcript-level/absolute quantification remained harder
That microarrays were more accurate than RNA-seq in every respect
That RNA-seq could not detect novel exon-exon junctions

explanations.a: The opposite was found — relative expression was largely reproducible across platforms and sites.
explanations.b: Correct — the FDA-coordinated SEQC/MAQC-III study (Nature Biotechnology, 2014) found relative expression measures reproducible cross-platform and cross-lab with proper filtering, while transcript-level and absolute measurements remained more challenging.
explanations.c: The study evaluated RNA-seq's own reproducibility; it was not framed as declaring arrays categorically superior.
explanations.d: SEQC/MAQC-III tested how well expression measurements agreed across platforms and sites; it did not evaluate junction detection at all. Splice-junction resolution was an established RNA-seq capability years earlier — Nagalakshmi et al. (2008) revealed splicing in yeast by mapping reads back to the genome, and reads spanning junctions are what let RNA-seq separate isoforms an array probe would blur together.

questions.prompt: Order these RNA-seq milestones chronologically, earliest first.

items.text: Nagalakshmi et al. sequence the yeast transcriptome
Mortazavi et al. introduce RPKM in mouse RNA-seq
SEQC/MAQC-III publishes cross-platform RNA-seq concordance study

questions.explanation: Nagalakshmi's yeast transcriptome paper and Mortazavi's mouse RPKM paper were both published in 2008, establishing RNA-seq as a viable transcriptome-wide method; the SEQC/MAQC-III cross-platform validation followed years later in 2014, once RNA-seq had become widespread enough to need the same kind of reproducibility check arrays had received in 2006.

lessons.label: Single Cell: Tang 2009 to the Human Cell Atlas

sections.heading: One cell at a time: Tang et al. 2009
sections.body: Every method covered so far — Northern, SAGE, arrays, bulk RNA-seq — measures an average over thousands or millions of cells ground together, which hides any real biological difference between cell types or states mixed in that sample. Tang et al. (2009, Nature Methods) broke that ceiling by sequencing mRNA from a single mouse blastomere, proving that a whole transcriptome-level readout was possible starting from one cell's worth of RNA rather than a bulk population. The method demanded extreme sensitivity — amplifying picograms of starting material without losing the signal in noise — and it worked cell by cell, so profiling any meaningful number of cells meant repeating the entire process manually, which kept early single-cell studies small, often tens of cells at most.

sections.heading: Droplets collapse the per-cell cost
sections.body: The bottleneck was throughput, and 2015 broke it with droplet microfluidics. Macosko et al. (2015, Cell) introduced Drop-seq: cells and uniquely barcoded beads are co-encapsulated into nanoliter droplets so that every transcript from a given cell is tagged with that cell's specific barcode before pooling and sequencing everything together, letting reads be sorted back to their cell of origin computationally. Their demonstration profiled 44,808 mouse retinal cells in one run, resolving 39 distinct cell clusters and revealing new cell types within a tissue that had already been intensively studied for over a century. Klein et al. (2015, Cell) published inDrop the same year, a parallel droplet-barcoding approach. Commercial platforms, notably 10x Genomics' Chromium system, then packaged this droplet logic into a turnkey instrument, moving single-cell RNA-seq from a specialist technique into a standard lab tool within a few years.

sections.heading: From one cell to every cell type in the body
sections.body: With per-cell cost collapsing from droplet methods, the ambition scaled accordingly. The Human Cell Atlas initiative, announced in 2016 by Regev, Teichmann and collaborators, set out to map every cell type in the human body — location, molecular profile, and lineage — using single-cell sequencing at a scale earlier methods could never have reached. The arc from Tang's single blastomere to a project cataloguing millions of cells across every organ tracks the throughput curve directly: questions like 'what cell types compose this tissue, including rare ones no one has named yet' were simply not askable until droplet methods made profiling tens of thousands of cells routine rather than heroic.

lessons.workedExample: A 2008 developmental biologist wants to know whether two blastomeres of an early embryo, which look identical under a microscope, already differ in gene expression. Bulk RNA extraction would require pooling many embryos and could never distinguish one blastomere from its sister — the signal would average out. Tang's 2009 method made exactly this comparison possible for the first time, sequencing each blastomere's transcriptome individually. A 2016 retinal biologist asking a different question — 'how many distinct cell types exist in this tissue, including rare ones under 1% abundance' — needs Drop-seq-scale throughput instead: Macosko's 44,808-cell run found 39 clusters, a number achievable only because droplet barcoding parallelized what Tang's method still did one cell at a time.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking about single-cell methods wants to hear that the student understands scale as the variable that changes what question is even askable — a handful of cells (Tang, 2009) can answer 'are these two specific cells different,' while tens of thousands of cells (Drop-seq, 2015) are needed to answer 'what are all the cell types in this tissue, including rare ones.' A student who cites a specific number — Macosko's 44,808 retinal cells and 39 clusters — rather than 'they sequenced a lot of cells' shows they grasp why droplet barcoding was a step change in throughput, not just an incremental improvement.

questions.prompt: What did Tang et al. (2009) demonstrate for the first time?

options.text: Whole-transcriptome mRNA sequencing starting from a single cell (a mouse blastomere)
Sequencing 44,808 cells in a single run
The first commercial droplet-based sequencing instrument
Mapping every cell type in the human body

explanations.a: Correct — Tang et al. (2009) sequenced mRNA from a single mouse blastomere, proving transcriptome-scale profiling was possible from one cell's material.
explanations.b: That scale of profiling (44,808 cells) is Macosko et al.'s 2015 Drop-seq demonstration, six years later.
explanations.c: Commercial droplet instruments like 10x Chromium came after the 2015 droplet method papers, not from Tang's 2009 work.
explanations.d: Mapping every human cell type describes the Human Cell Atlas initiative, announced in 2016, not Tang's single-cell method paper.

questions.prompt: How does Drop-seq (Macosko et al., 2015) assign sequencing reads back to their cell of origin?

options.text: By co-encapsulating each cell with a uniquely barcoded bead in a droplet, tagging every transcript from that cell with its barcode before pooling
By physically sequencing each droplet on a separate machine
By manually picking each cell under a microscope before sequencing
By color-coding cells with different fluorescent dyes before sequencing

explanations.a: Correct — each droplet pairs one cell with one barcoded bead, so every transcript is tagged with a cell-specific barcode before all droplets are pooled and sequenced together, letting reads be computationally sorted back by barcode.
explanations.b: Droplets are pooled and sequenced together, not run on separate machines per droplet.
explanations.c: Manual single-cell picking describes the earlier, low-throughput approach Drop-seq was designed to replace.
explanations.d: Barcoding is molecular (DNA sequence tags on beads), not a fluorescent dye scheme.

questions.prompt: How many mouse retinal cells did Macosko et al.'s 2015 Drop-seq demonstration profile, and how many clusters did it resolve?

options.text: 44,808 cells, 39 clusters
100 cells, 5 clusters
1 million cells, 200 clusters
44,808 cells, 1 cluster

explanations.a: Correct — the Drop-seq demonstration profiled 44,808 mouse retinal cells, resolving 39 distinct cell clusters including previously undescribed cell types.
explanations.b: This figure is far too small; Drop-seq's whole point was moving well beyond the tens-of-cells scale of earlier single-cell methods.
explanations.c: A million cells overstates the original 2015 demonstration's scale, though later studies did reach larger scales.
explanations.d: A single cluster from 44,808 cells would mean no cell-type resolution at all, contradicting the study's actual finding of 39 distinct clusters.

questions.prompt: Order these single-cell milestones chronologically, earliest first.

items.text: Tang et al. sequence a single mouse blastomere's transcriptome
Macosko et al. (Drop-seq) and Klein et al. (inDrop) publish droplet-based single-cell methods
The Human Cell Atlas initiative is announced

questions.explanation: Tang et al.'s single-blastomere sequencing was published in 2009; the droplet-barcoding methods (Drop-seq and inDrop) both appeared in 2015, collapsing per-cell cost; the Human Cell Atlas initiative, aiming to map every human cell type, was announced in 2016 once that throughput made such a project conceivable.

lessons.label: Live Debates: Function, Noise, and Clusters

sections.heading: 80% functional, or 80% transcribed?
sections.body: The ENCODE consortium's 2012 flagship paper (Nature) reported that roughly 80% of the human genome shows some 'biochemical function' — being transcribed, bound by a protein, or bearing a histone mark — and framed this as evidence against the idea of mostly 'junk DNA.' Graur et al. (2013, Genome Biology and Evolution) published a pointed rebuttal arguing ENCODE's definition of 'function' was far too permissive: a sequence being transcribed or bound does not mean that activity does anything selectively important, and by ENCODE's own criteria, evolutionary theory would require the vast majority of the genome to be under purifying selection, which comparative genomics does not support. The dispute is not fully settled — it turns on what 'function' should mean (biochemical activity versus evolutionary conservation versus phenotypic consequence), and reasonable scientists still weight the evidence differently.

sections.heading: The lncRNA question: signal or noise, gene by gene
sections.body: Thousands of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are transcribed across the genome, and the field remains genuinely split on how many are functional versus incidental transcriptional noise from active chromatin, promoter read-through, or enhancer activity. A minority of lncRNAs (such as XIST or HOTAIR) have well-established, mechanistically characterized roles, but extrapolating a functional rate from these well-studied cases to the thousands of catalogued lncRNAs is exactly the kind of overgeneralization critics warn against — low expression, poor sequence conservation, and no phenotype on knockout are common for many lncRNAs, which is consistent with either 'subtle function not yet detected' or 'not functional.' Judges and papers alike should treat this as an open, gene-by-gene empirical question, not a settled ratio.

sections.heading: Do clusters discover cell types, or manufacture them?
sections.body: Single-cell analysis raises its own live statistical debate: unsupervised clustering groups cells by similarity, and then the same data is often reused to test whether genes differ between those clusters — a form of 'double dipping,' since the clusters were defined using the very data now being tested, inflating apparent significance and risking clusters that reflect noise rather than real cell types. Selective-inference methods respond directly to this: Neufeld, Gao, Popp, Battle & Witten (2022) proposed count splitting, dividing each cell's read counts into independent parts so that one part defines clusters and the other tests differences between them, avoiding using the same data twice; Gao, Bien & Witten (2022) developed a related selective-inference approach for testing whether clusters from hierarchical clustering are genuinely distinct. A separate but related concern, raised by Squair et al. (2021, Nature Communications), is that differential-expression tests routinely treat individual cells as independent replicates when they actually come from a small number of biological samples — a form of pseudoreplication that can produce false-positive gene calls with artificially tiny p-values from inflated sample size.

lessons.workedExample: A student clusters their single-cell dataset into what looks like 6 distinct cell populations, then runs a differential-expression test between clusters 3 and 4 to find marker genes, and reports a tiny p-value as strong evidence the two are truly distinct cell types. A reviewer familiar with the double-dipping problem would ask: did you use the same counts to both define the clusters and test for differences between them? If so, the p-value is inflated by construction, because clustering was, in part, optimized to find groups that look different. A count-splitting approach (Neufeld et al., 2022) — clustering on one independent half of each cell's counts, testing on the other — or reporting whether the same pattern holds across independent biological replicates (addressing Squair et al.'s pseudoreplication concern) would make the claim defensible instead of circular.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing 'is this a real cell type or a clustering artifact' is testing whether a student knows double dipping is a real statistical failure mode, not a hypothetical — using the same data to both discover and confirm a pattern manufactures significance. Naming count splitting (Neufeld et al., 2022) as a concrete fix, or explaining pseudoreplication (Squair et al., 2021) when a student treats thousands of cells from three mice as thousands of independent replicates, shows the student can defend a single-cell result against the specific critique a statistically literate judge would raise — and framing ENCODE's 80% figure or lncRNA function rates as contested rather than settled shows the same intellectual honesty applied to functional genomics.

questions.prompt: What was the core of Graur et al.'s (2013) rebuttal to ENCODE's 2012 claim that ~80% of the genome is 'functional'?

options.text: ENCODE's definition of function (any biochemical activity) was too permissive and inconsistent with what evolutionary theory would predict if taken literally
ENCODE had made a simple arithmetic error and the true figure was 8%, not 80%
Graur et al. agreed completely with ENCODE and only clarified terminology
The human genome has since been shown to be entirely non-functional

explanations.a: Correct — Graur et al. argued that biochemical activity (transcription, protein binding) is a far weaker standard than evolutionary or phenotypic function, and that ENCODE's criteria would imply an implausible level of genome-wide purifying selection.
explanations.b: The dispute was about the definition of 'function,' not an arithmetic error in the underlying percentage.
explanations.c: Graur et al.'s paper was a pointed critique, not an agreement with ENCODE's framing.
explanations.d: Neither side claims the genome is entirely non-functional; the debate is about how much and by what definition.

questions.prompt: What is the 'double dipping' problem in single-cell clustering analysis?

options.text: Using the same data both to define clusters and to test whether genes differ between those clusters, inflating apparent significance
Sequencing the same cell twice by mistake
Using two different sequencing platforms on the same sample
Running a clustering algorithm twice with different random seeds

explanations.a: Correct — because the clusters were chosen, in part, to maximize apparent differences in the data, testing for those differences using the same data circularly inflates significance.
explanations.b: Accidental duplicate sequencing is a technical error, not the statistical double-dipping issue being described.
explanations.c: Cross-platform comparison is a different concern (addressed by studies like MAQC/SEQC), not double dipping.
explanations.d: Re-running clustering with different seeds is a stability check, not the double-dipping problem itself.

questions.prompt: What does 'count splitting' (Neufeld, Gao, Popp, Battle & Witten, 2022) do to address double dipping?

options.text: Divides each cell's read counts into independent parts so one part defines clusters and a separate part tests differences between them
Removes all low-count genes from the dataset before analysis
Doubles the sequencing depth to increase statistical power
Merges all clusters into a single group before testing

explanations.a: Correct — count splitting creates independent data partitions so clustering and downstream testing do not reuse the same information, avoiding the circularity of double dipping.
explanations.b: Filtering low-count genes is a standard QC step unrelated to the double-dipping fix specifically.
explanations.c: Increasing depth does not address the circularity of using identical data for discovery and testing.
explanations.d: Merging clusters would defeat the purpose of testing whether distinct clusters differ.

questions.prompt: What did Squair et al. (2021) identify as a pseudoreplication problem in single-cell differential expression testing?

options.text: Treating individual cells as independent replicates when they actually come from a small number of biological samples, artificially inflating apparent sample size
Sequencing too few cells per experiment
Using count splitting instead of standard clustering
Failing to use fluorescent barcodes on droplets

explanations.a: Correct — treating thousands of cells from just a few biological samples/animals as independent statistical replicates inflates the apparent sample size and can produce artificially significant p-values.
explanations.b: The pseudoreplication concern is about over-counting replicates, not about having too few cells sequenced.
explanations.c: Count splitting is a different, unrelated fix (for clustering double dipping), not what Squair et al.'s critique concerns.
explanations.d: Barcoding is a droplet-sequencing technique, unrelated to the statistical replicate-counting problem Squair et al. described.

lessons.label: How a Droplet Experiment Works

sections.heading: One cell, one bead, one droplet
sections.body: Droplet-based single-cell RNA-seq (Drop-seq, Macosko et al. 2015; inDrop, Klein et al. 2015; and the commercial 10x Genomics Chromium platform, Zheng et al. 2017) works by flowing a dilute cell suspension and a suspension of barcoded beads down microfluidic channels that merge into a stream of oil, pinching off tens of thousands of nanoliter droplets per run. Poisson loading keeps most droplets empty and most occupied droplets holding exactly one cell paired with one bead, so a typical run captures roughly 1,000-10,000 cells rather than every cell in the suspension. Each bead carries millions of copies of an oligo with a cell barcode identical across that one bead but unique to it, plus a random unique molecular identifier (UMI) attached to every individual oligo.

sections.heading: Why a barcode and a UMI, not just a barcode
sections.body: Inside the droplet the cell lyses and its mRNA anneals to the bead's oligos, which prime reverse transcription. Every resulting cDNA molecule carries the bead's cell barcode, tagging which cell it came from once droplets are pooled and sequenced together, and a UMI, tagging that specific captured mRNA molecule. The UMI lets a computational pipeline collapse PCR duplicates: five reads sharing a cell barcode, gene, and UMI count as one captured transcript, not five. Standard practice sequences to about 20,000-50,000 reads per cell, deep enough to saturate UMI detection for well-expressed genes without wasting reads on duplicates.

sections.heading: Capture efficiency, tissue damage, and the full-length alternative
sections.body: Reverse transcription and bead capture are inefficient: only a fraction of a cell's actual mRNA molecules, commonly cited around 10-20%, end up as detected UMIs, which is the root cause of the sparse, mostly-zero data matrix these experiments produce. Dissociating solid tissue into a single-cell suspension is itself stressful, and van den Brink et al. (2017) showed that the enzymatic dissociation step induces immediate-early stress-response genes like FOS and JUN, an artefact that can look like a real biological cluster if not recognized. For frozen or hard-to-dissociate tissue (adult brain, bone, fat), single-nucleus RNA-seq extracts nuclei instead of whole cells, avoiding fresh dissociation entirely at the cost of missing cytoplasmic and mitochondrial transcripts. Plate-based Smart-seq2 (Picelli et al. 2013) sacrifices droplet throughput for full-length transcript coverage and much higher per-cell sensitivity, sequencing hundreds of cells sorted into individual wells rather than thousands pooled in droplets. The low cell concentration behind Poisson loading is itself a deliberate trade-off: loading more cells recovers more of the suspension per run, but it also raises the odds that two cells share one droplet, so labs deliberately keep the cell concentration low enough that the Poisson-predicted multiplet rate stays under roughly 5-8%, accepting a lower cell-recovery ceiling in exchange for keeping most droplets single-cell rather than confounded doublets.

lessons.workedExample: A lab dissociates fresh mouse cortex, loads 10,000 cells on a 10x Chromium run, and sequences at 30,000 reads/cell. After demultiplexing they recover barcodes for about 7,000 real cells (Poisson loading never captures every cell 1:1) with a median of 1,500 genes detected per cell — a fraction of the ~10,000+ genes each neuron actually expresses, because low per-molecule capture efficiency (~15%) combined with Poisson sampling means genes expressed at only one or a few copies often yield zero captured UMIs, while abundant transcripts are still reliably detected. A cluster expressing FOS, JUN, and other immediate-early genes at high levels across otherwise distinct cell types is flagged as a dissociation-stress artefact, not a true cell state, and is either regressed out or excluded rather than reported as a discovery.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks how the sequencing data was generated because the droplet method's mechanics directly bound what conclusions are defensible: a student who can explain that a barcode identifies the cell and a UMI identifies the molecule shows they understand why duplicate reads don't inflate counts, and a student who knows capture efficiency is only ~10-20% won't overinterpret a gene's absence as proof it isn't expressed. Naming the dissociation stress-response artefact specifically signals the student checked their own clusters for a known confound rather than assuming every cluster is real biology.

questions.prompt: In a droplet scRNA-seq bead, what distinguishes the cell barcode from the UMI?

options.text: The cell barcode is identical across all oligos on one bead; the UMI is random and unique to each individual oligo
The UMI is identical across all oligos on one bead; the cell barcode is random and unique to each oligo
They are the same sequence, read twice for error correction
The cell barcode marks the gene; the UMI marks the cell

explanations.a: Correct — every oligo on a given bead shares that bead's cell barcode, so all cDNA from one droplet is tagged as coming from one cell, while each oligo's own UMI is random, letting duplicate reads of the same captured molecule be collapsed to one count.
explanations.b: This reverses the roles; the UMI, not the cell barcode, must vary per oligo or PCR duplicates could never be distinguished from independent molecules.
explanations.c: They serve different, non-redundant purposes and are not error-correction copies of each other.
explanations.d: Neither tag marks a gene; gene identity comes from where the cDNA sequence aligns in the genome, not from either barcode.

questions.prompt: A researcher finds a cluster of cells from many different tissue types all strongly expressing FOS and JUN. What should they suspect first?

options.text: A newly discovered universal cell type
A dissociation-induced stress-response artefact
A sequencing depth problem
A doublet of two real cell types

explanations.a: Immediate-early genes shared across unrelated cell types are a documented technical artefact, not a biological discovery.
explanations.b: Correct — van den Brink et al. (2017) showed that the enzymatic dissociation needed to make a single-cell suspension induces immediate-early stress genes like FOS and JUN, a pattern that can masquerade as a real shared cluster across cell types.
explanations.c: Sequencing depth affects how many genes are detected per cell, not which specific stress genes turn on.
explanations.d: Doublets show co-expression of two distinct cell-type marker programs, not a shared stress signature across unrelated tissues.

questions.prompt: Match each scRNA-seq approach to its defining trade-off.

right.text: High throughput (thousands of cells) but only a fraction of each cell's mRNA is captured
Works on frozen/hard tissue by profiling nuclei, but misses cytoplasmic transcripts
Full-length transcript coverage and high per-cell sensitivity, but only hundreds of cells

questions.explanation: Droplet methods trade sensitivity for scale (~10-20% capture efficiency across thousands of cells); single-nucleus RNA-seq trades cytoplasmic transcript coverage for compatibility with frozen or hard-to-dissociate tissue; Smart-seq2 trades throughput for full-length, high-sensitivity profiling of a much smaller number of cells.

questions.prompt: Why do UMIs matter for interpreting read counts in a droplet scRNA-seq experiment?

options.text: They let the pipeline collapse PCR-duplicate reads of the same captured molecule down to one count
They identify which species the cell came from
They increase the number of genes physically captured per cell
They replace the need for a cell barcode

explanations.a: Correct — because each captured mRNA molecule gets one random UMI before PCR amplification, multiple reads sharing a cell barcode, gene, and UMI are recognized as PCR duplicates of a single original molecule, not independent captures.
explanations.b: Species identity comes from genome alignment of the sequence itself, not from the UMI.
explanations.c: UMIs correct counting after capture; they do not change how much mRNA is physically captured from the cell.
explanations.d: UMIs and cell barcodes serve different, complementary roles and both are needed on the same bead oligo.

lessons.label: Sparse Data: Dropout, Ambient RNA, Doublets, QC

sections.heading: A matrix that is mostly zero, and what that actually means
sections.body: A typical cell-by-gene count matrix from droplet scRNA-seq is more than 90% zeros. The intuitive explanation is 'dropout' — that lowly expressed genes are stochastically lost during capture, as if the technology is unreliable in a way that needs a special statistical fix. Svensson (2020) tested this directly using spike-in control RNA of known concentration and found that UMI counts were well explained by simple sampling statistics (Poisson-like variance) without invoking extra zero-inflation beyond what low capture efficiency already predicts. In other words, most zeros are not a technology glitch to be modeled away — they are the expected consequence of sampling roughly 10-20% of a cell's mRNA molecules from a cell that may only have had a few copies of that transcript to begin with. This matters because analysis pipelines that impute or 'denoise' zeros as if they were errors can manufacture signal that isn't there.

sections.heading: Ambient RNA and doublets: signal that isn't from the cell you think
sections.body: Two other artefacts pollute the matrix in ways dropout does not.
