Ambient or 'soup' RNA is free-floating mRNA released by lysed cells during dissociation that gets randomly incorporated into every droplet, giving every cell a low background of transcripts from cell types it never was; tools like SoupX and CellBender estimate and subtract this background per sample. Doublets occur when two cells are captured in one droplet and their transcriptomes are read out as a single fake 'cell.' The doublet rate is not fixed — it scales with how many cells are loaded, and 10x Genomics documents roughly 0.8% doublets per 1,000 cells recovered, meaning a 10,000-cell run can expect close to 8% doublets. Computational tools such as Scrublet and DoubletFinder simulate synthetic doublets from the real data and flag cells whose expression profiles resemble those simulations.

sections.heading: QC thresholds are decisions, not facts
sections.body: Before any biology is asked of the data, cells are filtered on genes detected per cell (too few suggests an empty droplet or degraded cell), total UMI counts per cell (too few or implausibly many suggests background or a doublet), and percent mitochondrial reads (high mitochondrial fraction indicates a dying or ruptured cell, since cytoplasmic mRNA leaks out while mitochondria-enclosed transcripts remain). None of these thresholds are handed down by the instrument — a lab choosing '>200 genes' versus '>500 genes,' or '<5% mito' versus '<10% mito,' is choosing which cells exist in the dataset that every downstream figure is built from, and a paper rarely reports how sensitive its conclusions are to that choice.

lessons.workedExample: A team profiles a tumor biopsy and loads 12,000 cells on a Chromium run. At 10x's documented rate of ~0.8% doublets per 1,000 cells recovered, they expect roughly 9-10% of their droplets to be doublets before any filtering. Scrublet flags cells with hybrid expression profiles, but its detection sensitivity is imperfect, so it catches most but not all of the ~1,100 expected doublets, and the team removes about 900 of them. They then apply QC cutoffs of >300 genes/cell and <10% mitochondrial reads (looser than the <5% often used for hardy cell lines, since tumor tissue handling causes more stress). Reporting both the doublet rate and the exact QC thresholds in their methods lets a reader judge whether a rare cell population survived the filters by biology or was cut by the cutoff.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on QC thresholds because they are usually invisible in a results slide but decide which cells 'exist' in every figure that follows — a student who can state their exact genes-per-cell and mitochondrial-percent cutoffs, and defend why, has done real quality control; one who says 'we filtered out bad cells' has not. Asking about doublet rate specifically tests whether the student understands that doublets scale with loading density rather than being a fixed nuisance rate, which is the difference between a design choice (how many cells to load) and an unavoidable error.

questions.prompt: What did Svensson (2020) conclude about the >90% zeros in droplet scRNA-seq count matrices?

options.text: The zeros mostly reflect a technical zero-inflation problem that requires special imputation
UMI counts were well explained by sampling statistics without extra zero-inflation beyond what low capture efficiency predicts
The zeros are always sequencing errors and should be discarded from the matrix
Zero-inflation only occurs in plate-based Smart-seq data, not droplet data

explanations.a: This is the intuition Svensson's spike-in analysis argued against — the zeros did not require a separate zero-inflation mechanism beyond ordinary sampling.
explanations.b: Correct — using spike-in controls of known concentration, Svensson (2020) showed UMI counts fit simple sampling (Poisson-like) statistics, implying most zeros reflect low capture efficiency sampling a cell's mRNA, not a technology-specific dropout process needing correction.
explanations.c: Most zeros are a real consequence of sampling a small fraction of a cell's transcripts, not sequencing errors, and discarding them would discard the count data itself.
explanations.d: Svensson's analysis addressed droplet (UMI-based) data specifically; the claim is not restricted to Smart-seq.

questions.prompt: A 10x Chromium run recovers 10,000 cells. Using the documented rate of ~0.8% doublets per 1,000 cells recovered, roughly what fraction of droplets are expected to be doublets?

options.text: About 0.8%
About 8%
About 80%
Doublet rate does not depend on how many cells are recovered

explanations.a: 0.8% is the rate per 1,000 cells, not the total rate at 10,000 cells recovered.
explanations.b: Correct — scaling 0.8% per 1,000 cells recovered by 10 (for 10,000 cells) gives roughly 8% expected doublets, illustrating why doublet rate rises with loading density.
explanations.c: This overstates the scaling; the rate is per 1,000 cells, not per cell.
explanations.d: The whole point of the documented rate is that doublets scale with the number of cells recovered — denser loading means more co-encapsulation events.

questions.prompt: Match each scRNA-seq artefact to the tool or method used to address it.

left.text: Two cells captured as one droplet

right.text: SoupX or CellBender estimate and subtract background transcripts
Scrublet or DoubletFinder simulate synthetic doublets to flag suspicious profiles
Filtering on high mitochondrial read percentage

questions.explanation: Ambient RNA released by lysed cells is corrected computationally with tools like SoupX or CellBender; doublets are flagged by simulation-based tools like Scrublet or DoubletFinder; dying/ruptured cells leak cytoplasmic mRNA while retaining mitochondrial transcripts, so a high mitochondrial percentage is the standard flag for them.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson describe QC thresholds (genes/cell, counts/cell, % mitochondrial) as 'decisions, not facts'?

options.text: Because the instrument reports different thresholds for every run automatically
Because each threshold is a researcher-chosen cutoff that determines which cells are included in every downstream analysis, and rarely comes with a sensitivity check
Because QC thresholds have no effect on which cells appear in the final dataset
Because mitochondrial percentage cannot be computed from the count matrix

explanations.a: Thresholds are set by the analyst in software, not generated automatically by the sequencing instrument.
explanations.b: Correct — a lab's choice of, for example, >200 vs >500 genes/cell or <5% vs <10% mitochondrial reads directly determines which cells survive filtering, and that choice is rarely stress-tested for how much it changes downstream conclusions.
explanations.c: The opposite is true — QC thresholds directly determine which cells make it into the final dataset used for every figure.
explanations.d: Mitochondrial percentage is computed directly from the count matrix by summing reads mapping to mitochondrial genes, which is exactly why it can be used as a QC filter.

lessons.label: From Matrix to Clusters

sections.heading: Normalizing away sequencing depth, not biology
sections.body: Different cells are sequenced to different total UMI counts for purely technical reasons — a bigger cell, or one that happened to sit in a slightly more efficient droplet, yields more captured molecules regardless of its true biology. Standard log-normalization divides each cell's gene counts by that cell's total counts, scales to a common factor (often 10,000), and log-transforms, putting cells on a comparable footing. sctransform (Hafemeister & Satija 2019) replaces this with a variance-stabilizing transform built on regularized negative binomial regression across genes, explicitly modeling how a gene's variance relates to its mean expression instead of assuming a single scaling factor fits every gene equally well. After normalization, the pipeline selects a subset of highly variable genes — commonly around 2,000 — genes whose expression varies more across cells than technical noise alone would predict, since including all ~20,000 genes would drown true cell-type signal in noise from housekeeping genes that barely vary.

sections.heading: Compressing dimensions, then building a neighbor graph
sections.body: Principal component analysis (PCA) is run on the highly variable genes to compress thousands of gene dimensions into a much smaller number, typically 10-50, that capture most of the structured variance; an elbow plot of variance explained per component guides how many to keep, and choosing too few collapses real subtypes together while too many reintroduces noise. In that reduced PCA space, a k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) graph connects each cell to its most transcriptionally similar neighbors, turning the dataset into a graph rather than a table of coordinates.

sections.heading: Clustering the graph, and the parameter that decides your answer
sections.body: Community-detection algorithms — Louvain (Blondel et al. 2008) and its improvement Leiden (Traag, Waltman & van Eck 2019), which fixed a flaw where Louvain could produce badly connected or disconnected 'communities' — partition the kNN graph into clusters, interpreted as candidate cell types or states. The single most consequential knob here is the resolution parameter: a low resolution merges cells into few, coarse clusters (broad categories like 'T cell'), while a high resolution splits the same data into many fine clusters (naive vs. memory vs. exhausted T cell). There is no resolution the algorithm can tell you is 'correct' — it is a modeling choice the researcher makes and must justify against known biology. Finally, UMAP (McInnes et al. 2018) and t-SNE (van der Maaten & Hinton 2008) project the PCA space down to 2D for visualization; both are explicitly built to preserve local neighborhood structure (which cells are near which), but neither reliably preserves the distance between clusters or the relative size of clusters, so a small gap or a huge blob on a UMAP plot is not evidence of a small or large biological difference.

lessons.workedExample: A student clusters PBMC data twice, once at Leiden resolution 0.4 and once at 1.2. At 0.4 they get 6 clusters that map cleanly onto T cells, B cells, monocytes, and NK cells. At 1.2 they get 18 clusters, splitting T cells into 5 subclusters. Neither run is 'wrong' — the question is what the student wants to claim. If their hypothesis is about T cell subtype differences, resolution 1.2 is appropriate as long as they can point to known marker genes (e.g., CCR7 for naive vs. GZMB for effector) distinguishing the new subclusters; if they cannot find markers separating two of the 18 clusters, that split is likely noise, not biology, and should be reported as over-clustering rather than a discovery.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why did you pick that resolution?' is testing whether the student understands that clustering resolution is a modeling decision, not a measurement — a student who says 'we tried several resolutions and confirmed our clusters with known marker genes' has shown the number of cell types in their poster is a defensible interpretation, while a student who ran the default resolution without checking is reporting whatever the software's default happened to produce. The UMAP-distance question catches students who describe two clusters as 'very different' or 'close together' based on their spacing on a 2D plot, which UMAP does not guarantee reflects real transcriptional distance.

questions.prompt: What problem does per-cell normalization (e.g., log-normalization or sctransform) primarily correct for?

options.text: Differences in total sequencing depth between cells that are technical, not biological
Batch effects between different sequencing runs on different days
Doublets formed by two cells captured in one droplet
Ambient RNA contamination from lysed cells

explanations.a: Correct — cells are sequenced to different total UMI counts for technical reasons, and normalization puts gene expression on a comparable scale across cells before any biological comparison is made.
explanations.b: Batch effects across runs are addressed by integration methods like Harmony or MNN, a separate step from per-cell normalization.
explanations.c: Doublets are addressed by dedicated detection tools like Scrublet, not by normalization.
explanations.d: Ambient RNA is addressed by tools like SoupX or CellBender, not by normalization of sequencing depth.

questions.prompt: Order the standard steps from a raw count matrix to a 2D visualization of clusters.

items.text: Normalize counts and select ~2,000 highly variable genes
Run PCA to reduce to ~10-50 dimensions
Build a kNN graph in PCA space and run Leiden/Louvain clustering
Project into 2D with UMAP or t-SNE for visualization

questions.explanation: The pipeline normalizes and selects variable genes first, compresses that gene space with PCA, clusters cells using a neighbor graph built in the reduced PCA space, and only projects to 2D with UMAP/t-SNE afterward purely for visualization — clustering is not performed on the 2D UMAP coordinates themselves.

questions.prompt: What do UMAP and t-SNE reliably preserve, and what do they NOT reliably preserve?

options.text: They preserve local neighborhood structure but not between-cluster distances or cluster size
They preserve between-cluster distances but not local neighborhoods
They preserve both local neighborhoods and global distances equally well
They preserve cluster size but not which cells are near which

explanations.a: Correct — both algorithms are explicitly designed to keep transcriptionally similar cells near each other in the low-dimensional embedding, but the space between well-separated clusters and the apparent size of a cluster on the plot are artifacts of the layout algorithm, not measurements of biological distance or population size.
explanations.b: This reverses their actual behavior; local neighborhood preservation is the design goal, not global distance preservation.
explanations.c: Global distance preservation is specifically what these algorithms sacrifice in order to preserve local structure well.
explanations.d: Local neighborhood preservation, not cluster size, is what the algorithms are built to keep faithful.

questions.prompt: In Leiden/Louvain clustering, what does raising the resolution parameter do?

options.text: It increases sequencing depth per cell
It produces more, finer-grained clusters from the same data
It removes doublets from the dataset
It changes the normalization method used

explanations.a: Resolution is a clustering parameter applied after sequencing; it has no effect on how deeply cells were sequenced.
explanations.b: Correct — a higher resolution splits the same kNN graph into more, smaller clusters, which is why the number of 'cell types' reported from one dataset can change dramatically depending on this single choice.
explanations.c: Doublet removal is a separate QC step performed before clustering, unrelated to the resolution parameter.
explanations.d: Normalization method (e.g., log-normalization vs. sctransform) is chosen earlier in the pipeline and is independent of clustering resolution.

lessons.label: Annotating Cell Types Honestly

sections.heading: Marker genes and automated reference mapping
sections.body: The most direct way to name a cluster is marker-gene scoring: checking whether a cluster's top differentially expressed genes match a known cell-type signature, such as CD3D/CD3E for T cells or MS4A1 for B cells. This scales poorly by hand across dozens of clusters, so automated tools compare each cell's expression profile to a labeled reference atlas and assign the closest match — SingleR (Aran et al. 2019) correlates each cell or cluster against reference expression profiles, while Azimuth (Hao et al. 2021) maps query cells directly onto a Seurat-built reference through the same PCA space the reference was built in. Both tools fail in a specific, predictable way: if the tissue or cell state under study is not represented in the reference atlas — a disease-specific cell state, a developmental stage, a non-model organism — the algorithm still returns a confident-looking label, forcing the query cell onto the nearest available reference type even when none of the reference types are actually correct.

sections.heading: The judgment calls no algorithm makes for you
sections.body: Real annotation requires calls a pipeline cannot make automatically. Over-split clusters — two clusters differing only by a handful of genes with no clear marker distinction — are often merged back into one cell type after manual review. Doublets can masquerade as a biologically plausible 'intermediate' or 'transitional' state, since a droplet containing one T cell and one monocyte produces a hybrid expression profile that superficially resembles a transitioning cell; distinguishing a real transitional state from a doublet artefact requires checking whether the intermediate cluster's total UMI count and gene count are unusually high (consistent with two cells' worth of RNA) and whether its 'intermediate' markers are truly co-expressed within single cells or just averaged across the cluster. And sometimes the honest annotation is simply 'unknown' — a cluster with no clear marker signature and no match to any reference, which a rigorous student reports as unresolved rather than assigning a guessed label to make every cluster look identified.

sections.heading: Integration can erase the differences you're trying to find
sections.body: When combining data from multiple samples, batches, or patients, integration/batch-correction tools — Harmony (Korsunsky et al. 2019), scVI (Lopez et al. 2018, a variational autoencoder-based model), and mutual nearest neighbors (MNN, Haghverdi et al. 2018) — align cells from different batches so that clustering isn't dominated by which sample a cell came from. But these algorithms cannot distinguish 'a technical batch effect' from 'a real biological difference between conditions' — both look like systematic shifts between groups of cells. Over-aggressive integration can merge genuinely distinct cell states (a disease-specific activated state vs. its healthy counterpart) into one cluster, silently erasing the exact biological signal a study set out to detect.

lessons.workedExample: A team profiles tumor-infiltrating immune cells and runs Azimuth against a healthy peripheral-blood reference. Every cluster gets a confident label — but the tumor-specific exhausted T cell population, which does not exist in a healthy blood reference, gets mapped to 'CD8 T cell' with no indication that the match is poor. The team catches this by checking exhaustion markers (PDCD1, LAG3, HAVCR2) that are absent from the reference's CD8 T cell profile but present in their cluster, and reports the cluster as 'CD8 T cell, exhausted-like (reference mismatch, manually annotated)' rather than trusting Azimuth's clean-looking but wrong label.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'how did you know your cluster labels were right?' is probing whether the student trusted an automated tool blindly or actually validated marker genes against the specific biology of their sample. Naming the reference-mismatch failure mode specifically — that a tool like SingleR or Azimuth will confidently mislabel a cell type absent from its reference rather than flagging uncertainty — shows the student understands these tools answer 'what's the closest match' and not 'is this even in your reference,' which is the difference between using a tool and being used by it.

questions.prompt: A tool like SingleR or Azimuth is used to annotate a cluster of cells from a diseased tissue whose exact cell state is absent from the reference atlas. What is the most likely failure mode?

options.text: The tool will refuse to output any label and flag the cluster as unknown
The tool will confidently assign the closest available reference label even though none of the reference types is actually correct
The tool will crash and stop the analysis pipeline
The tool will automatically expand the reference to include the new cell state

explanations.a: Reference-mapping tools are built to output a best match, not to detect that no good match exists, so they do not default to 'unknown.'
explanations.b: Correct — reference mapping finds the nearest match in whatever reference it was given; if the true cell state isn't in that reference, the tool still returns a confident-looking label for the closest available type, which is why manual marker validation remains necessary.
explanations.c: These tools are designed to always return an output for query cells; they do not crash simply because a cell type is missing from the reference.
explanations.d: Reference atlases are fixed inputs; the mapping tool does not learn or add new cell types on its own during annotation.

questions.prompt: A cluster with an 'intermediate' expression profile between T cells and monocytes could be a real transitional cell state or a doublet artefact. What check helps distinguish the two?

options.text: Checking whether cells in that cluster have unusually high total UMI counts and gene counts, consistent with two cells' worth of RNA
Checking the resolution parameter used in clustering
Re-running sctransform normalization
Comparing the cluster's size on the UMAP plot to other clusters

explanations.a: Correct — a doublet contains RNA from two real cells, so it tends to show elevated total counts and detected genes relative to singlet clusters, which is a concrete, checkable signature distinguishing it from a genuine biological transition.
explanations.b: Resolution controls how finely clusters are split, but it does not by itself reveal whether a given cluster is a doublet artefact.
explanations.c: Renormalizing does not address whether a specific cluster's cells contain RNA from one or two cells.
explanations.d: UMAP cluster size is not a reliable measure of anything biological, including doublet content, per the lesson on UMAP's limitations.

questions.prompt: Match each annotation tool or method to its role.

right.text: Automated reference-based cell-type label assignment
Batch correction/integration across samples before clustering
Direct check of known genes (e.g., CD3D for T cells) against a cluster's top expressed genes

questions.explanation: SingleR and Azimuth automate cell-type labeling by comparison to a reference atlas; Harmony, scVI, and MNN correct for batch/sample effects so clustering isn't driven by technical origin; manual marker-gene scoring is the direct, tool-independent check against known biology.

questions.prompt: How can over-aggressive integration (e.g., Harmony, scVI, or MNN) distort a study's results?

options.text: It can merge a genuinely distinct disease-specific cell state with its healthy counterpart, erasing the biological difference the study aimed to detect
It can introduce new doublets into the dataset
It can lower sequencing depth per cell
It can prevent PCA from running

explanations.a: Correct — integration algorithms cannot inherently tell a technical batch effect from a real biological difference between conditions, so aligning too aggressively can pull apart cell states together into one merged cluster, hiding the exact effect the study set out to find.
explanations.b: Doublets are formed during droplet capture, before any computational integration step, so integration does not create them.
explanations.c: Sequencing depth is fixed at the sequencing stage and is unaffected by downstream computational integration.
explanations.d: Integration is typically applied on or alongside PCA-reduced representations; it does not block PCA from running.

lessons.label: Trajectories and RNA Velocity

sections.heading: Pseudotime: ordering cells along an assumed continuum
sections.body: A single-cell snapshot captures each cell at one moment, but many biological processes — differentiation, activation, disease progression — are continuous. Pseudotime methods like Monocle (Trapnell et al. 2014) and Slingshot (Street et al. 2018) take a static snapshot of many cells captured at different points along such a process and order them along an inferred trajectory through gene-expression space, assigning each cell a pseudotime value representing its estimated progress. Slingshot builds a minimum-spanning tree through cluster centroids and fits smooth curves (principal curves) through the data along that tree, while Monocle's later versions build a graph embedding it calls a 'reversed graph.' Critically, pseudotime is an ordering, not a measurement of real elapsed time, and the method itself already assumes the data represents points along a continuum — feeding it discrete, unrelated cell types will still produce an ordering, whether or not one exists biologically.

sections.heading: RNA velocity: reading direction from splicing kinetics
sections.body: RNA velocity (La Manno et al. 2018) adds something pseudotime alone cannot provide: direction. Pre-mRNA transcripts still containing introns (unspliced) get processed into mature, intron-free (spliced) mRNA over time, and because standard sequencing reads capture both forms, the ratio of unspliced to spliced reads for a gene in a given cell indicates whether that gene's expression is currently rising (high unspliced relative to spliced, predicting future increase in spliced mRNA) or falling (low unspliced relative to spliced). Aggregating this across thousands of genes per cell produces a velocity vector, drawn as an arrow on a UMAP plot, that predicts which direction a cell is moving in expression space in the near future — turning a static snapshot into an implied dynamic model.

sections.heading: Why the arrows can be wrong
sections.body: The original 2018 model assumes constant transcription, splicing, and degradation rates across genes and across the whole trajectory — a steady-state assumption that does not hold for genes with time-varying kinetics. Bergen et al. (2020) and subsequent reassessments documented that these constant-rate assumptions produce misleading velocity arrows in real datasets, including cases where arrows point in directions inconsistent with known biological ground truth, especially around cell-cycle genes and genes whose splicing kinetics genuinely change over a trajectory. The practical lesson: a trajectory or a velocity arrow is a hypothesis generated under specific modeling assumptions, not direct observation of cells moving through time. A defensible trajectory needs independent support — known marker genes for the proposed start and end states, or ideally an orthogonal time-course experiment — rather than resting on pseudotime ordering or velocity arrows alone, both of which will produce a confident-looking output even from noise.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs RNA velocity on immune cells from one blood draw and gets arrows pointing from a monocyte cluster toward a dendritic-cell cluster, which they present as evidence of a monocyte-to-dendritic-cell differentiation trajectory. A more careful check: monocytes and dendritic cells are both terminally differentiated in blood, not stages of one lineage, and known differentiation biology places their common progenitor earlier in the bone marrow, not visible in a peripheral blood sample. The arrows likely reflect noisy or violated steady-state assumptions rather than real differentiation. The student instead checks whether canonical progenitor markers appear anywhere in the dataset (they don't) and reports the arrows as inconclusive rather than as evidence of a trajectory the sampled tissue could not actually contain.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on trajectory and velocity claims because both methods are specifically designed to always produce an ordering or a direction, whether or not the underlying biology is a real continuum — so the output alone is never proof. A student who says 'we drew an arrow toward cell type X' has shown a plot; a student who says 'we checked that our two endpoints are known to have a real precursor-progeny relationship, and confirmed with marker genes independent of the velocity model' has shown they understand the tool's steady-state assumptions can generate a confident-looking but wrong direction.

questions.prompt: What does RNA velocity use to infer the direction a cell is moving in expression space?

options.text: The ratio of unspliced (intron-containing) to spliced (mature) mRNA reads per gene
The total number of UMIs detected per cell
The physical order in which cells were loaded into droplets
The percentage of mitochondrial reads per cell

explanations.a: Correct — a gene with high unspliced relative to spliced reads is inferred to be actively transcribing and rising in expression, while low unspliced relative to spliced suggests declining expression, and aggregating this across genes gives a directional velocity vector.
explanations.b: Total UMI count is a QC and normalization concern, not a source of directional information about gene expression change.
explanations.c: Droplet loading order carries no information about a cell's biological trajectory.
explanations.d: Mitochondrial read percentage is a cell-health QC metric, unrelated to inferring directional gene expression change.

questions.prompt: According to Bergen et al. (2020) and related reassessments, why can RNA velocity arrows be misleading?

options.text: The original model assumes constant transcription, splicing, and degradation rates, which do not hold for all genes across a trajectory
Velocity cannot be computed unless the tissue was flash-frozen
Velocity only works on plate-based Smart-seq data, never droplet data
Unspliced reads cannot be distinguished from spliced reads by any current method

explanations.a: Correct — the steady-state assumption of constant rates breaks down for genes whose splicing/transcription kinetics genuinely change over time, and Bergen et al. (2020) and later reassessments documented resulting misleading arrows, including cases inconsistent with known biology.
explanations.b: Freezing method affects RNA extraction protocol choices, not the mathematical validity of the velocity model's rate assumptions.
explanations.c: RNA velocity was developed and is commonly applied to droplet-based data, not restricted to Smart-seq.
explanations.d: Distinguishing unspliced from spliced reads by intron alignment is exactly what makes velocity computable in the first place; that is not the source of the critique.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to what it does and does not tell you.

right.text: Orders cells along an assumed continuum, but is not a measurement of real elapsed time
Predicts a near-future direction of change from splicing ratios, but depends on constant-rate assumptions that can fail

questions.explanation: Pseudotime gives a relative ordering of cells along a presumed trajectory, not real clock time, and will produce an ordering even for data that isn't a true continuum. RNA velocity adds directionality from unspliced/spliced ratios, but its steady-state rate assumptions can produce misleading arrows, as documented by Bergen et al. (2020) and related work.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest way to validate a proposed differentiation trajectory beyond pseudotime ordering or velocity arrows alone?

options.text: Rerun the same velocity analysis with default settings to confirm the arrows look the same
Check known marker genes for the proposed start and end states, and ideally corroborate with an independent time-course experiment
Increase the UMAP resolution so the arrows appear more clearly separated
Trust the trajectory if pseudotime successfully assigns every cell a value

explanations.a: Rerunning with the same settings just reproduces the same model assumptions and would not catch a systematic flaw like a violated steady-state assumption.
explanations.b: Correct — because both pseudotime and velocity will always produce a confident-looking output regardless of whether a real continuum exists, independent evidence such as known progenitor/endpoint marker genes or an orthogonal time-course experiment is needed to confirm the trajectory reflects real biology.
explanations.c: UMAP resolution/appearance has no bearing on whether the underlying velocity model's rate assumptions are valid.
explanations.d: Pseudotime methods will assign an ordering to essentially any input, including unrelated discrete cell types, so successfully assigning values is not evidence the trajectory is real.

lessons.label: Spatial Transcriptomics

sections.heading: Sequencing-based capture: whole transcriptome, multi-cell spots
sections.body: Standard scRNA-seq discards spatial location the moment a tissue is dissociated into a cell suspension. Ståhl et al. (2016) introduced spatial transcriptomics: a glass slide printed with thousands of spots, each carrying spatially barcoded capture oligos, placed under a thin tissue section so that mRNA diffuses down from the tissue directly above each spot and gets tagged with that spot's unique positional barcode before sequencing. The commercial descendant, 10x Genomics Visium, uses 55-micron-diameter spots, each large enough to sit under roughly 1-10 cells depending on cell size and density, and captures the whole transcriptome the same way standard RNA-seq does. The trade-off is resolution: a Visium spot's data is a mixture of whatever cells happen to sit above it, not a single-cell readout, even though its transcriptome-wide gene coverage matches conventional sequencing.

sections.heading: Imaging-based methods: single-molecule precision, fewer genes
sections.body: The alternative approach skips sequencing spots entirely and instead images individual mRNA molecules directly in an intact tissue section using rounds of fluorescent probe hybridization. MERFISH (Chen et al. 2015) and seqFISH (Lubeck et al. 2014) pioneered this by using combinatorial barcoding across sequential imaging rounds, so each gene gets a unique temporal color code that can be read out molecule by molecule, achieving subcellular resolution — individual transcripts can be localized to a specific position within a specific cell, even distinguishing nucleus from cytoplasm. Commercial platforms built on this principle, 10x Genomics Xenium and NanoString CosMx, bring the same imaging-based approach to routine use. The cost of this precision is breadth: these methods use targeted panels of a few hundred to roughly a thousand preselected genes rather than the whole transcriptome, so they can only measure genes chosen in advance.

sections.heading: Deconvolution, and a field-defining recognition
sections.body: Because a Visium spot mixes several cells, a key analysis step is deconvolution: using a single-cell RNA-seq reference from the same or similar tissue to estimate what proportion of each spot's signal comes from each known cell type. Tools built for this include RCTD (robust cell type decomposition, Cable et al. 2021) and cell2location (Kleshchevnikov et al. 2022), both of which fit a spot's mixed expression profile as a weighted combination of reference cell-type profiles, turning a blurry multi-cell spot into an estimated cell-type composition map. The importance of resolving expression in its native spatial context was formally recognized when Nature Methods named spatially resolved transcriptomics its Method of the Year for 2020, citing the technology's rapid maturation from a niche technique into a mainstream tool across cancer, neuroscience, and developmental biology.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher studying a tumor section wants to know which immune cell types infiltrate near the tumor boundary versus the tumor core. They run Visium (55-micron spots) across the whole section, then deconvolve each spot with cell2location using a matched single-cell reference containing T cells, macrophages, and tumor cells. A spot near the boundary is estimated as 60% T cell, 30% macrophage, 10% tumor signal — information no single-cell-only experiment could provide, since dissociation would have discarded exactly where in the tissue each cell sat. If instead the question required knowing whether a specific gene is expressed in the nucleus versus cytoplasm of individual boundary cells, Visium's multi-cell spots couldn't resolve that, and the researcher would need an imaging-based method like Xenium instead, accepting a much smaller preselected gene panel in exchange for subcellular resolution.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why spatial and not just single-cell RNA-seq?' to test whether the student understands what location adds — proximity to a boundary, a niche, or a neighboring cell type — that dissociated single-cell data structurally cannot answer. Pressing on the resolution-versus-breadth trade-off (multi-cell Visium spots with whole-transcriptome coverage vs. subcellular imaging methods with a targeted gene panel) checks whether the student picked their platform because it matched their actual question, rather than defaulting to whichever spatial method they'd heard of first.

questions.prompt: A 10x Genomics Visium spot is 55 microns in diameter. What does this typically mean for the data captured at one spot?

options.text: It captures the transcriptome of exactly one cell at subcellular resolution
It captures a mixture of roughly 1-10 cells' worth of mRNA, not a single-cell readout
It only detects a preselected panel of a few hundred genes
It cannot capture mRNA at all, only DNA

explanations.a: Subcellular, single-cell resolution is the strength of imaging-based methods like MERFISH or Xenium, not spot-based Visium.
explanations.b: Correct — a 55-micron spot is large enough to sit beneath multiple cells depending on cell size and tissue density, so its captured mRNA is a mixture from roughly 1-10 cells rather than a clean single-cell signal.
explanations.c: Visium captures the whole transcriptome via sequencing, unlike targeted imaging panels; gene panel restriction is a property of imaging-based methods, not Visium.
explanations.d: Visium spots capture polyadenylated mRNA via capture oligos, the same molecule class as standard RNA-seq, not DNA.

questions.prompt: What is the central trade-off between sequencing-based spatial methods (Visium) and imaging-based methods (MERFISH, seqFISH, Xenium, CosMx)?

options.text: Sequencing-based methods give subcellular resolution but only whole-tissue averages; imaging-based methods give single spots covering many cells
Sequencing-based methods offer whole-transcriptome breadth at multi-cell spot resolution; imaging-based methods offer subcellular resolution but only a targeted gene panel
There is no meaningful trade-off; both methods give identical resolution and gene coverage
Imaging-based methods always require tissue dissociation, while sequencing-based methods do not

explanations.a: This reverses the actual trade-off; sequencing-based Visium has multi-cell spot resolution, not subcellular resolution.
explanations.b: Correct — Visium-style capture reads the whole transcriptome but mixes signal across several cells per spot, while imaging-based methods like MERFISH/Xenium resolve individual molecules within single cells but are limited to a preselected panel of a few hundred to roughly a thousand genes.
explanations.c: The two approaches differ substantially in both resolution and gene coverage, which is exactly the trade-off the lesson describes.
explanations.d: Both approaches work on intact tissue sections; neither requires dissociating the tissue into a cell suspension, which is the whole point of spatial methods.

questions.prompt: Match each spatial transcriptomics tool or method to its role.

right.text: Introduced spatially barcoded array capture, the precursor to Visium
Imaging-based combinatorial single-molecule detection at subcellular resolution
Deconvolve a multi-cell spot's mixed signal into estimated cell-type proportions using a single-cell reference

questions.explanation: Ståhl et al. (2016) published the original spot-array spatial transcriptomics method that Visium commercialized; MERFISH and seqFISH pioneered imaging-based, combinatorially barcoded single-molecule detection; RCTD and cell2location are deconvolution tools that use a single-cell RNA-seq reference to estimate the cell-type composition mixed within each multi-cell spot.

questions.prompt: Why did Nature Methods name spatially resolved transcriptomics its Method of the Year for 2020?

options.text: Because it replaced the need for any single-cell RNA-seq reference data
Because it matured rapidly into a mainstream tool that adds spatial context single-cell dissociation structurally discards
Because it eliminated the need for tissue sections entirely
Because it was the first method ever able to detect mRNA in a cell

explanations.a: Spatial methods, especially spot-based ones, often depend on single-cell references for deconvolution rather than replacing the need for them.
explanations.b: Correct — the recognition reflected how quickly spatial transcriptomics matured into widespread use across cancer, neuroscience, and developmental biology by recovering positional information that dissociation-based single-cell methods inherently lose.
explanations.c: Spatial methods work on intact tissue sections; they require sections, they do not eliminate them.
explanations.d: mRNA detection itself long predates spatial transcriptomics; the recognition was for resolving expression in spatial context, not for detecting mRNA at all.

units.label: Applications, Case Studies, and Defending a Result

lessons.label: Functional Interpretation: GO, GSEA, and Pathways

sections.heading: Two ways to ask "what does my gene list mean"
sections.body: Over-representation analysis (ORA) is the older, cruder tool: you threshold your differential-expression results into a hit list (say, padj < 0.05), then ask whether a GO term or pathway shows up among those hits more often than chance, using a hypergeometric or Fisher's exact test against a background gene universe. The catch is that ORA's p-value depends entirely on two choices you make: where you draw the significance threshold, and what you call the background — the whole genome, everything on the array, or only genes actually detected in your tissue. Change either and the ranked list of "significant" terms shifts, sometimes drastically, because the hypergeometric test is a ratio comparison, not a property of the biology alone.

sections.heading: GSEA: rank the whole list, skip the threshold
sections.body: Subramanian and colleagues (2005, PNAS) introduced Gene Set Enrichment Analysis to remove the threshold problem entirely. GSEA ranks every measured gene by a per-gene statistic (fold change or t-statistic, no cutoff), then walks down that ranked list computing a running-sum enrichment score (ES) that increases when it hits a gene from the set of interest and decreases otherwise — mechanically similar to a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic. Significance is not read off a table; it comes from permuting phenotype labels (or gene set membership) hundreds to thousands of times to build a null distribution of ES values for that dataset, which yields a normalized enrichment score (NES) and an FDR q-value corrected across every gene set tested — critical, since MSigDB collections run into the thousands of sets and an uncorrected nominal p-value badly overstates confidence.

sections.heading: Where the sets come from, and the redundancy trap
sections.body: The Broad Institute's MSigDB Hallmark collection (50 gene sets) was built specifically to fix a redundancy problem: earlier collections overlapped so heavily that dozens of near-duplicate sets would light up together. KEGG supplies numbered pathway diagrams (originally metabolism-centric, now broader), and Reactome offers manually curated, reaction-level pathway detail. Gene Ontology itself is hierarchical, so a parent term ("immune response") and its children ("regulation of immune response," "innate immune response") are not independent — they co-enrich by construction, making a results table look more informative than it is. Broad terms like "immune response" or "response to stimulus" enrich in almost any experiment touching inflammation, stress, or infection, which is why a lone hit on one of these terms should be treated as a weak, generic signal rather than a specific finding.

lessons.workedExample: A student runs ORA on 40 differentially expressed genes against a default background of the whole ~20,000-gene genome and gets "immune response" at p = 1e-8. Switching the background to the ~14,000 genes actually detected as expressed in their tissue changes the hit-to-background ratio, and the p-value shifts along with the rank order of other terms — the biology didn't change, the denominator did. Running GSEA instead, on the full ranked list of all 14,000 detected genes by t-statistic with no cutoff, the same immune-related hallmark set comes out significant with an NES and FDR q < 0.05. That result is more defensible in a write-up precisely because no arbitrary threshold was chosen to produce it.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "what background gene set did you use, and did you correct for the number of pathways you tested" is checking whether a student understands that ORA's p-value is a ratio built from choices, not a direct readout of biology, and that thousands of gene sets tested demand FDR correction just like thousands of genes do. A student who can also explain why "immune response" topping their list isn't necessarily meaningful — because GO terms nest and broad terms enrich almost everywhere — has shown they read their own output critically instead of screenshotting the top row of a table.

questions.prompt: What is the core mechanical difference between ORA and GSEA?

options.text: ORA uses a full ranked gene list with no threshold; GSEA requires a hit list and a background
ORA requires thresholding genes into a hit list and comparing to a background; GSEA uses the full ranked list with no threshold
They are the same test with different names
ORA only works on single-cell data, GSEA only on bulk data

explanations.a: This reverses the two methods — ORA is the one that needs a threshold and background, not GSEA.
explanations.b: Correct — ORA needs a hard cutoff to build a hit list and tests overrepresentation against a chosen background; GSEA ranks every gene and computes a running-sum enrichment score without ever thresholding.
explanations.c: They differ specifically in whether a threshold is required, which changes what confounds each method.
explanations.d: Both can be applied to bulk or single-cell derived gene lists; the distinction is about thresholding, not data type.

questions.prompt: Why does changing the "background" gene universe in an ORA test change the resulting p-values?

options.text: Because the hypergeometric test compares the ratio of hits to background size, so changing the denominator changes the ratio
Because the background list determines which genes were measured in the experiment
It doesn't — background choice has no mathematical effect on ORA p-values
Because larger backgrounds always make every term more significant

explanations.a: Correct — the hypergeometric/Fisher's exact test is a ratio comparison between hits-in-set and hits-in-background, so shrinking or expanding the background changes the expected-by-chance rate and thus the p-value.
explanations.b: The background is a choice the analyst makes for the statistical test, separate from which genes were technically measured.
explanations.c: It has a large, well-documented effect — background choice is one of the most common sources of irreproducible pathway results.
explanations.d: The direction of the effect depends on the specific term and gene set overlap, not a fixed rule that larger always means more significant.

questions.prompt: Why do broad GO terms like "immune response" so often top enrichment lists regardless of the experiment?

options.text: Because GO's hierarchical structure means parent and child terms co-enrich, and broad terms cover many genes touched by almost any perturbation
Because the immune system is involved in every biological process at the molecular level
Because GSEA and ORA both specifically weight immune genes more heavily
Because immune genes are always the most differentially expressed genes in any dataset

explanations.a: Correct — GO terms nest (parent terms include all genes of their children), and broad categories like immune or stress response are large enough to catch genes perturbed by almost any stimulus, making them a generic rather than specific signal.
explanations.b: This overstates biology to explain a statistical/ontology artifact.
explanations.c: Neither method applies special weighting to immune terms; the effect comes from set size and GO hierarchy, not the algorithm.
explanations.d: Immune genes are not inherently the most differentially expressed; the issue is the breadth of the term catching many unrelated hits.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a GSEA analysis as described by Subramanian et al. (2005).

items.text: Rank all measured genes by a per-gene statistic (e.g., fold change or t-statistic)
Walk down the ranked list computing a running-sum enrichment score (ES)
Permute phenotype labels many times to build a null distribution of ES values
Normalize to an NES and compute an FDR q-value across all gene sets tested

questions.explanation: GSEA starts by ranking the full gene list with no threshold, computes the running-sum enrichment score along that ranking, establishes significance by permutation to build a null, and finally reports a normalized score with FDR correction across every set tested.

questions.prompt: Match each gene-set resource to what it actually contains.

right.text: 50 refined, low-redundancy sets distilled from earlier overlapping collections
Numbered pathway diagrams, originally metabolism-centric, now covering signaling too
Manually curated, reaction-level pathway database
Hierarchical ontology where parent and child terms are nested, not independent

questions.explanation: Hallmark sets were built by the Broad Institute specifically to reduce redundancy across earlier collections; KEGG supplies pathway diagrams historically rooted in metabolism; Reactome offers manually reviewed, reaction-level detail; and GO's hierarchy means terms are nested rather than independent, which is why child and parent terms co-enrich.

lessons.label: Expression Signatures in the Clinic

sections.heading: Oncotype DX and TAILORx: shrinking who gets chemo
sections.body: Oncotype DX measures a fixed panel of 21 genes by RT-qPCR from a formalin-fixed tumor sample and outputs a single Recurrence Score (0-100) for hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative breast cancer. The score existed for years as a prognostic tool before TAILORx (Sparano et al., 2018, NEJM) tested it prospectively: over 10,000 women were scored, and those in the mid-range (11-25) were randomized to endocrine therapy alone versus chemotherapy plus endocrine therapy. The result was practice-changing — endocrine therapy alone was non-inferior for most of that mid-range group, sparing an estimated majority of women a toxic treatment, though a secondary analysis found some chemotherapy benefit remained for women 50 or younger with scores in the upper part of that range.

sections.heading: MammaPrint and MINDACT: a different panel, the same logic
sections.body: MammaPrint uses a 70-gene expression signature, originally derived from microarray data, to classify tumors as genomically high- or low-risk. MINDACT (Cardoso et al., 2016, NEJM) enrolled 6,693 patients and specifically tested the hardest case: patients whose clinical risk (tumor size, grade, nodal status) was high but whose genomic risk was low. Withholding chemotherapy from that clinical-high/genomic-low group produced a 5-year distant-metastasis-free survival of 94.7%, statistically non-inferior to the 95.9% seen in the clinical-high/genomic-low patients who did receive chemotherapy — evidence that the genomic signature could override clinical risk factors and safely de-escalate treatment for roughly 46% of patients clinical guidelines alone would have sent to chemotherapy.

sections.heading: PAM50 and what makes a signature actionable
sections.body: PAM50 (Parker et al., 2009) takes a different approach entirely: instead of a single risk score, it classifies breast tumors into intrinsic molecular subtypes (Luminal A, Luminal B, HER2-enriched, Basal-like, Normal-like) from a 50-gene expression signature, and is now sold clinically as Prosigna. What separates Oncotype DX and MammaPrint from the thousands of expression signatures published as figures in papers is a specific chain: a locked, pre-specified algorithm (the gene list and scoring rule are frozen before testing, not re-tuned afterward), validation in a prospective randomized trial (TAILORx and MINDACT, respectively) rather than only a retrospective cohort, and regulatory clearance (FDA or equivalent) that lets a result change what a doctor actually prescribes. PAM50/Prosigna reached that same regulatory clearance by a related but distinct path: its prognostic value was validated retrospectively, on archived specimens from the TransATAC and ABCSG-8 trial cohorts, rather than in a trial that randomized treatment based on the PAM50 score itself the way TAILORx and MINDACT did for their signatures. A signature that stops at "correlates with outcome in our retrospective cohort" has cleared none of those bars — PAM50 cleared them through large, well-characterized retrospective cohort validation followed by regulatory review, a step behind TAILORx/MINDACT-style prospective randomization.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher publishes a 15-gene expression signature that separates a retrospective cohort of 200 archived tumor samples into good- and poor-outcome groups with a statistically significant hazard ratio. This is a real finding, but it is not yet an Oncotype DX. To become clinically actionable it would need: the gene list and scoring formula locked down (no more tuning on new data), a prospective trial that randomizes patients based on the score itself rather than just measuring it retrospectively, and a body like the FDA reviewing that evidence before a lab is allowed to report the score to a treating physician. TAILORx and MINDACT are exactly that missing step for Oncotype DX and MammaPrint — the trials that turned a correlative signature into a tool doctors could act on.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe "is this signature actionable or just correlative" because it is the single fastest way to tell a student who understands translational research from one who conflates a p-value with a treatment change. A student who can name TAILORx or MINDACT specifically — and explain that the trial, not the gene list, is what made the signature clinical — has grasped that a locked algorithm plus prospective validation is the real bar, not statistical significance in a discovery cohort.

questions.prompt: What did the TAILORx trial (Sparano et al., 2018) specifically test?

options.text: Whether the 70-gene MammaPrint signature predicted metastasis better than clinical staging
Whether women with a mid-range Oncotype DX Recurrence Score (11-25) could safely receive endocrine therapy alone instead of chemotherapy plus endocrine therapy
Whether PAM50 subtyping could replace hormone-receptor testing
Whether the 21-gene panel could be shortened to 10 genes without losing accuracy

explanations.a: That describes MINDACT's use of MammaPrint, not TAILORx's use of Oncotype DX.
explanations.b: Correct — TAILORx randomized the mid-range Recurrence Score (11-25) group to endocrine therapy alone versus chemoendocrine therapy and found the two arms broadly non-inferior.
explanations.c: TAILORx tested treatment de-escalation with the existing 21-gene score, not a comparison against PAM50 subtyping.
explanations.d: TAILORx did not test a shortened gene panel; it tested clinical outcomes at existing Recurrence Score thresholds.

questions.prompt: In MINDACT, what was distinctive about the clinical-high/genomic-low patient group?

options.text: They had the worst outcomes of any group in the trial
Clinical risk factors alone would have recommended chemotherapy for them, but the genomic signature classified them as low risk
They were excluded from the trial because their risk was ambiguous
They received both MammaPrint and Oncotype DX testing before enrollment

explanations.a: This group had a 5-year distant-metastasis-free survival of 94.7% without chemotherapy — a strong outcome, not the worst.
explanations.b: Correct — this was the group where clinical criteria (tumor size, grade, nodal status) said high risk but MammaPrint said genomically low risk, making it the key test of whether the genomic signature could override clinical judgment.
explanations.c: This group was central to the trial's design and analysis, not excluded.
explanations.d: MINDACT tested MammaPrint specifically; it did not require dual testing with Oncotype DX.

questions.prompt: What does PAM50 output that distinguishes it from Oncotype DX and MammaPrint?

options.text: A single numeric recurrence risk score from 0 to 100
A binary high-risk versus low-risk classification
A classification into intrinsic molecular subtypes such as Luminal A, Luminal B, HER2-enriched, and Basal-like
A direct measurement of tumor size and nodal status

explanations.a: That describes the Oncotype DX Recurrence Score, not PAM50.
explanations.b: That describes MammaPrint's genomic high/low risk output, not PAM50's subtype output.
explanations.c: Correct — PAM50 (Parker et al., 2009) classifies tumors into intrinsic subtypes from a 50-gene signature, a categorically different output from a single risk score.
explanations.d: Tumor size and nodal status are clinical-pathological measurements, not expression-signature outputs.

questions.prompt: Match each signature to its validating trial and gene panel size.

right.text: 21-gene panel, validated by TAILORx
70-gene panel, validated by MINDACT
50-gene panel, defines intrinsic molecular subtypes

questions.explanation: Oncotype DX's 21-gene Recurrence Score was validated for treatment de-escalation in TAILORx; MammaPrint's 70-gene signature was validated in MINDACT, including the clinical-high/genomic-low subgroup; PAM50's 50 genes classify intrinsic subtypes rather than producing a single risk score.

questions.prompt: What separates a clinically actionable expression signature from one that exists only as a paper figure?

options.text: How many genes are in the panel — fewer genes is always more actionable
A locked, pre-specified algorithm, prospective trial validation, and regulatory clearance
Whether the signature was discovered using RNA-seq versus microarray data
Whether the p-value in the discovery cohort was below 0.001

explanations.a: Panel size alone says nothing about validation status; a 5-gene and a 70-gene panel can both be equally unvalidated.
explanations.b: Correct — the chain from correlative finding to clinical tool requires freezing the algorithm, testing it prospectively (as TAILORx and MINDACT did), and clearing regulatory review before it can guide treatment decisions.
explanations.c: The underlying measurement technology does not determine clinical actionability; validation pathway does.
explanations.d: A strong p-value in a retrospective discovery cohort is a starting point, not proof the signature holds up prospectively or changes outcomes.

lessons.label: Atlases, Repositories, and Reusing Public Data

sections.heading: The deposit layer: GEO, SRA, and ArrayExpress
sections.body: Nearly every published transcriptomics paper is required to deposit its raw data before publication, and it lands in one of three linked archives: NCBI's Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) for processed and raw expression data with sample-level metadata, the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) for raw sequencing reads, and EMBL-EBI's ArrayExpress as the European counterpart that mirrors much of GEO. These are deposit repositories, not curated atlases — the data is exactly as the submitting lab processed and described it, with wildly inconsistent metadata quality, so pulling a GEO series means inheriting whatever labeling conventions (or gaps) the original authors used.

sections.heading: Purpose-built atlases and uniformly reprocessed collections
sections.body: GTEx (Genotype-Tissue Expression), in its v8 release, sequenced RNA from 54 tissues across roughly 950 postmortem donors — over 17,000 samples total — specifically to map normal human gene expression and its genetic regulation across the body, and it remains the reference atlas for "what does this gene normally look like in tissue X." TCGA (The Cancer Genome Atlas) does the equivalent for tumors, pairing expression with mutation, copy-number, and clinical outcome data across dozens of cancer types. The Human Protein Atlas adds a protein- and immunohistochemistry-level view on top of transcript data, useful for checking whether an mRNA signal actually corresponds to detectable protein. A newer, more powerful layer sits on top of raw GEO/SRA deposits: recount3 and ARCHS4 reprocess tens of thousands of public RNA-seq samples through one uniform alignment and quantification pipeline, which matters because two studies aligned with different reference annotations or different tools are not directly comparable no matter how similar their raw reads look.

sections.heading: Reusing public data without fooling yourself
sections.body: The practical workflow for a project built on public data is: identify a GTEx, TCGA, or GEO dataset matching your question, pull processed counts (preferring a uniformly reprocessed source like recount3 when combining multiple studies), and check what genome annotation build was used, since gene counts computed against different annotation versions are not safely comparable even for the same raw reads. The three traps that catch students hardest are annotation-version mismatch (combining a study aligned to an older annotation with one aligned to a newer one silently shifts which reads count toward which gene), unrecorded batch (samples processed in different labs, on different days, or with different library kits carry a technical signal that can masquerade as a biological one if you don't know which samples were run together), and metadata that doesn't describe what was actually done (a GEO entry labeled "control" that turns out to be a different cell passage, treatment duration, or protocol than the paper's methods section implies).

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to compare liver-versus-heart gene expression for a project and, rather than generating new RNA-seq data, pulls GTEx v8 liver and heart samples directly from the portal — already uniformly processed against one annotation build with donor metadata attached, so tissue comparisons are valid out of the box. A second student instead combines a liver RNA-seq dataset from one GEO series with a heart dataset from an unrelated GEO series, each aligned by different original authors using different reference annotation versions. Raw gene counts from the two series are not comparable without reprocessing both through the same pipeline (e.g., pulling both from recount3 instead of GEO directly) — otherwise, any tissue difference the student reports is confounded with which annotation build and alignment tool each lab happened to use.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "where did this data come from, and was it processed consistently" is testing whether a student understands that public repositories are not plug-and-play — GEO and SRA preserve whatever the original lab did, while GTEx, TCGA, and reprocessed resources like recount3 or ARCHS4 buy uniformity a student cannot otherwise guarantee. Naming the specific atlas used (GTEx v8, TCGA) and explaining why mixing raw GEO series without reprocessing risks confounding annotation or batch with the biological comparison is the difference between a student who reused data carefully and one who downloaded numbers and assumed they were comparable.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between GEO/SRA and an atlas like GTEx?

options.text: GEO/SRA are deposit repositories preserving whatever the submitting lab processed and described; GTEx is a purpose-built atlas processed uniformly for a specific mapping goal
GEO/SRA only contain human data; GTEx contains data from multiple species
GTEx is a raw-reads archive; GEO/SRA contain only processed, publication-ready figures
There is no meaningful difference — both are uniformly reprocessed collections

explanations.a: Correct — GEO and SRA are general deposit archives with inconsistent metadata and processing across submitting labs, while GTEx was designed and processed as a single coherent effort to map normal tissue expression.
explanations.b: Both repositories can host non-human data; species scope isn't the distinguishing feature described.
explanations.c: This reverses the roles — GTEx provides uniformly processed expression data, and SRA specifically holds raw reads.
explanations.d: GEO/SRA are explicitly not uniformly reprocessed; that is the entire distinction being tested.

questions.prompt: GTEx v8 sequenced RNA from approximately how many tissues, donors, and samples?

options.text: 10 tissues, 100 donors, 1,000 samples
54 tissues, roughly 950 donors, over 17,000 samples
200 tissues, 5,000 donors, 100,000 samples
54 tissues, 50 donors, 500 samples

explanations.a: This understates GTEx v8's scale by roughly an order of magnitude on every dimension.
explanations.b: Correct — GTEx v8 covers 54 tissues from about 950 postmortem donors, totaling over 17,000 samples.
explanations.c: This overstates GTEx v8's scale substantially; no GTEx release reached this size.
explanations.d: The tissue count is right but the donor and sample counts are far too low for v8.

questions.prompt: Why do recount3 and ARCHS4 matter when combining multiple public RNA-seq studies?

options.text: They add clinical outcome data that raw GEO entries lack
They reprocess many public samples through one uniform pipeline, avoiding the incomparability that arises when different studies use different alignment tools or annotation versions
They only host single-cell data, unlike GEO
They replace the need for any metadata checking

explanations.a: That describes what TCGA adds for cancer data, not the core function of recount3/ARCHS4.
explanations.b: Correct — running many public samples through one consistent alignment and quantification pipeline removes a major source of technical incomparability across studies pulled from raw GEO/SRA deposits.
explanations.c: Both resources primarily reprocess bulk RNA-seq; this isn't their distinguishing feature.
explanations.d: Uniform reprocessing solves the annotation/pipeline problem but does not guarantee metadata (like batch or condition labeling) is accurate — that still needs checking.

questions.prompt: Match each trap in reusing public data to its description.

right.text: Samples processed on different days or with different kits carry a technical signal that can masquerade as biology
Gene counts from reads aligned against different reference annotation builds are not safely comparable, even from similar raw reads
A sample labeled "control" in the deposited record does not actually match what the paper's methods describe

questions.explanation: Annotation-version mismatch changes which reads count toward which gene even with identical raw data; unrecorded batch introduces a technical confound tied to when/how samples were processed; inaccurate metadata means the label in the repository does not truthfully describe the sample.

questions.prompt: A student combines liver RNA-seq counts from one GEO series with heart RNA-seq counts from a separate, unrelated GEO series, each aligned by the original authors using different annotation versions. What is the main risk?

options.text: None — GEO enforces a single standard annotation across all submissions
Any tissue difference found is confounded with which annotation build and pipeline each original lab used
The comparison is fine as long as both series used Illumina sequencers
The risk only applies to single-cell data, not bulk RNA-seq

explanations.a: GEO does not enforce a uniform processing standard; submitting labs process and annotate their own data independently.
explanations.b: Correct — differing annotation builds and alignment pipelines between the two series mean apparent tissue differences could actually reflect processing differences, not biology, unless both are reprocessed through one consistent pipeline.
explanations.c: Sequencer platform alone does not guarantee comparable gene-level quantification; the annotation and alignment pipeline matter more directly.
explanations.d: This confound applies equally to bulk RNA-seq counts, which is exactly the scenario described.

lessons.label: Expression Meets Genetics: eQTLs and TWAS

sections.heading: cis- and trans-eQTLs, mapped tissue by tissue
sections.body: An expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) is a genetic variant statistically associated with the expression level of a gene. A cis-eQTL sits near the gene it affects (conventionally within about 1 megabase), typically acting through a nearby promoter or enhancer, and tends to have a large, tissue-consistent effect that is comparatively easy to detect with modest sample sizes. A trans-eQTL affects a gene far away, often on a different chromosome, usually by altering a transcription factor or signaling protein that in turn regulates the distant gene — trans effects are individually weaker, harder to detect, and need much larger cohorts. GTEx maps both classes across its 54 tissues, and the central finding is that a huge fraction of cis-eQTLs are tissue-specific: a variant that strongly regulates a gene's expression in liver may show no detectable effect in brain, which is exactly why GTEx sequenced so many tissue types rather than one convenient one.

sections.heading: Colocalization: does the GWAS hit share a cause with the eQTL?
sections.body: A GWAS hit and a nearby eQTL for some gene can overlap purely by coincidence of linkage disequilibrium, without being driven by the same underlying causal variant. Colocalization methods (such as coloc) formally test whether the GWAS association and the eQTL association are statistically consistent with sharing one causal variant, rather than two nearby-but-distinct variants that happen to travel together on the same haplotype. A colocalizing signal is meaningfully stronger evidence than a bare positional overlap — it says the same genetic change plausibly drives both the trait and the expression difference, pointing at a specific candidate gene and tissue rather than just a genomic region.

sections.heading: TWAS: imputing expression straight into a GWAS cohort
sections.body: Transcriptome-wide association studies flip the logic again: instead of measuring expression directly, a TWAS uses eQTL data from a reference panel like GTEx to build a predictive model of each gene's expression from genotype alone, then imputes that predicted expression into a much larger GWAS cohort that was never RNA-sequenced, and tests whether predicted expression associates with the trait. Gamazon and colleagues (2015) introduced PrediXcan using this individual-level imputation approach, and Gusev and colleagues (2016) built FUSION, which achieves the same result directly from GWAS summary statistics without needing individual genotypes. Both matter because roughly 90% of GWAS hits fall in non-coding, regulatory regions of the genome with no obvious protein-level mechanism — TWAS is the bridge that turns an anonymous non-coding signal into a testable candidate gene and tissue, handing GWAS's raw statistical hits (the domain of human/medical genetics) off to expression data for mechanistic follow-up.

lessons.workedExample: A GWAS finds a variant on chromosome 12 associated with type 2 diabetes risk, sitting in a non-coding region with no obvious gene nearby to blame. Checking GTEx pancreas eQTL data shows the same variant is a strong cis-eQTL for a nearby gene, and a colocalization test confirms the GWAS and eQTL signals share a single causal variant rather than two coincidentally linked ones — pointing specifically at that gene, in pancreas, as the likely mechanism. A TWAS using a pancreas expression model built from GTEx and applied to a separate, much larger diabetes GWAS cohort (never itself RNA-sequenced) independently finds that the imputed expression of that same gene associates with diabetes status, corroborating the colocalization result with a second, orthogonal line of evidence.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asking "how do you know this gene is the mechanism, and not just a variant that happens to sit nearby" is testing whether a student can distinguish positional overlap from colocalization — the difference between "a GWAS hit and an eQTL are in the same region" and "a formal test shows they share one causal variant." Naming GTEx's tissue-specificity, explaining why trans-eQTLs are harder to find than cis-eQTLs, or describing what a TWAS actually imputes (predicted expression from genotype, not measured expression) signals a student who understands why expression data is the bridge from a non-coding GWAS hit to a testable mechanism, not just a buzzword dropped next to "GWAS."

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a cis-eQTL from a trans-eQTL?

options.text: A cis-eQTL is near the gene it affects and tends to have large, easily detected effects; a trans-eQTL is far from the gene it affects, often acting through an intermediate regulator, and is weaker and harder to detect
A cis-eQTL only appears in cancer tissue; a trans-eQTL only appears in normal tissue
A cis-eQTL affects protein structure directly; a trans-eQTL never affects protein
There is no meaningful distance criterion — both terms describe the same phenomenon

explanations.a: Correct — cis-eQTLs act locally (often within about 1 Mb) with comparatively large, detectable effects, while trans-eQTLs act at a distance, typically through an intermediate regulatory protein, with weaker individual effects that require larger cohorts to detect.
explanations.b: Tissue type is unrelated to the cis/trans distinction; both classes are mapped across normal and disease tissues alike.
explanations.c: eQTLs affect expression level, not protein structure directly; this describes a different kind of variant (coding/missense).
explanations.d: The distance and mechanism between the two are a well-established, meaningful distinction, not interchangeable terms.

questions.prompt: Why did GTEx sequence 54 different tissues rather than one representative tissue?

options.text: Because eQTL effects are largely tissue-specific, so a variant's effect on expression in one tissue often doesn't generalize to others
Because sequencing cost is identical regardless of tissue count
Because trans-eQTLs cannot be detected in any tissue other than blood
Because GWAS variants only ever affect gene expression in skin

explanations.a: Correct — GTEx's central finding is that many cis-eQTLs are tissue-specific, so mapping only one tissue would miss most of the biologically relevant regulatory effects.
explanations.b: Sequencing more tissues meaningfully increases cost and effort; the tissue breadth reflects a scientific need, not a cost-neutral default.
explanations.c: Trans-eQTLs can be mapped in any tissue with sufficient sample size; blood is not a special requirement.
explanations.d: GWAS variants affect expression across many different tissues depending on the trait; skin has no special status.

questions.prompt: What does a colocalization test (e.g., coloc) actually determine that a simple positional overlap does not?

options.text: Whether the GWAS association and the eQTL association are statistically consistent with sharing a single causal variant, rather than two distinct but linked variants
Whether the gene is expressed at all in that tissue
Whether the variant is coding or non-coding
Whether the GWAS study had adequate statistical power

explanations.a: Correct — colocalization formally tests for a shared causal variant behind both signals, which is stronger evidence than the two signals merely falling in the same genomic region by linkage disequilibrium.
explanations.b: Basic expression detection is a simpler prerequisite check, not what colocalization tests.
explanations.c: Coding status is determined by variant annotation, not by a colocalization test.
explanations.d: Power calculations are a separate consideration from testing whether two association signals share a causal variant.

questions.prompt: What does a TWAS method like PrediXcan or FUSION actually do?

options.text: It directly RNA-sequences every individual in a GWAS cohort
It uses eQTL data from a reference panel to build a predictive model of expression from genotype, then imputes that predicted expression into a GWAS cohort to test for trait association
It replaces GWAS entirely by only using expression data
It measures protein levels instead of RNA levels

explanations.a: The entire point of TWAS is to avoid needing to RNA-sequence the (often much larger) GWAS cohort directly.
explanations.b: Correct — TWAS trains a genotype-to-expression prediction model on a reference panel like GTEx, then applies that model to impute expression in a separate GWAS cohort and tests for association with the trait.
explanations.c: TWAS builds on top of GWAS genotype data; it doesn't replace GWAS, it adds an expression-imputation layer to it.
explanations.d: TWAS predicts and tests RNA expression, not protein levels.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

right.text: Uses individual-level genotype data to impute expression and test trait association
Achieves the same TWAS logic directly from GWAS summary statistics, without needing individual genotypes
Roughly 90% of GWAS hits fall in non-coding regulatory regions, motivating expression data as the mechanistic bridge

questions.explanation: PrediXcan works from individual-level genotypes; FUSION was built to work from summary statistics alone, extending TWAS to studies where individual genotypes aren't shared; and the reason either method matters is that most GWAS hits are non-coding, with no obvious protein mechanism, so expression is the bridge to a testable candidate gene.

lessons.label: Perturbation Transcriptomics and Drug Discovery

sections.heading: The Connectivity Map: matching a drug's signature against a disease's
sections.body: Lamb and colleagues (2006, Science) introduced the Connectivity Map on a simple but powerful idea: profile the gene-expression changes that 164 well-characterized small-molecule compounds cause in a handful of human cell lines, then treat each compound's signature as a searchable reference. A researcher with their own signature — say, genes up- and down-regulated in a disease versus healthy tissue — could query the Map for compounds whose induced signature ran in the opposite direction, the "signature reversal" logic: if a disease pushes a gene set up, a drug that pushes the same genes down is a repurposing candidate worth testing experimentally, independent of whether anyone had ever considered that drug for that disease before.
