sections.heading: LINCS L1000: the same idea at industrial scale
sections.body: The Library of Integrated Network-Based Cellular Signatures (LINCS) program scaled this concept enormously with the L1000 assay, which directly measures only 978 carefully chosen "landmark" genes — selected because their expression statistically predicts the rest of the transcriptome — and computationally infers the expression of roughly ten thousand additional genes from those measurements. That cost-per-profile reduction is what let LINCS generate over a million expression signatures across thousands of compounds, genetic perturbations, and cell lines, turning the Connectivity Map's proof of concept into a searchable resource orders of magnitude larger.

sections.heading: Perturb-seq and the honest scorecard on repurposing
sections.body: A parallel line of work pairs CRISPR-based genetic perturbation with single-cell RNA-seq readout instead of small molecules: Perturb-seq (Dixit and colleagues, 2016; Adamson and colleagues, 2016) pools many CRISPR guides into one experiment and reads out each cell's transcriptome alongside which gene was knocked out or activated in that cell, giving a genome-scale, single-cell view of what perturbing any one gene does downstream. Signature-reversal repurposing has a real, named success: Sirota and colleagues (2011, Science Translational Medicine) applied this exact logic to public gene-expression compendia and flagged cimetidine, an already-approved H2-receptor antagonist, as a repurposing candidate for lung adenocarcinoma, then confirmed it slowed tumor growth in a mouse xenograft model. But the approach also has an honest failure rate, and the standing criticism cuts across both compound and CRISPR screens: nearly all of these signatures are generated in a small set of cancer cell lines, and a signature that reverses cleanly in a dish does not guarantee the same drug or target will behave the same way in a genetically diverse, physiologically complex patient, which is exactly why hits from these screens — including the cimetidine result — are treated as hypotheses to validate further, not conclusions.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher has a gene-expression signature for a rare disease (genes abnormally up- or down-regulated in patient tissue versus controls) and queries LINCS L1000 for any of its thousands of compound signatures that runs in the reverse direction. The top hit is an existing FDA-approved drug developed for an unrelated condition — a repurposing candidate identified purely from signature matching, with no prior biological hypothesis connecting the drug to the disease. Before this counts as anything more than a lead, it needs validation the signature match alone cannot provide: does the drug reverse the phenotype (not just the expression pattern) in a relevant cell or animal model of the disease, and does the cell line the L1000 signature was measured in resemble the actual disease tissue closely enough that the reversal is likely to generalize.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "was this signature generated in a cell line, and how do you know it will hold in real tissue" is pressing on the single biggest gap between a promising computational hit and a validated finding in this field. A student who can name the Connectivity Map's signature-reversal logic or LINCS L1000's landmark-gene design, and who volunteers — unprompted — that cell-line signatures may not generalize to patients, has shown they understand these tools as hypothesis generators rather than as an oracle that outputs proven drugs.

questions.prompt: What is the "signature reversal" logic introduced by the Connectivity Map (Lamb et al., 2006)?

options.text: A compound is a repurposing candidate if its induced expression changes run opposite to a disease signature
A compound is a repurposing candidate only if it was already approved for a related disease
A compound is ranked by how many genes it changes, regardless of direction
A compound is a repurposing candidate if its signature matches the disease signature in the same direction

explanations.a: Correct — the Connectivity Map's core logic looks for compounds whose gene-expression signature runs opposite to the disease signature, on the premise that reversing the disease's expression pattern is a plausible route to reversing the disease phenotype.
explanations.b: The whole appeal of the approach is that it can surface candidates independent of any prior disease connection.
explanations.c: Simply changing many genes, regardless of direction, is not the criterion — the direction relative to the disease signature is what matters.
explanations.d: This is the opposite of signature reversal; matching in the same direction would reinforce the disease pattern rather than counter it.

questions.prompt: How does the LINCS L1000 assay measure gene expression so efficiently at scale?

options.text: It sequences the full transcriptome for every sample but discards low-expressed genes
It directly measures 978 landmark genes chosen because they statistically predict the rest of the transcriptome, then computationally infers the remaining genes
It uses only single-cell RNA-seq, which is inherently cheaper than bulk assays
It measures protein levels instead of RNA, which requires no sequencing at all

explanations.a: This describes a standard full-transcriptome approach, not L1000's specific cost-reduction strategy.
explanations.b: Correct — L1000 directly measures 978 landmark genes selected for their predictive power over the rest of the transcriptome, then computationally infers roughly ten thousand more, which is what makes generating over a million signatures affordable.
explanations.c: L1000 is a bulk assay design, not a single-cell method, and single-cell RNA-seq is not inherently cheaper per sample.
explanations.d: L1000 measures RNA expression via a bead-based assay, not protein.

questions.prompt: What does Perturb-seq (Dixit et al., 2016; Adamson et al., 2016) add that pairs CRISPR screens with a transcriptomic readout?

options.text: It pools many CRISPR guides in one experiment and reads out each cell's full transcriptome alongside which gene was perturbed in that cell
It replaces the need for any control cells in a CRISPR screen
It only measures a single gene's expression per experiment, like a qPCR-based CRISPR screen
It uses small molecules instead of CRISPR guides

explanations.a: Correct — Perturb-seq combines pooled CRISPR perturbation with single-cell RNA-seq, so each individual cell's transcriptome is linked back to which guide (gene) was perturbed in that specific cell.
explanations.b: Controls (e.g., non-targeting guides) are still included in Perturb-seq designs; the method doesn't eliminate the need for them.
explanations.c: The distinguishing feature of Perturb-seq is genome-scale, single-cell transcriptomic readout, the opposite of a single-gene readout.
explanations.d: Perturb-seq is specifically a CRISPR-based genetic perturbation method, distinct from the small-molecule approach of the Connectivity Map and LINCS.

questions.prompt: What is the standing criticism that applies to both compound-signature repurposing and CRISPR perturbation screens?

options.text: Neither method can be run at more than a handful of samples per year
Signatures are overwhelmingly generated in a small set of cancer cell lines, and a reversal or effect seen in a dish may not generalize to genetically diverse, physiologically complex patients
Neither method has ever produced a validated repurposing candidate
Both methods require radioactive labeling, limiting their use to specialized labs

explanations.a: Both LINCS L1000 and Perturb-seq were specifically built for high-throughput scale, generating enormous numbers of signatures, not just a handful.
explanations.b: Correct — the cell-line-versus-patient generalization gap is the central, honest criticism: a signature reversal in a cancer cell line does not guarantee the same result in diverse patient tissue.
explanations.c: Signature-reversal repurposing has a real named success (e.g., the cimetidine lung-cancer repurposing hit from Sirota et al., 2011), alongside an honest failure rate — it is not a method with zero validated hits.
explanations.d: Neither method depends on radioactive labeling; both use standard sequencing- or array-based expression measurement.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the development of perturbation transcriptomics from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Lamb et al. publish the Connectivity Map using 164 compounds profiled by expression signature (2006, Science)
The LINCS program scales signature generation using the 978-gene L1000 assay
Dixit et al. and Adamson et al. publish Perturb-seq, pairing pooled CRISPR perturbation with single-cell RNA-seq readout (2016)

questions.explanation: The Connectivity Map (2006) established the signature-matching concept at small scale; LINCS L1000 later scaled that concept to over a million signatures using a cheaper landmark-gene assay; Perturb-seq (2016) then extended the perturbation concept from small molecules to pooled CRISPR guides with single-cell transcriptomic readout.

lessons.label: Designing and Defending Your Own Expression Study

sections.heading: Replicates over depth, and randomization to break confounding
sections.body: Given a fixed budget, more biological replicates (separate organisms, cultures, or patients) beats more sequencing depth per sample almost every time, because statistical power for detecting differential expression comes primarily from sample-to-sample variability, and depth cannot substitute for that — three replicates sequenced deeply still let you draw conclusions about exactly three biological units. The second design decision that quietly wins or loses a study is randomizing which samples get processed together: if every control sample is extracted, prepped, and sequenced on Monday and every treatment sample on Friday, the biological condition is now perfectly confounded with the processing batch, and no downstream statistical correction can fully separate the two. Randomizing condition across processing days, extraction batches, and even library-prep technicians is what makes batch correction methods valid rather than a guess.

sections.heading: Pre-registering the comparison, then validating the hits
sections.body: Deciding the primary comparison, the statistical test, and the significance threshold before looking at the data — a pre-registered analysis plan — prevents the specific failure mode of trying five comparisons, five thresholds, and five normalization methods until one produces a result worth reporting. Once a differential expression analysis produces candidate genes, the standard next step is orthogonal validation: picking a handful of the top hits and confirming the expression difference by RT-qPCR, an independent assay with a different failure mode than RNA-seq, rather than trusting the sequencing result alone. A hit that fails to validate by qPCR is far more informative than it looks — it usually means the original signal was a normalization or batch artifact, not a biological effect.

sections.heading: Reporting to a standard, not just to a folder
sections.body: MIQE (Minimum Information for Publication of Quantitative Real-Time PCR Experiments) and MINSEQE (Minimum Information about a high-throughput SEQuencing Experiment) are community reporting standards that specify exactly what must be disclosed for qPCR validation and RNA-seq experiments respectively — primer sequences and efficiency for MIQE, sample metadata and processing pipeline for MINSEQE — precisely so another lab (or a science-fair judge) can evaluate what was actually done rather than trusting a summary claim. Depositing raw and processed data to GEO with that level of detail is what turns a result into something reusable by the next atlas or the next TWAS, the way GTEx, TCGA, and thousands of individual GEO submissions became the reusable public layer covered earlier in this unit.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares gene expression between drought-stressed and well-watered plants using 3 biological replicates per group. A weak design processes all well-watered samples first, then all drought samples a week later, and reports whichever of five different normalization methods produced the most significant hits. A defensible design instead interleaves extraction and library prep so that condition is not confounded with processing day, locks in one normalization method and significance threshold before running the comparison, and after finding 40 differentially expressed genes, picks the top 5 by fold change and re-measures them by RT-qPCR on the same RNA samples. If 4 of 5 validate by qPCR, that is strong evidence the RNA-seq signal is real; if only 1 of 5 validates, the RNA-seq result was likely dominated by batch or normalization noise rather than biology.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge's rapid-fire questions — what is your n, what did you normalize to, how did you correct for multiple testing, is condition confounded with batch, did you validate your hits, and is the effect size biologically meaningful and not just statistically detectable — are not a checklist to memorize but a direct probe of whether a student's design can survive being re-examined by someone who wasn't in the room. A student who volunteers "n=3 biological replicates per group, randomized across two extraction days, FDR-corrected, top hits confirmed by qPCR" before being asked has demonstrated the entire chain of reasoning this unit builds toward; one who can only answer "the computer said it was significant" has not.

questions.prompt: Given a fixed budget, why do biological replicates usually matter more than sequencing depth per sample?

options.text: Because deeper sequencing always introduces more technical noise
Because statistical power to detect differential expression comes primarily from sample-to-sample variability, which more replicates directly address
Because sequencing depth has no effect on gene detection at all
Because journals require a minimum of ten replicates regardless of design

explanations.a: Deeper sequencing does not inherently add noise; the issue is that depth cannot substitute for having more independent biological units.
explanations.b: Correct — differential expression statistics are driven by variability across biological replicates, so three deeply sequenced samples still only describe three biological units, while more replicates directly increase power.
explanations.c: Depth does matter for detecting lowly-expressed genes; the point is that it doesn't substitute for replicate number when power is the goal.
explanations.d: There is no universal replicate requirement across journals; the tradeoff described is a statistical one, not an editorial rule.

questions.prompt: Why does processing all control samples on one day and all treatment samples on a different day create a serious problem?

options.text: It has no effect as long as the same reagents are used
It perfectly confounds biological condition with processing batch, so no downstream statistical correction can fully separate the two
It only affects qPCR validation, not RNA-seq
It makes the experiment take longer but does not affect the validity of the result

explanations.a: Batch effects (extraction day, reagent lot, technician, instrument run) can arise even with identical reagents, simply from day-to-day processing variation.
explanations.b: Correct — when condition and batch are perfectly aligned, any observed difference could be biological or purely technical, and statistical batch-correction methods cannot recover information that was never captured by the design.
explanations.c: The confounding problem applies to RNA-seq (or any expression assay) run this way, not specifically to qPCR.
explanations.d: This is a validity problem, not merely a timing inconvenience — it directly threatens whether the result means what it claims.

questions.prompt: Why does pre-registering the comparison, test, and threshold before looking at the data matter?

options.text: It prevents trying many comparisons or thresholds until one happens to look significant, a practice that inflates false positives
It is required by law for all science-fair projects
It removes the need for any multiple-testing correction
It guarantees the results will be statistically significant

explanations.a: Correct — deciding the analysis plan in advance blocks the failure mode of testing many combinations of normalization, comparisons, and thresholds until something crosses significance by chance.
explanations.b: Pre-registration is a methodological best practice, not a legal requirement.
explanations.c: Multiple-testing correction is still necessary within a pre-registered plan whenever many genes or gene sets are tested.
explanations.d: Pre-registration constrains how the analysis is run; it says nothing about whether results will turn out significant.

questions.prompt: A student's top 5 RNA-seq hits are re-measured by RT-qPCR, and only 1 of 5 validates. What is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: The RT-qPCR assay is broken and should be ignored
The original RNA-seq signal for the 4 non-validating genes was likely a normalization or batch artifact rather than a real biological effect
All 5 genes are real hits and qPCR simply lacks sensitivity
The result proves the RNA-seq platform is unusable for this experiment

explanations.a: RT-qPCR is a well-established, independent assay used specifically because it has a different failure mode than RNA-seq; a low validation rate is informative, not a sign the assay is broken.
explanations.b: Correct — because RT-qPCR fails differently than RNA-seq, a low validation rate points toward the original signal being driven by a technical artifact (normalization or batch) rather than genuine biology.
explanations.c: Dismissing a non-validating hit as merely 'qPCR being insensitive' avoids the more likely and more useful conclusion that the original RNA-seq signal was artifactual.
explanations.d: One experiment's low validation rate reflects on those specific hits and that design, not on RNA-seq as a platform generally.

questions.prompt: Match each reporting standard to what it specifies.

right.text: Minimum information for qPCR experiments, such as primer sequences and assay efficiency
Minimum information for high-throughput sequencing experiments, such as sample metadata and the processing pipeline used

questions.explanation: MIQE governs what must be disclosed for quantitative PCR validation experiments (primers, efficiency, and related detail), while MINSEQE governs what must be disclosed for sequencing experiments (sample metadata and the processing pipeline), so that another lab or a judge can evaluate exactly what was done.
